I'm going to keep this one short honestly.
Just Cause 3 will either be a make it or break it for you. For me personally, I feel like there's a lot LESS to do in this one there is in Just Cause 2, but of course I haven't really fully started up my own game yet.
So far, however, Just Cause 3 does improve on what matters: the graphics. The effects of explosions and the sheer amount of destruction that can be accomplished has been increased from its predecessor, and this does mark an overall improvement in the game itself.
Gameplay wise, there have been multiple things improved. The grappling hook now has some more uses, and there are more explosive weapons to use. While the physics and car driving still leaves much to be desired, I think that's just a staple of the series at this point and it just sort of adds to the insane action movie style of Just Cause.
In fact, the game even utilizes its rather weird driving mechanics to pull off some over-the-top stunts and action moments, so I can't really bash on the game too much for that.
Nonetheless I've enjoyed Just Cause 3, but I did indeed get it on sale. I recommend you do the same.

Transistor is Supergiant's second game, and they knocked it out of the park. Prepare yourself for an immersive and visually stunning playthrough, as well as a technical and intuitive combat system. Unfortunately, it is a very short game, but it does have replayability.

Like Bastion, but the gameplay is more solid, and the much of the story is infered, and not told. The characters are interesting, the setting is cool, and you are allowed the freedom to come up with your own explanations for why things work the way they do. I am very pleased with the soundtrack. Play this game with some headphones.

Bastion was a lovely surprise in the summer of 2011, easily weedling it's way to the very top of my list of favorite games. Supergiant Games was instantly put on my radar after their first game, so I was delighted to find out that they were making another game. However, I fell into this idea that it would just be impossible for them to make a game as memorable and creative as Bastion. I was very wrong. Transistor is simply a masterpiece.
Pros-
- Beautiful art direction and fluid animation
- Memorable characters and excellent voice work by Logan Cunningham
- Interesting combat with varied skills and combinations
- Satisfying progression
- Twists on gameplay via "Limiters"
- Quirky interactions between the main cast
- New Game Plus
- Great Developers
- Divine OST
Cons-
- Camera can (very rarely) be cumbersome due to architecture
- Story can be somewhat difficult to follow early on (didn't detract from my experience, though others may find it jarring)
- I wish there was more of it; completed my initial playthrough in roughly 6 1/2 hours.
In short: If you played Bastion and loved it, play Transistor. If you're looking for a game with great design and all around excellent craftsmanship, play Transistor. If you're looking for something different, play Transistor. And so, with all things said and done- play Transistor.

Transistor is a beautiful game with amazing art direction, music and a unique combat system. However, the story, in my opinion, is what completely falls flat. The premise of a female singer who's lost her voice is interesting but the storytelling is too one-sided. I understand Red can't speak but that doesn't mean she's incapable of responding or showing any emotion. At the end, we see what resembles snapshots of Red's life with the mystery man in the Transistor which should have, in my opinion, happened at moments throughout the game instead. There's a lot more I could say about the plot being lackluster but honestly the rest of the game - art, music and combat - make up for what the story lacks, and is well worth a playthrough. That being said, I don't know if I could stand to play recursion and go through the motions of listening to that narrator again...

Fotonica is a fun little first-person runner, with some great electronic music and a minimalist vector-based art style. The gameplay is extremely simple - you hold down a button to speed up, let go to jump, and can hold down again in the air to accelerate your fall back to the ground. Despite this, it has a fairly steep difficulty curve  - I've only completed all the levels on the easiest setting. It's a simple, arcadey experience.
If I have one complaint, it's that I feel there are too few levels. However, there are four difficulty settings and an endless mode, as well as a versus mode, and those do add some replay value.

I'd love to write a review of the actual game. But since Steam gave me a key for the PAL version, despite the fact I'm an American and my account both here and at Square Enix is for the US, I can't use my Steam key to activate the game. And of course my repeated attempts to contact Steam Support have gone unanswered, so I'm just out the $45 I paid for the product. Thanks so much Steam! You're my hero! D:
Update 6/26/2014: After nearly two weeks, Steam finally made good and refunded my purchase so that I could buy the right version of this game for my region. I criticized them when they were bad, so it's only fair I commend them when they do right. May have taken a little while, but they finally did right by me.
Now that I've been in the game, I can actually share some feedback. Character models and movements are some of the prettiest I've seen in any MMO, and the Emote system is phenomenal. It seems Square put a *lot* of effort into making the game very RP-friendly, between emotes and custom groups for chat channels.
Beginning quests are fairly easy, but there is a *lot* of running between distant points. The little crystals you can use tot eleport around are helpful, if a bit hard to get used to their naming scheme. But ti still seems I spend a lot more time running from point A to point B than actually playing the game, which is a bit frustrating.
As pretty as the character models are, the outfits and armor are just plain silly. It does a good job keeping in the style of previous Final Fantasy games, but it really doesn't fit here. With the more realistic-looking characters and backdrops, the clothing looks overly cartoonish and out of place. To be armored is to look ridiculous, in sharp contrast to the starter outfits you begin the game with.
As a player new to FFXIV, its pros and cons are pretty much a dead tie for me. I'll give it a nod towards Recommended only becasue the game does seem to have a good sesne of humor about itself, and that alsways helps. But it's barely a win so far.

The less goo you use to build your pathway to the exit, the more goo you can collect. It's a pretty simple concept but it can get pretty tricky to build a stable yet efficient structure when you're trying to obtain the maximum goo possible.

A masterpiece that is definately worth playing. If you have followed the alien story line, you will not be dissapointed. I have to give credit to the visual effects department and the art directors, because the game looks amazing, but more importantly, it feels like you are playing inside the Alien timeline. The interiors and environments you play in feels just perfect. Think Stanley Kubrick's "2001: A Space Odyssee", but still staying true to the Alien look and feel.
The game itself is pretty decent. It's not a first person shooter by definition, so let's just get that out of the way. The game has a first person perspective, however, focuses more on non combat manouvers such as stealth gameplay, tools and crafting to make the game more interesting. The game has a thoughtful and interesting storyline and has a lot of dialogue and audio recordings to fill in the missing pieces. You also interact with the environment in somewhat interesting ways in order to complete missions. You will use "weapons" but only when you really have to. They have done a great job in keeping the game challenging. There is only so much you can do inside a spaceship and within the setting which the game takes place, and I think they have done a pretty good job in creating an immersive environment for players to explore, especially if you explore a little further. And let's be honest, it's an Alien game, it's suppose to follow the plot and setting of what we would expect from the Alien timeframe.
If people complain and say the game is boring or not challenging enough, they have obviously not played the game on the most difficult level (nightmare). It is incredably challenging and really difficult at times. There were times that I got frustrated because it was somewhat impossible to complete some of the missions on the most difficult setting, but it's not called nightmare mode for no reason.
If you are a fan of the Alien anthology, just play the game, it's awesome.

Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs is disappointingly short on the first playthrough. Clocking in at about three hours long, the conclusion to the game is rushed and the enemies do not provide the same tension those in the first game do, especially with the removal of the terror metre and insanity scale. Enemies are easily shaken off and the AI is painfully dumb: taking far too long to react when light is being shone directly on them from a few feet away.
The puzzles are likewise easier this time around, the most challenging of them being shining a light on a tube of chemicals to generate electricity. It is all very straight forward, and the story the game tells isn't nearly as intricate as it's predacessor.
The game would be scarier if they had more 'enemies' than pigmen and tesla pigmen, both of which you will find ridiculous to several degrees upon examination. While not a bad game by any stretch of imagination, it failed to deliver the horror aspect completely after the first few minutes of gameplay, and I felt that too much of the game takes place without seeing a single enemy (the first enemy you encounter is 30-45 minutes in, and there is little tension building prior to this. If this was an eight hour game that wouldn't be a problem, but it's not)

An interesting experience. Having been a large fan of the prequel, I entered this game with great anticipation.
Did it deliver? In some areas, more so than the original. The map design was more diverse and interesting than the 'castle-locked' interiors of The Dark Descent. The Sanity meter was gone, as was the effects. While the Sanity was an interesting gameplay mechanic, it simply slowed the game down more than anything. It wasn't fun to sit and stare at a candle until the walls stopped breathing, every 20 minutes.
The enemies were meh. The monsters of the first felt more intimidating. The first set of enemies in A Machine for Pigs are 4-feet tall pig-babies. Not exactly the product of nightmares (though their audio was a different story).
The game improved in the second sections as the difficulty ramped up. Puzzles actually became a little more difficult, and enemies became bigger and deadlier.
Probably not as scary as The Dark Descent. The monsters had less effect and the gameplay was quite easy. Lack of lantern fuel and tinderboxes made exploration pointless and thus the game felt a little more claustrophobic and linear.
I would recommend this game, in spite of its short playtime. But I would recommend The Dark Descent more. This did not quite live up to its potential.

Short version:
The game is totally worth your time, if you enjoy a good story delivered in a dense atmosphere. If it's real horror you want, this game will probably disappoint you - horror is present, but not nearly as frightening as The Dark Descent.
More detail (no spoilers):
There are quiet a lot rather subtle things to discover regarding the story, which I really enjoyed (unlike in the first game, taking a closer look at pictures or  the stuff laying around can reveal new insight, much like in "Gone Home").
Now to the weak side of the game: The "Monsters" were not really frightening, and though the lights flickering when they are around can be spooky, I always felt safe when it didn't - which made the game even less scary for me.
The "Riddles" barely deserve that name, as they are really obvious (most of them are just activating a lever) and can be solved (if the answer is not given a priori) in under a minute.
The Difficulty is way too easy, if you consider basic guidelines, chances are good you won't get caught at all. (I got caught one time in the entire game, and I haven't been overcautious at all).
The length was ok for me, though I understand why some ppl consider it too short. I played the whole game in one session, started 10 p.m. and finished 3 a.m. - and I literally examined  every corner.

To start if you want a first impression of the game I have done a Let's Play:
Prelude:
Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is almost nothing like Amnesia: The Dark Decent. The only semblance of connectivity is that you have a lantern, the name, and the Amnesia. However, don’t let that dissuade you from buying this game, if it is on sale. $20 USD, is a bit much to ask for this game, however I bought it for $5 USD and I would say that it was worth it.
Review:
To start, if you have never played either Amnesia game, play The Dark Decent, it is the closest to perfection in the Horror genre.  A Machine for pigs cannot hold a candle to it that however, does not make it a bad game, just a not-so-good follow up.  For the majority of this review I will assume you have played The Dark Decent.
The real meat of the Amnesia The Dark Decent was the atmosphere which was only expanded upon with the Sanity meter, the longer you were in the dark or the longer you looked at an enemy the more insane you went, is gone.  The game starts in a similar way lulling you in, you’re in a large house that is almost castle like in a Victorian way that however, is quickly swept away as you start to venture into the steam powered machinery.   Now this atmosphere itself is quite eerie, all of the creaking machinery and the steam pipes bursting with unknown animal noises sounding off.  The atmosphere has changed and it doesn’t quite produce the same terror a dark, dingy, pink puss filled, musty castle has but it works for the setting.
The major element in The Dark Decent that really added to the atmosphere was the Lantern and the Tinder Boxes. The Lantern stays, however the oil, the finite source that powered the lantern, is gone. In this steam powered world the Lantern never dies, which doesn’t add anything to this game. In fact if you have played The Dark Decent you would know that this has actually taken something away the atmosphere. You no longer need to keep an eye on your oil consumption, which means that you no longer need to hide in the dark. There is no reason to be scared for most of this game.
You may have noticed that I didn’t say anything about the Tinder Boxes. Well that because there is also no inventory. At all, it’s gone.  Another finite source, that you used as back up to maintain your sanity and to see, is gone. You also no longer pick up keys, something is blocked, open or jammed. So basically every aspect that you had some sort of control over is gone. Which you might think would add to the horror, but it doesn’t. You may not have control over anything but you also have no finite sources you only have an unlimited use to your magical lantern.
Now one of my favorite parts of The Dark Decent was the puzzles. Luckily A Machine for Pigs kept this aspect. However, many of them are either too easy or offer no real direction.  Many of the puzzles are just turn this crank or pull this lever.  However there are some that really show how crazy Mandus really is, with corridors and objects disappearing after solving them. There were a few puzzles that made me feel great after solving them, which were quite a few puzzles in The Dark Decent.  There were too many that were on polar extremes unfortunately, either too easy or unexplained.
Another one of my favorite things about The Dark Decent were the enemy’s. For 90% of the game you need to NOT look at them, your sanity meter will thank you. For most of the game you can only seem them in passing or for a brief moment making them something elusive and terrifying, never knowing where they are going to come from or what is going to happen. With A Machine for Pigs, I only felt true terror and was unnerved about the enemy’s when they brought out the special variant enemy. The Pigs themselves however, just aren’t frightening.  They’re actually kind of endearing, which an enemy in a horror game shouldn’t be. They also don’t make many appearances, leaving the game to be unsettling but never really praying on your vulnerability.
In conclusion:
By now you would probably assume that I’m going to take a large dump on this game. Well, no. While it doesn’t have quite the same feeling as The Dark Decent, they did a good job with what they did. The story, which I’m not going to touch for risk of spoilers, keeps you in the dark for a very long time keeping you wondering what it really going on and occasionally punching you right in the feels. The unsettling atmosphere is great, it would just have been nice if they could have really instilled fear in me. It is definitely obvious that they focused on the story more than anything, which I appreciate.  It also made me want to go back and play The Dark Decent again, which I also love. So in the end, as game on its own I would say if it’s on sale play it, I beat it in 3.5 hours not worth $20. As an Amnesia game I would definitely say just watch a let’s play or buy it during one of the rare 75% off sales.

When I first played Grand Theft Auto III nearly 15 years ago, the open world concept was a revelation. The mini map full of icons was an open invitation to nonlinear mayhem. The emergent gameplay from primitive AIs reacting with hostility, terror, or even suicide attempts to your antisocial behavior brought a whole new concept to an industry full of on-rails experiences.
A decade and a half later, Ubisoft has boiled the GTA formula down to a thick, viscous syrup that is just pours all over whatever open world its massive teams build. The concept is played out. It's ripe for revision. Nintendo's first real stab at the genre has brought the beloved Zelda IP and survivalist elements to the mix. I see it as a high grain refinement of the idea.
Just Cause 3 is something else entirely. The series has been steadily iterating on its cartoonish physics and pyroclastic style - much like how the Saints Row series steadily cranked up the derangement of its social commentary - and I think the third entry has achieved something close to perfection. Example:
In a single half hour play session, attacked a small military base at night and easily took control of it and its attack chopper. I used the attack chopper to rain rockets down on a larger military base. When the base finally shot me down, I bailed into the water, hotly pursued by enemy choppers. Swimming and hookshotting, I hurled myself into a cliff cave, trying to escape. There, I discovered an enemy patrol boat, which I hijacked. I motored into the cave, trying to escape the choppers, who followed me inside. I quickly discovered that the cave was actually a tunnel, and another, larger patrol boat blocked the exit. I plowed my stolen boat directly into the blockade, jumping and floating away on a parachute as one of the pursuing choppers exploded into the boat wreckage with a gasoline fireball that lit up the night. I hookshotted my way up a cliff, dodging missile fire from the remaining chopper. I stole a small car and fled to a nearby town controlled by my rebel faction. I then hid in the police station while my NPC allies wrecked my remaining pursuers.
None of this was scripted. None of this was part of a sanctioned story mission. However, it was some of the most thrilling gameplay I've experienced in an open world game in years. JC3 is full of stuff like this. The game is littered with locations full of bright, red targets just daring you to start a rampage and dodge the fallout. The game even helps you out by radioing in support choppers and other units.
There's not a whole lot new here. Territory control, crazy mayhem, vast world with lots to do? All been done before. But JC3 tones down the limitations and difficulty level, encouraging you to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Up with impunity, and cranking up the consequences just enough to keep you moving. You can always easily escape for a breather if you like, so there's never the frustration of almost completing an objective and then getting stuffed at the last second...
... unless you take on a story mission. God, what a downer. Why do developers all think they have to be Naughty Dog? Just Cause 3 doesn't need some kind of hokey story-driven "action" plot. It makes its own stories with its crazy engine and its broad mandate of "See that? ♥♥♥♥ it up!" Too often, the missions state an objective and then pull a "surprise, now you have to do this ridiculous♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; twist. They have decent checkpoints, they aren't too hard, and they don't seem to gate your progress in any significant way. But they're completely unnecessary.
The time spent on developing these sad attempts at drama could have been put toward inserting triggered drama into the town and military base capture missions. I would love to be locked into a firefight with a town patrol only to have Mario (JC3 Mario, not Nintendo Mario) wheel up in a sports car and take me on a wild goose chase past the destructible objects I'd so far missed. Seemingly serendipitous events would have far more emotional impact in this setting than a mandatory slog through lame cinematic mimicry.

I have a thing for somewhat minimalist games. They isolate the element of fun and computer science.
Fotonica doesn't need much in the way of assets, texturing, storyline or branching plots. It's about running. More accurately, it's about FLOW.
Given a first person perspective or a "runner", your only control in movement is in the Y and Z plane (technically the -Z plane), where you can choose how fast to run, and when to jump, and how quickly to make yourself land (you can't move backward either).
Running like this produces incremental speed-up, a "flow", where you move faster and faster, and jump over obstacles or gaps between the platforms you see. The aim is to keep your "flow", not to fall to your death down a chasm, or to smash your face off a platform by mis-timing a jump (although this is an achievement).
The visuals are minimal but plenty for your needs (you can choose your level of minimalism, from just platforms through to some decoration to show the theme of the level), and allow some tuning (bloom, AA, etc). The audio is professionally made and presumably licensed (the credits and level options mention it), and matches the game feel and visual feedback wonderfully (slow to medium electronic, modernised chiptune almost).
Play with a mouse, keyboard or joypad (my cripped arthiritic hands appreciate the joypad option, PC purists *may* and *will* complain below), the only controlling you have is holding the button to run, letting go to jump and pressing again to control descent. Simple, but well implemented.
The game price is "pocket money" but worth it for people who like indie, retro or minimalist games which challenge the core aspects of your gaming ability: memory and response time. Recommended.

Smite is a 3rd person MOBA (Multiplayer Online Battle Arena) made by Hi-Rez Studios. While Smite mostly follows the normal MOBA formula, it differs in one major respect - the perspective. Instead of playing with the traditional top-down view, you are positioned behind your character in 3D. This completely mixes up the gameplay, as most attacks have to be aimed to deal any damage, and being behind your character means that you have to be more aware of your surroundings. In my opinion, this change makes combat more interesting and skill-based.
While the viewpoint differs, combat still remains much like many other MOBAs, albeit a bit easier to pick up and master. You've still got health, mana, items for power & protection against and for physical and magical attacks, and characters still fall into basic roles that have their own strengths and weaknesses. Mages, for example, rely on their abilities and have powerful magical attacks that can quickly burst down enemies, but usually have less health and defence to make up for it. In general, Hi-Rez balances roles and characters to an acceptable standard, but having a 3000 HP character burst you down within a few seconds leaves a sour taste in the mouth - the Smite balancing team leaves something to be desired.
Another point in which Smite differs from its competition is with it's roster of playable characters. Smite's characters are based around mythological figures from different cultures - Loki, the famous trickster assassin is part of the Norse pantheon, which includes Odin, Freya and Thor. It's a lot of fun to play as these characters, and Hi-Rez does well with incorporating the lore of each deity into their playstyle and abilities. Loki's playstyle is based around going invisible and backstabbing enemies, a nod to his untrustworthy and dangerous nature. He's also an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Like, a major ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Overall, I regret ever picking up Smite. I have over 1000 hours in this god-forsaken game, and I hate it. But I also love it. If you want a good, fun, and exciting time-waster then Smite is the game for you. If you want to have a life, don't play this game.

You play as an aged bounty hunter who stumbles into a saloon to tell his story to a bunch of patrons. The gameplay comes from you playing through his narrated story to the people at the saloon. I played it on hard my first playthrough because if not you can easily mow through the game in around 5 or 6 hours. Playing on hard forces you to not be as much of a one many army though the game still isn't too hard.
This game can briefly fill your shooter needs if you so desire. It's short length also helps with multiple playthroughs. It's a recommendation if you can catch it on sale.

When you look at the total package, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 is hands-down one of the best first-person shooters out there, and a truly amazing offering across any system. With that being said, our score comes with a disclaimer. For those planning to check out everything Modern Warefare 2 has to offer – online competition, full co-op Spec Ops mode, as well as the campaign – you’re looking at a no-brainer purchase. For the strictly single player crowd, however, Modern Warfare 2 is surprisingly short, and doesn’t live up to the standard set by previous Call of Duty games. The campaign can be completed in as little as six and a half hours, and the missions make better scenarios and moment-to-moment adrenaline rushes than they do a cohesive, well-told story. If you’re going solo, you’ve officially been warned. Look at the complete Modern Warfare 2 experience though, and there’s no denying its rightful place at the top.

Rating 7/10
Overview: First Person Horror
The Good:
+ Creepy atmosphere set at the very end of the 19th century. The game takes place mostly in factory like setting.
+ The narrative and plot is excellent, journal entries are scattered throughout the game providing pieces of the story. The story touches upon some interesting themes.
+ Light puzzle solving elements to keep things interesting
+The game doesn't overstay its welcome, it is roughly a 4-6 hour experience.
+ The music is excellent and really adds to the overall experience
The Bad:
- The game lacks a lot of the terror from the Dark Descent.  Despite the atmosphere, I never really felt threatened in any way. In the entire game there were only a few instances where the enemy would hunt you and even then it was very easy to just out run them to the next area. Part of the problem is that this game heavily streamlined many of the elements from the first game. Death has no consequence, sanity effects gone, refilling the lantern gone... . Many of the things that make the first game so terrifying no longer exist in this game.
- Technically and artistically the game didn't impress me. A lot of the later levels have the 'been there done that' feeling to them. Everything "feels" the same.
Conclusion
This is a game of expectations. If you were expecting the gameplay of Dark Descent then you will be disappointed. What you are playing this game for is the atmosphere, exploration and narrative, just don't expect anything more.
Let's be clear - this a is a vastly different game than The Dark Decent. Still. It's really dark and compelling even if the scares aren't laid down too heavy.
Play through a disturbing story. I thought this was better than Dark Descent. Tinderboxes are removed and the lantern has unlimited power. Monsters are not as easy to hide from.

I did not enjoy this game.  I was so looking forward to it, but it was a disappointment.  Even if I cannot convince you that you should not buy this game, at least this review may lower your expectations in a good way.
First off, I must concede that the art is lovely and I enjoyed the music in the game.  Everything else was problematic.
Obtuse
The plot moves very slowly, keeping the mystery until pretty much at the end, but the final reveal does not explain or justify the events of the game.
The in-game UI is overwhelming when you first get to use it.  The attack and moding system is not obvious, and the UI does nothing to help explain how abilities works or how to configure them.  Even worse, they use a lot of contemporary computer terms but with different meanings, so their terminology can be disorienting.  There are a couple of times early in the game that force the UI open and require you to fiddle with stuff before you can continue, but they don't explain what you have to do.
I need to explain a core combat feature before my critique will make sense.  The main character has two modes of fighting: real-time and pre-planned.  In the real-time combat, your character is at an extreme disadvantage.  Enemies move faster than you, have greater reach than you, and they definitely overwhelm you with numbers.  Most of your attacks have a short range.  In the pre-planned combat system, you pause the action and plan out one or a series of attacks.  After the plan is activated, it is carried out automatically in real-time, but your character moves much faster to let you accomplish things that you couldn't in real-time.  Also, all of your attacks do more damage in pre-planned combat and/or activate new combined effects.
Pre-planned combat is clearly superior to real-time, so the game limits it.  Each action or movement in the pre-planned system uses up resources on a special meter that refills over time when you are back to the real-time.  If you don't have enough of the special meter, then you cannot pause time or use the pre-planned combat.  This is where you get into trouble.
Planning combat attacks when combat is paused gives you feedback about how much damage each attack will do and whether it will be enough to eliminate an enemy, yet it is often wrong.  Enemies that choose to teleport themselves after being hit, bounce a random direction, or activate a defense are not reflected in the combat planning phase, so it is very easy to commit yourself to a big attack that uses up all of your special meter (leaving you defenseless for a period of time) which would have been OK if the enemies that you had planned to be defeated were defeated, but instead you end up dangerously close to enemies who punish you for believing the UI feedback.
Trolling
One of the main features of the game is a large selection of acquired abilities that can be used as either attacks or as modifiers for other attacks.  A big part of the user experience is mixing and matching of these abilities to find combinations you enjoy.
When fighting, if your health bar goes down to 0, instead of ending the fight, the game randomly removes one of your abilities and resets your health bar.  If it goes down to 0 again, then you lose another ability, and so on until you lose your last ability and are forced to reset the fight from the beginning with all of your abilities restored.
If you survive a fight with abilities lost, then they stay lost until you can explore your way to the next single-use restore terminal.  The game is extremely linear, so usually you can't backtrack and use a previously-skipped restore terminal.  It may require you to limp along with fewer (or less preferable) abilities for several fights before you can get your abilities back.
At first, I thought this was an innovative way to force you to mix and match your abilities after fights, but very quickly I realized that this is just the game devs trolling you.  Although every ability can be either an attack or a modifier to an attack, I found that many of them were useful only in a carefully balanced loadout of attacks and mods.  The removal of a single random ability often cripples an entire loadout, and after combat there may not be a way to rearrange the remaining abilities into a useful combination.
The better option in most fights where you lose even a single ability is to let the game completely kill you.  If you lose all of your abilities, then the fight resets to your previous state.  So you either finish a fight with abilities missing and hate your new restrictions, or you just stand still and let the enemies hit you over and over again until you can restart the fight fresh.  Neither option is fun.
An alternative would be to never allow yourself to lose an ability in the first place, but the game loves to give new enemies traits that you have never seen before and old enemies traits that they didn't have before, so I found myself constantly confused why my attacks didn't work and how enemies were doing things I had never seen before.  These changes are made without any feedback or forewarning, resulting in lots of cheap deaths (or ability loss in this case).  Variety is a good thing, but in a game where your character is so vulnerable unless you use your limited, time-stopping special ability, it is critical that you can accurately plan your attacks, and yet the planning system is inaccurate and intentionally hides information to misguide you.
Another way that I was tricked into overcommitting myself was when the game started adding multiple health bars to bosses.  Normal enemies only have a single health bar, so after hours of re-enforcing that system, the game started adding multiple health bars to certain bosses.  There's no tell that I could discover to know how many health bars an enemy has.  This led me to commit all of my special meter into an attack that the planning system told me would defeat them, but instead left me standing right next to the very-much-not-defeated boss and unable to do anything for a period of time (long enough for me to lose another ability from the barrage of boss attacks).
Poor Pacing
I already mentioned the bad plot pacing above, but there are other pacing issues with the game.
This game has a narrator, like in the developer's previous game, Bastion.  In Bastion, the narrator comments on what the main character does in present tense.  It was a fresh idea, and got lots of praise.  The developers must have felt that their next game needed to have a narrator too, but they really didn't know what to do with him.
In Transistor, the narrator really has nothing useful to say.  The narrator doesn't comment on what's going on, but rather fills in a little history.  If any of that history was entertaining, then it might have been worth having, but I did not enjoy it.  The devs even created multiple, un-skippable sequences that show the main character riding a motorcycle for long periods of time with no gameplay just so that they could have a situation where the narrator could talk, and yet he had nothing interesting to say.
There are puzzles in the game, which could have been a great way to change the pace from the extremely linear exploration and frequent combat, but there were not enough of them to help the pacing much, and the mechanics of the puzzles blended into the environment art so well that I found them more confusing than anything else.
Buggy
At least a couple of times I got my character stuck outside the playable space and had to reload the game.
Conclusion
Great art and music.  Everything else is a mess.

The art of this game is wonderful. (Characters. Areas. Songs. Story.) I will not elaborate further. I am sure others have.
I do have a terminology quibble: a transistor is a switch controlled by voltage. Yes, it is the basic unit of a digital processor. No, you can't stab people with it, much less
.
Nor, taken literally, should you be able to proc stun / charm / slow / vuln / knocked-into-air on them. Gameplay-wise, these are your basic tools. By artfully arranging them - some being cheaper than others, some affecting more enemies at once, some merely being available at the time - into useful combos, a pleasing variety arises.
Although the variety of (largely useful) abilities is remarkable, their tradeoffs won't particularly matter (due to some powerful, spammable late-game abilities) unless you up the difficulty. The system for doing so is remarkably flexible - rules of combat can be turned to the enemy's favor, or you can step outside the campaign (which you should be replaying at this point anyways) to pit a semi-fixed loadout against (yet )a(nother) set configuration of enemies.
Cloaking enemies (temporarily untargetable) are annoying for how they drag out fights, later on. Others, that boot you out of turn-planning, violate the premise of the game - the few encounters they participate in become mere button-spamming, converting tension to panic. This is the worst quibble I have with the game. (Except maybe for the name of its titular artifact.)
In summary: A fascinating post-mortem of a city that deserved to live. (Deserves, even. I'm imagining an art deco / cyberpunk life simulator.
) Coupled with the important, RPG-y business of blowing things up in increasingly efficient, then increasingly roundabout ways.

Every once in a while an indie game comes along that, to me, is not a clear like or dislike.  I started playing Papers, Please and go to day eight before quitting the first time. It is just a game though, why do I care?  I did not, really.  I played again, anyway.
The game kept my enthusiasm up as the difficulty ramped up, money was tight, and I seemed to be responsible for the lives of so many more pixel people than I anticiapted.  I enjoyed it up until the very end.  Good job, author.
I would recommend Papers, Please if you are type of gamer who does not need flashy graphics or rapid game play to be entertained.  If you are a fan of indie game development, Papers, Please is an enjoyable title that may grow on you as it has grown on me.

One of the most legendary games of all time, is Papers, Please. I would pay 20$ for this game, instead of 10$ just because of how good it is. The game seems pretty simple at the start, but gets more complicated and tugs at your emotions with people who don't have the right documents and need to get in. For example, one person is from your neighbor country, kolechia who betrayed the country and needed to come to Arstotzka to be safe because they would be killed if they returned to kolechia. You can deny them(and be a jerk, but do your job right) or you could let them in at the cost of a citation. You can recieve two warning citations each day and every one after is a 5 credit penalty. You are trying to keep your family alive with your job. The feeling when you let someone in and then a citation prints out is a feeling of epic failure as in YOU WERE WRONG! With all the side stories, the urgencies, and the twenty different possible endings, I highly recommend you buy this game as soon as possible.

A gripping and emotional story that seriously makes you question your morals. Also, the gameplay itself is surprisingly tough, with you having to pay attention to each and every detail, and rather than chucking everything at you at once and overwhelming you, it slowly adds more and more pieces of paperwork and rules, so you have plenty of time to understand each one before you have to learn a new one.

You'd think that making a game as annoying and banal as possible would make it uninteresting to play, but it's really not the case. Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is much more than just a run-of-the mill arcade shooter. Here's what it has to offer:
-A surprisingly fun and well told story, specially considering how arcade shooters usually have really crap stories. "Gunslinger" not only plays with narrative conventions to create a funny and enticing tale, it also teaches you stuff about the Old West through collectibles.
-Great visual presentation and sound design. The comic-booky feel of the graphics means that this game will stand the test of time much better than other games with realistic graphics, and overall the whole aesthetic is consistent and interesting. The music is great, and I don't think I've ever played a first person shooter in which the bullets sounded as good as they do in "Gunslinger".
-Incredible gunplay, wiith a variety of skills and guns so you can play how you want to. You will feel like you're playing the leading man in a Sergio Leone film, down to the revolver duels. No other arcade shooter has gameplay as solid as this.
-A lot of replayability. The story is short (about five hours long), but there are some differences between playthroughs, not to mention new game+ and collectibles. Arcade Mode and Duel Challenges make this a great pick-up and play title when you want to shoot some stuff but don't want to go play a lenghty story-based FPS or deal with multiplayer.
-There is no need to have played any other Call of Juarez games (I haven't, and honestly this could have been called anything else and it wouldn't make a lick of difference), and the game is really cheap, so there's very little reason not to try it.
-It runs well.

Played and beat this on console and I must say, for a cat and mouse game this is truly a breath of fresh air. This game is really itself is a great Alien game and a horror game. Being a massive fan of the Alien series, I played the game in a very unbaised profession and I must say, this game really works but has a few flaws. Let's start with the good. The Game drips with atomosphere. Every corner, every hallway, every room feels eerie and almost threatening. There's always a sense of "I  better keep moving because I'm being hunted" constantly going through your head. It's very good to say the least as far as creating a scary atmosphere. The enemy design is great. You face many enemies through out the game and you are constantly being thrown into situations in which you're told to simply just "figure it out" kind of. The game doesn't hold your hand and the way I view it, I have to say that this is a plus. With that out of the way, lets get to the bad. The game has a lot of back tracking which for some is really bad. Even for me the back tracking was a little much at times. I felt as though the game did this to try to stretch the game time but ultimately didn't need too. The game is too long. I don't normally say this about games but this felt like it could have been an hour or two shorter and I would have been more than ok with it. Overall, this game is a huge step in the right direction with horror and the Alien franchise.
+Atmosphere

I did not enjoy this game.  I was so looking forward to it, but it was a disappointment.  Even if I cannot convince you that you should not buy this game, at least this review may lower your expectations in a good way.
First off, I must concede that the art is lovely and I enjoyed the music in the game.  Everything else was problematic.
Obtuse
The plot moves very slowly, keeping the mystery until pretty much at the end, but the final reveal does not explain or justify the events of the game.
The in-game UI is overwhelming when you first get to use it.  The attack and moding system is not obvious, and the UI does nothing to help explain how abilities works or how to configure them.  Even worse, they use a lot of contemporary computer terms but with different meanings, so their terminology can be disorienting.  There are a couple of times early in the game that force the UI open and require you to fiddle with stuff before you can continue, but they don't explain what you have to do.
I need to explain a core combat feature before my critique will make sense.  The main character has two modes of fighting: real-time and pre-planned.  In the real-time combat, your character is at an extreme disadvantage.  Enemies move faster than you, have greater reach than you, and they definitely overwhelm you with numbers.  Most of your attacks have a short range.  In the pre-planned combat system, you pause the action and plan out one or a series of attacks.  After the plan is activated, it is carried out automatically in real-time, but your character moves much faster to let you accomplish things that you couldn't in real-time.  Also, all of your attacks do more damage in pre-planned combat and/or activate new combined effects.
Pre-planned combat is clearly superior to real-time, so the game limits it.  Each action or movement in the pre-planned system uses up resources on a special meter that refills over time when you are back to the real-time.  If you don't have enough of the special meter, then you cannot pause time or use the pre-planned combat.  This is where you get into trouble.
Planning combat attacks when combat is paused gives you feedback about how much damage each attack will do and whether it will be enough to eliminate an enemy, yet it is often wrong.  Enemies that choose to teleport themselves after being hit, bounce a random direction, or activate a defense are not reflected in the combat planning phase, so it is very easy to commit yourself to a big attack that uses up all of your special meter (leaving you defenseless for a period of time) which would have been OK if the enemies that you had planned to be defeated were defeated, but instead you end up dangerously close to enemies who punish you for believing the UI feedback.
Trolling
One of the main features of the game is a large selection of acquired abilities that can be used as either attacks or as modifiers for other attacks.  A big part of the user experience is mixing and matching of these abilities to find combinations you enjoy.
When fighting, if your health bar goes down to 0, instead of ending the fight, the game randomly removes one of your abilities and resets your health bar.  If it goes down to 0 again, then you lose another ability, and so on until you lose your last ability and are forced to reset the fight from the beginning with all of your abilities restored.
If you survive a fight with abilities lost, then they stay lost until you can explore your way to the next single-use restore terminal.  The game is extremely linear, so usually you can't backtrack and use a previously-skipped restore terminal.  It may require you to limp along with fewer (or less preferable) abilities for several fights before you can get your abilities back.
At first, I thought this was an innovative way to force you to mix and match your abilities after fights, but very quickly I realized that this is just the game devs trolling you.  Although every ability can be either an attack or a modifier to an attack, I found that many of them were useful only in a carefully balanced loadout of attacks and mods.  The removal of a single random ability often cripples an entire loadout, and after combat there may not be a way to rearrange the remaining abilities into a useful combination.
The better option in most fights where you lose even a single ability is to let the game completely kill you.  If you lose all of your abilities, then the fight resets to your previous state.  So you either finish a fight with abilities missing and hate your new restrictions, or you just stand still and let the enemies hit you over and over again until you can restart the fight fresh.  Neither option is fun.
An alternative would be to never allow yourself to lose an ability in the first place, but the game loves to give new enemies traits that you have never seen before and old enemies traits that they didn't have before, so I found myself constantly confused why my attacks didn't work and how enemies were doing things I had never seen before.  These changes are made without any feedback or forewarning, resulting in lots of cheap deaths (or ability loss in this case).  Variety is a good thing, but in a game where your character is so vulnerable unless you use your limited, time-stopping special ability, it is critical that you can accurately plan your attacks, and yet the planning system is inaccurate and intentionally hides information to misguide you.
Another way that I was tricked into overcommitting myself was when the game started adding multiple health bars to bosses.  Normal enemies only have a single health bar, so after hours of re-enforcing that system, the game started adding multiple health bars to certain bosses.  There's no tell that I could discover to know how many health bars an enemy has.  This led me to commit all of my special meter into an attack that the planning system told me would defeat them, but instead left me standing right next to the very-much-not-defeated boss and unable to do anything for a period of time (long enough for me to lose another ability from the barrage of boss attacks).
Poor Pacing
I already mentioned the bad plot pacing above, but there are other pacing issues with the game.
This game has a narrator, like in the developer's previous game, Bastion.  In Bastion, the narrator comments on what the main character does in present tense.  It was a fresh idea, and got lots of praise.  The developers must have felt that their next game needed to have a narrator too, but they really didn't know what to do with him.
In Transistor, the narrator really has nothing useful to say.  The narrator doesn't comment on what's going on, but rather fills in a little history.  If any of that history was entertaining, then it might have been worth having, but I did not enjoy it.  The devs even created multiple, un-skippable sequences that show the main character riding a motorcycle for long periods of time with no gameplay just so that they could have a situation where the narrator could talk, and yet he had nothing interesting to say.
There are puzzles in the game, which could have been a great way to change the pace from the extremely linear exploration and frequent combat, but there were not enough of them to help the pacing much, and the mechanics of the puzzles blended into the environment art so well that I found them more confusing than anything else.
Buggy
At least a couple of times I got my character stuck outside the playable space and had to reload the game.
Conclusion
Great art and music.  Everything else is a mess.

I do have a terminology quibble: a transistor is a switch controlled by voltage. Yes, it is the basic unit of a digital processor. No, you can't stab people with it, much less
.
Nor, taken literally, should you be able to proc stun / charm / slow / vuln / knocked-into-air on them. Gameplay-wise, these are your basic tools. By artfully arranging them - some being cheaper than others, some affecting more enemies at once, some merely being available at the time - into useful combos, a pleasing variety arises.
Although the variety of (largely useful) abilities is remarkable, their tradeoffs won't particularly matter (due to some powerful, spammable late-game abilities) unless you up the difficulty. The system for doing so is remarkably flexible - rules of combat can be turned to the enemy's favor, or you can step outside the campaign (which you should be replaying at this point anyways) to pit a semi-fixed loadout against (yet )a(nother) set configuration of enemies.
Cloaking enemies (temporarily untargetable) are annoying for how they drag out fights, later on. Others, that boot you out of turn-planning, violate the premise of the game - the few encounters they participate in become mere button-spamming, converting tension to panic. This is the worst quibble I have with the game. (Except maybe for the name of its titular artifact.)
In summary: A fascinating post-mortem of a city that deserved to live. (Deserves, even. I'm imagining an art deco / cyberpunk life simulator.
) Coupled with the important, RPG-y business of blowing things up in increasingly efficient, then increasingly roundabout ways.

____
My playtime for DS1 was about 110h.
I gave DS2 a several tries and finally completed brining a total playtime to 67h.
I guess in the end there are two major fractions of the Souls fanbase:
* The fans of the game (this group complains about stuff like lore and immersion)
* The fans of the metagame (this group very notably demand you to have at least 200 hours in the game to be able to voice any kind of opinion).
For the second group DS2 is on pair or maybe even better than the DS1 with better fps, better pvp, larger variety of weapons and overall better mechanic. I think they don't really care about the game itself as the artistic product, but merely as a medium for their metagaming experience. Convenience is all about metagame and DS2 is definitely more convenient.
For the first group DS is all about the game experience and the immersion. And from this point of view DS2 is absolutely abysmal. Every single design decision of the DS2 is simply not working in favor of game. What's worse, every bad design decision triggers a cascade of other problems and they snowball.
* Levels are poorly connected, and often make no sense thematically.
* NPC are completely uninteresting and too verbose.
* The lore and story are virtually non existing.
* Bosses are repetitive, often use the same movesets and are mostly recycled versions of other enemies.
* Soul memory is not really working in favor of local coop.
* Closely placed bonfires break immersion.
* You have to go back to hub to level up which breaks immersion even more.
* If you are using rings of protection you are completely deprived of any sense of challenge.
* If you are not using ring of protection, you are faced with extremely limited human effigies and inability to farm them (as monsters are limited in this game).
I can go on and on about it, but I guess you can get my point.

There is a lot of people that hate this game, and I know why:
TDD was a fad. The game became popular because of one thing, and one thing only: it was scary. Tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands likely bought this game because they wanted to get scared; they wanted a joyride complete with overwhelming fear. I don't blame them. The game is pretty scary, but here's the thing:
It seems that most people do not understand that Amnesia, and the games before it, were not just haunted-house amusement park rides like they like to act like it is. No, it's a lot more than that. The game has thick atmosphere, superb pacing and storytelling backed by a very dark story that keeps you curious from beginning and even to the end. To be able to truly appreciate TDD, you need to look further than the scare factor; it is not the only thing that made the game great. Guess what the Chinese Room capitalised on? The story. They wanted to tell a story, much like TDD did. MFP was much more of a psychological experience; the game did not need to scare you with darkness or spooky monsters, all it needed was an incredibly wicked story. This was fulfilled. I expected an atmospheric, thought-provoking horror experience that would keep me on the edge and this is exactly what the game did.
But what did everyone else expect? Probably something entirely different. They probably just wanted to get scared. Most of the fanbase is filled with people that appreciated TDD for nothing more than its scare factor, and therefor this is all they had expected from MFP. They are probably the kind of people that either skipped or skimmed through most of TDD's note readings, not givng a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the backstory whatsoever. They just wanted to get to the next "scare." The bad reception for this game purely comes from delusioned expectations, is what I believe. Horror is a much deeper genre than you'd think. Read up.

Smite is a 3rd person MOBA (Multiplayer Online Battle Arena) made by Hi-Rez Studios. While Smite mostly follows the normal MOBA formula, it differs in one major respect - the perspective. Instead of playing with the traditional top-down view, you are positioned behind your character in 3D. This completely mixes up the gameplay, as most attacks have to be aimed to deal any damage, and being behind your character means that you have to be more aware of your surroundings. In my opinion, this change makes combat more interesting and skill-based.
While the viewpoint differs, combat still remains much like many other MOBAs, albeit a bit easier to pick up and master. You've still got health, mana, items for power & protection against and for physical and magical attacks, and characters still fall into basic roles that have their own strengths and weaknesses. Mages, for example, rely on their abilities and have powerful magical attacks that can quickly burst down enemies, but usually have less health and defence to make up for it. In general, Hi-Rez balances roles and characters to an acceptable standard, but having a 3000 HP character burst you down within a few seconds leaves a sour taste in the mouth - the Smite balancing team leaves something to be desired.
Another point in which Smite differs from its competition is with it's roster of playable characters. Smite's characters are based around mythological figures from different cultures - Loki, the famous trickster assassin is part of the Norse pantheon, which includes Odin, Freya and Thor. It's a lot of fun to play as these characters, and Hi-Rez does well with incorporating the lore of each deity into their playstyle and abilities. Loki's playstyle is based around going invisible and backstabbing enemies, a nod to his untrustworthy and dangerous nature. He's also an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Like, a major ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Overall, I regret ever picking up Smite. I have over 1000 hours in this god-forsaken game, and I hate it. But I also love it. If you want a good, fun, and exciting time-waster then Smite is the game for you. If you want to have a life, don't play this game.
(Also, if you'd like someone to help you get the basics of Smite, hit me up in game! I go by JamHiggs, and I'd be happy to help you out. Oh, and use my name to sign up so that we can get them sweet sign-up bonuses <3)

Colorful, inventive and stylish, Gunslinger is a valuable edition to the Call of Juarez series. It has very realistic and imaginative level design. The in-game physics are very believable, as they reproduce very realistic effects. The dialogu and the accent of the narrator is highly entertaining and authentic. Whilst there could have been more period specific weapons, such as the 1887 Shotgun and the 1895 Winchester, the existing ones are pleasing to both the eye and are a joy to shoot. Gunslinger is more a visual perfection of the series, which attempts to add the graphic novel element to dramatic effect and succeeds. The reloading animation of the Winchester and the shortended Winchester are wrong and the Schofield is too quick, but the weapons otherwise work well and the powder barrel explosions are both effective and impressive to watch. Fans of the series and western afficionados will find a lot of things to like about this game.

Well, I can quickly state that while it's arguably one of the weaker titles in the franchise, it's definitely not the weakest PC release, despite being clear it's a console port. It runs very well, being not particularly tasking on HDD space nor performance by today's standards (Although being capped at 91fps may not be convenient for those with 120hz+ monitors or a real need for FPS, aswell as a select number of chipsets reportedly being unsupported for the Mac OSX port, which the PC Gaming Wiki article can detail if necessary). I certainly can't name any performance issues on my end.
The Singleplayer experience can be summed up as "Call of Duty 4 cranked to 11", as unlike it's more believable predecessor who rarely took away the player's control while the cinematic events occured, the setpieces are both in abundance & high spectacle, with numerous quick-time events to boot, for which many are memorable often thanks to the strong soundtrack composed by Hans Zimmer & Lorne Balfe.
The 2-Player co-op experience, "Spec Ops" is actually one of Modern Warfare 2's stronger features. It's a mission based mode with a wide variety of gameplay elements & objectives, which either originate from Modern Warfare 2 & Call of Duty 4 or occasionally are unique to Spec Ops, all with a Three Star system awarded based on either difficulty completion, time completion or other mission unique tiers. Such things as a Snowmobile race & time trail, covering a co-op partner from a Black Hawk or AC130, or getting All Ghillied Up together, along with the more classical eliminate all targets, survive or complete-a-mission affairs. Whilst most of these can be played solo, there are a small number of missions that do require a co-op partner (Along with some where a Co-op partner is ideal to completing Veteran difficulty, especially with being able to revive each other presents it's own strategies). With the right buddy, it can be quite the fun!
I can only give you my experience from the Xbox 360, but based on the brief return on PC just for experimentation's sake, not an awful lot has changed. I don't know how abundant hacking remains (To which on Xbox 360, it was utterly rampant!) but I have heard concerns from players that not only is hacking still rampant, but you yourself could be at risk from being VAC-Banned just by joining a matchmade game with or controlled by said hackers (I've had a somewhat similar experience in Gears of War 2 when my stats were permanently affected by being matchmade with illegitimate players, aswell as an occasion I was matchmade with hackers on MW2 [X360], which although neither resulted in any official bans, I'd say the concern should be at least considered valid), so it may be wise to proceed with caution if you wanna play Multiplayer outside of Private Matchplay, or be prepared to hightail it if you notice anything very unusual. Regardless, I can probably sum it up as a pit of out-of-control chaos with "noob-tubing" & death from above everywhere! (As this is Call of Duty 4 Multiplayer cranked to 17, which I personally classify as not a good thing). Perks have evolved from their more subtle kit choices to something comparable to super-hero powers, especially when you get their Pro upgrades (Commando Pro being among the most notorious). As for the Kill-Streaks, well, instead of being the assisting tools of winning the game, a significant selection pretty much is the gameplay & game-winners to anyone who can manage to avoid dying. You can rain death-from-above on a massive scale with AC130s, Attack Helicopters, Harriers, Bombing Runs, Stealth Bombers, Predator Missiles, maybe more. And of course, reel in 25 kills with all that and you have it equipped, hit the Nuke to win the game! (Provided your team or the enemy doesn't do it for you before the bomb drops).
Well, it's a limited recommendation. If you are willing to put your brain away for some utterly disorganised chaos of a multiplayer, eager to gear up for a potentially challenging co-op mode, or want a short & somewhat dumb (as a whole), but highly explosive & cinematic singleplayer experience, then I can recommend it.
If you're looking for something more exceptional and/or refined, I can gladly say that the PC platform has a large quantity of offerings to cater to that need.

Definitely one of the best games I've played in a very long time. If you like Skyrim, Dragon Age, Fallout, World of Warcraft, etc, there is a good chance you should try this game.
+ Character customization
+ Level scaling
+ Exploration
+ Graphics
+ Justice System
+ Add-ons
+ Story and quests
+ Generous subscription option
+ Crafting System
+ Resource gathering, farming, and economy
+ Day/Night cycles and weather systems
+ Audio, music, ambiance
+ Voice acting
+ Player Housing
+ Combat
Above are some of the things that I really like about the game. Character customization is amazing. Nearly on par with Skyrim and the likes. Level scaling is something not everyone likes, but so far I really love it. I just reached level 50 and barely made it through three entire zones. There is so much left for me to do and explore at this point, I don't see being done for several thousand hours. Exploration is rewarding with chests, skyshards (skill points) and lore books. Always something stuck in odd nooks and crannies. The graphics are phenomenal and remind me of Skyrim and Fallout series alot. The justice system is not very realistic, but interesting enough to make it fun. The consequences are light, but can be fairly expensive if you aren't careful.
Add-ons are great. While a few that I use seem like they should have been in the game to begin with, such as a minimap, it's nice to have the option to modify the game. The crafting system is quite deep and engaging, much moreso than most other games I have played, ever. Add to this the hunting and gathering economy and if you like to farm, this game makes that very rewarding.
The stories and quests are top-notch with very colorful writing and voice acting. I recognized many of the voices from other games and television series. Some of the best ever. The music is light and entrancing. Very moody and some thought was put into which music to play for which zone. I really love the audio in this game, as well as the ambiance and immersion of the day/night cycles and weather patterns.
While the game is buy to play, the sub gives you infinite crafting bag space and access to every DLC past and future as well as a 1500 crown stipend to use in the cash store where you can buy mounts, costumes, and loads of other uncecessary things. But if you like that sort of thing, this game has quite a lot to offer, even if it is mostly overpriced outside of sales and the monthly stipend, in my opnion.
I haven't gotten much into the player housing, but the fact that the game has it says something, because many do not. And from what I can tell, the system is very robust, with most if not all items being craftable. This makes for a very lucrative market as well as a nice gold dump for the economy. The one big drawback is that players are limited to the number of items they can have in each house.
The combat is good overall. Its fun and engaging and there are so many options it is pretty overwhelming at first. The classes are fun and unique and I like how there are cross-combinations depending on what weapon and armor the character is using. Gear sets make statistics junkies right at home. Although the combat is fairly fluid, it can become predictable after a time due to only having 5 skill slots available during combat. I feel like some ablities and combos are more powerful, which kind of pigeonholes some classes beyond the "magicka or stamina" decision.
- No Global Auction House
- Terrible search function/guild trader interface
- Drab looking gear
- Limited skill slots
- Year old UI bugs
Some things about the game I do not like as much, such as the guild trader system. There are things I like about it and things I don't. It's a little too cumbersome for my personal taste, but I do genuinely like what it's trying to do/be. Maybe in time it will get better. Thankfully there are add-ons that make this part of the game palatable for those that enjoy it.
Joining and leaving guilds is very simple and it wasn't hard for me to find several that I enjoy. The problem is with a 500 player limit in each guild, one may feel forced into joining 5 just to be able to trade all their goods every week. That doesn't leave a lot of room for the non-trading guilds that I would otherwise enjoy as well. The reason for this is because the guild traders have designated areas to sell, so each guild has to bid on those spots every week.
If a guild you are in doesn't win a bid, you can't trade with a guild trader in that guild for that week. And many of the guilds that are able to stay in good areas consistently charge very high dues/minimum sales. Its kind of supply and demand, and I get that, but for new players, it can be difficult when just starting out and trying to offload your trash for some upgrades or potions/food.
The gear is rather drab looking for the most part, at least at the lower levels. There are dye stations around towns to help spice it up, but you have to unlock the colors with achievements and some of the better ones are locked behind difficult or lengthy objectives. While I don't mind earning them (or not), it would be nice to not have to wear a costume all the time when my gear sets don't match.
The number of hotbar actions allowed is 5 plus 1 ultimate. At level 15 you get a second bar (both based on weapon type) with 5 more slots and another ultimate slot. This is good for some players and bad for others. Personally, I like games where I have access to all my abilities at all times and get to decide on the fly which one I use. I do appreciate the strategy involved with limited skills, but being that every skill had to be leveled up and morphed individually through using it, while very cool in itself, makes combat and skill levling more convoluted than I am used to or prefer.
I've run into a bug that shows one or more of the guilds I am in has no guild trader when they, in fact, do have one. Apparently this bug has been around since Morrowind released, a year ago. Some of the other UI are kinda janky as well, like when you are looking at your listed items for one guild, and you switch to another guild, and it shows no listings, so you have to click "sell" and then back to "listings" to be able to see the items. Annoying.

FOTONICA is a minimalistic runner game. It’s so minimalistic and simple, that controls consist of a SINGLE button. Holding down a button (you can use almost any button in-game to run) makes you run, releasing the button performs a jump and holding down the button mid air accelerates landing.
The game’s description asks: “Ever wondered what running at 140mph feels like?” But honestly, it doesn’t feel like 140 mph at all. I was expecting the game to be more like “Space tube” (a game available on Windows mobile and Android devices), where you can definitely feel the speed – on some levels you can even react in time after a boost. So when the description starts out with a question like that, you expect the game to be adrenaline inducing. Can’t say I felt a rush on any of the levels.
Although the animation is beautiful, the only mode that looks good on full screen is FLAT (you have a selection of three “QUALITY” options available for you). VECTOR and FLUID look poorly – especially on full screen.
3 modes are available to the player: arcade, endless and versus. Arcade mode consists of just 8 finite levels. The levels are very short – 1-2 minutes each. Endless mode has just 3 levels. Versus mode (where you can play split screen with up to 4 players) is a nice addition, but it’s not enough to compensate the lack of levels in other modes.
All in all, FOTONICA didn’t live up to my expectations. While the game indeed is a bit addicting, it still severely lacks content. It’s a decent game for mobile devices to pass time while waiting in line or riding a bus/train. However, I cannot recommend buying it on Steam for full price.

Fotonica is a port of a mobile game, and it shows. It has one button control - hold to run, release to jump, hold again to descend quicker. The game quickly goes from minimalistic to lacking when you realize there are only eight stages, and the imposing four difficulties presented only affect the speed. As the game progresses, the gameplay becomes increasingly frustrating, relying on memorizing the stage instead of reacting as you go, as one mistake near the end of the course can easily cost you the run.
The graphics aim for a retro vector screen look, but fall short because of lack of proper anti-aliasing - the wireframe lines are heavily pixelated and flickering. A clean look can only be achieved in "Solid" graphics mode, where white polygons are filled in, but even then the shaky particle effects appear somewhat out of place. Although the framerate seems to be uncapped, the camera movement appears jittery at times, especially at lower speed, further detracting from the game's promise of the experience of continous fluid movement.
The music is certainly not of bad quality, but quickly forgettable.
If you want this game, get it for your smartphone. It's good for short sessions, but not engaging enough for extended play.

while it's nowhere near as engrossing as its predecessor, this is still a fairly solid gaming experience and is definitely worth checking out if you're a fan of survival horror games in general.  as previous reviews have accurately pointed out, this is much more of a 'literary' game, as a huge portion of the story is revealed only through the scattered diary entries that the player can find throughout the game.  the story is much darker and far more depressing than anything in the previous game, although it is also much more tedious and long-winded due to the format in which it is revealed, so its ultimate impact is somewhat diminishesd by the time you reach the end.  the whole thing does occasionally seem to function more as an interactive novel than as a straight forward video game, but there are definitely a few moments that made me squirm in my seat, although none of them compare to the genuine frights that you can find in THE DARK DESCENT, not to mention that none of puzzles are ever even remotely difficult to figure out.  still, it's readily apparent that a ton of work went into creating the pitch black atmosphere and the dread-inducing sound design, which are unquestionably the best things about the game, as playing it with headphones on is an incredibly unnerving experience.
the $20 price tag is a bit steep unfortunately.

Finally got through this game. Its really challenging. Its not a first person shooter, its more of a first person adventure game that's really story driven. There's some problems, lets get those out of the way.
Negs:
The Voice Acting was good, not really mediocre, not consistently phenomenal.
Some of the hiding places were a little repetitive, especially the lockers. The cabinets all looked alike., and same pictures in each locker.
The missions had a little too much of find A to open B. way too much over-reliance on this mechanic that defines video games.  The exploring missions were actually some of the more interesting ones.
Scaring the alien away sometimes only worked for 5 seconds towards the end of the game. I think towards the end the invulnerability mechanic should have changed
Sometimes a little TOO much alien... there I said it. The game had a little oversaturation, making the creature less scary, and more repetitive. I don't think the designers thought about this during design, but breaking up the levels with more humans or androids might have broken the saturation enough.
Pros: This game was a blast to play. Good Plot -- really good story. Amazing Music, Original cast members. The Computer terminals were a little reminiscent of Fallout. The puzzles were good, the alien AI was very good. The devices and items were good. This game is scary! You have to look over your shoulder to save, or use a computer, or open a door. The environments kicked♥♥♥♥♥ This game will make you feel like you're in an alien movie. Its the closest thing to it--and I'll even go as far as to say that it had a better story than Alien, 3, Alien 4, Prometheus, or Alien Covenant. This game's story really could have been Alien 3 and I would have been perfectly happy to close that as a trilogy--thats how good the story is. If you're a fan of Alien, this game is worth the buy. It is THE only Alien game really worth getting. If you were looking for a good Alien movie sequel to Aliens.. this is probably the closest you'll ever get to one.
