Well, I can quickly state that while it's arguably one of the weaker titles in the franchise, it's definitely not the weakest PC release, despite being clear it's a console port. It runs very well, being not particularly tasking on HDD space nor performance by today's standards (Although being capped at 91fps may not be convenient for those with 120hz+ monitors or a real need for FPS, aswell as a select number of chipsets reportedly being unsupported for the Mac OSX port, which the PC Gaming Wiki article can detail if necessary). I certainly can't name any performance issues on my end.
The Singleplayer experience can be summed up as "Call of Duty 4 cranked to 11", as unlike it's more believable predecessor who rarely took away the player's control while the cinematic events occured, the setpieces are both in abundance & high spectacle, with numerous quick-time events to boot, for which many are memorable often thanks to the strong soundtrack composed by Hans Zimmer & Lorne Balfe.
The 2-Player co-op experience, "Spec Ops" is actually one of Modern Warfare 2's stronger features. It's a mission based mode with a wide variety of gameplay elements & objectives, which either originate from Modern Warfare 2 & Call of Duty 4 or occasionally are unique to Spec Ops, all with a Three Star system awarded based on either difficulty completion, time completion or other mission unique tiers. Such things as a Snowmobile race & time trail, covering a co-op partner from a Black Hawk or AC130, or getting All Ghillied Up together, along with the more classical eliminate all targets, survive or complete-a-mission affairs. Whilst most of these can be played solo, there are a small number of missions that do require a co-op partner (Along with some where a Co-op partner is ideal to completing Veteran difficulty, especially with being able to revive each other presents it's own strategies). With the right buddy, it can be quite the fun!
I can only give you my experience from the Xbox 360, but based on the brief return on PC just for experimentation's sake, not an awful lot has changed. I don't know how abundant hacking remains (To which on Xbox 360, it was utterly rampant!) but I have heard concerns from players that not only is hacking still rampant, but you yourself could be at risk from being VAC-Banned just by joining a matchmade game with or controlled by said hackers (I've had a somewhat similar experience in Gears of War 2 when my stats were permanently affected by being matchmade with illegitimate players, aswell as an occasion I was matchmade with hackers on MW2 [X360], which although neither resulted in any official bans, I'd say the concern should be at least considered valid), so it may be wise to proceed with caution if you wanna play Multiplayer outside of Private Matchplay, or be prepared to hightail it if you notice anything very unusual. Regardless, I can probably sum it up as a pit of out-of-control chaos with "noob-tubing" & death from above everywhere! (As this is Call of Duty 4 Multiplayer cranked to 17, which I personally classify as not a good thing). Perks have evolved from their more subtle kit choices to something comparable to super-hero powers, especially when you get their Pro upgrades (Commando Pro being among the most notorious). As for the Kill-Streaks, well, instead of being the assisting tools of winning the game, a significant selection pretty much is the gameplay & game-winners to anyone who can manage to avoid dying. You can rain death-from-above on a massive scale with AC130s, Attack Helicopters, Harriers, Bombing Runs, Stealth Bombers, Predator Missiles, maybe more. And of course, reel in 25 kills with all that and you have it equipped, hit the Nuke to win the game! (Provided your team or the enemy doesn't do it for you before the bomb drops).
Well, it's a limited recommendation. Following from their smash debut hit, Bastion, Supergiant Games raises the bar with yet another incredible title.
Transistor boasts uniquely hand-drawn artwork and visuals (which catches the eye with splashes of color and design), an absolutely fantastic soundtrack (which reacts and changes seamlessly according to ambience, scripted events, character progression and actions), simple yet complex mechanics (isometric viewpoint similiar to Bastion, but with an added layer of turnbased combat, as well as mergeable skills and abilities), on top of another astounding narrative and a deeply layered plotline. Transistor is a carefully crafted product, lovingly refined and polished by a dedicated, creative and passionate team of developers, as well as an exceptional performance by Darren Korb and vocalist Ashley Lynn Barrett. Transistor is unfortunately a very short game (but as was previously seen in Bastion), comes complete with specific attributes or "upgrades" resulting in a much tougher experience. Transistor also incorporates another layer of replayability - Recurse, which allows you to replay various parts of the story, or if preferred, new game plus.
All in all, Transistor is an absolutely fantastic, creative and unique video game and is deservedly a masterpiece in indie development! I highly recommend Transistor and it's seperately sold soundtrack as they are both most definitely worth the money and the time.

Emily is Away isn't fun. That's the first thing I want to say.
It's not really a "game", either. The "choices" you make all take you down the same path, and there are no mechanics beyond button mashing and pressing 1, 2, or 3 when necessary.
Having said that, I think it is a title worth giving your attention to.
First off, it's free. Free is great, and I think free is the perfect price point for this game type. I understand a lot of the reviews talk about the game giving you "feels", but I didn't really get that. I think I was too far removed from that period in my life for the nostalgia to be enough to make me actively feel something - and I'm the kind of person who cries at certain commercials.
That isn't to say I didn't understand the intended impact. I understood what I think the point was that the game was trying to make. I felt a retrospective ennui at the end, thinking back on old friends and old relationships.
I didn't think the game was great, I thought it was alright. I thought it was interesting, and I was at least semi-invested in the characters.
It's very short if you only do one play through, maybe 20 minutes long. I did 3 full play throughs and clocked in at just over 70 minutes, and a lot of that was spent with me slowly trying to predict what my character was going to type. If I had just button mashed I probably could have done the full three play throughs in 60 minutes.
Despite my own personal feelings regarding the game, I think this type of game is an important one. I can recognize how it will affect people, especially younger audiences. I also feel that perhaps a teen male will have a greater emotional connection to the game than I did. I don't mean that the game is immature in any way, but every game has a demographic and I think that is the one for Emily is Away. I actually think that it would be a great game for young men to play.
Overall I'd recommend the game. It's short and will raise some important questions for the player, especially if you are that demographic of 15-19, and doubly so if you're male.
P.S. After my first play through I felt bad, and wanted to fix what I thought was a mistake I had made. After my third play through I really didn't care if Emily was away. She's kind of annoying.

While, in many ways, not quite as good as the first Dark Souls (in my opinion, anyway), this one is still quite enjoyable.  You now aren't entirely dependant on the estus flask for healing (though that means starting with one measly charge for it, and a maximum of 12), and you can now use the humanity-equivalent item anywhere, though they're fairly scarce and don't heal you, instead just restoring any of your maximum health lost through your many deaths. Things the game has going for it include a better optimized engine, leading to smoother gameplay, and the enviroments are as gorgeous as ever, and with less "build area first, figure out how player will navigate it second" than the original, and you can warp to and from discovered bonfires from the outset of the game. On the other hand, there are some things that could be off-putting to new players, such as a reduction of your maximum hp with each death and having to return to the hub area to level up, rather than being able to from anywhere, and the combat, though generally smoother than DS1, can be a bit "floaty" at times and I personally dislike the changes to the parry/riposte system.
TL;DR
If you can get used to some of the mechanics, and especially if you're a fan of the franchise, I think you'll get a good deal of enjoyment out of this game, but if you don't find "firing yourself out of a cannon at a brick wall an infinite number of times" appealing, you can safely give Dark Souls II a miss.

Let me say in the beginning: "Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs" sure is a nice horror game, but mostly if you never played or saw the previous "part" The Dark Descent.
You play Oswald Mandus, the owner of an industrialised slaughterhouse in 1899.
While you proceed through the game, it already starts with the name of the game and continues with multiple bits of information, that you constantly think "What the actual ♥♥♥♥ is/was going on here". I liked that most in the game, same as in The Dark Descent. From the beginning to almost the last minute, you add pieces of information to finally understand what kind of **** is going on here.
On the other hand, after completing "Amnesia: The Dark Descent" multiple times, I was really disappointed in the horror-atmosphere, which was the strongest part in Amnesia, compared to other games of the genre. The Dark Descent was so strong, because it used a few simple mechanisms of fear. Most important, you almost never saw what was called "enemy". In TDD you♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants because you have no freaking idea whats behind you, what it can do with you, how close it is to you, and how long you need to run until you get rid of it.
Now, A Machine for Pigs and also, in my opinion, Outlast (I don't say it's a bad game, not at all) lack that kind of atmosphere since you know a lot about your pursuers. For me, the enemies in AMFP were neither scary nor did they chase me in a horrifying or atmospheric way, simply, if you know WHAT is chasing you, it loses way too much of its horror. The loss of atmosphere is in my opinion the biggest contra compared to TDD.
Too long, didn't read/All in all:
I recommend this game. The story is pretty cool for the genre, the music and sounds create a good atmosphere, but answer the following questions before you buy it.
1) Have you played The Dark Descent before and want to play the next part? Buy it.
2) Have you played The Dark Descent before and hope for an even better experience? You will not find it here in my opinion.
3) Have you never played or watched a Let's play of The Dark Descent before and do you look for a good horror game?
Start with The Dark Descent. Then go back to 1 and 2.

Gunslinger is a first person shooter with an excellently crafted, linear story line loosely based off of real characters and events, while Red Dead Redemption is a third person shooter in an open world experience, full of side quests and areas to explore. Alien Isolation got it absolutely right. I've seen complaints about this game that reveal more about what the reviewer wanted it to be than what this game actually tries to be. Sneak and survive. The setting is incredible. It capture the retro future from the original Alien movie to perfection. The designers and graphics team did their homework and it shows. The story is also spot on, as it moves through the chapters, hitting all the themes that we expect from the movies: Evil corporations, bad robots, flashbacks that reveal some very bad decision-making, greed, and ultimately a harsh survival story. Too often, little attention gets paid to the sound scape in games but this is a game that really highlights the importance of sound in creating tension, driving our emotions to the brink at the right moments. No matter how far you get with the crafting of tools and weapons, you are always left feeling a little bit vulnerable, which is just right. You need to feel helpless to get the crap scared out of you and this game scares the living crap out of you. Alien Isolation engages and manipulates our emotions in all the best ways. Play it in the dark, alone and with the volume way up. Be sure you've visited the bathroom before you start, though.

This game has its flaws - including multiple climactic moments after which the game bewilderingly continues, and a somewhat unsatisfying ending - but it is also the most loving, reverent depiction of both the setting and tone of the 'Alien' universe I have ever seen. To be able to walk around within this world is a stunning achievement.
I'm a wuss when it comes to horror games, and it took me a long time to get very far in this because I was quickly overwhelmed by its tense and oppressive atmosphere, but that is a
. This is one of my favourite games of all time. The Alien itself feels like a real thing. Even now with 150+ hours, I feel tense and nervous when it's nearby, and it feels like an active, malevolent presence.
The characters are mainly there to keep the plot going, so don't expect much there. Even the main resolution of the Ripley character isn't much more than a punctuation mark.
Later in the game, mission after mission ends with you discovering that Objective A you were looking for doesn't work for some reason, so you have to find Objective B to fix it and then return to Objective A, or worse, trek to Objective C because Objective B also doesn't work. This gets worse as the game goes on. I didn't mind this because I love drinking in the game world so much, but it does frustrate others and I can see why.
I haven't played much of the survivor DLCs, while the Nostromo DLCs are short and sweet. Again, it's fantastic to be able to walk around the actual Nostromo. The whole pack gets regularly reduced to silly prices in sales, so it's great value.

One of the best horror games I have played that falls flat at the end. I would only recommend this game to somebody who either really enjoys the Alien franchise or who really enjoys horror games.
Pros:
- The feel and enviroment of Alien Isolation captures the movies perfectly and the visuals are stunning.
- The atmosphere manages to keep you on your toes for the most part and can often make you feel paranoid
- The AI of the Alien is some of the best I have seen. It will learn from how you play and begin to counter your usual tactics by cheecking places you're likely to hide, it will stop falling for the same old tricks and will backtrack on itself to see if it missed anything. You can also use the Alien to your own advantage by having it clear out an entire room of humans for you.
-  Very few cheap jumpscares. It makes for a better quality of horror game when it can make you scared or on edge without spoon feeding you cheap jumpscares.
Cons:
- I encountered a bug that made my screen shake like crazy towards the end of the story, which made it very hard to aim and thus got me killed repeatedly. I had googled this bug and it seems this is a common occurence that has not (and probably never will) been fixed.
- Weak story. I can't say the story captured me all that much and further in I gave up on the story entirely. They focused on the gameplay and nailed it (mostly), but a better story would have greately helped the game.
- Extremely repetetive. Especially towards the end, you find yourself backtracking, going through the motions and playing the same minigame puzzles, pulling the same switches and pressing the same buttons over and over again. It felt very rushed towards the end and they just filled it with minigames so you'll rack up that playtime.
- The novelty wears off. After 15 hours the fear of the Alien, Androids and Humans were gone and I found myself not caring anymore. The more you're exposed to something the less scary it becomes and with this game taking me roughly 20hrs to beat it was enough time to wear the novelty off entirely long before it was over.
Conclusion:
I love this game, but I won't be replaying it again, and I can't say it's a bad game, because the gameplay is fantastic, but I couldn't wait for it to be over. After 12hrs I thought I was close to the end, but I was so wrong, I had another 8hrs left. In my final few hours I found myself literally running past androids and humans, because I wanted the game to so desperately end, but the games continued to just throw hacking minigames in my face and forced me to backtack all over the station to switch on power here, or overide cores there. It felt convoluted and seriously damaged the game in my eyes.
Combined with the novelty wearing off, the story lacking and the repetetive minigames/objectives I found myself playing a frustrating experience that I couldn't wait to be done, despite thinking it was one of the best (if not the best) horror games I had ever played up until that point.

TL;DR:  Emily is Away tries to be emotional, trying to get me to really care about this person on the other side of the chat, but fails due to the limitations of my choices and the predictable outcomes. It's free to play, so it's still a good 10 minutes to sink your time in.
This inherently is the problem with choice driven games and requires a well written (and varied)  plot to really reward the player into thinking the choices they made matter. Emily is Away really wants to put you in the seat of "just friends" and never wants you to be more than that. All the choices that percieve to let you always end up working against you. And while that's a great narritive for how that would be in real life, it's still upsetting that no matter what you do it always ends the same. It feels forced, and it loses all replayability because if this.
Giving the player choices, only in the end do those choices no longer matter makes the game less believable, and by extension enjoyable. It's hard for me to feel what the game wants me to feel if it forces it down my throat. The game gives you enough choices to choose how you feel about Emily (uninterested, mutual, affectionate) but because of how the narritive plays, all that doesn't play into the end because SPOILERS: You end up wanting her back. There is no option to "just be aquantances" or even end the relationship there. You're left with wanting a girl you're forced to want.
It is, however, free to play so it still is something worth checking out once.

Transistor is a rare breed of a game. To me, its sheer addictiveness comes from the fact that you can't really die, per se—instead, you lose access to abilities once your health drops below a certain point. Because your lost abilities return two access (save) points later, you'll start to hear a chorus of "two more access points, two more access points"...until all of a sudden you've beaten the game. Transistor is a very engaging but very short game.
The loss of abilities demands experimentation, which is a huge plus. Unlike Bastion, the number of possible setups seems massive in this game. The storyline will seem shallow unless you dig into the texts associated with functions and limiters, which provide insight into the world of Transistor. It's also worthwhile to explore every area as much as you can, to meet some amusing or interesting cutscenes.

It had been many years since I had played a good 2D game. Transistor did it for me. The turn planning is an incredible feature that adds playability, the game is visually enticing and has a really good soundtrack.
I enjoyed the gameplay, and the only thing that I regret is that ended so quickly for me. I could have stayed a little bit more in the game.
Now, as far as games go, this is not an RPG (even if they say so). It's an arcade game with a solid history and the possibility to tweak your character with different skills. But all the situations you're presented with have to be resolved fighting, there are no other possibilities there (you can't convince someone not to fight, for example). The story, if solid, it's quite linear. All this make it an excellent arcade game, but not an RPG.
In any case, it's totally worth it.

It's a really great game if you like the Elder Scrolls franchise, just don't expect Skyrim v2. If you like the TES franchise a lot but don't like MMOs, you can perfectly play through the story for many, many hours and enjoy the content on your own. The other players running around may or may not break the experience a little, but for me this is not the issue.
This game isn't exactly like a regular TES game: you pick a class and you have class-specific skills and weapon-specific skills. The possibilities of class/armor/weapon/skill are endless: want to play a robed healer with a mace and a shield? - go for it. Want to play a heavy-armor mage with a twohander? - go ahead. I'm not saying this is optimal play, but it is certainly doable.
Like in the traditional Elder Scrolls games there is level scaling, so you can ignore the main quest and level anywhere you want.
DLCs are released regularly and they are adding more and more events (like halloween, christmas, ...), so there is new content on a frequent basis. This combined with no monthly fee makes this an overall great MMO. If you want the best out of your money, wait for a sale and buy the gold edition.
Pros:
- In-game store is mostly cosmetic, not pay to win.
- Overall friendly player base.
- Very good soundtrack
- Character customization
- Amazing lore
- Good learning curve: new players can get around but each class/role needs to be mastered for optimal play.
- Graphics are very good for an MMO
Cons:
- ~80 GB storage needed
- Load times can sometimes be long
- PVP isn't really balanced: when you are max lvl and max CP you can compete better VS you being a fresh lv 50.
- Learning curve: while I like the learning curve personally, it seems to scare a lot of players.

Five years ago I bought this game in the blink of an eye, and the world  (people at Gamestop) just f****g watched.
CAMPAIGN - The campaign is a very good, action packed, fast paced, cliche thrill ride, like a Michael Bay flick, except instead of spectating, you get to participate in. It continues indirectly about 5 years (see a theme going on here?) after the events of Call Of Duty 4, and you play as a variety of characters and take part in a variety of over the top events in massive setpieces. One even is allowed to partake in the massacre of civilians, which might be in bad taste for sensitive individuals, but I honestly felt the whole sequence was an arbitrary catalyst for you to shoot stuff, and seems like IW just squeezed it in there for the shock value than actually advancing the plot. Not much else is to be said, but if you want a thrill ride, play it, it's a fairly short campaign, with a run on Regular lasting only about 5-6 hours depending on how fast you play.
There is also replay value in Veteran Mode, if you are an achievement hunter like I am, but be prepared to die, see lots of red jelly on your screen, and a lot of "eh eh eh eh eh ahhhh" when you get shot every 15 seconds. I find it odd and stupid you grunt and groan the same way no matter who you play as, but the real question is, who the hell does that? It sounds more like something else was going on when they recorded that clip, and that's been in every COD since 4. Get some new sounds going on IW. Other than that nothing else to be said about the campaign.
SPEC OPS - More replay value action here, run through a bunch of recycled maps and assets from the campaign, alone or with a friend. Get completely torn up by Juggernauts in the Delta and Echo ops on Veteran. Rage quit and try again for insignificant gratification of virtual stars. Great fun.
MULTIPLAYER - 2009, absolute fun, with almost 200-300 hours clocked on my console version, its a blast just jumping into a game and blasting people away with M1887'S or Glockin' someone's grill up by drop shotting them. Lot of unlock, lots of weapons and killstreaks to play with, and the gimmicky prestiging, if you're into that sort of stuff.
The maps are similar, but not wholeheartedly recycled from the campaign, and 90% of the maps I enjoyed, and varied from long sightlines to close quarters height based combat. I dare say it was probably the best MP experience of the time.
2011, 2012, 2013, 2014 - The multiplayer is absolute fecal matter exhumed from buffalos, its absolutely abysmal, plagued with hackers, boosters, cheaters, noob-tubers, the list goes on. 95% use OMA Pro, Danger Close with a TAR-21 GL and noob-tubes across the maps infinitely, and you'd be lucky if anyone is using a assault rilfe, or even playing this game now. Since COD has now become a epitome of FPS and dished out annually, it is expected that support will be relinquished for this game, but that just shows how much Activision and IW care about their products after less than 11 months on the shelves.
CONCLUSION - Good SP experience, OK MP experience, if you play spec ops or have private matches, but don't buy it for MP, even for 10 bucks save your money, and don't be a fool to also buy all the map packs that you'll never get to because the game is pretty much dead, only populated with sad lonely hackers that feel some gratification cheating on a 5 year old video game.

Let me apologize and say I am way late to the review party of COD MOD 2. This is my second playthrough of the game and I enjoyed it a lot on the 360. On the 360 it was my favorite multiplayer Call of Duty (with the exception of Black Ops 2, possibly) but it sure as heck was the most I played. I was a 10th Prestiege on the 360, where as a 2nd in BO2. However,  for my review on Steam I will not be reviewing the multiplayer. Haven't even touched it.
MW2 has 2 single player components, and sadly no zombies. Zombies are not in any Infinity Ward developed Call of Duty. The campaign is fun and and full of twists and turns to delight the player and leads directly into MW3 (which I will replay after I beat MW2). It's the sequel to Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare and picks up 5 years after. Modern Warfare (the first) had some amazing moments which were more dramatic than anything in MW2, though the end was pretty good. The campaign for a modern FPS is 4.5 out 5 stars. Spec Ops the Line was better, but you could argue first vs third person perspectives and how Spec Ops isn't a FPS. To say the least, the Modern Warfare games have better plots than any of the WW2 call of Dutys and most other FPS's.
Secondly, there is Spec Ops (the mode, not the game) in which you can play 1-2 players but comes downloaded with the campaign. It's short mission based levels that have difficulty stars leveled 1 to 3. After you unlock so many stars you    can unlock more levels for a total of 69 stars, I aced these on the 360 and have played some but they truely shine to be played with a friend (some even require 2 people). I don't think I will play many of these levels on this playthrough and it's not going to keep the game installed on my hard drive, that being said if you want a 4-5 hour interactive action movie. I recommend this game. I am sure by now you all have played it, if you haven't you must not play FPS games and if that the case this game isn't going to change that.

Papers Please is a game that is at once brilliant and depressing. It has multiple endings, of which I'm sure I may only truly play through to two or three.
It has a gripping storyline despite being about one of the most boring parts of any profession-- doing paperwork. That said, it is a game that goes out of its way to make you uncomfortable. The moral choices you have to make throughout, and the cramped, claustrophobic nature of the game's layout is brilliant, and unnerving.
In short, it is excellent, but not a game I would play very often after completing it. Definitely worth the purchase, however! It is one of the most unique gaming experiences I've had.

A very fun and creative game that has interesting storytelling elemenst similar to the Borderlands 2 DLC: Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep, but set in a western environment. The story mode can be quite quick, especially if you're acquainted with other FPS games and play at the easiest difficulty, but is supplimented by collectibles you can go back and search for in each level, 3 difficulty levels, an arcade mode where you can attempt to get the highest score, a duel gauntlet, and a NG+ mode.
Skills in this game actually feel rewarding and like they impact the gameplay, making the decision about which to get take some preplanning and consideration. The rifle, shotgun, and pistols all play differently and allow freedom on what playstyle you want, but the upgraded versions you get from skills feel only marginally unique and do little to differ from one another, except visually.
The visuals were appealing to me, not ultra-realistic but went in line with the storytelling and recollection elements of the game. Felt very satisfying to shoot something or for an explosion to go off, or to see bullets going by as you slowed time down and sprayed into a room. It is an old game, but that doesn't get in the way of playing it (except alt-tabbing, don't do that unless you intend on closing the game).
Honestly, the only downside would be the amount of hours you could put into this before having 'done' everything. To complete the story mode twice, 3 star all the arcade levels, and collect about half of the collectibles, took me about 15-20 hours (5-10 offline). However, this game is on sale often and can be found lower than the $9.99 pricepoint. But this game was definitely worth the time and money I put into it, and deserves to get a lot more recognition than it has so far.

Just Cause 3 is the third installment in the Just Cause franchise following the 2006 title, Just Cause, and the 2010 title, Just Cause 2. Just Cause 3 originally released in 2015 by the same development team of the past titles, Avalanche Studios and published by Square Enix. I personally enjoyed Just Cause 2 and I was expecting the same. Obviously it is not the same, but it is better. Make a note that this review will just have comparisons to Just Cause 2.
The gameplay in Just Cause 2 is similar to this game. Liberate towns and cities, bases and outposts and blow everything in your sight up. Of course the gameplay hasn’t changed but it can never get old. The unfortunate thing is that it is unoriginal and the exact same gameplay idea has been recycled and reused. The story is also very similar just like Just Cause 2 because in both games, the storyline is always like some Evil dictator taking over a country and your mission is to liberate every city until you liberate the entire country and kill the leader. It’s a very simple storyline and easy to understand. When you start the game, you are taken through a 30 minute tutorial. In each mission, you gain new technology for your character including a new and improved grappling hook, a wingsuit, airdrop beacons and more. It is a long tutorial and if you are only getting this game for the open world, do not worry. After the tutorial levels, you are unleashed into the wild where you can choose your own story. You could free roam around the whole island and play around with mechanics or you can continue with the story. There are multiple things to do.
The performance is the annoying part of Just Cause 3. Lets just say that the developers did not do the great with performance compared to Just Cause 2 which was perfectly optimised. Specific graphic cards can run it while others have issues. One graphic card that has an issue with running it at good settings in a GTX 1060TI. My secondary computer has the graphics card and runs the game at Medium Settings with fps drops to around 30fps when explosions occur. It has 8GB RAM. My tertiary computer which is not owned by me but my cousin with a GTX 1060TI and 16GB RAM and runs the game at Medium Settings with No FPS Drops. This is because of Memory Leaks.
Memory Leaks are often experienced in Just Cause 3 due to the optimisation. Any system with 8GB RAM will experience memory leaks the most often. My primary computer which I use all the time has an AMD R7 250X Graphics Card and at 8GB RAM at lowest settings. I run the game at 50FPS with fps drops to 16fps but to be honest, the fps drops are a rare encounter.
… This game is pretty great and probably the most decent open world game that you’re going to find in a while. I completely recommend it if you have 16GB RAM or more.

MY PERSPECTIVE: I started playing this game during its Alpha 14 patch (out of 22). I mostly played around it's Release 7-10 patches as a staff member on two of the top servers during that time period. Most of my experience was on RP servers, but I have talked with people who prefer the PvP aspects of the game, as well as some individuals who have done a fair bit of digging in the game's structure in order to create oxide modifications.
IN SHORT:
It's still the best medieval survival game out there, and it's still got a good skill-based combat system for being a survival game. I really want something else to dethrone this game on those two fronts, because:
It's buggy and laggy. I truly don't think the developers know how to make their game any better, but they also don't try anymore. New Content would help SO much; tools for community content would honestly be amazing. However, the community is leaving.
IN FULL:
THE GOOD:
Setting is a big part of a game for me. I don't think there are really any other contendors for a good medieval survival game of this style. It's a blend of Rush and Chivalry, and in some ways, it really works. From what I understand, every other game in its setting and genre is either less developed or even deader from a community standpoint.
Building is actually quite satisfying in this game, for me. It can feel really clunky at first; the entire map is on a cubic grid and you place blocks, and there is no terraforming. However, I found that once you get over having really thick walls to buildings, a lot of things really do work and look decent in game. There is more freedom to this than you have in ARK and Rust.
PvP is considered a strong point. I never really was well practised in this, but I do know that when the game's systems are in working order, PvP is very skill based (with bias towards equipment) and still remains a feature that people play the game for.
THE BAD:
The game is executed very poorly. It isn't optimized, which is an incredible hit to the good things in the game. I was lucky that I could always render my buildings. Other people weren't. Some people's game crashes upon finding a buidling too large to handle. other times, players can run inside someone else's base before it renders in so they could take their stuff. Maybe they are the lucky ones....
Servers typically slow down quite noticably at 20 people or more, but you see lag well below this also. The problem is, this has a huge impact on PvP.
Hackers, exploits, and bugs are things that are to be expected, with the assumption that patches will fix these things. However, these things don't get fixed at the rate they need to. There was a server-breaking bug introduced in their Release 8 Patch that was fixed until 11 or 12; about 6 months later.
There has been no new content since the Alpha stages, which makes sense. However, one of their 'lessons learned' from their first game, Starforge (noted below this all), was not to introduce content before it worked in-game. There are still a few important items, most notably, one of 3 siege items, that are NOT in the final product. There was no 'listening to the community' that was explicitly stated in their early access campaign. There is so much that should be added and fixed. It's a failed promise, and an unfortunate one. This game could have been something special for people outside of its niche.
SHOULD YOU BUY IT?
Read up on CodeHatch. They pulled something similar with their game Starforge, and it's a telltale case of why early access is easily abused by publishers. Reign of Kings is not quite as offensive, but it's still abuse of Early Access. It's not finished, and as a consumer, I feel like it was a cash grab in a popular genre.
Can you have fun with this game? Yes, you can. My best experiences, however, were largely EMERGENT, in that they came from the people I interacted with, and this game is a framework. I don't think it is a good game without that, and if/when the community does leave (which it mostly has), then that just simply means it is not a good game.

Transistor is a rare breed of a game. To me, its sheer addictiveness comes from the fact that you can't really die, per se—instead, you lose access to abilities once your health drops below a certain point. Because your lost abilities return two access (save) points later, you'll start to hear a chorus of "two more access points, two more access points"...until all of a sudden you've beaten the game. Transistor is a very engaging but very short game.
The loss of abilities demands experimentation, which is a huge plus. Unlike Bastion, the number of possible setups seems massive in this game. The storyline will seem shallow unless you dig into the texts associated with functions and limiters, which provide insight into the world of Transistor. It's also worthwhile to explore every area as much as you can, to meet some amusing or interesting cutscenes.
On the whole, I would strongly recommend Transistor. I found it to be just difficult enough to keep me on my toes, but engaging enough to keep me hooked.

Comfy med-low pop mmo with cute aesthetics and lots of grind.
The main drive in this game is the class variety and how classes work with each other. There are currently 4 main classes being your typical mmo swordsman/cleric/archer/mage that makes up the first "Class Rank". Each "Class Rank" allows the players to further involve themselves into the same class up to 3 "Circles" or pick from two new classes avaliable per rank. At the moment, 7 Ranks are in the game with an 8th on its way, 15 classes per class tree for a total of 60 classes and most of them have 3 Circles worth of abilities.
Players get permanent xp bonus from the combined levels of the player's characters, including deleted ones, making it easy to reroll and start new characters on a whim. Biggest downside is that character limit is at 3 unless you pay a small cash shop fee that averages at 3$.
PvE is solid and bosses is where your build really shines or fall altho dont expect anything serious before lvl 100.
PvP is broken as of now mages with heavy CC just rekt people up and the melee class is basically useless in that context, outside of a few gimmicky skills. PvP without mages is fair enough but could use some tweak here and there.
The F2P system is supported by the purchase of Cash Shop currency to buy costumes, hair dyes and some quality of life utlity items such as tp scrolls. Tokens can also be bought with bonuses like extra xp from killing monsters, increased dungeon instance avaliability and trading benefits on the market, mostly less tax and more selling slots. These Tokens can also be bought with ingame currency from other players on the market worth a day or two of grind for mid-high level players given said players know where and how to grind efficiently. Token benefits last for a month and once its ran out players can usualy buy another one right away from the market if they saved a bit.
Content is being released somewhat steadily and on the 26th of July there was a considerable update bringing balance to some classes and some new game modes and events.
I would recommend Tree of Savior to anyone looking for a comfy low effort mmo with a lot of class variety and cute animu grills with somewhat fair F2P at the moment.

The too-easy summary - Rez meets an endless runner.
It's a bit more than that. You run. Endlessly. Well, until you run out of platform to run on. Hold a button, run faster. Release the button, jump. Hold it again to cut the jump short & land again & start running. It's all about timing those jump/interrupts to land on the next platform you want.
Did I mention it's all first person, with a trippy rez-like vector graphic presentation where the world & environment builds up over the duration of the level in time with the music? It's tough arcade 'one more time' gameplay, with killer controls & level design.
It's not particularly deep, but it's a well designed challenge & is focused on doing one thing well - an incredibly cool kinetic feeling of powerful jumps.

What to say about Machine for Pigs.  Well... I guess i was a little bit dissapointed.  Lets start with the good stuff.  The atmosphere from the first game is back and (arguably) better than before.  Walking through a narrow pipe filled hallway while steam spurts out, trying to squint into the darkness is still unnerving as all hell, and the sound design is absolutely excellent.  It really does feel like the titular Machine (for Pigs) is a living, breathing organism and it becomes more so as you progress through its darkened passages.  Sounds good so far, right?
What really bothers me though, is the fact that so much has been stripped out from the first game that they feel like very different beasts entirly.  Gone is the sanity meter, which in the first Amnesia prevented you from hiding in the dark and, more imorantly, made the monsters feel more threatening.  After all, a creature that can drive you insane just by looking at them truly was a terrifying thing.  Not only that, the sanity meter also affected the way the game presented itself to you.  The walls would ebb, your teeth would grind, you would hear sounds that may or may not even be there etc etc.  Without that key mechanic, A Machine for Pigs feels overwhelmingly less dangerous.  Sure, the pigmen are creepy (sort of) but they don't mess with your mind nearly as much.
If Machine for Pigs was the first game in the series (which it kind of feels like), it would have been a much more effective horror experience.  As it stands now, it pales in comparison from its older brother.  Still worth a play through, but lower your expectations.

Pros: Excellent writing and pitch-perfect sound design combined with gorgeous creature design to make a creeping horror that sticks with you. Level design is twisty and well thought-out. Cons: It lacks graphical polish, mostly due to budget constraints, and the sanity meter is sorely missed, even if it would've been harder to pull off here than in Dark Descent.
Verdict: Highly recommended.

You are an alien, crash landing on a foreign planet. You survey the area to find that the planet has a stable ecosystem, standard minerals and run-of-the-mill wildlife that are very territorial if they feel the presence of others. You decide that you need to get back home and start gathering materials to make the technology neccesary to escape. You find that your weapons barely do any damage to the bigger wildlife and decide to go straight up gore the wildlife with trains to keep them away. It works for a while until they figure out the walls can be destroyed. Just as your on your last leg, you launch your new spaceship into orbit, searching for another planet, perhaps easier, to raze and destroy.
This is how this game is explained in my mind. Feel free to take your own interpretation of it but Factorio is a Marvel to play since the early modding days of Minecraft to me. I can not stress enough how much creativity is needed and how many hours is required to fully understand the different systems Factorio Vanilla has in play. It has Circut Networks relatable to how'd you connect redstone to your minecraft house to turn a light on if a creeper was nearby (this is what i did). It has logistic systems that combine with robots that are intelligent enough to replicate tasks you've created for them. It has an impressive rail system that I feel minecraft should have originally had as it is a sight to behold when you have 20 trains all backed up full with alien material to deliver to your base. In the end this is a wonderful game that even after 500 hours of gameplay I feel like I don't have the full grasp on everything it has to offer! This is an early access game mind you, but to me. It's a finished, modable, sandbox waiting for the right time to take your gaming soul.

Decent MMO. Fun. GREAT for RP-ing, since it's lore that I'm used to. Crowns are WAAAAY too expensive, also removed some key Elder Scrolls features that I think might be a dealbreaker for some.
I play quite a bit of it, and I think it's quite fun. Bit restrictive, lots of expensive micro-transactions, but believe me, it isn't pay to win. Even for the PvP, it isn't pay to win. It's really just... pay to get there faster. But it doesn't take long to build a character, if you don't mind grinding, which is what MMOs are known for. The game doesn't hold your hand, which is what I like about it.
Also, let me be clear. THIS. IS NOT. AN ELDER SCROLLS GAME. It's set in the Elder Scrolls' universe, but it is far from being an Elder Scrolls game. Great MMO! Terrible TES game. That's ok though. Personally, I enjoy that it isn't pay to win (I mean, thankfully. They already make you buy the game, and tbh having a subscription just makes your life hella easier, but I don't mind really, provides me with lots of fun.) and that the RP community is thriving. I appreciate that it's set in the TES universe, because it's lore that I know, and understand, and can really get into.
Let's see, as of the time of my review, here are a few pros and cons, starting with the cons.
-No Unarmed skill, which is highly underrated
-NO CHILDREN. ??? There are legit NO children in Tamriel. Ever. The closest you get are the shortest bosmer xD
-Crown store. Now, there are positives and negatives. First of all, there is a lot of... 'persuasive advertising'. They act like the crown store is the only way to get certain items. Luckily the crown store is mostly just cosmetic/aesthetic items. They make them all look super cool, but honestly if you just play the game and IGNORE the crown store, you end up getting cool stuff.
-The limitations on inventory space. Now, I get the need to limit inventory space, HOWEVER... in past elder scrolls games it was based on weight and the strength of your character. They did away with all that, and now it's a starting amount of 60 slots for items (at least you can stack those items in one slot? >,>)
-You can play as any race! Except Imperial... Yup, if you want to be an Imperial, you have to use crowns to buy the "Imperial Race Upgrade." which grants you the race, a white horse, and I think a few other silly things.
-Pets are useless. Non-combat pets are a thing. Why? Because money.
There is light in this story though...
+Pretty engaging quests, if you like lore. They even have a pretty prevalent Maormer presence, even though you can't play as a Maormer.
+Each zone is a decent enough sized, though the loading screens can get annoying from time to time if you travel quickly.
+For an MMO, it's great. For an Elder Scrolls game... well... eh. But, that's not so bad, because fans of MMOs can enjoy it.
TL;DR - Don't buy unless you like MMOs. This is not an Elder Scrolls game. Seriously. On the other hand, if you like MMOs and don't mind paying an initial price... dude! Get it! Also, there are less trolls since you have to pay to get in.
There's my 2 cents.

Smite is a third person MOBA (Multiplayer Online Battle Arena) developed by HiRez Studios. Despite the company's past, Smite is a well polished gem among the studio's line up of games.
In Smite, everything you do is a skill shot. You know how in traditional mobas where a general majority of attacks are automatic, as in basic attacks that lock on and home in on your target? That isn't how Smite handles things. You have to aim every basic attack and every ability. This creates for a completely different pacing and playstyle than other traditional mobas tend to offer, which is usually a hit or miss for a lot of people. Regardless, you shouldn't ignore this game.
The current roster boasts over 80 different Gods/Goddesses to choose from, all of which are from many different mythological pantheons (Egyptian, Greek, Mayan, Roman, Norse, Chinese, Japanese, Celtic).
The game modes it offers are relatively simple to learn, the easiest being Arena. The typical moba game mode, Conquest, has a steep learning curve, so I recommend starting off with Joust (3v3 one lane map with jungles) or Siege (4v4 2 lane map with a jungle) before stepping into it. Arena is a team deathmatch set in a giant circular map modeled after the Roman Colleseum, where your goal is to reduce the enemy team's ticket count to 0. Tickets are consumed whenever a minion dies, and 4 tickets are consumed per God killed. Assault is a game mode which focuses on a single lane with 2 towers and a phoenix. When you enter the lobby, every player has their God chosen at random among the ones you have unlocked. The focus of the mode is nonstop fighting, with the catch being you can't return to base unless you die. This causes spikes of power creep throughout the match, since players that go on killing sprees will come back even stronger once they finally die.
You have to give the game a try for yourself to determine if you really like this kind of game, although there's really nothing quite like it. It's very action and combat oriented compared to other mobas.
The graphics are adequate, the sound is memorable and does a fairly solid job at letting you know what's happening even if you can't see the source, and the art direction is faithful to the direction it wants to go in.
I recommend Smite, although it
have a steep learning curve to anyone new to the genre, and those who are familiar with moba styled games will still be a bit confused at the start. You have to be patient and take your time to learn the game, or you'll get frustrated very early on.
Good luck, and have fun.

I was playing this game about a week ago, and well… a game hasn’t made my palms sweat in a really long time. Not even Dark Souls. Apparently I was way into it. Sweaty palms, weak knees, heavy arms, sans Mom’s Spaghetti.
I really enjoy this game’s sense of speed, and the challenge of running through a new level trying to figure out the timing you need to pull off in order to advance is quite enjoyable. For the most part.
Most of my play time was probably stuck on one or two levels. THEY’RE SO DAMN HARD! I went into this game expecting it to be relaxing! Don’t get me wrong, it can be for sure… But, damn it’s rough sometimes. You really have to be on point to get through most of the game. Jump to early, miss the platform. Jump too late, hit the platform. Either way you’re falling into an endless void longingly reaching out to accept you.
The dream like sound design, and calming music betray that fact that this game will really screw you over if you’re not paying attention.
Fun Fact: your decreasing altitude is inversely proportional to your blood pressure.
Overall I really enjoyed my time with FOTONICA and would recommend it to anyone that really enjoys endless runner type games. However, the game is normally listed at $10! Which I feel is a little too expensive for the price, considering what is available. There are about eight or nine arcade levels, and three endless levels. All of which can be played on a variety of difficulties.
Interestingly you can also play with up to four other people, which is nice! But I don’t think that’s enough content to justify the $10 price. I would say it’s more along the $5 to $7 range.
So just keep that in mind. I would say if you’re interested, and like endless runners definitely give this one a chance. It’s super cool, well made, and pretty trippy, yo.

(long review -but its not a negative rant about item shop prices I promise! Saw so many negative reviews and I just thought Id pop my opinion on this game I love so much at the moment)
A very unique game - I have no interest in real life hunting either!
Yet... I find it almost impossible to spend less than 4-6 hours in this game at a time... it just draws me in... kinda lucky each hunt day ends and you run out of ammo eventually or I dont know how I would get out of this game... I would probably hunt with my bare hands when outta ammo if let me - its a vortex. Weird too because I can fire only 1 bullet/arrow every 10 mins or more/less and still be satisfied. (sometimes long times just wandering and tracking/waiting/chasing).
The atmosphere and creature AI are fantastic - the weapons feel satisfying, and kills dont feel too hard or too easy. Any bad things I have to say about this game are related to some items being too expensive, and draw distances being too low - but these things make sense when put into context I suppose, not the item shop so much (but I guess it is keeping them afloat). I doubt these guys are making these game updates inside mansions.
Its good value, unless you expect free to play in traditional sense, where you are the product, there to fill groups/be easy targets of paid members. You can pay a very small amount to custom tailor your experience if you want. This is mostly a single player session game, with multiplayer contests/leaderboards, with the option of multiplayer hunting with (not as many) multiplayer contests. So all the content is there for you to enjoy personally - and you dont get to play good games for free for the most part. Addictive and way too easy to spend money though - warning about that.
This game has been out for over 5 years but has had many graphics updates etc with new zones and animals (all for free) and the zones etc are very nice. AI/sound/weapons/contests etc are all outstanding also.
Consider the free to play a demo that lasts forever and lets you get a taste and a teaser. Then pay the $50 and get the best package deal and be just about set. Yes you can pay more, (or less) and yes if you dont you wont get all the items, but you dont need all the items. I am pretty sure a lot of the bad reviews for this game are people without money, or unable to understand that simple concept of games costing money, if they are good, and if people are prepared to pay. That said I think they went overboard on microtransactions in some ways.
Its a unique business model, but one that obviously works for them and their customers, not everyone understandably - but you cannot please everyone. Its nowhere near as pay to play as people make out - they just exaggerate... sure you can spend a LOT in the item shop, but you dont need most of it, and most of it just makes the game a bit too easy anyway...
Just buy one of the packs and you can kill almost anything (except bison with the most basic pack) with the guns provided - with few limitations - but spend another 10-20$ and u can get a decent rifle like a 7mm that can shoot almost anything you cant already shoot - and a backpack maybe some other items you wanted also. I recommend the $50 pack tho as it fills most things you will want to get anyway once you are hooked, lasts a year subscription and is by FAR the best value.
(I dont understand why people complain so much about these guys trying to make money from their game, yet the massive game market seem happy to pay $110 for a crappy annually released sequel and then a $60-70 season pass for games like battlefield, COD and fifa etc.) IF the hunter charged what those games did for the time it has been out, to pay for the current content you would be looking at $250-500 dollars EASILY. You can buy $15/3 month subscription to this and hunt on 10 reserves for 25 species. Pay another $10 and you can hunt anything.. game over for the animals but so much fun for you.

TRANSISTOR, is a Sci-Fi RPG game with elements of real time and turn based strategy incorporated into its game play. It's also known to be created by the same developers of the highly recognized and praised indie game, Bastion. Does its second game own up to their reputation?
Absolutely.
If you're looking for a highly complex RPG or an action game alone, Transistor is not the game you want. Instead, Transistor gives you a very unique game play experience all the while engrossing you in an original storyline. The best way to describe the combat, turn based and RTS being played AT THE SAME TIME is ... not too difficult or even annoying, it's just slightly unpolished. Honestly I had no trouble with it after a few quick rounds and waves of enemies, though it is an odd system.  If you find the combat too simple after a while, you can increase the difficulty of your enemies in exchange for gaining more XP points. (A great feature)
The customization of the abilities is very well done however, with new skills being acquired throughout. Testing and mixing skills for new enhancements was a blast and using every one of them is a goal as it unlocks background information for the story.
Putting the game play in the backseat though, it really is the atmosphere, themes, plot, art and soundtrack that make this an incredible game. Playing as the female singer Red as she journeys through the glamorous, beautifully illustrated cyber city Cloudbank, is an unforgettable experience. Having lost the two things that matter most to our protagonist, through the mysterious means of the sword she now wields, our story is about Red and her mission to take them back, by any means necessary.
Revenge, loss, control, utopia, change and even existence, are the themes of Transistor's story. And it’s a mature one, very different from Bastion. You play as the protagonist, but almost every character in the game is a grey one, when it comes to morals. Every single person, even the enemy, has a reason for what they're doing and it'll give you enough plot twists and surprises that should keep anyone engaged. From Red's voiceless stride, to the loneliness the city and the narrator express, all of this entwines to give off a near perfect tune.
And speaking of music, the game's soundtrack is one of my favorites. Electric guitar riffs to humming have never sounded so good to the ears. Transistor's music producer Darren Korb knows how to give sound to the world you’re in, and you'll definitely want to buy the soundtrack.
So, is there a downside? A full play through will take about four to five hours and after that, you can experience the game again for more difficult rounds and bonus stages. But that's about all there is to the game. The game took me personally about ten hours to beat “completely”, including achievements. (Friends of mine have played a little on my account too) If you're going to buy the game expecting an incredible combat experience, I will say it is a lot of fun, but some may complain given the oddness of it. AND if you're expecting Transistor tell to you everything it's trying to say right up front? Don’t. This is not a straight through plot and requires that you do a little reading of the back story to get the full effect.
Overall: Transistor is a game that shows, rather than tells and plays. It gives a mature storyline with incredible details and themes hidden throughout, and asks you strive to listen to its mute cries. I can easily say that this has become one of my favorite games, and my favorite all time indie game. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED

I eventually got rid of my XBox 360 and turned to my PC and Steam to get my gaming fix. Then CoJG went on sale...
I had seen it advertised on XBL and watched some of the ads for it. The ads don't do this game justice. This game is beautiful, with every locale thoroughly realized and perfectly crafted. The gameplay is plenty entertaining, mixing action and rpg elements perfectly making for a satisfying experience. If it had multiplayer, it would be damn near perfect.
Nothing will ever quite live up to the high bar that RDR set for Western games, at least not until Rockstar releases it much-rumored sequel, but Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a pretty damn fine alternative.

Fotonica is a first-person platformer at the price of 10$, if you want just go to the bottom of this review for pros/cons.
GAMEPLAY
As stated in the first sentence, Fotonica is a endless first person platformer/runner. You can choose to play its "story" mode (theres not an actual story being told though) which is kinda just a challenge mode. You can play endless in which the platforms are randomly generated and it's well endless. The game uses one button which you hold to charge your jump and release to jump. The gameplay gets INSANELY repetitive so I can't imagine someone having to pay 10$ for this game. It seems like a 2-3 $ game, luckily I picked it up on a humble bundle (check humble bundle out it's really cool) for just $1 plus a whole lot of other games. So yeah that IS the whole game, jumping one one platform to the next as the level speeds up. Fun but repetetive. 6/10
GRAPHICS
Omy god is all I have to say, and it's not in a good way. Now first things first I don't really care if a game has good or bad graphics, because frankly I have a horrible PC but still this was so horrible that I'm judging it. Now, if you have not seen the graphics from the screenshots it's really just a ton of lines put together to make a 3-D world, and it looks terrible. The background is none existent and it's really hard to see where you're jumping/going. 4/10
REPLAYABILITY
Really low, it's the same thing over and over again. 3/10
VERDICT
If you pick up Fotonica for 2-3 dollars yes it's recommended but for 10$ I just can't
+Good platforming
+Fun for first 30 minutes or so
-Visuals are blinding
-SO repetitive
-The price
FINAL RATING
5.7/10

Looks like Ragnarok Online, but it plays very differently. Combat is MMORPG-fun, and the only problem I had in performance was the lag in dense areas of the city (like Fedimian). Design-wise, it's more coherent than RO and has a simple storyline to it, but it lacks the open-world feel: different cities across the world to walk from and to.
Endgame and dailies are much like other MMORPGs. Gear variety is severely lacking, almost everyone is wearing the same optimal stuff. Doesn't really change anything if you stack up on Ice Defense, that Goblin Wizard is still going to freeze you to death. Much of the routine fun is in crafting the recipes, which you can sell in the market for good prices.
It's worth an experience if you're a fan of RO, but don't expect a renaissance.

The only thing I'll say against it is that I'm not sure listing it at the same price as it's predecessor is the right choice; many have been disappointed by this game in terms of it's length and the streamlining of gameplay in service of its story, and I think that charging the same price for both games compounds the view that it's a lesser game; get it in a sale, though, and if atmospheric storytelling is something you enjoy, I'm sure you'll find something of value here.

I wish there was an "utterly neutral option" for reviews. Oh well.
Now, I'm not a big fan of horror games. In fact, I'm a huge weenie. While playing A:TDD in a totally lit room with two of my best friends, I had to stop because I was hearing vague noises in other parts of the house that sounded like footsteps. This was after already having beaten the area with another friend, and knowing that there were no monster encounters whatsoever in the area.
That said, Machine for Pigs did make me feel pretty scared, even from the get go! But it wasn't the same feeling as A:TDD. It felt... very linear. There wasn't a lot of exploration. No things to pick up, no boxes to stack out of nervousness, no fear of using too much light and therefore no fear created by using too little. There were no characters mentioned for me to care about, all the dialogue sounded pretentious and confusing... I didn't really care about where the story went.
Now, that's said having played A:TDD.
If you DIDN'T play A:TDD, I'm sure it'd be a fine game! It's visually pleasing and pretty interesting, but considering the hype it got from A:TDD, it just doesn't live up to expectations.
So that's why I'm neutral. I didn't like it very much, but I don't feel I can judge fairly based on how much I liked A:TDD.

This is definitely not some kind of carbon copy sequel to The Dark Descent. It feels like more of a ''Dark descent inspired" kind of thing. The puzzles are simplified a lot compared to TDD, and I feel like the focus was put more on being scared to move to/from different areas to solve said puzzles. On that note, I did thoroughly enjoy the dread of having to keep going into the creepy hallway where you just saw that shadow.
This game is INCREDIBLY atmospheric and I feel like that's really one of it's best points, there were only a few times when I was in any actual danger and yet I remained nervous through most of the game. (I recovered towards the end, when you do start getting used to what the game throws at you, and start to kind of Rambo it out)
I think this game is mostly fun when it's scary to you, and you've got to be the right type of person to be susceptible to that scare. If you're really hard to impress on any kind of horror level you might get disappointed.
If you're someone who has a thing for stories involving slaughterhouses this is a total hoot though.

Although not nearly as frightning as the first game, Machine for Pigs is however, much more story driven, and honestly, much easier to keep up with.
Now, I did beat the first game, but once it ended, I had no idea what the heck the whole thing was about. I'm not sure if it is just me, and it was simply too complicated for my feeble mind, or if this game really based on a fever dream one of the developers had one night, but in short, I was totally lost with the story, but damn if I didn't wet my britches while running away from sheer terror.
Anyways, Machine for Pigs (No, I have not finished it) so far is a much simplier story, one of which a father is looking for his children, while exploring the giant slaughter house that he inhiereted from his father's rich pork business. Yes, there is not that many scares, and with the few there is are harmless.
So pretty much just flip-flop the two focuses of the two games. Dark Descent: Terror > Story;  Machine for Pigs: Terror < Story. Since there was a diffrence between devlopers, there was bound to be diffrences, and I, for one, liked the change of pace, and am eager to see the next projects of the game devs.

TRANSISTOR, is a Sci-Fi RPG game with elements of real time and turn based strategy incorporated into its game play. It's also known to be created by the same developers of the highly recognized and praised indie game, Bastion. Does its second game own up to their reputation?
Absolutely.
If you're looking for a highly complex RPG or an action game alone, Transistor is not the game you want. Instead, Transistor gives you a very unique game play experience all the while engrossing you in an original storyline. The best way to describe the combat, turn based and RTS being played AT THE SAME TIME is ... not too difficult or even annoying, it's just slightly unpolished. Honestly I had no trouble with it after a few quick rounds and waves of enemies, though it is an odd system.  If you find the combat too simple after a while, you can increase the difficulty of your enemies in exchange for gaining more XP points. (A great feature)
The customization of the abilities is very well done however, with new skills being acquired throughout. Testing and mixing skills for new enhancements was a blast and using every one of them is a goal as it unlocks background information for the story.
Putting the game play in the backseat though, it really is the atmosphere, themes, plot, art and soundtrack that make this an incredible game. Playing as the female singer Red as she journeys through the glamorous, beautifully illustrated cyber city Cloudbank, is an unforgettable experience. Having lost the two things that matter most to our protagonist, through the mysterious means of the sword she now wields, our story is about Red and her mission to take them back, by any means necessary.
Revenge, loss, control, utopia, change and even existence, are the themes of Transistor's story. And it’s a mature one, very different from Bastion. You play as the protagonist, but almost every character in the game is a grey one, when it comes to morals. Every single person, even the enemy, has a reason for what they're doing and it'll give you enough plot twists and surprises that should keep anyone engaged. From Red's voiceless stride, to the loneliness the city and the narrator express, all of this entwines to give off a near perfect tune.
And speaking of music, the game's soundtrack is one of my favorites. Electric guitar riffs to humming have never sounded so good to the ears. Transistor's music producer Darren Korb knows how to give sound to the world you’re in, and you'll definitely want to buy the soundtrack.
So, is there a downside? A full play through will take about four to five hours and after that, you can experience the game again for more difficult rounds and bonus stages. But that's about all there is to the game. The game took me personally about ten hours to beat “completely”, including achievements. (Friends of mine have played a little on my account too) If you're going to buy the game expecting an incredible combat experience, I will say it is a lot of fun, but some may complain given the oddness of it. AND if you're expecting Transistor tell to you everything it's trying to say right up front? Don’t. This is not a straight through plot and requires that you do a little reading of the back story to get the full effect.
Overall: Transistor is a game that shows, rather than tells and plays. It gives a mature storyline with incredible details and themes hidden throughout, and asks you strive to listen to its mute cries. I can easily say that this has become one of my favorite games, and my favorite all time indie game. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED

This is maybe the most confusing game ever. It has a somewhat healthy playerbase, somewhat okayish reviewscores and is still being updated. So after a long break of it because I thought the game will die pretty quick I returned to it with hopes of improvment..... This game is INSANELY stale. The combat, the story, the NPCs.... I really don´t know where the fun is all the reviewers talk about.
The combat is incredibly boring, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥it´s boring. I´m just standing in front of the boss and singlehandedly bring it down by spamming Ransack, which is an Ability. No tactics, no risk of death, no gameplay at all. I was told that combat would get better with higher levels so I thought to myself "Okay, I´ll give it a try.". Take a guess, nothing friggin changed except I occacionally press 2 for a Stamina/Mana regen buff. And if I am not fighting I stand back with my healingstaff and spam my group heal and contemplate life until the boss goes down with absolutley no effort. "Go to the dungeons for 4 players" you might say. Okay let´s do that. I did nothing different aside from seeing more stuff going on but still spamming healz (I am a Templar with a support focus) and my warhorn. Aside from that I have a suspicion that the dungeons are not designed for 4 players because it was so incredibly easy. Sure it wasn´t a high level dungeon but if I literally do nothing and spam my 1 and 2 keys without any other action while being able to make a sandwich then there is clearly a huge con.
The loot you get from quests and combat is not satisfying. The loot from bosses and other quest related events is unique, but have no unique appearance. I´m a huge loot♥♥♥♥♥ and adore my customizations, but this is abysmal. For the first time ever I am purposely ignoring loot with the knowledge that it has no impact whatsoever. Inventory managment is a mess if you don´t upgrade to premium. I spend so much time on micromanaging my inventory it´s ridiculous. The best items for customizing your char are behind paywalls with so many other features (who the hell thought locking the Dark Brotherhood behind a paywall is a good idea?!). The worst part of this is you can´t get these things by normal means, that´s right, you have to pay because ♥♥♥♥ YOU GIVE ME MONEY!
The story is laughable. I couldn´t do it because it was so boring and I couldn´t do it with my friend for comedic relief and some sort of diversion because "you are expected to do this alone". I don´t even know who all these people are I worked with and don´t care about them. There is absolutley no connection between player and those characters. Granted the voiceacting is somewhat passable, but I want substance and the storyrich experience everyone is talking about. Where the hell is it?! Did I join the wrong faction? Am I the wrong class? Do I have to pay more? WHERE THE HELL IS THE FUN IN THIS GAME?!
The atmosphere is fitting for its regions, but then things happen that just are so ridiculous that I have to tell them. A city was apparently under siege and the city-main-guy told me to help defending it. I walked out of the gate and there were literally 3 guys outside with 1 trebuchet.... ARE YOU ♥♥♥♥ING SERIOUS?! This is not a one time only thing, it happens so often that you can´t immers yourself into the world, which is the whole point of a RPG, MMO or not.
The only really outstanding good experience I had were the sieges in PvP. Damn. They are quite impressive and a lot of fun in my opinion. But again, I dont get why I need an eternity with my uptodate equipment to dent someone and my enemy player just oneshots me ( not literally but it´s so fast I don´t know what happens). Aside from this I loved skulking around with my buddy in Cyrodiil.
If someone can please tell me where the hidden gem of this game is, please tell me! I can´t find anything redeeming in it and I feel I only waste my time with it. I really love PvE and this is so unbelievably boring, bad, stale and unintuitive. I actually have more to say about it like the Levelsystem, the graphics, the music and crafting, which I find ok but on 1 good thing 1000 bad things follow. As it stands I can´t recommend this game. Ok, so this could be a very good game. It has amazing graphics, realistic shooting, and great weapon and animal varieties. This game is meant to show what hunting is like, and to provide a chance for people who can't go hunting to get the experience. You also don't have to kill real animals if you don't like the idea of doing that. It does that well, but the biggest flaw of this game can completely bring it to the ground, and it's starting to already. Here it is. You have to pay to hunt most of the animals. You also have to pay to get better weapons and clothing. The creators, Expansive Ways and Avalanche Studios, just want to reel in money, and don't get me wrong, money is a big factor in creating games. It's a big factor in all of our lives. It pays for the development of the game and the creators. But, you can't make gamers pay to even play the game at all. Many users have already complained about the fact that it's "Free to Play" because it's basically not. They've just uninstalled it right away. This game has such a big chance to get to the top of the charts, but the money issue is holding it back. All in all, it's a very good game already, but you have to pay to get past the very basics of the game.

Beautifully polished with interesting gameplay mechanics although some unfortunate innovations prevent a perfect review.
Combat lends itself to both creative tactical gamplay and on-the-spot improvisation with a smooth fusion of turn and real-time, if skewed towards the former. Storytelling is vague but very atmospheric. Few things will make sense until the end of the plot or the second run and even then there will be lots of unanswered questions. Parts of the story are unlockable only via experimenting with different strategies which is a nice way to connect gameplay and storytelling.
Before you start: forget about grinding. Sandbox mode becomes available only later in game and the overall difficulty is rather low, so it's better to just learn how to play as you go with the story.
Difficulty can be increased trough the use of "limiters" which enhance your enemies or limit your options in exchange for an increase in experience gain. I find that the former increase the overall fun factor, while the latter tend to become a drag by removing the creative component that is the highlight of the game. Sadly limiters have to be unlocked too, so the initial sections might feel a bit too easy depending on your skill level.
After the first game it is also possible to play in recursive mode with all of your abilities unlocked from the start and even tougher enemies if you want to give a chance to that combo you never got around implementing the first time around.

Only a Meta Score of 83/100? This game shows how much "game critics" are paid off.
Edit for people who might not understand: The game is 110/100.
