A wonderful game that I can spend hours on.

Where to start with Factorio?
Factorio is one of those games where you buy it, play for ages, then close down to play a different game with your friends. Factorio then sits and gathers dust in the corner of your game library to be played again a month later. I mainly have 3 different ways for playing games. Short but frequent bursts, Meduim lenght plays often enough and Very long playtimes now and then. Factorio is the last one. A game that will be played for hours at a time but only every so often.
On to the game then!
The first time you boot up factorio you get to start your first world. Sure, there's a campaign but it's around average and nowhere near as good as the real deal. Your first world is fun and exciting and all around a giant mess because you have no idea what you're doing. Doesn't matter though. It was a blast. Who cares if a conveyor belt track is way longer than it needs to be or one part of your factory relies on somthing at the complete other end. It still worked, didn't it? You start anew, armed with what knowledge you could gather and set off. You realise that it takes longer and longer each time in the beggining because you're used to automation now. Don't worry, it'll be back the way it was. You actually plan your factory this time instead of going in willy nilly. Your factory is way more efficient.
Uhoh, here comes the aliens!
Your base is under attack by ruthless aliens and you didn't prepare defences because there were more important things like research. Your factory is half dead when you manage to kill the last alien. It was a good run. You now have 2 options. Restart or Rebuild. Either way it'll be better than last time. It's the aliens again but this time you have a turret. You kill them all and keep going. As you keep tearing down trees and creating pollution, the enemies grow. You evolve with them with better armour and guns, more defences and a tank. It was a close battle but you won. The taste of victory on your lips. You start to get better, start using trains, robots and whatever else you can get your hands on. It's up to you. Maybe you'll go on a psycopathic rampage and kill all aliens. Or maybe set up a train circling the entire factory just for protection. Who knows. Maybe you'll escape, or maybe the panet's grown on you a bit TOO much.
Will you be the hero of your own story? Or will you rot on this planet and be torn to pieces?
The choice is yours.

I've got to say. I like games with a unique, even story telling type, style. That being said, I don't like this game. Not because it is a bad quality game. But, I didn't find it fun. This game puts you in charge of a border control station. All that stands between a terrorist attack and safety, is you. As you progress, the game get's harder, giving you more and more information to check in order to carry out your duty. Did i mention this is a husband simulator as well? No? Because you have to get through as many people as possible in the time limit in order to get payed enough to feed, heat, and care for your family. Oh, and also pay rent. But, I am terrible at this game. I can't slow down and enjoy the atmosphere, or the writing, because i'm too busy trying to speed through this "Job." both aspects are unique, both are clever, but put them together and it kills both parts of the game. I might give this game another shot. I've learned and grew my skill, but this game plays like a proof reader job. And focusing on just gameplay, it's a little boring. The writing would definitely pick things up, but I can't enjoy the writing because of the "come on, move it" nature of the gameplay. Maybe adding an easier mode would change this. I know some people will enjoy this game. Many already have. But, it's not for me.

Alien is in my top 10 movies and I was totally convinced that you couldn't make it into a game.
There had been an uninspiring attempt with a top-down view about 20 years or so ago, but I can't find it back anymore or remember who made it. You have 1 bad guy and you can't beat it, only run and hide. Good luck making a decent game with that premise.
Did Creative Assembly succeed against the odds ? Mmmm, sortof. The first half of the game is without a doubt the stronger one. The tension building in the first few stages, followed by hide and seek gameplay with the most dangerous animal in the universe is unprecedented.
I can't stress enough how the mix of perfect sound effects, the hunt and the brooding visuals turns the first half into one of those gaming experiences you'll never forget. It's scary and you often have to force yourself to keep sneaking around instead of doing stupid stuff, like running or stay to long in hiding. I realise the alien-AI cheats a bit (it basically respawns in the area you're in) but I personally didn't notice. It looked like the alien was hunting me down, intent to deliver a horrible, painfull death.
Unfortunately, the game branches out by throwing androids in the mix, and guards, and psychotic humans, lots of them. Firstoff, I was unable to communicate with the humans. They're scared, shouting at me, almost begging me to say something, but no, although I'm safe behind an iron gate, I won't say a word and keep hiding in the shadows, like some demented stalker.
Alien was an intelligent movie that handled human interaction near perfect. It's really painfull to see the game rather takes it's cue from half-brained zombie-movies in which all humans hate eachother and the game doesn't provide any options to interact with it besides shooting.
Allow me to explain how to turn horror into comedy :
There was a scene in which some unarmed civilians are cowering and crying for help, while they're being slaughtered by synthetics. At the same time a security guard is shooting at the civilians  and when they're dead, the synth turn on the security guard and kill him. So... instead of killing the synth while their busy, he rather shoot people and then get killed by the synth....
Why not make the  non-aliens sparse and pop up unexpectedly, guard keypoints or whatever. Lots of options instead of turning it in some third-rate splinter cell episode. And the ending ? No, just no.
Special :
* Outstanding music and sound effects. Perhaps the best I've encountered in a game.
* Great visuals, movement and design of the station.
* Incredible tense atmosphere, the alien is the imposing creature that gave birth to the franchise.
* the alien is watching you
* "lovely" flashback-mission that reconstructs "finding" the alien at the derelict.
Annoying :
* not enough options to deal with humans
* second half of the game is run over by synths and they're a lot more annoying than scary
* ending... pfff, seen that kind of ending too many times now.
In conclusion : Creative assembly did (in my view) the impossible despite a couple of errors and I would buy the game at full price again without hesitation. It looks like a follow-up isn't going to happen, which is a shame. As it is, this is your only chance to play a role in the alien-universe before Cameron shot it to pieces.
Just don't try to kill the androids with melee...

When this game came out it was at a time when the Call of Duty series was in the height of its popularity and arguably the prime of the games themselves. Modern Warfare 2 smashed sales records and was one of the most played games on the platforms it was released on albeit less popular on pc. The single player has always been my favorite part of the Call of Duty series harboring back to the days of Finest Hour on Playstation 2. Its basically an action movie that you can play. For the people who say "its not realistic, its completely insane to think this would ever be possible!" that's the point. I enjoy the hell out of the whole game but the single player is my favorite. You play as various characters in an epic globe trotting campaign that picks up right where the first modern warfare ended. Its a bit short (4 to 5 hours and more if playing on veteran difficulty) but its a satisfying single player. The multiplayer on the other hand is a very mixed bag. There are so many design decisions that Infinity Ward made with this game that blows my mind. Guns that are insanely overpowered, perks that are insanely overpowered, really easy quickscoping which is absolutely infuriating in my opinion, overpowered kill streaks i mean the list goes on and on. Counter Strike pisses me off to no end but at least its balanced. This game is not balanced at all when it comes to the multiplayer. To be frank, the multiplayer is a complete mess and there are tons of hackers in this thing. The worst things about this game are the fact that there is no way to change the field of view so if your a person who gets sick from a narrow (65 to be exact) field of view, your going to have problems with this game. There is however a tool that you can download that changes the fov to whatever you like but unfortunately it only works for multiplayer. I will say that this tool makes the multiplayer much more playable. There is no dedicated servers, just a very bad matchmaking system. The multiplayer is very fun but its heavily flawed. The final mode is spec ops. This is very fun because its short little missions quite often based on single player campaign levels and you can play it with a friend which makes it much more fun. When you start there are 5 levels unlocked and as you go through you earn stars on each level you complete. Once you earn enough stars it unlocks the next set of missions and so on. All and all i say if you like the Call of Duty brand of gameplay you won't be disappointed or maybe you will i don't know. But if you don't like the Call of Duty style then there isn't one thing that will change your mind in this title. I do recommend it for the single player.

Call of Juarez is a first person shooter that resembles somehow, Call of duty in it's mechanics, regenerating health, going around shooting at the enemies while getting XP that will then transform into perks that will make you into a deadlier man killing machine, but this isn't bad in any way, this game has very unique features in it that make it a worthy game.
PROS:
Call of Juarez counts with a pretty straight forward story, I won't spoiler anything in here, but I can just tell it is simple and functional, it makes it up enough to make you want to keep going and know how everything will end, the way it's told is also pretty unique, as it is always narrated by the same character you are playing as, it makes you your own hero of the story, which I found pretty cool.
The art style, OST, voice acting and art direction in general are flawless, it really makes you get into the grip of the old west, the voice actors sound professional, which I truely apreciate, voice acting in videogames is often ignored or not taken as seriously as it should, I'm glad to see it's not the case in this game.
The gameplay is simple, fun, and addicting, you'll find that you have a leveling system that rewards you depending on your skill, the better your aim, speed and combos are, the more XP you'll earn, which can be then used to buy skills that will give you more satisfaction while killing bandits and other scum of the west.
CONS.
Now, just as I said, the game has a simple story, which is good, but bad at the same time, none of the characters are really interesting, as you barely hear anything about them, even the protagonist himself has almost zero development, he just shoots at bad guys and gets bounty, sometimes I got extremely confused because the story went way too fast, you didn't get to know your enemies for longer than two minutes before you get to kill them, and that felt a little off.
This game also counts with a ''Dueling'' mini game that will appear every time you fight most of the bosses, if you expected boss battles that involved using the same FPS mechanic, oh, dear, you are mistaken, it feels gimmiky and it's not really fun to play, I know that they intended to make it feel like a compelling and suspense inducing system for bosses, but it just doesn't do what it should, as most of the times you'll find yourself confused on what the hell you are supposed to do.
One big flaw that I found is that the game is waaay too short, I got to complete it on five hours only on normal mode,  after that, you only get to play the other difficulties and an arcade mode.
They failed to add a multiplayer mode, which is a HUGE let down, this game could give Fistful of frags an amazing competition, but oh well, can't have it all right?
7.5/10, while it has it's flaws, it's worth the buy.

TLDR
As MMO - the game is sadly  repetitive, bugged and unrewarding.
As Single player's game - any other elder scroll game is way better.
Why?
It is presented as MMO - but your interaction options are poor and limited, sharing items is limited, splitting mission goals is impossible and trying to coop with another player is sadly useless, since you end up either stealing each other's harvests or breaking up each other's quests (You talk to an NPC and the other player has to wait for it to respawn since sometimes his quest updates and sometimes it doesn't. You kill some BOSS and sometimes your friend gets the chest and sometimes he gets nothing - not even the update). You find yourselves in different phases of existence and spend time to run to your "party" etc..
There are tons of bugs - which might have been forgivable if the game wouldn't literally make you PAY for them (you get STUCK IN A *** WALL and have to teleport to a shrine (and pay for it). You "fall" through a rock and spend 10 minutes waiting to find out if you end up on the floor or  beneath the bottom of the world. Your controls lag during fights and sneaks causing your timings to get you killed or "disreputable" over and over again - and so on.
At the game's current status, it is not "pay to win" so much as it is "pay to not be a second hand citizen".
The world is huge and beautifully made with huge amounts of content, but it keeps reminding you that to experience everything (be that races, mounts, map zones, chests etc..) - you need to pay and pay more and more.

I gave FF14 an honest try, I really did. (For some reason Steam says I only have an hour in the game but I've spent well over 20+ hours on it.) I had a friend who recommended I get into this game. I hopped on to play with her with high hopes and expectations after reading reviews, guides, etc. Regrettably my hopes were not met nor does FF14 fulfill any expectations I would have for a MMO. The graphics were nice, but I've never been big on graphics, with that said, the *only* redeeming thing I found about FF14 was the graphics.
I joined on a popular legacy server so I expected to see plenty of people. People were almost non-existent and difficult to find anyone to quest with. Even going through the starter areas it felt like a ghost town, only running into one or two other people outside of the main town. The community itself I had no desire to be apart of. The interaction I did have, joining my friends Linkshell, I found maybe one or two people I actually enjoyed speaking to and found the rest rude and downright mean most of the time. To be fair, it could of just been the people in that Linkshell, but I found no other pleasant people even after joining two separate guilds.
The gameplay was downright awful. I have *never* been so disinterested in a combat system than I have been with FF14. It is the most absolutely boring combat system I've had to experience. The basics for every class seem to be some sort of combos, I played Warrior after hearing they had more variation than the others, and jesus. If that's variation I would hate to play any other class. Killing ANY mob, whether in a dungeon or questing, was just so boring and uninteresting. They felt like they took forever to die and there was literally 0 challenge. I died maybe once taking on a mob 8 levels above me for a hunting log in the time it took me to get from level 1-37. There is no challenge for the content I experienced.
I heard repeatedly from my friend the game is good once you get your first level 50 but I have no desire to do so. On other games, even if it's a little slow to start, leveling is at least somewhat enjoyable. Not the case for FF14. There felt like there was no reward. The skills I unlocked as I leveled only contributed to my combos for the most part and made the game More repetitive, locking you into set combos to even be successful.
Add in all of this AND it's $15 a month I feel this game is not even worth *thinking* about. I would not pay $5 for this game let alone the current $30 price tag it has currently. I would never recommend this to anyone I know and wish I had looked into this game further before I bought it.

As an avid MMO player, I came into Final Fantasy XIV with mixed expectations.  I had friends who had played before ARR and I had friends who had played after the release.   While one set said the game had been terrible and they were never touching it again, those who played after ARR's release said that the game was well worth the monthly sub.   Deciding to see for myself; I, my significant other, and our friends decided to buy the game and check it out.   It suffices to say, I was not disappointed.
FFXIV: ARR takes points from all current MMO's, polishes them, and then puts them on a pedestal for all their players to view and enjoy.   I've played GW2, WoW, RIFT, Terra, and SW:TOR, but nothing comes close to the pure satisfaction of embracing a truly well made Final Fantasy MMORPG.   FFXIV: ARR has recovered from all of it's mistakes in the past, to bring out a wonderful game that sticks true to it's Final Fantasy roots and will leave you begging for more.
From the game soundtrack to the storyline, FFXIV: ARR has shown itself as a competitor to take place among the "legends" of the MMO industry.  The Dungeons are paced wonderfully, and show challenge when you need it, the quests are fulfilling and give you a sense of purpose within the game and objectives like FATE's and Guildhests give players exactly what they need; smooth enjoyable fun.
From furthering yourself in crafting items and gear, to fighting monsters and bosses, each task takes an enjoyable amount of time.  Having only put in about 75 hours, I've found myself enthralled by  the depth of each action, and the amount of polish that has gone into the game to make it the work of art that it is now.
+ Great Storyline.
+ Battle system is enjoyable.
+ Wonderful music.
+ Enjoyable community.
+ Smooth gameplay.
10/10.

I played the original FF XIV Online game in Beta, and quit on account of horrible story start and client performance issues which extended into the free play sessions. The Realm reborn came out on the PS4 recently, and I decided to try it again. This time I enjoyed it playing  with friends...the gamplay is fun, and combat flows fairly well; grouping is a cinch! Intitally, all was well.
However, after 30 hrs in-game, I realized that we were doing nothing but hard-core MMO grinding with a few dungeons interspering the drudgery. While cut-scenes were a-plenty (too many for this veteran MMOer), the horrible navigation gaps, disjointed voiceovers/non-voiceover cutscenes, and a story had made no real effort to make me care about the game world just got to me.
To get through it, I stopped reading and started clicking through everything just to get to the next quest so I could get my mount...then I was told I needed to grind for 3-4 hours to get my mount. I just can't grind like this in a world and story that is so all over the place that it cannot grow on you. I am not sure what lead reviewers to cast an 83 MetaScore for this one...I would put it in the mid-70s, as it is a generally tollerable title on other counts. If it were less of a grind-fest, I would have stuck it out regardless of the poor storytelling.
If you are e FF/Zelda fan, this game caters to you. You are already used to the FF story flow, and the awesome stylizations of the game world will appeal to your Inner-Mog. If you are a veteran MMO player, you will probably find this one as enjoyable as I did.

If you're looking for the sequel to Amnesia: The Dark Descent, I'm sorry but you're horror game is in another spooky mansion. If you're looking for a spooky atmosphere that can only be created by combining the spook-masters at Frictional Games and the narrative masterminds at The Chinese Room (Dear Esther), you've come to the right place.
It is true that this game disappoints in the scare department, after experiencing the last Amnesia's diaper fest, but if you go in without those standards it becomes a very enjoyable, narrative driven, atmospheric, horror game. The Chinese Room masterfully uses the sound and ambience of this world to create a spine tingling adventure that isn't so much a "Scared to go into the next room" experience, but creates a general nervousness about what's going to happen next.
This is one of those games where, if you took off the "Amnesia" from the title, it would have been much more critically acclaimed as a worthy successor to Dear Esther. But if you go in with an open mind and no expectations that the name "Amnesia" creates, you will enjoy A Machine for Pigs. If you want to play the successor to Amnesia: The Dark Descent, wait for Soma.

The game starts off with you awakening in a strange land called Drangleic, after being branded with the "Darksign" - an emblem that turns you into an "Undead", a being who cannot die, and eventually will lose all hope and go hollow - no memories, no feelings, no emotion - just suffering. You're told by a mysterious figure known only as the Emerald Herald that the only way to stop it is to seek out the King, Vendrick. Who is this mysterious king? And does he have the power to stop one from going hollow? Find the answers yourself in the second installment of the Dark Souls series, Dark Souls II!
Pros:

Cons:
- Steep learning curve
- Sometimes hackers don't get softbanned
- You have to place summon signs to get placed into your friends' game, and anyone can summon you.
- You can get ganged up on (Regulars call it a gank, winning a gank is called a gank spank) when invading others' worlds.
TL;DR - Great game, if you want difficulty this game is full of it!

Transistor is one of the greatest singular visions I have seen in some time.  Set in what was a high-tech sci-fi utopia, melding futurism (and *nix computer geekery) with lots of jazz, this game has beautiful, imaginative artwork, a great story, and brilliant mechanics.
Each function you unlock for the transistor (your sword) has an associated character, and using their function (move) in different positions (active, passive, upgrade) will unlock their backstory.  Getting a full understanding of the world Transistor is set in means using every function all three ways.  With every level you gain, you earn a new function, and often a new permission (upgrade) and a new limiter.
Better yet are the little touches.  As in so many games, the main character is mute.  Here you have a good reason: she was an influential singer who had her voice stolen by the Camerata.  She can still hum, though, and if you hold TAB, she'll hum with whatever tune happens to be playing.  You can listen to all the different songs in a backdoor, and hum with every single track.  Transistor has amazing voice acting, so this was one of my favorite parts of the game.

Day 42
Last night I had a dream. I flew high above the Earth and I gazed down at Creation. 'Twas not the Creation of a superior being, free and clean, clear and majestic, beautiful, bright, a world of magic and wonderment. No, the creation I looked upon was chaotic, frightening, full of over-complication and madness, dark, made by the hand of a lowly creature who's mind was twisted with the thoughts of the Unspeakable Creatures from the Other Places. Motivated by the inability to stop, he toiled away, adding to the monster he was creating, with no thoughts of orginization or coherence; it just had to fit. The veins of this creature covered the land, ever moving, little hands grabbing all as if for nourishment, but never satisfied. I watched the lungs of the beast breathe energy into it's nerves, fueling it's desire to consume the world. I could hear the scraping of it's jaws as it chewed at the Earth, swallowing it's riches only to spit them back up moments later.
As I watched from the ethereal, the Mad One ran about this leviathan as if he were a crazed Frankentein, bringing Life and movement to things that should be kept still. All of a sudden, he stopped. His eyes turned up to observe me, and I knew at once the horrible truth: this small, tireless worker for the Dark Ones, who's life was driven only by pain and insanity, this creature was me.
...
I awoke in a panic, sweat pooling around me. I knew I could never rest, never sleep; They won't let me. I can only build, only continue Their work. The designs don't make sense, but it doesn't matter; it works, and I must continue. We are close to our Goal, They say, though I know not what it is.
I log on once more. Peace will come only when I'm done...

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a relatively short (~5 hours campaign) episodic bullet time western shooter story about Silas Greaves, the infamous man that took down the legends - if you can believe him. Playing as Silas as he recounts his past in a bar to whoever will listen, you chase the men that tore your life apart. Be wary though, as the crazy gets crazier, this unreliable narrator changes his tune rewriting your game in real time. This aspect in the game makes this extremely linear and relatively repetitive game feel new each time. You may be fighting through an outlaw packed mine only to find out that you actually went around the mine after-the-fact, changing your progress.
Gunslinger also utilizes some really fun gameplay mechanics to help liven up the shooting including random bullet time reactions, QTE's, duels, and over the top machine-gun-wielding/dynamite-throwing/mountain-pass-sniping boss fights. Although i wish this game was more of an rpg (similar to the previous games) or had more diverse/non-linear map exploration, Gunslinger truly makes you feel like an Old Western legend.

I love this game, find it to be very enjoyable, and reccomend it to any fps lover, but I also have to say some things to pottential buyers. First, in my opinion, Borderlands is the better game. If you have been looking for a well-made, not too serious but still gritty, fps go buy the first game; the only games I can think of to compare it to are Mad Max and RAGE. Borderlands 2 improves upon the gunplay and abilities but loses any grit and solitude and replaces it with goofier enemies and terrible jokes written for 12 year olds.
Here's a breakdown of my exact thoughts.
What I liked better in Borderlands 2:
The gun variety- They really amped up the ante when it comes to how many different types of guns you can get in this game. I really enjoy all the wacky effects you get with uniques. I also like how powerful you feel when you use some of the legendaries. Also MORE LEGENDARIES!!!!
The classes- They improved all of the classes and I enjoy them more than the originals.
The bosses- I appreciate just how many tough bosses there are in this game, especially enjoy the amount of raid bosses. I will add one issue to this since it does not apply to the first game- Every single boss is, "Invincible" like come on, you can come up with better epithets than that. Here I'll do some: Terramorphus the Unstopable, Pyro-Caustic Pete the Immortal, Hyperious the Indestuctable, Master Gee the Wise. That was just a huge pet peeve of mine  ¯\_(ツ)_/¯
Main antagonist of the main campaign-Handsome Jack is awesome, I loved every moment I got of him.
Things I liked better in Borderlands:
The tone of the first game. While I know a lot of people had issues with the first game, mainly that they neede to be walked through a story and couldn't piece it together themselves, I loved every moment of it. The first game had this real desolate feeling to it. Borderlands gives you this very real sense of issolation. You don't feel like a super badass when you first start out. You feel like a merc who came to a planet seeking fortune only to find out how dangerous the world you are on truly is. I hate the feel of the second game.
The music: The dry guitar will always be better for me than the constant dubstep, and my favorite type of music is electronic so I'm not just a music enthusiast.
CL4P-TP/Claptrap- He was barely in the game and he said almost nothing. Prefer it that way.
The side characters- Most of them didn't talk, when I was younger I wanted them to talk and move. I got Borderlands 2 and I wanted them to stop talking again. Also they ruined Scooter. in the first game he was pretty funny and interesting, second game his brain regressed to an unrecognizable state.
The DLC antagonists- General Knoxx is tied for the best when it comes to antagonists in this series. He was a grumpy, borderline suicidal old soldier that you would love to have as your grandfather. Also hearing him read out what he had to deal with when it came to his commanding officer always put a smile to my face. Oh will admit that I enjoyed Claptrap as the villain in the final DLC.
The writing- Borderlands' story was more enjoyable for me b/c of the lack of story, I was more focussed on exploring anyway. The humor was also better and it came in bursts. Borderlands 2 was written for teenagers and people with under-developed brains. This is how I look at Borderlands 2, I found it kind of funny when I was 16 but now I'm in my 20's and most of the jokes pi.ss me off rather than make me laugh.
The cars- The cars drove better, did more damage, died less frequently, and felt like they were on the ground instead of floating.
Borderlands: Better tone, better music, better writing (imo), better humor, better DLC villains, better side characters, very little Claptrap, and better driving
Borderlands 2: Better gunplay, better abilities, better story plot, better main antagonist, better boss battles
Boderlands the Pre-Sequel: Stop

text:
tl;dr: Is Just Cause 3 as good as the truly fantastic Just Cause 2? No.
Is it a good game despite this? Yes.
I've been a fan of the Just Cause series for a few years now. Just Cause 2 is, in my mind, one of the best open-world games ever made. The actual missions were mediocre at best, but when it came to free-roam, just exploring the lovely (more than slightly inspired by North Korea) island of Panau and reducing everything to rubble, it was a fantastic romp that very few games could match.
So, you can imagine how excited I was to finally get around to playing Just Cause 3. Now that I'm mostly done with the game, I feel like I'm in a good place to review it. If I were to sum up the game in one sentence, it would be this: Just Cause 3 improves on a lot of problems that Just Cause 2 had, but also drops the ball on a lot of the things that made Just Cause 2 great.
Let's get one of the biggest issues out of the way right now, and one of the biggest reasons this game has a Mixed rating-- the game has a horribly shoehorned in online mode that causes no shortage of problems. It's easy enough to get around; simply blocking the game's online mode through your Firewall solves the problem nicely. Unfortunately, if you don't, then the online servers will make your life miserable. Even two years after release, the online mode is wildly unstable. Losing connection pauses the game, and if you
to open your map during a server hiccup, you'll be forced into a lengthy loading screen as it tries to reconnect you.
What do you get for playing online mode? Nothing, except for an online leaderboard and frequent notifications to tell you that other players have beaten your score in some way or another. Hard as it might be to believe, Square Enix, I don't care that a random player by the name of "420BlazeitNachoFlava" has beaten my personal best BASE jump record by .2 meters. I really don't.
So yes, turn this off immediately, you'll thank me later.
The gameplay itself is, for the most part, as good as it's always been. Getting around with the grappling hook and parachute is as fun as ever, and the new wingsuit is a great addition. There's a decent number of land, sea, and air vehicles. The DLC even adds mechs and jetpacks to the mix, which is always a good time.
Of course, getting around in Just Cause is only part of the fun. The real main meat of the game is breaking things and freeing settlements from an evil general, and there's well over 100 towns, military bases, and outposts to blow up. It's still fun, though I personally feel like the variety of destructible objects is smaller than it used to be. You'll be breaking into a lot of the same prisons, calling in your fellow rebels time and time again, and breaking a lot of the same propaganda speakers, billboards, and fuel tanks from one town to the next. Some of the outposts are stupidly small and easy to clear just by hijacking a helicopter equipped with missiles and strafing the place. But, for the most part, it's still entertaining, just a bit repetitive.
"Repetitive" is a word that a lot of people have used to describe Just Cause 3 compared to Just Cause 2, and, to be honest, I can see why. The Islands of Medici are a beautiful place, but they lack the sheer variety of sights that Just Cause 2's Island of Panau had. The vaguely Italian scenary is beautiful, to be sure, but it's a lot of the same old rustic fields filled with wheat, small towns overlooking the ocean, and military bases with a lot of the same buildings. Panau had a much wider arrangement of sights, from lush jungles to beautiful mountain retreats to vaguely Middle Eastern deserts-- while Just Cause 3 does have more than just oceans, fields, and vineyards, the variety is sorely lacking in comparison.
But enough of the negatives-- there's plenty of good things to say about Just Cause 3 as well. Where Just Cause 3 blows its predecessor out of the water is the game's actual missions. Just Cause 2 was a great game, but its story mode was not particularly great, and its side activities were very lacking. Just Cause 3's story is much better in almost every way-- better missions, better voice acting, and a much healthier variety of things to do when you're taking a break from just liberating areas. The main antagonist, General Di Ravello, is a legitimately unnerving threat-- a modern day Mussolini, a cold-blooded psychopath who rules Medici under martial law, and one with access to (totally-not-Uranium) Bavarium, a fictional material exclusive to Medici that can be used like a superfuel, or to power warheads. Unlike Just Cause 2, the protagonist, Rico Rodiguez, takes this fight personally, as Medici is his home.
The missions themselves are actually pretty fun this time around. At several points, battles between Di Ravello's forces and the rebellion break out into large scale open warfare, which is a welcome improvement. Many of the awful escort and delivery missions from the previous game are gone (and while there are still a few of them, most of them are much less cheap than the previous game), replaced with good old fashioned direct combat. There's still a few duds, but overall I enjoyed the story much more than I did Just Cause 2's.
Even the side activities have had some welcome improvements-- while the same old "drive X vehicle through hoops, Superman 64 style" time trials are still around, the driving mechanics are much better this time around, and there are some really cool additions, like minigames where you have to drive a bomb car to a target while trying to find shortcuts or stunt jumps to keep your score high, or "Destruction Frenzies" where you destroy military bases under a time limit, trying to chain together targets to keep your score multiplier high. All of these minigames give "gears", which provide universal bonuses (more tethers, more nitrous for vehicles, reduced damage from smashing into solid objects while gliding, etc.), replacing the clunky vehicle upgrade system from the previous game (I do wish there was an upgrade to increase Rico's health, though, he feels much more fragile than he used to)
Unlike the previous game, there's no currency system, which means you're free to call in weapons and vehicles without worrying about running out of resources (there IS a "beacon" system, though those are easily restored at any outpost you've liberated, and a cooldown system to prevent you from calling in the same thing over and over again within a short timespan, which is reduced with the aforementioned upgrade system). So long as you've unlocked that vehicle or gun, you can use it almost as liberally as you'd like.
Overall, Just Cause 3 is a lot of fun, with a lot of content, even if it gets repetitive at times. While I think Just Cause 2 is still the better game, this one's still totally worth checking out, especially with its (absolutely bonkers) DLC. Hopefully, if we ever get a Just Cause 4, it'll blend together 2's better environments and destruction with 3's better missions, but for now, this is still one of the best ways to drop a shipping container on a cow, have the container explode to reveal a jumbo jet, drive several small cars into the cargo hold, load them with explosives, fly over a military base, and let them rip.
Why? Just (be)Cause.

Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs, (AMFP), is good, if it didnt have the Amnesia title. Its like taking a movie, that is low budget, low quality, has its good moments, but overall isnt the greatest, and slapping Steven Spielberg's name on it. You took something that was alright, and put it into a stantard that cant be beat. Amnesia: The Dark Descent was rated one of the greatest horror games ever, and I completely agree with that. This one, however, when held up to the Amnesia stantard, isnt nearly as good. I liked it and it was scary at parts, but it lacked all the best parts of Amnesia. It took out the hunt for things like tinder boxes, and oil, and santity potions, and replaced them with never-running-out lamps and flashlights. Which I get... Its in the time of electricity, so thats somewhat understandable, but to literaly remove the inventory and physical/mental health entirely?! Its crazy. I did like however adding lots of cool features. It added plenty of "secret passage way" architecture, which included secret doors, levers behind painting, ect. I also like how it had plenty of different enviroments. Whether it be a castle like the original, or the streets of London. This game had mutliple level maps. There were a lot of stuff that was overlooked, when people (including myself) complained about the lacking user ability, or the more linear story. If you absolutely love horror games, and know and have played all the best of the genre, then go ahead and buy it. My only request of you, wait for a sale. I would price this game at about 12-15 bucks. Its not worth the full 20. Overall, it was an alright experience, that is a severe dissapoint relative to The Dark Descent.
The best thing about this game, is that it's short. You won't waste too much time.

Final Fantasy XIV: A realm reborn is a really fun MMO. Being a WoW player from late vanilla and jumped to GW2 but got bored from it after a couple of weeks later when it was released and then jumped to Final Fantasy XIV: A realm reborn when it came to steam.I can say that i have more fun playing this MMO then when i playing GW2 and what WoW is becoming today.
To be honest i never played a Final Fantasy from the main series before but did played some DS spinoff games and came to this game and the main series as a stranger but i always wanted to try out a FF game from the main series. From have completed the main story in this MMo i think i can make a review of this game.
The first thing you should know is that if you were expecting a different MMO then World of Warcraft you gonna be disapointed but if you liked WoW from what it is you can feel a bit comfort here. You got your Kill X creatures and Collect Y things and also some talk to NPC quests but the game does not take the amount you need kill or collect as crazy as most MMo's. At later levels you mostly need to kill like 6-10 while at early levels not even more then 3. Also this game has just like WoW the Holy trinity (Tank,DPS and Healer) where also you can also play dungeons with people from other servers. But unlike WoW the normal instances are 4 man and the bigger instances 8 man but you also got a 24 man raid.
One of the key differences from WoW is that you can change to every class in the game on 1 character meaning that you dont have to make alts. I personally like this a lot and you can also be every gathering and crafting class aswell. if you level more classes you can even share some of the skills they have with other classes but not all of them, Kinda replaces the game from having no talent tree or talent skills.
The game does have a story and you progress through it by completing story quests. The game kinda forces you to follow the story quests because most of the game features are only unlocked by doing these quest making the first levels from 1 - 30 on your first class a long tutorial but after that games opens more up and the game does not really feel that slow. The game does feel a bit slow on every class first levels but as you go on the class becomes a lot more intresting.
The game also have guilds but here they are called Free Company's in this game but as you go through the story you also need to choose a Nations Grand Company wich you discover more from as you go on with the game.
Lastly if you are more of a PVP person you gonna also gonna be a bit disapointed because right now the only PVP is a 4vs4 Arena battle like in WoW and there is no way to duel people in the world and Open pvp is also not in the game.
So that kinda concludes my review on this game. if i tell about everything then this review goes out of hand. Overall i really like this MMO and wishes it to even improve more in the future. And i cant wait to do all the end game content now that i completed the main story but to be honest the story does go even further after you completed the real main story of the game. If you are unsure if you can run this game you can download a benchmark from the official site of the game where you can also Create a character beforehand so you dont have to that when you buyed the game and the benchmark is free..

This is like rapid-fire Phoenix Wright. You have to check dozens of immigrants for contradictions in their paperwork, and determine whether they’re accepted or rejected. You’re paid (poorly) for however many passports you stamp correctly. If you don’t perform well, your family will die of sickness or starvation, or you’ll get arrested for going into debt. (Yes, going into debt is illegal now.)
But it’s a game that’s less about how well you check papers, and more about why you’re checking papers. You won’t get very far before the story starts getting really complicated, and you’ve got to start making some tough ethical decisions. Are you a true patriotic Arstotzkan, willing to uphold the law to the letter? Are you only in it for your family, willing to take juicy bribes from illegal smugglers? Or are you willing to help the shadow cult overthrow the Arstotzkan government?
This game files in the face of everyone who’s ever said that story and gameplay can’t be the same thing. It really makes you feel like you’re shaping the fate of a nation, or succumbing to it, just by sitting in a booth and deciding who gets across the border.

Now that I have played it to fullest, I decided to give it a non-joke review.
PROS:

CONS:

Factorio is a sandbox puzzle game in which you try to make a fully-automated factory, with a small mix of survival (optional). You gather resources with your mining drills, transfer them through conveyor belts, smelt them into intermediate products, then use those products to make actually useful procuts, and use those products to make more advanced products. Further into the game, you can make trains to transport said resources from far away outposts and deliver them to other parts of your base. Then a bit more later, you will have logistics and construction drones that automate maintenance of your factory by doing things like transporting items, fixing broken things, and building stuff.
However, there will be obstacles in your way. You will eventually run out of resources and will have to venture far into the wilds where creatures known as Biters await. They form hives of varying sizes and are usually found near patches of resources. If your make too much pollution, they will swarm your factory and destroy everything in it, making defenses a necessity. However, as this is a sandbox game, you have the option to enable "peaceful mode", whichi causes biters to behave and not attack your base out of the blue.
The best part about this is the *very* active modding community. There are mods that improve the sandbox experience, make the game more complicated than it currently is, or even make biters very threatening. You can pretty much customize your own Factorio experience to suit your tastes.
Oh, and I almost forgot about multiplayer. Factorio allows you to play with your friends and even online with other people. It even has dedicated servers! Some servers even manage to reach 400+ players at the same time. Factorio lends itself to multiplayer due to its "role" driven nature. It's good fun to play with friends and assign them different tasks such as who will manage the train, expand the smelting, handle base defenses, etc.
The ever-expanding mega-factory and the continuous problem solving is what sold the game for me and for $20, this game is totally worth it.
Original Review: "Start Factorio an hour before dinner and you're sure to lose weight."

I had this one on my radar for quite some time. What initially grabbed my attention was the minimalist art style. I’m generally a fan of anything that can look cool by using minimal amounts of colors or contours and
is about as simple as it gets. The bold black and white (and sometimes yellow) vector graphics invoke a bygone age, where the smooth lines of the Vectrex were a serious competitor to the blocky raster graphics.
But beyond that initial wow-factor, I’m not sure if I can fully recommend the game based on its gameplay alone. In the grand tradition of games where you have to run around in a straight line as fast as possible,
’s gameplay boils down to a single button. You either press it to accelerate, or you let it go to jump. In essence, you’re playing an old school 2D platformer from a first-person perspective.
While this idea does have its charm, I feel that the game has a lot of somewhat missed potential there. The stages feature some verticality and multiple levels, which becomes apparent when increasing the difficulty which basically means you’re going to be running faster. Thus, certain paths you’ve carved out for yourself on lower levels aren’t feasible anymore. But other than jumping from platform to platform, there’s no challenge in there. If I may be so bold as to compare this to another very popular runner game,
, you’ll notice that that game features a variety of hazards, direction changes and power-ups. All of this is absent in
, you merely run in a straight line and avoid falling off the path.
One goal that Fotinica definitely manages to achieve is that it provides the player with a sense of speed. Running around in first-person will always be a more dramatic thing than having the camera float behind the character or racing car. It’s just a shame that this aspect, along with the gorgeous art style, are underserved by the minimal gameplay it has on offer, along with the very few levels. 8 regular levels and 3 infinite ones. There’s room for replayability there because of the difficulty levels, but overall I still feel that there aren’t enough levels, because the arcade levels are all fairly short.
I guess I’ll give a mild recommendation for the title, since I like the central concept and the art style a lot, however with the caveat that I don’t think that
is worth the full price of $10 or €9. I had the good fortune of buying it during a Humble Bundle, which is why I’m more lenient in this regard.

World of Goo is an adorable, charming, and above all, inventive puzzle game developed by a couple of guys sitting in a coffee shop. It was born from a much simpler game posted on the Experimental Gameplay Project
entitled Tower of Goo, in which you attached little balls of oily 'goo' to one another via stiff strings of the stuff, in an effort to create a tower that's as tall as possible without causing it to buckle and fall.
World of Goo takes this mechanic and applies it to a somewhat more varied kind of puzzle solving, introducing a myriad of different varieties of goo in addition to the basic black. (There's still a Tower of Goo mode, though, so worry not!)
Basically: buy this game. It is wonderful and you will love it.

Amnesia A machine for pigs is a good game, but unlike the dark decent not a great one. The dark decent set the standard too high so that nothing would ever be able to compare to it despite a machine for pigs having alot going for it, but also a few problems that in my mind defenitly affected the overall gameplay.
First the negatives:
1) if you look at how many hours ive played up to this point your probably thinking: "3-4 hours? how can you have an educated opinion on a game youve barley played" well thats my point. I finished the entire game in a night. A machine for pigs (amfp is how i will refer to it from hence forward) is way too short, and while i dont mind a more linear story (which amfp definetly is) at least stretch it out I was expecting at least a 10 hour story and with no custom stories there will be very little too come back to.
2) repetition, In The dark decent there where a sh** ton of puzzels but atleast they were different and in my mind much more creative. In amfp each puzzle is completed in very simalir fasion and I think this not only made the game much easier but also was one of the major reasons as to why the game was so short. In TDD i spent nearly an entire hour trying to solve one of the puzzels. In amfp the longest it ever took me was 10 minutes. long story short some puzzels in tdd took longer for me to complete than the entire first half of amfp.
The Positives:
1)TDD heavily depended on atmosphere, in amfp atmosphere is the games saving grace. the music and ambience is just absoulutly increadible and there where countless times were i found myself shaking JUST because of the ambience or mood in an area, combine that with manpigs and youve got yourself one terrifying experience.
2) the story in amfp was in my mind scarier than any mosnter or beast that attacked you in the game. the very premise scares me just thinking about it. even now, almost a day after i completed amfp, i still feel horrified and sick. I wont spoil anything but the twist about half way through the game made me stop the game and listen to soothing music for atleast an hour. the story in this game fully surpassed any prevoius expectations i had before the game and i love discouvering it piece by piece. It also has some social commentary in the game about religon, wealth and coruption, going where the first game never dared to go... and i loved it
3) the graphics: not much i can say other than i thought the game looked awesome.
Final verdict: 7.5/10 -a good game with some minor yet noticable set backs.

I am not a fan of survival horror, first person games or stealth-gameplay and I actually flat out refused to play A:I at all when it was released - eventhough I really love the IP and consider ALIEN (1979) as one of my favourite movies of all time. But the premise of being there, personally facing one of cinemas greatest creatures seemed just terrifying and not much else.
In a funny turn of events I got to see ALIENS (1986) on the big screen and on that very same weekend the Humble Store offered A:I for a low-low price and being all hyped from the movie and Sigourney Weavers kickass performance, my curiosity got me registered on the Sevastopol space station.
Let me just say that I am very positively surprised how much I actually enjoyed A:I. Basically, you play hide and seek with the xenomorph, gradually building up an arsenal of tools for distraction and destruction as well as uncovering a lame plot about corporations willing to end hundreds of lifes for profit. Seriously, the plot is just a megamix of every idea the original two movies had and you can sense the plottwists hours before they happen.
Gameplay consists of finding safe and secure areas, checking out waypoints and avoiding any actions that draw attention to your position. A:I demands both patience AND nerves of steel. It is also a game about choices and deadly consequences should you choose poorly. In order to help you make those decisions, Creative Assembly gave you a bunch of tools - like the motion tracker and an excellent map. However, your most important asset for survival are your ears. Up to this point, I haven't played a game that put so much emphasis on its sound as a means of navigation and well, deciding what to do next. The xenomorph makes a lot of distinct noises that allow you to "read" the current situation (like: is it even there, is it currently in the vents, is it busy murdering other people or is it actively hunting you). You may be just running back and forth between checkpoints, restoring power and opening doors - but it sure feels intense. And they managed to do that without artificially crippling your actions - so, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to take control out of the players hands and make matters more "EXCITING!" by making them more awkward to handle.
Another reason why A:I works better than other games of this genre that I have tried, is the fact that you know A LOT about your surroundings and most of the imminent dangers in them. In fact, I love the level design for the most part - it strikes the perfect ballance between being linear but allowing you a couple of different tactical options and routes to take. Mind you, there are exceptions to this and later levels have a tendency to introduce choke points where you are forced to encounter hostiles - but the first half was really great. In fact, all levels do a splendid job of conveying that you are being inside the bowels of a massive, man-made, mechanical mega-structure floating in space. All areas feel like real places that had a purpose before they were abandoned (or... shall we say... redecorated by certain creatures) - there are floor markings and signs helping you navigate and further turning Sevastopol into a place that makes sense, becomes believable.
What really sets A:I apart from the competetion (and is ultimately the reason why I got it in the first place) is its license and the way that license was used. A:I is all about atmosphere and looks as well as sounds fantastic - Creative Assembly did a near flawless job of recreating the ALIEN universe aesthetic of retro-futurstic spaceship corridors, computer terminals and heavy machinery. Some of the corridors look so great, you can almost feel the damp air, the heat of fires, and the frizzle of electric sparks on your skin. Now you combine the insane artdirection with the awesome sounddesign and you got your current benchmark for every upcoming science fiction game. All those rumbling sounds, sirens, shutters and alarms - they really make Sevastopol feel alive. As much as people praise (and fear) the xenomorph, for me the real star of the game is the space station itself.
Talking about fear, I actually didn't find the game to be as frightening as everyone makes it out to be. In fact, I was more afraid of those goddamn Working Joes (because harming them makes either a lot of noise or isn't very healthy, and it gets worse when they start wearing hazmat-suits). I think the game is rather light on jumpscares and shockvalue - if you pay attention and move cautiously. This might be different on harder difficulties - but then again, it "just" insta-kills you even more - so, what is there to be afraid of? And this doesn't mean this game isn't exciting or intense - it is the thrill of getting caught instead of being paralyzed with fear.
Finally, there are a bunch of issues I have with the game that need to be mentioned as well.
First of all: the anti-aliasing in A:I sucks. I am talking PS2-era jaggies here - not cool. Also, the lighting did wonders on the levels - but did not really work too well on the Alien itself, it looks kinda flat - even though the model seems to be pretty detailed - you just never see much of that quality.
Occasionally I had a bunch of clipping issues - the worst was when the alien suddenly clipped into me while I was hiding under a desk, making the ai go berserk and immediatly kill me. There were a bunch of other weird occurences, mostly when Androids were around - if they spotted me and the Alien was around, the xeno would never calm down and suddenly know exactly where I was, almost like androids and alien shared the same info. What made matters worse was that I wanted to open a vent security door (from inside the vent) and all enemies "knew" exactly where I was (even though that was impossible) - they just couldn't get to me because of that security door, but once it was open the alien took a dive straight into the vent, three times in a row. In the end I snuck through the "harder part" of that area without encountering either Alien or Android. Weird and annoying.
At times the controls are a bit finnicky, running (with the Alien in hot pursuit) into an elevator, I died because despite the control buttons being in the center of my screen, the button prompt didn't show up because I wasn't properly looking at them - same goes for some vents, standing exactly in front of them won't do - you gotta look at 'em right.
Needless to say, A:I is a game with tons of potential for frustration as you will be playing a couple of areas a few times before you figure out how to best tackle them. Wether or not you will enjoy it depends mostly on your admiration for the Alien-IP. It is definitely a good game and is quite a departure from the stuff I usually play - and seeing how I am quite happy that I actually did play (and finish) it, says a lot about its quality. It's a unique experience and does wonders with the license - reason enough for me to recommend it, even to all those people that normally would not touch a game like this.

Completed the game on normal in 20 hours. Died a lot. Had fun.
The game has stunning visuals and style as well as excellent sound effects. The plot is mostly ok, but could have been improved with more character development and slightly improved writing & voice acting. Still the atmosphere, 70's retro scifi style and consistent art & sound style create a great experience.

Except when the level designer has failed and the Alien's AI seems to be "trapped" in a very small area or spawns near you because of a scripted event or "difficulty". There are some silly places where the Alien just spawns periodically from a single vent every half minute or so, even though it has free roam on the station and no reason to check the place repeatedly.

The boring ending feels like wasted potential, even though it's a great Alien game, which captures the horror perfectly at it's best bits.

Welcome to Arstotzka, a country that has recently opened its border after a war with Kolechia and thanks to the labor lottery, you are the newest immigration inspector in this tumultuous region. Bluntly stated, 'Papers, Please' is a job simulator that has you checking for discrepancies between information. You'll look over permits, IDs and passports. Reading to what the people say vs what is in the information. After you look over everything, you will either approve or deny them. If you find anything questionable, you can have the game check for dependencies, by clicking on two specific things, such as their photo doesn't match their face and then ask them about it. Later in the game, you will unlock things such as searching people and finger printing them.
Each day will have a new issue that you need to check for. Another layer that you look for. The game first starts out by only letting your own citizens back into your country. Then opening the borders to everyone with a ticket, then people need a permit, then a work permit for those working and an ID for your own citizens. You'll see the issuing city that you'll need to check your rulebook to see if its really an issuing city, a gender that you'll get to search their gender even if it looks like a woman, they could be a man, detain people with contraband, question identities and fingerprint them, look at the date of entry vs the expiration date of their passport, look at when their work permit says they'll leave vs how long they told you they'll be in the country vs what they told you. Eventually, forgeries will happen that will force you to see correct official seals are there. It is a lot of information you need to look over.
The major controls are just mouse clicks and drags. You have a rulebook that you can click and drag onto your desk. All information you are given from people needs to be click and dragged into your work desk to look over. Then approving or denying requires you to click to take out your stampers, then move the passport into place and click the approve or deny, then give everything back to the person, by clicking and dragging it back to them. Once you've approved or denied them, then its time to click the speaker to call up the next person in line. Its a very click heavy game, but as time goes on you can purchase booth upgrades that lets you click space or tab to call up things you'd normally just click and drag.
Each person that you process earns you $5. If you make mistakes and approve or deny someone that you shouldn't you will receive no penalty the first two or three times. After that, you start losing $5. Why does money matter? You have 4 people at home with you, your wife, your son, your mother in law and your uncle. You spend money on rent, heat, food and medicine. If you don't have enough money you have to start sacrificing things. If you don't have heat, your family will start getting sick and need medicine. If you don't have food, eventually your family will die. When your family dies its game over. You need to be both thorough and efficient in the game, because you only have so much time in a day. Some days get stopped short with unavoidable terrorist attacks and bombings that cause new rules such as searching every Kolechian.
There are other game over states, like doing something incorrect in front of the wrong person. If you get a game over, you can restart from any previous day. This makes the game pretty forgiving.
As the days go on, a stories will unfold and you'll be responsible for the course of mini stories. You'll meet interesting characters such as diplomats, soldiers with bribes, inspectors, angry people cursing you out, human trafficers, secret agents, mysterious men.
In all, this is a very unique game if not job simulator with a good story, good art style and music that matches the game and back story. I can understand if this game isn't for everyone, but if you can get into it, Papers, Please will keep your attention in a lot of ways. Once you get endless mode unlocked, you have 3 categories: timed, perfect and endless complete with leader boards.

Papers, Please is an indie game developed by Lucas Pope, in which you play an immigration inspector whom is working at a border checkpoint in a country named Arstotzka . The goal of the player is to inspect documents using a set of tools and in some occasions to inspect the individual per se, in order to keep criminals out of the country . Everything is a bit unknown, until it will be disclosed , the more you play .
Every work day, you receive a document with informations about particular things you have to notice about, the arrival of important people and/or if you have to take some measures if a specific occasion happens, like having to do body scanning to all civilians who belong to the country of Kolechia . We also have a rule book all the time, so we can know what is allowed in the documents we inspect and if there are any discrepancys, you have to reject the entry to the person and later on, if you want, arrest them . A situation with a spy, terrorists and smugglers with not be uncommon, and you will decide if you will let them pass by, because you can bribed and even threaten .
After a day of work, you receive a wage, which depends on how well you did your job, and you will have to decide where your wage will go, some option include 'food', 'medicine' and 'heat', also as you progress in the story you will be able to choose to move to a better house, but it will also have bigger expenses . You also have freedom of will in basically everything since the game changes with your decisions .
Be careful too, this game will play your emotion and will play mind games with you, sometimes you must choose between doing your job or doing the right thing sometimes, there will be families slip apart because of you, but if you decide to let someone passe the border without the correct documents so he or she can be with her/his family, you will face the consequences . Your gaming experience with this game could end in 20 different ways, each occur depending on what decisions did you take in a certain way because you actually have a lot of choices throughout the story, some of them may include, being part of a conspiration group named EZIC against the government of Arstotzka, accepting bribes and even saving money on medicine or food, which will let to the starvation of members of your family .
This game is worth all your attention, since its incredibly addicting, has a great plot and the gameplay its really original, you will not regret it .

If I were to be locked out of my account, this would be one of the 1st games I'll buy with my new account. I don't mean the standard edition, I meant the full GoTY edition with all the DLCs. That's how good this game is.
TONS of enemy variety. It's not your usual FPS where you shoot someone, and they shoot back. Of course, you could always go in an shoot everything, but unique tactics are required to take some down faster. You either have to flank them, switch between different weapon element types, force them to kill off each other and have them level up for greater exp (Goliaths), kill them fast before they evolve (or just have them evolve for better loot)...etc. Killing them never gets old (well it does, but by then you'll have poured hundreds of hours into the game).
TONS of guns! The game uses a combinatorial system to generate it's guns, granted there are a few rules to keep the balance in check, but mathematically speaking this games has the one of the most guns of any FPS.  However, this would be quite boring, since the guns would be slightly different versions of each other. To account for this, they have "Legendary" and "Unique" items where the guns or grenades would have unique attributes. Ex: There's a gun that shoots there axes (Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep DLC required) and a grenade that spawn homing projectiles (like a wasp nest). Nuff said.
TONS of replayability. There's 6 characters in total, 2 of which are DLCs. Each have unique skills and play differently for one another, so each playthrough with different characters will feel different. There's also 3 modes to play through, in increasing difficulty: Normal, True Vault Hunter, Ultimate Vault Hunter. There's also unique enemies in each mode, such as the "Armoured Psycho" that exists in TVHM and UVH. Honestly, it's worth having multiple playthroughs.
The story is also awesome. There are several plot twists that are quite surprising, but makes perfect sense. The antagonist will comment and mock you throughout the story, like the Joker in Arkham Asylum. The dialogue is hilarious, and very well written, although it can be quite dark. The antagonist (Handsome Jack) is somewhat relatable. An egotistical maniac whose goals and actions are understandable, but is very unorthodox. At the end, I was left feeling sorry for him, despite the horrendous crimes he has committed.
Now to the only thing I hate: Movement. I've sunk nearly 1500 hours into TF2, and have grown accustomed to the movements: Air strafing, and rocket jumping. I know rocket jumping is possible with the Badaboom, but I haven't tried it, so I will not comment on it at this moment. There is a tiny bit of air strafing, but the results are negligible. It is also impossible to stop in mid-air. This game could use more "air control".

Just skip Dark Souls II, and buy Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin. It's essentially the complete version of the game, and it isn't compatible with this old version. They are effectively two different games in Steam.

I bought it this morning, it was both on sale and on my list, so why not.
I bought it for for some challenge, regardless of the overall experience.
POSITIVE :
And I have to admit I'm hooked ! I produce electronic music, so I always pay attention to sound-design. Most of the games I play have either no sound-design like Super Hexagon, or a really awful one, like Hero Siege and those mp3-quality swords and voices.
And here, it's clean as hell, I was very surprised and very delighted ! Voices and shouts, breathing, motion, it's very, very precise and well-designed. And music is so good. I like this abstract, but heartful modern design.
I went thru the first levels, nothing difficult, you run, you jump, with one button. It's not about the gameplay and the difficulty. You have to find the perfect timing (and you can take 4-5 different paths every level) for catch all the red circles and reach 10k points. You'll access next level without 10k points, and even if I think it's a mistake (at least for me), it keeps the game doable for somebody who don't want to play the same level for hours.
Default difficulty is 2, then 3 and 4, I'd have like 5, definitely.
I think this game is about the pleasure of execute each jump with perfect timing, not for the performance or achievement but for feeling it. Feel the air, the gravity, and the overall quality of the way you move, of the code they wrote.
If you want a challenge and only this, it's not for you, you'll beat the game, you'll say it's easy and it isn't worth 9 bucks. I  think I would not buy it this price, since I'm more skill-side. But for 1,70 Euro, I have fresh air in my hands, thru a unique game.
ABOUT GAMEPLAY :
I read a review about the fact that you only have to push one key for running, and release it for jumping. And the fact it's boring, and it gets old really fast. In fact, you can change the behaviour of the game and frankly, it really changes the way you play. Default is touch/release gameplay, but in the options, you can change it : it will run automatically, and it will jump when you press.
NEGATIVE :
- Each time the jump ends and I'm back on track, it's difficult to see what's in front of me. It's really immersive, yes, for the better and the worse. I just have to stick with it and to get used to it but still, I consider this is annoying.
- Why always black background and white/gold people and road ? It gets visually boring really fast. I think one can maintain this minimalist look all the game, and still can make it more interesting for the player. It's kinda weird I'm saying this because I actually enjoy the overall look of this game, but... I dunno, I feel it deserves more spice.
So, I probably won't play more than a few minutes between two games. Or maybe I'll take a day for exploring it in depth and see what lies there. But definitely, for 9 bucks, it lacks something. Say, I would have loved a voice from time to time, since the shouts of the runner are so greatly designed. Or random events. Or something which breaks the rythm you take after one or two levels. Beginning/Straight-up level/End. Not so much.
If you're still there (I don't write short reviews, sorry), should you buy this game ?
Yes. Even for 9 bucks : the last game I played with this amazing feeling of sound-design clarity was Skyrim, one year ago. So even if you don't like the game, see it like a gesture for an amazing sound-designer.

For Deaf/hoh gamers, I rate this game a 10/10!
Supergiant knocked it out of the park again.  In Transistor, you play as Red, a lady whose voice was stolen by a group who intended to kill her.  Obviously that's a bit odd, but the game takes place inside of a computer-ish environment.  Telling more would be giving things away for those who, for some reason, have yet to play it.
Since this review is largely oriented toward acciessibility for deaf/hoh gamers, I will stop there and just say that it is a great game with a great story that has significant replay value both in terms of further understanding the story and additional challenges, as the game gets harder on additional playthroughs.
My overall rating for gameplay experience is 10/10. :D
This game has been called semi-isometric.  Basically, you control Red in an angled-down view using WASD, Q for a 'flourish,' and the number keys 1-4.  In place of WASD, you can left click to have Red go somewhere.
For mobility-related issues, you have the option of keyboard/mouse OR a controller, and the game can realistically be played using real-time combat and the Turn() function or just through Turn(), though it is slightly harder, since the enemies will still attack outside of your Turn() actions.  Further, all keys can be rebound.
Turn() basically pauses combat so that you can plan and execute an attack using 'movement points.'
For overall accessibility, I give Transistor a 10/10.
Transistor starts with subtitles turned off, so make sure you enable them before playing.  As the game has no opening cinematics prior to the start menu, you will not miss any of the story.
Subtitles appear at the top of the screen in very large, clear, outlined text.  No concerns with white-on-white or otherwise unreadable subtitles.  Further, subs are colored according to who is talking and images accompany the voices to indicate the speaker.  In scenes with multiple speakers, nobody is shown actually talking on screen, so there are no concerns with differentiating on-screen vs off-screen subtitles.
Although I was confused when I first started playing, when you see off-white captions with no indication of the speaker, pay attention to the sword glowing.  Since Red has no voice, the sword is the speaker, and it acts as a narrator-in-being in the game, pushing the story along by talking to Red.
Red actually uses the OVC terminals to talk back to the sword via typing, so you can consider that a shoutout to TTYs or using text/notepad on a smartphone to communicate.
For its effective use of subtitles that leaves no confusion about the speaker or the story, I rate this category a 10/10.
Transistor is a single-player game.  No chatting or voice comms exist.

I concur with aforementioned reviews acknowledging the fact that A Machine of Pigs is different than The Dark Descent. Having played 'Dear Esther' (also from Chinese Room), I noticed the similarity that the game focuses largely on the narrative and their excellent ability to tell a story that can almost be classified as virtual literature. This causes the game to lose some ground in the interactive part. In itself I don't find this to be a negative point, since too much interactivity can interrupt the flow of a game if not done properly, but I expected the game to have the same balance between scary moment, storyline and interactivity as The Dark Descent. And I think that is the reason why the reviews might be a bit more negative than they might have been if it wasn't so closely related to the Dark Descent. If you can set aside your expectation for the game and play it with an open mind, you're in for a treat.
The game is short, for me it was about 5 hours. Thing is, if a game lacks interactivity or the story loses its pace, it might be a good thing to not have the game taking 10 hours. While the story might be good, you don't want to get the reputation that folks want to finish your horror game to see how it ends, but are bored throughout it instead of scared stiff every once in a while. So all in all 5 hours is a good time for a decent horror game.
Catch the game on a sale if you want the money to match the amount of game time (I have this arbitrary rule that 1€ = 1h game time to make it worth my while, but that's just my idiosyncrasy).
Final verdict: Play it without expecting it to be like The Dark Descent and you will have about 5 hours of good creepy fun.

Running, jumping, running, jumping, running aaaaand jumping.
That´s what Fotonica is all about...kind of.

FOTONICA doesn´t rely on a huge amount of polygons or fancy color-schemes.
In fact, because of the low-poly look and "the lack of color", FOTONICA is one of the few that are able to pull it of right.
The only time, where color is shown in the game is, when you reach the so called "Golden Speed". The once colorless background and properties now turn into yellow-ish ones with a neat but sometimes distracting and bugging animation.
Filled with electronica soundtracks made by Michael Manning, Nicolô Sala and Baiyon, the game lacks other sorts of music, which is kind of sad.
Some of you will argue, that this is no big deal but i would like to have some variety in fast-paced games.
Apart from the music, there are only a few other sound in the game -->  running-sound, a jump-sound coupled with a human "hugh"-sound, sound of your body hitting the floor or an object, sound of collecting bubbles and a sound when reaching "Golden Speed".
There´s not much to do in FOTONICA.
The game is divided into four chapters/difficulties and eight different levels.
You run in a straight line for the entirety of the game while jumping and collecting bubbles.
While running, jumping and falling you increase your speed as long as you dont hit any objects with your face.
At a certain speed-level you reach the so-called "Golden Speed" where everything around you turn yellow-ish/golden and your momentum builds up even faster.
Like all other aspects in the game, the controls are minimalistic, too.
Just hold down a button to build up momentum, release it to jump and hold it again in mid-air to dive and land.
Apart from running and jumping you can collect red "bubbles" to increase your score.
They are scattered all over the track and are more or less hard to collect, while trying to finish the race.
A rather unique-looking game about running, jumping and competing against other, trying to get the Highscore of a level.
With its minimalistic and easy controls it is engaging for casual and "highscore"-gamers.
