-Landing is simple, and jumping is easy to judge (see the bad for a brief comment on this, though)
-Music is appropriate and helps keep ya going.
-You know when, in Mirror's Edge, you'd get a really good string of perfect jumps and mounts, gaining speed and flowing through the world in one of the best gameplay experiences ever? Remember how rarely that happened and how often it was unpleasantly cut off? Well, the only way it happens here is if you screw up or fall into oblivion.
THE BAD
-when you go Super Saiyan and the screen goes♥♥♥♥♥♥Yellow, the sudden speedup pushes you forwards, and can make you 'misjudge' your landing. This can be day-ruining in frustration.
-The 'dots' or Pacman Pills or whatever they are - the fastest route doesn't follow this and is a tad arbitrary, though enjoyable most of the time.
-Making the sides of a linear path wobbly to make the map drastically different does not a cake make.
-bit more variance? Maybe some aesthetic variance? Sure, the look is good, but a bit of something more 'out there' might be worth considering in the future.
-collision with ledges can be hard to judge at times. Whether or not you automatically mount is sometimes just 'up in the air'.
I am big on first-person parkour and this simplifies everything to core principles, and then turns the simple result to 11. Thoroughly enjoyable and worth playing. 6-6.5/10. Would pay full price.

Whether you're a fan of the series, looking for a new MMO to invest yourself in, or both, FFXIV is definitely a good choice. Some will get tripped up over the subscription fee and not give it a chance as a result, and I would tell those people they are making a sore mistake. Once you get into the game, you'll immediately experience some of the best visuals that you've ever seen in an MMO, which in itself is reasoning to stay. Plus, you get the first month free.
The plot actually plays a significant role in FFXIV, again unusual for an MMO, and is actually quite interesting IMO. As stated, the game is absolutely beautiful and I've found myself on many occasions stopping, going into first person, and just absorbing the beauty. The player community is very friendly, and you'll find yourself joining a Free Company in no time. In fact, I'd recommend it, but I digress.
But the most interesting thing about FFXIV is its Job system. One of the most unique character specialization systems I've seen in an MMO, where you need to thread together 2-3 different classes to create a job unique to that class combination. although there are only around 8 or 9 jobs as of now, the possibilites are vast, and I am optimistic that it will gain many more with future expansions. The game is still in its vanilla stage and is already working MUCH better than its predecessor MMO. I have high hopes for the future in this game, and enjoying it thoroughly as of now. I recommend to any fans of MMO's or Final Fantasy.

I have had some mixed feelings about this game, and have seen very mixed reviews of it. I want to start off by saying, however, that I do think buying this game is worth it.
The disappointing thing about Machine for Pigs is that a lot of the gameplay elements that I personally (and I'm sure many others can agree) found very fun in Dark Descent were taken out. There is no sanity meter, no inventory, you can't pick up anything other than objects required to complete puzzles, and there is no hiding in wardrobes. As such, the gameplay suffers, making it less appealing, especially after you have played Dark Descent.
What Machine for Pigs does well though, is story. I don't want to say too much to avoid spoiling, but it deals with morality and personal struggles much like Dark Descent does. In fact, Machine for Pigs may have an even darker, more disturbing story than Dark Descent once you are able to put everything together and realize what has been going on. The ending of the game was very dark, dramatic and intense, and I found certain parts to be quite creepy. There were a couple of cheap jumpscares, but the atmosphere was still heavy and had me on-edge.
Overall, the gameplay wasn't quite as fun (particularly if you enjoy puzzles like I do), but the ending left me satisfied and glad I had spent the time and money (full-price, even) on it. In fact, once I had beaten it, I ran to the Wiki to read up more on it in case I had missed anything. If you are still unsure, which I'd understand, perhaps wait for a sale, but do still consider it!

For Deaf/hoh gamers, I rate this game a 10/10!
Supergiant knocked it out of the park again.  In Transistor, you play as Red, a lady whose voice was stolen by a group who intended to kill her.  Obviously that's a bit odd, but the game takes place inside of a computer-ish environment.  Telling more would be giving things away for those who, for some reason, have yet to play it.
Since this review is largely oriented toward acciessibility for deaf/hoh gamers, I will stop there and just say that it is a great game with a great story that has significant replay value both in terms of further understanding the story and additional challenges, as the game gets harder on additional playthroughs.
My overall rating for gameplay experience is 10/10. :D
This game has been called semi-isometric.  Basically, you control Red in an angled-down view using WASD, Q for a 'flourish,' and the number keys 1-4.  In place of WASD, you can left click to have Red go somewhere.
For mobility-related issues, you have the option of keyboard/mouse OR a controller, and the game can realistically be played using real-time combat and the Turn() function or just through Turn(), though it is slightly harder, since the enemies will still attack outside of your Turn() actions.  Further, all keys can be rebound.
Turn() basically pauses combat so that you can plan and execute an attack using 'movement points.'
For overall accessibility, I give Transistor a 10/10.
Transistor starts with subtitles turned off, so make sure you enable them before playing.  As the game has no opening cinematics prior to the start menu, you will not miss any of the story.
Subtitles appear at the top of the screen in very large, clear, outlined text.  No concerns with white-on-white or otherwise unreadable subtitles.  Further, subs are colored according to who is talking and images accompany the voices to indicate the speaker.  In scenes with multiple speakers, nobody is shown actually talking on screen, so there are no concerns with differentiating on-screen vs off-screen subtitles.
Although I was confused when I first started playing, when you see off-white captions with no indication of the speaker, pay attention to the sword glowing.  Since Red has no voice, the sword is the speaker, and it acts as a narrator-in-being in the game, pushing the story along by talking to Red.
Red actually uses the OVC terminals to talk back to the sword via typing, so you can consider that a shoutout to TTYs or using text/notepad on a smartphone to communicate.
For its effective use of subtitles that leaves no confusion about the speaker or the story, I rate this category a 10/10.
Transistor is a single-player game.  No chatting or voice comms exist.

I bought this game because I was bored, and I was pleasantly surprised. The cartoony borderlands-esque visuals of this game worked nicely in contrast with the blood that flies across the screen, breaking the tranquility of the distant landscapes. The legendary gun skins are very pretty, which were nice to have along with the stat boosts, and each weapon felt different and unique in itself.
Bosses and upgraded enemies were a fair fight, and probably quite tough on the higher difficulties, which I have not had a chance to play. However, I did not understand the nonsense of "stand behind this conveniently placed rock and wait until you can throw a piece of dynamite behind an armoured gatling gun," those parts were just asinine to me. The majority of bosses are very well done, though.
The second chance ability was a way to just straight up cheese your enemies, and is pretty hilarious when you are being riddled with bullets from some random Native Americans and then you magically dodge their bullet, regain your health and headshot them. It made me laugh.
General gunplay feels very John Woo- where killing things allows you to have more slow motion. The slow motion can be quite useful in the later missions when there are many people shooting at you and then they are suddenly highlighted red. I mostly ran with dual-wield pistols for the hell of it, aside from that pesky gatling gunner on the train, who I promptly shot in the face with a rifle.
The narrative in this game is perfectly executed, and I could not be happier that it is told in a light hearted sort of way. For example "I walked into the barn on a plank, but I slipped off. Well how did you get out? The door was open," my short period of confusion was ended when a whole side of the barn disappeared in front of me. It isn't funny as such, but it's enough to crack a smile at.
As a whole, you should definitely get this game if you are considering it. It's nothing short of brilliant, and combines well liked elements from all genres of games. For a game of this standard, for this price, it would be criminal not to get it.

Where to start with Factorio?
Factorio is one of those games where you buy it, play for ages, then close down to play a different game with your friends. Factorio then sits and gathers dust in the corner of your game library to be played again a month later. I mainly have 3 different ways for playing games. Short but frequent bursts, Meduim lenght plays often enough and Very long playtimes now and then. Factorio is the last one. A game that will be played for hours at a time but only every so often.
On to the game then!
The first time you boot up factorio you get to start your first world. Sure, there's a campaign but it's around average and nowhere near as good as the real deal. Your first world is fun and exciting and all around a giant mess because you have no idea what you're doing. Doesn't matter though. It was a blast. Who cares if a conveyor belt track is way longer than it needs to be or one part of your factory relies on somthing at the complete other end. It still worked, didn't it? You start anew, armed with what knowledge you could gather and set off. You realise that it takes longer and longer each time in the beggining because you're used to automation now. Don't worry, it'll be back the way it was. You actually plan your factory this time instead of going in willy nilly. Your factory is way more efficient.
Uhoh, here comes the aliens!
Your base is under attack by ruthless aliens and you didn't prepare defences because there were more important things like research. Your factory is half dead when you manage to kill the last alien. It was a good run. You now have 2 options. Restart or Rebuild. Either way it'll be better than last time. It's the aliens again but this time you have a turret. You kill them all and keep going. As you keep tearing down trees and creating pollution, the enemies grow. You evolve with them with better armour and guns, more defences and a tank. It was a close battle but you won. The taste of victory on your lips. You start to get better, start using trains, robots and whatever else you can get your hands on. It's up to you. Maybe you'll go on a psycopathic rampage and kill all aliens. Or maybe set up a train circling the entire factory just for protection. Who knows. Maybe you'll escape, or maybe the panet's grown on you a bit TOO much.
Will you be the hero of your own story? Or will you rot on this planet and be torn to pieces?
The choice is yours.

The concept of the game is very nice. If you enjoyed playing Ragnarok Online, you would enjoy playing this game. HOWEVER, there are an absurdly large number of flaws that would deter many players, and even force players to quit this game very quickly:
- Poor server stability and location. For some reason IMC has lumped the servers all in the east coast for US servers. This means that anyone playing on the west coast will consistently have a ping of 150+ms. In addition, lag spikes due to memory leakage (or whatever the heck they are doing) can cause your ping to skyrocket to 6000+ms. ALOT of rubberbanding ensues due to this.
- Poor optimization. In this day and age, one would expect a game to be running fairly smoothly. For example, TF2 (a game fro 2007) still runs decently even in non-vanilla severs that holds 32 players, with particles and projectiles flying left right and center. With this game, a boss fight with no more than 32 players degrades to a slide show. You would probably get a better framerate using Microsoft Powerpoint, hitting F5, and mashing the right key.
- Management and team working on the game. I don't know what in God's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ these people are doing. An autistic person coupled with Down Syndrome could probably manage this better. There are countless bugs that the community brings up (party questing bugs, weapon swapping lag just to name a few), and none of the them are resolved.There are no updates from the development group to inform on the progress. Instead, we typically receive disappointing updates (such as more costumes that you must use real money to pay for, and their associated loading screens to advertise them), and the Q&A sessions answer absurdly trivial questions that they probably pulled out of the deepest pits of their♥♥♥♥♥  Bots are rampant in the game and IMC's attempt to deal with these bots results in the player experience and quality of life to be quite deplorable. There are no GMs to actually deal with said issue. Seeing a GM is basically like seeing a unicorn: you'll never see one, because they're probably aren't any.
All in all, while the concept of the game is very good, poor management and the inability to optimize this game's coding will send it to its deathbead. I wouldn't be surprised if the game kicks the can by September or October.

I follow a personal rule that for every dollar I spend I should be able to get at the VERY least 1 hour of gameplay. Though the gameplay in FOTONICA is enjoyable for the time that you're new to the game, once you play through all the levels (that took me about 1 hour) the game gets dull.
The gameplay is good, but it's too short a game for is regular retail price.

Is it worth 10 bucks? Hell no. Only get this if it's on sale.
That said, this game has a sort of intoxicating quality to it, something that most AAA titles seem to lack, and a lot of indie games with similar mechanics (such as Super Hexagon and Boson X, just to name a few), carry quite frequently. Regardless of that, though, Fotonica still feels unique because of its artstyle, suprisingly innovative one-button gameplay, calming soundtrack, and beautiful, diverse levels. While all these things have been done before, none of them have been incorporated into one game so expertly. Fotonica deserves your time if not only for that.
There are issues with the game, though; most notably how the artstyle interferes with your ablility to see platforms at a distance when playing on a smaller resolution monitor, and other things of that nature that really can't be helped, but said things never bothed me, even if they did end up hindering my experience. That was because the game itself, in combination with all of the elements that I listed previously, ended up being so relaxing that I just stopped caring about any objective flaws I might have come across. Maybe that's because the flaws just weren't very significant, but regardless of whether or not that's true, this game gets two thumbs up from me.
Whether you're a casual or hardcore gamer, I strongly recommend Fotonica if you feel like destressing or just having some fun with an artsy little experience.

Whether you're a fan of the series, looking for a new MMO to invest yourself in, or both, FFXIV is definitely a good choice. Some will get tripped up over the subscription fee and not give it a chance as a result, and I would tell those people they are making a sore mistake. Once you get into the game, you'll immediately experience some of the best visuals that you've ever seen in an MMO, which in itself is reasoning to stay. Plus, you get the first month free.
The plot actually plays a significant role in FFXIV, again unusual for an MMO, and is actually quite interesting IMO. As stated, the game is absolutely beautiful and I've found myself on many occasions stopping, going into first person, and just absorbing the beauty. The player community is very friendly, and you'll find yourself joining a Free Company in no time. In fact, I'd recommend it, but I digress.
But the most interesting thing about FFXIV is its Job system. One of the most unique character specialization systems I've seen in an MMO, where you need to thread together 2-3 different classes to create a job unique to that class combination. although there are only around 8 or 9 jobs as of now, the possibilites are vast, and I am optimistic that it will gain many more with future expansions. The game is still in its vanilla stage and is already working MUCH better than its predecessor MMO. I have high hopes for the future in this game, and enjoying it thoroughly as of now. I recommend to any fans of MMO's or Final Fantasy.

The game-play sounds boring compared to the sheer number of action games; however, the game-play is actually quite addicting. That being said, the multi-branched storyline of Papers, Please is the biggest selling point. With various endings, players are encouraged to replay the game, and experience other possibilities.
YOUR DECISIONS MATTER. When pitted against difficult decisions, players must decide what is more ethically important to them. Do you believe the government or the pleas of individuals? Do you purposely make a mistake to ensure the safety of others? Your actions greatly changes the outcome of the game.
It's not by mistake that Papers, Please grabbed the attention of many gamers. It's a big change from typical games, but it's a change worth taking. Glory to Arstotzka.

You're a tiny cog beneath a soul-crushing bureaucracy. I struggled to manage the ever-increasing immigration controls and paperwork yet still move the line along. You're paid per person. I faced corrupt guards, mysterious visitors and various others at the gates, all while my family died from cold, starvation and illness. I took bribes, looked the other way and sent strangers to their doom just to eat and maybe keep the heat on. At last, I gave up and just let everyone in. Being sent to prison was a reprieve.
What this game set out to do, it does well. Glory to Arstotzka.

Having seen many immigrants in my own country that is located somewhere next to the South China Sea, Papers, Please is a great thriller that challenges you to be an immigrant officer who either approves or reject immigrant for the glory of Arstotzka.
The UI is simple to understand and use while the overall presentation reminded me of the good old school graphics of the late 80s which I enjoy a lot (brought up with Sierra adventure games). The low resolution display couple with the limited colour help to enhance the abstract feel of the game with the player filling in the extra details in their own mind.
Papers, Please can be quite addicting one you get to know the core gameplay with "one more immigrant to process" that will leave you wanting for more.

First thing's first - I don't understand the angry rant about this game. People literally drown it in pig♥♥♥♥ while other really crappy titles manage to get away. Often the reason why players hate AMFP is that they beleive it's far worse than the original Amnesia. I suggest you should consider these two as completely different games. The Chinese Room (the developer I put highest hopes on and will defend) did their thing. OK, they got rid of core Amnesia gameplay elements (lantern oil, thunderboxes), but I think they did it for the good sake of the story. For story and atmosphere are the basis for Machine For Pigs. Storytelling is just plain dark, almost pitch-black and somewhat Lovecraft-ish as it's predecessor. Game is sophisticated as it is asks global and complex existential questions. Ominous atmosphere is here allright, driven by classy frightening sound desing and music. And YES, this Amnesia is scary - not too scary, but still.. Although it's hard to terrify a Survival Horror vet like me, AAMFP did that. And this what I ♥♥♥♥in' expect from a horror game! Ain't no need to throw ♥♥♥♥ at gamer's face, more of that - no need to drop them off their seats. Freeze them on the spot so they are afraid to move a finger! That's the real horror. And here's the thing some will consider DarkDescent-blasphemy: maybe removing oil tanks, thunderboxes and difficult puzzles was necessary for this particular project, like blinding a man makes his hearing sharper. Cutting the gameplay elements allowed story and setting take the spotlight. IMHO it's better than solving riddle after riddle after riddle in similar tunnels in Penumbra: Overture. Amnesia AMFP isn't an interactive movie though - you do things besides walking. I will however admit it lacks some hard puzzles. And dying. Yeah, I dropped dead TWO (!) TIMES. Anyway, it helped me to percieve the story better. Game's not short too - if you take time and won't charge your ♥♥♥ forward you'll get your healthy 8 hours as I did. Amnesia watches you play...it smiles as you begin your descent into madness. it laughs at your frustration, and totters when you are fearful. It is dark. It is abysmal. It is disgusting. It is beautiful in a monsterous way. Its soundtrack: Fantastic, its voice acting: Superb, its story: magnificent-the lovechild of Poe and Stoker. What is lacks in puzzle and gameplay elements it makes up for with a more polished and thrilling experience. If horror games are remotely in your realm of interest, Machine for Pigs is a must play.

While Amnesia: The Dark Descent was a fresh gasp of air for the horror genre, A Machine for Pigs felt like a casualized knock-off of it's rather brilliant predecessor. I'd recommend it, if it was sold at at least half it's price. Fortunately for myself I bought it when it was on sale, so I got my money's worth.
It honestly felt like a mediocre mod to the original Amnesia and I wish I knew better than to buy it. Examples to it being that way are poorly designed monsters, weak storyline, non-immersive gameplay and trivial puzzles. In the end, it was not at all what I expected to buy, it is advertised to be the exact opposite of what it actually is, and the trailer shows all (read ALL) the strongest points of the game while hiding the weak spots.
I'd absolutely give it 4/10, I admit that my view of it is warped, but I'm sure that those bias are forgivable if they're based upon how much of an blast of fun the previous game was.
EDIT: I also forgot to mention that by paying full price for this abomination, you're not only getting DLC quality, but also DLC playtime, grand total of which consists of 4 hours.

I used to have hobbies.
I used to have a life.
Now I have a factory.
Great game, I keep forgetting what time it is... Making automatic factories to take iron, copper, and oil, then make solar panels and laser weaponry. Super fun.

Take the best parts of Transport Tycoon, the geek-elements of the extended patches with train-signalling, path-finding and complex schedules, the building of a working network to transport cargo.
Now shove that cargo into buildings to craft further items and transport their results.  Rocket fuel.  Drones that can help you build or deconstruct anything.  Research vials to help you unlock the tech tree.  Vehicles.  Pumps.  Guns.  Ammo.  From basic ore, coal and wood, you build a system to manufacture circuits and trains.
Manage it all in a massive, endless world, collating the resources you need to get to the right places to be processed and fulfill your current needs, while exploring for that crucial oil well.
Now imagine that everything you do pollutes the planet.  And the locals aren't at all happy about that.  The more pollution, the more unhappy they are.  And they grow, expand, and up-sticks in your direction like the populous of Populous.  And after a while they come hunting and you have to man the barricades and send out the repair drones and hope you're producing ammo at a fast enough rate to keep them at bay, without dwindling the resources that let you take your defences to the next level.
Everything can be automated, from the collection of wood from trees to the creation of a train from raw parts.  Everything can be controlled and processed.  Set up in-game sensors and circuits to make sure you don't run out of one resource, or that you don't churn out masses of one required substance when the other critical one isn't available.  Make automated trains go and collect resources from your far-flung outposts and bring it to one point, with the help of the drones and conveyor belts, while building safe computer-controlled crossing points so you don't get run over by your own trains.
Keep your power networks up to keep firing the lasers, while not burning through your coal.  Or move to solar to keep the aliens from getting mad at that cloud of smoke coming from your factory, if you can manufacture enough and balance the power overnight.
Hundreds of items, a large tech-tree, an infinite map, a challenging enemy, and a factory to manage in the middle of it all, while trying to stay alive and get an SOS message off the planet.
Great fun in multiplayer too, sharing the burden and taking turns on the purging of the nearby alien spawns or the patching up of the base, or establishing a new outpost.  Always something to do, always something to be made more efficient, more automated, more productive so you can build that new flamethrower or have the better drones help you out in taking out the enemy.
And, yes, you can just storm in, raze their village to the ground and steal their precious artifacts.  But you better hope that they don't find a way in the back while you're out there.
One of the best games ever, and I've sunk thousands of hours into things like OpenTTD and all the RTS games of old.  Tuned resource management, simple or complex networks, simple or complex interactions (move this type of resource over there but only if there's enough to build one of those and we're not short on the source material, etc.), and a hostile horde at the gates vying to get in and wreak havoc.
Cannot recommend enough, and it only looks to be getting better as time goes on.

I wasn't a big fan of Just Cause 1 or 2. The first game caught my interest because - released in 2006 - its huge world and addition of flying and driving mechanics were still novel additions to the FPS genre. Its gameplay wasn't particularly well done and its world was fairly shallow, but the scale and newness of the franchise were enough to carry the game. Just Cause 2 upped the ante with an even larger world and the addition of a grappling gun (a feature singularly uninteresting to me, but apparently a fan favorite). The story and characters were even more ridiculous than the first but it kept me interested enough to invest the necessary 30 hours or so to complete the game.
I tired of Just Cause 3 in less than two hours.
I know there are a lot of people who get undue joy from the destruction and chaos they can wreak on the virtual world and I will be the first to admit the game utilizes some impressive technology. It's not quite up to the high-water mark set by the Red Faction games, but I quiet enjoyed being able to blow apart guard towers, fortress walls and giant dish antennas. The action can get quite frenetic and the gunplay is solid, if not particularly noteworthy. But beyond that, there really wasn't much to keep me invested in the game.
That the characters would be annoying caricatures was evident just from the introduction, and they did little to improve themselves during gameplay. The setting remained as superficial as ever; for all its vast scope, there's little to differentiate one tiny village from the next; they are all hollow shells whose only purpose is to serve as liberation points. Too much of the game is locked behind in-game challenge modes, few of which were enjoyable and all broke the game's feeling of immersion. Odd control choices and unequal game performance didn't help, nor did the brain-dead AI. The game feels far more a chore than a fun experience.
I'll admit, the two hours of blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up and killing the moronic AI weren't completely without merit, but - even at the sharp discount I received - it's not enough. I purchased the game at an 80% discount and I still don't think I got value for my money.

Other than that, I loved it. Challenging and deep stealth gameplay, great visuals, great soundtrack and sound design, and a generally faithful recreation of the original Alien (although occasionally it dips its toe into Aliens as well, which seems to dilute the appeal somewhat, especially as I wasn't the biggest fan of Aliens). Story wasn't much and the characters aren't particularly interesting, although it could be argued that this is equally applicable to the original Alien film, and horror media with interesting characters are rather the exception rather than the rule.
Alien Isolation is one of those media properties that isn't entirely sure if it's a sequel or a reboot (not dissimilar to Metal Gear Solid or The Force Awakens) and hence tries to hedge its bets a bit, which feels a little uncanny and disorienting, when the story hits most of the same plot beats as the original property - and yet they've "already" happened in this continuity, so it feels like history is repeating itself for no good reason. But suffice to say that if you've seen even one of the Alien films, the plot will never surprise you.
Two little quibbles: the game generally performed quite well on my mid-range laptop, except that the audio cues in the pre-baked animations are timed to specific frame intervals: hence, if your computer can't comfortably and reliably hit 60fps, the audio will be out of sync during the pre-baked animations (but otherwise in sync). It was a little distracting for me, but not a deal-breaker. The only other quibble was that the smoke bomb is the only one of the craftable items which is more or less useless, all the more jarring given that the other items are, for the most part, quite well-balanced.
Took me about 18 hours to complete the main campaign on hard mode, planning to play the DLC next.

A really fun arcadey shooter taken to a whole other level by its clever use of narration; events unfolding on screen will change in real time, like taking one fork in a path and then later recanting and having to play through the other path, or enemies changing from Apaches to bandits when a listener points out that it wasn't Apache territory, or running through an endless loop of train cars when the narrator steps away for a moment to go to the bathroom.
The core gameplay is plenty fun on its own, and the experience system lets you unlock perks related to whatever weapons and tactics you like so you can play however you like whether it's accurate long-distance rifle shooting or quickly mowing down crowds of bandits up-close with double revolvers or dynamiting groups and shotgunning the survivors. And the regenerating health system rewards skillful play by letting you automatically dodge shots that would otherwise kill you if you've built up enough kills.
The only real issue is that some of the puzzle bosses are frustrating at first and will require a few deaths for you to figure out their gimmicks, and that some of the later quick-draw minigames can be prety tough unless you mess around with sensitivity settings or use a controller.

Summary:
Graphics: 7/10
Gameplay: 4/10
Sound: 7/10
Design: 3/10
Story: 2/10
Disappointed to say the least for this veteran gamer. I just about played everything on the market and how this one stacks up against the rest is a merely okay. WoW is king for a reason. Their design was brilliant. GW1 broke the model for subscription. DDO made the first F2P. Regardless of this, FFXIV doesn't bring anything special to the table.
Graphics:
Very nice graphics. It's no skyrim, but still very nice. They have some good special effects for weapons and spells. And they were pretty reserved when it came to mass implementation which is good for video latency issues. Animations are smooth and they went with the flashy factor when it came to special effects and clothing design. My one gripe about the clothing design is that it's designed by the mind of a metro/homosexual whom assumes heteros will embrace it. Well excuse me, but I don't like wearing black leather thongs and the game forces us to wear it at the first level depending on your class. Other than that, the monster designs were merely okay. I'll talk more about that later.
Gameplay:
First thing I noticed was the slow 2.5 second global cooldown rate which made things slow and boring. The skills are limited, which is a good thing against overcluttering and gamepads. I did like the camera angles though. The default for gamepads was a monster focus shot with the player on the sides. Limited range though, but it gives the feeling of an actual FF game, but only slightly. The gamepad took getting used to because I found far more efficient ways to implement all its features with an Xpadder configuration as a substitute. The fights themselves as I said slow, but somewhat interesting. It's not always stand there and button mashing. Sometimes the monsters do area-based attacks and gotta move outta the way. Slightly more interesting to the dullness of it all. However, when it comes to healing and customization, that's where this game drops the hat. Healing is limited. Potions but no skills. Customization? None. You use what they decide to give you at the level you achieved. But you can make your own looks. Which is alright I suppose given the deep customizations from the mind of a metrosexual artist. Overall... there is a lot to improve upon and no one sure way of doing it.
Sound:
The first music was the crystal theme which was meant to invoke FF nostalgia. But for some reason, it didn't really work with this game. The game design and art vastly drifted from the FF path long ago. The creators are different. The fans are different. Everything is different and mixing old music with new graphics desynchronized the effect and created a strange mood. So it didn't work. The rest of the music is fairly well done. A bit grand for non granduous events, however. But it gets the job done and keeps the ear entertained.
Design:
The initial tutorial aspect of the game was tedious, long, and boring. The size of the settlements did the game no justice. It could have been reduced by half or to a third and still maintain streaming play with a shortened time span. The explanations of the game's features was rather forced. Instead of players being allowed to discover features on their own, the game hits it over the head and merely forces you to read through blobs of texts. They change names around from what was conventionally used, adding to the confusion of clueless gamers. And when the gameplay starts, the lengthy tutorials were not even needed in the first place. This is a result of poor gaming design. Once you're on the field, the world is not open ended. The battle area feels like strings of sandboxes walled in and connected together and teases the eyes with backdrops of expanse when there really isn't any. The design for monsters were graphically and artistically alright, but the choices of which monsters to present to the player is absolutely horrendous. Who thought fighting a big toad would be fun? Or a couple of anorexic dogs? Or a couple of flowers? Where's all the goblins? Ogres? Drakes? Monsters of great badassery? There aren't any. It's like walking into a telltubby/pikachu zoo and beating on things that squeak.
Story:
Square-Enix has sucked balls with stories ever since Final Fantasy 8. They did mediocre jobs with FF9, FF10, and FF13. But the rest of it was horrendous!! FFXIV: ARR is no different. Most characters are cliches that invoke manga fanaticism. Their dialogue is flat, boring, straight-forward, and verbose. Their story nodes are unmemorable and completely uninteresting even with flashy cinematics. And its evolution completely makes no sense at all. Most MMOs arent any different, but SquareEnix tried to put the story in the fore-front and it fails.... horribly.
Conclusion:
Don't buy this game. You're better off spending dollars on Guild Wars 2 or some other game that's at least playable without a subscription fee. This game is a disappointment and should not be charging a subscription fee due to its failures.

As far as MMORPGs go, FFXIV is not at the same level as it's main competitors. Yet. The world is still lacking in scope, the endgame needs more variation, and lots of features like player housing hasn't been implemented yet.
But I still give it my wholehearted recommendation. The graphics are great, the content that IS there is really fun, the production values are as good as any MMORPG I've ever played, and I can't stop playing it. If you're the type of player who rushes through content, you may find yourself hitting a wall at some point, but if you dial it back to somewhere between "hardcore" and "casual", this game is a true gem. Heck, even if you DO breeze through it all, it is a game that grows with every patch, every content update, and every (eventual) expansion pack.
The monthly fee might seem discouraging, but not since Final Fantasy XI (also an MMORPG) have I ever got so much playtime and content for my money. If you love Final Fantasy and MMORPGs, you owe it to yourself to at least give it a try.

i played many MMORPGs, and after a game like Guild Wars 2 this feels like a step back. On the upside, you can call it oldschool, and for slower players it is surely the right thing. But if you like games with action in your gameplay/fights, that depend more on skill than on items, this game is outright boring to play.
Example 1: most skills depend on a global cooldown of approximately 1.5 seconds (at least that's what it feels like). So you execute 1 skill... then... wait... wait.. wait... finally a second klick... rinse and repeat.
Example 2: The skills can be queued up to do chains of skills. While this in itself is nice, in this game this ends in most classes pressing 1-2-3 (wait 1.5sec between each skill mind you) then 4-5-6 .. rinse and repeat. oh perhaps once or twice a fight i press also 7 or 8. Thats about it. In a game like GW2 this would be about your auto-attack, and everything else you do in GW2 is on top of that. And you do a lot on top of your auto-attack in GW2.
Long story short: If you like nice graphics, cute questchains and dialogue (reading, no voice acting, 90% of the time) with sometimes funny reasons for NPCs to request something from you, and like solo playing in your own speed most of the time, then this game is for you.
If you like challenging gameplay, and like to play the whole game together with friends (outside of random dungeon finder queuing), buy something else.

A breath of fresh air in the MMO scene, or rather, a reminder of what it was that made MMOs popular in the first place.
What makes FFXIV:ARR so good, is not what it does have, but rather what it doesn't.
Gimmicks.
Ever since World of Warcraft became such a large player in the MMORPG scene, competitors have risen which attempt to dethrone it with new and "exciting" mechanics, but in doing so forget what an MMO even is.
FFXIV:ARR learns from the mistakes of others and sticks to the known strengths of the genre. The holy trinity of Tank/DPS/Healer, Strong and challenging end-game content, deep storyline and world lore, an abundance of content to sink your time into along with major content patches every 2 and a half months.
It should be noted, that major content patches in FFXIV:ARR usually contain the same amount of content an expansion for WoW would contain at launch.
Yes, the game has a subscription model, but given the spetacular failures of numerous F2P and Cash Shop MMOs that have popped up over the years, combined with how this money is funneled into frequent and high quality updates to the game, is this really a bad thing? Honestly, it's well worth the money.
However FFXIV:ARR doesn't just stick to old core values, it does so while breating new life into them that don't undermine their integrity. The holy trinity of MMOs is refered to as holy for a reason, to mess with it is to dance with certain doom. FFXIV:ARR conquers this perplexing problem regarding the need for re-interpretation without becoming gimmicky by altering the way experience works in the game.
In traditional MMOs, you make a character, you select your class and you start getting experience points. As you gain experience, your character levels up thus expanding your capabilities with your selected class, until you hit max level then you move to end-game content.
XIV:ARR does away with character experience, instead replacing it with class experience. You have an active class, determined by the weapon you are wielding and any experience gained will go into the experience pool for your active class. You don't level your charcter, you level your class. For example, I'm currently a level 50 conjurer, specialising in the advanced healing class "White Mage" and I am also at the same time a level 18 Thauterage, the predecessor to the DPS class "Black Mage".
This doesn't make me some weird DPS/Healer hybrid, I can only be one at any one time. If I have a WHM weapon equipped, I'm a WHM and I have access to all the abilities of a WHM of my level and can equip gear for my class. I do not however have access to abilities for classes I have also leveled (except certain cross-class abilities which are sort of how this game does talents) nor can I equip gear meant for a Black mage while I have my white mage active. At the same time, when I switch to my black mage, it is as if I am a fresh character still leveling and only at level 18, the fact I have a class at max level does not affect my game play at all.
This is great since it allows for alts without having to give up your character, your identity, your friends, your guild etc, you have it all in one place, without ever undermining the holy trinity.
FFXIV:ARR shows that it's possible to approach MMORPGs with a "Don't fix what isn't broken" philosophy without simply remaking yet another WoW.
On a final note? I pre-ordered the imperial edition for The Elder Scrolls Online, that set me back $75 USD, I did that before I started playing this and you know what? I've decided to just swallow that purchase and play this instead.
It's THAT good.
Saying all that however, the game is certainly not without it's faults.
FFXIV:ARR is a remake of the 2010 game FFXIV, which frankly? Was absolutely terrible.
The original game suffered from poor UI, poor world design, a dull and slow (Even by MMO standards) storyline and terrible optimisation leading to significant technical issues.
There is only so much you can do with this and this shows when we look at the current game world.
The current world is made up mainly of what was the original open game world which has had the massive bloat cut from it, the areas worth keeping turned into zones which are seperated by zone transitions.
These aren't instanced, which is good, but still it does break immersion a bit.
Thankfully, this isn't likely to be an endearing issue as developers have acknowledged the size of the world which though acceptable, could use a bit more to it and have said that we will be seeing significant increases to the world's size in major expansions (the first of which is expected in the second or third quarter of 2014).
There are also some key class types which are noticably absent from the game, for example the stealthy ambusher, (thief, rogue, ninja etc), however once again the developers have acknowledged this issue and said plans are in place to bring in new classes in future patches and expansions.
Typically, I would count this as a major negative when forming my opinion on a game but I have been very impressed with how reliable Square-Enix are for following through on promises and fixing or introducing things where needed.
So I'm willing to take their "We are aware of this and we have plans in motion to meet these requests" in good faith, something I am VERY hesitant to extend to many if not most game developers these days.
Overall?
FFXIV:ARR is the equivilent of a miracle in gaming. Not only rescuing a title otherwise doomed to ridicule, but improving it to such an extent that it deserves a place in the genre's historybooks on account of it's merits.
It has it's issues sure, but nothing that comes close to being considered a major con against it's abundance of pros.
I highly recommend buying this game, or at the very least, putting it onto a watch list and keeping a very close eye on it over the next few months to see just how well it is cared for for yourself.

OOOOooo.  This one was a hard one to review.  Keep in mind I have never palyed the other Amnesia game nor the Penumbra games.
For the first like 80% of the game, I was really only impressed with the nice graphics and way the game moved.  Allbeit, it chugged on my dated dual core CPU but worked okay once i set it at 720P.
Even on my laptop A10 quad it chugged, so best to have at least an nice 3+ quad to run it at 1080P.   So, it looked nice.  BUT. It was becoming a walking simulator with a few spooky things here and there - a few jump scares ( thank god not too many ) and super duper easy to figure out puzzles.  If you have FOV issues, this will give you a headache,  it did me.  Could only play a bit at a time.
Now, then at the 80% I was thinking to myself - "it's sorta nice with the well written story, just not really scary".
A lot of work went into this game, it's not just slapped together.  I waited for more.  And then....kinda past the point where you meet some actual piggies - and they don't really kill you as you re-spawn right about where you died - it started getting seriously creepy.  Not in the "boo!" sense, but storywise it did not turn out exactly how I had envisioned.  I won't spoil it.
The mood changes as you get horrid scenes of death, massacre, waterfalls of blood!, chased from piggues A LOT, and then just the vile realization of what the guy is and what he did.  It's nota  " OH. MY. GOD" surprising horror feel, but you'll get a definte "Man, that's like really sick. " out of it.  And then the ending...i thought it was over, but kept going.  And I personally liked it.  It does not rush and not does stay to long in one area.  Well paced for what feels mostly like it was stretched a bit at the end.   You have to esacpe from certain clutches and sneak around Hitman style somewhat without any weapons...I liked that the most.  Puzzles, etc just kept me busy but I really liked sneaking rather than kill kill kill bang bang bang which is what most scary games involve ( Rez Evil 5 on up I am looking at you ).  It kept me going to the end.  So, for my $0.02 it's worth it...for $5. Honestly, a $20 price tag?  C'mon.  $15 would have been better to start.  $5 on sale for me was justified.

I love this game, find it to be very enjoyable, and reccomend it to any fps lover, but I also have to say some things to pottential buyers. First, in my opinion, Borderlands is the better game. If you have been looking for a well-made, not too serious but still gritty, fps go buy the first game; the only games I can think of to compare it to are Mad Max and RAGE. Borderlands 2 improves upon the gunplay and abilities but loses any grit and solitude and replaces it with goofier enemies and terrible jokes written for 12 year olds.
Here's a breakdown of my exact thoughts.
What I liked better in Borderlands 2:
The gun variety- They really amped up the ante when it comes to how many different types of guns you can get in this game. I really enjoy all the wacky effects you get with uniques. I also like how powerful you feel when you use some of the legendaries. Also MORE LEGENDARIES!!!!
The classes- They improved all of the classes and I enjoy them more than the originals.
The bosses- I appreciate just how many tough bosses there are in this game, especially enjoy the amount of raid bosses. I will add one issue to this since it does not apply to the first game- Every single boss is, "Invincible" like come on, you can come up with better epithets than that. Here I'll do some: Terramorphus the Unstopable, Pyro-Caustic Pete the Immortal, Hyperious the Indestuctable, Master Gee the Wise. That was just a huge pet peeve of mine  ¯\_(ツ)_/¯
Main antagonist of the main campaign-Handsome Jack is awesome, I loved every moment I got of him.
Things I liked better in Borderlands:
The tone of the first game. While I know a lot of people had issues with the first game, mainly that they neede to be walked through a story and couldn't piece it together themselves, I loved every moment of it. The first game had this real desolate feeling to it. Borderlands gives you this very real sense of issolation. You don't feel like a super badass when you first start out. You feel like a merc who came to a planet seeking fortune only to find out how dangerous the world you are on truly is. I hate the feel of the second game.
The music: The dry guitar will always be better for me than the constant dubstep, and my favorite type of music is electronic so I'm not just a music enthusiast.
CL4P-TP/Claptrap- He was barely in the game and he said almost nothing. Prefer it that way.
The side characters- Most of them didn't talk, when I was younger I wanted them to talk and move. I got Borderlands 2 and I wanted them to stop talking again. Also they ruined Scooter. in the first game he was pretty funny and interesting, second game his brain regressed to an unrecognizable state.
The DLC antagonists- General Knoxx is tied for the best when it comes to antagonists in this series. He was a grumpy, borderline suicidal old soldier that you would love to have as your grandfather. Also hearing him read out what he had to deal with when it came to his commanding officer always put a smile to my face. Oh will admit that I enjoyed Claptrap as the villain in the final DLC.
The writing- Borderlands' story was more enjoyable for me b/c of the lack of story, I was more focussed on exploring anyway. The humor was also better and it came in bursts. Borderlands 2 was written for teenagers and people with under-developed brains. This is how I look at Borderlands 2, I found it kind of funny when I was 16 but now I'm in my 20's and most of the jokes pi.ss me off rather than make me laugh.
The cars- The cars drove better, did more damage, died less frequently, and felt like they were on the ground instead of floating.
Borderlands: Better tone, better music, better writing (imo), better humor, better DLC villains, better side characters, very little Claptrap, and better driving
Borderlands 2: Better gunplay, better abilities, better story plot, better main antagonist, better boss battles
Boderlands the Pre-Sequel: Stop

I really don't write a lot of reviews, like, at all. But I enjoyed this game so much; it physically compelled me to do so. Rarely has a video game caused me to spout praises about it to millions of strangers on the interwebs. This one did, big time.
It's hard to talk about this game without mentioning the stylized presentation. Transistor shows influences from Supergiant's previous game, Bastion. Whereas Bastion's toon-like presentation contrasted with the somber themes the game explored, in Transistor, the developers made the game feel almost impressionistic. Cutscenes and plot elements are introduced in parts and pieces on a background palette of neon lights and gilded society. Much like how Bioshock gives you the choice of picking up optional voxaphones, the clarifying parts of Transistor's story are introduced via optional newscasts and recordings. The female protagonist looks like she stepped out from the Roaring Twenties, and the game feels and plays like a jaunt through The Great Gatsby if the book also featured murderous enemies at every turn. The protagonist's accomplice will narrate and banter with her throughout the game. Plot elements are introduced organically, and it's almost too easy to feel the emotions behind choices and actions the protagonist takes despite her being pretty much mute for the entire game. I found myself satisfied in almost every artistic aspect.
The original soundtrack. Is. Awesome. The writter and producer of the soundtrack, Darren Korb, describes the music as "old-world electronic post-rock." Ashley Barrett, who sings many of the lyrical songs in the game, is suberb at giving the protagonist's (past) voice. The music strikes that rare balance where if you stop to appreciate it, it may just steal your breath away, but it's never intrusive when you're getting mauled by enemies in the heat of battle. Narration by the protagonist's accomplice is sassy, hilarious, conversational, and at times heartwrenching. It gives a sense of how the two interacted with one another in the past. Other characters who make appearances are memorable and unique; each character has their own linguistic quirks that differentiate their speakers. Nothing cookie cutter here.
Combat is tight, clean, and rewarding. Gameplay happens in real-time, but the protagonist has the ability to pause time and lay out a series of combat moves reminiscent of KOTOR or X-Com. Battle abilities are acquired sequentially through plot and with every level the protagonist gains, and they can be mixed and matched to create endless variability, damage potential, and combat philosophies. Each ability is linked with character backstory that is unlocked through use, which encourages you to try novel combinations of skills. Enemies scale in difficulty reasonably and foes behave logically. They will heal damaged allies. They will buff their tank as he smashes your face in. And they will cause headaches for you if you aren't careful. For added challenge, the game features handicaps that make gameplay much harder but will reward the protagonist bonus experience. There is also a built-in, plot appropriate haven of sorts that the protagonist can access for scenario battles and a sandbox practice mode. After the first playthrough, you have the option of starting over again with a game-plus mode, retaining all progress with enemies starting out much stronger. It is one of the few games where I didn't think twice about playing the game again right after I beat it. And I played it until I got every single achievement and searched every single corner. It made me neglect basic necessities like eating. And sleep. And personal hygiene. And I didn't mind.
While writing this review, it was actually quite difficult for me to separate discrete pieces of this game into music, gameplay, etc. It is such a well integrated package that one aspect is in complete alignment with another. Gameplay introduces plot. Narrative augments gameplay. And the art pulls you into the gameplay. And the feels. Oh, does this game have the feels. The only other game that I can remember that has left me feeling like this is Portal. They are both a bit on the shorter side in terms of gameplay length, but the density of gameplay is tremendous. The white dwarf star of games really. Every moment feels meaningful, nothing is drawn out. There are no ♥♥♥♥♥♥ parts to this game. It is pure, concentrated fun with a shot of the feels right where it hurts. But it hurts so good.
10/10 would (and did) play this game again (and again). And I honestly think this game is worth its full retail price.

Have you tried Bastion? If you have, why are you even reading this review? Just buy Transistor already!
The artwork of transistor is largely in the same style as Bastion. That means pretty damn good, for those who hasn't played Bastion. The music is great, and if you paid attention to the lyrics, there's a fair bit of foreshadowing in them. There's nothing in the aesthetics of the game that should deter you from buying Transistor.
However, it's in the game mechanics that Transistor really shines. Like any normal RPG, you run around, shoot, and hack enemies until they drop dead. Except that now you can freeze time as well. When the time is frozen, you get to plan out your next few moves, stringing together devastating combos. Each skill costs a certain amount of energy, listed as a bar at the top of the screen. To prevent massive abuse, there is a short (approximately 5 seconds) cooldown period before you can use most of your skills again. But I spam it all the same.
The customizability of Transistor is truly amazing. Your weapon has four active slots, each active slot comes with two upgrade slots. Along with that, there are four passive slots as well. As you progress along, you pick up 'functions' which give your weapon different fighting abilities. Each function can be placed into either one of the active, upgrade, or passive slot, alowing immense customization. The game actually forces you to try different builds, as each function comes with its own lore. To unlock all three parts, you have to have equipped the function in all three slots at least once. So you have this skill that you'd really love in your weapon active slot, and in the passive slot? On your second playthrough, you get to earn the skill again. Double the functions, double the fun!
As with Bastion, Transistor has a very forgiving, but highly scalable combat system. If you're terrible at RPGs like me, Transistor initiates an emergency turn before your health hits zero to save your♥♥♥♥♥from being kicked by The Jerk. Of course, if you really suck, you still 'die', although all it does is to make you temporarily lose one of your active skills. You get 'Limiters' as you level up in the game. Much like the gods of Bastion, enabling the limiters on your weapon gives a boost to your enemies. If the game is too easy, stack up all 10 limiters and try it again.
The storyline of transistors is very linear, without any sidequests. Not that I feel this diminishes the game in any way, I'm just stating that theres only one path to reach the endpoint. There are a handful of optional battles, but that's about it. In the Cloudbank, the world of Transistor, there are many computer terminals which you have the option to interact with. This doesn't further the story in any way, but does help to paint a picture of what is going on. The ending of Transistor is not as ambiguous as Bastion, however, the entire world of Transistor is much more open to speculation.
The only thing I hoped Transistor had is a sandbox allowing you hack down waves of enemies. It's as though there's all this possibilities of different weapon setup, but nothing to try it out on. Sure, you could replay the whole game again, but sometimes you're just lazy and want to stand in one spot to try out new builds for your weapon.
Oh by the way, there's a hum button. Because screw the bad guys and all those bots chasing me down, sometimes all I want to do is stand around and hum a tune.

I wasn't a big fan of Just Cause 1 or 2. The first game caught my interest because - released in 2006 - its huge world and addition of flying and driving mechanics were still novel additions to the FPS genre. Its gameplay wasn't particularly well done and its world was fairly shallow, but the scale and newness of the franchise were enough to carry the game. Just Cause 2 upped the ante with an even larger world and the addition of a grappling gun (a feature singularly uninteresting to me, but apparently a fan favorite). The story and characters were even more ridiculous than the first but it kept me interested enough to invest the necessary 30 hours or so to complete the game.
I tired of Just Cause 3 in less than two hours.
I know there are a lot of people who get undue joy from the destruction and chaos they can wreak on the virtual world and I will be the first to admit the game utilizes some impressive technology. It's not quite up to the high-water mark set by the Red Faction games, but I quiet enjoyed being able to blow apart guard towers, fortress walls and giant dish antennas. The action can get quite frenetic and the gunplay is solid, if not particularly noteworthy. But beyond that, there really wasn't much to keep me invested in the game.
That the characters would be annoying caricatures was evident just from the introduction, and they did little to improve themselves during gameplay. The setting remained as superficial as ever; for all its vast scope, there's little to differentiate one tiny village from the next; they are all hollow shells whose only purpose is to serve as liberation points. Too much of the game is locked behind in-game challenge modes, few of which were enjoyable and all broke the game's feeling of immersion. Odd control choices and unequal game performance didn't help, nor did the brain-dead AI. The game feels far more a chore than a fun experience.
I'll admit, the two hours of blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up and killing the moronic AI weren't completely without merit, but - even at the sharp discount I received - it's not enough. I purchased the game at an 80% discount and I still don't think I got value for my money.

A breath of fresh air in the MMO scene, or rather, a reminder of what it was that made MMOs popular in the first place.
What makes FFXIV:ARR so good, is not what it does have, but rather what it doesn't.
Gimmicks.
Ever since World of Warcraft became such a large player in the MMORPG scene, competitors have risen which attempt to dethrone it with new and "exciting" mechanics, but in doing so forget what an MMO even is.
FFXIV:ARR learns from the mistakes of others and sticks to the known strengths of the genre. The holy trinity of Tank/DPS/Healer, Strong and challenging end-game content, deep storyline and world lore, an abundance of content to sink your time into along with major content patches every 2 and a half months.
It should be noted, that major content patches in FFXIV:ARR usually contain the same amount of content an expansion for WoW would contain at launch.
Yes, the game has a subscription model, but given the spetacular failures of numerous F2P and Cash Shop MMOs that have popped up over the years, combined with how this money is funneled into frequent and high quality updates to the game, is this really a bad thing? Honestly, it's well worth the money.
However FFXIV:ARR doesn't just stick to old core values, it does so while breating new life into them that don't undermine their integrity. The holy trinity of MMOs is refered to as holy for a reason, to mess with it is to dance with certain doom. FFXIV:ARR conquers this perplexing problem regarding the need for re-interpretation without becoming gimmicky by altering the way experience works in the game.
In traditional MMOs, you make a character, you select your class and you start getting experience points. As you gain experience, your character levels up thus expanding your capabilities with your selected class, until you hit max level then you move to end-game content.
XIV:ARR does away with character experience, instead replacing it with class experience. You have an active class, determined by the weapon you are wielding and any experience gained will go into the experience pool for your active class. You don't level your charcter, you level your class. For example, I'm currently a level 50 conjurer, specialising in the advanced healing class "White Mage" and I am also at the same time a level 18 Thauterage, the predecessor to the DPS class "Black Mage".
This doesn't make me some weird DPS/Healer hybrid, I can only be one at any one time. If I have a WHM weapon equipped, I'm a WHM and I have access to all the abilities of a WHM of my level and can equip gear for my class. I do not however have access to abilities for classes I have also leveled (except certain cross-class abilities which are sort of how this game does talents) nor can I equip gear meant for a Black mage while I have my white mage active. At the same time, when I switch to my black mage, it is as if I am a fresh character still leveling and only at level 18, the fact I have a class at max level does not affect my game play at all.
This is great since it allows for alts without having to give up your character, your identity, your friends, your guild etc, you have it all in one place, without ever undermining the holy trinity.
FFXIV:ARR shows that it's possible to approach MMORPGs with a "Don't fix what isn't broken" philosophy without simply remaking yet another WoW.
On a final note? I pre-ordered the imperial edition for The Elder Scrolls Online, that set me back $75 USD, I did that before I started playing this and you know what? I've decided to just swallow that purchase and play this instead.
It's THAT good.
Saying all that however, the game is certainly not without it's faults.
FFXIV:ARR is a remake of the 2010 game FFXIV, which frankly? Was absolutely terrible.
The original game suffered from poor UI, poor world design, a dull and slow (Even by MMO standards) storyline and terrible optimisation leading to significant technical issues.
There is only so much you can do with this and this shows when we look at the current game world.
The current world is made up mainly of what was the original open game world which has had the massive bloat cut from it, the areas worth keeping turned into zones which are seperated by zone transitions.
These aren't instanced, which is good, but still it does break immersion a bit.
Thankfully, this isn't likely to be an endearing issue as developers have acknowledged the size of the world which though acceptable, could use a bit more to it and have said that we will be seeing significant increases to the world's size in major expansions (the first of which is expected in the second or third quarter of 2014).
There are also some key class types which are noticably absent from the game, for example the stealthy ambusher, (thief, rogue, ninja etc), however once again the developers have acknowledged this issue and said plans are in place to bring in new classes in future patches and expansions.
Typically, I would count this as a major negative when forming my opinion on a game but I have been very impressed with how reliable Square-Enix are for following through on promises and fixing or introducing things where needed.
So I'm willing to take their "We are aware of this and we have plans in motion to meet these requests" in good faith, something I am VERY hesitant to extend to many if not most game developers these days.
Overall?
FFXIV:ARR is the equivilent of a miracle in gaming. Not only rescuing a title otherwise doomed to ridicule, but improving it to such an extent that it deserves a place in the genre's historybooks on account of it's merits.
It has it's issues sure, but nothing that comes close to being considered a major con against it's abundance of pros.
I highly recommend buying this game, or at the very least, putting it onto a watch list and keeping a very close eye on it over the next few months to see just how well it is cared for for yourself.

What starts off as an entertaining little arcade shooter ends up filling a void I never realized was missing. As someone who doesn't often touch a modern FPS game, I may not have a whole lot of experience to describe why I think this game is worth so much more in $15 than most games earn for the $60 they demand, but I can at least describe why I love this game immensely.
To start, it's a fairly linear narrative-driven shooter, and that alone would have put me off in the light of Medal of Battle: Dutyfield games that have defined the genre in the past couple generations. But this game manages to stand between the modern conventions of shooters and the classic mechanics I remember from sneaking onto our old Compaq PC to play Doom or Duke Nukem when I was supposed to be in bed.
Games these days can't get away with some kind of RPG progression system, but Gunslinger does away with the tedium of it by offering little perks that don't define how you play the game but just enhance it in non-essential ways. The exception would be the titual Gunslinger perk that allows you to dual-wield revolvers, with that being the only gain that offers a genuine mechanical difference. Otherwise, leveling up gives you slight advantages that make the game feel a bit more action-heavy and faster paced.
The levels in the game are surprisingly massive, which actually comes as a drawback to the experience, as in many cases I found myself lost until I hit a point where I was told I was leaving the story zone and had to turn around. Why these levels allow you to reach places so far from the objective is beyond me, as there is rarely anything to find outside of the scripted mission path. There are a load of secrets to find in each level, but they are placed in little nooks and crannies amidst the mission zone that it makes no sense to let you wander so far away.
The showdown mode, which stands in place of a boss fight in several levels, is what it is. You stand there, waiting and observing your enemy, baiting them to draw first yet finish last. It requires you to focus as much on your character as on your enemy, so there is a good bit of skill involved, but there is an artificial difficulty added by the immense sway of your crosshairs that is incredibly difficult to predict or compensate for. This system could use a lot of work, mechanically, but it's hard to fault them when I haven't quite seen anything like it since the original Red Dead Revolver, at the very least.
The gunplay is a load of fun. It's a fast-paced shooter where the simple objective is to out-bullet your enemies. Stealth is usually only a mechanic at the very beginning of a level - once you fire a shot, it's all out chaos. This is mitigated by a bullet-time mode that, with perks, can allow you to dodge bullets, line up headshots, and reload or swap weapons in a blink. Apart from that, the game occasionally sucks you into a QTE-mode to dodge bullets in a life-or-death scenario, or in scripted events that depend on precise reaction to button prompts to take out enemies quickly. I hate QTE's with a firm passion, but at least this game almost never relies on instant-death ones, instead requiring you to take them down the old fashioned way.
Being such an action-focused game, it's hard to believe that it has a surprisingly deep story. At first, the depth presents itself in its history-rich narrative, involving characters from classic American Western folklore, played up in a balance between recorded history and the first-hand account of an unreliable narrator. It's incredibly entertaining to watch how everything from the narrative to the enemies to the landscape itself gets reimagined as the player character recounts his tale to his imaginative audience. Your protagonist, Silas Greaves, presents his account of the downfall of just about every famous Western outlaw or folk hero as he regales his tale of revenge. How much truth you choose to derive from his boasted tale is up to you, but it all culminates in a unique opportunity to define how it all ends.
TLDR version: Gunslinger is a fast-paced, action-packed shooter with a simple narrative that nevertheless drew me in deep and left me with a burning desire for more games of its caliber. I dearly hope that this franchise (which I will admit I've never played before this game) continues in such a direction, as I have not played such a compelling and satisfying single-player shooter in a very, very long time.

*Sigh* Where to begin. I have been a fan of Final Fantasy franchise for more than a decade, and have played WoW for a while, so I will compare WoW and FF14 and see how FF14 stacks up against WoW.
First of all, graphics. I think FF14 is visually gorgeous looking, and this is most likely the most advanced MMORPG in terms of graphics. PC optimization is well done as well, so I think a lot of PCs with weak GPU can run this game. In fact, my PC is not even a gaming PC to begin with, and yet, the graphics still look amazing.
Gameplay. Well, I was aware of the fact that the new producer of FF14 learned a lot from WoW to create 2.0, and well, I guess that kind of shows in the game. The quests function more like WoW now, when 1.0 was more of endless grinding and all. But my goodness, I am not sure if it is just me, or also the same for the others, but at level 15 or something, I have lost interest in this game, as I had to keep doing boring quests in the places that are always the same spots. In WoW, you move on to a new map if you are done with the quests in that region and basically there are many places to explore in WoW but this game? I don't really think the map is all that different from 1.0? Is it? Sure, some places look different. But honestly, can you tell me that the map is big in this game? Because it's not. The game focused way too much on graphics, it totally ruined the size of the map.
Story. Is there a story in this game? WoW has a story for "every" race, but what about this one...? It just shows some cut scenes that say "oh, you are strong. You might be that some hero or something blah blah" and such, and seriously, that crap is getting old. The story is....compared to something like FF7, FF8 or FF10, this game fails, miserably (And what's up with the opening scene, where it reminds me of the opening scenes of Skyrim?)
Yes, I have played this game since 1.0, and that really was one of the worst games I had ever played. So, I was basically looking forward to this game, as I have been a big fan of FF franchise, and SE stated that they promise they will bring a better one with 2.0. But really? All I can say is, this game is not something that I would pay 10 or 15 dollars a month for, it is more like a free to play game at the very least.
The story is not there. It is, just NOT there. And the quests should at least be a bit more entertaining. I already am aware of the fact that the Square-Enix today is not really capable of making decent games anymore (I mean, FF13-2? FF13-3? Really? WHO said we wanted those? And I actually bought FF13-2, and I stopped playing after playing for 30 minutes). So, really wow, I do not see the point of paying monthly fees to play this game. I basically can not find the same quality that can be seen in FF7, 8 and 10. So how is this even called "Final Fantasy"?
And the endgame contents? Is there any?
Maybe the game will get better later on. Who knows. But all I can say is that, I would never play this game again.

I don't mean to demean Techland but, given the checkered history of the Call of Juarez series, Gunslinger is better than it has any right to be. The soundtrack is an excellent mix of bluegrass and rock with both electric and acoustic guitar abound, augmented by percussion driven sequences to drive the action along.

One of the most fun FPS I've played in a while. Mechanics are solid, the story is interesting. I even read all the nuggets of truth because they were so interesting to read. The game really sells its atmosphere. It really encourages you to go guns blazing most of the time. I think one of the reasons the gun play is so enjoyable is because there aren't any automatic weapons. Bullets in this game feel more significant, especially with the edge of death mechanic where you're able to dodge a bullet that would've ended you. Good voice acting, and good times all around.

First off, yes, this is a ubisoft game and it doesn't have UPlay as a feature jammed up it's throat, let us rejoice!
I absolutely loved this game! Solid gunplay and nice mechanics that make it a bit more interesting, like some sort of 'focus' mode that let's you highlight and shoot the ever loving f*ck out of baddies.
The storytelling is definitely the strongest point of this game, you go along Silas' stories and meet interesting characters (that existed in the ACTUAL wild west) along the way. It's a very linear experience though, with little to no exploration or sidemissions in the storymode, sure there are the extra challenges that you can access in the main menu but those will give you 6 hours of extra playtime at most (or like 25 hours if you're a perfectionist like me).
I did like the inclusion of "New Game Plus" which let's you keep all your upgrades while starting a new storymode, which still made it worth replaying once or twice.
That brings me to another weakness of this game: you can play through the entire storymode in about 3 hours, so while it's a fun game to knock out in one sitting (believe me, I just did, for the 3rd time) It doesn't hold much replay value other than bragging rights for completing the game on all difficulties, which even at the highest difficulty level, isn't all that hard.
While it's a short and linear experience you find yourself shooting and blasting through, it does look pretty, with cell-shaded graphics giving it a borderlands-ish feeling which I definitely liked, you can even make your guns look prettier by upgrading your skills and you'll end up with beautifully engraved and gold-plated machines of DEATH!
+Good graphics
+Good upgrade system (that let's you have nice and shiny weapons in the end)
+Great gunplay
+Interesting storyline
+Outstanding presentation of said storyline
+Interesting characters
+NO UPLAY
-Quite linear
-Not a lot of replay value
-Really short (you can knock this game out in 3 hours or so)
-Not difficult, even on the highest difficulty setting
Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a fun game, that is fun to play if you're looking for an easy, quick game to play, it's not gonna challenge you, test your abilities to the maximum but it's definitely a fun story-driven experience, no matter how short that is.

IMO there's more chance, with the way the publisher/dev are treating the game right now (minimal improvements, more cashgrabs), they're just trying to milk the remaining, dwindling playerbase of money to fund the mobile version which will likely then make them more money considering the massive mobile market especially in SEA.
