I am a total war fan and this game is sadly so casual, its ui and campaign map are designed to simplify it and focus on battles only. THe campaign maps on the other old games were rich, not perfect like paradox in complexity but enough to keep you busy and building your provinces and cities how you want them. Here is a logistical complicated and simplify mess where your cities don't matter but only for choosing efficient buildings that don't consume food and create negative public order. that is not freedom of choice, diplomacy is bad and simple.
The battles are ok formations work, and keeps thing organized, be careful with the mouse box it sometimes doesn't work and selects units instead of the group is a feature i hate because of misclicking on the heat of battle. Naval battles are a good addition not amazing but still fun.
Family tree is gone, senate tab is a confusing mess, like it was added last minute with no though. Armies have a limit, I left the game with max at 20 units for land and sea. The generals are not important in a sense of caring for them since they die of age too quick unless you mod this feature. Cities are pretty much boring the new system is province where all the value of the cities sums up in food production and public order, if neither is balance you have slave revolts or a random enemy take a city you left open. You can't control or upgrade garrison, it took me a while to understand that through specific buildings you create garrison. Again expanding is a pain since every building punish it you for that need more public order or more food. Tech tree is another after though very boring
Overall this Rome compared to the old one and worse compared with complex and rich mods like Total Realism and Barbarorum make this sh**T a mediocre and boring experience. Is sad how people like this without realising how much has been lost compared to the last Rome 1. I really don't recommend it to die hard fans, if still are curious buy it on sale otherwise from now do your research, find playthroughs and see if this and the new generation of Total War games is worthwhile. I mean why have a campaign map if you barely do anything to forge it has you see fit and you are forced to choose building that does not alter the food/public order, I try to play more hours to justify this review but the victories and playthrough feel so boring I couldn't keep up with this sad idea of how much Total War Rome 2 lost to simplify and satisfy the casual multiplayer market

"Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs", huh. Who could have thought that I will write a positive review for this game.
I actually bought it in bundle with the game I really loved - "Amnesia: The Dark Descent", so that was quite an accident.
I was kinda frustrated with all negative reviews for this game and I didn't want to play it or even watch a playthrough.
Well, that was unfair thing to do.
The reason people dislike this game is wrong expectations. Which is not someone's fault.
Gamers who played the first "Amnesia" liked it, because back in those days "Amnesia" was the scariest game ever made.
But the thing is - "Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs" was made by another team and they didn't really tried hard to make this part of the game scary. So when a lot of people haven't found the "scary component" they were disappointed.
But still "Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs" is pretty good game. I think it should be considered as an independent product. And that's it. Just give it a look from another angle.
The goal developers were trying to achieve is creating another game in "Amnesia World" . The game with diffirent characters, but with still with a great story inside. And this goal have been achieved.
This game is filled with the "Amnesia style" even if it's not scary. You can still feel this creepy atmosphere, the depressing mood and thoughts about man's sins and man's nature.
And without "scary component" developers created new "Amnesia". "Amnesia" with touching story.
There will be people who still don't like this game and that's their right. But as for me, I think "Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs" is a masterpiece. A little bit different. But a masterpiece.
I can't say that it's one of my favourite games. I can't say that it doesn't have drawbacks. But I can say that it still worth checking out. Unless you're afraid of making up your own opinion.

I've been avoiding reviewing this game, being my number one favourite I couldn't think of a way to make it unbiased. But after the resurgence of Open world games, the downfall of AAA and the battle between TF2 and Overwatch, I think I can finally pinpoint what makes it so beautiful.
The art style is an obvious starting point. Everything is cartoony and exaggerated, it's filled with colour and despite being cartoony it feels more realistic than the grim grisley greyness of Skyrim, Morrowind, Witcher etc. It's not perfect of course, with clipping and terrible lip sync but with the cartoony atmosphere it adds to the exaggerated charm that it provides.
The characters themselves are also important. If you compare how they were designed to Mass Effect: Andromeda, the way it has been presented is genius. There are a lot of gay characters, black characters, female characters- but these characteristics do not define who they are. The characters still have peronalities, they just happen to be these things- they are not just addons, it just adds to the depth of the world.
I suppose the most important thing in a game is the gameplay, and this Borderlands nails too. A lot of games can't tell whether they want to be simple or complicated, they can't tell what gimmicks they want to use, so they use everything and it turns into an incoherent mess like Undertale. Borderlands knows exactly what it wants to do. It's a Single Player or Co-Op FPS with RPG mechanics with levelling and loot systems. The RPG mechanics make it feel more open worldy than most open world games. It defines what towns exist, and gives you fast ways to get to them, and while games like Skyrim use the open world idea to make you travel for hours, Borderlands 2 just adds a lot of depth with; secret loot boxes, experience, Cult of the Vault logos or mini easter eggs.
Something that I noticed in my most recent playthrough is how much freedom you have throughout and how this can appeal to both new players and veterans. One example is the first area, the entirety of Southern Shelf. You fight Knuckle dragger, to a new player they find out how brilliantly designed the bosses will be: They aren't walls of health, they aren't stupidly damaging, they are balanced with weaknesses and phases. An expert player on the other hand could then debate whether they would want to farm Knuckle Dragger for the legendary pistol Hornet, or just move on. This can also be seen in Southern Shelf Bay when you have to kill Midgemong. A new player could rush right towards Midgemong or maybe explore the boats, while an expert player would take the long route around for some extra loot and instead of calling the bridge over to get across the lake, they can just run across the chain, significantly increasing the pacing and replayability of the game.
Of course Borderlands 2 isn't perfect, the majority of the fun is in the UVHM playthrough which is a DLC. The bugs might throw people off while I enjoy discovering two or three new ones every new playthrough. Even despite this, just the first playthrough with a friend is highly worth your time. Let's hope Borderlands 3 will be another great one. Iron out the issues of Borderlands 2, while still being able to provide replayability where Borderlands: The Pre-sequel couldn't.

I generally do not review games, but I NEED to review this.
I spent about 30 hours playing JC3 over the last month, as can be seen from my playtime. This was the SP campaign, I did not attempt MP because I did not care. I think that I'd have more fun if I tried it, but I am an SP person.
Yes, there were moments when it crashed on me (I did not lose progress, it was usually during missions, so I simply started them from the beginning) and yes, there were moments when the game paused because connection to the servers was lost, and yes, I do have a strong PC (i7 4770k, EVGA GTX 1070 SC, 32 GB RAM) so many of the optimization issues many other people experience were not there for me. There are many more problems with the game that I obviously never saw or noticed, so I cannot speak for those.
I will say however that I had a great time playing it and I enjoyed it immensely. Even the repetitiveness of liberating settlements was enjoyable, and the explosions, the variety of weapons, the dumb fun, the extremely good and detailed graphics and locations, make me want to come back to this game at some point in the future. The DLCs/expansions are also very good in terms of content as well as the rewards they give - the jetpack is a great addition and makes cars and the parachute obsolete.
Don't get me wrong, there's quite a few issues with the game that many other reviewers who had a negative experience with it, will point out. Personally I had so much fun that I am willing to overlook the roughly ten crashes I had.
I would recommend this game. For £15 it is a steal with the amount of fun you can have.
Edit: Just get it. Currently on sale for £7.

A surprisingly fun Source zombie game.  Yeah yeah, I know Steam's crawling with them but this game actually ends up being really suspenseful.  This analogy is done to death, but it really is like Left 4 Dead 1 with more dread.  Guns and their ammo are a rarity unless you know where to find them, melee is a struggle with every individual zed, and keeping everyone alive and in good health becomes problematic if there isn't a whole lot of trust going around (though that might be a plus if you're looking for drama and tension).
One of the mechanics this offers over most other similar games is the ability to actually be infected.  Having an infected person in the party flips everything on its head and causes everyone to think differently.  Rationing health items requires more time and thought, and scrounging for pills (an item that keeps it at bay temporarily) or gene therapy (an exceedingly rare item that cures it permanently) takes up more time and places your wellbeing further on the line.  A nice touch is the ability to put your gun to your head and take one for the team if you don't feel too lucky, but if you're out of guns or ammo you don't have such a luxury, so keep an extra round on you in case things go south.
The inventory is unique in its presentation; rather than a weight limit you have a scrollwheel with space being taken up by items.  This prevents inventory clutter while still encouraging organization.  Guns can be unloaded, ammo can be dropped in individual boxes rather than dropping the entire reservoir of 9mm.  Reloading throws away the whole mag (and all ammo in it) on higher difficulties, but funnily enough you can mitigate this by unloading the gun and then reloading it with a full mag.  This isn't advised when you're surrounded but if you're surrounded by dudes you're probably not going to have any shots left in the magazine anyway.
The ingame voice chat system functions on a realistic basis, people far away from you become harder and harder to hear (though this can be mitigated with the walkie-talkie item which takes up ammo or health item space) and dead people can't talk at all.  I haven't tried using the ingame chat in its entirely intended method at the moment, since my friends and I would be crippled if we couldn't talk to eachother at all distances, but we do shut off our mics when we die.  Being unable to talk when dead adds whole new levels of tension to the affair; if someone dies and they don't tell you, you might not even know.  They're just silent until the next round.
Unfortunately, movement gets clunky and the melee feels slow and sticky, guns are a bit of a fuss to aim but I let it slide since this is survival horror; combat isn't your main suit.  Granted having powerful weapons still turns tides drastically in your favor, but if you can't aim worth a damn and you're not paying attention, an obnoxious kid will bite your ankles and you'll turn in a matter of minutes.
It's not perfect and definitely a bit buggy and sometimes obtuse, but it's easily one of the best zombie games I've played, as it's one of the only ones I've played that does its job - it worries you, it makes you uneasy, and sometimes it can really scare you.

Dark Souls is one of my favorite games, and as such I've tried my very best to like Dark Souls 2 as well, but I just can't. So, if you're looking at this review wondering if you should get into the series with Dark Souls 1 or 2, my short answer is: absolutely avoid DS2.
I got into the series myself with DS2, but it gave me such a bad impression that I didn't bother to try DS1 until over a year later, only because of somebody else's insistence. Yet fast forward to today, and I'm on my third DS1 playthrough (and am also loving Bloodborne), while I've never even been able to stomach half of DS2 -- and I've tried, over half a dozen times.
DS2, to me, feels like more of a fan game than an actual sequel. I believe its main issues stem from the team (which was not led by the same person as DS1) wanting to uphold the series' misappropriated "omg so hard" image for some reason. To make this less rambly, here is a list of things.
Things I liked:
- Many individual levels have interesting and kinda cool concepts.
- I really liked the lore, despite its issues with relying way too much on "subtly" referencing DS1.
- The principles of the combat system are there and they are good.
- Well-optimized PC port, much better menus, good character creator.
- Dogs aren't literally satan.
Things that ruined my experience:
- Frustrating combat due to enemies' ridiculous movement tracking, annoying movesets, and your much less reliable rolls.
- Over-reliance on multiple-enemy encounters, even in boss fights, removing all challenge in favor of a test of patience.
- Plenty of weird level layouts with terrible flow, levels never loop back or feel interconnected.
- Occasional trolly moments that you can't anticipate, that will very possibly kill you.
Other things that I really disliked but can be ignored:
- World layout is nonsense and devoid of personality; You take an elevator up from the top floor of a decrepid windmill, directly into the sky, somehow landing you in Bowser's castle in the middle of a lava land.
- Nearly every enemy is a humanoid, probably a form of Large Knight.
- The plot makes no attempt, NPCs are lifeless, and who even are the bosses? You get nothing like Sif, Seath, or Nito here.
- Music is generally lackluster and unmemorable.
That's about it. I think a person who has no experience with DS1 *might* still enjoy this, though I see no reason to recommend DS2 over it; it's not more accessible. If you've played DS1 and didn't like it, this is NOT going to be better for you. I can only recommend this game if you liked DS1 *AND* you're not overly fussy about the mechanics.

FOTONICA is an adrenaline rush, at the very least. A high speed running game with one button as the sum total of a player’s control. Don’t think of that as a limitation. Quite the opposite. Since this is first and foremost a sensory experience type of game, deriving much from little, it would be unfortunate if even the smallest part of a player’s attention were taken from the screen.
The player, as “runner”, travels very minimalistic landscapes. Some are vaguely identifiable, such as rooms in a sort of building. (The more identifiable the terrain, the faster landscapes seem to go by as the eye/brain connection struggles for context.) The runner also jumps, but I hesitate to call this a platformer. It does have platformer characteristics, such as the pink dots one attempts to acquire by contact. And the varying size and levels of platforms. Some game levels, in fact, are almost entirely platforms. These are generally the more difficult; as players struggle to attain the secondary goal, SPEED.
The primary goal of FOTONICA is scoring points. Every run scores points, even those ending in failure (carefully recorded on the Statistics screen.) Points are composed of distance traveled, dots attained and how much of the distance was in “gold” mode, above 60 mps. (There may be exceptions beyond the lower levels I’ve seen so far.) There are numerous levels, each beyond the first being unlocked through performance (so I hesitate to give too many details.) As well, there are 4 skill levels. Though they have Italian names, I presume them to be Agile, Energetic, Furious and Impetuous. Perhaps someone can clarify. Each game level at each skill level has its own leaderboard. A player can seek their own ranking, overall, or compare with any friends that have played. In addition to Arcade mode, composed of various tracks or terrains to run, there is Endless (presumably as described, though hitting 10,000 points (oddly enough) does indicate “completion”, but not the end. Each Arcade level also has a point of completion in which the player joyously jumps into a world of horizontal lines, not tracks or platforms.) FOTONICA also includes a third mode, multiplayer, which I am unable to comment on at this time.
Each skill level is essentially an increase in speed, requiring different paths and strategies, often seeming almost as if a completely new level of the game involving new terrains. That’s the real excitement of FOTONICA, finding the BEST (perhaps only) path to the end, by exploring all the possibilities at the various speeds. Hints are offered. Sometimes the placement of a pink dot can offer a clue, as can the position of flag-like markers to indicate a jumping point. But be careful, sometimes a dot seems, at least at certain speeds, to sucker you into a dead end move.Very often the appropriate path or action is counterintuitive, such as jumping before maximum speed, in order to land more strategically. Or kicking off instead of running, for a similar purpose. Strange as it may sound, all movement is, as mentioned earlier, controlled by one button, ANY button. But that button does even more. It also controls landing from each leap, presumably to provide a smoother, less momentum disrupting transition. When at some point a leap goes too far, “the button” will also act to land the runner sooner (though at a cost to speed) to avoid leaping into space, the most common conclusion to a run. (After two days I have nearly 1,000 such “space leaps”.)
In real life I can’t run without a price, and have been severely limited in doing so for about 40 years. Perhaps that increases my enjoyment of this game. For others with limitations this game is nearly perfect with its simplicity of control and color. It also offers a feature by which a player can offset the timing of their input, in either direction, by 2 degrees each. This feature certainly deserves examination by any player, impaired or not.
The achievements are interesting and esoteric. One, in fact, is a total mystery, and the developers AREN’T talking. Ultimately what’s not to love in a game that gives an achievement for a huge number of face plants at high speed? (Which, incidentally, frequently leads to new discoveries.)
A great game to be played with or without external controls, for a minute or for hours. Portrait mode is suggested, though you’ll need familiarity with the menus first, as it seems to have been an afterthought. Perhaps not the greatest of its type, but a darn good one that I certainly suggest, especially if it’s still so cheap. Hope to see you there.

Fotonica is a surreal rail-runner, and while it´s clearly influenced by
(similar animations, Hands visible, moans), it is extremely unique. The gameplay mechanics are based on
. By holding it, you run foward and gain velocity (on the ground) or dash down (in the air) Releasing the button makes you jump.
I had my doubts when I was introduced to this concept, but it works pretty well: The overall steering is responsive, and even with a single button, you feel in control of your character´s movement. If you fall down, it´s your fault most of the time, not the game´s.
There is a total of ~10 levels in the game, each one playable in one of the 4 difficulties. The game is not unforgiving, and coming to a complete stop due to a collision doesn´t necessarily force you to restart the level. Your main objective is to get as fast as possible and collect as many red dots as you can in every level.
If you just run through every level to unlock the next one, the game will take ~1 hour. But the real satisfaction comes by trying out new routes, getting a new highscore and optimizing your "finger´s performance".
Every level is split into
, between which you can switch as you run. Split-second reflexes and good hand-eye coordination are reqiured to reach some harder (and more rewarding) passages.
The Soundtrack was created by 2 artists, and it fits perfectly in the game´s atmosphere; (mostly "Minimal"). Ambient sounds like moans, footsteps, and the characters breathing make the experience perfect. You can almost feel the wind in your face then you propel yourself into the air
The graphic style is very interesting, the devs have created a surreal and touching world with basically only 3 colors (white, gold, blue) The surroundings are diverse and in 3D, reaching from mountain paths to appartments, churches and so on.

No me canso de recomendar Alien Isolation. Es mucho más que un juego basado en el universo de Alien, es un producto que derrocha calidad por donde se lo mire: desde las detalladas representaciones de los entornos, hasta la escalofriante inteligencia artificial del Xenomorph que nos da caza. La criatura es imposible de matar, eso nos da una idea de adónde apunta este juego: a que nos sintamos constantemente bajo amenaza. Podemos matar a los Working Joes (androides) y a los humanos que eventualmente nos crucemos y presenten un problema, pero no hay manera de deshacernos completamente del Xenomorph, sólo podemos ahuyentarlo e intentar ser más listos que él. El hecho de no poder matarlo puede parecer una contra en este juego pero definitivamente no lo es, nos obliga a estar pensando un paso adelante siempre. Insisto con la inteligencia artificial: la criatura tiene mejor visión, mejor oído y sobre todo mejor olfato que cualquier otro enemigo del juego. Esto significa que si estamos escondidos y pasa lo suficientemente cerca nuestro podrá olernos y comenzar a buscar en la zona. Lo mismo sucede si tenemos el detector encendido: los beeps los escuchamos nosotros... pero también él.
En definitiva: es uno de los mejores survival horrors y de los mejores juegos ambientados en el universo Alien que he jugado.

This game is the pure definition of horror.
A lot of people give this game hate, and I can understand why people might dislike this one as opposed to The Dark Decent. A Machine For Pigs takes away quite a few of the main gameplay factors from the first, such as the sanity meter, your inventory, and lantern oil (your lantern never dies out). A Machine For Pigs also is not as 'frightening' as The Dark Decent, there are FAR less "fall out of your seat" scares in this one, but A Machine For Pigs greatly makes up for all of this.

The horror in this game comes from the atmosphere and the story. It's no doubt one of the most atmospheric games I have ever played, and sometimes atmosphere subtlety delivers that dread and pit in your stomach that nothing else can. I have to say that the scenery is almost perfect, the lighting, the shading, the textures, hell all of it. Except for the water, but thats not a bother unless you're an uptight nitpicking jackass.
And as for the story, it left me speechless almost the entire way. It builds up fantastically. There were moments where I had to pause the game and process what I had just seen or discovered, and when the climax comes around it will leave you shouting "what the ♥♥♥♥ is happening" for 20 minutes straight, but not the confused "what the ♥♥♥♥ is happening" the in complete shock kind.

To wrap it all up, if you appreciate the more subtle and atmospheric scares, this is 100% worth playing. However, if you're hoping for the same gut-wrenching chases and scares like the last game, maybe pass. This one is all about suspense, atmosphere, and being as disturbing as possible. It's very difficult to compare the two Amnesia games because of the approach to scare the player, so I can't say which is better. But in my opinion, I give A Machine For Pigs an 8/10.

Where Amnesia The Dark Descent excelled at scares and intense gameplay, Amnesia A Machine For Pigs is wonderful with story and atmosphere. This is coming from somebody who was a huge fan of The Dark Descent. Amnesia A Machine for Pigs seems to be far more of an exciting sequel to Dear Esther fans than it is to Dark Descent. This game is far simpler than Dark Descent. They have taken away limited light sources, sanity, and almost everyhing so that you can focus on getting through the game. This game does a fantastic job of building up the tension with an atmosphere, sound, and story, which I believe, is far better than it was in Dark Descent but does not really do much to scare you at the end of all the tension. This isn't a game I would replay for the scares as I have done plenty of times with Dark Descent but everyone should definitely check this game out. This game has some interesting mechanics that help it stand out. First off, the multiclassing system is pretty neat. At around level 10 your character gains the ability to level up in other classes simply by equipping the weapon associated with that class. All of your stats and gear can also be independently associated with those other classes, which basically means that other than race, gender, or name, you can experience all the content of the game with just one character.
The graphics are quite nice, although not spectacular. The textures are a bit soft and the game has a fairly stylistic, cartoony feel. However, aesthetically the game is beautiful. There's not a single ugly character to be found anywhere, except perhaps the giant or tiny races, and that just depends on your taste.
Combat doesn't stray far from standard "Diku-MUD" style tab-targeting / hotbar combat like you'd find in almost any other MMO since EQ. They do manage to mix it up a bit, however, with attack chains and synergies, encouraging you to mix up your rotation depending on the situation. Many enemies also telegraph their attacks, which is a trend that is becoming more and more common in the genre.
Questing is fairly standard, with only a few very special quests featuring cutscenes or voiceovers. Quest objectives usually consist of escorts, defending against waves of enemies, run and fetch, click on various sparkly objectives scattered around, or kill X number of mobs. Again, this is pretty much what you'd expect from almost any MMO.
There are a few interesting twists on the standard questing model, however. Scattered around the gameworld are various public quests called "Duties" which usually automatically activate once you get in range. Sometimes they're triggered by speaking to an NPC. These work almost exactly like the public quests of Guild Wars 2 or the rifts and invasions in Rifts. Aside from that, each class has a monster journal which tracks various enemy kills. The enemies you need to kill in order to fulfill the various objectives in your journal are marked with a special icon, and when you complete a set, you get a fairly decent amount of XP. This makes it fun to just run around hunting for these mobs and doing the public quests.
Speaking of mobs, the enemy designs are fantastic. The various types of creatures you're likely to encounter often have surprising and very creative designs. This is fairly typical for Asian MMO's, but fairly rare here in the West. This, combined with the beautiful character designs, is where FFXIV shows its chops by blending Eastern and Western sensibilities to create a compelling overall experience.
There's also a player housing system, and although I haven't tried them myself, I hear the dungeon encounters are really well done.
All that said, I find that this game hasn't really managed to get me hooked for some reason. Maybe it's the stale controls and format, which is almost too reminiscent of almost every other mainstream MMO of the past 15 years. Another problem is the quest tracker. While it's pretty good about showing you where quest objectives are on your map, if you have quests located in another zone, it's not always easy to figure out where to go. I also found myself frequently having to do a lot of backtracking. I'd be questing around in a certain zone until I'm too low for the content. Then  I'd have to run all the way back to a central area and then head off in a different direction to find quests I missed which by then would be several levels below me. This might not be as much of an issue if you're not a completionist and you decide to do more leveling with the duty and achievement system, or you've already leveled up a couple times and you're more familiar with where the quest hubs are. I guess I've gotten too spoiled by "breadcrumb" style questing, which was first popularized by WoW.
I decided not to pick up a subscription and continue past the trial. This is a great game, don't get me wrong, but it's just not for me. There are too many great games out there to justify another subscription. I'm already subscribing to 3 or 4 other MMO's that I rarely ever play.  Personally, I think a better model would be for MMO's to let pre-pay, maybe at a rate of 5 or 10 cents per hour for full VIP access. Then you can spend those hours however and whenever you like, without the pressure to keep playing to justify your subscription.
Do I recommend this game? Yes, if you're looking for an MMO with tons of content and features that you can sink hundreds of hours into, absolutely. If you're a "one-game" type of person and you're looking for a great fantasy MMO, you can't go wrong with this one. However, if you have a huge steam library and/or you're already subscribed to one or two other MMO's, this one doesn't really offer anything new and interesting enough to justify another subscription. Even though I'm uninstalling, I'm still going to give this game a thumbs up. Square Enix really did an excellent job and they deserve kudos.

Fun at first, but you soon realize that the entire game is the same. Over and over again, you shoot faceless mooks. It's almost a rail shooter. And there is almost no enemy variety; you don't really care if they are firing a pistol, or two pistols, or a rifle, or a shotgun, because you deal with them all the same way. The only enemies that require an ounce of awareness to kill are the ones with shields, which come with a gaping hole right in front of their face to shoot through. The enemy AI is pretty basic; take cover, shoot, with each enemy usually running back and forth between two different cover. They don't flank you or ambush you or line up careful shots; they either shoot blind, or step out and shoot like a light gun game at an arcade. There IS an RPG element, but it's very shallow, most of the skill gains are just minor boosts, and you barely notice them. Oh, but if you want all the XP, you have to hunt down "Nuggets of Truth", little factoids about the real Wild West; these are literally the only reason not to just run straight from fight to fight, because these things are increasingly hard to find, buried in little corners, perched high up on a little plank, way off at a dead end path. They do nothing to contribute to the actual story, they just give you more XP. And as for the story...it's kind of fun, inventing a new character and weaving his story into the real lives of numerous Wild West legends, but it starts to become a drag. The narrator talks too much, he gets into pointless tangents, and the game refuses for far too long to actually explain to us who our hero is. Starting in median res I can understand, but he just keeps hitting the action notes without getting around to explaining what our motivation is, why we are killing hundreds of people and criss-crossing one of the largest countries on earth. Oh, and then there's the dueling; mostly easy, very tedious. As for weapon options, they have a tendancy not to give you the ones you want, which is stupid in a game that has you spending XP to unlock weapon-specific skills. That said, there's only 7 guns, one of which is extremely rare, so there's not much going on, and the pistols aren't really THAT different from each other. Bullettime works fine, although I'd argue it charges and burns out too fast, because when I really felt like I needed it, it was never enough, so it mostly just sat there unused. And the shooting mechanics themselves are mostly fine, but it, frustratingly, it is possible to miss even with a dead-on shot, for some reason. Also, bullets do catch the edge of hit boxes pretty easily, so don't try shooting through a hole in the wall or just barely around a corner, it doesn't work.
Yeah, short review, but this game was literally fun for two hours, then I just kept playing expecting, just, more; more story, more enemies, more fun, but no, that well had run dry, it was just the same formula over and over again, precious little variety, and looking for those stupid collectibles really got irritating after the first few levels.

What made the Dark Descent such a wonderful game was the exploration. You would get immersed in the world having to search high and low for oil, tinderboxes, and keys. Machine for Pigs completely removed the exploration from Amnesia. You just keep going forward while letting the story unfold around you. You don't feel like you are in this world; you just feel like a bystander watching everything happen around you. You don't explore at all, you just go on the linear path the game has set up for you to follow exactly. Go watch a scary movie, because this game has just as much gameplay as a watching a movie.

I'm not sure if it's because I was new to the franchise, and had to fumble my way around figuring things out for the first Amnesia, but I clocked about 12 hours in the original. While I only clocked around around 5 hours for A Machine for Pigs. However, I think it has to do a lot with cutting a lot of filler rooms to explore, and giving you a straightforward path for the most part, and to be fair, I was speed running this one and really didn't take my time like I did with the first one. Don't misunderstand me, there's still a bit of puzzle solving here and there, and running from enemies much like in the original.
What this game does not contain however, resource management and sanity effects have been removed. This was the only feature I really missed, and you can't really move as many objects as you could in the previous title. Despite the seemingly downgraded gameplay, I found the story itself to be far more personal and enjoyable than that of Daniel. The atmosphere itself is still incredible, and the creepy sounds and psychological aspects are still present, although in a different fashion.
Anyway, if you're a fan of the many custom stories of Amnesia, or you are a diehard Amnesia fan, and or like light gaming and RPG horror type games, and prefer more story over gameplay, then I say get this title. If you're the type to read every note, letter then you should enjoy taking your time and really taking in the story.
However, I strongly advise avoiding this one if you prefer action, guns, and don't like puzzles. This is a different kind of feast, and one some will enjoy, and many others will not. If you know the difference between classic Resident Evil and RE4, or if you know the difference The Last of Us over Silent Hill, then you're more than likely the type to enjoy A Machine for Pigs...if you're someone who preferred RE4 and up over the classic titles, well, this isn't going to be very fun for you.
Basically, if all you want is a good horror story and don't care too much about the gameplay, then by all means, get this one and play through it.

Overall Tree of Savior is a good game with its fair share of problems. Despite the current flaws, it's still been a fun experience so far. If you're considering trying it, I think you should go ahead and give it a shot.
Pros:
+
. I'm constantly enthralled by the scenery of almost every map I'm in.
+ Fantastic soundtrack.
+ Large variety of classes with a large amount of combinations. Several classes have a very unique feel. Of course, not all builds are created equal.
+ Nostalgic for RO players. If you enjoyed RO, you'll likely enjoy ToS.
+ Game requires some actual exploration, most quests you will find by talking to NPCs, not by looking for quest markers. There's a few maps throughout the game that are more like puzzles than regular quest maps. You are also rewarded for exploring such as getting 100% map exploration, or finding and completing collections. You can occasionally find things like statues that give you an extra stat point.
+ Personally, I enjoy the storyline and I look forward to seeing how it will progress.
+ I do see IMC making changes that have improved things and answering player concerns. (Drop in token price, allowing non-token users to trade, better ability to block and report bots....) However these changes have felt slow so some people say IMC doesn't listen ever or fix anything.
Cons:
- Still has a fair amount of bugs that should have been handled sooner. (i.e. party quest bug at the time of writing this)
- Restrictions made to fight bots/gold sellers have more of a negative impact on players than actual bots. I am hopeful this will change someday in the future..
- Not a con for me, but for others. ToS requires some research before jumping into the game if you don't want to have to reroll your characters.
- Related: If you mess up on your character, you'll most likely just have to reroll.
- Guilds are created by leveling a swordsman to a rank 7 class, Templar. This is something I really dislike, I'd rather it be a cost in silver or a hunt for a rare drop. This way for a group of friends, someone doesn't have to put all the work into it themself. I still like the idea of a class with guild-related skills but not that they are the only ones to create it. Because of this, you also can't change guild leaders.
- Bots are a problem, but then again I don't think I've ever played an MMO without 'em... especially F2P.
- While I think IMC has been trying, it seems like improvements/bug fixes/etc. just happen too slow.
Some things may be a pro or con depending on perspective, such as needing to explore and seek out quests. I enjoy it, as do many people. However many people also complain about it.
Despite what I've seen people say, you don't need to use a guide to level your character! Just explore, actually TALK to NPCs to get side quests, and look for maps your level around both Klaipeda and Orsha.
While this game is reminiscent of RO, it is *not* RO, so please don't judge everything by comparing it to Ragnarok.

You play as Red, a singer who lives in the art deco cyberpunk city of Cloudbank.
Cloudbank is an apparent democratic utopia where the citizenry vote on everything. 'Everything' including things such as the weather, the colour of the sky and the daily layout of the city. Here is a city which is almost certainly a step sideways from our reality and into the virtual, much like The Matrix movie or the TV series Reboot. There are 'back doors', loopholes and hacks much like one might find in software. The game locations are named after coding terms, and the names of your abilities and the ubiquitous Process, your primary antagonist throughout the game are reminiscent of faulty or malicious programming. Then of course there's the name of the city itself: Cloudbank being reminiscent of something ephemeral and unreal, a distributed network of servers which may be real or virtual.
The game opens with Red having survived an assassination attempt by four individuals who call themselves the Camerata, and her voice has been stolen.
Red is kneeling next to a man impaled by The Transistor, the weapon that they attempted to kill her with, a blade reminiscent of a circuit board. The blade hums to life at her touch, and her not-exactly-deceased friend speaks to her from it. He’s character, narrator, and your only weapon of choice. However his memory is corrupted and with Red unable to speak the nature of their relationship is built up gradually over the course of the game. Red takes the Transistor and sets out looking for answers and vengeance against the Camerata as a mysterious force known as 'The Process' seeks to stop her and corrupt and unravel reality.
Visually this game is a joy to behold, with a rich colour palette in a semi painterly style with an isometric viewpoint and a glorious attention to detail. Transistor is a digital world, a cyberpunk art deco utopia in collapse with a plot of vengeance running through it. This is like playing through painting, one that turns from contemplative and sombre to dynamic and sharp with the neon bright light show that combat brings to the fore. Holographic effects and stylised programming glitches also help sell the virtual reality you romp through.
The music and sound infuse a soul into Transistor which goes beyond a beautiful score. Much of the music is that of Red’s and, word of advice, pay close attention to the lyrics as they are more integral to the storyline than it may appear. This is especially true at pivotal moments where a track may ‘corrupt’ and alter, providing insight and subtext to a situation, or foreshadow coming events.
As an ARPG, combat takes the lion’s share of gameplay as Red cuts a swath through the Process in her hunt for members of the Camerata.
Each ability gained can be used 3 ways with the Transistor: an active attack, a modifier for active attacks or a passive ability that augments Red. You slowly gain information about the world by using abilities in each of these ways, giving you a new incentive to change up your build. This information helps paint a vibrant and culturally rich world – a fusion of 1920s art deco and democratic utopian cyberpunk gone wrong.
The twist, is that Red is able to pause the flow of time and modify the world through abilities. Red can even later acquire super user access with glorious results. During ‘Turn time’, Red can queue up actions (movements, attacks and other abilities) with action points and then unleash them rapid-fire on your enemies.
Movement is important in both modes of combat, so turns and real time are one part positioning, one part offense, and one part “NONONONO RUN RUN RUN.”
One could sit still, but efficient movement and punching through the abstract high tech nightmare programming of the Process with planned out status effects and backstabbing will give you a significant upper hand. One could also play solely through real time, but you would miss out on the glorious satisfaction of watching Red execute your plan (and multiple unlucky foes) in a bullet time moment of neon samurai fury.
Gameplay death is also handled in an interesting way. When your health bar drops to zero (and it will) you won’t die, rather an active ability will get burned out of the Transistor for a few checkpoints. Only once all active abilities are burned out do you start again from the last checkpoint. This temporary loss of an ability forces you to experiment and find new strategies and this helps keep the gameplay from stagnating.

The combat is broken up with contemplative treks through this apparent utopia in collapse (apparent as even before the impending process wrought apocalypse there are indications that prejudice, inequality and a lack of personal agency were more present than Cloudbank’s citizenry would care to admit).  Here, the interactions between Transistor and Red really shine.

The relationship between Transistor and Red is the core of the game’s story and how they communicate is really what makes it – how Red expresses herself despite being mute is especially compelling. Body language involving the sword, clever use of message board terminals, split-second decisions she makes. Red is a complex, interesting character whose personality is drawn in assured and precise strokes. Quiet moments and sudden decisive actions reverberate with equal strength and land home with an intimate touch and the force of a sledge hammer respectively. She may have been a singer, but her response to tragedy is what outlines who she is. She is action and silent fury with burning purpose. The only thing left when the world and everyone else is long gone.
Transistor provides a contrast to Red. A sword with the power to alter reality, a weapon of enormous power is one of the more subtly vulnerable characters I’ve come across, one that speaks fondly and protectively of Red, and tentatively speaks heartbroken confessions in dire situations. Having the narrator in the form of Transistor on board for the ride and his interactions with Red makes this very compelling and I think more intimate. His writing is excellent as is delivery of the voice acting. Transistor and Red really are a perfect match. A body and mind without a voice, and a mind and voice without a body.
The overarching plot as well, is told in a very minimalist fashion and is deceptive in its depth. It is a larger world from a lore perspective than one might think. One which is subtly told and implied through character exchanges, terminals, and abilities. The latter is quite interesting, a good union of gameplay and narrative exposition, although the ability exposition can be a slog at times. as it is delivered via text.
The gameplay is near perfect the story compelling, and the presentation flawless. If I were to lay criticism at Transistor it would be a desire for more solid and defined chunks of lore, world building and narrative. The storyline can be completely incidental and missed if one does not seek it among the sublime ARPG romp.
That said, I’m still thinking about world, the story, and its myriad meanings. It is an experience which has really stuck with me after the credits rolled. It is also one of the only games that I have felt I needed to play through again immediately after, to ‘Recurse’ as the game tantalisingly puts it.

I tend to dislike FPS games. So when I feel an itch to to run 'n gun, I want something slick, well-written, and not bogged down with a ton of exposition. Call of Juarez Gunslinger fits that bill quite nicely, thank you very much.
The story unfolds almost like a Quentin Tarantino script while the narration keeps your action in tune with the story. The gameplay is very straightforward and the gunplay is very satisfactory. There's an almost tactile, visceral feel when using the late 19th century weaponry in this game. Whether you're aiming down the iron sights of a Winchester rifle while taking a bead on a bandit lying in wait, firing from the hip to take out a back-stabbing desperado, or simply blasting buckshot at close range to deal with bushwacker who just leaped out at you, it all feels great as you're firing lead down range at the enemy.
There isn't a map or a radar, there aren't any quest-givers with exclamations marks over their heads, there's nary a health pack or even a health bar in sight, and inventory management is non-existent. However, there's no denying that the gameplay is polished, fast moving, and very fun.
My only serious dislike would have to be the relative length of the game - I finished in just under 8 hours. Some of the aforementioned features were sometimes a detriment to gameplay as it would've been nice to know my location or how I was doing on health, but, at the end of the day, their lack probably enhanced my overall enjoyment.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is essentially a mostly-linear FPS that takes place in the Wild West. It's a highly exaggerated tale of heroic exploits by a famous bounty hunter who met all the lawman/outlaw folk heroes of the late 1800's.
It focuses on doing what it does extremely well, with very enjoyable gunplay compared to most FPS games. You can use a variety of period specfic weapons and throw dynamite as grenades. And at the end of every chapter, you engage in a duel minigame.
The story is a breath of fresh air. It feels similar to Bastion, with the main character constantly narrating. The narration changes depending on what path you take, and even changes the game itself if the narrator decides to say something different. The graphical effects for when the story changes are fantastic, and the setting itself is absolutely breathtaking and rendered in bright color.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone who is even remotely a fan of FPS. It's definitely one of the best FPS I have played, gameplay and story wise.

FFXIV definitely takes its time to get started, but once it gets going it's ridiculously easy to get swept away by the setting. The world is beautiful and the soundtrack even more so - this is one of the few MMOs I've actually turned UP the music to listen to, rather than turn off and play my own. It all comes together to give it that "Final Fantasy" feel, which is either your cup of tea or isn't. If you long to rush into battle between White Mages and Black Mages, and face off against classic Final Fantasy bosses such as Ifrit, then FFXIV is the game for you.
However, it's far from perfect. With the exception of the absolutely stellar opening cinematic, cutscenes are generally quite atrocious, and the voice acting even more so. Not only are they overly long and painful to watch, but the writing is also sloppy, which just makes every cutscene a bore and every time I reached one I just wanted it to end. I also found I had to turn the graphics down a fair bit just to reach 60fps, which is not something I usually have to do, but even when I did hit 60fps certain parts of the game were still choppy.
On the gameplay side of things, there's nothing FFXIV does that isn't standard for the MMO genre. The hotbar-based combat is as generic as you can get, but still fun, and you'll find no shortage of baseline MMO kill this, fetch that quests. Where the game really shines is in its story quests, which while not the most elegant considering their reliance on cutscenes, are far more interesting than the grind.
If you're a fan of MMOs or a Final Fantasy fanboy, you'll find a lot to like about FFXIV. Is it the best MMO out on the market? Not in my opinion. but damn it if I wasn't having a lot of fun anyway. I always had that "just one more quest" or "one more dungeon" feeling in order to progress the storyline, which is nice to have in the current paradigm of "gogogo loot slot machine" MMOs.

Take the best parts of Transport Tycoon, the geek-elements of the extended patches with train-signalling, path-finding and complex schedules, the building of a working network to transport cargo.
Now shove that cargo into buildings to craft further items and transport their results.  Rocket fuel.  Drones that can help you build or deconstruct anything.  Research vials to help you unlock the tech tree.  Vehicles.  Pumps.  Guns.  Ammo.  From basic ore, coal and wood, you build a system to manufacture circuits and trains.
Manage it all in a massive, endless world, collating the resources you need to get to the right places to be processed and fulfill your current needs, while exploring for that crucial oil well.
Now imagine that everything you do pollutes the planet.  And the locals aren't at all happy about that.  The more pollution, the more unhappy they are.  And they grow, expand, and up-sticks in your direction like the populous of Populous.  And after a while they come hunting and you have to man the barricades and send out the repair drones and hope you're producing ammo at a fast enough rate to keep them at bay, without dwindling the resources that let you take your defences to the next level.
Everything can be automated, from the collection of wood from trees to the creation of a train from raw parts.  Everything can be controlled and processed.  Set up in-game sensors and circuits to make sure you don't run out of one resource, or that you don't churn out masses of one required substance when the other critical one isn't available.  Make automated trains go and collect resources from your far-flung outposts and bring it to one point, with the help of the drones and conveyor belts, while building safe computer-controlled crossing points so you don't get run over by your own trains.
Keep your power networks up to keep firing the lasers, while not burning through your coal.  Or move to solar to keep the aliens from getting mad at that cloud of smoke coming from your factory, if you can manufacture enough and balance the power overnight.
Hundreds of items, a large tech-tree, an infinite map, a challenging enemy, and a factory to manage in the middle of it all, while trying to stay alive and get an SOS message off the planet.
Great fun in multiplayer too, sharing the burden and taking turns on the purging of the nearby alien spawns or the patching up of the base, or establishing a new outpost.  Always something to do, always something to be made more efficient, more automated, more productive so you can build that new flamethrower or have the better drones help you out in taking out the enemy.
And, yes, you can just storm in, raze their village to the ground and steal their precious artifacts.  But you better hope that they don't find a way in the back while you're out there.
One of the best games ever, and I've sunk thousands of hours into things like OpenTTD and all the RTS games of old.  Tuned resource management, simple or complex networks, simple or complex interactions (move this type of resource over there but only if there's enough to build one of those and we're not short on the source material, etc.), and a hostile horde at the gates vying to get in and wreak havoc.
Cannot recommend enough, and it only looks to be getting better as time goes on.

AFter the awesomeness that was Amnesia came this game; A machine for pigs.
I have to say, I'm dissapointed.
To start with, the game is extremely predicable as far as the story is concerned. From the very intro and first few chapters you'll most likely guess where things are headed, leaving little surpirise in store as the story unfolds.
While the game does have some gruesome scenery it just doesn't capture the same sense of horror as in the previous Amnesia game, which is something I guess most fans wanted. You're definitely going to get a few scares out of this one and I have to admit that there *are* a few well executed horror segments, but at the same time everything else has been dumbed down somehow. This leads to limited gameplay and therefore a lack of enjoyment.
If you want a good horror game, look elsewhere.

Fans of the series be warned: This is not The Dark Descent.
The difference between these two games can be best be described like this:
a) Monster appears in The Dark Descent - you run, and you hide. You look away when it comes close and you pray it doesn't check the cabinet where you're hiding.
b) Monster appears in A Machine for Pigs - you stare at it as it walks away.
With a new studio at the helm, A Machine for Pigs takes a massive detour from its predecessor. While the atmosphere is rich and the level design remains fantastically disturbing, this new installment strips away many of the game play mechanics that made the original so memorable. Light, sanity, and most of the puzzles and traps of The Dark Descent have been removed - creating a more stream lined, and sadly less engaging experience.
The story is interesting and the atmosphere is creepy and unsettling, but the machine has been too well oiled for a horror game. The creeks in the metal removed and the cringe inducing grinding quieted, and all that's left to do is walk from the beginning of the game to the end. If you played the first this is still worth the six hours it will take to beat, but this is not the direction the Amnesia series needs to continue. 3/5

Tree of Slavior and no that is not a typo . I really really wanted to like it and some of it I did but so much of it I didn't. This is where I was going to rant on and on about how much potential it had to be a good game but I'm not  because there are so many other negative reviews that have already done it for me . Maybe I'll check back in a few months if the game is still going and if anything has improved but as of now don't even bother.

EDIT: I realize that I may have painted a negative picture of the game and IMC in general, but please don't let it turn you away from at least trying out the game. I do not mean to insult the publishers and the developers, and to their credit, they have listened to the community during the beta phases of the game. Tree of Savior is still relatively new and unpolished, and the full release of the game was greatly rushed. I recommend you give the game a few months time to see how much or how little the game actually improves.
The game itself is enjoyable yet flawed.
Pros:
- The soundtrack, artwork, and story are all very well done,
- There are so many areas to explore and the game rewards for exploring the map through obtaining exp cards and map collection bonuses.
- The is a wide variety of classes to choose. You start with the basic classes: Archer, Swordsman, Cleric, Wizard, and advance to other classes later on.
- At it's core, Tree of Savior has the potential to become a very popular game reminiscent of Ragnarok Online.
However, there are quite a few gameplay issues that may turn some gamers away.
Cons:
- For one, there is quite a bit of grinding in the game. While for some people this may be a great aspect of the game, the grind isn't for everyone.
- Despite having a wide range of classes, only some really stand out while the others are clearly inferior choices, and players cannot redo their class choices unless they want to make a new character.
- Another big issue is the prevalence of bots and goldsellers that flood the main towns and the market.
While there are other problems these are the ones that stand out to me personally.
Despite these flaws, I do love Tree of Savior and I would put more hours into it... if it weren't for the publishers IMC. Time and time again they have proved themselves to be less than adequate in dealing with problems regarding the game. Some examples are:
-Poor server optimization. Countless players would experience lag in the amount of damage dealt, item drops, skill cooldowns, etc.
-When they announced that the game would go free to play, they ended up pushing the release date back a week or two (I don't clearly remember)
- When the game was fully released, there were restrictions for free to play gamers. They were not allowed to directly trade with other players, 30% fee on market items, etc. The only way to get around these restrictions was to get a token which can be bought with real money or for a fairly large amount of the in-game currency.
-Goldsellers and bot farmers were everywhere. To their credit IMC did at least try to deal with them. But instead of working on a real fix, they just banned them. This proved ineffective as they would always be back a few days later.
However, IMC is not all bad because they have listened to players during the beta phases. There are times where they did go above and beyond for the game such as adding an entirely new region (Orsha). Its just that lately they have made a lot of questionable decisions that have negatively affected the players for the most part.

My opinion about Dark Souls II is evenly torn between good and bad. I like it a lot because it's not a reskinned, expanded copy of the prequel. I really like how different the combat mechanics are. Neat movesets, brutal backstabs, all that healthy dose of violence I need. Most of the bosses aren't enormous monster creatures. Taking on duel-like bosses is much more challenging (and rewarding) for me because they have a different fluidity than a 20m tall creature stomping and thrashing about. But sure, what's a fantasy game without dragons and slimy creatures blocking your way. The variety of items, builds, stats, online play modes is fantastic. Still, with all the new cool bling and witchcraft you have, it's still extremely punishing if you don't balance your gameplay right; stick to a pure-whatever build and you'll find yourself stuck in an area not before long, teaching you to be flexible and resilient. The DLCs help it put it all together, both the lore and the world exploration.
However...
The world is a tedious, linear bunch of roads. At the beginning you have an open-world where you can choose which area to tackle first- wrong. You have multiple branches that all take you to a dead-end, meaning you've no choice but to drag your behind to Majula and choose the next branch. Then you go on a one-way linear path all the way to get pancaked by a golden bell hammer multiple times. In Dark Souls the world is almost entirely free for you to explore -- and learn the hard way why you shouldn't go there yet, and every single area is part of an enormous map. In Dark Souls II  it feels like I'm in a Megaman game: select your boss, make your way to it, beat it and get your buns back to the hub. It's not a bad thing, but it does NOT fit the style of the game at all.

FFXIV definitely takes its time to get started, but once it gets going it's ridiculously easy to get swept away by the setting. The world is beautiful and the soundtrack even more so - this is one of the few MMOs I've actually turned UP the music to listen to, rather than turn off and play my own. It all comes together to give it that "Final Fantasy" feel, which is either your cup of tea or isn't. If you long to rush into battle between White Mages and Black Mages, and face off against classic Final Fantasy bosses such as Ifrit, then FFXIV is the game for you.
However, it's far from perfect. With the exception of the absolutely stellar opening cinematic, cutscenes are generally quite atrocious, and the voice acting even more so. Not only are they overly long and painful to watch, but the writing is also sloppy, which just makes every cutscene a bore and every time I reached one I just wanted it to end. I also found I had to turn the graphics down a fair bit just to reach 60fps, which is not something I usually have to do, but even when I did hit 60fps certain parts of the game were still choppy.
On the gameplay side of things, there's nothing FFXIV does that isn't standard for the MMO genre. The hotbar-based combat is as generic as you can get, but still fun, and you'll find no shortage of baseline MMO kill this, fetch that quests. Where the game really shines is in its story quests, which while not the most elegant considering their reliance on cutscenes, are far more interesting than the grind.
If you're a fan of MMOs or a Final Fantasy fanboy, you'll find a lot to like about FFXIV. Is it the best MMO out on the market? Not in my opinion. but damn it if I wasn't having a lot of fun anyway. I always had that "just one more quest" or "one more dungeon" feeling in order to progress the storyline, which is nice to have in the current paradigm of "gogogo loot slot machine" MMOs.

Damn, is this game tricky. Not in the "How do I get past this jump that looks impossible?" way, but the "How the hell did I miss that?!" way.
Your goal is to get as many people through the border checkpoint as possible without breaking the rules. The more people that you deal with, the more you get paid. But the rules change day by day and based on what actions you take; let a bomber through? The day ends and you have new rules to follow. Miss a violation? Do that 3 times and you lose money for the 3rd time on. If you were on your own I could care less, but you have 4 other family members to take care of so every penny counts. 5 days into my first playthrough and my Son is dead, my Uncle is sick and everyone is cold and hungry... holy♥♥♥♥♥♥
It's bleak, the art style has you wondering where the nearest suicide booth is and generally it's just a dull trudge to get your guy through each day on the job and not kill your entire family... so in that sense, it's what I imagine working in the formor Soviet bloc was like.
Definatly a game that I count as an "art game", but not one that relies on weird visuals and wonky mechanics to try and evoke something in the player. This game has smile mechanics and a washed-out color pallet that, again, makes it feel as if you really are trudging through each work day and just managing to get by. Just from that, it does what it set out to do and evokes something in the player.
It's worth picking up if you can find it cheap or on sale. There's not a lot of story here aside frrom the newspaper articles you get at the start of each workday to help you ID potential problems and some interesting dystopian elements mixed in with the immagrants, but it's worth playing to see a simple concept done right.

Papers, Please had me hooked for a short while. In a weird, yet fun way I would start it up, bob my head to the music, and pretend that I was "going to work" again.
The game starts you off tame and picks up momentum, forcing you to remember initial tasks and methods while learning new ones each day that passes. I had great fun in these mini-games (if that is what you would call them) such as denying a citizen or finding that tiny discrepency that allowed me to use an X-ray and find that contraband or weapon only to have the poor person hauled away (most likely for execution).
However, for whatever reason I stopped playing and although I have thought about picking back up where I left off several times over the past few months, I haven't been able to get myself to do so. This is where I ultimately land with this game, that is, its fun if you play it and stick with it (and if you have an interest in this sort of puzzle-ish, organizational memory-game). However, if you allow any amount of time in between playthroughs that is too great, I think you'll find it somewhat tedious and difficult to get back into the swing of things. If I were to go back now, I'd have to basically re-learn everything from the beginning just to keep up with where I was when I left off - and this is not the most appealing thought, at least to me.
Papers, Please is unique and definitely well crafted. The gameplay is tight, the visuals have a pleasing, retro feel, and the challenge is definitely there for those that love to one-up themselves on a second or third playthrough. It just, for several reasons mentioned and not (as I'm sure I missed a few), doesn't hold my interest enought to want to actually play it - and this is why I'd give P,P a 7.5/10.
Maybe it's just not for me after all.... :/

FOTONICA introduces a really unique gamestyle, "It's like mirror's edge on drugs".
Such a simple concept, yet so fullfilling.
The game on itself has a lot of replay value, having multiple difficulties where you can either finish the pre-made levels, or play an endless running mode that gets harder the faster you go, even compete with up to 4 players to finish first the level. Doesn't matter how many times you'll play it, you will always find at least some enjoyment out of running and jumping over an infinite void.
Don't get me started on the art, which is the reason I first picked up the game; it's constant eye-candy for those who like dark, ethereal, psychedelic kind of art. I've always been fond of the use of simple geometry on games and art, and this game in special has amazing bright, sharp figures creating amazing fictional landscapes that almost induce vertigo on each jump.
The music is pretty fitting, and has a relaxing feel to it that goes perfect with the game. Some games fail to create a good visual-auditive connection, but this one in special is an exception on that. It has simple entrancing melodies that go perfect with the ambience the game tries to create.
The game is also pretty cheap, paying $10 or ($5 if the game is on sell) is pretty worth it, I'd rather love to be able to support the developers in more ways that just buying their game.
On the grimey side, it can sometimes get a bit repetitive, but you still gotta play quite the constant hours before you memorize all there is to memorize and learn in this game.
If you're wanting to play something casual during your free time, FOTONICA will bring you hours of learning how to jump through surreal landscapes, and will take your breath away everytime you fail that one jump you needed before finishing the level. You can even stay still, look around the level, and will still enjoy the art and music of the game.
8.5/10 - Unique & Hypnotizing.
For such a simple concept, this game is both endlessly fun and frustrating (in the  best way possible). If you're looking to 100% this game and you're not instantly amazing, prepare to take a while.

Whether or not you will like this game depends very much on what you are looking for.
This game is a polarizing one.  You will likely laud it, or hate it.  If you have to look up the word 'laud' in the dictionary, you should probably pass, (or better yet, buy the game and start the processes of understanding nuanced and subtle literature)
You will probaby enjoy this game if
- you appreciate enviormental atmosphere
- you enjoy literature
- you like horror that builds more on deep issues and less on 'shock' or 'camp' gimmicks
- you like Dear Esther
- you want to support developers that are pushing the boundaries on games as a literary medium
- you enjoy a game with puzzles that feel 'real-world' and don't call attention to themselves or hinder the pace of the
narrative
You will probably not enjoy this game if
- you don't like not having a gun in your video games
- you don't enjoy having to do your own critical thinking to come to conclusions concening the story or how it ends
- you think it will be very similary to The Dark Descent (the game feels much closer to Dear Esther in my opinion)
- you want something with puzzles that requires you to scratch your nogging
- you want a horror game where things jump out at you often
In short, if you value deep narrative experiences in games, and feel familiar with literature and coming to terms with your own underlying meaning, you will find an absolutely matchless gem here.  Although narrative indie games are on the rise, this  one is still leading the pack.  If you don't value these things, or are looking for something that doesn't require you be knee deep in your mind, thoughts, beliefs and opinions, it may not suit you.  Either way, consider this tale a gothic horror tale in the traditional sense, as anyone familiar with the novels Frankenstein or Dracula could tell you, the 'horror' is less about bloodshed or constantly spooking you, and more about building a sense of dread over the whole canvas.

Making an MMO interesting and enjoyable is a complicated art. Zenimax and Bethesda did not really master it.
THINGS I LIKE
- Compared to any other Elder Scrolls game, this title is a significant technical improvement. Say, it has very good visuals, while not being extremely demanding resource-wise (for a modern game, at least). I often stop somewhere in the middle of exploration and save a screenshot. I mean, like, wow, they even made flowing water, so now a river is actually a river rather than a body of static liquid. The combat is a bit more diverse, too: they added actual dodging, so you can evade enemy hits instead of taking them all. Exchanging blows until somebody dies has always been the default combat mode all the way up to Skyrim, and it always felt stupid to me. Some effort has been put into usability as well, so the game is more comfortable as far as interface is concerned.
- Another positive feature is, obviously, the unlimited Tamriel. Save for a few of territories which are DLC-only, the entire continent can now be explored. This ensures you an eternity of discovery, treading everywhere and looking around, finding new places and seeing new people. It’s an explorer’s dream. And it’s the Elder Scrolls universe, a true magnet for any fan of the franchise.
- I can also note an interesting approach to balance, which was designed to keep all players equal no matter how far they have progressed. Thus, any region and any quest can be done anytime, and the amount of challenge it’s going to provide will remain the same. It has some drawbacks, though, of which I’ll be writing below.
THINGS I DISLIKE
- Combat is boring. Encounter an enemy, perform your usual routine of battle moves and see it dead. Well, sure, having a set of abilities in addition to the ordinary left mouse button clicks is great, but it doesn’t improve the situation a lot. The difference, basically, is as follows: in Skyrim your battle succession was like “attack – attack – block – attack – attack”, and here it would be “ability 1 – ability 2 – ability 3 – ability 4 – ability 5”. You will repeat this ‘12345’ dozens of times, and that’ll be it. I could also add that the abilities themselves are not quite spectacular, so I don’t really find a lot of enjoyment in practicing them.
- Magic is very unremarkable. The rich variety of Skyrim spells is replaced by a small bunch of dull skills, most of which have quite limited usefulness. Tactical use of spells is nowhere to be found: you can’t exhaust enemy stamina with frost or drain enemy mana with lightnings. Visual aspect of magic hardly exists at all: it’s rather basic, I might even say featureless.
- Balance has a major psychological flaw: there’s no progression worth speaking of. This will require a couple of examples.
1) You’re level 10 and you crafted a sword. The sword does 1000 damage. You have then progressed to level 12 and can now craft a ‘better’ sword. However, your old level 10 sword now deals 900 damage, and the new level 12 sword does exactly the same 1000 damage. You can develop your craftsmanship to great heights and forge yourself a set of level 40 dwarven armor, but it will have exactly the same stats as the rusty iron cuirass you had when you were level 5. Basically, you cannot become better – you can only keep up to be as good as you’ve already been before.
2) Most combat-relevant stats are measured in thousands or tens of thousands. Bonuses you gain from developing your skill lines or from using special items are usually lying somewhere around 3-5%. This effectively means that your attempts to improve will hardly improve anything. Yes, you had 10 000 health before, and now you have 10 500 health. Technically, it’s an improvement, but actually, it’s the same 10k as before.
- Speaking of armors, different types of equipment don’t have any drawbacks – they only have benefits. You will not move slower or spend more stamina in heavy armor compared to light armor.
- Group challenges are achieved through simple multiplication of enemy health. If a dungeon is intended for a group of 10 players, the mobs will have x10 health. This is your challenge. Sounds exciting, right? Big bosses will also have skills that would oneshot you; somebody obviously thought that it would add complexity to the gameplay.
- Many mobs are all the same, just having different exteriors. Here’s a bandit throwing a dagger at you, here’s a dremora throwing a dagger at you, here’s a goblin throwing a dagger at you. The same set of skills is often found throughout the entire range of enemy variations. Wildlife does add some diversity, but to a certain extent only.
- Presence of other players is often annoying, especially in public dungeons: every new visitor makes enemies respawn. They will often respawn right on top of your head and overwhelm you with numbers; you won’t even be able to run for your life, because the mobs you killed before have also respawned behind your back.
- A number of quests is not very well developed either lore-wise or logic-wise. Some look as if they were hastily compiled. It’s a minor thing, but it breaks immersion sometimes.
OVERALL
For an Elder Scrolls game, this is a good product. It’s perfect for walking and sightseeing, and whenever the servers are not very populated, you can just imagine that it’s simply another singleplayer title in the series, where the entire world belongs to you only. It preserves some traditions too: for example, Ayleid ruins are reproduced with exceptional attention to details – exactly the way they looked in Oblivion. It will appeal greatly to any explorer-type player.
However, even though it might seem to be enjoyable at first, the gameplay is not very entertaining. Many things are boring and repetitive, and interactions with the environment do not provide much excitement. Of course, there are player-to-player interactions as well, but they can just as well be found in any other MMO.

This game is as obscure as it is interesting.  You move little goo-balls around, connecting them to one another to get the flow of them from point A to point B.  Catch is, usually you have to build them in weird ways so it doesn't topple over or get hit by things that destroy the cute little goo-balls. Tons of fun!

If you like balls, this game is for you.  You can play with healthy balls, sick balls, black balls, sticky balls, pretty balls, hairy balls, big balls and small balls.  There aren't any  blue balls though.  That would be overtly sexual.

Loved Lemmings? Loved The Incredible Machine? Loved Bridge Builder games?
If yes, then World of Goo is the logic-and-skill game for you.
There's approx. 50 levels with about 10 different types of goo balls -- some form ropes, others are flammable or explosive, yet other can be detached and re-attached later.
You can skip up to 6 levels if you get stuck, which prevents the infamous problem of blocking off entire sections of a game due to too hard a level.
The storyline in the game, albeit entirely unnecessary, is actually very funny and if you follow it through all the signs and messages, you may get a few laughs as well.
But keep in mind that sometimes you'll need quick reflexes besides a working brain - this is NOT chess.
