Final Fantasy XIV, the original one, was a mess. The servers were terrible, payments were unfair and confusing, and the game just made it so difficult for you to enjoy. Square Enix realised, "holy hell, this is bad" and revamped the game, leading to the release of A Realm Reborn. And boy did they do good.
A Realm Reborn is not only a more polished FF XIV, it is a new game. It offers so much more than the original. Better service, better gameplay, more engrossing quests, everything an MMO can offer is in this game. A Realm Reborn is by far the best Final Fantasy of the last console generation, and it is perhaps the best FF I have ever played. It stays true to it's roots, but still manages to not be a total copy cat of previous FF games. It borrows alot from the orginal series, when Final Fantasy was at it's best, but adds a sense of freshness so that FF new-comers could pick up the game and play it as their first FF and still have a wonderful experience.
Detail is where this game excells. The amount of effort into making this as refined as possible is staggering. You could honestly sit at the character creation screen for an hour, picking the tiniest things about your hero. The environments are fantastic, and it's hard to believe that an MMO looks this good.
As well as being the best Final Fantasy in years, it is also groundbreaking in the MMO genre. It offers so much to the genre as a whole, it has made a name for it's self as one of the greatest MMOs in recent years. It is addicting. It is enchanting. It is simply bliss.
Square Enix have really made me regain my faith in them, and I hope that they let future Final Fantasies learn from A Realm Reborn. I cannot wait until more content is added into the game, and clock in a few more hours. Get yourself this game now, even just for the free trial, it's worth it. Even if you're a hardcore FF fan, or a newcomer looking for a game to start with. This is the one.
+ Essentially has it all. Near enough limitless gameplay hours
+ Environments look stunning, attention to detail is incredible
+ Smooth gameplay, easy to learn mechanics
+ Makes great homage to previous Final Fantasy games
- A lot of fetch quests
- Occasional bug here and there
10/10. This is a fantastic game. Get it. Now.

Lucas Pope's Paper's Please is an oddity, in that it's a "Dystopian Document Thriller". Reminiscent of Orwell's 1984, Papers Please takes place in Arstotzka, a fictional country that resembles an Eastern European country during the Cold War. Here in Arstotzka, you are a border checkpoint officer, looking over the passports and documents of all citizens attempting to cross into glorious Arstotzka, making sure they have all proper paperwork, whilst also making sure you family doesnt starve to death or get sick.
Whilst this seems like it would make for a boring game, Papers Please is probably one of the tensest games i've played. It riddles you with moral choices, decisions that affect your future (and that of your family), and the stress of taking care of 5/6 individuals, being paid based on your performance. You have to decide if you are going to let you're family go hungry so that you can help you co-workers, or maybe not have any heating, in exchange for letting in one too many people whose stories touched you. Maybe you'll find yourself aiding a terrorist organisation, or even a vengeful father. Or perhaps you will stay a hardworking, productive member of Arstotzka, with all which that entails.
Papers Please is an excellent game, with unique gameplay, hard moral decisions, a large amount of replayability and a fantastic audiovisual aesthetic. It is truly unique, and definitely a game that everyone needs to play.
Glory to Arstotzka!

There is so much to be said about Papers, Please. I prefer to say it's the most mind-rattling and gut-wrenching game out there, for the people looking for games that leave you emotionally scarred, this is what you're looking for. There's no great tragedy, no brave hero turned evil. Just you, trying to support your family, and being forced to make decisions. One day in the newspaper you get a profile on this man named Vincent, who killed some people in a different country. Then, the next day you might see him in the booth. Do you let him in? Or, are you willing to potentially take a citation? These many, small, choices affect your entire playthrough, and it's a wonderous experience throughout.

This is a simple, yet complex game. Even though there are scripted triggers, the multitude of endings increases the replayability.

I love this game, find it to be very enjoyable, and reccomend it to any fps lover, but I also have to say some things to pottential buyers. First, in my opinion, Borderlands is the better game. If you have been looking for a well-made, not too serious but still gritty, fps go buy the first game; the only games I can think of to compare it to are Mad Max and RAGE. Borderlands 2 improves upon the gunplay and abilities but loses any grit and solitude and replaces it with goofier enemies and terrible jokes written for 12 year olds.
Here's a breakdown of my exact thoughts.
What I liked better in Borderlands 2:
The gun variety- They really amped up the ante when it comes to how many different types of guns you can get in this game. I really enjoy all the wacky effects you get with uniques. I also like how powerful you feel when you use some of the legendaries. Also MORE LEGENDARIES!!!!
The classes- They improved all of the classes and I enjoy them more than the originals.
The bosses- I appreciate just how many tough bosses there are in this game, especially enjoy the amount of raid bosses. I will add one issue to this since it does not apply to the first game- Every single boss is, "Invincible" like come on, you can come up with better epithets than that. Here I'll do some: Terramorphus the Unstopable, Pyro-Caustic Pete the Immortal, Hyperious the Indestuctable, Master Gee the Wise. That was just a huge pet peeve of mine  ¯\_(ツ)_/¯
Main antagonist of the main campaign-Handsome Jack is awesome, I loved every moment I got of him.
Things I liked better in Borderlands:
The tone of the first game. While I know a lot of people had issues with the first game, mainly that they neede to be walked through a story and couldn't piece it together themselves, I loved every moment of it. The first game had this real desolate feeling to it. Borderlands gives you this very real sense of issolation. You don't feel like a super badass when you first start out. You feel like a merc who came to a planet seeking fortune only to find out how dangerous the world you are on truly is. I hate the feel of the second game.
The music: The dry guitar will always be better for me than the constant dubstep, and my favorite type of music is electronic so I'm not just a music enthusiast.
CL4P-TP/Claptrap- He was barely in the game and he said almost nothing. Prefer it that way.
The side characters- Most of them didn't talk, when I was younger I wanted them to talk and move. I got Borderlands 2 and I wanted them to stop talking again. Also they ruined Scooter. in the first game he was pretty funny and interesting, second game his brain regressed to an unrecognizable state.
The DLC antagonists- General Knoxx is tied for the best when it comes to antagonists in this series. He was a grumpy, borderline suicidal old soldier that you would love to have as your grandfather. Also hearing him read out what he had to deal with when it came to his commanding officer always put a smile to my face. Oh will admit that I enjoyed Claptrap as the villain in the final DLC.
The writing- Borderlands' story was more enjoyable for me b/c of the lack of story, I was more focussed on exploring anyway. The humor was also better and it came in bursts. Borderlands 2 was written for teenagers and people with under-developed brains. This is how I look at Borderlands 2, I found it kind of funny when I was 16 but now I'm in my 20's and most of the jokes pi.ss me off rather than make me laugh.
The cars- The cars drove better, did more damage, died less frequently, and felt like they were on the ground instead of floating.
Borderlands: Better tone, better music, better writing (imo), better humor, better DLC villains, better side characters, very little Claptrap, and better driving
Borderlands 2: Better gunplay, better abilities, better story plot, better main antagonist, better boss battles
Boderlands the Pre-Sequel: Stop

"Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs" is a pure horror experience. Not the trivial horror in which the player is always firing with a shotgun, but a deep and perverse psychological experience that dig into the player's darkest thoughts. This second chapter differs in many ways from "The Dark Descent": the sanity meter, the inventory and the oil/tinderboxes related difficulties have been removed, probably with the intent to create a more realistic atmosphere. A great limitation. This was not the best choice to me, since puzzles can't be satisfactorily complex and does not require much effort to be solved. Overall the gameplay result a little too linear but is compensated by a breathtaking atmosphere created by the story, the lovely and disturbing graphic, the dark sound environment and the superb music.
"A Machine for Pigs" is a very compact and well designed game, that have only one misfortune: be the successor of a perfect game. A lot of people didn't expect Amnesia to change it's way of being.
I replayed this game 3 times now and I would definitely recommend it.

Score: 56
Concept: Survival Horror Adventure
The original Amnesia sort of jump started the horror genre for video games back into life. After Amnesia: The Dark Descent we would be given Home, Outlast, Don't Starve, Limbo, Daylight, and others. So when this one came out I was expecting either more of the same or a better game overall. Well... I'll tell you right off the bat what the problem I had with this game was, I'm still playing and very close to beating it, so my opinion has not changed. This game is boring. I fought sleep through the entire game. I'm only slightly interested in the story and they took too much out from the original game.
The original game could be tedious at times, but at least it was difficult and actually scary. This game removes the sanity meter. So, now you can chill in the dark, without freaking out. This would be okay, but it removes that tense nature from the game. You have a lantern that never runs out of fuel. Again, cool concept, however it removes the survival aspect from the game. Fuel was one of the resources in the last game and in this game you're never frantically searching for resources. You don't lose and gain health. The only things you have as a 'resource' is the letters and notes from the first game. But I'm so disinterested in the story that I haven't read any of that crap.
Here is another peeve, its the same monster. In the first game there were several monsters. In this game there is one type of beast, the pig monster. C'mon, change it up. One point in the games favor is the setting. While the game is obviously very dark, you actually get to spend time outside at one point. The surroundings are incredibly varied, one point you could be in a mansion, then in a factory, then in the inner works of a large machine. I suggest not wasting your money on this pill of bore unless you are a die hard survival horror fan, even then...
Second Opinion: It's like a Myst... Dark Myst. Yeah. So if you're expecting to be scared, find something else. However, if you want a really well written adventure game look no further. I personally can't play Myst because I fall asleep two seconds into the game, but I am aware that it has a fan base. Enjoy you crazy Myst fans.

Some notes for those curious:
Elder Scrolls Online takes place millenia before the events of TESV: Skyrim, so don't expect to see any dragons (because they're not back yet). Similarly, please realize that the Aldmeri Dominion alliance isn't any more evil than the other alliances you can choose from. They're not high elven supremacists in this game (source: Queen Ayrenn literally condemns high elven supremacy in one of her dialogues). You're the prejudiced one for thinking so. :)
Extra words from me:
I'll be honest, when ESO first came out, all it took were a few screenshots and some bad early reviews to get me to stick to the single player games. I figured it would come and go like The Matrix Online, but, like that One guy, it persisted. I probably wouldn't have liked it at launch, but when it had a free weekend at the beginning of summer this year and I was burnt out from a tough semester of pretending to like ancient philosophy, I tried it out. I ended up buying Gold edition for myself and my wife (I've always been partial to the Thieves' Guild and Dark Brotherhood), and we played it together (which I highly recommend, playing a TES game with a friend is amazing). I'm not sure how many things they've changed since launch, but it's caught me.
This game's got quests and sidequests with engrossing stories and memorable characters, beautiful landscapes and cities with music to match, and not everything looks the freaking same like in Skyrim. You can fight bears, run dungeons, drink mead with the Nords; not once will you ever be bored. There's crafting, cooking, enchanting, alchemy, stealing, killing, adventures, achievements, everything.
And listen, because I know some people care about this, the game doesn't try to tell you anything about your character except that Mannimarco killed you and trapped your soul in Coldharbour. People consider that an Elder Scrolls staple, and it's in this game, so you're welcome. There are even user-created add-ons to enhance the experience, though they aren't quite as wild as the mods for the single player games can get (as far as I know, I haven't gone down that rabbit hole and don't care to because ignorance is bliss).
So, especially if you like the Elder Scrolls games, I highly recommend ignoring all the sorely uninformed negative reviews and buying this game. If you have always wanted to explore Tamriel, not just confined to Skyrim, or Vvardenfell, or Cyrodiil, you should absolutely get this game. If you need that sweet succulent lore, you need this game. If you have friends that also like Elder Scrolls and you wish you could play together, you should all get this game.
Whatever your choice, I wish upon you Bright Moons, walker!

The game focuses on being a MMO that it forgets that it came from a line of RPGs and large scale adventure, and hey, maybe there is a larger picture, but from the 7 hours I played it all I got was fetch quests and walking town to town.

Been a huge fan of the Elder Scrolls series, still got my old Xbox 360 and an engine-chugging copy of Oblivion (Along with a slightly less chugging version of Skyrim from WAY back in 2011), so it's lovely to see not just the whole world of Tamriel in some damn fine looking glory, but also get to go back to Cyrodiil with a fresh coat of paint and a half. While the grindy aspects of the game can really put you at a standstill from time to time, and the Alliance Wars map is CRAZY huge (To the point where an in-game mount is a necessity), it still functions as a fun and wholly needed addition to your 'Scrolls collection. The use of skill lines, whereby you can develop all manners of skills and tactics for weapons, crafting, armor proficiencies and your own class/racial benefits (The only two features you really do have to stick with after character creation) means you never feel limited in what you can learn and craft. There's a multitude of items and equipment to wear and make, and plenty of dungeons worth exploring.
Two notes, or rather caveats; the game is huge (80+ GB for storage), as it should be for an MMORPG. Secondly, Alliance War: While the game is always online, with you able to interact and see other players constantly, the Alliance PvP sections are it's main focus. Part of this means that your character will be scaled on a different level of power than they are in the non PvP sections, and as such will usually be weaker than you were. This can mean that a character of starting levels are going to essentially turn into some light cannon fodder when you're ganged upon by three enemy characters all sitting about 10+ levels higher than you. Which can mean that battles feel like a case of 'I spent five actual minutes of my life running to join a siege, to find it out it had failed and I was immediately blasted into non-daedric Oblivion by my vengeful foes.'. Yeah, it gets like that.
But also what it gets like? The sheer joy of setting up a half dozen trebuchets as you and a group collapse a keep wall, storm the front gates and, braving flaming oil, burst in the door and conquer a fort for your alliance. The combat is exciting and there is a host of magical spells and abilities you can do that make your character unique.
There's a lot more to say, but suffice that I've put in 50hrs and feel like 100 more would be no sweat at all. And once you buy the game, there you go. No membership required (though often tempted by all the DLC I could I get with it), and you still get plenty of content as it is. Grab a group, or not, and go take on a dungeon and put a sword in a demon's face. It's fun, it's kinda grindy, it has occasional connectivity issues, it feels like coming back home.
I just couldn't get into it. Maybe it was the graphics, maybe the atmosphere, maybe the loot. Or maybe I'm too used to LOTRO.

So im just going to start my review of jc3 by saying this:  just cause 2 is, has been, and likely will be my favorite game of all time. so im a bit biased toward this series. with that being said, i also realize that both number two and three are arguably terrible games in terms of glitches, compatability, and failed expectations. however, i think that the Just Cause series gets too much of a bad rep for all the wrong reasons. when #2 came out, it was the first game i ever was so hyped for i bought on release day. i watched alot of the pre release footage, interviews with the devs, ect, and from that learned a few things that, in my opinion, alot of people overlooked when buying these games.
First and foremost, the series is purposely cliche and "cheesy." if you want character development, good voice acting, and a riveting storyline, BUY A DIFFERENT GAME. however, if your the kind of person who likes endless destruction, lame action catchphrases, and  hillariously terrible physics, this is the game for you! if you go into buying one of these games with the expectation that its going to be rough around the edges, i can guarentee you will be pleasantly supprised. whereas if you buy it expecting a polished masterpiece with no issues whatsoever you will be very let down.
Now that i have that cleared up, heres my take on JC3 from the perspective of someone who loves this series.
Pros:
-JC3 is GORGEOUS. absolutely some of the most beautiful in game scenery of any game ive played
-better weapon selection than jc2
-wingsuit is a briliant addition to an already awesome way of moving about (grapple/parachute)
-DLC has added enough fun stuff between mechs, the jetpack wingsuit, and the eden spark to make any destruction addict satisfied
-i have been lucky enough to not be plagued by the numerous glitches and performance errors that so many seem to have with this game. (16gb ram and a 970, so im not really running top tier hardware either)
-replayable settlements (something i wish was added in JC2)
cons:
-the WORST i repeat WORST driving physics of any game in existance GUARENTEED. motorcycles are practically undrivable, as any controll input will barely move the bike unless held for a long duration. however, once you get it to turn past a few inches to each side, there is no middle ground. the bike makes a sudden and unexplainable 90 degree turn, sending you careening off the clifside and resorting to your parachute
-the biggest issue i have with this game by far is that it feels like the designers just stopped trying when they reached the top half of the map. the bottom chains of islands are densely packed with all manner of locations, and things to do, where the top half feels empty and repetitive
-takes quite a beefy PC to run anywhere close to max settings
-the typical Just Cause glitchyness
Overall, i love this game and play the hell out of it, however i understand its not for everybody. i recomend this game immensely, and give it a solid 8/10

Letting go of the run button sends you leaping into the sky and pressing it down again makes you hit the ground, which is how you make your way through the tracks of empty highways, apartment buildings, a forest, whatever. The game emphasises the importance of landing after you jump up. It's pretty important.
All of the Arcade Mode maps eventually end with you reaching the finish line and then falling into the same emptiness you were maybe trying to run away from. It's kind of philosophical, really.
After I had played through all the maps I found out the game comes with different difficulty levels but I feel like they make very little difference. After you learn to land your jumps properly it doesn't matter how fast the game moves because you can nail the jumps anyway.
I guess like most running games FOTONICA rewards you for not bumping into things. If you try to jump for a higher ledge but you don't have enough speed you will smash against it and lose momentum. If you run well you gain speed and you can see the white lines around you change color. The best and most thrilling moments of FOTONICA are those where you run towards a ledge at great speed – everything around you shining in gold – you can hear the music get more intense and you see the road end in front of you and beyond that there's nothing but the empty void so you just have to go for it.
Run to the very end of the ledge, let go of the keyboard, take the leap of faith and hope your jump will carry you on to the other side. If you don't make it you just need to try again from the beginning.
FOTONICA is no Mirror's Edge but you should probably still play it.

Supergiant Game's second take on Adventure RPG games brought many ideas from their previous work, Bastion, and set them in a futuristic sci-fi theme. This time the player plays as "Red", a singer whose voice has been stolen, aided by the "Transistor", a sword-like weapon, that can absorb "lost souls" to gain new powers.
The game is built upon a pretty isometric 2d style engine (maybe Bastion's), the graphic and the art style are, once again, polished, well defined and definitely unique. The whole world, as in Bastion, seems to be handcrafted - and maybe they are - and as you venture through the many areas, you'll have the chance to notice how small details make that game worth spending time on it.
The sounds are good, music's the best part of the game's "audio aspect": an original soundtrack where the vocals singer is Red herself.. smooth, chillout-like and ambient are the defining characteristics.
Gameplay-wise the game relies much on its "spiritual predecessor's" mechanics: though this time there's no hub to navigate the world through, they chose a classic area-after-area mode, the player can upgrade the Transistor with an awesomeness of abilities and swap them using specific "terminals". Abilities are known as "functions" (...) and they can be used as "active", "support" and passive". The first one, let you use the function's main ability (as many as four); mid one's, let you put a function in support to another one, creating a new effect (you can have up to two support functions); the latter let you gain a passive effect that auto-activate and you can unlock four of them. You can stack as many functions as memory capacity let you have; memory can be increased leveling up and choosing to upgrade it; other options are also available, like different functions, more support slot, limiters.. what in the heck limiters are? Ever played Bastion and divined any god? Well, limiters are Transistor's shrines: they give you % xp bonus.. but also activates malus like stronger Process (main enemies AI)..
Red explores the world areas in real-time though, during combat, the actual moving area is restricted; combat can be executed in real-time and/or aided by the Turn() option: she can stop time and use a combinations of moves and attacks that she will then executes in real-time, allowing for greater gameplay experience and differentiation.
Honestly, as with Bastion, there's no point in looking for negative aspects  as positives' more than successfully pawn cons. If you liked Bastion, want a unique adventure, a fresh take on RPG.. you definitely want to give Transistor a try. You'll love it.
Overall:
Graphic: 7
Art: 9
Sound: 7
Music: 8
Gameplay: 8
Replay value: 8
Uniqueness: 9
Partial: 8
The partials and so the final score are identical to Bastion's and that is soon explained: I see Transistor as a transposition of Bastion's mechanics and feats to a new world; there's no real "reinventing" but the story, the world, the themes.. they all are unique and different from each other.

Lucas Pope's Paper's Please is an oddity, in that it's a "Dystopian Document Thriller". Reminiscent of Orwell's 1984, Papers Please takes place in Arstotzka, a fictional country that resembles an Eastern European country during the Cold War. Here in Arstotzka, you are a border checkpoint officer, looking over the passports and documents of all citizens attempting to cross into glorious Arstotzka, making sure they have all proper paperwork, whilst also making sure you family doesnt starve to death or get sick.
Whilst this seems like it would make for a boring game, Papers Please is probably one of the tensest games i've played. It riddles you with moral choices, decisions that affect your future (and that of your family), and the stress of taking care of 5/6 individuals, being paid based on your performance. You have to decide if you are going to let you're family go hungry so that you can help you co-workers, or maybe not have any heating, in exchange for letting in one too many people whose stories touched you. Maybe you'll find yourself aiding a terrorist organisation, or even a vengeful father. Or perhaps you will stay a hardworking, productive member of Arstotzka, with all which that entails.
Papers Please is an excellent game, with unique gameplay, hard moral decisions, a large amount of replayability and a fantastic audiovisual aesthetic. It is truly unique, and definitely a game that everyone needs to play.
Glory to Arstotzka!

There is so much to be said about Papers, Please. I prefer to say it's the most mind-rattling and gut-wrenching game out there, for the people looking for games that leave you emotionally scarred, this is what you're looking for. There's no great tragedy, no brave hero turned evil. Just you, trying to support your family, and being forced to make decisions. One day in the newspaper you get a profile on this man named Vincent, who killed some people in a different country. Then, the next day you might see him in the booth. Do you let him in? Or, are you willing to potentially take a citation? These many, small, choices affect your entire playthrough, and it's a wonderous experience throughout.

I wanted to like it- I did like a lot of it (I love the idea of the combat being an action ARPG type of affair with a controller)  and the skill and class mixing is pretty great, but the company is the most incompetent, least motivated and utterly lethargic  mass of nothing I've ever seen. And IMC has handled their game worse than single person indie dev teams.
For months after launch they could not properly set up a payment system for their own game's premium system- And they kept the restrictions in place during the whole time. So if you weren't a founder even if you wanted premium benefits and to support the game- Tough ♥♥♥♥♥♥s- They didn't even do 5 minutes of research about how steam works, when every other few dozen F2P MMOs with a cash shop that funnels through steam somehow figured it out just fine- Without having a 2 year beta cycle to do so.
Let's not even go down the rabbit hole of idiocy that is iTOS having harsher penalties and restrictions and lowered spawn rates and less allowed dungeon runs a day than kTOS- Along with being in a permanent patch, content gear and balance lag much akin to the dandy days of iRO vs kRO. Where an international player pays full price for a cut down and poorly managed version of the real deal that's always going to be 6 months behind.
IMC... Real talk, you're like that manager who comes into work with his hair sloppy, shirt half buttoned and he just watches the clock until it's time to go home- You have no passion or drive for what you do and you know it and you didn't even have it at the peak of the game's hype train which does NOT reflect well on the product.
Nothing spurs them to action, not losing the majority of their playerbase, not the failed launch and the need to turn their image and PR around- Even open talk of making a private server for ToS right on their very forums doesn't seem to phase them from their sluggish death march into doing the bare minimum effort to get their money from the game while even the most hopeful, patient, sunk cost or otherwise invested players are sick of it.
Things that should be solved with internal QA- Much less make it to the live game often go a week without a correction or hotfix, from things as "benign" as a marketplace not showing items unless you change tabs a few times first. Or things as crippling as PARTY PLAY in a MMO being broken because any quest that triggers a cutscene or event (80 percent of the content FYI) can freeze the other party members in place randomly where they cannot act, use skills- But can be killed and have their time and money wasted. This is goddamn embarrassing and would not be accepted in any other game for an entire day, much less a whole week.
If we want to talk about the core game itself?
There are also a ton of class abilities and skills which are buggy, blatantly broken or have improper interactions since beta- And tons of "working as intended" choices which are low powered trash at best, or outright wastes of skill points and traps at worst even amongst the most creative and discerning character builder.
And there are circles of classes littered with these borderline vestigal skills which have no scaling or proper ability attributes tied to them and no plans to do a damn thing about it. And the fact the game is "incomplete" with only 7 out of 10 ranks and 280 out of over 500 levels really comes home to roost when you want to make a character build and always have a nagging feeling you are missing core abilities or making a wrong turn no matter what you make unless you make the most straight forward cookie cutter possible.
In addition to several of the classes in the trailers and hype up vids outright not actually being in the game "yet" and tons of core gear for certain classes and circles not being in the international game's drop tables adds to a frustrating experience where you're never fully satisfied with your choices and character.
Dungeon content is a weirdly gated affair where the party finder will jam together people with little rhyme or reason and often put together confusing mishmash parties of all archers, healer-less warrior groups and all wizard based characters- The real challenge of doing dungeon content without a static party is using the group finder.
Dungeons are typical mobs-in-a-clump-who-run-at-you faire and the only difficulty comes not from their abilities or interactions but how much health they have to sponge up damage and how much they can hit you for.  And if you're in a competent group the bloated HP pool feeling is really apparent as you are boredly looking at helpless masses of enemies steadily die as they drop a piffling amount of money for your efforts as Dungeon mobs have no loot drop tables at all barring the dungeon's bosses.  The bosses of which have 3-4 abilities and maybe two phases tops and despite being the most simple overly telegraphed things on earth- Most rando parties will eat their AOEs every time and die. Making you wonder when they started training bonobo apes to play videogames.
If you defeat these fantastically simple bosses you only receive a cube and another paltry sum of money from them. The cube is a gamble to get an item of merit tied to that boss and dungeon or the game's trash loot currency. "Talt" which can be used as an item to upgrade player guilds, or used as a scrip token to trade to players in liue of money as each one vendors for 5K (And you can't trade money in this game so....)
Talt is the item you will get almost every time because when you have three items with 1 percent, 5 and 10 percent drop rate in a drop table. And a fourth occupying the rest of the remaining percentage- Congratulations. You now have a boss which drops effectively garbage 84 percent of the time. Especially seeing as you only get one item per cube.
They are also self aware of this as there is an achievement for running a lot of dungeons called "Talt, my love." (Protip: Being self aware of a part of the game being broken doesn't change the fact it's broken.)
The fact they include a padding item to screw you over in regards to boss loot on top of limiting you to 3 dungeon runs  (Not per dungeon.... FOR ANY DUNGEON. So if you help a friend run a lower dungeon- grats, you just screwed yourself out of a higher level dungeon run.) a day is a painfully obvious way to put a poster over the crack in the game to try and hide the fact there's a dire lack of content so they have to distract you with another treadmill.
Gear in general- There are very few useful pieces of gear- The game largely having statless filler grays and pointless bonused blue items. You will see the same 8-9 item names for the rest of your ToS life largely enough- And there are core items for some classes with no other alternatives with abysmal drop rates off of relatively trashy mobs (00.1 percent for a sage wall for example, a magic def heavy and spirit heavy shield for caster or cleric types.. There are no other shields with spirit in the game, period.) So as a result the few decent items have VERY inflated values as they are often the only good items you will see for over a hundred levels.
TL;DR: The game is a neat concept and gameplay "Skeleton" with no meat on it's bones  The entire game feels like it should have stayed in development for another two years without bothering with the CBTs as they clearly didn't get any input or work done during those times anyway.
Edit on 07/27/2016: GUESS WHAT? The party play breaking cutscene freezing bug persisted and continues -even after the patch and database merges-  from kTOS to iTOS. IE: Despite the versions having patch parity finally- They still have something broken which is obvious they don't know how to fix.
Update on 08/09/2016: This is beyond parody- This is a new level of incompetence. The aformentioned bug STILL persists.

NOTE: as I write this the server is down for maintenance. GAH!!!
Now 130 hours in, 2nd character: generally the game's largely enjoyable. Visitng Valenwood has been a clear highlight. Most areas are reasonably well layed-out, the graphics are good but distinctly fantasy rather than grim reality. The story is well thought-out and satisfying. I'm mostly positive about my time there and feel like it's largely money well spent.
Guild Merchants can be incredibly helpful. The game just doesn't tell you that items are delivered via in-game mail. I discovered this by complete accident while doing something else.
But there are problems, and they're huge.
Skills: you can slot 5 [later 10], with one special. That means you have to carefully select between class skills, racials, weapons, and magic. Unlock a new skill in any set and  you have to choose what you lose. This *massively* sucks in terms of progression. Playing as a Warden I have Guardian perma-slotted. There's no point in unlocking the other specials. I can't slot them so they're utterly worthless.
You do get to unlock a second weapon slot, for sure. That increases your lot to 10, as you have 5 per weapon. But again you hit the same issue: you'll have probably 3 skills you consider essential, leaving you with a still severe limit on the others you'll use.
Quests: far too may involve running the length of an area map, doing something incredibly minor [read a note, speak to someone] then running back. This is unavoidable and a total pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥
Boss fights tend to scale badly. You'd expect them to be more difficult, but  many seem overwhelmingly so. I started a new character because I had a stack of 6 bosses with my Nightblade that I just could not kill. I'm still not sure whether I just built a bad character. My Warden has now completed the main quest and is at a lower level. This is largely because the Guardian bear acts as another character - which I love, but which makes the game feel horribly unbalanced compared to my Night blade.
Extra content - not just DLCs, is stupidly expensive. I bought the game with Morrowind, which is great, and discovered I need to spend actual money on 'Crowns' to by utterly trivial things like differently coloured horses. So I just don't.

Want to play the next installment of the Elder Scrolls series?! Want to be the 'Vestige' along with countless other 'Vestiges'?! Want to explore Tamriel's hidden secrets while Level 660 Master Wizard's ride on by on their ethereal steed?! Want strangers with ridiculous and crude names getting in your way?! Want to trudge through awkward co-op with your friends who have to be at the same point of the same mission with you?! Want to see the guy you're supposed to kill standing next to his own dead body?! Want 37 people standing around a quest giver?! Want failed pickpockets butchering civiliians?! Want nerf'd skillsets that basically render everyone a wizard?! Want to be crippled by the one of two servers you decided to play on being down for maintenance?! Want to lust after those glory days of Morrowind, Skyrim and Oblivion (or even Arena and Daggerfall for the old kids)?! Then this game is for YOU!
As you might have guessed, I'm not a fan of MMORPG's, but I got it on sale and gave it a try. In all truth, it's not that bad of a game -  so long as you can ignore everyone else. The things above literally form the basis of this game, or happen all the time. After about 30 hours of playing, I still have yet to see a real purpose of ESO being solely an MMORPG (other than being a DRM measure / cash cow exploiting players' vanity). I know there are multiplayer elements, but for those who are interested in the storyline, other people just serve to get in your way and break your immersion.
But then again, I'm an anti-social introvert. It's in my nature to say that I would have been overjoyed for Bethesda to have made the exact same game with private server capabilities (with some better co-op functionality for the one or two friends I have). If you like this kind of stuff, it might be for you - but if you're looking for the next standalone, this is just a drug that will get you by for now.

Dark Souls II is a well known old school action RPG that has earned its reputation from more than just masterful fighting mechanics, wonderful graphics and fledged out world, but also for its notorious difficulty. This review will cover both Dark Souls II and Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin. The latter is essentially Dark Souls II with a portion of extra content, varied enemy placements and some entire new enemies. It also contains all standard Dark Souls II DLC content.
Even at a glance at this game you will immediately notice how visually stunning it is. The in-game textures are eminently crisp, even the backgrops are particularly realistic; from mountainous volcanos to vast oceans. With that said, the actual textures are not even the star of the game's visuals, the actual level design is probably the most breathtaking part. The way developer From Software has laid out these magnificent landmass is a sight to behold. At no point did I ever feel lost during my journey through this winding scape of land. Bonfires, (essentially the game's checkpoint system,) are set apart strategically throughout the world and there is always a large segment of content to explore between each. For the most part the world feels like it has been created apace with enemy placement. Enemies are, (for the most part,) well situated as well as expertly modelled, well textured and competently animated. Finding a new enemy is always a pleasure due the clear-cut quality and effort put into each.
Gameplay wise, Dark Souls 2 is all about the combat. Traversing through the enormous world all to unlock that next boss, that next challenge that you know is going to be difficult but oh so rewarding. Reigning triumphant over bosses never gets old. Killing a boss in Dark Souls is up there with the most rewarding feeling I've felt playing a game. You always feel like you have accomplished something. Being able to tell your friends you've beaten a Dark Souls game is a fulfilling feeling. That said, for those players that don't care about bragging rights, it is entirely possible to summon other players into your game to assist you with the game's tougher content. There is even a way to summon your own friends using a special in-game item which means playing through the unabridged game with a friend is achievable.
Whilst a lot of focus of the game is on the enemy mechanics, there is also a lot of other features in Dark Souls, including player vs player combat, lore and probably most importantly, gear collection. Aside from overcoming well designed bosses, Dark Souls II is largely about unlocking and obtaining gear to wear, use or otherwise hoard. From unlocking boss souls to be traded for legendary items, to finding items to enchant your weapons, to finding that amazing set of armour you've always wanted, Dark Souls II always gives you the feeling that there is something amazing hidden around every corner. Chests, hidden passageways, enemies, corpses. All of these things may potentially contain the armour piece you've been waiting for and attempting to collect every item in the game will drive you insane. (In a good way.)
The PvP in Dark Souls is by no means one of the highlights but it can create some memorable moments. If you are playing online, other players may potentially invade you at almost any time, and it is terrifying. The enemy player is able to roam around the level and hide amongst monsters to attack you; they are essentially an aggressive NPC except far smarter. And sometimes much laggier. The moment I got invaded whilst attempting to clear a room full of spiders was both frustrating and exciting, but what really killed my excitement was when he one-hit-KO'd me by stabbing me in the back. While I was facing him. Sure, Dark Souls may have some lag issues but I still feel that the multiplayer is a welcome feature in Dark Souls especially for those out there who are more interested in PvP, (player vs player,) than PvE, (player vs everything.) That said, I would not recommend this game to someone who is only looking for PvP chiefly due to how lag is compensated for, but also because to have any chance at competitive PvP, you will also need to defeat many bosses to unlock gear strong enough to fight other players. You will also need to obtain a high enough level to even get matched with interested parties.
Once you have officially "completed" Dark Souls II to a degree you're happy with, whether that be by simply defeating the final boss, or by defeating every optional boss, collecting every item, and full upgrading your favourite weapons, and completing the very well made DLC From Software has released, the game offers you New Game Plus. "NG+" for short. Each time you finish the game you are offered the opportunity to restart the game with all of your items, gear and stats. In this mode there are a number of changes to the game that will make your experience far more intense. Perhaps the most noticible amendment is that there are amplified numbers of foes added throughout the game, even new enemies you may not have even seen before. Even the beginner's zone is absolutely riddled with aggressive enemies giving you a hasty feel for how the game is going to be from then on. As well as new enemies, some bosses have obtained powerful new abilities and increased health that will make defeating them a second time a much larger challenge than it was the first time through. Finally, NG+ will add a large number of new items that were not available in your first playthrough, including some new boss souls obtained by the milestone bosses throughout the game. New Game Plus also allows you to obtain items you perhaps missed or accidentally lost in your first run. New Game Plus can be activated every time you defeat the final boss so replaying the game infinitely is entirely feasible.
One of the least talked about features of the Dark Souls series is its lore. The lore in these games is extremely subtle, leaving a huge portion of it to the beholder's imagination. Although From Software never blatantly tell you what the game is about or what the story is, they allow you to discover it through a mixture of your own logical conclusions and the NPC character's fully voiced stories to do the work for them, and I must say it is an elegent addition to the game. It is a wonderfully different style of storytelling that not many other games have attempted much less succeeded at. It is yet another reason Dark Souls II is so compelling and addictive.
The leveling system in Dark Souls II ties in with its currency system. As you progress through the game you will obtain souls. (Hey, it's in the name.) Everything you kill will reward you with a number of souls. These souls are able to be spent at numerous merchants around the world for spells, weapons, armour and usable items. As well as this, souls are also used to level up. You read correctly. You have to resolve between using your souls on leveling up or buying well needed gear and items. This mechanic means that you are always weighing up your options rather than just blindly leveling up each time you hear a ding. You could go through the game focusing all of your souls on leveling up, sure, but you would be missing out on new weapons and armours and you'd be too destitute to upgrade them at the blacksmith. I feel that this constant balance is interesting enough to keep even the newest RPG fan attentive throughout an entire playthrough.

It is my opinion that the original Alien film is one of the greatest horror movies in all of existence.  A truly disturbing creature, a cast full of nervous wrecks and dysfunctional hotheads, and a setting full of retro "70's future" technology.  It creates an atmosphere like nothing else, and set off a wave of copycats and industry influence still felt to this day.
The sad part is that the franchise peaked at the first two movies, with Cameron's sequel being one of the best sci-fi/action films.  It has since sputtered-out drab, disjointed, and dismal sequels, spinoffs, and Ridley Scott's "George Lucas" prequels taking a massive crap on the mythology and tied up way too much in an unnecessary focus on Michael Fassbender.  Not to mention horrible videogame adaptations that have tarnished the franchise even further.
This is not one of those.
Alien: Isolation is probably the purest distillation of the original film in a videogame form.  Amongst a swath of games trying to capitalize on the blood-pumping, bullet-spewing action of Aliens, "Isolation" instead opts for the slow burn, the crawling dread, the dark hallways that might hold a horror unseen, and the held breath as you pray the menacing cosmic monstrosity right next to you does not find you.
From the get-go, the true visual beauty of this game is how it captures the 70's style of Alien.  The clunky, dirty, vinyl-covered corridors and technology are absolutely perfect, and it's a gorgeous treat to just admire the scenery when you can.  Every tool you get and piece of technology you use feels like it leapt out of a "Popular Mechanics" catalog from four decades ago, with CRT monitors, chunky buttons, clicky dials, handles to crank, and cards to slot.
Added to this is the cast of characters on the verge of falling apart, and a relentless hunter that is almost ever-present.  There are a few sections of the game where you're given reprieve, and have to face-off with human and synthetic enemies, but once you hear that tell-tale clunk in the air ducts above you, you know exactly what you're facing until you get out of the area.  Slow, quiet stealth is key, as the slightest noises can bring the titular alien down to lope about, heavy footfalls and hissing growls alerting you to its presence.  Distraction is largely your weapon here, as you cannot hope to fight the thing, only fend it off, hide form it, or escape it for a while.
SUMMARY/TLDR:  If you like slow, hyper-focused games, where you have to keep track of every noise and be aware of your surroundings at all times, rather than being a bug-stomping Rambo . . . or if you're just a fan of the aesthetics of the original Alien flim, this game cannot be beat.  It's more the pity to me that Fox doesn't look to this for direction on what's good about the Alien franchise.

Still, if you like terror movies, or if you liked any of the alien franchise movies, you should try this one too. I guarantee it will leave you breathless more than once.

Fotonica is endless runner perfection in a most blissful series of beautifully crafted lightspeed stages, the warm vector lines and hallucinatory neon waves that illuminate from the sides of your vision like some kind of adrenaline induced euphoria. When you finally reach that zen-like state of focus things begin to speed up even more, the colors and movements are intensified for a wonderful audiovisual overload that sets it apart from the rest.
The music comes from a plethora of incredible artists (including the very talented
of Pixeljunk Eden fame) and ranges from shimmering, gorgeous soundscapes to heavy pulsing electric rhythms with infectious bass and they compliment the array of different environments and backdrops you'll encounter between each visually shifting level perfectly. The minimalistic yet abstractly complex interconnected series of lines in the classic vector style needs to be seen in motion and lends itself to the very reminiscent feel from the Death Star trench run section of Atari's Star Wars that most endless runners give.
Fotonica moves away from the single boring stretch of hallway players may be used to from other games in the endless runner genre, instead giving us varying heights of platforms. The player character runs at increasingly faster speeds with the holding of a single button, and releasing causes you to bound into the air and leap over gaps in the broken pathways before you. Aiming and timing your landings is the key to success, and overshooting your jump by even the slightest is enough to ruin a good run. The longer you keep your momentum up the faster you go, and the more complex these breaks and gaps in the trail become as they stretch out to seemingly infinite lengths.
The game features two main singleplayer modes including Arcade and Endless as well as a split screen Versus mode that makes for some great living room multiplayer. Arcade mode features eight stages of increasing difficulty as shorter, more rapid platforms are thrown at you forcing you to think on your feet. As you fly and leap past these deadly gaps you collect various score increasing orbs tucked in hard to land spots, spicing up how score chasers will approach the leaderboards. Endless mode is just as it sounds, giving players who have already mastered the several Arcade mode stages and want to put their endurance to the ultimate test.
You'll run again and again, jumping from cascading catwalks to other layers of psychedelically colored platforms only to watch your arms flail in terror as you plummet to your death. When you get back up again and check your score against your friends, you'll run again with reinvigorated motivation and eventually find that ultimate
. From the incredibly creative minds behind MirrorMoonEP, Fotonica further proves that Santa Ragione has the potential to craft unique and memorable experiences in a multitude of genres and stands as what is most likely my "Runner of the Year" due to attractive, straightforward and addictive design.

FOTONICA has an arcade-y, crisp feeling to its vector-style graphics. It is minimalistic, yet somehow still fairly elaborate when it comes to the track building, the only thing that is going attract your attention. Speaking of the track, it is outlined in white (golden-yellow when you reach a certain speed) but is not colored in anything but black, which is a bit confusing to say the least. Fear not, for once you die enough you will no longer be confused by these seemingly semi-translucent blocks. In later levels it becomes a bit tougher, when the game starts to spawn different, more complex kinds of "terrain". It's not an issue that would stop me from playing, but I would love to see the track change color or be colored differently from the background.
The game doesn't use a complex control scheme by any means. You will only use 3 buttons: any button to jump (I will talk about this in the 'Mechanics' section), M to mute and R to restart the level. You are able to invert the controls if you so desire (hold button to jump instead of hold to run). FOTONICA doesn't require many graphical options since it's very minimalistic, and most of them can be changed in a separate launcher. Navigating the menus is a bit weird with the keyboard, but you can navigate them with the mouse as well, so no problems here.
While this is a completely subjective argument, I did not enjoy the soundtracks FOTONICA offered.
Sure, I might not be into that kind of music, but I only heard the same 1-2 soundtracks for the 5-6 levels I got to play. No, they didn't SOUND the same, they were literally the only two songs I saw playing throughout the game (the name of the song is displayed at the beginning of each level). I do appreciate the effort put into creating them, hence giving Music a 5/10. The sound effects in general were decent, nothing too special.
In my opinion, this is the biggest downfall of this game; you either really like it, or you don't. There's no in-between. As you can see, I didn't. Basically, you hold a button to run, and you release it to jump when necessary. It's all very very simple, and I feel like people who aren't looking for depth will enjoy it a lot. It takes a short while to get used to the jumping, but once you figure it out it becomes great fun to play...
you realize the levels aren't randomly generated, and there are only 11 of them.
This was a major turn-off for me personally. There is a limit to how many times you can fail/beat a certain level and not get bored. The game puts an emphasis on score-beating and being on the leaderboards, which I don't really like. If you're a score-attacker, FOTONICA is most likely your kind of game. People really like it because
a) you can play it with the Oculus Rift, and
b) you can play the game locally with your friends.
If you don't have a VR headset, friends, or score-attacking tendencies, you will probably find this game shallow, repetitive and boring.
As already mentioned in the Mechanics section above, the levels aren't randomly generated and there aren't many of them to begin with, a thing that significantly shortens the amount of time it'll take you to get tired of the game. There's barely any depth to the mechanics or the terrain itself, and there's no storyline to support them and make you want to continue playing. It takes a while to get used to the controls, and after that short period of time beating levels becomes lots of fun, hence the 5/10. Other than that, if you don't score-attack, you don't have much to do; you either fail a lot and replay the same levels to beat the game, or you quit trying. Playing (local only) co-op adds to the Replayability aspect, but then again, you're just playing on the same levels with another player.

Now, let me start by saying I do recommend this game. Whew, now that's done, let me tell you that I was sorely disappointed with this coming from the world of Amnesia: A Dark Descent. Don't get me wrong, the storyline was great and had sinister and grity tone all the way through. A haunting ending with beautifully erie sounds to keep you on edge all the way through with your dim lantern. That all sounds wonderful and great for a game right? Wrong! I'll explain. Now, as of this review, I've yet to see a Custom Stories mode. Not to say you can't mod it for one, but still, it made the first Amnesia replayable, so you can try out all the other chilly chapters yet unplayed. Another thing, Amnesia: AMFP took away the sanity meter. Now, the first time you play Amnesia: Dark Descent, and you even look at a monster, the music and the image effects are what spook you. Not to mention the creatures running after you and you know you're toast. This game...not so much. It lost that fear factor for me in playing it. I wasn't so scared to die and run around the corner, because I didn't lose my sanity to the brink where I was seeing faux creatures trying to gnaw my face off. The terror of cowering inside a closet as an atrocious sound was ripping away at the door to your little room is lost and forgotten. Moments like this made Dark Descent scary for me and adrenaline pumping. I digress. Overall, if you're a fan of the series or creepy tales, buy this. But if you want a replacement for your Amnesia Custom Stories, don't do it.

Everything about this game is much more fleshed out and better-written than Skyrim, even without dragons.

Dark Souls II is the sequel for the almighty Dark Souls, where the player has his adventure on the merciless Drangleic, fightning hollows, mages, dragons and more fantasy monsters. This is one of my favorite games of all time (possibly my most favorite game), so this review is going to go into a lot of details. If you want a true experience of Dark Souls II, play it blind, without reading any guides or reviews. Good luck.
The storytelling of Dark Souls II is similar to Dark Souls I, where the player is the chosen one who will sit on the Throne of Want so that the age of fire will continue on, and the world will be in peace. For that, the player (who is a hollow) gets his humanity and his soul from the Fire Keepers, then the player proceeds to the 4 corners of Drangleic to find the 4 monsters who have the Lord Souls inside of them (the Lord Souls are from Dark Souls I), and after that, having acess to the Shrine of Winter, heading to the Throne of Want inside of Drangleic Castle.
The different styles of playing are very vast. You can be your average mage, or a super strong and slow warrior, a tank for damage, or a quick rogue with fast reflexes, and more. You could do over 200 playthroughs to test each weapon and what works best for your style. There is no best weapon in the game, just a weapon that requires less skill than others. With good play, you can make your bare fists work on PvP and PvE.
The controls are simplistic, having a improved jump button compared to Dark Souls I, having your usual roll to give yourself invicibility frames to not take damage, and having attack buttons and other regular buttons. The enemies have different attacks, some can be parried and easily taken out, others require for you to stay away and wait for the correct time to attack them, others just sit there and wait to die, others just kiss you (it's not that hot).
The graphics are very nice. Everything is pretty detailed and the atmosphere is amazingly set up. The OST is also great, it greats a nice atmosphere during boss fights, knowing you're fightning a honorable knight or a uncontrollable beast. One of the main concepts of the game is the "always online" feature, which can help the player be aware of what's going to happen, via bloodstains, which let you see where other people died, or via messages.
The covenants are groups in the game, and each of them have a different purpose. Some are for tha champions, they make the game harder for youself, for no reason, except the final reward of the covenant, other let you explore pieces of the abyss (which was destroyed on Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition), others just want the blood of others players, others serve as the "police" of the universe, trying to kill people who seek the blood of others, and more.
Most of the complaints are it's netcode, which has been improving since the release of the game. All in all, a excellent piece of artwork, that everyone should try. Just make sure you have a controller and a lot of patience on your hands. You wouldn't like to break your whole room, would you. Just make sure to remember that YOU WILL DIE. A LOT.

The monetization of this game is unconscionable. It is actually cheaper to go hunting than the buy all the items in this game. There really is not a viable way to play the game for free. The tracking and hunting section itself is brilliant. I desperately want to like this game, but the cash grab of these transactions is just immoral. 1 em$ is a cent. Most weapons are about $4.50. The basic rifle is deplorably basic in its stopping power. It actually feels inhumanely inadequate because it is unlikely to take down an animal at any range greater than about 90m. Thinking about the 10 minutes of suffering that it goes through is pretty rough. There is one other weapon you can purchase through hard work alone. It is only possible to get through missions. It is clearly meant to be embarrassing and largely unusable. There's also a time limit to how long you can play with animals other than the basic guest creatures because they require their own licenses that expire in 1-28 days. You cannot repeat missions and there is no other way to accrue money at this stage of the game. Also, it isn't just occasional microtransactions, there is a membership to give you the privilege to hunt the animals other than the basic 3. Also you can't even hunt rabits since your basic weapon doesn't fire acceptable ammunition. This game is not free to play. The content is extremely gated by rather large amounts of money. The level of blatant money grubbing in this game's monetization feels deeply insulting. I wouldn't be this verbose if it weren't for the incredible potential of the game. If they did cosmetics for monetization like every other successful free to play game, that would acceptable. Some of the gear actually looks very cool. To make the free to play tag viable they would have to ungate about 50% of their content, they would also need to make a progressive way of gaining money outside of the missions that is repeatable and useful. Actually letting you sell your trophies that are shot through the mechanic already available would be a good step. Even then, it the gm$ prices would need to be about 25-30% of their current price to be remotely accessible to casual players. The mechanics of tracking, leveling up, shooting, and spotting are rewarding and challenging. The game itself is pretty slow paced and would be a relaxing time killer if it were actually playable as a free to play.
I hope they turn it around with their monetization, I deeply want to say only good things about this game, but for now, it simply is not worth your time, and certainly not worth your money at the prices they ask.

these ideas so that they actually have impact and make the world feel real and unique.
I think it would be interesting if you did not

The character creation and voxel building are good the way they are, and I enjoyed the combat when I played as well. The maps are cool as well, especially the procedural ones.
All in all, I think Reign of Kings is at an important position in the crafting/survival world; They have all the means to make their game
definitive medieval crafting survival game, but it is currently stuck as Medieval "Kill-the-man-with-the-ball" and I fear that will not change any time soon. Oh Hell Yes. This is another gem from SuperGiant Games, another hit from those that brought you Bastion. Same seamless narration (and possibly, narrator, I'm not certain). Same use controlled in-game difficulty options. The (Turn) system is a novel addition to combat, with a few wrinkles for you to figure out. My accountant has informed me that I should mention the price tag, as this is quite a deal for the game, and even more so if you get it on some sort of sale or deal. It may be possible to not enjoy this game, but I do not see how. I only finished it as late as I did because of graphics card driver issues, unrelated to the game: the version of updater I had for my card was corrupted and did not in fact update my drivers. So if your IT hung-fu is superior to mine -which is likely, since I'm an artist, not a technician- you should run it just fine.
The story and soundtrack are great, both very well done. The game is executed in such a manner that you gain access to more elements of it as you progress, and does not spoon feed you with exposition. You are left to figure it out on your own, but be ye not afraid. Unless you have written more books than you've read, you should be fine. Overall, I thought that this game was pretty decent and well worth my $5. It started off strong and I found myself a little scared in some parts. The music, the lighting and the music all worked well together to achieve this. However, as the game progressed, it became a little repetitive. Navigate this room, find a note, flip some switches, open doors and occasionally run away from the enemy. What kept me going to the end was the story. I wanted to know the ending.
Controls were fairly simple. Move forward, point and click your mouse, occasionally use your lantern and sprint. I had a lot of fun playing it until about 3/4 through where the game got buggy. My game kept crashing at one loading screen, which is apparently common for this game. A few changes to my graphics settings and I was able to continue. I didn't hit a problem until the 2nd last chapter where I encountered a bug that caused my map not to load properly and me to fall to my death. That would have been okay.....but then on respawn, that same bug made it impossible for me to move on to the next stage. A fact that didn't dawn on me until an hour later after dying to the electric Manpig a bunch of times while trying to open a door that was bugged shut. A reload to an earlier save point fixed this however. And almost 7 hours later.... game finished.
So, if you're looking for a cheap scare for a few hours and enjoy a decent story, I reccommend this game. I give it a solid 7 out of 10. Points lost for the bugs encountered.

Fotonica, correction, FOTONICA is a one button runner game with interesting graphic style and fitting soundtrack. I find the one button implementation kinda unique - it's not like you're non stop running and you have the one button for your jump, no no no - you run while holding the button, you jump by releasing the button, and you fall down faster, if you press the button while airborne. It works for almost any key on your keyboard, and there is even achievement to use different keys, while completing a level. It was a little bit counter intuitive for me at the start, nothing a few deaths couldn't fix :p and also produces fun sounds, if you decide for whatever reason to start mashing a key!
I couldn't find any background story on who is running and why are they doing it, but I did notice that the gender of your runner alternates ( or maybe I'm delusional) from track to track (although I've only played the first 3 for now) going female male female. I was able to tell that ( or delude myself of it) just based on the moans your character does, while jumping. Now beware - the rhythmic music and the moaning can sound totally out of context to a person who has no idea, what are you doing on your pc :p In light of that fact, the game does offer you a one button (Q) instant exit with no confirmation required, for your plausible deniability!
The biggest plus for me though, are the online leaderboards - you have 5 min spare time and you can go for a couple runs ( the first 3 maps I've played don't take long) to beat that pesky neighbor, who topped your highscore once again :p
There is a local multiplayer, but I haven't had the pleasure to test that one yet.
The price tag might seem just a big high, in light of recent (Halloween) and upcoming (Xmas) sales, but if you're just a little bit competitive, I'm sure, you'll get your money's worth out of this game!

This review is in September 2017, so ESO is almost 4 years old and still going strong.
I don't like MMOs as a rule.  I tried quite a few of them, including WoW, and they were all too grindy to be enjoyable.  At first I would like them, but as I leveled up the grind would get worse.  Eventually I would quit and find that I actually felt much better after quitting.  That has happened to me when changing jobs, suggesting that the MMOs become too much like work rather than entertainment.
I resisted ESO for a couple of years.  I am a big ES fan and I did not want a MMO game because it would prevent single player game development (which it has).  Eventually my daughter talked me into trying it.  I was pleasantly surprised.  The main reasons I like ESO are:
1. Progress can be made even with casual play.  It is easy to get to max level compared to many MMOs.
2. There can be grind for top tier items, but the game is designed so that those top tier items are only ~3% better than items that are fairly easy to acquire.
3. There is a lot of single-player content.  The quests are very good (better than Skyrim, imo).
4. PVP is optional.  I was never interested in PVP but I tried it and it is fun in small doses.  There is no penalty for being killed.  It is also possible to gain PVP rank even if you suck (like me).
5. There is no pay to win.  There is a little pay for convenience, mostly storage space.  The real world money only stuff is limited to costumes and some exclusive houses.  The costumes are not really better than items you can find/make.
6. There are 4 player group dungeons and 12 player group dungeons.  It is easy to get a group for the 4 player dungeons using the group finder tool.  I do not do the 12 player dungeons because I do not have time; they are not essential.
7. I have never grinded once.  Sure, you can grind, but it just means you get to a place you will get to anyway, only sooner.
8. The in game community is pretty great for a MMO.  Sure, there are jerks, but it is easy to find guilds that are full of helpful people.  You can join up to 5 player guilds, which allows you to try a guild to see if you like it.
9.  You can respec your character, so no being stuck with something you no longer like.  It costs about 12000 gold at max level, which is about the amount you would earn in a few hours of play.
Here are what I perceive are the cons of ESO:
1. It is a MMO.  It is not Elder Scrolls 6.  That said, I actually like it much more than I did Skyrim.
2.  The biggest con is simply than other people can ruin the immersion.  You might want to be a thief on a stealth mission, but another player might run through the same area just killing all the guards.
3.  Some of the costumes, pets and mounts are not terribly lore-friendly imo, so you might be a brave knight ready to lead your group into the deadly dungeon, but your group consists of a guy wearing a towel, a drunken jester and a brightly glowing cat.
4.  I said that end game items did not need grinding, or the ones that did are not needed.  There is one exception: Veteran Maelstrom Arena is a max level single player challenge that rewards you with weapons that can be better than alternatives.  It takes a long time to complete, it is very grindy, and I have never heard anyone call it a "fun" experience.  The worst part it that your reward is random, and it can take many runs to get what you want.  Luckily it is not essential.
5. I do not think the PVP is that great.   The open world PVP consists of either surprise attacks (ambushes) or steamrolling smaller groups with bigger groups.  There is little in the way of skill or tactics.  Although fun at first, taking castles and resources gets old quick.  It lacks a meaningful overall goal.  Small group PVP was added recently, called Battlegrounds, which may appeal to hardcore PVPers.
Overall, I think ESO is a very good game, and a great MMO for casual and semi-casual players.
Edit: The hours played in Steam does not reflect my overall hours played, which must be 1000 or so.  That does not sound very casual, but it is about 10 hours a week for 2 years.

While the first Modern Warfare’s story was implausible at best, Modern Warfare 2’s story was downright silly. This was the first Call of Duty game that truly started to feel like a string of set-pieces. However, at this point, the series had not yet fully developed into the farce it would become.
Modern Warfare was known for its big twist, which made its story great. Modern Warfare 2 tried to capitalize on that infamy by doing the exact same thing, multiple times. It did not have the same effect.
There are some filler missions in the campaign that you will not ever go back to after the first time, but some campaign missions are genuinely fun to play over and over again (Wolverines!, for example). There is replay value here. Also, they finally removed the infinitely respawning enemies that previous installments were known for, which is a big plus.
The Spec Ops missions were actually a highlight of the game, if you could find a friend to play with. Playing as a sniper team together, or having one person provide fire support from an AC-130 was truly enjoyable.
Modern Warfare 2 is silly, but it’s probably the last still-enjoyable Call of Duty installment.

Let me start by saying I'm a HUGE horror fan, and love some of the games most people universally hate in the genre, based on their own merits anyway. I've done it all from Alone In the Dark, to Silent Hill. A lot of negative reviews for this game, and why? Because it doesn't play quite like the original, and that it's more about the overall story telling and the atmosphere?
Well to me, atmosphere will make or break a horror game, and it's probably the very first thing that needs to be done well and established in one, before even gameplay. This game nails that. This is a bit less of a "game" than The Dark Descent was, in the sense that it's more like a horror adventure game rather than a survival horror game. But that's ok. Some of my personal favorite horror games have fairly poor gameplay, but are loaded to the gills with deep atmosphere and sharp storytelling. Games like Silent Hill 2, Rule of Rose, The Fatal Frame series, Haunting Grounds, Siren, etc.
Yes, in terms of actual gameplay, this game is a step back from The Dark Descent, there's no argument there from me. In fact, overall, TDD is a superior game in most every way, I'll easily admit that. TDD is one of, if not my absolute favorite more recent horror game. That doesn't mean this is a bad game, if you had to pick one Amnesia game, it's an easy choice to pick the first over this, but you don't have to pick just one. In fact, if you enjoyed the first, I'd encourage the second.
I feel this one has a richer story, or at least one that's a bit better told, and relies on it more. It's atmosphere can sometimes be better than TDD, sometimes not as much. But it oozes it regardless. Controls are pretty much the same. Gameplay is where things change a bit. It's pretty similar, but some small differences are what really separate it.
For one, your light source doesn't run out now. A big part of the tension, and an element of the overall survival horror experience in the original game was having to manage your lamp oil, as well as finding tinder boxes to light candles and lamps around the game. As well as darkness quite literally driving your character mad. That's gone here, and I'll admit, I DO miss the old way, and it is a bit worse off without it.
Secondly, pretty much all of the major monster encounters are scripted. This is also a real bummer. I mean, it's still cool, but you lose that tension of never knowing when a monster is going to randomly attack. To be fair though, in all honesty, all of the best encounters in TDD were scripted too.
So what this leaves you with is like I stated above, more of an adventure game, it's certainly a horror game, but less on survival horror, and more on the adventure. See, it does story telling better than the original, it's just too bad it couldn't have retained a bit more of the original game's gameplay on top of that.
All in all though, it's still a wonderful game, and as a horror fan, I feel you owe it to yourself to try it out. If you're trully a horror fan anyway you know these games aren't about the actual gameplay. They really never have been. And when they do focus on the gameplay we often end up with games like Resident Evil 6 and Dead Space 3.
Don't bother.
If you're a fan of the original, then just steer away from this mess.

This review focusses on one part of this game in particular: its controller support. Steam says partial controller support, and unfortunately that's accurate. The game really seems to have been designed for m+k, with controller support tacked onto it. All the hints at the start of the game refer k+m controls even when you set the ui to controller.
There is a screen you can open from the options menu showing the controller bindings, but it doesn't have everything. It does have a LOT though, with your triggers and shoulder buttons as modifiers you can bind 20 skills or items to your abxy buttons, and then you can swap between pages if you need even more. It gets very confusing though, with other combinations used for certain actions (like right trigger + shoulder is resting). Still, you run into things that have you reaching for the mouse or keyboard again.
It may be possible to play this mostly with a controller, buf if you're looking for an MMO you can play while lazing about on your couch, I'd say this is not it.
