I'm gonna start out the review by saying that this game met my expectations.  If you were expecting it to be a riviting story with a huge climax and lots of entertainment, then you completely missed the point.
"Papers, Please" is a brilliant take on the mundane job of being a border crossing guard.  The thrill of the game comes from looking at every little detail in the ID's and paperwork you're handed and trying to find some kind of inaccuracy.  It could be as glaring as their Date of Birth being in the future, to as subtle as a "0" instead of "O" in their registration number.  Your job is to sort through it all and only admit those who present the proper information.
That's not all though!  You are also having to take care of a family at home, and you're paid by the job not by the hour.  Every person you admit/deny gives you income.  Make too many mistakes and they start docking your pay.  It's quite the challenge to be fast, yet accurate.
Add to this your work area, which is far from efficient.  It's virtually impossible, expecially later in the game, to have all your documents open in your workspace.  You have to determine what to look at, and what to leave closed on the counter for the time being.
You also have little side events, like one of the guards making deals with you that'll net you a little more income.  You also get approached by people and organizations who want you to allow/deny admitance to others no matter what their credentials.  Do something wrong and you can land yourself in jail. This is a sequel of the well-known Amnesia: The Dark Descent, and differing from the previous title, this game was not done by the same indie company, Frictional Games, as far as I know. Frictional Games were the publisher and/or end-user testers, or something along those lines, and the whole development process was done by The Chinese Room, known of Dear Esther for example.
If compared to the original Amnesia title, this one experienced some sweeping changes. For example, whole inventory system is chucked, the game levels are rather straightforward, and the sanity system has been removed. I also took notice that the puzzles we are also somewhat simple compared to the original title.
The atmosphere is good. Great in some cases. I have to say that the game was scary. REALLY scary. But to a point. To the point when the monster arose. The monster moves clumsy, it can be outran and outsmarted easily. It was not as scary as the game implied to me during the few first levels. But in any case, the game was really scary at some points, and not because of the monster.
The story is quite brilliant. I'd say this game is more close to a visual novel than a game. The Chinese Room-people are ingenious at doing these story driven games. The maps and soundscape upholds the story in a great way, and I must tell these people know what they are doing.
Conclusion: If you are a follower (or might be) of story-driven horror games, then yes, try this. But if you want to be TRULY scared (and somewhat frustrated at some points), then try on the first title, in case you already haven't.

Got the game as part of the summer sale. I was a fan of The Dark Descent for its storytelling, even though I probably wouldn't say it's the scariest game I've ever played. A Machine for Pigs doesn't change the priority, focusing on story rather than strict scares, although the atmosphere and its world are certainly unsettling in and of itself. The visual design of the locales you explore have so many details its hard not to see a story forming from the objects themselves.
In that regard, these aspects of the game interest me the most; the realistic physics of objects, the creaking of old wood and the clinking of machines, it makes the game breathe its own thick and heavy air. If you're a fan of immersive storytelling, A Machine for Pigs continues on its predecessor's praises and makes for a memorable experience that succeeds not in breaking the mold, but further cementing Frictional and The Chinese Room as some of the greatest storytellers in game design.

Kingdoms is still a shell of a game full of nothing but potential.
Visual
I run this game on a newer AMD R9 390 and 16GB ram. On the highest setting and with all optional visual effects enabled it rarely drops freme rate below 30. No crashes or graphical glitches. There are occational floating bushes and animals, and missing trees but nothing a quick game reset doesn't fix for at least 1-2 hours.  The character models are still potatoy and unappealing but I imagine they are not the final concept. The world looks great and the buildings and landscape textures and models are very nice to look at. The day/night sky is nothing special and there is no noticeable weather yet.
Overall for an early stage development it is doing well in the looks department.
Audio
Subpar at this point with repetitive music and soundfx. Really not something I consider when looking at Early Access Games.
Game play
The build mechanics are nothing special but at least functional and clean. A simple foundation is placed and you add material until everything is there and pop goes the building.
Crafting and gathering leave much to desire with repeating animations or no animation at all.
AI is something that Kingdoms is priding itself on and thus far it is doing well. NPCs work at a frustratingly slow pace, often seem to have no focus, face the wrong direction when doing something and get stuck on building corners. Despite this there is an underlying complexity to the AI that just seems in need of further development.
Combat is obviously on the back burner atm. It is much akin to minecraft with simple swings and simple DPS race fights with wolves. Ranged combat isn't any better.
Potential
As with most Early Access Games it is potential that I rate on the most. And as with all Early Access Games it is more about the developers drive to see their goals met then IF such mechanics can be implimented. Kingdoms has huge potential and if all the road map markers are hit the game should do really well. Right now it is worth a $5-10 investment. You'll get 4-6 hours of good gameplay as it stands and you can shelf the game between updates and get more game time exploring each new progression.
Devs, Keep up the good work!

I've been watching Kingdoms for some time now, and though I've seen the comments for it, both positive and negative, with it being on sale right now, I decided to try it out. The last update happened all of a week ago, so there have been some changes, and while, yes, Kingdoms is very much a beta, the game has a lot of potential.
Pros:
- I kind of lost track of time and didn't realize I'd been playing it for a few hours (has a certain addictive quality, comparable to Minecraft)
- There's relatively enough to do to keep you going. If you aren't building, you're doing things to help npcs, or you're gathering food/hunting
- With all the warnings about bears, wolves and bears are fairly balanced and don't cause as much concern for enjoyment of the game
Cons:
- Yes there are bugs and glitches still. I wouldn't consider it a glitch or bug, but I spawned in a new world right beside a wolf (not cool!). My first and favourite glitch had to be getting stuck in the trees, which is reatively easy to do when jumping off a hill. If you get stuck, your best bet is to try and get your axe out and cut down the tree, as reloading the game didn't seem to work. Trees are glitchy in general as I've also witnessed 2D trees up close, and trees that can't be cut down.
- Yes the animal spawns are still an issue, and that did eventually lagg my game a bit, but I never had game-breaking crashes as described by some, and I am using a laptop computer, and was expecting it as a possible problem.
- The only thing I could add is the fact that the game still lacks a robust economic system to keep a player busy. It didn't take long to end up with all the town's money by selling stuff to all the stores, but then there is nothing worth spending money on yet within the game, and little to reward you for completing the limited number of quests available. I'm sure these are issues that will be addressed in time, but it would certainly add to a reason for building or assisting in the development of an existing town and investing in the shops if the player gains something out of it.
All in all, it's actually a good start to a potentially great game, and I would recommend it.

If you enjoy wasting your life trying to fully understand everything about a game, only to get put into games with people who don't know what they're doing, this is the game for you.
Seriously though, the gameplay in smite is amazing. It has flawless controls, and everything feels really smooth and perfect to use. The controls being so perfect allow you to play every god to their highest potential, provided you're good enough. That is the reason i have so much time in the game. There are almost 90 gods in the game at the time im writing this, and even after all this time there is room for me to improve on almost all of them.
Despite the gameplay being so good, it is let down by every other aspect. Balancing is a joke. Hi rez don't aim to have all gods on the same level. Quite honestly, i don't think theyre really aiming for anything. Some gods aren't too good, and they will stay not too good, whereas some gods are perfect in almost every aspect, and will stay that way. Take thor for example. He has been in the top 3 junglers for 4 years, but then there's bastet who has way too high mana costs to keep up with any other junglers. Mana problems wouldn't be too bad if it wasn't also for there being little thought put into items. There is only really one item that you can get to help with mana, but it is one of the most expensive items in the game. So even if you are the best player in the world, and amazing at bastet, you still won't do as well as you would if you picked thor.
Some items are absolutely required, and some never get touched. You have 6 item slots, there must be over 100 items in the game, but only about ten items are usable in each of the five classes. If you don't pick your 6 items out of the 10 good ones, you won't do very well. There isn't room for variety or trying something new, or surprising your opponents with something they didn't expect, you have to choose from the few items that hi rez refuse to nerf. For example, Polynomicon. This item makes your next normal attack do additional damage after using an ability. The damage it does scales based on how much power you have. Late game this item alone will do a quarter of a mage, hunter or assassins health. Thats not including the damage the ability you used did, just the single basic attack. The item is also on a 3 second cooldown. Compare that to similar items, and they don't do nearly as much damage, and have much longer cooldowns. But item balancing is essentially non existant.
Now we can move onto the matchmaking in this game. I know almost everything there is to know about this game, and i have fairly good mechanical skill. Despite this, i will get placed into games with tanks who end the game with less damage mitigated than the hunters, mages who finish the game with the least damage because they don't know what items to buy, and the items they do buy are in a bad order (most expensive items first for example. They don't buy boots, they buy items that do damage based on how much power you have like polynomicon before they have any power, etc). In some cases people who haven't even reached level 30 (the highest level) will get into level 30 games and, unsurprisingly, lose the game for whoevers team they're on. I understand every god in the game, i know what to buy for every god, im fairly good in general with aiming and map awareness, etc, but i only play games with people who dont know what most of the gods do, and dont know what items to buy.
Despite matchmaking being so bad, hi rez refuse to listen to any complaints about it, and refuse to improve it.
You can avoid that altogether by playing ranked however. You have to be level 30 to play, and you can only play with people around the same division you are in. The division you get placed in however is determined on the first few games you play, so if you get unlucky, you will be placed in a low division and have a lot of trouble climbing out. There are also only 3 modes for ranked. 1v1, 3v3 and 5v5. If you solo queue 3v3, you will lose. And you recieve a lot of toxicity while losing. 1v1 is boring unless you enjoy playing only the best 3 or 4 gods. 5v5 requires luck, or queueing with a friend who is really good. The biggest party you can have when searching for ranked 5v5 is 2. You can't guaruntee a win if youre alone, and you will still have a hard time with 2 of you, so its largely luck based. Because of it being so innacurate because of what i just said, the match quality won't improve. The only difference is there will be more toxicity.
In addition to the terrible matchmaking, smite is always very unstable. About twice a week the servers shut down completely; sometimes games will close; if you are in america you can't guaruntee good ping, and will get matched with people from outside of america; sometimes you will have a big delay between when you do something, and it actually registering that you did it; one of the relics is currently very inconsistent with whether it wants to work or not; and the match of the day (special gamemode that changes daily) sometimes wont work for up to a week at a time.
There are still more issues than those though. Some gods don't always work as intended. The most well known example of this is thors second ability where a wall will appear in a line infront of him. You are supposed to get knocked to either side of the wall and be stunned for a moment if it hits you. That doesn't always happen though. A lot of time you can get stuck inside of the wall or ontop of it. And if you get knocked up next to it, both will happen. You get stuck on top of it. I already mentioned that thor has been one of the best gods since the game was released but hi rez still hasn't fixed the issues with him. Another god, ne zha, takes you up into the sky for his ultimate. You can use a relic to prevent this however. Or at least you should be able to, it almost never works. There's the morrigan who isn't allowed to be played in the smite pro league because spectating games with her in it doesn't work properly. There are a few more, but i won't go on.
Now onto the community. As i just mentioned, there is a lot of toxicity. Hi rez do nothing about this. There is a mute function, but if you mute them you won't be able to hear the commands theyre putting in chat to let you know if youre getting ganked, or if a certain enemy just used their ultimate or whatever useful things they may have to say. They can also just message you directly if they want. Thats not much of an issue though, you can mute and you can disable messages from people who arent on your friends list, but for a game that cares so much about the pro scene and wanting to be a relevant e sports game, it won't be surprising for people to take the game extremely seriously, in which case muting your teammates will put you at a disadvantage. And even if you don't take the game seriously, you just want to relax and have fun, there is so much toxicity that you won't be able to unless you mute everybody at the start of every game, or only play with friends. And if you choose to only play with friends, there is a laugh function in the game (for some reason), so you will still be able to hear the enemies laugh at you if you don't mute them. Either way, there is so much toxicity that you will not be able to have a good experience in this game.
There is a report function however. You can report people who break the rules or the ToS. Hi rez don't do anything about the reports though. Some streamers for example will even break the ToS live without consequence. You can contact hi rez directly and provide evidence of what has happened, in which case they will listen. The most i have seen them do is a 3 day ban though, which was for death threats and racism.
Overall, smite is a great game, but it has the worst community i have ever came across, and its made by the worst developers i have ever came across.

Transistor is one of the best non-traditional RPG experiences I've ever had. The trailers might make it look complicated or intimidated, but it's actually very fluid and only ever becomes as complex as you want it to. I highly recommend that if you're on the edge, you dive right in. Your trusty sword will be at your side to guide you throughout the Process.
If you're a narrative-focused gamer that doesn't like to get into deep customization and wants to mostly focus on the story, you can do that in Transistor, and the experience is extremely rewarding, as there are many aspects of the plot which are only revealed to those who are dedicated to searching for them.
Conversely, if you're a mechanics-focused gamer who couldn't care less about plot but loves to customize characters and really "play" the game, Transistor is also for you. Instead of getting generic combat abilities, you earn Functions in Transistor, which can be used in three different ways: actives, upgrades, and passives. Depending on how you use Functions and combine them together, you can create drastically different playstyles and create your own unique way of defeating enemies. You can even use Limiters to change the way the enemy fights you for a more challenging experience.
Despite those two points, I think Transistor is most enjoyed by the completionist. While it's true that the game can be "finished" in as short as four hours, Transistor allows you to build the game the way you want to play it. If you want to 100% complete the game and experience all it has to offer, you'll be here for a while, and you'll love every step of the journey. In Transistor, the sky is only blue if you want it to.

I bought this game hoping it would have something in common with the classic vector based arcade game Rez, and it does, but not enough.
The visuals are gorgeous and the music is okay. (Thankfully it's not actually dubstep, as another reviewer has erroniously written.) The controls are responsive and engaging as well, and suit the sort of first-person-unicorn-dash gameplay that the designers chose.
And that brings me to my one major gripe. Unlike Rez, whose arcade shooter game style was challenging and varied, FOTONICA is pretty much a one-trick pony. The single-button control scheme (somehow incompatible with the XB360 controller - whether through laziness or evil) means that each level amounts to repetitive trial and error with the ultimate goal of course memorization. This in turn means that in order to progress in the game, you will need to know each level so well that the element of urgency and adrenaline (an area where this game excels) is pretty much lost. Nor are the collectibles an entertaining distraction; there is only one variety, an inornate red sphere. This, plus the lack of checkpoints and the game's tendency to put the most difficult obstacles at the end of each course, is why I can't recommend this game.
TL:DR?
It's not completely non-fun, but probably fun and non-fun in equal measure.

Probably my favourite runner game!
… It takes a more dream-like approach on running. Playing Fotonica makes me feel the way how I fly in my dreams. Unlike going to sleep Fotonica – as a runner game – is an energetic game though. The clue of the game will be the inverted 'jump button': flying by default you need to push a button 'to land and run'.
Simplistic in many ways it offers a great atmosphere.

There’s a sublime beauty driving Fotonica at all times.
It’s simple vector graphics twist and contort into images and designs which far succeed the simplicity with which they’re drawn, even more impressive in motion as you speed through levels barely having time to take it all in. The artistry and style expressed in these moments is at times stunning and always stimulating, mesmerizing and drastically different in tone and setting in each passing scene. Minimal sound design serves as a constant reminder of the speed and velocity with which you move, being both an invigorating source of feedback when you successfully land a jump and make it to top speed, and a sudden jolt should you miss and slam headfirst into a platform before beginning a fall into nothingness. Being in this world is in itself something of a wonder and a thrill, though one that constantly wishes to throw you out before you have a chance to behold all there is to see.
Controlled via a single button, Fotonica is an runner which compensates for its simplicity in design with challenging, extremely fast, multilayered levels with a very small margin for error. Finding the best paths and secrets within each level is an interesting and engaging element that extends your goal beyond the omnipresent fear of missing a jump and falling to your doom, and an aspect I would have liked to have seen more focus put upon besides effecting your score. Successfully making your way through these levels is invigorating, but more often than not it falls into punishing loops of trial and error, punctuated by occasional success as you incrementally make your way through levels memorizing your path and planning your jumps to the exact second.
It’s a challenge that’s certainly passable in time, but one which rarely feels fair. The monochromatic environments are often difficult to tell apart from the background and the draw distance painfully short, making judging distance and timing jumps frustrating and tedious. With how exact jumps tend to need to be to land, not having enough input to make the call of when to jump is a huge detriment to the experience.
Split into just ten very short levels (though it will of course take you longer to clear them at first), Fotonica feels like almost a prelude to a larger game. Its lacking so much content as to feel empty and possibly even unfinished, leaving me wondering what I was intended to do after completing them all in only an hour or so. The endless mode is a rather disappointing and throwaway addition, ditching the involved multifaceted platform layouts from the arcade mode for bland, single platforms which I grew tired of traversing almost immediately.
The multiplayer mode actually fixes my biggest issue with the game, that being its relentlessly punishing nature, by only setting you back a short way when you fail and then making the challenge about being the first to get to the end instead of memorizing and clearing levels on your own. Sadly it’s local only, and I doubt many will sit down with a group to spend much time with it, but the one button control scheme does mean there’s no issue of not having enough controllers as everyone can play with a single keyboard (or gamepad, if you’re dexterous enough).
I have a lot of problems with Fotonica, ones which fundamentally hurt my enjoyment of the game and have me incredibly confused on if I believe it’s worth anyone’s time to bother with. In that same instance though I’m reminded of just how artistic and imaginative running through these levels are, which caused me to continue playing far after I stopped having any great amount of “fun”. Is visual design alone enough to carry the game? I’m not sure I could give you a sincere answer, but even now I’m finding myself drawn back into it, no matter how loudly every other aspect is telling me to leave.

By many aspects it feels like the run for the closest description of reality is over* — even though human eye can still distinguish artificial from realty. So beside story-telling, what's left for creators to conquer ? VR probably and on the other hand I'd say “Descontruction”.
belongs to the last category. Using the endless running theme, FOTONICA is one of those game that masterfully recreate specific feelings thanks to great care for complementarity between motion, pace and sound.
Your eyes shall always try to predict what's beyond game's horizon, your mind will stumble and fall many times before it catches the “one-key” control. One unique original track for each level - mostly from minimal genre — even close to neural beats sometimes — brilliantly emphasize the global idea behind FOTONICA: Simplcity, the reprensation of scene only using white lines on deep black background.
Proceduraly generated level? In the case of FOTONICA I'd say : irrelevant. Still 3 “truly” endless runs await you. But you don't play F. for endless ...!
But pragmatically what does Fotonica offer? Jump and land, many alternative routes will be offered to you — creating the most effective one is rather complex. Goal? Achieve great speeds, never lose acceleration by hurting something or by satying in the air for too long while jumping. You'll need to pick-up purple patch, the faster you go while grabbing, the more marks you spare.
> 8 “handcrafted” levels >< 3 types of Endless >< 4 difficulty >< tweak your visual experience in option >< Steam-wide ladderboards >< split-screen multiplayer >< sharp & polished experience (so far, 9h)
It's like having an itch, and every time you scratch that itch, the itch becomes more and more complex. But in a good way.

I have a lot of tolerance for early access games,  as a game that has only existed for 6 months, and appears to be developed by a single person, this is a brilliant effort.
When compared to retail release games, it still has a long way to go. If you are a person that can respect some guy for taking on the challenge of building a game on his own, then certainly you will appreciate the effort that went into this game. If you have no idea what goes into game making.. then you need not apply; move on now...
The basic framework for addictive gameplay is there, most core logics are working, graphics still has some bugs, as does logic.  But I can see where he is going with this game.  I actually got this game as some of the building layouts reminded me of minecraft.  The gameplay itself seems to be similar to the millionare/village building and trading addon of tekkit (minecraft) where you can provide supplies to villages and see the materials used to build and upgrade the village.  Players can help or create villages, and there is a basic skill tree already in place.
On the other hand if you have some strange expectation for early access games to be polished and professionally put together.. then aside from the fact you are totally missing the point - you will probably not like this game .. yet.
Still lots of graphical glitches, trees not aligning with ground and breaking up realistically, NPCs placing two houses in a single tile, an inventory that doesnt tell you when it is full nor can be expanded in any obvious manner, NPC menus that appear to only be designed for one specific screen mode which isnt the game default, and looks all buggy and overlapping when you try to go into the NPC training screen.   Animals spawned so frequently i often found animal "towers" stacked 10 high.  Players and animals can walk on water, NPCs founding invisible villages, NPCs being both alive and dead etc.
Ignoring that, the game strikes me as only really needing basic menu alignment tweaks, and some graphical tweaking, and the game seems so far along already for a 6month effort.
I hope the developer keeps at it, as the game even in its current state is appealing in a simple survival style sort of way.  There is enough depth to be interesting, and it has managed to avoid the tendancy of other games to be overcomplicated, which makes it a fresher game for casual survivalist fans. Even my daughter liked the look enough that she had a go before bedtime and probably wants a copy herself now.
This game is also single player.  That is not a bad thing, makes it more of a casual flavor.  The skill tree is actually part of game play too not just a badge collection.
overall with some ui polishing and maybe something more interesting for mines/ruins added; and less crazy spawn rates, and more durable npcs (i keep finding dead ones) this looks to become a fun casual survival game.
it is also good they are supporting modding early on.
i may be crazy but i liked it

I have since given some more time to this game only to be bombarded with more and more issues. I'm changing my recommendation from "Has Potential" to "Most likely another money grab", simply because I do not understand why any developer would release a game, even in Early Access, when I discovered the first three problems within the first 5 minutes of gameplay.
All of the issues I am experiencing are so easily triggered and should not have been overlooked by a developer who actually plays his own game. It's almost like the developer hits compile, assumes it's okay, and publishes it.
This game was built with Unity. It's the first thing you see; "Made with Unity" upon start the game. Whilst not important to most, there are some who dislike Unity games due to a certain "feel" the games have. I understand this, and agree to some extent so I'm making it known this is a Unity game.
One of the first things the game throws at you is what will be available in an upcoming update. In this case it's Taverns. You've already seen them, it's that lovely interior screenshot on the store page... That's right, it's not even in game yet.
Okay, so maybe some of you are thinking 'who cares, it'll be added eventually'.. Sure. But this isn't the first time I've seen developers misrepresent with screenshots of "upcoming" content and run off with your money before that "upcoming" content is added to the game. We're not allowed to mis-sell in the real world of economics and advertising, it shouldn't be allowed here.
That certain "feel" of Unity as mentioned earlier is prominent in Kingdoms. Animations are slow and everything feels sluggish. It takes so long to swing your sword almost everything will outrun you before you finally follow the swing through. All animations just feel so slow and as a result, weak.
Combat is equally lazy. I was killed by an unarmed peasant, despite mashing his face in with an Axe. To be fair, I had no idea I was hitting him, or vice-versa, because there is a lack of combat sounds, flinching etc. The best you get is an awful blood-splatter effect around the screen which is so bad it literally blocks 80% of your vision... not kidding.
The worst part about this game is not the amount of bugs and glitches I have encountered, but how easy they are to find, replicate and ruin your game. I appreciate it's an Early Access title, but any competent developer who play tests his own product for more than five minutes would have found and sorted these issues.
During my first playthrough I quickly found a cave. The caves are more like mazes, being generated in a very typical dungeon crawlereqsue "corridor and intersection" like grid. That said, my first reaction was to open my map to see if the game had maps for underground areas.
It did not and my map simply displayed the very botton left hand side of the world. Upon leaving the cave and opening your map you will discover that the map is still stuck in the bottom left hand corner.
A save and reload fixes this one.
Don't you just hate it when you put something down, only to find it's still in your hand? No?... What do you mean that doesn't happen?.. Well in Kingdoms it does, with Torches at least.
Upon leaving the cave in which I discovered the map bug, barely a minute later I discovered this bug.
I've left the cave so decide to put my torch away, dragging it from my hand in my character screen back to my inventory. The torch is unequipped now and is in my inventory, but also magically and annoyingly, blinding the crap out of me in my left hand..
A save and reload fixes this one.
Not a bug, but something basic that any compentent developer will have done with no excuses.
Wait for it........... theres no confirmation on the load button... *audience gasps*.. I know, I know.. Click carefully..
When speaking with NPC's you have the option to see their skills. When i was finished viewing this NPC's skill I pressed ESC to exit the dialogue; the problem here is that in Kingdoms, pressing ESC doesn't close dialogues like most games. Instead it just brings up the menu.
This creates an annoying bug.
You see, when you pressed ESC the second time to close the menu, it unfrees your mouse so you can move around the world again, but, the skill window reopens. You're not running around with this window slapped on your screen.
Moving away from the NPC giving the dialogue will close it, but it will automatically re-open when you get back within range.
A save and reload does
fix this one.
This one is weird.. And makes me question the integrity of the save/load system of the game.
Whilst trying to get rid of the skill window mentioned in the previous bug above, I tried to click the NPC (difficult with a massive, non-transparent window up in your grill). Eventually it closed, but now the NPC was hostile. Clearly all my clicking about initiated an attack on him, no biggie, I'll jsut reload and carefully click him now I know it's possible..
That god damn NPC is still hostile! Even after a reload! (And no, he wasn't hostile before the save, as after the save I followed him and watched him build for a while before the bugs, we both reloaded in the same place and the building was back down to it's initial progress when I arrived, but he was still hostile after the load!)
I'm now 50 minutes into the game. Never built anything; never mined a single ore; never cut a single tree; never killed a single animal... And I don't intend to. That's enough early bugs for me.
It was at this point, ladies and gents, I closed this game, wrote this review, grabbed a beer, and thanked the Lord I didn't pay for this game.
UPDATE: Game is more stable now, doesn't abuse my hardware, and it's pretty fun in it's current state.  Devs are very active, and there's even a Discord for reporting bugs and stuff.

I'm a newbie, I've read about all the negative threads, and know of most of the negative points of this game. Lack of endgame, massive amount of bugs, performance issues, network issues, awful class balance, no stat resetting potion, no way to reset the circle of a class if you screw up your build, tons of bots, restrictions that affect us players more than the bots...
Reading negative threads isn't healthy, but you can't just hide your eyes from the reality since you'll have to experience it at some point.
But I'm still having fun. The OST and the art quality are both top notch and the mmo is really set up like those japanese light novels with special events, cutscenes, hidden quest and "freedom". Honestly that's a really cool concept.
I have a few friends that play the game with me, and I've found a casual and fun guild to play with too. I've had to do a lot by myself from crafting gear, farming mats/exp cards, grinding, and the progression so far (I'm level 96 right now) felt really good.
Because I knew of the unforgiving build system, I did my homework and made myself a build up to rank 7 that looked good and would please me along the way while being useful during parties, and I asked advice about it on the reddit and on the official forum of this game. So far I'm not disappointed by that.
So is the game worth playing as a newbie? If you got nothing else to entertain yourself with, I'd say yes. Go in blind except for your build (and that includes also stats distribution) and you'll enjoy the ride.
Will I quit upon reaching 200+ because of all the issues mentioned above? I'm not sure, but it wouldn't be the first time I quit an mmo after hitting the cap. I'll still have fond memories, but I'll move on if there's nothing else waiting for me, and if IMC decides to not support their game.
Anyway, just words from a newbie.

I've been meaning to sit down and write a review up for Machine for Pigs for a while, so here goes.
The best way to review Machine for Pigs is to compare it to its predecessor first.
What Machine for Pigs does better:
+ Story
+ Graphics
+ Characters
+ Immersion
What Dark Descent does better:
+ Fear/Dread/Scare Factor
+ Monsters
+ Soundtrack (OST) & Ambience
+ A generally better horror game
Now of course both these games are very different, but unlike Dark Descent, Machine for Pigs feels more like 'Dear Esther' than it does, say Penumbra. The story is very interesting and the level designs are also really nicely done. That aside, i didn't find the Pig Monsters all that intimidating or scary in comparison to that of the Brutes/Grunts/Suitors in Dark Descent. The level designs are well thought out and the unique touch in the landscape sets it apart from the other games, but again, i didn't find it to be that good of a horror game, which it really is supposed to be. Don't get me wrong though, there were times where i was running for my life and had my heart racing, but the real sense of dread due to ambience and tension was lost after the first monster encounter (Before the first pig monster appears, it really was scary!). If anything, i felt sorry for these monstrosities rather than fear.
Machine for Pigs is its own game, and i'd recomend it to players who enjoyed Dark Descent, like story and immersion and want something that will keep them on their toes. It's not as good as Penumbra: Black Plague or Amnesia: Dark Descent, but on its own it is still a noteworthy title.

When Frictional Games let The Chinese Room take hold of this, one of the few good things that came out were a very nice artistic appeal. Amazing graphics, and a slightly intriguing story(and I emphasise on slightly heavily).
The thing is, the wandered away from the atmosphere, which is the heart and soul of the Horror Genre.
They primarily focused on the complexity of the story, the contraptions, hiding places, I could go on.
As soon as I was dropped into the game, I felt that I was being held along the game all the way. No helpful hints in-game to help me, but it was as if there were huge arrows pointing towards the 'complex' puzzles. This can be a nitpick depending on the gamer, for me, it is annoying to see this. But, this is just versatile to the gamers.
Overall, this game isn't as good if you played the previous, but is quite nice graphics-wise. I say that Frictional Games should have worked on atmosphere and story, while The Chinese Room worked on graphics. It may have been able to be one of the few best Horror games of 2013.

For those who are accustomed to horror games like Outlast will draw some parallels to its overall feel and controls.  A lot of the scares comes from what you see as well as what you don't. You get freaked out when you hear an enemy has spoted you and you jump at the small sounds indicating an enemy is near by.
There are some deviations as well. In Alien Isolation there are very few jump scares which keeps the game fresh for multiple playthroughs (I played through multiple times to 100% complete the game and still left shaken bye the end of it).
The AI is extreamly smart and every death feels deserved, discounting a few as youtube has made well aware. The dialog and characters further the immersion which subsiquently heightents the fear factor. The only glaring downside I can recall from my hours of play was a bug which made it impossible to progress (only fixed after two reloads) and the lipsync (which essentially boils down to moving the mouth up and down when the character talks).

Just be sure to get the DLC as you gewt to play as Ripley on the Nostromo (if your a true fan that should already make you nerdgasm). If I haden't gotten this on Humble Bundle I would have bought it anyways. Just some tips for those of you who do bye, look in the community guides for the ultimate graphics tweaking guide and save often.

I am giving a quick review because I strongly believe that after what CA did with the game post-release it has become one of my favourite TW games.
The Good: Graphics, Varied Factions, New Province System (Gives you mini-objectives that add some structure to the campaign), Army System and Traditions, Great audio and music, Lots of DLC
The Bad: Performance (This game will eat your PC alive), Agents (They are both too powerful and their risk is not satisfying at all), Diplomacy (Better than before but still feels random), Lots of DLC
Overall: It's easily become my favourite historical Total War game. I like some of the new systems they have in place and the wonderful setting means you get to fight with/against Legionnaires, War Elephants, Horse Archers, Chariots, Heavy Cavalry, Ballista - So much variety!
Recommended for: In its current state, every TW player must try this game. It is a good starting point for new TW players as it is by far more streamlined than the old games (For better or for worse)
And for those that bought this on release or were turned off by the release problems - I ask you to try this game again. With the fixes and changes in place (And maybe with some mods) it is now a great and authentic Total War entry.

Being a part of the legendary Total War series I expected nothing less than an amazing game, however this game falls below the standard previous games have set. Many of the mechanics are basic and just absolutely ridiculous (for example the province system, which renders settlements useless on their own which is annoying as well as unrealistic and tedious) which is the biggest problem. Furthermore is the AI known to be weird.
It is not all bad though: it offers a wide variety of factions and it'll take you more than a 100 hours to discover each one. The battles are pretty good as well, and even though it goes without saying with a Total War game: the visuals are great.
Overall conclusion: This is one of the lesser games of the Total War franchise. If you want just any game of the series I suggest Shogun II over this one. And if you specifically want a game set during the rise of Rome I even prefer the original Rome: Total War. It's a bit outdated graphics-wise, but it plays so much better.

I'm gonna start out the review by saying that this game met my expectations.  If you were expecting it to be a riviting story with a huge climax and lots of entertainment, then you completely missed the point.
"Papers, Please" is a brilliant take on the mundane job of being a border crossing guard.  The thrill of the game comes from looking at every little detail in the ID's and paperwork you're handed and trying to find some kind of inaccuracy.  It could be as glaring as their Date of Birth being in the future, to as subtle as a "0" instead of "O" in their registration number.  Your job is to sort through it all and only admit those who present the proper information.
That's not all though!  You are also having to take care of a family at home, and you're paid by the job not by the hour.  Every person you admit/deny gives you income.  Make too many mistakes and they start docking your pay.  It's quite the challenge to be fast, yet accurate.
Add to this your work area, which is far from efficient.  It's virtually impossible, expecially later in the game, to have all your documents open in your workspace.  You have to determine what to look at, and what to leave closed on the counter for the time being.
You also have little side events, like one of the guards making deals with you that'll net you a little more income.  You also get approached by people and organizations who want you to allow/deny admitance to others no matter what their credentials.  Do something wrong and you can land yourself in jail.  Do something right and you can come out on top, while not quite following the rules.  Work too slow and you might start to loose family members to illness or starvation.  It's quite the puzzle!
There isn't really any excitement to this game.  The enjoyment comes from working out a strategy that sees you staying out of jail, your family staying healthy, and your patritism remaining intact.  It even has an "Endless" mode if you just want to keep going and going.
I absolutely recommend "Papers, Please"!

This game has simple mechanics and a simple goal; clear as many people from your line as possible before the shift ends.  The more people you process, the more money you get at the end of each day.  If you mess up and let someone through who shouldn't have been able to, you'll get a penalty and too many of those will start to cut into your income.  Where does the money go?  It goes to providing for your family who you have to keep alive in order to continue on with the game.
Simple enough.  But the catch is the increasing difficulty of each day as more and more regulations are put into place and changes being made to established policies.  When you first start out, it's a breeze getting everyone through and making good money.  As the days roll, the new documents and procedures needed to gain entry into your land become more and more and your skill in managing these new tasks as well as maintaining old ones in a timely fashion become much harder and mistakes will likely be made numerous times costing you money and in some cases, your families life which means game over for you.
One of the cool things in this game is the stories of the people you're processing.  At one point, you get someone entering your country that mentions not to let a certain person in because they mean to harm them.  You eventually meet that person and even though their documents check out, do you allow them access or do you forbid them entry?  Whatever you decide during your time in the booth will have ramifications on the news stories of the following day.  Sometimes the paperwork checks out and in your haste to get more people processed, you overlook something subtle but suspicious that results in a major event, like a terrorist blowing himself up because even though the paperwork checked out, you didn't take the extra time to scan him when he was acting strange.
I'm calling this a casual game because everything is super simple but effectively difficult and tense when trying to get as much money each day so you can feed, shelter, and warm your family.  The days generally last about 5 to 10 minutes so you can jump in and out after each day and pick up where you left off no sweat.  I'd recommend this game to anyone that likes games that require your full attention and attention to detail.

AquaNimble is everything you could wish for in a shoot 'em up game, and even more. In addition to the singleplayer mode, it features local multiplayer for up to four players, three fixed campaigns, two procedural campaigns, six difficulty levels, more than 70 enemy types, over 20 submarines with different unlockable skins, eight types of special items, more than 30 weapons, over 50 Steam achievements, leaderboards ,full controller support  and Steam cloud support.
The game has so much content that even quoting everything that it offers still can not give an idea of ​​its grandeur. Yes, it is that giant, both in the size of the campaigns (which last about an hour and a half, which is a well above average time for this kind of game) as in its replayability. Even the three fixed campaigns brings variery to the table, as weapons and powerups will always be chosen randomly, and although you can memorize the order in which the enemies appear, they can come from any corner of the screen. The Daily Campaign (a campaign generated every 24 hours for all players) and Forever Abyss campaign (which brings 200 hordes of enemies to be defeated) are totally procedural.
Besides the high replayability that AquaNimble provides, it can be fair to any kind of player, be it casual or hardcore, as there are many, many options of customization beyond the levels of difficulty. The player himself will decide whether he wants something with lives and continues to spare or a more serious challenge with few lives, except for the difficulty level Nightmare (the highest), which requires that the chosen campaign be completed with only one life and without Continues. Another positive point is that even customized games allow you to unlock achievements, which does not take away the freedom to choose the best way to play. The scores of these matches also go to the ranking, and the accumulated points are calculated according to the options selected, and the choice for a bigger challenge also guarantees a higher score.
Graphics are all made in pixel art, a very exotic one by the way, with all the screen space taken advantage of. The soundtrack, composed by PurpleFreezer, unites masterfully common instruments common with chiptune soubds and has a handful of songs that will stay in your head for a long time. The result of the whole is  game that manages to be more than the sum of its parts, that is, right away it brings an ambitious concept that does not disappoint.
* Fun and accessible for all players
* Captivating visuals and soundtrack
* Responsive and fully customizable controls
* High replayability, always with unpredictable matches
* Able to offer both a traditional shmup experience and bullet hell
* The boss order is exactly the same in all campaigns, including the procedural ones

This game is absolutley amazing! But don't let the "Free to Play" title fool you. You have to pay for literally EVERYTHING with real money. I've already dropped about 30 bucks getting a 3 month membership and a compund bow with an improved sight. Once you break past the pay wall this game is wonderful (and worth paying some money for). Also a membership will give you acess to hunt any animal, make your own servers, and have your ammo refilled for free everytime you start a new hunt (unless you have premium ammo such as tracers!).
This game is about as real as it gets in terms of a video game, and yes I have hunted and killed animals in real life so I would know. Wind patterns can make animals smell you. If you're quiet enough they only see you if you're coming from a certain angle. Animals will either die or run and eventually die depending on where you hit them. There are many more reasons I could show but my fingers would fall off before I could finish the review.
Keep in mind this game pertains to a certain set of people. You must grow patience if you want to get a good kill, otherwise you'll mostly find females or smaller males, but take that statement with a grain of salt. You can most definatley run around the woods like a crazy person and have a good time killing animals, but rare animals can hear you much easier than say a pheasent or a roe deer.
The maps are absolutly amazing, from snowy enviroments to summer, there is something for everyone (The Hammeldel and Australia maps have the best animals in my opinion, Reindeer, snow hare, moose, kangaroo etc). There is no shortage of detail and they're extremely realistic.
There is no shortage of weapons in this game, from rifles to bow and arrow there is most definatley enough to suit anyones taste. Also I stated earlier that you're going to have to pay some money for this game. Thats only true to a point. You're not going to be shelling out mad money on this, you only need 2 guns, a big rifle and a smaller pistol in case you run into small game ( I would recommend to buy a highpowered rifle and a bow, because a bow is able to legally kill any animal in the game and a rifle can kill bigger animals much easier from an even further distance than even the best bow).
Thats about all I have to say about this game, I havent really found any cons yet and I'm sure I will eventually. Thanks if you took the time to read this review and I hope all the negative reviews dont sway you away from getting this game ( all the bad reviews are from people not willing to pay money for this work of art) :).

Most bad reviews seem to come from people with little-to-no hours in the game who haven't fleshed the game out, not getting to experience the real fun of the game; which is, seige wars between guilds, fighting for the throne, teaming up with the community to over-throw a corrupt King or Queen, and the list goes on...
That all being said, this game is not polished yet, and anyone fighting a battle in the flaxfields playing on a mediocre laptop is going to have a bad time. Furthermore, the other negative reviews of the game that don't come from salty players have merit, where if you don't take satisfaction in grind and results, this isn't the game for you. Combat is a steep learning curve for anyone who hasn't played Chivilary, but it is oh so satisfying when you decapitate your opponent and become a skilled fighter.
All-in-all, excellent game, and if you like being King, sitting on the throne and yelling, "Off with his head!" as the executioner sends the guillotine blade down on your opponent, then pick up a copy and give it a go.

I enjoy myself a nice little western game every once in a while. I don't mean a western game as in a game released in the west, no, those are kind of the only games I really play xD I mean a nice little trip through the old wild west. For some sad reason, there aren't many western games out nowaday. There's Red Dead Redemption, and I freaking love that game, but other than that, I can't think of a mainstream western game out there. I can only really name two games that I can say are definately good western games other than Red Dead. One is Westerado: Doubled Barrelled, an 8-bit romp that is the closest thing a PC only gamer can play to RDR and is probably going to be in my Top Games of 2015. I should really review that game sometime. But anyway, the second game is the one you read the review on right now. Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a kind of silly linear shooter that has the best duel system since Red Dead Redemption without a doubt, and while it is nothing special, I say you should try it out sometime. Why that? Well, let me go into it a bit more.
STORY: Your name is Silas Greaves. One day you walk into a saloon and, in order to mooch drinks off some people, decide to tell the story of his life as a bounty hunter and how he took down the greatest villains of the old west. Or at least, how he says how it goes down, since half of the time the stories he tells seem a bit... off, from the usual stories on these people's demises, and a few of the guys he tells the stories to start to figure out that this guy might be lying. The story is kind of neat, nothing really astounding other than a neat little twist near the very end, but it isn't anything bad. I like how we have to take each story he tells with a grain of salt, because we have no idea when this guy tells a true story or when he just makes it up. Story will keep you occupied for around 4 hours I suppose, but that's fine enough.
GAMEPLAY: First person perspective. You carry a revolver and a main weapon, though I prefer the revolver for most situations, and dynamite, which acts like a grenade essentially. You can also unlock an option to duel wield revolvers via a skill tree, which is awesome. There is a Max Payne-esque Bullettime mode here where you can slow down time and line up your shots easier, which is a nice feature as well. A really neat feature is that, sometimes if you are close to death, time slows down so you can actually dodge a bullet that flies towards your head and would otherwise kill you, and if you succeed at dodging it, you'll get some extra health. The afformentioned duels I mentioned before are fun as well and are set up very well. Overall, it's good fun.
GRAPHICS AND PERFORMANCE: The game has a kind of cell shade look to it, like the Borderlands games, though they don't necessarily go all out with it. The scenes in the saloon are still images of some usual character sketches. Both look fine and do the job well. Game runs decently as well.
CHARACTERS AND VOICE ACTING: Silas Greaves is voiced well enough. The other people in the bar are voiced decently as well. All of them look fine enough, the unique baddies in the games look pretty good and unique. Nothing really special I suppose, but it's decent enough.
EXTRA: There are some arcade modes that you can play once you beat the main games. None of them necessarily interested me, except for the Duel mode, but maybe you can get something out of them. There are Nuggets of Truth hidden throughout the levels, which tell you how the stories they talk about actually went down in real life, which is pretty interesting. Decent amount of stuff here if you can get interested in doing so.
FINAL: It's a nice little game, should get more attention than it does. 7.5/10, nice game, might want to pick it up around sale time. I say it's worth it.

Easily one of my favorite games of the year. Bastion absolutely amazed me, and supergiant games somehow stepped it up with Transistor. The whole experience -gameplay, music, artwork/visuals are absolutely breathtaking and original. The combat system is similar to VATS in the fallout series, in that you can either play real time or freeze time and plan out your moves. What amazes me the most is the sheer number of combinations of abilities. There are 13 functions, which can be combined in 13 * (12 choose 2) = 858 unique combinations. That means there are 858 UNIQUE SKILLS in the game. You have 2 passive slots and 4 ability slots, meaning the total number of loadouts is... a lot.
Gustav Klimt did the art for this game, every bit as good as Bastion.

The gameplay is V.A.T.S. from Fallout 3, except that Supergiant took it and made it strategically interesting.  It's seriously the best thing ever.  I wish all RPGs were this sophisticated.
Obviously this game has other merits, but they're covered in other reviews.  Like, lots of other merits.  I just don't want praise of the story, graphics, music, etc., to make anyone think that this game isn't just plain fun to play.

I've had Papers, Please installed on my system since Winter 2013, but always resisted actually playing it because of its reputation for being grueling, not fun, feeling like work, etc. Well, this game is indeed those things, yet it's incredibly engaging and deserves every bit of the praise it has gotten. The story has various branching paths and events, and a typical playthrough has a manageable length (around 4 hours) which gives it a good amount of replay value. I definitely intend to play through at least a few more times.
I appreciate how the game finds a lot of (admittedly often dark) humor and humanity in such a bleak environment. Papers, Please may be an unlikely inspiration for cosplay, fanart, mods for other games, etc.,  but I wasn't surprised to find that its story and characters have resonated with a lot of people.
Plus, the satisfaction you get after receiving one of the "good" endings makes all the tension worth it. The Victory music (which I'm listening to right now) is a reward unto itself. Looking forward to Lucas Pope's next game.

It was my first hunt.
I was roaming the big, dense forest looking for wildlife, keeping my eyes and ears peeled, but after hours of searching I had not yet found my prey, and it was getting dark.
The forest was not the same, like it was before it got dark, and a slight feeling of discomfort came over me.
That was the moment I should have gone back, I should have left and never come back.
But I didn't.
Around midnight, in the light of the big white moon, that seemed to be wathing over me, I finnaly saw something that seemed to be an easy kill, but never had I been so wrong.
It was a wild rooster, unaware of me, as I was on my belly in the thick bushes preparing my first kill.
I held my breath, pointed the cross of the scope at the roosters body, and slowly squeezed the trigger.
That was when it happened, something beyond comprehension, that made sure I will never, no, can never, play this game again: when I squeezed the trigger, it was not the sound of gunpowder igniting that I heard, nor the muffled impact of the bullet.
All I heard was silence, and all I saw was the screen telling me I had to buy a license to be able to hunt in a game about hunting.
2/10

I liked this game a lot, in a way that is not easy for me to describe, but I think the best way to do it is not to compare it to its developer's predecessor title Bastion.  Bastion is its own game and while there are some similarities, Transistor is its own title.
The game is an isometric 3rd person action title putting the player in the role of a mute female protagonist named Red, on a mission of revenge towards a group of persons who killed her friend who takes the role of a personality trapped inside a cyberized sword, set in a fantastical retro/sci-fi digital-esq world.  The presentation of this setting is in my opinion absolutely wonderful, and genuinely inspired feelings of awe.  The use of narration, music, sound, and cutscenes all combined well, and the story presentation felt very true to itself.  The game does not go out of its way to explain its world to the player in the way a lot of RPGs do by breaking character, the characters behave and use figures of speech as if they were themselves and the player can sort out what that means as he plays the game.  Some people might hate it and its not always done well in games, but here it was done right.
Gameplay wise, you have a mix of real time action and a core ability which lets you pause the action to play and queue up actions.  This is probably where the game's main flaw lies for me, but that reason is NOT because it breaks the pace of action (a complaint I have heard others voice).  The problem is that when played with a KB+M, the planning element of the game is very fluid but the action is not.  When you use a controller the action is fluid, but the planning element is not.  Overall I think that it is better to play with KB+M, and try to find a set-up that works for you.
You gain new abilities in this game in an RPG-lite way, with some gained from level-ups and some gained from story progression.  Each power can be one of four usable active powers, one of two possible upgrades for an active power, or a passive benefit, and you can mix and match these as you please at save points.  It adds a very nice level of customization, and also serves as part of the game balance as when you lose all HP you lose one equipped power for a period of time but get to immediately continue playing rather than being served with a game over.  The game also lets you optionally make combat harder in a number of ways if you like a challenge, and without these difficulty customizations the game is fairly easy.  Aside from combat there are no puzzles, it is purely an action game.
The game performed perfectly fine on my rig (2.8ghz * 6, AMD Radeon 6850 HD, 8gb RAM).  There is only moderate replayability in the form of a New Game+ mode which allows additional progression and starts at a higher difficulty, but as much of the game is the amazing presentation and initial experience you probably wont find this game to be an hour sink.  Length wise is about 10-12 hours or so, if I recall correctly, but absolutely worth the money.  Maybe even consider picking up the soundtrack.  I'd reccommend it.

This game pulled me in straight away. I played through it once and immediately after the credits played through it again in an NG+ file so I could get all the achievements associated with the game. And I will likely be playing through it again and again with no regrets.
This game has so much to offer.
The artwork for this game will leave an imprint in your mind and heart long after you stop playing. To start, world of Cloudbank has a very authentic futuristic feel to it. Random polls dictate the set-up of the city,  so Cloudbank is filled with terminals where the cityfolk can take polls and voice opinions. Cloudbank is a colorful, ad-filled world where everything seems perfect. The white sterility left in the wake of the Process set against the color of  the city only further sells the future setting of the game as the city's digital-built beauty is slowly chipped away. The cutscenes are quick and simple, but they are the real knockouts of the game. Still illustrations (hand painted) have the look of a watercolor painting come to life through simple animation, but that effect tells a story with a big impact.
The combat was fun and refreshing throughout both playthroughs for a few different reasons. First, it mixes both real time fighting elements with tactical planning. You can switch between these two types of fighting styles freely and as best suits the player. Next, because you are given an array of different trace functions() in your arsenal to assign to the Transistor as you see fit. Each function() can be assigned/used as a combat move, an upgrade to add on to a combat move or a passive ability. This gives you a lot of flexibility in how you fight you can completely customize which moves you use and how you upgrade them! Finally, it was a little overwhelming at first to learn which function() did what and how to effectively use them. But you are given a great motivation to try each function() in all three different combat/add-on/passive assignments, since as you use them in different configurations, you will unlock data files about the person the trace data originated from (which adds a great deal of background to the story and the motivation of the Camerata.)
You are thrown into the aftermath of a tussle that has left you (the protagonist Red) voiceless and her beau on the wrong end of the Transistor. Some part of you and most of him seem trapped as trace data in the overblown flash-drive of a sword. Your bond allows you to communicate with him despite his current state, he provides emotional support and talks you through your arduous journey to face the Camerata, get to the bottom of their plans and possibly get back the precious things you have lost because of them...  Though by the end of the game, you will understand everything that has transpired – in the beginning I found it a bit jarring to figure out what was going on. I understand that this was most likely done on purpose to make you feel more like Red would be feeling at the start of the events, but I think maybe a little more background story on her or (the fact that she knew/was friends with a member of the Camerata prior to her being targeted) the world of Cloudbank would have been nice to start…  I actually enjoyed the story MUCH more the second time around, as I was already familiar with the world and its ways (i.e. Cloudbank is a digitally constructed city, who Red is in the community, etc.) so I found I could focus more on the little details. But this is not a knockdown, just an observation. Red and her beau’s love/devotion for one another was quite moving to put it simply. I absolutely felt their connection throughout the game, even though Red couldn’t utter a word to that affect. Logan Cunningham really sold a solid character as the beau through his wonderful voice acting; there was definitely history, deep love and loss in his narration to Red. The villains motivation for theirs schemes were rather understandable. The story was overall, very deep and the theme/morals touched on some modern-day issues of a technology-driven society.
Songs fit the world of Cloudbank and the mood of the story as it progresses. They are often very beautiful and sad in equal measure, giving them a very haunting quality. For someone who likes to listen to VG soundtracks, this one is worth the additional purchase.
As mentioned previously, the customization of the combat abilities adds a fresh element to a second (or third) run through Cloudbank with TONS of configuration combinations. The Recursion mode (New Game +) and the self-inflicted Transistor limiters add additional challenge to the game runs as you go. The Test/Challenge Rooms were fun to find/beat. The achievements were also fun to obtain, and at least 2 full playthroughs are needed for 100%. And though the story doesn't change, it is still a lovely journey to go on again and again.

Following on from Bastion, Transistor is yet another brilliant piece of gameplay and art, and is just a truly great experience. However, there are a few things that make it different from Bastion.
First of all, the perspective is the same. The gameplay, however, is different. Instead of running in and hitting everything, your approach should be more careful because enemies tend to be a lot more deadly than they are in Bastion. You don't really have any form of instant healing (other than a few lifesteal upgrades you can find for your weapon) so you have to be much more careful. What allows you to do that while still destroying all these aggressive and powerful enemies is the turn-based system that you can switch to at any time. Time is paused while you plan your moves, and each step you take and attack you set up spends a bit of the bar at the top, which signifies how much you can do in one turn. Stronger moves generally take up more of the bar. You then end the turn and watch it all unfold as you quickly decimate your enemies... that is, if you set it up right.
The challenge of the game is trying to kill your enemies as quickly and efficiently as possible, because if you finish your planning phase and you're out of energy for another turn, you may die very quickly as enemies rush to kill you. There is far more strategy than hacking and/or slashing to be found in Transistor. If you wanted to do the whole game without the  planning system, it's probably possible except for maybe the final boss fight. It will be very difficult though.
Of course, the music in this game is even more spectacular than that of Bastion. You play as Red, a singer who has lost her voice completely. Although she can no longer sing, she can hum, and there is in fact a button that lets you start humming along to the current music playing in the background. Each track fits each level and the situation you're in, and each track is also expertly well done. I LOVE all the aspects of the music in this game. Without it the atmosphere wouldn't be quite the same.
Speaking of atmosphere, art style is comparable to Bastion but has its own unique elements. The attention to detail is still there, however, which makes it beautiful to look at. The level design is similar throughout the whole game. However, it's not boring, just consistent. The world is very unique and futuristic, providing a strong contrast to Bastion. Supergiant Games are clearly trying to cover more than just one theme of games which is always interesting to see a developer do. In this case it works spectacularly. The enemies are also varied and you are introduced to more as the game goes on, each with their own special behaviours and attacks. The enemies fit very well with their environment as they are all robotic-looking. The boss fights are also very different from each other, which was something Bastion generally lacked. The game manages to give you plenty of action to keep yourself entertained. There are also small training rooms that you can progress through to get rewards.
The story is told similarly to Bastion; a narrator guides you through the whole game, but this time the narrator is actually with you the entire time. In a way you feel less lonely, but in another way, you feel more lonely. You and the narrator are in this together, but you are alone together. The world is full of nothing but danger and despair, but there is the glitter of hope that you may somehow fix this in the end. The voice acting is fairly good, but not totally on par with Bastion's. However, the story is compelling and well written, keeping you playing and listening the whole way through.
The game is amazing. I am going to be keeping a close eye on Supergiant Games in the coming years, and I hope to more excellent entertainment from them. If you like art in all forms, as well as gameplay that provides a perfect mix of action and basic strategy, then this is for you. Buy this game, support these developers, have a lovely time humming the soundtrack in the shower after you beat Transistor.

I really wanted to enjoy this game, I really did. It is beautiful, the animations are great and the details are breathtaking.
But alas, there are just too many bugs. Too much non-intended frustration.
I started playing this game at least 3 years after its release. Here are just a few of the problems I've encountered.
The AI is just bad. And often just plain broken. You have enemies sieging your city and they're coming by sea. They're coming to land on your shore so you bring up some long-ranged units to fire upon them as they do. But it seems your units are far too curteous. It is not possible to order your units to fire upon disembarking enemies until EVERY SINGLE UNIT has unloaded and got into correct formation. Until that very moment, you cannot order your units to attack the enemy unit.
This time you are the one attacking the enemy's city. You arrive with transport ships full of troops and you order them to disembark on the shore. Some of your ships carry out your orders. Others? They sail right up to the shore and... just stay there. On the boat. Your units are now 'landed' according to the UI so you can't order them to sail anywhere else, but neither can you order them to move onto the land. So they're now useless.
In the same battle, your enemy has a huge army all situated in the city centre - a very good strategic position if I might say so myself. For some banter you send two ranged units to start picking a few of their units off from afar. This pisses them off - so much in fact, they send their ENITRE army after these two archer units! That's right. They send a few dozen spearmen, swordsmen, archers etc after your two weak long-ranged units, leaving the city centre unprotected and up for grabs. Clever.
Aside from this there are crashes (I have a very high-spec PC. No, I didn't need to turn my graphics settings down), terrible UI which is hard to read (the unit cards don't clearly describe what the unit does at first glance).
This could have been such a good game. You can tell people put a lot of work into it. So it's such a massive shame that it's let down so severely by the developer neglecting its most core components.
I'm going to try out Attila next and pray that it doesn't repeat these problems. If it does, I think I'll probably give up on the Total War series until Creative Assembly get their act together.

Ok, so I've only played this game for a few hours... but this game is actually really fun. It's open world, so you actually have to track creatures and use tactics to take down your target, which I absolutely love. I've played hunting sims where they basically show you where the game is and all you do is point and shoot; not so with this game. In this you actually hunt, *gasp*.
I really, really wanted to love this game, I really did. But there is a serious flaw that I just can't get past: Pay-to-win microtransactions (more like macrotransactions).
Playing this game "for free" means that you cannot hunt anything other than mule deer and rabbits. From what I've seen you cannot buy any equipment or weapons (aside from a shotgun which is priced exorbitantly) at all with the ingame currency that you aquire through the missions. Buying licenses with ingame currency is really a joke. For example, you can buy a 7-day Whitetail license for 110em$ (real money) OR 4399 gm$ (ingame currency)... considering you only get around 100-300 gm$ from the missions that you can actually complete, I consider that utterly ridiculous. I don't really see the point of the ingame currency at all.
Now, I understand, developers need to make money. They work hard creating games and I totally respect that and I love supporting developers. What I don't respect is sucking all the money they can out of their supporters and players. I honestly wouldn't mind paying for this game if the devs weren't openly shysters and sucked all the fun out of their own game. If they want money, just make it a full subscription-based game, and use the ingame currency for the store items. Or just charge a flat price for the game and remove microtransactions from common necessary items and make a premium shop for those people who want special or really cool items. But as it stands now it's just a really horrible set up.
In summary: theHunter is really fun, great environments, challenging hunts, cool items (if you don't mind shelling out the cash), the animals are nice looking. BUT the whole pay-to-win-or-do-anything aspect is a total deal breaker.

Let me preface this by saying I am really hard-pressed to enjoy a RPG for any significant length of time, as I typically prefer shooters. I am also someone who loses interest extremely easily. That being said...
I have had this game installed for two weeks and have five and a half days of active, in-game playtime (215 hours is because I forget to close the launcher & tend to leave it up even when I'm not playing). Aside from some issues when I first started playing that resulted in the servers being down (they had just released the new expansion when I stated), I have had an absolute blast and my interest is not waning in the slightest.
For me, ESO is wonderful because I'm partial to MMOs, be they shooters or otherwise - I have a great preference for playing with other people. The community in ESO is friendlier than I have encountered in other RPGs (and everyone knows shooter communities are cancer) and I've always been able to find someone willing to help or give me pointers in the event I can't find something online. However, I also really enjoy ESO's solo-play. It's engaging and I have actually found myself curious about the lore and storyline where I have never had an interest in any Elder Scrolls game before.
Graphically the game is beautiful, even on the lower graphic settings, and I was pleasantly surprised to learn that the system requirements for the game are as low as they are (I had expected them to be much higher). I also really enjoy the fact that I was able to play comfortably without all the DLC.
If I had to point out a few negatives, I'd say the servers could be better - the random loading screens get really annoying, and the length of time for maintenance leaves quite a bit to be desired.
Overall I'd give the game a 7/10 and would highly recommend the game.
