This game is one of the greatest pyshological horro stories I have ever had the pleasure of experiencing. At its core, it is about a man trying to do the right thing and failing horribly. It is about what can drive us mad, how our best laid plans can turn on us, and the lengths we are willing to go for love. This is not a horror game, in the sense of truly scaring the player away from the screen. It has few jump scares and downright "crap-your-pants" moments, which is obviously a far cry from the original Amnesia, one of the scariest games of all time (one where I literally leapt out of my chair multiple times). However, this game is a different beast entirely, and well worth the attention of anyone who's into psychological horror and  storytelling and writing on par with the best movies and literature.
It's honestly a shame this game was branded as a sequel to Amnesia: The Dark Descent. The only similarities I could find between the two games are that the main character has amnesia, has done some horrific deeds in the past, and... has a lamp. If this game were not tied up with the original Amnesia, I think it would have been much more positivley received.
The game has done away with many of the gameplay mechanics that made the original such a terrifying experience. Your lamp has unlimited fuel this time around, so there are no more hurried searches for oil as you desperately try to conserve your remaining fuel. There is no sanity meter; your character does not go insane from staying in the dark, witnessing unsettling events (of which there are plenty), or looking at the enemies creatures. There is still some light puzzle-solving and exploration, although the puzzles are simpler (which might be a good thing, because I found a few of the puzzles in the original a bit contrived, which broke my immersion) and the spaces to explore are nowhere near as vast and open-ended. There are still enemies that you have to hide and run away from, which accounts for the meat of the gameplay (I even died a few times) although these encounters are not numerous either. So yes, the gameplay has taken a back seat to the story, but this is not all for the worse.
These changes and simplifications of the gameplay make sense within the context of the story. A sanity meter simply doesn't make sense within the story of the game. Your character is already insane - he has witnessed and commited horrifying acts. Seeing a Manpig or two - or being alone in the dark, god forbig! - isn't going to suddenly send him further into the depths of madness. It would just be too "gamey" and break the immersion and the character.
Since insanity is no longer an issue, it would then follow that there is no reason to have limited fuel resources, as the primary reason for your lamp in the original was to keep from going insane in the darkness. Thus, having limited fuel would only serve to make some parts of the game unnecessarily dark, which would be nothing but an annoyance - and a shame, since the art design in the game is so amazing.
I would have liked to see more exploration in the game, yes. That is my one big gripe with it. Being able to explore a mansion and the immense factory and machine underneath at your own discretion - discovering the different places and parts and horrors in your own order and at your own pace - would have been much more disconcerting and haunting than following a mostly linear path, seeing everything the game has to show you precicesly when it wants to reveal it.
So there is just enough gameplay to serve the story. And what a fantastic story it is. Much like in the original Amnesia, the story is told mostly through found documents and through memories that come back to the protagonist. This time around, there are also phonographs to be found, which are a welcome addition because the audio allows the player to hear the emotions in the voice of the protagonist. The writing in this game is excellent, just as it was in the developers previous game, Dear Esther. In my mind it is unmatched. The writing is smart, layered, gorgeous, and at the same time visceral and unforgiving. There is no end to the amount of the times people mention brutal acts, and blood and♥♥♥♥♥♥and child murder. It is like reading a great literary work, and interacting with it to experience this unforgiving world.
I could talk about this game for days, but I have said enough. Clearly I think it's fantastic, and you will too if you love a good story and are fine with not having deep game mechanics. I can fully understand why it's not for everyone, but that's OK: it was never meant to pleave everybody. I have one last thing to say though: this game has one of the great sequences/set pieces I have ever encountered. It's called the Den of the Wretches, and it completely disposes of any suppositions you may have about the enemites in this game. It was one of the most haunting and unsettling things I have ever experienced. Be prepared.

The game keeps you on a very linear path. There are some cool and creepy moments in the ~5 hours it took for me to complete it, but I doubt I'll remember the game 5 years from now. I paid $5 for it, maybe wait until it's $2.50 possibly in the winter sale.

This game was one that I was excited for since its announcement and when I finally got the game my excitement only grew but things went downhill incredibly fast.
Story:
You awake in a room and have amnesia, (in case that wasn't obvious enough,) then you start finding journals that will talk about this spooky machine and you must find out what this machine is and how much you were part of it, (you were a huge part of it in case that wasn't obvious enough,) you are also looking for your kids. The story isn't much but hopefully the scares and immersion will make for it (Spoiler, They don't.)
Scares and Immersion:
Scares are incredibly weak since most of it is sound effects and nothing else (but I will admit the game did scare a bit only because of the sound effects). The enemies themselves aren't even scary because the game does a nice job of making you see them a lot before they become an actual threat also the lights around the place warn when an enemy is nearby. Immersion is a bad one also since the game focuses sound only on loud noises and the environment doesn't draw in at all.
Puzzles:
Puzzles are almost nonexistent. The "puzzles" are merely carrying one object to another room, placing said object into where ever it goes, and hitting a switch when you're done. The lack of an inventory destroys all possible puzzles there could have been and instead makes them all too simple.
Exploration:
Since the game doesn't have an inventory, there is no real reason to explore besides to look at the area even then the areas are so linear that there is still no reason to explore. The game doesn't reward exploration and the only thing to gain is journals entries except you still don't need to explore since most of them are in plain sight.
Mechanics that were in Amnesia: The Dark Descent but removed:
-Sanity Meter: While the sanity meter was sort of annoying in the first game, it encouraged you to stay out of the dark and to not look at the monsters but with this removed, you can stay in the dark as much as you want and stare at the monsters all you want once again making them less scary.
-Inventory: This had no reason to being removed since it helped the game out with puzzles and encouraged the player to explore and collect objects.
-A limited lantern: The lantern got changed in such a way that took away most of the horror in the game and that being it has unlimited light. Dark Descent's limited lantern encouraged the player to only use it when it was really needed while in this game the lantern can be out at all times and the worry of it running out isn't there also the lantern is key in knowing when a monster is nearby since it flickers when one is close once again taking away the fear of the enemy.
-Large amount of physics: This game will hardly let you pick anything up or move anything
-Custom Story Support: This one thing is the main reason I still play Dark Descent since I know that when I'm done with one story, I can go download another. Some custom stories are incredibly well done and playing those provides whole new experience with the same game.
The Monster:
The monster is nothing to be scared of in appearance or sound (unless you think an angry pig snort is scary.) The enemies look like humans with pig features such as snouts and hooves for feet. The monster ‘s AI isn't the best either, at times they can stand right in front of you and not notice anything. There was also this time where I flashed the lantern in its face and stood directly in front of it and it didn't notice me and instead went the other direction. Also the monsters despawn incredibly fast.
Outside sections:
The game lets you go outside and its' a great new feature but the Amnesia engine is great with inside buildings only so the outside parts don't look amazing and even when you're outside, you still get this feeling of being boxed in.
The Wrap-up/ The TL;DR:
This game is complete let down when comparing to Dark Descent but when not comparing, it still doesn't do that well. To be honest, this game felt more like a mod for the first game than an actual stand-alone game. This game really shouldn't even have Amnesia as the title since it is nothing like it should or could be. I suggest not buying this and instead getting the first game or wait till Frictional's next game.
(I know that it isn't Frictional's fault that the game ended up like this and I know the Chinese Room is to blame.)

Once you automate one thing, you can then automate another, and another, and eventually you will have a sprawling, massive factory that you didn't plan very well. Then you'll look outside, or at your clock, and realize you haven't left your computer to eat, drink or sleep for five days. I'm not kidding, this game is better than crack.

Unless you have hundreds of hours to spare, don't play this game.
And if you plan to use more than one character, better have thousands of hours to spare.
The appeal of this game, for me at least, is the depth of the class system. You really have to plan out what path you're going to take through the classes beforehand, once you make a class choice, you can't change it. That's not necessarily a bad thing, I enjoyed looking at all the options and planning it out, but unfortunately it just feels wayyy too slow to get somewhere. It seems decently paced at first but it quickly turns incredibly slow paced. Oh, the quests don't feel slow... but I don't feel like I'm getting anywhere, it's just going from one quest to the other... one map to the other. It wouldn't be as much of a problem if I had more skills or things to play around with, but it takes just so long to get the class levels..
And it's hard to experiment because of all this.. you pretty much have to ditch those hundreds of hours and restart if you're not satisfied with what you got, or want to try something different.
The social side of this game isn't very good, because of just how linear it is, and that you can't just jump in with some high level friends, they lower the exp you get if you're 10 levels away from the monster levels.  So you just have to team up with people around your level.. which might work for some, but I just thought more about the social aspects...
It's too bad, because the art in this game is gorgeous, and the combat system isn't all that bad, except when the lag kicks in and doesn't register the damage correctly.  The reason I'm not recommending it is just because the progression, character-wise especailly, is just too slow, and I can tell it's going to take hundreds more hours just to see more interesting development I want for my class and skill choices.
If for you it's incredibly rewarding to spend incredible amounts of time to finally get the character developped like you wanted, and don't mind simple quest after simple quest just to progress, then you might really enjoy this game because no other games have a class system like this one, from what I've seen, but for most, it'll just feel too tedious.

By doing so you create machines,research new technology, and while you do all these cool things, you essentially have industrialized the whole planet and removed its beauty with vass amounts of pollution. There is so much content in this game that it would take me 25 pages to explain it all, and if that isn't enough, there is a growing and very active modding community for the game. After playing a considerated amount of time into this game, i think it's time i leave a review here!
Have u been looking for a grind mmo for years now? Nothing seems to satisfy ur grinding hunger? are you tired of going to lvl cap just questing? Well Tree of Savior is one of the only games out there that has potential and has this type of grindy gameplay that games started to stay away from!
So Lets start!
Pacing:
- The game starts with a really fast pace, until you get to lvl30~35 , but don't worry this game has a weird exp curve reset(lvl46,lvl86,136,186,236) after u hit those lvls the lvling pacing gets better and then worse as u keep getting closer to another one, keeping the game with a nice pace until you hit cap, and giving you a nice character progression!
Controls:
-Are the controls intuitive? Yeah to the point the control tutorial is about 5 seconds long !
-I love being able to play a game with a controler and this game allows me to,however i think the keyboard mode is better and then you have the mouse control for those who are used to playing PoE, Diablo...etc still crancky with some quests but better overall for ranged classes!
Story:
-Another generic story of you being the hero, has some interesting arcs to say the least, because the story is not bad in itself, simply generic.
Gameplay:
-We do have some bugs still but it's open beta yet so no big deal, If you play with a controler the gameplay becomes smooth for most part of the game, and it fells rewarding something i havent felt in so many years playing mmos, the best way to explain it would be a refreshing breeze with a nostalgic felling to it!
Experience:
- I'm having a blast as a grind fanatic, i have started with some friends , which some quited because they prefer quest based mmos, but the ones who stayed are having a blast , we have tons of diffrent combination of builds and combos we still want to test and get to end game, overall like almost any mmo played alone can be quite boring, as when i try to grind off alone, i can't keep my interest in that character as much as i wanted to, so try to make friends , as you hit 208~210 you will be starting grinding parties until you hit cap and this is when you start metting more people and the game overall becomes more fun (taking in cosideration u started alone).
Balance:
-We need some balance issues as it stands, some builds are really stronger than others making all that Game depth in terms of builds kinda fall off, however those non meta classes always bring something new and if you can build a party according to that non meta classes you will be able to succed, but if you don't have a decent build or a meta build people wont really want to party up at least 50% of the people, which i think its a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ behaviour, but as long as your build as synergy it will work, so invest sometime into a build before starting because we don't know what will be meta tomorow, so just use something that works and its to ur liking!
Overall, I love this game , it has tons of issues and it isnt a game for everyone , but if you like grinding mmos then don't let this gems escape you, IMC has been trying their best and when this gem gets polished im pretty sure ToS will become a big hit, it has the potential for it!

Prepare to experience a paramount in auditory terror.  Alien: Isolation grabs your eyes with it's sharp attention to the look and feel of Ridley Scott's classic films.  Alien can be considered a first-person stealth game with more focus on the later.  The graphics are goregous but what really gets your heart pumping isn't what's necessarily here, but what isn't.  That's to say the game creates an astounding sense of emptiness that accompanies space and made hairs stand up on the backs of necks during the first movie.
*Intro Spoiler*
-  You're on your way to a space station/service center that is in the late stages of being decomissioned.  Upon arrival, you guessed it, everything seems to be in disarray.  Profane threats are scribbled on the walls and you begin to learn about the actual events that occured before your arrival.
The graphics are stunning (SEGA is consistent with this stuff) but really the sound effects are really where this game shines.  Our beloved antagonist can be heard approaching and you're forced to decipher those movements through sounds in a eerily empty space station.
Great adaptation that stays true to Scott's iconic asthetic.

World of Goo is a nifty little title that has you moving small blobs around the screen so that they connect to each other thus forming little structures like what you might make with toothpicks and some chewing gum. The goal is not to use up all the blobs available to you, though, because the extras must traverse your bridge to an exit point on each map. You must rescue a certain number to proceed. The maps eventually develop interesting environmental hazards, starting with spikes and gaps and continuing until entire screens rotate. Of course, it starts introducing things like balloons or reusable goo balls to help you overcome such difficulties. It's full of odd little bits of humor and quirky style.

I am a very avid hunter in real life, and so when I saw this game I thought, this might be fun. The Game is beautiful, with amazing graphics, but it's super-realism is it's own downfall. The Developers spent so much time making this game realistic, that they forgot to also make it fun. You WILL go walking for 30 mins real time and not see anything. You WILL get busted by animals because you don't have any money to buy decent camo to hunt in. And You WILL get irritated with the stupid HunterMate thing for not being capable of telling you which animals you're tracking until you start tracking them. (You can only track one animal at a time, and you start the game basically only being able to hunt Mule Deer unless you take part in the millions of micro-transactions in the game to let you hunt the fun stuff. So when you're tracking a Mule Deer Buck, and a new track shows up, you want to track it but it's actually a feral hog that you can't shoot and now you just lost your buck.) Another Thing, In Real life hunting, you don't go into a new Area to hunt with 0 knowledge of the landscape or the animal's patterns. I never go hunting without leaving my trail camera in the field for at least 6 months to give me a good indication of the deer's usual routine, and i can manipulate the routine by planting Food Plots or setting feeders up. the Deer feeder in this game costs you about $30 real money just to get. Great Concept, Terrible execution. And I put 6 hours into the game so I gave it a good chance to impress me.

Technically this game is F2P. Yes. When you start you can only hunt whitetail deer, but if you complete missions you'll earn ingame currency (GM$), which can be used to buy hunting licenses, ammo and scents. Winning competitions gives you EM$, which you can use to buy firearms.
Sure you can pay for membership, which gives you all hunting licenses and unlimited ammo for X amount of months. 3 months is 10 euros, which isn't really that expensive considering how much you all pay for new games, play them for 50-80 euros and never open them again (or pay another 20-30 euros for each DLC). If 10 euros is too much for you, then maybe you should have buckled down a little bit more in high school?

I recommend this game, but here's the thing.
It's most definitely NOT Amnesia by any means. There is no inventory system, and there is no fueling system for your lantern. It  seems as if everything on your character is an unlimited resource, and that takes away the challenge of the game.
Another thing, the game is VERY short. I never expected a game like this to be short considering The previous Amnesia, and the Longevity of the Penumbra series. Though this was developed by TheChineseRoom, who also made Dear Esther, which was also a very VERY short game (1 hour roughly).
On the positive side, the game is very immersive and promoted horror quite well in it's own way separate from The Dark Descent's technique. The story really drags you in but at times it can be difficult to understand with overwhelming literary devices and figures of speech.
The reason why I recommend this game is that I respect it in the Non-Amnesia point of view. The game for me just didn't feel like Amnesia. It was still a very good game though, although I wish it were longer.

Interesting first-person horror game that is grounded in social/political commentary about the ills of society and man's effort to save humanity from self-destructing (albeit in a morbid way involving lots of pigs). Also deals about the consequences of playing God in order to make that happen. Play this game for the slow-building tension and suspense that accompanies a profound story about one man's quest for redemption in an unforgiving world.
Overall, this game is nowhere near as scary as the first Amnesia. The first game was more focused on instilling a constant fear and dread in players, while this sequel is more focused on having players slowly unravelling the sad story of one man's ambition. Puzzles are boring but easy (I rarely ever got stuck and the lantern in this game has endless energy so you won't have to worry about finding matchboxes like the last game. Get this game on sale for 5 bucks because I bought it for the same price and spent 5 hours to complete it, even as I explored the levels for the notes that added to the games' story.
The game lacks action in parts but the story and ending make up for that greatly. I wish it were a bit longer.

Start a world, picked my specs i wanted. little do you know if you dont get "chopper" and "worker" at least...........well...you dont get to play this round
Spawned in, grabbed some berries, got framiliar with controls and such. Then bear attack! no big deal...I got a sword, stood behind a tree cus i knew i couldnt take him since he gets you with 5 bites, 14-19 stabs for your sword to kill him. And sure enough just like i suspected he glitches into the tree (every tree and any tree) and you just stand still and stab till you get him....okay so boring start but im sticking with it!
Go find my first town(2 npc's and the frame of a house) and chop some trees to fininsh the towns peoples main house. Although the house is only good for sleeping. It does nothing else and neither does the quest board.
Then Bear attack 2! mind you i've traveled about 500yrds and its been 10minutes since bear attack 1.
I can hear him but idk where he is, so naturally i run in the house to spice things up. And behold, bear is in the middle of the house biting me with half his body under the floor boards except this time he can glide right through the house and walls no problem. So then i run, 1 bite of health to my name and my sprint bar goes out so i try for the tree trick from before but my sword is bugged and wont swing or un-equip....im doomed, but not quite! I didnt die, but why? well because the bear is faster then me, yes so i should die, but the bear cant bite while hes moving- he will stop everytime to attack. So if i dont stop, i dont die. I can even walk, I didnt even have to sprint, I just had a pet angry bear follow me for 25 minutes while i looked around for other towns. I leap off a little hill into the water and check my six and see the bear take a stutter step and walk off. I lost him!! But i look down and im not underwater, im not even swimming...Im literally running on top of a fairly large rivir with a decently strong current, but i aint got time for swimming....psshh im walking!

This is the most fun game on the face of the earth.  It's so much fun.  Lots of games look pretty or make you tear your hair out in frustration, but factorio (while still accomplishing both of these things very very well) just comes across as "fun."
There is no way I would tell someone "you may not enjoy this game" whether they are the most enthusiastic spacechem record setter or the ios clash of clans candy crush game novice.  It takes the most satisfying formulas in games and mushes them into one (survival, sandbox, organization, replayability, and well-balanced progression) and the mods just make the whole experience even better after a few vanilla factories.  It's satisfying, it's fulfilling, it's exciting, it's frustrating, it's mind-melting, but it's mostly fun.

In the moment of writing, I have 83 hours logged on Factorio.
Usually, I'll get tired of a game pretty quickly, or I'll just play for a few hours at a time.
None the less, this was my Saturday night:
1900: All right, it's 7 in the evening. I'll go play some Factorio.
2100: Man, I love this game. I'll go to bed soon. Just have to optimize these transport belts.
2300: Oh, right, I was going to go to bed. Hm, I'll just fix this electricity shortage first.
0100: Pretty sure I was supposed to do something now... Oh well, better crush some aliens with my tank.
0300: Hot damn, those aliens are getting pretty angry. Better put up a proper perimeter defence. And then go sleep.
0500: Okay, right, right, I've finally got some clever designs. Better redesign my entire factory. WAIT, WHAT TIME IS IT?
0630: WHAT DO YOU MEAN IT'S 0630 IN THE MORNING? BUT IT'S STILL DAR... No, okay, apparently it's light outside.
0640: Okay, okay, okay, I'll just write a Steam review for Factorio. Then go sleep. Yeah. Sleep. And dream. Of Factorio.
Somebody once asked if androids dream of electric sheep. I can assure you that Factorio players dream of factory optimization.

One of the best, if not the best, western shooter! Very well optimized, stylish, and very fun Western FPS with fantastic storytelling.
Western shooters now days are hard to come by. I feel this genre is underrated as there are lots of possibilities both gameplay and story wise to explore. Call of Juarez Gunslinger in perticular is a fantastic western FPS.
The story telling in this game is perfect. It is told in game, not as cutscenes, as a fireplace story by a infamous bounty hunter drinking a few beers in a saloon. He may not remember the events that happend realistically so he may exagerate, but this really makes the game more fun. If he says he fought a whole entire army on a boat, by god you do actually fight an entire army in the game. He also tells events that could have happend if he made a choice he did not, and you actually play that choice then play what really happened. Again, this is one of the best storytellng in a game I have ever experienced.
Gameplay wise, the game is awesome and full of action. It feels like an arcade type FPS shooter as you try to rack up combo and creative kills to earn points so you can upgrade your skills and weapons. This arcade type gameplay is a real welcome to me as the action is always intense. The game is also very well optimized. I have been able to play this game at 1440p on high settings with a 770 GTX and never going under 100 frames per second, even when there is a lot of stuff going on.
The graphics are great! It has a cartoonish cell shaded look that makes the western art style pop. When you fight a boss, the boss is introduced through a very short stylish graphic novel cutscene. Again, I feel this is a welcomed style to this game.
Overall, I believe this Call of Juarez game is the best of the series and one of the best western games. If you have been a fan of Bound In Blood, this game will not disappoint.

As great as the game may be, this release is so unstable, I'm floored the developers would not only release the game to begin with, but also have the audacity to stand by it without fixing the issues. Don't waste your money on this game, I beg you. Don't make my mistake. As great as gameplay may look, and as fun as it may seem, your paying $50 for a virtual paperweight that serves no purpose other than to shorten your hardware's life expectancy.

Want to sail trough the air on your badass wings suit while literally everything blows up behind you? Ever felt that useless left hand would be better for unrealistically zipping around the landscape with a grappler/gaunlet/arm-computer-thingy combo? Well, now you can. Welcome to just Cause 3. First off, the game has a lot of replayabilty, and has a good amount of sh*t blowing up. Just Cause 3 is the next-gen title for the "blow crap up just because you can series", and it does not dissapoint. Having played Just Cause 1, it was a good concept ruined by a lot of bugs and half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥physics, graphics, and gameplay, (like the grappler only hooking onto cars, being able to drive through trees, etc.). Just Cause 2, couldn't have been more different. Just Cause 2 payed a lot of attention to detail, had great car physics, explosion physics, solid trees, above others. But, it began to feel dry, with the grappler (Which then lached onto anything) only having one weak, non-retractable thether. In JC2, Your only means of transport was this grappler and a parachute, Just Cause 3 ups the ante, giving players the new wingsuit. The wingsuit controls fantastically, and is an overall blast to use. The new retractable tethers are amazing for physics based chaos, and result in a hours of fun. You can also take any civilian  vehicle to a chop shop, and then you can order one ahytime trough the new rebel drop system. Unfortunately, the items have a cooldown of fifteen minutes, wich is a bit too long. You can do challenges to obtain gears, which unlock gadget mods (including mods to reduce and later remove the RD cooldowns). These are a grind to collect, easily the most boring and tedious part of the game.  Most of the cast are not done by their original voice actors, but I found the new actors to be more convincing and overall better in quality, so I will not complain. Just Cause 3 does lack of the graphics side of things, but with such a massive world, you need to make sacrifices. And man sh*t, is this game huge. The world is one of the biggest I have ever seen, beating out games like Grand Theft Auto V and Watch Dogs 2 by a mile. Some parts do feel empty at times, but there is still s lot to see. Now let's talk JC3's multiplayer: It has none. NO couch or even online, which is a huge missed opportunity. PC players do get the JC3 multiplayer mod (from the same makers as the JC2, Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim MP mods), and it works surprisingly well, and can even be downloaded directly trough steam. Square has stated the game was never going to see proper multiplayer on PC, so console players are even more out of luck, as JC3 does not suppport mods on PS4 or XBOX ONE.
THE VERDICT:
Just Cause 3 is the definitive Just Cause experience. Those who want a massive open world to explore and explode will find exactly what they want, even though at times the may be looking at nothing, and never with friends proper. People who don't like to grind though, may want to avoid entirely.
THE GOOD:
+Great Destructibility
+Huge World
+New gadgets are a blast
+Better voice acting
THE BAD:
-Rebel Drop cooldowns are too long
-Gadget upgrades boring/tedious to collect
-Feels a little empty in areas
-No proper multiplayer support
>Need a mod for multiplayer on PC (online only, no local)
>No multiplayer on consoles period
THE SCORE:
8/10

The best game available on Steam, the crowning achievement of indie gaming and the best PC game made in years.
Far more than just a puzzle game or a physics toy, it uses its surreal world and its many abstractions to tell a kind of story. There's no way to say or even know just what that story is, but the result is somehow an emotionally draining experience, and a thing of beauty on a level with Shadow of the Colossus or Homeworld.
It's also a lot of fun, consistently inventive with a wide variety of challenges and settings. A branching worldmap and relatively easy base requirements make it nearly impossible to become stuck, but the brutal requirements for true "OCD" completion make it a game almost no one has managed truly to beat.

I was very dissapointed with this game.  I have been an Elder Scrolls follower since Morrowwind and was looking forward to something new.  This is not what I was hoping for.
The game has no single player mode.  I like to use single player to get familier with a new game.  By starting in multiplayer mode  you must join with players with a much higher level.  Since the game is set to accommondate the higher level player,  you don't stand a chance against many of  the npcs.
Another problem is the number of players.  You frequently have to stand in line to talk or react with a npc.
The loot system is in my openion,  inadequate.  You fight and kill a nps,  but you cannot claim his weapon or armor.  To get decent armor or weapons ,  you have to buy them from the crown store.
There are to few places to sell your surplus loot.
There is no provisions waiting or sleeping.  If you need to do something five or six hours later,  you just stand and wait.
Frequently there are five or six players doing the same quest at the same time.  If you are a level 5 and other players are higher,  your enemies are at the higher level and you don't have a chance.  You constantly die and have to restart.
The provisions for fast travel are very limited and expensive.  You can only travel from wayshrine to wayshrine and in most instances there is a fee involved.  If you can't afford these fees.  you must walk.   If you play 10 hours,  you walk about 7.
I am totally against paying to play a game that I have already paid for,  but in this game,  the best armor and weapons must be purchased.  This ruins the game for me.
For those who don't mind the inconviences I pointed out the,  game has some good points.  The graphics and voice acting are great.  The storyline not so much.

I'm sorry to say all the bad ratings are true. Here's my experience up to level 36:
-Story makes little sense, and isn't worth reading almost immediatley.
-The translation is iffy at best, even untranslated at times (that's what you get when you don't pay your translators).
-The layout of all of the maps feel exactly the same. So rather than getting excited reaching a new level area, it feels depressing.
-All the bosses act almost entirely the same.
-Some classes just don't function well the way mobs work in game. Meaning, you could need to start over entirely if you picked the wrong one.
-Targeting is probably the worst I have seen in a modern MMO. You'll constantly waste SP shooting off screen, or hit the wrong mobs entirely.
-I have seen more botters than I have seen real players. It feels like a 10 year old MMO, where the entire community has left except for bots (this is not an exaggeration).
-The market issus is pathetic. I NPC nearly everything, and save just the best for trade. However, I have made no friends, or even got a response from anyone in game because of the above mentioned bot problem.
-There are not actually 80 classes. There are 4 classes (archer, warrior, healer, mage) with different skill sets. So, there really isn't any way to make any sort of creative build that crosses these barriers like a battle mage, or a trap healer, etc..
-Every map constantly lags and tears at the screen, even when there is no one there.
-Moving between maps is really awkward.
-Mobs feel like the same thing, over and over, just reskinned.
-The spawn rate on some maps is extremely slow. I'm writing this close to 4 months after release, and absolutely no one was on the channel I was in, yet I would walk around for minutes on end not finding any spawns at all. You have to play on channel 1 or 2, just to get any sort of spawn. The rest are apparently for botters that don't seem to mind the long wait.
This game looked as if it would have been like Ragnarok. However, it's only good in it's appearance. This was one of the most pathetic MMOs I have seen in a long while. I expect it to be shut down within 2 years.

As thou this may not be the best Total War game, it's definitely my favourite one. Right from the beginning you have a huge option of factions to choose from & most of them are wastly different. For example the Suebi tribes are barbarians, but if you compare them to the Arverni (also barbarian tribe) you find that their units have maximally one similiar unit, which really gives good sense of replayability to all factions. This TW game also has your generals & spyes aging so your main & upgraded general can die of old age right before his battle, thus maybe even losing the battle for you, because your newely recruited general doesn't have as much experience or morale. As with all TW titles as you progress deeper in the campaign & your empire expands you have higher income, but you also spend way more on many armies & new buildings to protect your realm. You can finish the campaign by many goals - warfare, economic victory & more. Then when you finish your campaign you can also play new free campaign Emperor Augustus which is set in the roman civil war & adds few more cities to the map. If you don't like singleplayer you can also play the amazingly constructed multiplayer. Where you can fight 4v4 battles with huge 20 or 40 unit armies. Obviously by playing againts players you can create tactics that would normally never work in singlepayer to defeat your enemies. Overall this game had a lot of problems on its release, but the Emperor Edition upgrade really made this TW a game that you would gladly return to from time to time.

Some people don't like how resources are now managed at the province level, and you can no longer build every little town into a rival of Roma, but really, it's a non issue once you get the hang of managing food and learning what to build and where.
Also worth noting that the Workshop has tons of mods, from minor music enhancements, to complete overhauls. This certainly extends the replayability of the game once you get done with the included scenarios (which are good, especially teutoburg forest).

One of my favourite games so far for this year and it has a hell of a lot of potential, with a decent amount of current playable content. If you enjoy First person sandbox survival RPG's with a strong crafting base, then please read this review.
Pro's and Con's
First Person Sandbox Survival RPG
- A rewarding leveling system, where your choices influence your ability to construct a variety of building, affecting in turn what you can craft.
- Mount and Blade type of atmosphere with animals, survival and settlement building thrown in.
- Procedurally generated world, will the slaughter of bears never end  ?! mwahahahar...
- The world regenerates, trees will grow over time, ores will reappear somewhere and animals respawn
- A tad buggy.. some Animals will be invincible ( FLEE, run for your life, ... this bear isn't taking any damage ) but when you find a Wildberry bush that has an enormous amount of fruit to give you won't complain hahahah nomnomnom..
- Some perks are ineffective, or rather do not give you the listed bonuses, such as Yager and Skinner.
- So i've built a Settlement... but im rather alone.. /tumbleweeds... how do we attract people to our Settlement ? good question :P This is why I suggest starting at another Settlement and expand with them for now.
- Framerate issues / Lag.  It's an issue for quite a lot of folks.  I will suggest you Choose "Fastest" for Video / Graphics options when you run the game.  Try removing the Bloom setting in game as well.
Firstly.. choosing your beginning perks with the 20 points you get.. well, much can be said here, but i'll try to spare you some time.  I understand a lot of people will do w/e they like and discover what works for them. I've started several times myself in order to either dump a corrupt save and start again or retry new perks from the beginning. The faster you get exp the better imho ( in my honest opinion )
I recommend starting with Chopper, Scholar & Scrivenr ( giving you a 25% exp bonus )
You will start at a random point on the map with an Axe, a sword and a torch. Allow me to give you some advice on where to go from here..  Look around and find a tree that is NOT near a bear hahahah... no seriously.. you need to make a bow and arrows..
TAB opens your inventory and the one the left hand side you'll find tabs, the topmost tab is your inventory, pickup and place the axe in your left-most hand slot to equip it, close inventory with TAB again and press 2 to weild the Axe.  Walk over to the tree or Hold Left Shift while you move ( W,A,S,D ) towards it to run.  When you reach the tree a circle will appear for your aiming reticle signalling that you are in range to begin harvesting it.  Chop Chop Chop.. ( hold left mouse ) you'll notice the circle filling slowly... when it fills you will receive 1 Wood ( 2 x wood and chopping speed if you chose the Chopper perk ).
When you've fulfilled your lumberjacking fantasies enough ( 6 wood is a good enough start ) you open your inventory again and pick the tab at the bottom for crafting, choose to craft on the right hand page without a bench and you turn wood into planks 1 wood = 5 planks = 1 self crafted wooden bow,  1 plank = 1 arrow etc, leave the arrows in your inventory while you are crafting more arrows and they will continue to stack to 20.
Place your new bow in the left slot and the arrows in the right slot and you are ready to hunt bears ( cackles maniacally )
Lets face it.. in this game there's no point hunting anything but the creature that gives you the most EXP.  Bears will give you 200 exp without any of the Scholar tree perks.  Press 2 to wield the bow, click ( or hold ) the RMB ( right mouse button ) to prepare the bow for firing in your other hand and hold RMB to arm an arrow and raise the bow. Now at this stage you can either click LMB to fire or unhold RMB to lower the bow thereby not wasting the arrow.  Alternatively you can use LMB holding down to ready the bow and release to fire the arrow, but you cannot lower the bow from this stance and save the arrow.
Find a Settlement asap ( M to open map.. if it looks like a Chapel ( not a greek Pantheon ) run to it,  the faster you get there the sooner you can begin to take quests from the board, earning you gold and exp. I have personally not experienced any reputation / Fame increments from completing quests for the population, but i've been more of a wanderer around the map, searching for a perfect place to build my own settlement.
Now you're ready to explore.. make a name for yourself in this world of infinite bears... will you become Master of the hunt, roaming the land and setting up rudimentary shelters to rest before you again set off to explore.. Or will you become Jack of all Trades, buying from towns, crafting their produce into something better to resell again elsewhere. Or an owner-builder taking a piece of land for yourself and establishing a Settlement, building it the way you see fit. ?
Either way this game is certainly a great way to spend your days, immersed in the survival, crafting and hunting. Pick it up and see for yourself
In this Early Access state I give it a 6 / 10.  The more content and patches it receives, the better.
Good luck out there, may the wilderness be gentle with you ^_^

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger was a blast to play. Not only is this the best Wild West game i've ever played, but also a contender for best FPS of all times I've witnessed and arguably the best Cowboy Game currently available for the PC.
You play a character that could might just be Clint Eastwood in a spoof similar to "Hang 'em high" with the goal to pump every Motherfûcker full of lead who wronged you or is unfortunate enough to cross your way. Back in the day when men were men, guns were guns and the law was your trigger finger and not your trigger list of hashtags and your filthy posse of absolutely disgusting degenerates. You have 3 game modes. All single player. Fully heavily narrated Story mode with cutscenes. Arcade mode with Global Score lists and High Noon Duel Mode, with score lists as well.
The graphics of this game are anything but hot stuff. Its fairly basic. But id rather play a smoothly running game with fluid gameplay than a graphics best that runs like âss. The engine seems to have some cell shading with black outlines to it. Also some Black bars. you can argue if these enhance the movie feel for the game or not, but an option to remove them would have been nice. Some terrein graphics are poor, but that is made up for with the character design and guns. You can see these people but effort into the designs. Wished though they would have added facial features and more gore effects in addition to the head shot gush.
The guns are a real feast. Not just the looks. They look Marvelous. They sound fantastic and feel comfortable. Dare i say these are the overall best designed and best feeling guns I have ever seen in any game of all times. Aiming is pinpoint, shooting feels great. Never felt bored with it in my whole 25 hours when i was enjoying this treat. The sound of bullets whizzing around your ears and the meaty impact when you put a bullet into someones skull is probably the closest I can compare to shooting a real weapon.
The gameplay itself is very fast paced. It will remind you of an old arcade style shooter. Except this plays more like a modern FPS. Yes, it has regenerating health, but that doesnt break the game. You are anything but a bullet sponge and can die anytime with one single well placed shot of if you get caught in some deep shît. An Essential part of the game is not just the aiming, shooting and well timed reloading, but the key feature of bullet time. You have a charging meter that gives you the opportunity to take down enemies Matrix style. This is mandatory to get decent scores for streaks in arcade mode, but will also help you to gather experience in Story mode. To know when and how long to bullet time is key to success. And of course to refill the meter for it.
Call of Juarez Gunslinger is an excellent game. I never imagined i would enjoy it as much as i did when i bought it during steam sale, its a short, but intense experience for little money. Probably the best deal i striked since i bought Metro Last light for 5 bucks. If you even remotely like Cowboys or Guns, you will like it. Its like a rising knee to the face. Easily worth 30 Euros. You can get it any time for half this price. Touching Wild West story with outstanding Gunplay. Speak volumes that it needed a competent european company to create it. Apparently USA doesnt know how to present it's own heritage properly. Doesn't even need U-play to run. Give it a 9,5 out of 10.

I personally love the game. It's one of the most fun Total War games I've ever played, alongside Shogun 2 and Napoleon. There are some aspects of the game which feel a bit broken, but it is nowhere near as bad as Empire or Medieval II (oh God, why?); the likeyhood of success when auto-resolving battles is definitley skewed in the favor of the enemy, and even if you lose the engagement you stand to inflict a lot more casualties fighting yourself than via auto-resolve. The use of agents by the enemy can be really inhibiting in some cases... I personally think they should be more of a nuisance instead of being capable of halting and virtually destroying an entire army. The diplomacy can also use a bit of fixing; it gets annoying when certain factions ask you for the same thing every turn, even if you reject them every time. My biggest issue was with the lack of unit diversity; both in the sense that there are not enough different units within each faction as well as the fact that all 'Eastern' factions are lumped into the same archetype as well as all Hellenic, Latin and Celtic/Barbarian. Some units are very annoying to use, especially horse archers which require constant babysitting lest they get killed off by standing infront of a stationary tower. Micromanaging happiness/order, food and money making buildings can get a bit annoying if you are trying to expand quickly, but if you take it one region at a time I find it quite managable. Seige units are a bit over-powered in my opinion, they should only be highly effective... well, in seiges and not be capable of devastating units on the battlefield before they are able to reach them. One final complaint is that there should be more factions, but it seems they are continously adding more in DLC so it's starting to balance out.
Those are all the negative things I can think of off the top of my head. Other than that, the game is stunningly beautiful, both on the campaign map and in battle. There is a wide array of weather effects and unlike previous titles, not all cities look alike. (I think that's one of the best things about this game). Some cities like Athens, Rome and Carthage are completley different from the rest. The ability to land naval units in a battle is pretty cool as well.
In conclusion, anyone who loves the Ancient world will have a good time playing this game, with the mild annoyances here and there. I find that it isn't enough to take away from the overall positive experience I've had playing this game.

Tree of Savior is an MMORPG that serves as somewhat of a spiritual successor to Ragnorak Online. It is an asymmetrical top-down, sometimes unforgiving, game that has a lot of potential to provide hours of fun. Its artstyle is one that can either be found gorgeous or sickening depending on personal preference, but it is definitely catered to anime fans.
When first creating your character in ToS, you have the option of 4 different (non-genderlocked) classes:
The swordsman, the archer, the wizard, and the cleric. Each of these classes provide different playstyles. To top it off, ToS has a unique progression system in that each time you get to a specific level, you have the option to branch off into one of 3 classes, or stay the same. All these classes make up a total of
. Out of all of those, you should be able to find one that plays exactly how you want.
One thing worth mentioning though is that once you pick a skill, there's no going back. So it would be a good idea to research a build beforehand, or at least give careful thought before picking that skill; it
haunt you forever.
The rest of the game is just grinding quests and mobs till you hit level-cap. Now, there are several dungeons that you will journey through, and in addition to them you will be able to find over 128 boss monsters, each with their own custom animations and strategy to defeat. (The term strategy is used usely, most of the combat in this game is mashing F along with a combination of different hotkeys until the poor thing dies.)
-Loads of class customization; you will definitely find a class, or several, that really get what you crave.
-Beautiful artstyle
-Amazing soundtrack
-Diverse monsters and areas
-Helpful UI makes it easy for beginners to grasp
-Trading. You CANNOT trade items or anything unless you purchase a recurring subscription from the cash shop
-The combat can get boring quite quickly what with it being so simplistic
-Gold farmers can get ridiculously annoying in the two major cities. (Klaipeda is already difficult to navigate)
-Very instanced. This is a personal pet peeve of mine. Loading screens litter the world.
All in all, I would recommend this game. All cons aside, its a great game to get into the MMORPG genre.

For such a short game, it managed to feel drawn out and unnecessary.  If there is one thing that we can learn from this narrative, it is that wordy and intelligent are not synonyms.  It brushes against interesting themes, but does not reach any conclusion worth noting, aside from the classic video game trope that "evil is bad."  The few encounters with enemy creatures devolve from an intial tense atmosphere to an annoyance, as the player realizes they can always outrun their opponent, and will never be challenged with completing a task while an enemy is present.  Heaven forbid you stumble on one of the half-dozen safe points from which you can view the underwhelming models of the creatures you have been running from.  In the final hour, there is a two-part boss battle which is mind-boggling in both concept and execution, and clashes harshly with the game's established world.  Then you get on the pork shuttle to watch the game play the final act through on its own - though why the final scene concludes the game as the protagonist wishes is not obvious to me.  This is not a technically challenging horror game, and it is not an intellectually challenging narrative adventure.  This is a drawn out and densely crowded narrative-heavy gameplay-light experience, which manages to come across as half-baked.

The next issue (which many games will always suffer from) is the community. FFS, I understand that for some in fact probably many, this is their first try at a MOBA game. I understand that. There is a level system wish "matches" (i use that term lightly) simaliar skilled (coughs) players against each other. The problem comes in the form that leveling up in this game is easy as heck and thus you'll get stuck with many on a high level that still have no idea how the game is played. Let's not forget the toxic comments being made before, during, and even after a match. I've had to report so many people and I swear nothing is ever done since people can make a new account and join right back in being toxic.
After so many years I've put into this game, I can't say I'm having fun with it anymore. I've left and come back but things are only getting worse it seems.

But I need to be honest and say that I'm not that active in the community for this game.
So, conclusion:
Do not buy it at this time if:
- You want to play the game right away and have fun doing it
- You have an "older" pc (upgrade first)
- You get easy frustrated by laggy gameplay and a lot of bugs (reduce the risk of hurting you pc)
- You can't stand flying animals (deers, bears and other)
I also need to make a list of reasons for why you should buy it now:
Buy it if you:
- Like laggy gameplay

At this point in this game's progress, even asking for $10 is too much. In the limited amount of time I spent playing this game, the following annoyances led me to request a refund for this purchase:
1. Animals and people clip through objects and float about anywhere they like.
2. The bow's reticle vanishes, perhaps when you are in a settlement, perhaps not. Aiming becomes a farce at this point.
3. Bears. They spawn inside settlements, where they don't bother attacking villages (or vice versa), but are more than agitated by your presence. The two good things about bears is that, when I shot it in the face with an arrow, the collision detector kept registering between the bear and the arrow as I kited the bear and it basically committed suicide, and the meat from the bear completely removed my hunger.
4. My hunger bar jumped back to 50% when I went to sleep after eating that bear meat.
5. You can't do anything in the game unless you have the matching basic skill choice. This means you need to pick the gathering abilities during character creation. If you don't, even chopping wood becomes a monumental task. To wit: you cannot start a character that is not a gatherer unless you like chopping wood for three days in order to make a campfire.
6. When you chop wood, it quickly fills your inventory. Queue the crafting screen. This point is going to have sub-points.
(A) When you are crafting, you cannot see what resources you have because it closes all access to inventory and doesn't bother telling you anywhere how many resources you have.
(B) Each item takes what I assume to be in-game time to craft. During that crafting period, you are completely locked in that crafting window while time in the game continues to roll on at an accelerated pace. The blurry rectangle in the center of your screen allows you to watch at daylight changes and blurs of NPCs zoom by.
(C) Let me reiterate: you are stuck in the crafting window. If you craft something that takes 2-3 hours in game, you are going to wait in that window until it is done. Do NOT try to interrupt crafting by pressing the escape key. This will simply open up the game's main menu BEHIND your crafting menu and completely bung up your ability to manipulate the crafting window once your item is finished, even if you press the escape key again to close the main menu.
Please look at the majority of the other reviews for this game. Even the positive ones repeat the word "potential" until the word begins to lose meaning in your head. Potential is great, sure, but I'm not going to purchase an empty, dark, dank corner and hope that a delicious mushroom grows there.
Also note the amount of time most of the reviewers have spent playing the game, including myself. Keep in mind that these reviews are written after that much gameplay. The numbers aren't very high because there is nothing to do in this game yet that is worth your attention and money.

A suprisingly strong comeback from what I am told is a subpar series, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a singleplayer-only FPS that ranks among the top Wild West-flavored games I've played- and there are admittedly not many. You take the role of one Silas Greaves, quick-shooting, hard-drinking bounty hunter who rolls into Abilene, Kansas one day in 1910 for a drink and winds up relating the story of his life to his fellow bar patrons. This provides the framing device for a series of pitched gunfights as the fictional Silas goes on a Forest Gump-ian trip through the old West, coming face to face wth a long list of real outlaws of history. Gunslinger takes advantage of the cult of mystique that time in history has accrued, and the mysterious circumstances surrounding the deaths of some of these outlaws, to weave a tall tale of robbery and revenge that is just far-fetched enough to be plausible. Silas earns experience from his kills and levels up, giving the player a point to spend in Gunslinger, Ranger and Trapper skill trees, which upgrade revolvers, lever-action rifles and shotguns, respectively. You can also throw dynamite, and use bullet-time, upgrades for both are seeded through all three skill trees. It is possible to earn all skills eventually, though this will take more then one playthrough. When Silas comes up against a legend of the west, the player will engage in a duel minigame that has you focus his sight on target, adjust his hand for a faster draw, and then choose to shoot before or after your opponent draws for a dishonorable or honorable kill. Scattered throughout the story levels are collectibles called "Nuggets of Truth" that when found confer an experience bonus and give you some real historical background about the people, places, events and objects you see on your journey. In addition to Normal and Hard, there is a "True West" difficulty mode unlocked after completing the game once that disables your hud. Aside from the story, there is an arcade mode with pre-made levels distinct from the story, and a duel mode that comprises additional dueling challenges. Gunslinger is alive with a vibrant, cell-shaded art style, excellent voice acting, sound and music, and overall presents an incredible deal for the price. If you have not played a Call of Juarez game before, as was the case with me, you should probably start here. A must play for any Western fan.

Short but perfect experience.
Art style - beautiful. SG team created a really unique futuristic vision of city that is not gray/blue/black but using a variety of colors. The most dominant symbol - 'triangle' also contributes to this.
Music - soundtrack to Transistor works very with the game. Music for exploring is nice on ear, and combat has some very dynamic tracks. Songs in the game - they are awesome and can be listened as a complete separate entity. And the humming mechanics....nice.
Story - can't say anything without spoilers. Partially is like Bastion - you don't know everything from the beginning, you learn the world as you play. But Bastion was more like listening to the story of a good storyteller. Transistor is much more personal experience.
Gameplay - way better than a Bastion. Combat can be played in real time, but it shines in the turn mode. Main character can stop time to plan actions and then execute them very very fast. The fight takes in closed arenas (a part of game world is being enclosed in force fields - you can't escape until you win). The health system is also unique - your health is tied to your equiped abilities. Each time you loose full health bar, you loose this ability. It will be disabled until next checkpoint (access point). So basically you can take some punishment but next fight can be more difficult with some skills/functions lost.
Time/content- some people complain this game is short. Yes, the main story is short - it feels shorter than the bastion. It's also more linear. But this is only one playthrough. There is NewGame+ mode. There also unlockables like background information about characters etc. There are also limiters that grant bonuses but make combat/enemies stronger.
Very personal opinion - I love this game. The story, the presentation, gameplay mechanics - everything is awesome.
I' played some good and bad games. I've played some great games. Yet, for games I have a special category - masterpiece. And for me Transistor is a masterpiece. It takes the same place on the same shelf as Chrono Trigger and Deus Ex.
Good job Supergiant Games!.

I did not expect to stick to this game as much as I did; merely decided to give it a go since I didn't feel like playing anything else in my library at the time and this game had some pretty great reviews. The magic hit me around 30 minutes into game when I built my first steam engine and saw my electric drill work on its own. It was such a trivial hurdle, but that particular feeling of success carried on into all parts of the game. My first run was very obviously a complete wreck, mostly since I didn't automate anything really. But my second run is where that magic came back, realizing that I could build in such a way that the system takes care of itself. Almost like nurturing a baby until it can feed itself. It was such a beautiful thing and the best part is it didn't stop there. It never stopped there. I was always inclined to find ways to further optimize my design, to make it take less of my manual labor to work. Even when I reached the point where it all worked without my help anymore, there was still so much to do. I play with a set of mods called Bob's mods which further complicate the tech tree and add many new materials and forms of refining to the amazing base game that is Factorio. With these mods, it was never an easy task to automate anything past the first couple hours of the tech tree, and there was always a bottleneck in the design somewhere that needed extra care and thinking. With every new resource being brought into the base came the challenge of refining it and putting it to use. More often than not, its presence affected the priorities of my other materials already being refined in the base, forcing me to reconsider my design every time. It was a spectacular balance of expansion and resource management that I had never found in any game before...
Then the fire nation (aliens) attacked.
Stupid things were ruining everything! Destroying a single tiny component of my base could easily make the whole system come to a screeching halt, and so I could not let them go, as I call it, "unsupervised". My supervision usually consisted of pumping lead into their hideous heads or cooking alien meat for dinner with flamethrower turrets (all of which also required some level of resource management, it all works so well together!). Even still, the rowdy aliens got bigger and uglier over time, forcing me to have to repair things often. Eventually I stumbled upon the robotics part of the tech tree, and man did I feel like I was in some sci-fi planetary terraforming factory (well technically I am). Repairs were done automatically, and materials were now being carried by flying robots where they needed to be according to my commands. I even managed to automate the robots into creating more of themselves! Everything was fine and dandy, until the next bump in the road...
We dun goofed and ran out of steel.
I had taken such a simple material for granted and paid the price since that was one thing I never further optimized. I tried desperately to enhance its production, but it was futile. Aliens were storming our base every few seconds and repair robots were all being destroyed. Single pipes were being destroyed and as a result most production was slowing down. Eventually I only had 200 logistic robots with nothing to do, since there were no materials being made and none left to use. I watched as my base was engulfed by aliens and my legend wiped off the planet.
10/10 make sure to tell your steel you love her

This is a fun single-player shooter with some caveats. I love the fact it's a Western, for starters, and that it doesn't turn into yet another endless zombie shooter. The story is engaging enough the first time around, though the whole game is very linear. You can never go more than a few dozen feet off the chosen path, and you're effectively spoon-fed the tale as you go.
Graphically it holds up quite nicely. You can tell it's aged a bit, but it's still very nice.  The audio and voice acting are pretty good.  It's not at all realistic. It's a bit like playing a low-budged Western. The guns are very visceral, and I swear you can feel the kick through the mouse. :-)
The environments are also nice. I'd recommend having your gamma up a little past their defaults though. Possibly it was my PC, but that made the colour palette a lot less jarring for some reason.
Pros:
+ Engaging story, at least on the first play-through.
+ Nice graphics. Not amazing, but nice.
+ Nice arcadey gun mechanics.
+ Feels like you're playing an over-the-top Western movie. This is not a bad thing.
+ Responsive, and reasonable controls.
+ Fun flash-backs and "Actually it didn't happen like that" moments.
+ Enjoyable duels.
Cons:
- The story is very short. About five hours on normal difficulty for me, and I wasn't rushing.
- It's *almost* a rail-shooter. The very opposite of "open world".
- Sometimes the story interrupts the action a bit too much.
- The damn 'ghost' level. Almost a game-breaker for me.
- When the main character says "Then I saw a ladder I didn't spot before." - That's because it wasn't there.
- Did I mention how linear it is?
It's well worth it for the super-cheap price I paid (About NZ$6) and it was fun the first time through. It's not holding me for the second play-through though, because I found I was playing it for the story, not for the action... which was OK but nothing particularly special.
It worked out to just over a dollar an hour for me, which is more value for money than a movie... and that's ultimately why I'd recommend it.

Coming from a relatively not well know franchise, Call of Juarez Gunslinger comes in guns blazing. Set in the Old West, you take on the role as Silas Greaves as you take on legendary outlaws as you try to make things right in the world. The way the story is told is the narrator is Silas Greaves and he takes you through the story. The story is told in real time so anything Silas will say will happen, whether or not it makes sense. This way of telling the story is unique and it works.
The gameplay is tight and flows well. The game features a combo system that rewards quick kills and precision aiming. As you earn xp you level up and you unlock perks. If you unlock enough perks in that category you get a legendary weapon. The game also features arcade mode which is certain sections of story in which your objective is to score as much points as possible. The last mode is Duels, where you go through 15 duels and you try to score as much points as possible.
There are some gripes I have with this game is that to change the FOV you have to go into Video.scr to change it. Not many people are aware of this. The AI isnt the best, they just spawn and shoot you. I have experienced a couple crashes with the game.
If you are a fan of first person shooters get this, if you like Wild West shooters definitely get this.
1) Go to C:\Users\YOURNAMEHERE\AppData\Local\tech­land\cojgunslinger\out\Settings
2) Open Video.scr with notepad
3) Add the following 2 lines to the bottom of the list
ForcedHorzFov(INSERT FOV NUMBER HERE BETWEEN 80-110)
DisableScreenBorder()

This is the membership policy, specifically, the fact that the time you buy is not game time, but real life time which ticks away even when you are not playing.
I am someone who will spend $50-80 bucks on a sim game I like easy.
Simulating hunting to the fidelity level of purchasing license and memberships is cool actually. But this recurring payment maintenance model is totally not cool  as it runs out whether I am playing or not!
So much so that my initial decision to break from my own hard rule of not getting into a 'recurring x period' payment model for a sim/game was challenged but ultimately I cannot get past the poor value proposition the model offers!
There is upwards for $50 waiting for the game developer here when a solution where I can buy the game [or even game time] and play it as I want to.
Clearly, this is not going to happen with theHunter so, just to be clear, I'll play the free game until I'm bored with hunting mule deer and rabbits and then removed it from my computer.  Just saying.
Sad really. No money will pass to the developer!

The experience demands patience, one of the attractions for me. The stalk is well designed and it can get quite tense on occasion as the worry of spooking your prey grows.

Check YouTube, the game graphics & environment are simply amazing overall.  Fantastic job.
It is really rather sad that such a great sim is hamstrung by such as pricing model ..... if they are making dough this way, then shame really ..... because this endorses other devs to do the same.
As for recommendation, I've struggled with my choice here before deciding on "NO" by way of communicating my dis-satisfaction with the pricing model. For what good it will do LOL.
I will follow this up with saying that I would recommend playing the free version as it really is a superb Hunting sim.

This is a builder game, but on a scale not typically seen. You start off small, chopping trees and digging coal out of the dirt by hand. You quickly get set up with a machine to automatically mine, and start smelting some iron. Then you make something that automatically moves the iron to your smelter. Then you research a machine to construct items for you. Then you automatically move your iron, copper, and stone through appropriate smelters, on to assemblers that make more assemblers, smelters, miners, and things that move items around. Then you make trains to supply your smelters from far away. Then you build robots that can simplify your supply chain within your factory by moving items between any two points as needed. Then you build power armor and carry the robots with you. Then you have them build entire solar farms in seconds, from components built automatically in your factories. Eventually you've built enough infrastructure that you're measuring your iron consumption in hundreds or thousands *per second* and start launching rockets into space on a regular basis. About the only thing you can't automate is deciding where/how to expand your base.
It's rather telling that it takes literally millions of item crafts to launch your first rocket, but it can be played indefinitely with as few as 101 of those crafts being performed manually, and speed runners can beat the game in a couple hours.
The way it manages to transition you between these stages without telling you what to do is rather fantastic, albeit rough at times as you struggle to figure out the best way to lay out your factory. My only significant complaint is that proper management of trains is decidedly unintuitive. Or rather, it doesn't give good feedback on *why* it's failing if a train can't find a path. But this game has already improved over time in so many other areas that I can't see that being a problem forever. And once you find a pattern that works, the game has built-in capabilities for copy-pasting your designs elsewhere so you don't have to worry about it anymore.
Oh, and there are aliens to fend off the entire time you're doing this, so good luck with that (though you can technically choose to play with them on "peaceful" so that they will not attack first.)
If you're worried about getting bored, don't be. There is a very healthy mod scene in this game, with mods adding everything from tameable aliens, to dozens of ore types, to entirely restructuring the tech tree to make them game 5 times as long. And the game itself isn't done yet, of course, with plans to eventually expand out beyond your initial planet.
TL;DR - If you like builder games, you'll love this. Just be prepared to voluntarily lose some sleep.

I have no experience at end game so my review is just from the starting 40-50 levels or so
Pros:
- combat is fun. played as a mage first and swordsman. 1 shotting a big group of monsters after grouping them up just right is a good feeling. However, my swordsman seems to just buff itself then auto attack until one of us dies, hopefully there'll be more to it later, was planning on going dragoon, but after reading all the reviews saying anything other than tank is pointless, im a little worried.
- Music is pretty good. a few zones have the fantasy feeling down, theres some odd techno going on in the mines but i enjoyed it. It's very korean sounding if that makes sense.
- Art is pretty. the 2d sprites and maps have a pretty watercolor effect that reminded me of saga frontier 2 back on PS1. Monsters range from cute to...less cute? was farming some big red onions in a zone and noticed a few of its frames of animation hadnt been colored in though.
- Collections. I really like this feature. Find a treasure chest in most maps and it has a box for that map, bring it back to the main city to unlock it and you need to gather some monster drops to unlock a permenent bonus to stats and such. It can get a bit grindy when they include some rare weapon, but it gives you a reason to run around killing stuff other than exp.
.
Cons:
- Translation issues. Theres been quite a few issues understanding what the hecks going on or how things work, it takes some investigation on forums or experiments to figure out things.
- Freemium. I cant mail items to an alt, or at least i havent figured out how yet. theres clearly a mail system but theres no mailbox that ive found to send stuff. If you sell something on the market, you will not recieve the money for 2 whole days. thats just silly. I also can't buy things on the market without buying a token. the only way to do that in game is with in game silver on the market, which i cant buy anything without a token. How is that supposed to work? The alternative is to buy 300tp for around 30 bucks in the steam store and use a third of that on the tp store. I'm just not willing to go that far to buy some level 15 armor.
- Could be pro or con depending on your preference but the game is grindy. As with all Korean MMOs they have the habit of putting more emphasis in killing groups of monsters rather than running from quest to quest. At 40 i followed the questline till it took me from a level 38 zone into a 50ish zone, was getting destroyed and had to go back and try to find a grind spot. If they wanted to add quest grinds they need to smooth the level transitions. Unless i missed it, they needed to have the questline go into a 40 zone, then head to the 50, but oh well.
- Grouping. I prefer playing by myself, so it hasnt bothered me much, but when ive looked at groups, theres only ever 4-5 listed, and theyre mostly 100-200 levels above me even at peak hours. feels like either everyone just plays in their own little groups or no one bothers till closer to max level.
- Bots and goldsellers. As with all Korean MMOs, you will get lag in the main cities just from gold seller spam. My first day i found a bot farming in the mines. switched channels and found another bot in the same place, same class, same hairstyle, did this for about 4 channels till i found an empty one. They arent so bad if you switch channels but its annoying. I always play on the middle or last few channels for that reason.
So far its been fun to play, but the comments about endgame, or lack thereof and how i'm unable to do basic MMO things like Buy and sell items on the market or mail things is turning me off. Ill try to enjoy it for what it is and not what its missing, at least till i get to higher levels.

An absolutely amazingly well done shooter that holds up to the test of time. Someone who loved Wild West American history put their heart and soul into this game. On the surface it's your typical shoot'em'up. Shoot, shoot, shoot, reload, and shoot some more--my favorite. Of course, it sports a Wild West Americana theme through the story telling of Silas Greaves.
The people in the story are actually real people. There's history and speculation behind these people back when we weren't so great at logging our past. This allows the story teller to stretch the truth as we see our plot unfold. Secret collectables known as "nuggets of truth" reveal factual history on these characters and more, so it's also educational and full of intrigue.
The combat is solid. I wasn't a big fan of the quickdraw segments. I had to repeat these a lot because you have to keep track of three things at once while trying to pop the bad guy. Normal combat is visceral and action packed! Bad guys have great aim, though they don't flank around too much. They use cover and reload appropriately. Your "health" meter is very well represented by paper tears on your screen that heal over time. Weapons feel powerful and kinetic. There's very little variety, unfortunately. Three revolvers, two shotguns, and two rifles. There's a level-up mechanic in the form of skills. Unfortunately shotguns are way too limited and the gunslinger tree focuses too much on spray-and-pray, so if you want to play this game on the hardest difficulty you are going to default to "Ranger" and focus on longrange combat and precision.
The game has a points system for gaining experience in the same way that Bulletstorm does. The "cheat death" mechanic is a lot like Max Payne. You get to see who's about to gank you and you can turn the tables and get yourself back in the fight.
The game isn't realistic by any means, but that's what makes it such a fun shooter. If you like FPS games and Western themes then you need to give this game a try.
