Despite the generic name, questionable English and lack of content, this game holds a lot of promise. As it stands now, you can wander through a living world where you and a few thousand NPCs seek to find purpose. As far as I can tell the NPCs can do most things you can do, and they can be found wandering the wilderness and starting their own settlements.
As of the writing of this review, it is possible to build a settlement with basic structures such as homes, farms, tavern, etc, craft a decent number of items, gather resources and food and be killed by bears.
If what you want is a medieval game that strives to allow you to do anything and go anywhere in a world that feels alive, this game is absolutely worth the investment. Buying early access is always risky business, but this game is far enough along to get your $10 out of it, and you'll be helping the developer continue to make what could be a very compelling finished product.

In the moment of writing, I have 83 hours logged on Factorio.
Usually, I'll get tired of a game pretty quickly, or I'll just play for a few hours at a time.
None the less, this was my Saturday night:
1900: All right, it's 7 in the evening. I'll go play some Factorio.
2100: Man, I love this game. I'll go to bed soon. Just have to optimize these transport belts.
2300: Oh, right, I was going to go to bed. Hm, I'll just fix this electricity shortage first.
0100: Pretty sure I was supposed to do something now... Oh well, better crush some aliens with my tank.
0300: Hot damn, those aliens are getting pretty angry. Better put up a proper perimeter defence. And then go sleep.
0500: Okay, right, right, I've finally got some clever designs. Better redesign my entire factory. WAIT, WHAT TIME IS IT?
0630: WHAT DO YOU MEAN IT'S 0630 IN THE MORNING? BUT IT'S STILL DAR... No, okay, apparently it's light outside.
0640: Okay, okay, okay, I'll just write a Steam review for Factorio. Then go sleep. Yeah. Sleep. And dream. Of Factorio.
Somebody once asked if androids dream of electric sheep. I can assure you that Factorio players dream of factory optimization.

Not so much the 'survival horror' of the first Amnesia: the Dark Descent; A Machine for Pigs does away with many of the elements its predecessor had in that vein. So, there are no limited resources to grab, no sanity to keep or torches that run out of oil.
This time, the game would prefer to let its intense story at atmosphere scare you, instead of relying on the prospect of running out of torch light or a monster chasing you through a corridor for its scares. You will either love or hate this change. Fans of survival horror may be dissapointed if that is what they are expecting - it is no longer this type of game. Fans of the original game who want something new and different will certainly enjoy it.
I think most will agree after playing both games that the Dark Descent is more immediately terrifying. It is unlikely that there will be YouTube videos of people jumping at this game, as there was with the original. Saying that, although I never felt as insanely frightened playing A Machine for Pigs as when I played the original game, I felt a more lasting and meaningful sense of unease. The story takes a hold of you in the same way as the monsters did previously. It is a much more interesting and disturbing game than the Dark Descent, and something which I spent a long time thinking about after finishing.

enjoy this chicken stir fry recpie
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan

I had very high expectations going into this game. It was made by Supergiant, everyone I know ever has reccommended it to me, and from the bits and pieces I've seen of them, the game's OST and visuals are VERY good. That said, did Transistor deliver? In every way, shape, form, and more. Like a number of games these days, you're just tossed in, dazed and confused, and left to your own devices. The game has a lore, as well as a defined plot of the events leading up to where you, the player, join in. After the beginning, the game does a good job of showing and explaining the world to the player, and I found understanding that to be a key part of the experience. Now as for the gameplay, it's a pretty unique take on JRPG elements. You can fight enemies actively in gameplay, or use a one-sided turn system. Fighting enemies actively is MUCH harder, the one sided turn system is a bit difficult to describe, but I'll do my best. What happens is you get a Turn ability, which lets you pause the fight, only for you, and dictate the next few moves in battle. Everything you use in your Turn takes up a chunk of a universal bar at the top of the screen, moving, using an ability, everything takes up part of your bar. After you use your Turn it's on about a 3 second cooldown. You get new abilities as the game progresses and you level up, each of which are unique. GRAPHICS: The art style is Ragnarök Online, kinda 3d terrain with fixed camera, cute-ish monsters, rotating character sprites. Character customization seems to be a joke. It has serious optimization issues: dropping frames with 1280*720 resolution with a R9 290 graphics card for an almost completely 2d game is insulting (I'm not sure if this is an actual graphic-pipeline issue or if the game just handles lag in a stupid STAHP EVERYTHING manner). Also the anime graphics style is highly weaboo and sexist. The narration sprites of female NPCs are usually showing a lot of chest and skin.
STORY: The story is cliché and simple. Save the world! Oh noes, bad ugly races attack! Go kill them! Also you are the chosen one (of the chosen million).
CLASSES: The class system is a mess. Once you choose a class quest you're locked in. Miss-Click? Tough luck, better reroll your character. Most advanced classes have ridiculous cooldowns on their skills, meaning you are using the skills of the new class... one third of the time. Also many classes use items per skill-cast meaning you are constantly burning your in game currency.
SKILLS: You can (and must) burn in-game currency to buy passive upgrades for your skills. Most of the important passives then "start to be learned" and take anywhere from 2 - 30 minutes to learn (and this time increases with each passive level). During this learning time you can't learn any other passive skills (but you can learn 2 at once with a cashshop item). Also you can turn many passive skills off... understandable for the warriors provoke but not so much for many other passives.
COMBAT: The combat gives off a good vibe at the start but gets really old really fast. There are serious targeting issues if you are ranged and play with a controller. In many cases your skill rotation is reduced to 1 skill or just auto attack which is horrible for those who expect an exiciting time but maybe great for those who want to experience the "flow" feeling.
OTHER: The collection system is interesting (getting permanent bonuses for completing item collections) but the way it works is completely bureaucratic (deliver collection box to town, then get items, then deliver them again). Also it's odd that every collection you complete is also completed for all of your party members but not for your other characters. This was confusing for me because I thought these passive bonuses would work well if you want to level a 2nd/3rd character (but the grind must remain).
CRAFTING: horrible, primitive. Every time you craft you eat the recipe. You can put some text on the crafted items. As far as I crafted the items were useful but the materials were grindy (yes, everything here is grindy).
RECOMMENDATION:
- Don't fall for the Ragnarök hype
- Ruthlessly Grindy (xp, planned xp scroll uses, money, materials, gear)
- Strict and Cruel system when it comes to skill and talent choices
- Multiple systems which want to burn your in game currency AND drain your time passively
- Higher level play almost always requires a party that is working together (1st for leveling speed, 2nd for survival)
- Higher classes have interesting skills with greater power but cooldowns force you to rely on your lower tier class-skills
- Party synergy will most likely limit your possible class choices to comlement your team.
Final grade: 1 screeching halt at the end of hype out of 10.
I'm not even sure if the studio really planned on keeping this game alive or if they just wanted to make as much money as possible with the pre-purchase cash. I don't expect anyone to remember this game after a year expect as a some murky fog of disappointment from the past.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is a mixed bag. Did I enjoy my time playing it? Yes. Was it anywhere near as good as the first game? Not even close.
The Chinese Room succeeds at telling a compelling story but fails utterly at the execution of tension and fear in many ways due to the removal of the "gamey" elements from the previous Amnesia. Gone is the inventory and any item management. The few puzzles that occur in the game are pitifully simple and that's really sad considering the original Amnesia puzzles weren't really that difficult either. Every enemy encounter is broadcast via the flickering of your lantern from miles away, making every scare there fall completely flat.
The linearity of the game is also totally noticable. Amnesia did this too but they at least tried to hide it. A Machine For Pigs seems to revel in the fact that you can tell how linear it is. The belowground levels at least attempt the illusion of non-linearity, barely, but the outside areas are awful in this respect. I recall a specific sequence where I was funneled from small London building to small London building via a series of straight pathways bordered by fences. If The Chinese Room's goal was to immerse me by removing the video game elements of this video game, then maybe they should actually try to hide their game's linearity instead of playing it up.
But by far, the biggest crime is the removal of the sanity meter. You can look straight at monsters now, and while they are indeed disturbing to look at the scare factor there is gone and there is no penalty. Frictional knew that showing your monsters kills the atmosphere and that The Chinese Room ****s this up is mindboggling to me.
I could go on and on about why the removal of the original Amnesia's game elements is Awful and Never Should Have Been Done but it's been discussed ad nauseam at this point.
TL;DR Since there isn't a "meh" or "disappointingly competent, I guess" button I've hit recommend, but with the huge caveat that it is inferior in every way to the original Amnesia, but if you're looking for a story being told in a fairly creepy way, this game is passable.

No, under no circumstances is it acceptable to pay 20 dollars for a 3 hour long, slightly spookier version of Dear Esther, which was also a narrative walking simulator. The game itself is good and I hadn't any trouble. But I do not recommend to buy it on steam for various reasons:
1) The steam download is not up to date! After downloading ~63gb through steam the eso launcher redownloaded ~45gb and replaced the steam files. So as long as you don't have a fast connection don't buy through steam. Also if you want to test the game and refund it if you don't like it keep in mind that the launcher counts as play time. So redownloading the game reduces the time you have to play the game before you can't refund it anymore.
2) When I managed to play the game it worked fine, but until now I had a problem EVERY. SINGLE. TIME. I pressed on play in steam. Some of them are directly related to steam (e.g. steam not even starting the launcher) others are issues of the launcher itself (e.g. error to download the patch manifest) which are harder to solve because of steam. For example you can bypass the launcher and therefore every issue you have with it by starting the eso.exe directly. Not so if you bought the game on steam because now you have to start it through the steam launcher, which, again, has a lot of issues.
3) While searching for solutions for the issues I had I found a lot of complaints about other problems. The launcher itself has obviously a lot of problems, but there also seem to be a lot of issues related to steam besides those I experienced myself.
So do yourself a favour, don't make the same mistake as I did and don't buy the game on steam. This has been the worst experience I've ever had with steam!

Don't be mislead by the whole 'art game' thing. It has (more than?) enough gameplay going for it to be an actual game. This game actually is fairly solid at it's core, with interesting gameplay mechanics. You'll quickly be amazed by how easy it is to make mistakes in judging someone's legal documents and how many layers of control this game offers. It has more depth than meets the eye. It's great even at what it does. Do keep in mind that the aesthetics are a bit rough in this pixel art style and it remains to be seen how all things combined will influence the game's longetivity. But I've already had a good few hours of fun with this and probably will occasionally play some more. It's also the only game I know of in it's genre of 'border patrol' style gaming. Add to that random events like terrorist bombings, people you have/can detain for human trafficking and it's quite a cool spin on the simulation genre. The stalinistic setting is nice and adds to the overall experience. The low pay with a direct impact on your own family can be a bit crude at times, but it's a nice touch.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 is my favorite Call of Duty that I've played. I feel that it is a nice sequel to Modern Warfare 1 with a fantastic storyline and the addition of Spec Ops, a series of short challenge levels. There are a variety of guns to choose from and different levels to play through. For the most part, none of them feel repetitive in any way. It looks great and plays great.
On the other hand, multiplayer is a let-down. Its been a few years since release and many people have gone on to other titles in the series leaving Modern Warfare 2's multiplayer dwindling. They have the servers and the players but failed to incorporate some sort of anti-cheat. Multiplayer is filled with hackers. Not every game has them, but they are there (and you can definitely tell when its enabled). For whatever reason, they also got rid of the server browser so there are no more modded servers.
The single-player and co-op experience is great. Multiplayer can be so-so. It's worth a few re-runs to beat Veteran and get all the intel!

One of the most exciting games i played this year, finaly a reason for me to play an mmo that isn't Maplestory or WoW.
other mmo's usually get boring after or during the tutorial where they fail to get you excited from the ground up start and every moment after that.
This game learns the lesson by using fun combat that is satisfying, and starts where you have already gained your powers (example wizard already has a staff and does magic) and doesn't ruin the flow of the game like most new 3d mmo's do.
I like this games camera and graphics, really nice art style.
Optimization needs some work, frame stuttering issues near alot of people which is weird since theres nothing graphically demanding compared to something like a battlefield 4 match with more than the same number of people.
overall i find this game alot more fun to play alone, in a lonely channel. but if you do want to find allies you'll definitely find.
Rewards from are a bit different this time, instead of getting exp, you get a scroll that gives you a specific amount of exp whenever you wish to use it, this is unique because it lets you grind and save an specific number of exp scrolls untill you want to spend them on a level that you're really having trouble on.
Controls are great, everything feels just right.
Music is alright, nothing you've never heard before, but it does fit the flow of the game and is nice listening to.
I was a bit dissapointed of the graphical options, i wish i could change resolution in fullscreen, or change rendering settings, how about low-medium-high-ultra and not just few checkboxes to select that are pretty much ultra-settings of the graphics.
Another thing i have to point out is the controller support, finally a way to use the controller in an mmo without slow downs and stopping in combat. This might be surprising but i actually prefer to use my logitech 360 styled controller for this game, it's very fun.
to sum it up
PROS:
*Eye candy - beautiful graphics , nice style.
*Gameplay - Satisfying combat, fast and fluent, platformish with some beat em' up, if you do like the style of maplestory, *and dislike the slow combat of most mmos' , you'll definitely like this one , and this one even more because it's not *button mash 1 skill to grind, variation does matter and is satisfying.
*Quests are fast and fun to do.
*Music - i guess i just listened to everything that this just doesn't excite me anymore, but it is good.
*Controls
*10/10 Controller support in an MMO
*A spirtual 3D successor to pre big-bang Maplestory & Ragnarok Online
CONS :
*Optimization issues
*Not many graphical options, like rendering % settings or resolution on fullscreen, it's 2016 and every game should have that
*Long loading times on some areas, distrupts flow of gameplay

I came home from work one day, I'd had a long day ,and I'd played maybe a couple of hours of this game so far. I decided to put some pasta on the boil, and then thought I'd play while it cooked. I became absolutely terrified and engrossed in gameplay. I was busy trying to escape from the Alien's clutches by hiding in a cupboard and holding my breath while it stalked by, and before I knew it I hear - BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP!  I immediately though it was coming from the game, and began to wonder what new horror was about to rear it's head, but no, this was coming from....inside the house. Bewildered and frightned I ran and opened my door ,(half expecting an Alien to devour me),  but all I saw was thick smoke filling my hallway. I ran into the kitchen and saw the culprit - some thoroughly burned pasta and smoke streaming from a burning pot on the hob. I rushed to fill the pot with water and then proceeded to have to open all my doors and windows and let the smoke filter out. My housemate came home and faced with every door open and the smell of smoke, immediately thought we had been robbed. Chaos and panic were the menu for that evening. It took 2 weeks and more then a few bottles of febreeze to get rid of the stench of smoke.
I became so enraptured with this game, that I nearly burned the house down. An absolute joy to play and still haunts my dreams, (and my nostrils), to this day. I hugely reccommend it.

I am among those people that love this game, Just as I loved Dear Ester. I give Amnesia: A machine for Pigs 10 out of 10. Maybe this game shouldn't be compared to the other Amnesia at all. This game just works perfectly, no bugs at all. The graphics are very good. The sound and voice acting are first class. The atmosphere is very creepy, gloomy, and scary. My heart was beating and I jumped many times during the game. There are problems to solve (puzzles) lots of thinking to do. Some are quite difficult, and you never know what exactly is going on here. Is it a nightmare ? is this man insane ? Is the whole world insane ? Slowly but surely you are given notes, recordings, and journal entries to help somewhat. I enjoyed every minute of this game, which lasted about 14 hours. My hats off to the Chinese Room for making another masterpiece. I highly recommend A Machine For Pigs to anyone who enjoys thinking about our world, and the human condition. Anyone who has no knowledge of the Industrial Revolution working conditions, Child Labor Laws, Life at the turn of the 20th century, right before the slaughter of WW1, wont enjoy this game, because they won't understand it. I advise you to play in a darkened room, with good headphones, on the highest volume you can stand, to hear all the sounds, if you dare.

Amenesia the Dark Descent was an amazing game that created an internet phenominon. With all the Youtube press it recieved and barrage of indie horror games mimicking that followed. It's hard to deny it was an influential, innovative, and fantastic game. This game was a huge letdown in contrast. It's not all this game's fault however, the original Amnesia came out of nowhere as a suprise and thus I had no expectations from it other than was most likely going to be frightening to say the least. So it's hard to achieve something bigger than what the original had. That being said, I was still excited from the coverage I had been following online concerning this game so I was nonetheless pumped about it. It was a day one purchase for me out of pure faith. The opening seemed interesting to say the least but as soon as that was over and the gameplay segment had begun it didn't take long for me to notice changes in the series... changes for the worse.
First off I almost immediately noticed you could not interact with most of the furniture and objects laying around the rooms. In the first Amenesia you could mess with almost anything whether it was form or function related, it was still fun to toss vases at the monsters as you were trying to make a break for it. In this sequel you can open very few drawers and cabinets, and the only other objects in rooms you can move are the chairs. I know thats a nitpick but it gets worse.
After accepting that slight change I was trying to figure out how to open the inventory. I tried looking at the controls in the game and found nothing. I then read forums that said the inventory was removed. This simplified the game too much for my taste and seemed like it only made the game more bland.
With no inventory to open I then wondered how I would check my health and sanity... then I read more up on the game. There was no sanity meter... I mean what the ♥♥♥♥ man that was half of the fun of the original. Hiding in a corner wondering if you were going to either go ♥♥♥♥ing insane from the darkness or have to turn on your lamp to relieve yourself only to have a god damned monster with googly eyes staring you down. Pick your ♥♥♥♥ing poison! It was awesome. But no, no sanity meter here more watering down of what made the predecessor so great. Oh and that's another thing... your lamp, or old timey flashlight device, has an infinte source of light. There is no oil to fill it up with or anything you have to replenish it with at all in the game. On top of that your flashlight torch lamp thingy magiggy flickers on and off when a monster is near or about to appear taking away yet more tense build up moments. Also no god damned tinderboxes. I guess it doesn't matter anyway since half of the game's envirenment is lit and you don't have a sanity meter anyway. What a crock of♥♥♥♥♥♥
The story is even more far fetched and bizarre this time around, but it's ok I had no issues with it. The monsters are pigs instead of jawless, leather bondaged, flabby♥♥♥♥♥white things. They act the same though so again that change is purely aesthetic. On the plus side though is awesome atmosphere of late 1800's industrial London, you get to venture through a mansion, factories, a church and catacombs, slaughterhouses, sewers, even the streets of London itself. The music was also pretty intriguing. And the graphics were obviously better being it came out nearly 3 years after the first game.
Overall this game is not bad by any means. It's fun and worth playing. The problem with it is that its just a watered down version of the first game with a different setting and characters. It brings nothing new to the table gameplay wise, it only takes things away. It's worth buying on Steam if you get it during a sale I'd say, otherwise I would invest my money in another title.

This game is a sandbox, with story elements.
The story isn't great, it gets boring fast, however, that's not the selling point of this game, it's the massive sandbox, I mean, in what other games can you attach a sports car onto a helicopter, fly it into the mountains and then ramp off the top? Hijack a military jet, cover it in bombs then fly full speed into a military base, bailing out at the last second? And in what game can you zip around the massive map, with a combination of your grappling hook, parachute, and wingsuit?
Onto the combat.
The parachute adds a new dimension to traditional gunplay by allowing you to soar into the sky then rain missiles onto your enemies, the grappling hook also lets you grapple onto targets and deliver flying kicks. The tethers are also really fun to play with, attaching people to a jet and watching as they are flown of into the distance...
However gunplay without these aspects can beome quite boring.
The Graphics are amazing, and the map is so masterfully crafted that you will enjoy finding quite mountain lakes, and soaring of cliffs.
There are cons however, you need 8 Gb of Ram, I would recomend 12. Also Sadly this game crashes however, not too often. Also youre going to want an SSD as load times are large, Upwards of 1.5 minutes.
In summary, this is a great game, with amazing sandbox potntial and lots to do.
I also recomennd the DLCs as they add really fun missions, some of witch are more fun the the regular story.

Transistor...
The next perfect game by Supergiant Games.
This time the developers put some more effort into the gameplay than in the story I personally think, but that's no problem at all! Maybe I shouldn't even compare Bastion and Transistor because Supergiant Games might wanted do something different... Anyways.
You start right away in middle of the game and the story. The setting is a Sci-Fi world, more precisely I guess it's something like an online world.
In Transistor you experience the story chronologically. In the beginning there are some minor gaps, which get filled soon. The story catches you and you want to know what happens next. Nevertheless, to be honest I have to say that I liked the story of Bastion better but the story of this game is not bad at all!
The gameplay is quite cool. Transistor's gameplay contain some nice features that underline the story and the atmosphere. That includes electing something on a terminal or some breaks for the protagonist. These breaks are implemented as beautiful pictures.
What I liked the most is the combat system.
Time to time you get more attacks and can combine these like you want. This mixing provides a great variety to fighting in Transistor. Also, there is a "plan mode" in which you can plan moves and then perform then fast. That looks very cool and is fun too.
Lastly, you can, as well as in Bastion, increase the difficulty on your own.
Supergiant Games games always catch you with their atmosphere so I didn't write anything about the atmosphere here.
Okay, I can not write this review without mentioning Darren Korb and his great job on composing marvellous songs for this game. The music matches perfectly to the game and is an essential part of it, just like in Bastion.
I come to the conclusion that Transistor is another awesome game by Supergiant Games. It's a perfect game that doesn't need improvements at all! If you liked Bastion or you want to play something different but brilliant buy Transistor now!

The game itself is good and I hadn't any trouble. But I do not recommend to buy it on steam for various reasons:
1) The steam download is not up to date! After downloading ~63gb through steam the eso launcher redownloaded ~45gb and replaced the steam files. So as long as you don't have a fast connection don't buy through steam. Also if you want to test the game and refund it if you don't like it keep in mind that the launcher counts as play time. So redownloading the game reduces the time you have to play the game before you can't refund it anymore.
2) When I managed to play the game it worked fine, but until now I had a problem EVERY. SINGLE. TIME. I pressed on play in steam. Some of them are directly related to steam (e.g. steam not even starting the launcher) others are issues of the launcher itself (e.g. error to download the patch manifest) which are harder to solve because of steam. For example you can bypass the launcher and therefore every issue you have with it by starting the eso.exe directly. Not so if you bought the game on steam because now you have to start it through the steam launcher, which, again, has a lot of issues.
3) While searching for solutions for the issues I had I found a lot of complaints about other problems. The launcher itself has obviously a lot of problems, but there also seem to be a lot of issues related to steam besides those I experienced myself.
So do yourself a favour, don't make the same mistake as I did and don't buy the game on steam. This has been the worst experience I've ever had with steam!

TheHunter. I think you can figure this out. You hunt. Simple as that. Alright, I'll get rolling. TheHunter is a F2P hunting game. A decent hunting game but the micro-transactions are horrid.
There, review over.
Fine, I'll keep going.  I'll start with graphics. The game looks nice. Not the greatest I've seen, but definitely not the worst. For a F2P, not bad at all. It isn't hard on your hardware either, which is nice for the lower-end systems. On a 5 year old laptop with no dedicated graphics, medium settings is where it's at. But on my new GTX 960 system, maxed out. Nice to see. The mechanics are nice in this game too. The HunterMate is nice for hunting (no wonder). It works fine. The shooting mecanics make sense. Right-Click scope. Left-click shoot. Mouse-aim. Simple as that. Everything sounds great until... micro-transactions.
Now, I usually don't bash a F2P on micro-transactions because it's free, and the developers need money somehow. But, you only get 1 gun, and can only shoot Mule Deer. Unless you pay money. Yes, real life money. Even then, after a certain time period, you'll have to pay again (memberships). More bad things though. Time in-game. Or should I say, real-life time. 30 minutes in real life is 30 minutes ingame. Not a problem but it typically takes a while to find an animal. Realistic yes, but not really a good impliment to a video game. And, lastly, private servers. I don't get why you have to have a membership for a private server. I just want to play with my friends, and only them. Makes no sense.
Time for conclusion I guess. I say I recommend it but I wish there was a neutral button, or percentage, or out of 10 stuff. I think you will have to be an avid hunter to actually really enjoy this game. Yes, it's nice, but I don't want to empty my wallet over it. Final statement-It's good for what it is, which is a F2P, but it feels restricted in a way. I would put it in your descretion when it comes to recommending.

Oh boy, this game. How do I begin with this game? Well as everyone already knows Rome II had a TON of problems. Most of which were already fixed and the game in this state is playable. It's not only playable, it is quite fun, otherwise I wouldn't spend hundreds of hours micro managing my gigantic empire/republic trying to keep all my different people happy and not destroying my enemies primary "city" box that dictates how a city looks culturally. I was determined to not be like the romans see. The game can be fantastic in ways that can surprise you in a world full of different factions, people, landscapes, and battle strategies and yet I feel like Rome 2 just seemed the same. Yes there were different factions but they felt like they were just a copy and paste of the four subcategories in the game, hellenic, barbaric, eastern, and roman. The armenians were just a slightly different parthians, the marcomanni were just a slightly different suebi. Ok the barbarians of the celts and germans felt a bit different and there were mixes like that sprinkled through the game but it was just far too few to really note. The whole diplomatic intrigue between nations is... non existant, the intrigue between your family and the other houses is forgettable. Trust me I tried to keep track of who, I love to roleplay like that, to create my little worlds in my head as I play and I couldn't tell you a single thing what anyone did or how they were important to me except the first general that I got whose name was Zenon by the way. Ah yes Zenon the magnificent, stout defender with a kind heart. But that's the thing everyone felt the same, I didn't feel attached to anyone, apart from Zenon, and I guess I wasn't really supposed to, this isn't skyrim after all, but I just feel like the game missed a great opportunity here. The battle maps were... stale, like my yesterday's bread. It's all the same really, one gigantic pine forest, A desert with some variation, Plains with some trees in between, Water. It felt like I was playing on the same map regardless where I was, be it Dacia or Italy, Gaul or Iberia. The maps were also kind of small, yes small, it was fine for 1v1 but when it gets to 4v4 it kind of shows. You can't manouver your men (or women) as much because of a magical red line and it kind of felt dissapointing. But what of the combat? What of the actual gameplay? Well as I stated, it feels the same, the AI is MUCH better but it is no Alexander the Great, it rushes your army and it feels great in the first hundred battles but then you kind of see a trend, the strategy for the AI doesn't really change, not really, it doesn't matter if the AI has infantry or cavalry it just kind of rushes you, all you have to do is employ the same strategy to beat it, and it kind of loses that magic or illusion that you are fighting a high level general or just some dude with a broom who stumbled upon the sign up sheet for the "We need a general" fair they were holding that week. Sure the combat is epic, seeing your units individually slug with each other and you root for your favorites to survive the fight as you see the masterfully done animation and motion capture. But after a while if you start to pay attention you start to see problems (just like if you stare at yourself in the mirror for too long) the individual soldiers in the unit aren't individual soldiers they are a unit. A solid entity. A big block trying to pass as a group of men. When they move they move as one and sure this is army discipline but that's not what I am talking about. What I am talking about is the fact that they do stuff as a collective. When two units clash and fight, they attack an enemy kill them and just kind of stand there rotating around. Then they find an enemy smack them once and continue staring at them. Then they smack them again turn 180 degrees smack another guy and then get killed from a blade that didn't even touch them traveling at the speed of my grandmother's cooking. (Her cooking is delicious by the way and well worth the wait). That is kind of...sad. It doesn't feel like a battle between individuals, it feels like a pushing contest between two blocks, two bacterias trying to consume each other. The individual units can't go too far away from the main block either, otherwise everyone just goes into metabolic shock and just doesn't know what to do. Which then glitches out the cavalry charges that the attacking person is doing. Because they try to get to the center of the block instead of hitting the eighty dudes in front of them, their charge animation doesn't start until they are half way through those eighty guys and then they stop because they realize that there are enemies there. That doesn't allow for a proper charge or skirmishes either, the archers don't really know what to aim for so they try to find that spot where they can fire at the unit instead of the 3/4 of the  unit RIGHT IN FRONT OF THEM. Combine this with AI AND sieges, oh boy sometimes you are in for a treat. So then to overlook that you just have to fight against a human opponent right? You are correct go find yourself a cookie. The multiplayer is really where the gold of the game lies, the time you spend with your friends conquering the world, only to stab or get stabbed in the back by them (I was the one always getting stabbed in the back)(but thats what friends are for). Or just the plain quick matches or 4v4 or 2v2 or 3v3, or naval battles, siege battles, land AND naval battles, all of that gets your blood pumping, you get excited, you have TONS of fun. But that's pretty much it to multiplayer, there is really nothing else, its barebones. I WISH for free for all I WISH for avatar conquest, are you kidding me? Avatar conquest would have been perfect for this game. And the full experience of the game is kind of not there, not without the truckload of DLC, there is a huge difference in my game and the game of my friend who has all of these fancy units because he bought all of that dlc. And I understand that for factions and units that are entirely new. But for the factions that are already in the game? LIke suebi? What if suebi is some little boy's favorite faction? (Little boys can't play this game but just imagine) He can't really get the full suebi experience unless he pays for the other dlc, he can't pay for that, he has to pay for college! Anyway, sidetracked, what of the price? why is this game still 60 dollars? It has been out for years and two games later it is still the same price as it's release date. And I feel like that's because of the dlc and Emperor Edition, which prolongs the life of the game superficially, don't get me started on the Ultimate Edition with the Spartans.  But what kept me playing? Well the game. Despite everything the game is fantastic and the community that supports it just makes it that much better, the mods that are out for this game are phenominal with what the mod creators work with and it is just really astounding. Unfortunately I cannot recommend this game, not really, I really want to, but I just can't. There are games out there now by this company with the same price that are much better than what you are getting here. Look at the upcoming Warhammer Total War releases they are phenominal and add so much more and have so much more depth and fix most of the issues that I talk of here with a great modding community with grandiose maps straight out of a storybook. If you are not into the fantasy genre and want to play as the romans look at Attila, they have such a great modding community because of the tools that they have received and there are mods of that game that basically make this game, and improve upon it with features you can't get here. I really wish I could recommend this game but I can't because compared to the other titles of the same series it just dissapoints, and that's the main issue really it just dissapoints because it could have been so much more. This game is just
. I'd like to give kudos to the creator, Lucas Pope, who did about everything (code, artwork, sound, story) this is a darn good accomplishment, and even more so with its success.
However, like many games it's
. Its not an action/shooter/platformer twitch reaction type game (though a few segments are reflex based). Its closer to a "point and click" or a 'spot the differences' type game, only many times there aren't any differences and/or there's multiple actions you could perform with various results some long term.
What would normally be considered work is somehow fun in this game. I don't quite understand it which piques my interest even more. Verifying passports and documents and stamping them sounds like a terrible game, but somehow its not. Trust me after the first few days/levels you'll be questioning why this is fun.
The story mode is great and builds up the difficulty as you progress. It is also rather humorous and as previously mentioned some decisions have reprecussions later in the game. The save system is great; saving for each day and allows you to go back to any previous day and start a new timeline and make different choices save each day of the new timeline.
Once you 'beat' the game, basically finish each levels/days
you unlock the endless modes. Where you can compete globally or locally/against yourself or just play for fun in 4 different modes with 4 different difficulty levels (in effect 16 combinations).
There are 20 different 'endings' I believe, several are being jailed/executed for different reasons, some have a 'happy' ending at least as happy as an ending can be in a dystopia, some are based on decisions you make halfway through the game. On top of the endings to complete there are various tokens and achievements to get if you are into that sort of thing. These last few things and endless modes give replayability but not an enourmous amount; 5-15 hours I'd say maybe more if you're a completionist and/or very competitive.
If you are into puzzle/mind thinking games pick this up. If you just want to kill terrorists/robots/aliens/monsters/etc then as I said at the beginning, this isn't for you.

It's difficult to describe this game and get across the reason why it is such a great experience. To put it literally, you are an inspector at a checkpoint which has recently been opened, one which makes entry into the country possible. People wishing to enter the country come to you with papers - at first just a passport, but then they need more and more to enter - and it is your job to check through them for mistakes or 'discrepancies'. If a discrepancy is found, you use your 'decline' stamp on their passport. If not, you can use your 'accept' stamp to let them into the country.
This is basically the game. However, the developer has done an amazing job of showing the people coming into the country - people with lives, worries, and reasons needing to get in. You could deny the woman who really wants to see her son, or the wife of a man who you just let through - but when they turn away, and walk off you will feel it. You also have to keep your family alive, however. At the end of each day you can choose whether to buy food and heating, both, or neither - if you're out of money for, say, allowing people to enter because you felt sorry for them.
This is a truly fascinating game, one which I would definately recommend to anyone - you probably won't quite understand what it is until you've tried it.

Dark Souls 2 is a visually and aesthetically impressive game that definitely builds off of the first dark souls in a good way as far as visual design and atmosphere. However this game lacks the core elements that made the first game so immersive and engaging.
The combat in Dark Souls 2 misses the core ideals that the first Dark Souls created. The developers seem to have just made attributes of the bosses and the enemies more annoying in order to increase the "difficulty" of the game itself. The mobs tracking system is one example of this. Mobs will track the player until the very last moment that they attack even if they are wielding a large heavy great sword or mace. This defies one of the principles that the first dark souls created which was to create a weighty and realistic combat structure that focused on precise movements and smart defensive gameplay. The combat in dark souls 2 doesn’t really feel very weighty when fighting mobs because they do a 360 degree turn to hit you when they are using a heavy cumbersome item. I find this kind of lazy design in my own opinion.
The story feels disjointed and pointless which i suppose goes with the apparent theme of melancholy and anomie that the game tries to push. I can understand the ambiguity of the direction in the game but it does nothing for me as the player. In the first game the story was equally ambiguous but at least there was some end goal, which was to fulfill the prophecy told to you at the beginning of the game. This simple request and then the subsequent requests to find the two bells of awakening and eventually succeed Gwinn were purpose enough to continue to explore the game world. In dark souls 2 you have to search for four powerful souls for some reason to get to the kings palace for some reason and etc. there is no motivation no dying man’s request to fulfill a prophecy. I felt as though my character was a pointless nobody just wreaking havoc for no apparent reason except to advance through the game.
Overall this game lacks what I loved about the first dark souls and while this is its own game I still can’t feel a sense of annoyance and frustration for what this game could have been when I play it.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs in many ways alters the formula of the original, The Dark Descent. The game infuriates me in so much as it both surpasses and is surpassed by its predecessor.
Much of the alterations made in A Machine For Pigs come in its structure. Lamp Oil, Tinderboxes, and the Sanity Meter are gone. This makes the darkness the player's best friend, which is surprisingly not a completely bad thing. While the original Amnesia consisted of fairly open and explorable levels, A Machine For Pigs forces the player to follow a single path in most circumstances. The Dark Descent also had a high degree of interactability, where most objects could be picked up, examined, and used in some fashion. A Machine For Pigs, on the other hand, limits interaction to objects associated with progression. Combined, these latter two game changes reduce much of the mystery and trial and error of the original, which was one of its strongest points. The original Amnesia's poor puzzle integration also persists in this game.
However, A Machine For Pigs does improve on some aspects which, at the time of playing The Dark Descent, appeared unassailable. The gritty industrial machinery is in many ways much more atmospheric than the somewhat sterile Brennenburg Castle. The clanging of pumps and shots of steam create an environment in which the original Amnesia's use of sound becomes nigh obsolete. To remedy this, A Machine For Pigs plays with light to instill fear in the player. When a monster is in the vicinity of the player, surrounding lights and the player's lantern begin to flicker. Eventually, one responds to even a single flicker of the lantern by turning it off and crouching in the nearest dark area, even if a monster is not patrolling.
A Machine For Pig's story is also, surprisingly, an improvement on that of the original. Many of the somewhat camp over-exaggerated elements of The Dark Descent are replaced by deep characterisation and emotion. Even the monsters are humanised to some extent in one sequence. A Machine For Pigs' story delves into themes such as industrialisation and class with notable skill. There are a few references to the world of The Dark Descent, but A Machine For Pigs is, by and large, a break with the original.
Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs is an excellent, if somewhat short, continuation of the world of The Dark Descent. While an improvement in some areas, it does however regress in others.

Transistor...
The next perfect game by Supergiant Games.
This time the developers put some more effort into the gameplay than in the story I personally think, but that's no problem at all! Maybe I shouldn't even compare Bastion and Transistor because Supergiant Games might wanted do something different... Anyways.
You start right away in middle of the game and the story. The setting is a Sci-Fi world, more precisely I guess it's something like an online world.
In Transistor you experience the story chronologically. In the beginning there are some minor gaps, which get filled soon. The story catches you and you want to know what happens next. Nevertheless, to be honest I have to say that I liked the story of Bastion better but the story of this game is not bad at all!
The gameplay is quite cool. Transistor's gameplay contain some nice features that underline the story and the atmosphere. That includes electing something on a terminal or some breaks for the protagonist. These breaks are implemented as beautiful pictures.
What I liked the most is the combat system.
Time to time you get more attacks and can combine these like you want. This mixing provides a great variety to fighting in Transistor. Also, there is a "plan mode" in which you can plan moves and then perform then fast. That looks very cool and is fun too.
Lastly, you can, as well as in Bastion, increase the difficulty on your own.
Supergiant Games games always catch you with their atmosphere so I didn't write anything about the atmosphere here.
Okay, I can not write this review without mentioning Darren Korb and his great job on composing marvellous songs for this game. The music matches perfectly to the game and is an essential part of it, just like in Bastion.
I come to the conclusion that Transistor is another awesome game by Supergiant Games. It's a perfect game that doesn't need improvements at all! If you liked Bastion or you want to play something different but brilliant buy Transistor now!

Main character Red, is strong, resilient, and graceful, even though silent trough out the game (like in Bastion), trough her (players) actions becomes adamant in her mission.

You walk to work and begin your work day as an immigration officer. You sit down and buzz though the first person trying to pass though your boarder, they present you with their papers and now it is up to you to see though their deception.
When I first heard about Papers Please I thought it would be the world’s most boring game, IT IS NOT! These are some of the things I love about.
1) Story: There are different paths which you can take each with their own ending meaning your actions have consequences. This also gives you the incentive to try out all the different possibilities.
2) Art Style: The art style in this game I personally love, it's dark and cold which gives the true feeling of working within an oppressed country.
3) Emotions: I guess this can be connected with the story but there are a lot of people which you can feel for, you feel oddly connected with them and their plight.
4) Difficulty: This game can be confusing, you need to stay on your game and look for the miniscule details and stay on top of your countries ever changing foreign policies.
5) Replay-ability: I warn you; once you start you may never stop. Although you may play little by little the hours add up and even after playing this game for a long time I can still come back to it and play again.
6) Soundtrack: There is nothing better to get you in the mood for playing in an oppressed dreary country than the drumming at the start of the game with classic eastern feel.
I hope those of you who have bought the game enjoy it as much as I did, it was developed by Lucas Pope I urge you to check out his other games.

"Papers, Please" is a 2D adventure game rendered with old school graphics that allows you to follow the life of a border inspector in the fictional country of Arstotzka. Your objective is to control the papers and documents of every person trying to cross the border and interact with the other characters you will meet through several days of work. While at the beginning the controls you are tasked with are pretty simple, later on you will recive new orders that will require you to examine the papers you are given more and more carefully, in an effort to let pass, detain or reject the right people.
"Papers, Please" features an evolving story: you will recive tasks or orders from several characters and your actions will reflect the final outcome of your adventure. The game itself has a total of twenty different endings and you can choose to replay whatever day of work you wish, should you want a different outcome.
Another important element of the game is your outcome: at the end of each day you will be noticed with all the expanses you can cover, especially the ones involving the well-being of your family or the opportunity to purchase automatic control systems. Neglecting some of them could bring an abrupt end to your career, as well as accepting money and gifts from the wrong people. Making several mistakes during your dury is also sure to cause you some trouble.
All in all, "Papers, Please" is an excellent adventure game, with a simple but engaging gameplay and a branched story that offers a lot of replay value

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is an enthralling work of fiction about a wealthy man coming to grips with his own evil right before the turn of the 20th century.
This work's position as a video game makes consideration of gameplay an unfortunate factor in its appraisal. You really don't do much in the way of normal gaming during your experience with Pigs. However, you will find yourself engaged by what you might call narrative/ambient puzzle solving. You aren't asked to find a clever way around a locked door, or trick enemies into sucide, or rearrange parts of a painting to reveal a secret message. Instead, the intellectual satisfaction you'll find in Pigs comes from examining the game's environment and reading cryptic journal entries to understand this narrative's disturbing truths. That is, running through the game without paying enough attention and without thinking critically enough will result in failure--you will have missed the game's point. It's in careful methodic analysis of the narrative elements that you win and experience the pleasure of the game's reward--deep fear and revulsion about your character's tale and even what the story says about the nature of our own lives.
I believe this game's only material shortcoming is technical--it is deceptively resource intensive, despite its lack of visual sophistication. It's not particularly pretty (Outlast, however, is particularly pretty), but slowdown is frequent nonetheless. Routinely, the frame rate would dip on my pc, from around 60fps to something closer to 30fps. I'm not sure if this is the result of visual tricks that I simply didn't appreciate enough to notice, or if it's because of less-than-optimized code. Vision blur never triggered the slowdown. Slowdown occurred most often in the large, more decorated rooms of Mandus's mansion, and in some of the larger chambers below.
Play this game, though. Its terror doesn't come from visceral, instinctual tension as it does through Dead Space and Outlast. Instead, it disturbs the conscious mind only after reflection and understanding of the story's premise. You won't spend your time with Pigs with white knuckles and a tight stomach. Instead, you will spend days afterward dwelling on dread and the loathing you were meant to feel through Mandus as he rediscovered his own past.

text: If you loved the first game and are looking for that same experience, look elsewhere, because you won't find it here.

BASICALLY:  Poorly done monster encounters, but excellent atmosphere; would recommend ONLY if you have the patience to become immersed in games.  Grab it when it's on sale.
If you love games with a dark, suspenseful atmosphere, look no further, 'cause this game definitely delivers in that respect.  Better than in The Dark Descent, IMO.  Of course, in order to find this game to be "scary" you will have to allow yourself to suspend disbelief and put yourself in the main character's shoes.  The horror almost completely relies on that.  If you just run though and don't look at or read anything, you're not going to get many scares.  There aren't that many monster encounters, and the ones that are included are very short (and frankly not well thought out).  Plus, the game is pretty short as it is (~4.5hrs for me).  If you take your time with this game, I'm sure you will have many thrilling moments.  Hopefully we'll see some extra content like in the previous game.

Amnesia: AMfP manages to surpass its precedessor with an even more unique atmosphere, a dark story, and well-designed gameplay that keeps you on edge all the way through.  Very rarely do horror games make you more nervous or terrified to continue as this game does.  There are little jump-scares here; this kind of terror creeps slowly towards you, and you only aware of it enough for you to doubt yourself.  Thus, the scares aren't so much from some monster in your face, as it is the noises in the walls, the scraping of feet on the floor, or the extremely menacing sounds of the machine below.
The game does do away with some of the more troublesome aspects of the first game, which is sometimes a blessing, sometimes not.  Your (electric) lamp is no longer going to just run out of fuel / power at the worst time just because you used it too much, thankfully.  Also gone is the sanity system, which was not a huge nuisance in the previous game to me, but did lend some to the atmosphere in certain places.  However, AMfP doesn't even need such a system; often you feel that you are going crazy, but its subtle, like hearing voices in the walls or the like.  The game does lack the nice inventory system of its precedessor, however, meaning you will physically carry some objects around for a short (and I mean short) while.
Fortunately, though, the game is extremely well paced, both in story and terror.  Descending in the darkness (haha) alone is intersperced between the excellent writing in some of the dialogue and in most of the notes.  Reading such notes lends credence to both the game's themes and the world's lore.  Then you go back to exploring the dark and intimidating buildings, tunnels, pipes, holding pens, and even some rather amazing steampunk-ish houses of horror.
If you liked the original's story, Amnesia: AMfP will impress you even more.  If you liked the mechanics of the first, don't expect all of them in this one (which is both good and bad).  More importantly though, if you love atmospheric experiences, it truly does not get much better than this.

is a survival horror video game developed by Creative Assembly and based on the Alien science fiction horror film series. It was published by Sega and originally released for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, Xbox 360 and Xbox One on 7 October 2014.
Alien: Isolation emphasizes evasion over direct combat by providing the player with limited ammunition, and occasionally the use of a revolver, a shotgun, a bolt gun, and a flamethrower. P.S.
In addition, there is a crafting system in the game where you can use items like; EMP mines and Noisemakers, Molotov Cocktails and Pipe Bombs, and of course... MedKits among others to help the player deal with enemies and the alien. I found the game mechanics to be pretty good! No real complaints to mention.
In 2137, 15 years after the disappearance of the Nostromo spacecraft, Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley, is approached by the android Christopher Samuels of the Weyland-Yutani corporation. Samuels informs her that the flight recorder of the Nostromo was recently located by a ship named the Anesidora and is being held aboard Sevastopol, a remote space station owned by the Seegson Corporation, in orbit around the gas giant KG348. He offers her a place on the Weyland-Yutani team sent to retrieve it so that she can have closure regarding the fate of her missing mother... Now starts the "Roller Coaster Ride" to find out what happened to Mama!

For some sense of time scale, my main character is Lv105 in fediman and I have another character in the 30s. And I only use cards at the optimal levels, otherwise they'd be a higher level since I have a lot saved. I played the game at release and have lost interest...
A few issues I faced (and maybe you will too):
-Botters, especially in town spamming chat (Thank god for the add-on to quick report and mute)
-Mob spawn timers. I (far too often) find myself switching channels due to lack of mobs to complete my quests.
-Optimisation, The frame drops is too much in towns that are only moderately busy and it's just as horrendous in common grinding spots.
-The grind. Low frames rates? Ok, I can survive that. But the grinding is futile when you don't 'feel' the progression. I've played in iCBT, I've read guides on using cards, exp spots, doing party dungeons, etc. Basically, I KNOW what I have to do to progress. But say if I invest another 100 hours, what will I be doing? Grinding exp still? OFC! IF the end game content is somehow different but it takes 700+ hours to get there, then this game totally f'ed it's approach to keeping players interested.
-The social aspect. It's lacking. A LOT of maps are incredibly empty. I might come across a player or two but it's still silence. Many times I wonder if I'm playing a solo-player game in disguise. I for one, don't enjoy soloing 90% of my time playing.
-Your character identity and progression. A big issue. Many classes are redundant, a wrong choice will screw you permanently and there's no reversing it. And even if you pick a useful class, there is an optimal build you
should follow otherwise your character becomes useless. In other words, character variation is limited, unless you want to get called trash by party members.
You could make yourself another character, but only if you can survive the grind. -_-
-The combat. This is more personal, but the combat is just dull after the first 15 hours. And it makes grinding even more of a chore.
-There's more stuff to complain about but I've had enough.

I tell myself "I have to level up to get stronger and access more content!" BUT what content?! I'm still grinding my♥♥♥♥♥off! There's PvP but like I said about classes, there are specific optimal builds for that too. IMO, 100 hours is more than enough for a game to showcase itself. TBH, it just feels like a chore to carry on playing.

I give transistor ⅗ stars.
I bought Transistor solely because it is from the same developer that made one of my favorite games, Bastion.  While Transistor is still a good game I was somewhat disappointed.
The Good:
-As of mid November 2014 I didn’t encounter ANY bugs or instability issues, a common complaint at launch
-The graphics are good, but should still work on lower-end systems
-The turn based gameplay is well done for the most part
-Reasonable price for a game at 6 hours of play
-Has some replayability to it
-While not the best story, and a little confusing at times, I think the ending ties everything up nicely and makes you think a bit. Even though the story was lacking it kept me coming back for more to finish the game.

The Bad:
-The graphics, in my opinion, are not nearly as clever as Bastion.  Bastion used beautiful bright cell-shaded/watercolor style graphics to illustrate a strange and troubled world.  Transistor relies heavily on a beautiful but dark watercolor style that looks more sophisticated but is less enjoyable to look at for 6 hours of game.
-The characters aren’t as likeable, developed, or funny, as Bastion’s.  The narrator of Bastion was one of the best features.  In this game the transistor character makes soft-pointless observations throughout the game that don’t add very much creative value
-The turn style gameplay is again, in my opinion, a step back.  In Bastion I spent hours mastering the various weapons in the proving ground.  This game has a similar proving ground structure but the turn style combat feel easy and disconnected.  I imagine many gamers will  disagree with me on this point.
-Music is a large element to the game and passing various tests unlocks more music.  However, I found the music itself to be pretty boring and uninteresting.  I have fairly broad taste in music so I imagine many will agree with me.  I’m glad I didn’t pay extra to get the boring soundtrack because I cannot imagine wanting to listen to it at any time.
Based on these reasons, I give the game ⅗ stars.  Yes, it is fun, and it is well done; but it could be so much better.  I will likely follow this developer and buy future titles with the hope that they are a bit more fun than this one.

I can understand some players issues with this game but they are flawed views. This game has a very useful Wiki which has a page dedicated to those who are playing for free Guest), it outlines everything you can do which is a surprisingly large amount. There are restrictions to playing the game for free, most of these are based on what you have a licence to hunt. But you can still play many enjoyable hours hunting free licence animals such as mule deer and two types of rabbit. Although it is a little more difficult when you are trying to track animals and don't come across tracks of animals you are allowed to hunt, I feel that adds a level of difficulty that increases the games challenge.
You do get in game money which you earn through confirmed kills which you can earn to buy ammo. To buy all other equipment including guns you can buy in game money or earn it through filling in online questionnaires for third party companies. That may seem annoying but it is at least an option to further your progress in the game with no cost (keep in mind that mobile apps also do this with advertisements to allow you to play their games for longer).
Based on the game itself it has good graphics, and solid gameplay. Tracking and hunting takes time but is very rewarding when you finally get a kill. The game has good mechanics and allows an open variety of methods to get a kill. I would advise checking out the Wiki to see how in depth the game really is.
It’s definitely worth trying out for free, just be aware of what you can hunt and where to look for animals and its great fun if you’re into long gameplay.

This is a great game for several reasons:
- The game is not that easy, as being able to hunt an animal every 30 seconds like in some hunting games would become boring really fast...
- It's free to play, although much of it's content must be purchased separately (more on that later).
- The graphics are great for it's age and the devs are constantly improving them to keep up with the technology advances. In fact the graphics were among THE BEST and looked realistic when the game came out.
This game has only one flaw: Micro Transactions.
While the game is free most of the contents must be purchased by the players with paid currency (em$).
Now, why does this not bother me as much as most of the players who reviewed this game negatively? Their only reason for not recommending this game is the "Pay 2 Win" model but in fact I don't think the game is P2W at all. When the game came out, way before it was available on steam, the free players could only hunt with one rifle, one species and limited ammo, a demo in it's purest design. A few years later the game allowed the player to hunt with that very same rifle and species but this time with unlimited ammo for that specific rifle. All the other rifles do not have that perk, so you must purchase ammo for them.
Now, Q3 2016, you can hunt with the same rifle from the old days, a shotgun, a pistol, a different type of deer, one bird species and one rabbit species, all for free and with an extra 2 species that are free in a rotation, so every now and then you get to hunt 2 different species.
Not to mention that you can purchase consumables with the ingame currency you earn by completing missions, and the purchased currency you can also earn for free if you participate in the tournaments and challenges, if you manage to win or get a decent score that is...
TL:DR:
Yes, the game is still a money hog, BUT
The game has improved a lot since it's birth and is helping more and more the free players.
You CAN still have fun in this game even with it's limitations, so give it a try! It's free!

You walk to work and begin your work day as an immigration officer. You sit down and buzz though the first person trying to pass though your boarder, they present you with their papers and now it is up to you to see though their deception.
When I first heard about Papers Please I thought it would be the world’s most boring game, IT IS NOT! These are some of the things I love about.
1) Story: There are different paths which you can take each with their own ending meaning your actions have consequences. This also gives you the incentive to try out all the different possibilities.
2) Art Style: The art style in this game I personally love, it's dark and cold which gives the true feeling of working within an oppressed country.
3) Emotions: I guess this can be connected with the story but there are a lot of people which you can feel for, you feel oddly connected with them and their plight.
4) Difficulty: This game can be confusing, you need to stay on your game and look for the miniscule details and stay on top of your countries ever changing foreign policies.
5) Replay-ability: I warn you; once you start you may never stop. Although you may play little by little the hours add up and even after playing this game for a long time I can still come back to it and play again.
6) Soundtrack: There is nothing better to get you in the mood for playing in an oppressed dreary country than the drumming at the start of the game with classic eastern feel.
I hope those of you who have bought the game enjoy it as much as I did, it was developed by Lucas Pope I urge you to check out his other games.

"Papers, Please" is a 2D adventure game rendered with old school graphics that allows you to follow the life of a border inspector in the fictional country of Arstotzka. Your objective is to control the papers and documents of every person trying to cross the border and interact with the other characters you will meet through several days of work. While at the beginning the controls you are tasked with are pretty simple, later on you will recive new orders that will require you to examine the papers you are given more and more carefully, in an effort to let pass, detain or reject the right people.
"Papers, Please" features an evolving story: you will recive tasks or orders from several characters and your actions will reflect the final outcome of your adventure. The game itself has a total of twenty different endings and you can choose to replay whatever day of work you wish, should you want a different outcome.
Another important element of the game is your outcome: at the end of each day you will be noticed with all the expanses you can cover, especially the ones involving the well-being of your family or the opportunity to purchase automatic control systems. Neglecting some of them could bring an abrupt end to your career, as well as accepting money and gifts from the wrong people. Making several mistakes during your dury is also sure to cause you some trouble.
All in all, "Papers, Please" is an excellent adventure game, with a simple but engaging gameplay and a branched story that offers a lot of replay value

- This game DOES have some really scary moments. However, whereas Dark Descent was pretty much "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I'm gonna♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants" 100% of the way through, A Machine for Pigs has MUCH less of those types of experiences, and those moments are sprinkled out over several hours of play instead of being constant. The game also starts out incredibly slow and you will probably want to quit within the first hour unless you're patient like me. It DOES ramp up eventually, but boy does it take its time to do so. The game as a whole also feels dumbed down compared to Dark Descent, as you don't have an inventory (and as a result, puzzles in general are also much easier to solve). Your light never runs of oil either (infinite flashlight!), and the sanity system is nowhere to be seen.
- The game has some absolutely amazing environment design, especially the lighting and the sound effects. For example, the wails and screams you can often hear off in the distance really add to the atmosphere around you. If you play this with surround sound prepare to be truly immersed in its world.
Overall, if you can get this for $5 or less, this game is definitely worth it IMO. I wouldn't pay more than that though unless you're okay with a much less-scarier, more-dumbed down experience than its predecessor, Amnesia: Dark Descent. A Machine for Pigs unfortunately totally deserves the label "Walking Simulator."

I'm going to lay it right out. I think A Machine for Pigs is a master stroke in video game horror and storytelling. I consider it a far more captivating experience than The Dark Descent. Where TDD relied more on chase scenes and jump scares, AMFP focused far more on crafting a dark, Lovecraftian world to enthrall the player with.
A Machine for Pigs drops the tiresome sanity meter, which at no point in its predecessor enhanced the experience. This artificial system only served to remove me from the experience. It accomplished nothing but making you feel like your character was extremely drunk. AFMP, on the other hand, approaches the question of sanity organically within the game. You will encounter situations that will make you question your character's sanity and perhaps even your own. Along with losing the sanity meter, it curbed the need for tinderboxes and oil because your lantern is permanently powered now. At no point did I consider this a weakness of the game. Collecting oil and tinderboxes was practically useless in the original even with the lighting settings correctly calibrated.
The soundscape in this game is truly stellar. The music is haunting and beautiful and greatly adds to the atmosphere of the game. Outside of the music, it has superb sound effects. From the groans and shrieks of the machinery to the otherwordly sounds that come from the pigs, it is all done superbly.
In another contrast to its predecessor, this game has far less focus on puzzles. And this is another thing that seems to have been very controversial for people. My reply is that this is a horror game. It is not a puzzle game. Puzzle games do not need to have horror sections. Why do horror games need to have puzzle sections? Beyond that, let's not kid ourselves about the puzzles in TDD. They were infantile and even the most challenged player could solve them easily without consulting a walkthrough. So let's not act like this series is famed for its amazing puzzles.
It is not without its problems, though, It is a very short game. I completed it in 3.4 hours on my first playthrough and that was with seeking out everything and reading everything. While I consider it worth it even at full price, it is still quite a flaw. Another problem is that you cannot back track, so you have to make certain you fully explore an area before trying to move on or you will miss stuff.
Still, this game is amazing. I completely adore it and hope that people will look past all the unwarranted negative reviews it has received. It is superior to The Dark Descent by far.

I have a confession to make.
I never finished the first Amnesia. It's more accurate to say that, according to Steam, I have played 28 minutes of Amnesia: The Dark Descent. That includes times spent setting up options in the menu. So in reality, I've gotten far enough that the first strong gust of wind howled through a corridor before I quit. I'd like to say that's because I didn't like the controls. Admittedly, I do prefer gamepads to mouse and keyboard, but the atmospheric elements of Amnesia: TDD kinda scared me.
Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs recently went on sale for 66% off on Steam, so I decided to roll the dice. It does, for the record, support gamepads. As far as the technical aspects of the game, Frictional teamed with The Chinese Room, creators of Dear Esther (developer of 2008's popular First Person Walking Simulator Dear Esther). It's got a fairly hefty options menu, and the game looks gorgeous (when you can see it).  It ran well on my GTX770, and once I'd nailed down a particularly nasty case of screen tearing (disable in-game Vsync, both regular and adaptive, and enable it in the Nvidia Control Panel or your ATI equivalent), the game ran at a smooth 60 FPS with no screen tearing. The gamepad controls were responsive and simple to learn, and even the object manipulation mechanic of the first game translated well from mouse to thumbsticks.
This is not an overly complex game, though. It's pedigree shows through, as many sources have said that this game is far simpler in its gameplay mechanics than the previous Amnesia title. Your lantern has unlimited oil. There are no items to pick up, no laudanum to keep you sane. Your character is obviously far more mentally stable, seeing as the monsters in this game doesn't affect your ability to cope with the world around you.
Where A Machine For Pigs really shines is its storytelling. You wake up in a caged bedroom of a properly posh Victorian mansion, and bits of story are slowly fed to you throughout your descent (a dark one!) into the heart of a Steampunk monstrosity of brass tubes, gears, pistons, and oh-so-many nauseating swine carcasses. Like many dark horror stories, there are aspects that fall apart if you look at it too closely, but the game wraps up before most people have time to question those aspects. The game runs about 4 to 4 and a half hours, but that's a tight 4 and a half hours, with very few wasted moments, and a hectic (if overly obviously scripted) sequence later in the game where the monsters really come into play. Overall, it's dripping (quite literally at times) with atmosphere
Is it worth the usual $20 price tag? That's all going to depend on whether you're a big horror buff. Personally, I'm not. That I only paid < $7 for the game, goes a long way to my personal valuation. I feel I got my money's worth, even though it didn't quite hit that “dollar-per-hour” magic mark. If you're a fan of horror, I recommend this at a higher price than I paid, especially if you like your horror to come from the storytelling as much as the gameplay.
