Good:
Bad:
This game is the spiritual successor to Ragnarok Online in the sense that the game revisits all of your negative experiences from RO. If you like chat spam, botters, rubberbanding, and crashing, this game is for you. Like IMC's previous games, Tree of Savior is a game with potential that will never be realized. It happened to Grenado Espada, and Tree of Savior is no exception.
Let's start with the controls. You can pick a keyboard-only scheme, or mouse and keyboard scheme. Immediately it becomes clear that mouse and keyboard become optimal. You can instantly target AoE skills anywhere by simply pointing the mouse instead of navigating slowly with arrow keys. However, some quests are simply not completable with the mouse and keyboard controls. Some quests require you to interact with mobs. To interact with quest objects, you typically need to press left click. However, left click will attack the mob instead of interacting with it. You will then need to switch to keyboard-only mode and press space on the mob instead of left click. Some bugs do overlap between keyboard schemes though. If you tap an AoE skill, it simply doesn't come out. Period. You need to hold the key down for at least a 0.5 seconds, which instantly slows down the pacing of the game.
Auto attacking is bugged. Sometimes wizard auto attack will animate, but no projectile comes out, therefore doing nothing. If you have focus-targetting on by pressing ctrl, you will have only a chance of auto attacking successfully. If you try to be smart and use the mouse to attack instead, you will sometimes be stuck in an autoattack animation you cannot get out of.
Walking is bugged. Stairs and elevators will sometimes put you in a random position in the map. Some stairs will act as walls and you cannot walk them without going at them at a specific angle through a specific pixel.
Jumping is bugged and useless. It's not clear what you can jump on. You can scale mountains in one jump in some maps, but you can't get over a pebble in others. Jumping sometimes sticks you or other mobs in the air and keeps them there. At that point it becomes unclear if they are flying or if it is lagging and you're waiting for their position to update.
Typing is bugged. The censor will completely ruin you when you type words like 'cumulative'. It's always great to see a game censor words you type, but will have those same words in their game text. Typing in numbers in the marketplace is bugged. If you highlight any text and type, you have ruined the marketplace and will need to restart it. Typing in a message and pressing enter will leave the message box open. It's not like I need to fight a mob or anything....
Some skills straight up bug the game. Try Telekenesis while players are moving around. Their positions will randomize and you will not know where they are in the map.
The minimap lies about party members' positions. Look at the minimap, and press M. Player locations are completely different. Which one is right?
Friends list reports people being online without them actually being online, or vice versa.
I can write more bugs but that will take me hours. On to the game design...
Chat bubbles have priority rendering on the screen, even above loading screens. Chat bubbles will cover crucial UI elements like the settings menu, and you simply can't click on anything until the chat bubble goes away and uncovers what you were trying to interact with. This magnifies when bots spam long chat sequences that cover 1/4 the screen.
There are quests that have a chance at completion. Donate silver to this statue. Pick an amount to donate. It wasn't the right one, try again. Giving 1000 silver didn't work? Try again. 1/9 chance means you have to try 1-999999 times to complete the quest.
Attacking nothing (no target) decreases an item's durability. Just.. why? Also, the cost of repairing an item is static no matter how damaged it is.
Gems and other special items drop on death. Not sure why. It doesn't clearly say which items drop on death other than gems.
Marketplace is horrid, I'm sure everyone already mentioned that though. (Huge commissions, limitations on pricing and amount, etc.)
There are hidden skill interactions that you wouldn't know about unless you tried them yourselves, meaning you've invested your character into the build. Pyromancer's Fireball + Psychokino's Psychic Pressure makes a nifty nova that sometimes emits flames that take up half the screen, but most of the time the flames are the length of the fireball itself. It's random.
This game says you need to think carefully about your build before persuing it. Fine advice, but there aren't any resources out there to make an informed decision on what build path to take. If you make a mistake, you have doomed your character and wasted 100s of hours. There are also hidden classes in the game that not many people know about. It's almost as if they want you to build wrong.
You need to plan and build a max level character to create a guild, because there is a class specifically to do this basic game feature. Same for crafters (alchemist). These characters are useless for PvE and PvP and are there to waste your time to enjoy features other games would have given you straight away.
Dungeons are limited to two runs per day, but still have item drops that have less than 1% chance of dropping. 2 runs per day, 0.1% chance.. guess I'm playing game for decades.
There are pay to win elements of the game. You can enchant gears with premium enchant scrolls. The enchantments are also random, so you'll need to pay a lot of money to get lucky and roll for the enchantment you want, like +50 magic attack x 3.
Class EXP. It's an outdated mechanic. There doesn't appear to be any variance between Class and Base exp either (e.g. you will hit class circle 5 at base level 126 regardless where you grind). It would be nice to have all the circles to start with, and then have class exp levels to enhance any circle of your choosing. That would have been a decent use for this mechanic.
I play this game because it is like watching my favorite B-movie. I get to see a train wreck of a movie slowly happening to quite hilarity. They consistently make poor choices over every detail and it makes me wonder if the developers have played any video games at all.

Transistor first strikes with its splendid art direction and ambience.
Sound design is brilliant, one of the best I've seen in a game and the Transistor dialogues, reacting to your actions, is really immersive.
If the story was told a little too crypticly for me to really care, I still got attached to both the main characters, even if one of them his just a sword with a voice and the other a woman who lost hers.
Where Transistor also really shines it's in its game mechanics. You can use your abilities either in real time or use the planning mode to unleash more firepower upon your foes at the cost of a serious cooldown afterwards.
Choosing your spells is pratically a game within the game as you will try to figure out the best combination to match your play style or the enemies you're facing.
Because this is how you will be able to fully enjoy the depth of the game, I would really recommend you to play the "recursion mode" (which is Transistor's new game+).

I originally bought Transistor as it was one of the few games on discount that had a 9/10 rating on IGN
The game took me less than 8 hours to finish (not complete, since there is still much to explore)
Gameplay was solid; you will learn anything you need to know for combat from the start
Many combinations of functions (skills) make the gameplay clever, and possibilities limitless (seriously, limitless!)
The art is another aspect which is great. This is further complemented by its soundtrack which is amazing as well
Finally the story, which is just masterfully put together. You will begin to realize how deep and good the story really is only after a few hours of playing. And I must say the ending of Transistor was something truly special!
Conclusion: Transistor is an artistic masterpiece, I'd recommend it to any gamer

Transistor is the most enjoyable RPGs I've in a very long time.

The sound is just as amazing. From the wonderful voice-overs to the music. The music fits the atmosphere and having Red hum with the music is lovely to listen to.
I absolutely loved the gameplay. I enjoyed being able to switch between freezing time, planning my attack, and watching it execute and being quick on my feet. The mechanics surrounding how you can build your own playstyle and change it up made the game constantly enjoyable to play.

This game is one of the best games of 2014, if not the best. If you have even a remote interest in this game, it is well-worth picking up.

It's important to make two points very clear, given their contradiction: One, "A Machine for Pigs" isn't scary. Two, I still absolutely recommend it.
While "A Machine For Pigs" fails in the same places its predecessor did (lack of variety in the monsters chief among them, there being a grand total of four enemies in this game, two of which make very limited appearances and two of which I had to check the wiki to even learn they were seperate creatures), and even in some new ways (no need to manage light supply, puzzles are reduced mostly to "press the button" or "put the thing in the thing and then press the button"), it makes up for it in atmosphere. Between the design of the eponymous Machine and the incredible sound design, "A Machine for Pigs" does a fantastic job of creating a tense, oppressive environment as you wander the vast, claustrophobic passages of the groaning behemoth.
So with the understanding that any sense of actual fear (though not unease, by far) will evaporate after about the third Manpig encounter, and that the game isn't that much longer than a Peter Jackson film, I still recommend giving this game a try.

This game is amazing, so don't buy it if you've got things to do or places to be. I remember I hit the 30 hour mark about half a week after getting it, and I saw from the reviews I wasn't the only one.
In a way, it's a bit like Minecraft in that you start with nothing and have only your hands to survive with, but the whole point is to be lazy and build machines to do everything for you. If you enjoyed using redstone to do awesome stuff, then you'll definitely enjoy this game. If you didn't or have no idea what redstone is, then you'll still probably enjoy this game.
Since the devs have done such a good job at optimising it all, there is virtually no limit to how much stuff you build. A factory that burns through 1000 ore per second can still happily run on a laptop. You will undoubtedly end up with a ridiculously complex factory that only you can figure out, which feels kind of like your own artwork (either that or you'll keep starting a new game to do things better).
Despite the lack of end game content, it feels like a finished game, and already has hundreds of mods to pick from if you want more things to do. The devs are very active and are constantly listening to and replying to feedback, so you're not in danger of buying an abandoned broken game if you get this.
Also the trains are awesome, but I had to watch a 10 minute video tutorial to find what they were capable of.
The good:
- (Almost) infinite procedural world
- Multiplayer support
- Really good sense of progression
- Build huge factories and set up defenses
- Automatic train system with pathfinding
- Logic system with combinators (like redstone but more advanced)
- Active devs
- Hundreds of mods
- More complete than some fully released games
The bad:
- Multiplayer doesn't support separate factories
- Enemies are quite basic
- No real goal aside from launching a rocket
- Lack of higher tier items

"First, you say 'where are your papers?' If it goes further than that, it's too late to be saying anything at all..."
Welcome to Paper's Please, a game about being a low level beaurucrat whose job is to make sure that people who enter your country have legitimate papers, are not criminals, and are not smuggling contraband.
Working at your post pays poorly, and you are overworked by an uncaring, faceless government, but you need the money. Your family is at home, and you provide for all of them. If you don't make enough money, they will starve, grow sick, or simply be forced to scavenge for whatever they can because you have been taken to prison because of your debts.
Of course, if that's not enough, there are terrorists who want to tear down your government, and they think that you might be perfect for a new position that just opened up...
Papers Please takes the form of a simple eight bit game where the screen is split into three parts. The top part shows you your workplace, and everything that's going on around you, from the massive line trying to get in, to the armed, poorly trained guards there to keep order and shoot anyone who breaks rules. The left side shows the person trying to get in, and a small desk where all documents are placed, and the right side is your workspace, where you drag documents to and check them against a list of rules that is prone to politics, random changes  to fit world events, and other problems.
Not only, however, must you keep these rules in mind, but corruption is the game of the day, and between trying to make more money in not entirely honest ways, to having to bow down to a corrupt superior, life is hard. And your job keeps getting harder.
You only have twelve minutes per level to process as many applicants as possible, and they have a lot of paper work for you. You only get paid for who gets in, however, so be careful not to send too many away. Of course, you can choose to activate an easy mode that sees you get 20 dollars a day regardless of performance, but that's not enough to cover everything.
Ultimately, this is a surpisingly tense game that is more about atmospshere than action, a game that asks hard things of you, and makes you question the rules. How far will you go to feed your family, and how much will you do to help others in a world where there are penalties for doing so?
That's up to you, I suppose.

I almost have 16 hours on record and I have achieved basically all the achievements except for four. I really love this game.
The story and the gameplay itself is solid. One can continuously change their functions to play differently for each battle or one can just keep a combination of functions to storm through the entire game. Regardless, it's quite fun to experiment with different combinations and whatnot.
In terms of replayability, it doesn't fare too well. Once you finish the game through once, you have the option to recurse through the story again. In doing so you get to unlock functions you didn't unlock the first time around, get the rest of the achievements and etc. However, replaying the story the second time around is basically the same like doing it the first time around. The story itself doesn't change, though one does have the ability to pick new functions and create new combinations to replay through the game once more. Once you get all the achievements and unlockables you really don't have anything else to do in the game unless you want to experiment with function combinations and try to see if you can create the most productive and devestating ones. You can also enable limiters to make the game more difficult for you. The game is very customizable in difficulty, which is an upside for those who like to control the difficulty.
Regardless of its replayability, I recommend the game for people who are looking for an interesting story and fun, overall gameplay.  I will admit, I was confused initially about what was going on story-wise, but if you replay through the game at least once after you finish it initially, you get a better sense of what's going on story-wise.
I really love this game, it's got great visuals/detail/aesthetics, some incredible music and it's just fun to play overall. If you're into RPG style games, you'll love this too. The story itself can be finished under a few hours, perhaps 3 or less. I'm not sure how long it took me since I did a few of the tests you can find as you visit the beach area. That keeps you busy for a while, some of the tests are challenging but fun as well.
Anyways, I recommend this game. It was a great experience for me personally and I'll probably replay it a few more times just to get the rest of the achievements and just because the game is amazing.

Dark Souls II takes an interesting step from the Dark Souls I feel and gameplay.
While I recommend this game and at times enjoy playing it, I feel like they missed the mark on a few things:
- Multiplayer was something that was a total miss to me and something that's becoming more of a standard. In that regard its not improved nor worsened from DS1.
- Unlocking the bonfires was a great idea, however I feel that unlike DS1 which had some amazing level design that made you feel like you were connecting parts of a world as you progressed, with creatively linking areas to one another as you explored, it feels more like they leaned on the bonfire transportation as a crutch. It does give you the ability to sprawl out the world more, but it also makes me miss the original level design.
-  Increasing difficulty (ex: much smaller parry window) and increasing punishments (every death decays your healthbar's max, with annoying methods to regain it) was something I feel was natural to this type of game, but I found myself more annoyed with the hallowing effect than challenged by it. If I couldn't kill it the first time I tried, why make me eventually fight it with 50% less health?
Overall it's a great game and recommended, but since it is a sequal that will be compared to its predecessor I feel like it's not really a step up in anything more than length and graphics, with other aspects being slightly worse. The frustrating aspects of DS1 are just more aggrivating in this game, the ambiguity of the story is not clarified and lack of direction from the start is even worse. Read / Watch some guides if you're starting this game, because it will only get more frustrating as less people play it online making one of your options of reversing hollowing less appealing. The game could have increased difficulty without increasing aggrivation, but it didn't.

A note before reading this review:
I am, by no means, a frequent player of horror games. I am quite a wimp. Only rarely do I venture into the genre myself, mainly due to the abundance of games reliant on jumpscares to create the 'horror'. As one who greatly prefers psychological horror games as opposed to the rather cheap jumpscare variety, this was the main appeal of Amnesia: The Dark Descent, and so this review is written by a player who had expected an atmospheric, psychological horror game in its sequel, Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs.
Game: Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs
Traditional Rating: 5/10
Recommended: Yes
Firstly, it is important to note that Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is pretty much only an 'Amnesia' title in name alone. While the controls remain perfectly similar to that of The Dark Descent, this serves as one of the few reminders of its predecessor throughout the whole game, save for the occasional reference to the original title in the story/lore. If you found the controls in The Dark Descent to be good and practical, it is the same in this title. If this is your first delve into Amnesia, you will find the controls easy to learn and manage.
In terms of gameplay, however, A Machine for Pigs is quite limited. It essentially consists of the barebones of The Dark Descent - exploring your surroundings to find out how to progress, while hiding/running from any monsters that you encounter. You are defenceless - much like in the original Amnesia - and this serves as a source of the horror found within the game - if you're spotted by an enemy, there is nothing that you can do but run. While the essence of an Amnesia title exists in this respect, A Machine for Pigs feels quite lacking. There is no 'sanity meter' in this game, which served as either an excellent mechanic in the original, or a mild pain, depending on your preference. There is therefore no need to try and avert your character's view from disturbing events, or even any need to stay in the light to preserve your sanity. The lantern which you obtain very early on in the game serves as an unlimited light source, removing any need to scavenge for tinderboxes or oil containers to illuminate your surroundings. It feels like part of the horror is therefore removed - entering a new area with limited light sources would be much scarier than having an unlimited, portable light source. If you found it difficult to progress in The Dark Descent, or if you aren't great with puzzles, then you can find solace in the fact that the 'puzzles' in A Machine for Pigs are incredibly simple, easing your progression through the game.
The atmosphere of A Machine for Pigs is sometimes unsettling, but not overwhelmingly so. It uses many tried-and-tested tactics of previous horror titles to create this atmosphere, so those who frequently play horror games will not find many surprises in the tactics used by the developers to unsettle the player. Indeed, considering my inexperience with the horror genre and the fact that I am quite easily scared, A Machine for Pigs did not really seem particularly scary to me. It is significantly less scary than its predecessor, so if you were expecting an escalation of the atmospheric horror found in the original, you will not find this in A Machine for Pigs. However, there were some rather creepy ambient sounds and pieces of music used throughout the game that could make you a little nervous, though these aren't particularly distressing. The music, too, fit the mood of the game quite nicely.
The story in A Machine for Pigs definitely picks up towards the end - as you might expect, you begin with little-to-no memory of previous events and put the pieces together throughout the game. The majority of the story is told naturally throughout the game, while additional writings and pieces of information can be found scattered around the game's various locations, never far from the intended path. While the story was quite good, it was also quite predictable. Initial hunches (which I won't divulge) about a couple of aspects of the game's narrative were proved to be correct, which unfortunately removed any real chance of surprise from a narrative point of view. The game's ending was more satisfactory than the rather lacklustre ending to A Dark Descent, I found. However, it is a very short game, clocking in at around 4-5 hours at a fairly slow pace, including hunting down the additional notes throughout the game.
To conclude: although the game is a step-down from its predecessor, I would recommend A Machine for Pigs if you wish to experience the story of the game and explore an additional sample of the Amnesia universe. As a horror experience, however, you could do a lot better. There is little horror to be found in A Machine for Pigs, even when the monsters are present. It is perhaps akin to dipping your toes in the water of the Amnesia universe - if you want to take the plunge, look no further than The Dark Descent.

The first RTW game got me through some of the most angst-filled years of high-school.  I stayed up late playing it all the time, and I distinctly remember playing it when my first girlfriend broke up with me :(.  The many hours spent playing RTW taught me more about European Geography than any class, and I am still fascinated by the innards of this complex beautiful machine.  I've never played the Civilization games, but I've spent a lot of time with vanilla RTW2 and would like to share my experience.
Rome Total War 2 looks great, I typically run it on my laptop (with a 970m) and play on my 4k T.V. (60hz).  The game crashes occasionally, but not enough to interfere with what I am doing.  On the legendary difficulty battles and the campaign offer a curve that is surprisingly easy, and if you are practiced at the RTW series style of command, you should be able to win pitched battles, even when the odds are stacked against you (sometimes).  Winning an important battle against a superior foe feels great, and is the peak experience of the series.  If you like your histories, and never understood exactly what the military tactics were, battle command in RTW2 is as close to experiential learning as you can get.
Historical accuracy is a big deal.  I'm somewhat of a history buff, and just finished listening to "The History of Rome" podcast by Mike Duncan which I highly recommend (179 Episodes about 30 minutes each), and still enjoy his "Revolutions" podcast immensely.  Back to the game, 272 B.C. is a great year to start the campaign.  If you're playing as Rome, the characters available to your faction were actually around that year (more on this in a second).  Julius Libo was a consul in 269 B.C. and fought on the tiny peninsula south of Brundisium.  Lucius Papirus Cursor was consul in 272.  Scipio "Asina" led the first Roman Navy to a debacle during the first Punic War and was captured earning him the cognomen "Asina" or "The♥♥♥♥♥quot; (He never lived it down but he was freed in a prisoner exchange and went on to capable army command).
This last point is indicative of the game that CA made... If you believe that the Rome campaign is 100% accurate, that's crazy because even though the Republic might be possible to model, the Late Empire would be insanely difficult, and there's no way I believe that CA did this.  However, nothing about my experience with the game has indicated that the campaign is completely randomized, or even highly randomized.  For example, if I chose to build a Villa at Consentia, it seems as though I suffer diplomatically with Carthage.  I don't know if this is true or not, but one that I have reproduced with regularity is that if I march Legio II away from Syracuse, that I am able to gain a non-aggression pact with them (go ahead, try it).  Like I said, I do not know the innards of Warscape (the engine), but I do know that any programming involving the variables in RTW2 is very involved.  The probability and statistics behind the campaign and battle mechanics are beautiful, and lend themselves to forcing you to think like an ancient leader.
The campaign map on Legendary sort of reminds me of a Rube Goldberg Machine... you know, one of those machines that uses kinetic energy to roll a ball through a maze, knock a bucket off a ledge, etc. etc.  The reason I have so many hours in the game is because the campaign AI is very impressive.  By no means is the AI perfect: sometimes a random war-dec will throw off my plans to invade Sicily, Africa, Corsica, etc... figuring out what you did to upset the balance of civilized power or the barbarians is frustrating.
Are there other problems with this game?  Of course, it's large, time-consuming, purely representational of the actual history...  Without background knowledge, its difficult to express why the Romans started the 1st Punic War just by looking at Syracusae and saying "Oh wow that Grain Farm is awesome, lets take it."  272 B.C. Rome had virtually no navy, and Scipio was not yet an Asina.  There are mods to improve historical accuracy, and I've been meaning to try a 4 turn per year mod as well.  However, the mod this game would benefit the most from (or that would attract the most new players) is a mod that turned the history of Rome into a visual novel.  The game recreates some of the most famous historical battles, but reproducing that on the campaign map would be a feat worthy of the greatest game designers, historians, and writers.  Don't go crazy like I did, but play some RTW2, if only because its a great strategy game in an amazing period of history.

I first went into this game shortly after release, having just finished JC2 a few days ago so I had high expectations.
At first, I was disappointed by bad performance, visual glitches and general stability issues so I opted out real quick.
Now that some time has passed I tried it once again and actually finished the game and all its DLCs so I feel like I can form a relevant opinion:
Pro:
• Great Graphics
• Amazing flexibility b/c of the tethers
• Fun wingsuit
• Rather big map
• Regions differ in design
• Fun little easter eggs
• Collectables
Con:
• Trash performance
• FPS drops
• (some) crashes
• Some bugged challenges (making it unreasonably hard to accomplish them)
• Mostly garbage vehicle handling (few exceptions for certain vehicles)
• Whatever could be identified as a story could have been expanded massively (doesnt really matter, you play the game to destroy stuff anyway)
• Leaderboards are basically useless unless you have a large amount of friends who play the game
• DLC are kind of overpriced (the "Air" one for sure)
• (entirely subjective) sadly they changed the voice actor for Rico, I really liked the one in JC2 ;/
If you're looking for a real story, look elsewhere. But if you want to blow up a bunch of stuff in different ways for 50hrs this is where it's at. The performance is just unreasonable for the price but if you play around with the settings and give it high CPU priority (task manager) you should be okay.
I enjoyed my journey to (blow up) Medici and even though I liked JC2 better, I still think this is worth a play (especially if you can get it at a discount).

Hello world!
Supergiant comes back with another installment, same narrator (or at least the same actor), world still falling apart, but this time, it's in the future!
For Bastion fans, Transistor has all of the flavors of  Bastion, with a whole new story and significantly changed combat elements.
Combat this time often time involves the usage of the "Turn()" ability.
Turn() is essentially a planning phase where you can plan out your attacks, then when you execute, it happens instantaneously, then you have a recharge time before it can be used again.
Being in the non-discript space future, there are a decent amount of programming references embedded into the game.
As a programmer, I thought that was kinda cool, because I felt like I had a secret hand shake with the developers saying "Hey, I got that!"
Even if you're not a programmer, those minor references don't really effect the story at all, so nothing will be missed by anyone that plays this game.
So to break down the pieces, gameplay, I would say is equivalent to the level that Bastion output.
Music, dare I say, better than Bastion. The song for the trailer, We All Become was fantastic. Old Friends was great as well.
Combat, personally, I liked it. I've heard some friends that preferred Bastion's combat system to Transistor, but I'm definitely a fan of RPGs, and Transistor feels more like an RPG with its system.
Story, I'm kind of mixed. Shortly in, it becomes apparent that there are elements of romance. My video game taste palate initially wasn't expected a romance, but grew to accept and even really like where it took the story.
All of those elements combined, it makes this game one of my absolute favorites.
I would absolutely recommend it.

For the sake of context I think its important to state that I am coming into ESO fresh. I never played the game when it first launched, though I am aware of some of the criticisms directed towards the game upon release. I came to this game having played other MMO's like World of Warcraft, Guild Wars 2, etc. I had just leveled 5 characters in WoW to 110 and was looking for something a bit different. (Make no mistake I will return to WoW, but for now it's just nice to have a bit of a break.) I had read this game was quite different than when it first launched. Given my love for the Elder Scrolls series I decided to give it a try. Now after having spent 30 hours with the game I feel comfortable in sharing my thoughts about my experience thus far.
The first thing that is apparent is the amount of character customization and control you have over how your character looks. Upon creating your character you are deposited in a starting zone. This can be pretty lengthy, however upon completing this area once, you are able to skip it should you decide to roll an alternate character.
Also apparent is some pretty decent voice acting. I noticed the likes of John Cleese as well as the fellow who played Albus Dumbledore in Harry Potter.
The character models are generally decent enough, though there are some low res/quality textures here and there.
The questing is on it's own, generally a mixed bag. There are some really good ones and there are also some really bland ones that feel a bit anticlimactic. Fortunately there are some really interesting characters. My personal favorite thus far has been Raz'um Dar a khajiit who's sharp witted humor makes for some entertaining conversations.
I've seen many people consider this an MMO. And while they aren't wrong, I do think the game still has a bit of an identity issue. Much of the game can be played as a single player RPG with some co-op elements. In that sense I think the game does feel a bit more like a co-op Elder Scrolls game. That's not a bad thing though and there is a lot of content here to keep you occupied.
The player interaction from my brief time with the game seems to have vastly improved from what I heard about at release. There appears to be no more phasing issues and you can at least group up with a friend to complete quests together (save for solo quests which you have to complete on your own).
I have only done one major dungeon thus far and some of the bosses were surprisingly difficult, though still manageble for just a friend and myself. The game's character progression isn't so much tied to gear acquisition though it is there, but you are utterly free to build a character how you see fit, selecting from a variety of active and passive skills and distrubiting skill points.
On top of this, there is an extensive crafting system that allows you to craft and forge armor and weapons as well as furnishings for the in game player housing.
The combat is decent and places a lot of emphasis on positioning and it feels really dynamic. If I had one gripe it's that the sneaking and stealth sections of some of the Dark Brotherhood quests can be downright frustrating because of some of the enemy AI. You can be ever so careful only to find a guard spawn or seemingly spot you through objects, causing them to ring a bell and ruining your day.
The Tamriel Unlimited update allows you to purchase the game at one price and play indefinitely. The only thing is that you then have to purchase DLC separately. These pieces of DLC are included however in the ESO+ which is the subscription model. It's not a bad way of going about it to be honest. If you don't like paying the $15 a month, you can simply buy it all up front. It offers the consumer options which is always a good thing. You don't need the DLC right away and can pick it up later. Among these DLC's are some guilds like the Dark Brotherhood and Theives guild.
You are also no longer restricted to playing with friends of the same faction/race either which adds that much needed social aspect that any MMO depends on.
Finally it has to be said that ESO does have microtransactions. These can range from inexpensive XP Boosts, etc. to more expensive things like the DLC. For the most part a lot of it is cosmetic. I've seen worse in other games. However, what I do have an issue with is the absurdly low conversion rates for Crown gems which can be acquired from items that drop from Dwarven chests. If it sounds convoluted? It is. Basically there are two forms of in game currency. The crowns themselves can buy things like DLC and other stuff, while crown gems generally can be accumulated and used for things like mounts, outfits, etc.
Even after 30 hours I feel like I have only begun to scratch the surface of what's on offer. I have yet to try PVP or delve into the player housing yet. I only know that I look forward to 30 hours more. WIth the recent patches, I feel that ESO finally has earned that "Elder Scrolls" in it's title.

I have to admit though, if I were to choose one game from the present that was near it's greatness, it would be Call of Juarez : Gunslinger.
Now, the
sort of took me by surprise. I was expecting the typical scenematic every now and again between shootouts. This wasn't the case. The cut-scenes aren't fully animated, but are animated enough to give you a rough idea of what everyone looks like. Within the game, Silas's voice narrates the action while his friends will sometimes pipe in with a question or a comment. The game is definitely unique in it's approach to telling a story.
I was extremely skeptical before I even tried out the game. I've heard a few positive reviews but haven't seen anything to make it substantially stick out. I gave it a shot and am glad. The game play will keep you immersed, but depending on how much you like what they give you, depends how long it will suck you in for. I haven't been bored yet as they do a good mix of allowing you to use all of your weapons (or explosives) at a given time. There are times where the game play will stop and the player will have to have a duel with an enemy. This brought me back to the good old days of Red Dead. Instead of simply copying former versions that have included dueling, CoJ rather has you and the opponent sort of circling one another. At this point, the player tries to focus in on the opponent (with one joystick) and adjusts their hand position over the gun with the other joystick. Carefully watching the opponent, once he draws then you can draw. Draw first and lose honor. The game play itself is done in first person and the guns move relatively to where you move, meaning if there is a wall in the way of one revolver, Silas will hold the left revolver up (for example) while the right one can engage enemies.
The guns themselves are sort of basic but slowly upgrade throughout the game. Basic guns include revolvers (you can have dual-lies), rifle, sawed-off shotgun, and the double barreled shot gun. Explosives are also available such as sticks of dynamite. Within the map, there are explosive objects which can be shot to damage opponents within the proximity. There is also a feature which slows down the game and gives the player a chance to take out as many opponents as they can before their "focus" stamina runs out. When a player's health runs low, you're given a final chance to redeem yourself and get back on your feet. This happens by focusing in on one opponent (automatically) and he fires a single bullet at you. If you dodge the bullet, you can keep the mayhem going. If you get hit, you're sleeping with the fishes. I absolutely love this portion of the game as it keeps you on your toes and engaged within the game play almost at all times. Just because that dynamite is flying in the air doesn't mean it has to explode by you. Shoot it before it gets near you! The RPG element of the game deals with improving your skill with the revolvers, rifle, or shotgun. Choose wisely as you may favor a gun more than the others.

The first RTW game got me through some of the most angst-filled years of high-school.  I stayed up late playing it all the time, and I distinctly remember playing it when my first girlfriend broke up with me :(.  The many hours spent playing RTW taught me more about European Geography than any class, and I am still fascinated by the innards of this complex beautiful machine.  I've never played the Civilization games, but I've spent a lot of time with vanilla RTW2 and would like to share my experience.
Rome Total War 2 looks great, I typically run it on my laptop (with a 970m) and play on my 4k T.V. (60hz).  The game crashes occasionally, but not enough to interfere with what I am doing.  On the legendary difficulty battles and the campaign offer a curve that is surprisingly easy, and if you are practiced at the RTW series style of command, you should be able to win pitched battles, even when the odds are stacked against you (sometimes).  Winning an important battle against a superior foe feels great, and is the peak experience of the series.  If you like your histories, and never understood exactly what the military tactics were, battle command in RTW2 is as close to experiential learning as you can get.
Historical accuracy is a big deal.  I'm somewhat of a history buff, and just finished listening to "The History of Rome" podcast by Mike Duncan which I highly recommend (179 Episodes about 30 minutes each), and still enjoy his "Revolutions" podcast immensely.  Back to the game, 272 B.C. is a great year to start the campaign.  If you're playing as Rome, the characters available to your faction were actually around that year (more on this in a second).  Julius Libo was a consul in 269 B.C. and fought on the tiny peninsula south of Brundisium.  Lucius Papirus Cursor was consul in 272.  Scipio "Asina" led the first Roman Navy to a debacle during the first Punic War and was captured earning him the cognomen "Asina" or "The♥♥♥♥♥quot; (He never lived it down but he was freed in a prisoner exchange and went on to capable army command).
This last point is indicative of the game that CA made... If you believe that the Rome campaign is 100% accurate, that's crazy because even though the Republic might be possible to model, the Late Empire would be insanely difficult, and there's no way I believe that CA did this.  However, nothing about my experience with the game has indicated that the campaign is completely randomized, or even highly randomized.  For example, if I chose to build a Villa at Consentia, it seems as though I suffer diplomatically with Carthage.  I don't know if this is true or not, but one that I have reproduced with regularity is that if I march Legio II away from Syracuse, that I am able to gain a non-aggression pact with them (go ahead, try it).  Like I said, I do not know the innards of Warscape (the engine), but I do know that any programming involving the variables in RTW2 is very involved.  The probability and statistics behind the campaign and battle mechanics are beautiful, and lend themselves to forcing you to think like an ancient leader.
The campaign map on Legendary sort of reminds me of a Rube Goldberg Machine... you know, one of those machines that uses kinetic energy to roll a ball through a maze, knock a bucket off a ledge, etc. etc.  The reason I have so many hours in the game is because the campaign AI is very impressive.  By no means is the AI perfect: sometimes a random war-dec will throw off my plans to invade Sicily, Africa, Corsica, etc... figuring out what you did to upset the balance of civilized power or the barbarians is frustrating.
Are there other problems with this game?  Of course, it's large, time-consuming, purely representational of the actual history...  Without background knowledge, its difficult to express why the Romans started the 1st Punic War just by looking at Syracusae and saying "Oh wow that Grain Farm is awesome, lets take it."  272 B.C. Rome had virtually no navy, and Scipio was not yet an Asina.  There are mods to improve historical accuracy, and I've been meaning to try a 4 turn per year mod as well.  However, the mod this game would benefit the most from (or that would attract the most new players) is a mod that turned the history of Rome into a visual novel.  The game recreates some of the most famous historical battles, but reproducing that on the campaign map would be a feat worthy of the greatest game designers, historians, and writers.  Don't go crazy like I did, but play some RTW2, if only because its a great strategy game in an amazing period of history.

A great marriage of turn-based strategy and real-time hack and slash. Like Bastian, the graphics, voice work, and music are all spot on. The mechanic of being able to have your character hum along to whatever track is playing at the time is a nice touch to the story and atmosphere. Speaking of story, I love how the story is revealed in tastey morsels throughout the game’s progression instead of being crammed down your throat from start to finish. If you really want to know the whole story, you’ll have to explore every facet of the game. I’m not just talking about the terminals you find in back-alleys, but also the ability combos and enemy-modifiers you unlock. That leads me to the coolest feature of Transistor. Every ability you unlock can be used as an attack power, and enhancement of another attack power, or a passive character enhancement. This creates an amazing amalgamation of tactical planning, RPG power-leveling, and story progression.
Not terribly long but amazing enough that you’ll want a second play through.
PS Get the accompanying soundtrack if you like good music and clever writing. The lyrics in those songs that have them make further implications surrounding the events of the story.

Transistor is much more refined, well-polished and cleaner than SuperGiant’s previous title. The game implicates relevant, political messages of man’s current struggle against technology.
Bad Points: Although visually and artistically refined in comparison to Bastion there is just less to do. The story, voice-acting and music seem more sterilized and subdued than most action adventure games.
Unique Strengths: The presentation and visual elements are some of the best in the sci-fi genre. Although not as good as his previous SuperGiant soundtrack, Darren Korb still demonstrates that he is one of the best musicians in the gaming industry. Rarely do I see such an artistic heroine (Red) in a leading role.
Gamer Tastes: Diehard SuperGiant and Bastion fans, indie-gaming enthusiasts, cyberpunk and sci-fi junkies and well…if you’re a gamer that likes kickass female leads.
Worth Buying? - If you’re an indie-gaming enthusiast who prefers the sci-fi/cyberpunk genre this is right up your alley otherwise you’re not missing much by skipping this one.
Theme: 9.5/10 – The visuals, gameplay, story, voice-acting, music all followed the same thematic direction of high science-fiction fantasy. Albeit painfully nihilistic, minimalistic and emotionless at times; these are the flag posts of any futuristic dystopia. By the end of the game you will have a strong grasp as to what Cloud City really is but more importantly what its inhabitants are. My only gripe is with the repetitive and admittedly uncreative enemy designs.
Story: 4.0/10 – The story exists in places where gamers may never venture; character profiles, kiosk dialogue boxes and the transistor’s very terse commentary (which I would not even consider voiced narration). The latter half of the game’s story feels rushed and I cared little for any characters outside of Red and the voice inside her transistor device. Musical lyrics, some sort of formally presented backstory and more dialogue in general all could have added logic to the plot but unfortunately none of this was significantly presented.
Gameplay: 9.0/10 – I have a love/hate relationship with turn based combat but fortunately it is designed very well in Transistor. Many gameplay elements were borrowed from Bastion such as the cover system, active abilities and delimiters (which have replaced relics) but everything else feels different and new. The ability to easily combine, recombine and experiment with abilities actively, passively and as weapon upgrades is done incredibly well and easily the most notable aspect of Transistor. I just wish there was a defensive and healing system that did not take away from such a well-executed combat system.
Soundtrack and Acting: 6.5/10 – High quality music and mediocre voice acting is met with failed expectations. SuperGiant Games is known for their use of voice acting and music in videogames and yet these are not strong points of Transistor, made unfortunate by the fact that your main character is a professional singer. I know what SuperGiant and Darren Korb is capable of. I just need to hear it but didn’t playing this game.
Technical Quality: 10/10 – The design of this game is mind-blowingly good. The imagery, actions, animations and visual effects are elements that could have been taken out of a well-established comic book or cartoon franchise but is SuperGiant’s original creation. If anything about Transistor is going to stick with me long after the credits it is the visuals and art direction.
Replay Value: 6.0/10 – The game plus mode and challenge rooms are directly ported mechanics from Bastion. But all-in-all there is just much less to do in comparison and generally not much to do after beating the core storyline. It is very fun to experiment with different abilities in the practice room and grind experience to gain new ones but this feels like a fleeting interest rather than anything to draw me back after the game is beaten.
Conclusion: Transistor is a good game in its own right but I’d rather return to its more likable videogame brother, Bastion. Much of Transistor’s story, gameplay and animations are spiritual successors to Bastion so it is sad to see that although it has a more focused, cleaner and understandable art direction it fails in lack of story and the distinctive voice that Darren Korb and the narration of Rucks gave Bastion. SuperGiant Games took its two strongest abilities, music and voiced narration, and merely ported them to a game that could have better utilized both. Despite these apparent weaknesses, the superb visual design, varied and tight gameplay and, though not amazing, music still puts it a cut above most independently developed games. Diehard SuperGiant, science-fiction and independent gaming fans will love Transistor, for everyone else I suggest you put it on your “play later” list of games.
Overall Score (based on an average): 7.5/10

For the sake of context I think its important to state that I am coming into ESO fresh. I never played the game when it first launched, though I am aware of some of the criticisms directed towards the game upon release. I came to this game having played other MMO's like World of Warcraft, Guild Wars 2, etc. I had just leveled 5 characters in WoW to 110 and was looking for something a bit different. (Make no mistake I will return to WoW, but for now it's just nice to have a bit of a break.) I had read this game was quite different than when it first launched. Given my love for the Elder Scrolls series I decided to give it a try. Now after having spent 30 hours with the game I feel comfortable in sharing my thoughts about my experience thus far.
The first thing that is apparent is the amount of character customization and control you have over how your character looks. Upon creating your character you are deposited in a starting zone. This can be pretty lengthy, however upon completing this area once, you are able to skip it should you decide to roll an alternate character.
Also apparent is some pretty decent voice acting. I noticed the likes of John Cleese as well as the fellow who played Albus Dumbledore in Harry Potter.
The character models are generally decent enough, though there are some low res/quality textures here and there.
The questing is on it's own, generally a mixed bag. There are some really good ones and there are also some really bland ones that feel a bit anticlimactic. Fortunately there are some really interesting characters. My personal favorite thus far has been Raz'um Dar a khajiit who's sharp witted humor makes for some entertaining conversations.
I've seen many people consider this an MMO. And while they aren't wrong, I do think the game still has a bit of an identity issue. Much of the game can be played as a single player RPG with some co-op elements. In that sense I think the game does feel a bit more like a co-op Elder Scrolls game. That's not a bad thing though and there is a lot of content here to keep you occupied.
The player interaction from my brief time with the game seems to have vastly improved from what I heard about at release. There appears to be no more phasing issues and you can at least group up with a friend to complete quests together (save for solo quests which you have to complete on your own).
I have only done one major dungeon thus far and some of the bosses were surprisingly difficult, though still manageble for just a friend and myself. The game's character progression isn't so much tied to gear acquisition though it is there, but you are utterly free to build a character how you see fit, selecting from a variety of active and passive skills and distrubiting skill points.
On top of this, there is an extensive crafting system that allows you to craft and forge armor and weapons as well as furnishings for the in game player housing.
The combat is decent and places a lot of emphasis on positioning and it feels really dynamic. If I had one gripe it's that the sneaking and stealth sections of some of the Dark Brotherhood quests can be downright frustrating because of some of the enemy AI. You can be ever so careful only to find a guard spawn or seemingly spot you through objects, causing them to ring a bell and ruining your day.
The Tamriel Unlimited update allows you to purchase the game at one price and play indefinitely. The only thing is that you then have to purchase DLC separately. These pieces of DLC are included however in the ESO+ which is the subscription model. It's not a bad way of going about it to be honest. If you don't like paying the $15 a month, you can simply buy it all up front. It offers the consumer options which is always a good thing. You don't need the DLC right away and can pick it up later. Among these DLC's are some guilds like the Dark Brotherhood and Theives guild.
You are also no longer restricted to playing with friends of the same faction/race either which adds that much needed social aspect that any MMO depends on.
Finally it has to be said that ESO does have microtransactions. These can range from inexpensive XP Boosts, etc. to more expensive things like the DLC. For the most part a lot of it is cosmetic. I've seen worse in other games. However, what I do have an issue with is the absurdly low conversion rates for Crown gems which can be acquired from items that drop from Dwarven chests. If it sounds convoluted? It is. Basically there are two forms of in game currency. The crowns themselves can buy things like DLC and other stuff, while crown gems generally can be accumulated and used for things like mounts, outfits, etc.
Even after 30 hours I feel like I have only begun to scratch the surface of what's on offer. I have yet to try PVP or delve into the player housing yet. I only know that I look forward to 30 hours more. WIth the recent patches, I feel that ESO finally has earned that "Elder Scrolls" in it's title.

TLDR; I wanted to love this game so very much, but it fails on too many counts. Go check out a classic RO server or something, it'll be a lot more fun than this.
Old Review:
I have 66 minutes of staring at a patcher as it crashes. The game is not properly called and crashes on launch every time. Have never managed to get the game to start. Tried everything recommended by support, as well as every voodoo thing mentioned on the internet by people who had had the same issue. Only support step I haven't tried is to reinstall Windows, which isn't gonna happen for a dumb game. Nothing worked. Support ticket was unhelpful. Devs seem completely unconcerned that there are people wanting to play but can't - there have been 4 or 5 patches without a word of them even acknowledging this is an ongoing issue. I have no idea why I've spent this much time on a completely broken game.
New Review: After finally getting into the game (after a total 89 minutes of patcher) and spending some time playing, I still would not recommend it to anyone. Its been a few weeks since I last played so some of the following may have been fixed, but I highly doubt it.
Partying was broken: every single time a cutscene was set off while in a party, all party members other than the one who set it off would be stuck in place, unable to use any skills. This, obviously, would make a party of a mage and cleric completely useless. This issue had been effecting people for weeks before I made it in game, and continued for the weeks I played. Devs wouldn't even acknowledge it as a known issue, never mind actually fixing it. Don't bother playing if you wanted to play a multiplayer game.
The controls are rather stupid, and obviously designed for you to use keyboard mode, and never switch to keyboard+mouse (I never tried with controller). Event npcs were completely broken unless you switched back to keyboard to interact with them, cause they just did not respond to the mouse at all, irregardless of what control scheme you're on.
Which leads to: the events were dumb. They tried to make an even spread of PvE and PvP events, but, after months of no events, they decided to spam, like, 8 all going at the same time. The PvE events I did try out were excessively boring. If you like fetch quests and wander around in an area spamming space quests, you might have enjoyed them, but thats all they were, without even any sort of amusing story. The events starters were also in both of the two major citys, but couldn't keep themselves straight, often sending you to an area around the other major city. Not a big deal if you've leveled up enough to make decent money, but any lower level characters would be screwed out of the event, even though they were all set in starting areas in an obvious attempt to make it so everyone could participate.
The game is stupidly linear, and I couldn't care less for the story. I was an avid RO player for years, and in RO the game never forces the story on you - you seek it out. I loved and enjoyed doing quests just for the stories. In ToS, the story is forced down your throat and is rather bland - though even if it was okay I would still hate it being forced on me. The maps literally follow a line of "if you are X level you go to this map, then at Y level you go forward one to that map!". There was no choice at all in where to level. Technically you had once choice, depending on which main city's line you were following. It felt stupidly restrictive, especially since a large number of the maps had invisible wall dead ends that seemed like they had originally been intended to lead to more maps.
The maps and monsters were also rather boring. None of the maps felt truly unique or interesting. If I was shown a screenshot theres no way I would be able to tell most of them apart even. A large number of them also had some serious design flaws, including places where there is a raised up platform that if you walk to, you just walk right through it, your head just floating along the ground. A lot of the monsters were equivalent to Minecraft zombies - they just ran their faces at you to hurt you until you popped them, and those that didn't used nice obvious, easy to avoid red "I'm attacking there!" targets. Even the bosses that I encountered were largely like that. (Though, since I didn't play long enough to get to the higher levels, there is a chance that higher level bosses are smarter). It was just boring and samey-samey.
If you're a support-type player who enjoys a big party to run with, this game is not for you. My party was capped out at 5, so no giant dungeon raids. As a cleric-type, I was bored out of my mind. I ran in a party with 2 other people, and most of the time I just sat there, alt-tabbing and leeching experience. Buffs were largely nerfed to the point of uselessness, and heals were rarely needed. (Also, wtf is up with my heals hurting non-demon monsters? I don't understand the logic there.) I've been a support/priest-type in a number of games, and this was the most boring any game has ever made support.
They have also taken measures to kill any community that could form, making items only able to ever be traded once. And did you find an awesome bow while out on your cleric character that your archer would love to have? Welp, too bad. You're a team, but you're a greedy team that doesn't share and theres no way you could get that bow to your archer without paying real-world money. And if you want to form a guild, better hope someone in the group is willing to use up a character slot and spend time to make a character solely for that purpose since only one class can do it.

Okay, I'm sick of all the negative reviews this game is getting from users. Yes, the first one is scarier. That's about it. Does that mean this is a sh*t game? Nope. Amnesia is scarier than EVERYTHING, so if that's your lowest expectation, good luck in enjoying horror, ever. The sequel IS scary, it still has that ominous, oppressive atmosphere, sound design is fantastic, and the sense of vulnerability is present. The game drip-feeds the tension, and as potentially comical as the monsters sound, when you meet them, you will still sh*t your pants.
The removal of the sanity system is to the game's credit, I found it annoying and artificial in the first game. Why should the game tell me when I am scared? I can get scared for myself, thank you very much.
The "bad" is that the game is very simple when it comes to puzzles. No more inventory, no more combining and thinking, just carry this one object to the place you need to use it.
The "good" however, is that all this is in favour a story which is leagues better than the first. The voice acting is incomparably superior (the first was laughable), and if the puzles don't make you think, the story sure as hell will. It's the type of game plot, after which the first thing you do is hit the forums and have huge discussions about the meaning, the detalis, the who-s, the why-s... I remember how absolutely anti-climactic and flat the first game's ending was. This one is almost cathartic, especially if you played close attention throughout.
The bottom line is, if I had to recommend one of the two games to someone, I would go for the first, as it remains the definitive horror gaming experience. But dismissing this game as horrid because it can't match some of the very very good aspects of the first, is simply foolish. In some aspects, this one is better, and the rest really isn't bad at all. Give this underrated gem a  try.

As mentioned by other reviewers, this game is a let down for the fans of the previous amnesia game. Being a HUGE fan of horror, it's rather hard to scare me. However, Amnesia the Dark Descent did just that. Not only does it have you searching around a maze of tortured bodies while avoiding hidden monsters, but it literally brings you in psychologically with the ambiance and sound effects. I didn't want to play the game because I was terrified, but I loved to play the game because I was terrified of it. It had me jumping out of my seat! HOWEVER, this was the Dark Descent.... A Machiene for Pigs (amp) fails to do this. Having loved the first one, I anticipated more horrifying monsters and more puzzles and options to get lost. I wanted a less linear path to follow with more intricate stories and decisions to be made. But I didn't get this. In fact, I was given the same game with everything I wanted, taken away. I'll ask the devs, why can't I move this barrel? Why can't I wiggle this mirror? Why can't I explore? Where are the monsters?! The game's 'scary factor' comes solely from the fear of darkness and blurs moving in said darkness. I want to walk into a room and have to figure out what piece I need to collect... not have it be the only thing in the room that I can move as well as be glowing saying "hey! I'm important! you should touch me!"
I urge you, if you are new to this series, go back to Dark Descent. If you are a fan and coming to this one... Brace yourself... Disappointment is coming.

I'll start this recommendation by plainly saying that this is one of my favorite games of all time. Now, into the review. This is a first person linear horror game made by the Chinese Room, and their signatures are all over this game.
The game is beautifully written, every document fascinating, every bit of dialogue engaging. This game masters immersion, and it simply makes sense. This is not a leap at you horror, it is not jumpscare based, it is not overly gorey (not at first anyway), and it is not overly forward with it's horror. It is more conceptual, and a good amount of the horror is lost to all those who rush through the game without reading the documents. This game makes me think of a lot of eastern horror games, less am onster in your face and more one breathing down your throat, as if the very world was against you. The factory is well crafted, the story is superb, the atmosphere coats you like a blanket and tries to suffocate you in fear. I honestly found this game more scary than A:TTD, and I even played through a second time to find stuff I did not see before.
I do admit, this game is not without it's flaws.  The puzzles of A:TDD are heavily reduced. The puzzles here are straightforward without a lot of wandering about. To me this is great. It makes it a little closer to an interactive novel, but the puzzles of A:TDD mostly just took me out of the game. A:TDD was closer to those old point and click games where you used everything against everything else and got a bit frustrated, removing all the horror. This game has nothing of that, so the fear is able to sink in. It is very "Chinese Room"-y to focus less on the gameplay and more on the story aspects (the world and whatnot). For a more extensive review, here's a link.
All in all I love this game, but I understand the fact it has a limited audience. If you enjoy horror, great story telling, the chinese room, or you're even mildly interested and willing to explore I'd say pick it up. I don't regret gettting it and I'm certain I'm far from done with it.

Borderlands 2 was also developed by Gearbox Software and published by 2K Games and was released on September 18, 2012. Like the first installment, Borderlands 2 is a "shoot and loot" game with a series of central quests and numerous side quests. Once again you must choose one of four (or six if you download the two additional characters) vault hunters and take them to a new vault.
However you are not the only one looking for it, Handsome Jack is venturing for it as well and he is a piece of work. Handsome Jack is, in my opinion, one of the best video game villains ever created.
The first character you can choose to be is Axton the Commando. Much like Roland in the first game, Axton's Action Skill deploys an automated Sabre Turret that fires on any enemies within its range. After a few upgrades he is allowed to deploy two turrets at once and can even stick them to walls and ceilings.
The second vault hunter is Maya the Siren. This is the character I chose for my first play through because of her healing abilities. She is also beneficial for herelemental effects and crowd control. Her action skill is Phaselock, which will suspend and immobilize enemies.
The next vault hunter is a short little Mexican named Salvador the Gunzerker. Salvador resembles Brick from the first game as far as abilities are concerned, but instead of powerful melee attacks Salvador's action skill allows him to dual wield any two firearms. Upgrading his skill can allow him to throw multiple grenades at once, regenerate massive ammounts of ammunition and health, or attract enemies with a double middle-finger taunt.
The last vault hunter is a Zero the Assassin whose origins, species and gender are completely unknown. Zero's skills are based on sniping and using a sword for melee attacks. His action skill creates a decoy and turns Zero invisible so he can sneak past or attack enemies.
That completes the list of playable chatacters that are included with the game. The next two can be downlaoded as add on content. The first downloadable character (and my favorite) is Gaige the Mechromancer. Mechromancer? What's that? Well Gaige's action skill is to summon a hulking, floating machine called "Deathtrap" to attack her enemies.
The other downloadable character is Krieg the Psycho. His action skill allows him to go on a rampage using his Buzz Axe to deal highly increased melee damage and refilling his health entirely every time he kills.
The story begins with the vault hunters answering a call from Handsome Jack to find the vault. Unfortunately it's a trap and Handsome Jack attempts to kill all the vault hunters by blowing up the train they are riding.
From that point on he constantly tries to take you out, and in turn the vault hunters try to take him out. You aren't alone though, the original vault hunters from the first game help you out periodically throughout the game. And there are a couple of twists involving certain deaths that really keep you on your toes.
Handsome Jack is a very twisted individual, but damn he is funny. This game is definately good for many laughs. Naturally Handsome Jack gets to the vault first and opens it when you arrive unleashing another giant alien creature that you have to kill. Once you kill it you get to kill Jack. In addition to the two extra characters, and countless character skins, there are also four downloadable add on campaigns.
The first one was "Captain Scarlett and Her Pirate's Booty" which, like it sounds, puts you on a treasure hunting quest.
Next was "Mr. Torgues Campaign of Carnage." The objective here was to get sponsored in an arena tournament, and of course enter the arena and leave a champion.
The third add on was "Sir Hammerlocks Big Game Hunt." It is what it sounds like, basically a safari.
And last but definately not least was "Tiny Tina's Assault On Dragon Keep." This one is the best by far. much longer and more content than the rest. The story for this add on revolves around the vault hunters from the first game and Tiny Tina playing Bunkers and Badasses, a table top paper and dice game parody to Dungeons and Dragons. The player is dropped into the Bunkers and Badass world, Tiny Tina, as the game master, narrates the story and modifies it as she sees fit. The world is fantasy themed with dragons, skeletons, orcs and giant spiders.
The graphics, sound and gameplay are very similar to the first game with some improvements. The humor and story are fantastic, keeping me interested enough to play through the game several times on different difficulty levels.
Very high replay value. I rate this one a 9/10.

Speaking of story, I love how the story is revealed in tastey morsels throughout the game’s progression instead of being crammed down your throat from start to finish. If you really want to know the whole story, you’ll have to explore every facet of the game. I’m not just talking about the terminals you find in back-alleys, but also the ability combos and enemy-modifiers you unlock. That leads me to the coolest feature of Transistor. Every ability you unlock can be used as an attack power, and enhancement of another attack power, or a passive character enhancement. This creates an amazing amalgamation of tactical planning, RPG power-leveling, and story progression.
Not terribly long but amazing enough that you’ll want a second play through.
PS Get the accompanying soundtrack if you like good music and clever writing. The lyrics in those songs that have them make further implications surrounding the events of the story.

Good Points: Core elements from Bastion’s gameplay and story are retained acting as a “spiritual” alternate universe. Transistor is much more refined, well-polished and cleaner than SuperGiant’s previous title. The game implicates relevant, political messages of man’s current struggle against technology.
Bad Points: Although visually and artistically refined in comparison to Bastion there is just less to do. The story, voice-acting and music seem more sterilized and subdued than most action adventure games.
Unique Strengths: The presentation and visual elements are some of the best in the sci-fi genre. Although not as good as his previous SuperGiant soundtrack, Darren Korb still demonstrates that he is one of the best musicians in the gaming industry. Rarely do I see such an artistic heroine (Red) in a leading role.
Gamer Tastes: Diehard SuperGiant and Bastion fans, indie-gaming enthusiasts, cyberpunk and sci-fi junkies and well…if you’re a gamer that likes kickass female leads.
Worth Buying? - If you’re an indie-gaming enthusiast who prefers the sci-fi/cyberpunk genre this is right up your alley otherwise you’re not missing much by skipping this one.
Theme: 9.5/10 – The visuals, gameplay, story, voice-acting, music all followed the same thematic direction of high science-fiction fantasy. Albeit painfully nihilistic, minimalistic and emotionless at times; these are the flag posts of any futuristic dystopia. By the end of the game you will have a strong grasp as to what Cloud City really is but more importantly what its inhabitants are. My only gripe is with the repetitive and admittedly uncreative enemy designs.
Story: 4.0/10 – The story exists in places where gamers may never venture; character profiles, kiosk dialogue boxes and the transistor’s very terse commentary (which I would not even consider voiced narration). The latter half of the game’s story feels rushed and I cared little for any characters outside of Red and the voice inside her transistor device. Musical lyrics, some sort of formally presented backstory and more dialogue in general all could have added logic to the plot but unfortunately none of this was significantly presented.
Gameplay: 9.0/10 – I have a love/hate relationship with turn based combat but fortunately it is designed very well in Transistor. Many gameplay elements were borrowed from Bastion such as the cover system, active abilities and delimiters (which have replaced relics) but everything else feels different and new. The ability to easily combine, recombine and experiment with abilities actively, passively and as weapon upgrades is done incredibly well and easily the most notable aspect of Transistor. I just wish there was a defensive and healing system that did not take away from such a well-executed combat system.
Soundtrack and Acting: 6.5/10 – High quality music and mediocre voice acting is met with failed expectations. SuperGiant Games is known for their use of voice acting and music in videogames and yet these are not strong points of Transistor, made unfortunate by the fact that your main character is a professional singer. I know what SuperGiant and Darren Korb is capable of. I just need to hear it but didn’t playing this game.
Technical Quality: 10/10 – The design of this game is mind-blowingly good. The imagery, actions, animations and visual effects are elements that could have been taken out of a well-established comic book or cartoon franchise but is SuperGiant’s original creation. If anything about Transistor is going to stick with me long after the credits it is the visuals and art direction.
Replay Value: 6.0/10 – The game plus mode and challenge rooms are directly ported mechanics from Bastion. But all-in-all there is just much less to do in comparison and generally not much to do after beating the core storyline. It is very fun to experiment with different abilities in the practice room and grind experience to gain new ones but this feels like a fleeting interest rather than anything to draw me back after the game is beaten.
Conclusion: Transistor is a good game in its own right but I’d rather return to its more likable videogame brother, Bastion. Much of Transistor’s story, gameplay and animations are spiritual successors to Bastion so it is sad to see that although it has a more focused, cleaner and understandable art direction it fails in lack of story and the distinctive voice that Darren Korb and the narration of Rucks gave Bastion. SuperGiant Games took its two strongest abilities, music and voiced narration, and merely ported them to a game that could have better utilized both. Despite these apparent weaknesses, the superb visual design, varied and tight gameplay and, though not amazing, music still puts it a cut above most independently developed games. Diehard SuperGiant, science-fiction and independent gaming fans will love Transistor, for everyone else I suggest you put it on your “play later” list of games.
Overall Score (based on an average): 7.5/10

This is one of those games that from the outside seam like nothing special, just another fps, but once you begin to play it turns out to be one of the most fun things ever.
Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a short 'All killer, no filler' arcade fps game. You are Silas Greaves - one of the fastest gunslingers in the wild west. A man who has spent most of his life in bullet-time.
This game has a unique way of telling it's story. Game starts in a saloon where Silas ends up telling his life story to a bunch of people. As he speaks you get to play through his life's events that he is narrating. Every now and again one of his listeners will interrupt Silas and tell his own version of the same story he has heard it somewhere. And that will effect the game word. The level will shift or time will rewind and the scene will play out in an entirely different manner.
Also thanks to this manner of story telling there is almost no downtime. You are always in action and the story is narrated while you are lining up headshots.
Visually this game is also neat. It may not be the most graphically advanced game around, but what it lacks in graphics it makes up with good art design. The colors are bright and sharp. Environments are beautifully designed and quite varied.
When it comes to visuals the only three sins this game commits are:
Lack of fov slider. The default fov is not terrible, but it's definitely not 90.
No anti-aliasing.
And there's a weird black border around the screen at all times.
Luckily all three of these issues can be fixed by the player. Fov and that border can be modified in a .ini file. And AA can be forced through you gpu's control panel.
And while the story mode is good and definitely worth a playthrough, where the game really shines is it's arcade mode. Arcade basically is an score attack/speedrun mode where you compete with your friends for the highest score. You get to play through more linear version of story modes levels where the objective is to kill everyone as fast as possible meanwhile maintaining a as high as possible combo.
All in all this is a short (~5h for the story mode and ~13h for a complete run) and super fun fps. If you are in a mood where you just want to shoot some people and feel super bad♥♥♥♥♥while doing it you can't go wrong with Call of Juarez Gunslinger.
