It's one of the best total war game out there in my own personal opinion.
If you enjoy controlling large armies as you crush the ai, sacking rome, and playing
diffrent factions with their own unique cultures(diffrent units) then I'd recommend this game.
It's not that hard to get into it as a new player but you may encounter some
difficulties(buildings, army comp, battle formations) at first, eventually you'll get
used to it and become decent enough to enjoy the game.
One concern of mine is how repetitive the gameplay can be especially the battles. Ai
does the same tactic every time, you attack the ai the ai sits still, the ai attacks you
it marches forward hitting your frontline along with it's attempt at flanking. Yes, a
working ai although it may seem that way but after a while it's easy to predict it's
movement becoming a little boring at times.
Sieges are fun too as long as you have a great amount of troops and hit autoresolve
because most of the time the defending force are small in numbers that it's not
worth the time. If your lucky and meet a large force then there's a challenge
you might think to face or autoresolve it like I do sometimes cos i suck at sieges.
Pyrrhic and close victories man I tell ya.
It's not impossible but make sure you have a large quantity of men that and a
brilliant army composition along with a good strategy
Also the ai likes full stacked armies so be sure to have yours stack as well.
Lastly the victory conditions, unlike other tw games it doesen't let you choose
whether you want a long, short campaign or domination. You're stucked with 3
victory conditions: military, economic, and cultural. Which is unfortunate cause
achieving one can take forever especially on your first try. I'd prefer if they had
the old victory conditions considering you'd want to try other factions as well
and by the time you did manage to try another one it felt like you've done all
there is to be done.
Tldr:
Great game
Diffrent factions with diffrent cultures(diffrent units)
Gameplay can get repetitive
Victory conditions can take a while to achieve atleast on
my first try

The concept is simple... verify everyone's documents before you let them enter your country. You are basically just a paper pusher. The 1st day is easy... so is the 2nd day... but don't think it stays that way. Each day, a new "rule" is added on what you have to check... who gets thru, who has to be searched, who is detained, etc. There is even a criminal you have to keep an eye out for. There is a little story line going on. And someone wearing a hoodie gives you a a cryptic message.... and someone may give you somehing to help decypher it, if you know how. You may even be bribed every now and then. People lie so pay attention to what they say. Make sure the picture on the passport matches the person who hands it to you. Make sure it isn't expired. After about a week, you may be having to look thru 4 or 5 pieces of paper to make sure everything is in order. Those rules that are added each day carry over to the next day, which may have other rules you have to follow..... things get hectic real fast..
You can't spend too much time verifying everything. You get paid for each person you CORRECTLY approve and let through. But if you lapprove someone that isn't supposed to go thru, you get penalized and money is taken off your paycheck. Each day ends at 6pm.Your paycheck is important... you have to pay rent, buy food, and heat for your apartment.... for you, your wife, your child and your mother-in-law. You may have to skip food for a day, or heat, and that makes it hard for your family. You may even have to decide if you are going to buy medicine for a sick family member, or pay your rent. Too many mistakes, and things get rough at home.
Don't let the 1980's graphics keep you from getting this little gem of a game. It is worth every penny.

It's not Red Dead Redemption.
It's a linear shooter that plays well but without the freedom of Red Dead Redemption and unfortunately I got bored really quickly. There is an interesting story telling mechanic where the narrator who is telling his life story keeps altering it. This leads to essentially going back to a check point but progressing down say a different road than you originally did. In the end if you want a Call of Duty style game set in the 1800s then this is your game. I've just grown tired of linear shooters.
Another note, I'm probably the only one who notices or cares but no game seems to get 19th century firearms correctly. When you reload a revolver in this game your character rotates the cylinder while placing new cartridges in but without emptying the weapon of the spent ones. On the Winchester you reload through the extraction port not the loading one, when you fire the revolver he pulls back on the hammer of the single action revolver rotating the cylinder for the next shot but if you fire to fast the gun just works without the hammer moving, black powder revolvers are loaded with cartridges yet don't seem to have been R and D converted to accept them and more.
If you buy a western then your probably looking for some sort authenticity to the weapons that never seem to find their way into westerns. The only game so far to get it right has been a futuristic game called Fallout New Vegas.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs. Well, what can i say? Being the second game after Amnesia: The Dark Descent, it has kept the same charisma of its forerunner. But many things have been changed in this game: now you don't have to pick up oil for your lantern or any item that can make light, but you have an electric lantern with infinite light; the only things you must pick up are the papers, and this aspect makes the game a bit less interesting than the precursor. Accordingly to this, you don't have an inventory anymore, and the icons of the phisical health and mental health are disappeared, and this is one of the worst points of this sequel i must say. The riddles aren't hard to solve like the ones in Dark Descent, and with the fact that you don't have an inventory, you can't bring items with you, and many times you only have to push levers or turn valves. But speaking about the positive aspects, A Machine for Pigs keeps the suspance with a very good plot and awesome musics; the monsters are well designed and the sounds that the pigs make are pretty scary. The ending was unexpected, and I was much surprised by all the philosophical concepts which are inserted into the game, expecially in the final part.
In the end, it's a good game, not good like Dark Descent, but it has its good points. Try it out, it deserves to be played.

Introduction:
Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is the first person horror sequel to Amnesia: The Dark Descent. The game is also set in the same dark and twisted universe as the previous one, though in an entirely new time setting and features a new cast. The game features a rich and breathtakingly horrifying story.
Where the first game took place in Prussia in 1839, the second installment to Amnesia is now set in London 1899 on New Year's Eve. The protagonist, Oswald Mandus, who is a wealthy industrialist and butcher, has returned from an expedition to Mexico and has contracted a fever. At the beginning of the game, Mandus finds himself awakened in his mansion from his fever, which has lasted for several months. Only guided by the voices of his two sons, Enoch and Edwin, Mandus ventures out to find them, all while they lead him deeper into the abysmal depths of London...
The story is the main drive behind the game. Exploring the dark underworld of London is a thrilling experience. However, going through the game a 2nd time is less exciting, as all of the mystery will be gone. The replayability of the game is therefore nothing to brag about.
Control & Gamplay:
Amnesia is a first person game, where the main goal is to explore and delve deeper into a frightening world, and survive. You are armed with nothing but a lantern, thus rendering you utterly helpless should you be confronted with the horrors that await you. Therefore, running and hiding are your only options. This is one of the defining elements of the game. Being unable to defend yourself, you feel constantly threatened, danger lurks behind every corner and you are always on your toes, ready to run away and hide and beg god the thing chasing you doesn't find you.
The game itself is not difficult. The real challenge is in actually daring to advance further in the game before you get another heart attack. There are no real puzzles as in the previous Amnesia game, which is a shame. The "puzzles" that are present are very obvious and annoying. For the most part, the controls are good. However, when you have to use the few items in the game, the controls can feel clunky and difficult to coordinate.
Graphics:
The visual aspect of the game is not impressive. However, the slightly dated graphics create a more gloomy and sinister atmosphere that fits very well with the overall mood of the game.
Sound:
The soundtrack is my favourite aspect of the game. It is deep and melancholic and it fits the dark and twisted mood of the game.
Conclusion:
The game offers hours of horror, mystery and heart attacks. Amnesia is a horrifying and exciting universe that must be experienced, especially under the cover of night and preferably all alone. However, in light of its predecessor, The Dark Descent, this game offers little new in terms of mechanics and features. The puzzles feel little more than inconvenient stops in the progression and they have been unnecessarily simplified. On the other hand, the story plays a more significant role, as it often comes across as eluding and perplexing. Thus, even after the credits have rolled, Amnesia will keep you pondering about what exactly has occurred throughout the course of the game.
For both old and new players to the Amnesia universe there is a twisted, yet compelling, story in wait, which is definitely worth the money.

First of all, thank you for building up such an entertaining and great game.
As a gamer the most important aspect of a game is "playability" and if it has this, it will have a long-lasting play time.
The good things about the game are, it has lots of things similar to our life. There are lots of stuff and things to make. Building part is really nice since it provides the player a wide range of materials and creativity. The voice and mic thing is really nice for Role Playing.
However, there are too many parts in game to be improved for stable playability. For instance, at first, it is not so much important to have so much items and so much graphics. In alpha version, the game could be more suitable for older computers (which I have one right now) so that more players can join and test the game without lagging and "paralyzed-screens", and freezings etc. What I mean is that the game MUST be fluent to play. This is the most important thing for many gamers. The graphics can be altered and improved later on.
Secondly, the very first thing to improve is to OPTIMIZE the game engine as soon as possible. There must be more graphical options (Medium textures i.e.). Additionally the game takes too much RAM to run, so this must be, again, fixed at the very beginnig.
I also played ROK in a more advanced computer (My brother's computer and he also has the game) but the problems are nearly the same.
To conclude, the game engine MUST be optimized so that the game can run on most of the computers (even in the older ones). This will make your game suitable for the top numbers (players). And there can be more options in character creation screen. But this is not so necessary for now.
I think this game will start a new era for "free-world type" games and when those improvements above are done, it will reach a wide number of players around the world. In my country, Turkey, I heard about the same complaints from many players. So your team should focus on the optimization.
In the future if any help needed for "Localization" ( I mean if you need Turkish Language option) I gladly help you with this.
Looking forward to see most of the problems solved in BETA!
LATEST NOTE: The game is open for hacking. So this MUST be fixed at very first so that players do not leave the game FOREVER.

I woke up on the beach and found myself fighting for nothing.  I didn't know what to do or anywhere to go.  The global chat was alight with people cussing each other over griefing and offline killings.  In games like this, that is to be expected.
Then, I start trying to find my way.  I begin building my own little ?hovel?.  As I am naked, chopping a tree down, nearly dead because of the work that my character has done, along comes this guy (looking like a gangly freak) dressed in full armor and weilding a huge 2-h sword comes through and starts attacking me.  I run toward my house thinking about diving in.  Then it dawns on me, "Don't do it, he'll get in and steal your stuff".  Well, that didn't help.  He just lock-picked his way in and stole my 570~iron, my 20+ meat, all of my wood (3k at the time) and left me for dead.
I called him a d*ck in global.  He frowny-faced me and asked "why would you call me that?".  I explained to him that his type (stealing from those who are not capable of defending themselves from him) and just ransacking for the fun of it makes him a♥♥♥♥♥♥  His response was something like, "Oh. Griefing is normal in a game like this.  I understand there are going to be power trips.
Final though:  This game is awesome!  The polish is great.  The climate is exactly what you would expect of a "Naked and Afraid al~la 1400's" setting.  I was told this was made on Unity3D, which is what I use for my development.  You guys rock!  Keep it up!

I've now played this game for several days, and I came to some conclusions:
First, the good points: the graphics are very nice, the island, even in lowest graphic level, is still beautifull. The farming system is well made and very immersive, as well as the construction mechanics which will keep you busy for hours, and the fact that you have to keep an eye on your hunger and thirst makes it even better.
But there are also a lot of points that needs improvement, and if you, game developpers, are reading this, this part is also a little for you:
the servers seems to be too weak for the increasing number of players, ths consequences are massive lags for every players on it, or players getting disconnected for no reasons, which makes it kind of annoying. the consequences are also visible on the combat parts of the game: chivalry fight mechanics are nice...if you have a VERY good connection, one lag, and it's faster to wait the finishing blow from your opponent than trying to touch him.
After the server problem, the game itself: the game, even knowing it's very immersive, and very fun when you play with your friends, is quite empty: no NPC, always the same map, the same lake in the center of the map, the same plains near the king's castle, it's boring... adding maybe a greater map, or the possibility to reach different other islands, smaller or bigger, by building boats for example, would increase the durability of the game. About the NPC, adding NPC can improve the immersive side of the game, and the interest for "teamplay": if you can associate with a village of NPC to survivre, or enter in conflict with the king guard's, it might improve the need for the players to group in order to establish themselves nicely or to take the king's castle. Or maybe by organizing events: in the trailer, you show a town destroyed by a bunch of undeads, why not make similar events in the real game too? It will add more fun to the need of building an entire base and good weapons.
The last point is the protection against hackers, which needs improvement: even knowing we now have to install "easy anti-cheat" in order to play, adding a better protection to the programs of the game can be only a good improvement, for players and developpers.
My conclusion, is also that satisfied players, and I mean by that: players who have fun, don't particularly feel the need to hack just for the pleasure of it, it works the same with the PVP: players try to hack or permanently murder every other player they meet just because they're getting bored. Think about the points I spoke and you'll see that I'm not wrong about them. Try to improve the game in order to satisfy the players, and the number of "social" problems will decrease fast.
I still recommend this game, but for now: only to people who have friends to play with, playing alone is stressfull, boring and being killed all the time by older player when you just started the game is not fun at all. If you still wants to try it, then go at it, but don't buy it right now, wait for price reductions. I regret to say it, but for now this game isn't worth his price. Day 1: Hmm... Factorio? What idiot would buy this crap? I'll give it a shot.
Day 2: I've been playing for hours now. How on earth can this game be so fun? 12:00AM Already? Dang... maybe I should stop.

Day 6: My girlfriend told me to make a choice, her or Factorio. Why would she do such a thing? Can't I love both? She gave me a day to decide. I only needed seconds.
Day 7: She looks longingly into my eyes, waiting for my final answer. I tell her I'm sorry. I simply cannot live without finishing my work. It has consumed me. I hurl myself into Factorio's strong arms, our bodies join in a Holy embrace between man and machine, it caresses my hair with it's machine-like hands, it tells me that I'm special. Oh Factorio, I will never leave you.
Day 8: The Aliens have come back again... I fixed that problem.
It's started to rain. I look up into the sky, thousands of corpses lay at my feet, I've done it, my factory is now autonomous, it no longer needs me. I wipe the remainder of purple blood from my gun as I walk towards my factory, the making of my own hands. I have done it.
The End:
The moon shines through my window, glistening on the metallic skin of the creature I have come to love so much.
"Did you like it?" it asks.
"I loved it, but now what?" I respond.
Factorio stands and extends its hand towards me, how many times have I felt those hands guide my own?
"It has only just begun, my child. Come with me, I have more to show you."
I reach out my hand, but it is no longer my own. I look into a mirror before taking that final step over the edge, I expected to see myself, but I did not. Instead, looking back at me through lifeless eyes, I saw a metallic creature. The Human Factory, everything I have ever created has led up to this, I have become a factory.

Yes, you can only hunt rabbits and mule deer with the free to play version. That's what you start hunting anyways. The sub is only 3 bucks a month and it's worth it. I have only put about 6 hours into this game and I love the scenery and detail they put into it. You can get a shotgun with in game currency that you can hunt most game with if you get slugs. However, most f2p's do require you to pay something so they can afford to keep up the game. I mean expecting a full game of this caliber for free just seems silly.
I will caution that this is not a Cabela's style arcade hunting game. You don't walk around and shoot stuff every 5 minutes. It can take hours to find yur perfect target. It just makes it more rewarding to do so.
With teh standard .243 rifle they give you it allows you to hunt a lot of game if you pay the small sub (10 bucks for 3 months is nothing). You can hunt coyotes, any kind of deer, kangaroos (yes, I said kangaroos), and foxes. Once you do the daily quests you can get a shotgun and you can hunt everything from ducks to bears.
When you hitan animal with a shot it shows what organs you hit, and if it wasn't a kill shot you can track it by the blood it leaves behind. This game accounts for everything from the wind bringing your scent to a deer to poor visibility in the raid (which the rain has varying degrees of intensity which I found really cool). You can also hear everything from mosquitos, woodpeckers, crickets, and cicadas while you're out in the wild.
So far I give it a 7/10 if you pay the minimal sub fee. DOn't let teh bad reviews fool you. You get more than a 3 bucks a month game.

This is NOT a game.  This is a game engine.  A wonderful 2D game engine that has that Cortex Command physics, pixel eating magic, kind of procedural character movement.  From the guides looks like easy to make objects and characters, LUA scripting, sharing via workshop (embedded in PNGs), level (terrain) editing with all kinds of deformations to make your round planets with caves and radial gravity (I think that's what it's called with gravity in the center of the planet), or regular gravity to make a side scrolling game or level, or no gravity for a top down game or level.
There is a learning curve, maybe more because of the LUA scripting if you are dumb like me, but so far having fun just blowing up stuff, playing with the rovers, the grappling hook, the jet pack, the different guns that are already in the game (like the bee gun).  I am going to try to learn some scripting and make something terrible.
If you like playing with game engines as much as games and have $40 burning a hole in your pocket this might be for you.  If not, just wait a couple of years for the game this engine creates.  Peace.

If you want a unique experience, this is definitely the game for you. Though there is not as much quick event actoin going on, you, being the border control agent deciding who is and isn't allowed into your country, faced with the moral choices of doing your job properly so you can pay the bills to keep your family alive versus allowing battered women with bad paperwork escape their pimps or saving political prisoners escaping an enemy nation, aren't exactly calm. You have to do everything perfectly or your superiors will simply fine you or, worse yet, fire you for incompetence, leaving you and your family to starve. Still, if you tick off the wrong people, they may not have any gripes with simply blowing up the border in search of better lives, regardless of your possible death. This game creates such a specially stressful environment when you play it that there isn't quite anything else like it, and nothing else that is as satisfying. It's not totally possible to convey the correct level of worry you get from playing this game, and, as such, I definitely recommend it to anyone interested in experiencing a game that isn't like anything else out there.

Plenty of Potential. This game is honestly been one of the better mmorpgs out there & also the true successor to RO compared to RO2. Diverse range of jobs/classes with many different ways of playing each character depending on the jobs you take (complementary or diverse its really up to you). New updates are done weekly to allow for more content to arrive & make the game more enjoyable, Lovely graphics, cute outfits, interesting in-depth story lines, & overall 10/10 fun,
However! Be prepared for lag, bugs & glitches. Due to an overwhelming increase of players since the servers opened to the public, the servers are unable to support the large amount of ppl wanting to play this game; IMC is working hard to fix this but with not much success, or is rather slow with this. Recently the lag has been reduced minimally & they have been having alot of maintenance almost daily, but there is still lag - I wont deny this. It took me 15 secs for a mana potion to take effect after consumption lol, & also had to keep switching servers to hand in quests due to lag, although this seems fixed for now.
If you have slow internet, I wouldnt recommend you playing this game at all; you can try, but probably without much success. If you are like me, & have relatively decent internet, its still doable & I would ask you to patiently try the game out with the 4 different starting jobs - you wont regret it, I assure you.
Tl;dr - Very fun, but very laggy at the same time. Play at your own risk.

I'm someone who played Ragnarok since 2004 and stopped last year because the game is basically done. Tree of Savior is definitely what RO2 should have been like and not the abomination of the game that it actually was. Lots of the negative reviews of this game focus on stuff that isn't the fault of the actual game or it's content and is instead the fault of IMC Games; things like too many bots that aren't banned, really laggy servers, and the awful way they set up the auction house and treated their community. This is valid negative feedback of the game overall but I'm much more interested in the game's systems such as classes and leveling.
- Classes and Skills
Lots of classes to choose from, almost too many, you get to choose between Archer, Cleric (has healer classes), Swordsman (has tank classes), and Wizard class trees. These trees have 13 different classes to choose from that you unlock as you level and all of them have different skills. There are also a handful of hidden classes in each tree that you can access by doing special hidden quests. Most classes can also be chosen twice or thrice as you progress through your leveling which unlocks further skills and skill buffs for that class if you like the class that much and really want to commit to it. Each class you choose also comes with a unique cosmetic costume that you can swap out for each other any time. I only have experience with the Archer tree at the moment and I was planning on turning it into a Rogue later down the class tree but I spent too many skill points in a particular skill that I should be spamming and so I run out of mana quite often. Ragnarok had a skill system where you could select which level of the skill you want to cast and this game doesn't have that so if I continue playing I'll have to play IMC to reset my skills eventually. It's very easy to screw up your character if you don't know what you're doing by putting a skill or status point in the wrong place, so do your research and make sure you know where all your points going before you start.
- Leveling and Exploration
This is one of the most beautiful worlds in this type of game I've seen in a long time and combined with the BGM it easily gives me flashbacks of Ragnarok in it's prime. In Ragnarok you would explore the world while killing monsters wherever you went, however in this game you level mostly by questing on appropriately leveled maps and receiving EXP cards that you can redeem at a later time if you wish. You get experience from monsters too but it's only optimal to grind them at certain levels and the most optimal way to use your EXP cards is at certain levels as well. In Ragnarok (before Renewal at least) you could just kill any monster and it would give you the same amount of experience and the well-populated and expansive maps meant you could farm them the whole way to max level. I feel many players liked this because you could set your own goals; you could grind your levels all night or simply a level or two a day. Tree of Savior doesn't really facilitate that because you're almost always just plodding along through endless and sometimes pointless quests without the sense that you've achieved much. This was the big turn-off for me as it made the game seem boring and I just wasn't having fun after a while. Even going back to grinding professions in WoW or skills in Runescape ended up being more fun because they have better structured reward systems.
- Summary
This game falls into the trap of the newer generation of MMOs where they try to ape other games instead of coming up with their own creative gameplay. Tree of Savior is like someone awkwardly put WoW's questing system and Ragnarok's class and skill systems in a room together and forced them to make a baby. The result was a more lame version of both. The art, music, and characters in the game are truly beautiful but that can only carry the game so far before you notice the gameplay flaws. I got bored of it because it failed to capture my attention. Will I be back? Possibly, but I've already quit games like GW2 and SWTOR for much the same reason. They try to recapture the feel of the MMOs of old in their heyday but ultimately fail. What they should be doing is trying to make a new heyday with new and creative ideas.

I think Machine for Pigs gets a bit of a bad rep from those who fell in love with the first Amnesia game, though I understand their reasoning. Machine is an entirely different beast in comparison to Amnesia: The Dark Descent since it was headed by two different teams. Machine is more story-driven and Dark Descent is geared more towards game mechanics – but both are designed to scare. It's...just in different ways.
Machine was made to horrify you more from an ethical standpoint, while Dark Descent was more visceral. While I think Machine was a beautiful, if not masterful, game, it was not the same thing as Dark Descent and affixing their story with "Amnesia" was its biggest failure. If it were a stand-alone game without the mild tie-in with the Brennenburg Formula, I think this game would have been better received by the gaming community as a whole.
Overall, I really do recommend this game a lot. It's not terribly long, but if you're looking for a good spinetingler and something that's more than jump scares (though there's plenty of those in here, too), then you should give this title a shot. Just... hold your thumb over the word "Amnesia" and you'll be fine.
+ Pros +
• Amazing story
• Tons of psychological and ethical horror
• Interesting character
• Beautiful and scary atmosphere
• Great creature design
• Great sound
- Cons -
• Being tied to the Amnesia franchise hinders an otherwise great game
• Compared to "The Dark Descent", Machine is low on the visceral scares after a while
• Length of game (4-6 hours) may be a detractor for some.
Overall: 8 out of 10

All of these negative reviews are because you do  need to pay money to play the game.  The game is awesome. For about 25 bucks you can be able to hunt all animals, and buy a shotgun and rifle package (which will let you hunt any animal in the game). For a total of 50 bucks you can get a bow too, scopes for both, tree stand, calls, etc.... Everything you need to be set up to go anywhere you want for any animal.  It probably is unfair for them to say free to play. All the negative reviews are probably right IF you are only going off of free to play and that experience.  But games cost money, and for 50 or 60 bucks, the same ammount as any other game, you will have a great experience.
Now for the actual game.
The game is a hunting simulator, and its a really, really good one. You start off at a camp of your chosing depending on where you want to hunt, and what animals you want to go after. This is where you can change your gear or swap anything out before you get going.  I bring a shotgun with the different ammo loads, and a bow.   With the bow you can shoot any animal you find. If you see it,  go for it.
From here its pretty simple... you head out into the woods and see what you can find. The game has an execellent tracking system. It doesnt take a long time to track an animal and there are plenty of animals around.   When you run across animal tracks or signs, It flags them with a red marker on screen.  You walk to the red marker and use your handheld computer/gps to ID it. It will tell you what kind of animal it is.  If you want to go find it,  follow the red markers until you get in the vicinity of it. Pop up a tree stand and start calling it, or scout around until you see it.  It works great. It takes a small ammount of paitence, but it doesnt take a long time to find animals.
The graphics are great. I have a 980, but im way over 150 fps with everything maxed.   It is very well optimised and any midrange card should be able to get great results.
Sure the game obviously wants to make money on everything, but most of that stuff is random junk you dont need. Just go ahead and accept that the game will cost a little money like every other game, and everything will be fine.

This is essentially paperwork and double checking... but I can't recommend it enough! The first time you look at your bill and have to decide how to use your meager hard-earned money, you feel the weight of the game, your family, and eventually the country. With so little on display, Paper, Please manages to suck the player into a dystopian world. While the concept may be simple, the gameplay is surprisingly deep.

tl;dr: This game is not awesome, but it captures your heart with simplicity, humour and a few sadness.
And Jorji. Don't forget about Jorji.
Papers, please is NOT your ordinary game.
Is it awesome? No. But it's interesting.
It has a simple, yet interesting story that will bore you to death if you're not interested
in stories but will keep you asking for more if you dig these stuff. I'd love it even if it is a novel.
The game mechanic is seemingly easy (check papers, deny, repeat), but it isn't.
This game actually makes you think about checking, double checking and triple checking.
Not only that, but you would also have to think about your decisions to either follow the rules or have a heart.
I just love how you can make such choice in a game. It may be just an illusion of free will, but still... (no rhyme intended)
From all the seriousness, you can also get humour, romance, thriller and suspence.
And unlike most steam games, it's so tiny! Like a mini squid girl!
This game also has a nostalgic 8-bit graphic. I love that.
But from all this great things that i said, there must be something negative!
But what?
Well, here's one:
This game is NOT for perfectionist.
Why? Because there is one citation that is forced into your face. (damn you, Jorji)
Other than that small thing, it's a pretty boring game that is totally worth your time unless you like mindless action.
I will recommend this to deep thinkers, but not RATATATATATATATATATATA-ers (FPS peeps who hates thinking)
No offense. I love you guys too.

You would never expect a game seeming as simple as this to have such a moving plot, forcing you to choose whether to help people and risk losing money or even your job or to obey the corrupt Communist goverment in order to keep your job and keep your family alive. It was suspicious enough after Bastion that the guys at Supergiant know something. This game has ambience, immense fun, fine-grained control of difficulty implemented as an in-game feature, different play styles and combos, etc.

A brilliant piece of work. I would really want to spend an afternoon in the Sandbox() with the developers just talking.

Art, music, voice work all what you'd expect from the folks who made Bastion. I love the focus on configuration, enabling you to put together your own moves and combinations thereof. It can be played as a straight action game if you wish,  but it's meant to be played as a sort of hybrid between that and turn-based combat.
But it's short... very short.  The story feels like it should have been two or three times longer than it was.
There's a new game plus type mode enabling you to start with all the stuff you had at the end of the first play through, but unless you stack on limitations (which give you more XP in return for increased difficulty) it's a cakewalk, even though the enemy is much more powerful. And, of course, NGP mode doesn't really replace having a long first game, especially for those of us who aren't really interested in replays...
That said, it's not a bad game at all - it just doesn't live up to it's potential.
Verdict: Get it on sale.

I tried Terraria, it was alright. The learning curve was pretty steep, and I had trouble playing on my own without help from the internet. I stopped playing because I didn't find any element of replayability or growth, something I value a lot in my indie build-em-up games.
I saw this game on my Discovery Queue, almost discarded it because it looked at first glance like a Starbound or Terraria clone. Hooooooo boy its a rougelike. The game starts out like a point-and-click defense game, and progresses nicely into a challenge of supply and demand as you try to develop your own automation systems and efficient material transports. You can play it for hours just trying to make a stable steel factory.
I can expect loads more playtime from this, and their world generation options are perfect for changing what kind of game you want to play. There are actually no bugs or performance issues I have experienced at all, other than some slightly large GUIs which can be shrunk in options for oddly-sized screens. There aren't a ton of requirements on the system, either. I can run Factorio on a Surface 3 for hours without lag or crazy battery drain, and multiplayer has been awesome as well.

First of all, I played the game on difficulty 2/3 (middle, since 3/3 was not unlocked from the beginning [-]).
Let's start with the positive:
+ Narrative story telling during and between missions.
+ Comic like looks/graphics.
+ Different play styles (story and challenges).
+ Different skill trees (pistols, long range, close combat).
+ Duels, in which you have to control your hand for speed to reach your gun and focus on the enemy.
+/- Fast paced gameplay (see below).
That's about it, which is more than just sad, it is pathetic for a gaming series with history like this. Now the very bad
of it:
- Overpowered AI (if you can still call it that), which shoots you as soon as any part of your body pops out of cover or around an unsuspecting corner - or you stand behind thick bushes. This often means instant death.
- Quick time events everywhere, which lead to death when not perfectly performed.
- Awfully linear levels, which do not allow one single step of the path, or else it is either death or invisible walls for you.
- Although levels are painfully linear, it is often not clear, where a before not visible path will open up. This can be more than stressful, when under fire.
- Skills help you very restrictively (more ammo, faster reload and stuff like that) and thus are more a gimmick than real help.
- Killing enemies "honorably" (= let them draw their guns first) in duels often seems impossible. This might be due to the percentage for drawing speed and accuracy, which you have to crank up while keeping your hand near the gun (via keyboard) and your focus on the center mass of the enemy (via mouse). Sometimes I had the feeling, that there was just a mm wide discrepancy of either increasing percentage or lowering it tremendously. Plus, mouse movement was delayed so that you could not follow your enemy accordingly, when he took a step to the side, which resulted in fast dropping percentage for your accuracy.
- Boss fights are uninspired. It is basically "take cover and let them discharge their magazine on you, then take action". Action meaning either throwing dynamite, shooting them multiple times or just approaching them until they give up. Between all that, you always have to crouch down and wait for the hail of bullets to end. Otherwise you'll die within two to three rounds hitting you. Now, this would be fair if the game wasn't so fast paced.
- As I mentioned it: Fast paced gameplay. This is good on the one hand, because it suggests action and pressure. But it fails with the overpowered AI, the unclear pathing, the unfair hit&shoot system (cover, cover, cover, shoot, etc) and overall overpowered weaponry.
- Totally confusing HUD. Broad black frames (mostly on top and bottom of your monitor to underline the narrative story telling), "Found a secret" message clear over your crosshair so you can't see anything anymore for several seconds, Mission objective marker (which should be set to "permanent" under options) is elusive, arcade messages ("long shot", "headshot", "running shot", etc) pop up everywhere and blend in with the coloful graphics.
- Bullet time events triggered by the player deplet so fast, you can only hit 3-4 enemies. The skill tree does not help here either.
I think, that is about it. I might have forgotten minor negative aspects, but you get the picture. I wished for a game more like the second Call of Juarez or even the first, which was mighty better! Instead, we got a dead clone of a Wolfenstein original, which can not live up to its potential.

A textbook case of trying too hard. I hoped I'd have learned by now that when the vast majority of user reviews cites a game's story as a strong point without any concrete supporting reasons, it typically means that the story is, in actuality, flawed and whatever quality makes it that way is masked by other elements of the game such as music, atmosphere, visuals and other story-enhancing elements that aren't actually part of the story.
It's not hard to see why a lot of people would like this game. The skill system is incredibly clever in its simplicity, variety and potency. It's the only game I've ever played where I haven't found a single skill to be useless or ineffective. This system alone merits praise and hopefully future emulation. The visuals are enchanting and the score haunting and every other superficial and mechanical element is in place to make someone enjoy this game...but beyond that is where things fall apart.
The mystery of the story stretched all the way into my apathy as by the time the world revealed itself sufficiently, I had long stopped caring. It's not impossible to successfully push the exposition of a mystery all the way to the end, but there needs to be adequate engagement in the interim and SuperGiant did not provide. All they gave was an empty world with only the skeletons of characters, minimally fleshed out and ultimately not meriting sympathy or interest.
Worst of all, the conflict made ZERO sense. *PSEUDO-SPOILER* High ranking public servants from the "government" plot to imprison influential, celebrity figures with the goal of abolishing a capricious democracy that renders their work meaningless. *END SPOILER* Are you kidding me? Government drones have an existential crisis and accidentally destroy a city? They should've known when they took their posts that government is ineffective and should be dissolved. In all seriousness though, no suspension of disbelief can make me take this plot seriously. It's like if a waiter reflected on the pointlessness of his job and decided to imprison all restaurant owners to end the drudgery of waiting forever. It just doesn't make sense! And the heroes are a singer and her talking-sword-lover, niether of whom had sufficient backstory to make me care about their relationship?!?...fighting against an army of robots who are just doing their job at the behest of a NON-VILLAIN who accidentally let them run wild?!?!?!?! All of this adds up to a conflict that simply doesn't exist, let alone make sense and all the beautiful music and scenery couldn't pull me back into this heap.
The last - and a minor grievance - is that the gameplay, even the walking speed, could've been a little faster. It felt almost like a turn-based strategy game that ran too fast or an action game that moved too slow.
The most effective stories have a simple premise but are delivered effectively with relatable, interesting, sympathetic characters as the agents of delivery. Transistor had an overwrought premise and failed to deliver it on all fronts and that's what I call trying too hard. Might be worth a purchase at $5 just to see some of the clever ideas implemented and, for aspiring story writers: how NOT to deliver a story. For me, it was too disappointing and even the sale price of $10 now feels like a cold slap in the groin.

Transistor, like Bastion, is one of those games where if someone asked you if games were really art, you'd point them straight here. Stunning visuals and captivating music makes Transistor one of the most aesthetically pleasing games I've played. However, a game isn't all visuals of course. Transistor's gameplay is easy to pick up and diverse, with a system that allows and encourages the player to combine abilities in different ways, with a difficulty system decided by the player with the use of "limiters". Although Transistor has many good points, there are some flaws. The game is short, around 4 hours for me, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but can leave some players wanting for more. There are some challenges to complete and a NG+ which I haven't played yet, but the main story is over quite quickly. Speaking of the story, the story is very vague. Many parts of the story I was lost at, especially the final battle, which didn't make any sense at the time. The story is heavily dependent on the player's intepretation and isn't quite clear, which can turn some players off. All in all, this game is something I'd recommend. If you liked Bastion, you'd definitely love this game, and if you haven't played Bastion, play Bastion, and then play this game. 9/10

I did not wish for the 6 hours of my life back, but I do hold a lot of issue with this game.
When I went into Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs (from here on referred to as MfP) I expected an exploration, suspense game that utilizes mechanics in order to protray a story. Would I say MfP is /not/ that game? No. It is that game, but the mechanics in MfP were poorly designed at best, the story was not adequately portrayed for how complicated it was, and the suspense was lacklustre at best.
This game, first of all, does not follow in anyway the mechanics from Dark Decent. There is no sanity, so the player has the wonderful ability to really focus on the story and watch it unfold. The joke is absolutely on you though because you can't do anything with this new found freedom except read the same note style plot entries in a terrible font just like DD. The notes make it so all plot points are exposed to the player equally. Major or minor, significant or non. This means that perhaps thorughout the game I was a bit confused because I didn't disect every inch of every note along the way.
In the beginning I felt I was given a lot of information. There were a lot of monologues from our protagonist, but as the game progressed the monologues decreased in frequency and so did my understanding of the plot. As the chapters progressed past about 5 or 6 the monologues stopped and the information flow basically ceased. We learned about the slaughtering process, the components of Compound X, how the pig people are taken care of, but none of these are really /plot/ related. So at this point you are 10 or 11 chapters in (out of 17) and you STILL don't know why you are here. You are looking for your children in a slaughterhouse or a sewer because that's where children go, right? There's someone trying to break the machinery and you need to fix it to get your kids which are trapped in it? These things are logical gaps in story-telling that made continuing forward infuriating at times. Lack of tangible character motivation is inexcusable, tell me why I'm here. It should have been laid out at the beginning of the game who you are and what the machine was to you so that the twist that occurs 3/4 of the way through was even bigger and hit the player even harder.
It is inexcusable to have a luck-of-the-draw, guesswork level. And that was the pitch-black pig level. You can't use your lantern, there are no lights. Good luck. It's never scary, it legitimately stupid and lazy on the designers and I nearly gave up playing at that point.
Mechanics. Mechanics, mechanics, mechanics. You have the constant and readily available ability to pick up and rotate chairs, but WHY? This is wasted effort. This is wasted time and money and it is a useless mechanic in a game that really could have used a few more mechanics to it. You have a lantern, the lantern flickers when there's a threat, that's a good mechanic, but then you can't use it when you need it. Playing in complete darkness is not scary, it's not suspenseful and it's JUST. NOT. FUN. I feel like Chinese Room and Frictional forgot halfway through that they were making a game. Do not make me play in darkness when your settings are so neat. Your doing both you and I a major disservice. There were times you need to pick something up and bring it somewhere and I relished those times. A GAME. FINALLY. But they were rare. There were times the surroundings played tricks with your mind and I awaited moments like those around every corner but they were fleeting and infrequent.
My ultimate review for this game is that I wanted more. I wanted more cutscenes, deeper plot drops, and better portrayal of information. I loved the story, I loved the setting, but you made me somehow come out of it frustrated and confused. This game had a ton of wasted potential.
It would be wrong of me to harp on the negative solely so I'll briefly touch on the positive.
This game had several awesome, beautifully designed and intricate settings. The slaughterhouse parts, the machine cores, the streets, the house, were all very very well done. I am impressed with the design capabilities of this developer and I appreciate their hard work in creating a town built above the pits of hell.
The story, in and of itself, was very compelling. I loved reading about the slaughter process, the machine's past and birth lurred me in like a siren's song, Mandus's sickness and later insanity was a welcome disturbance in what would normally be a boring rescue plot. I loved this story, I wish that it could have been told to me in a deeper way given its inherent depth.
The length of the game was perfect for what it was. It could be played in about 4-6 hours and that's exactly about as long as I was willing to put up with it. Well done cutting the cord before I hit the uninstall button out of infuriating frustration.
The nuances. Though the game did a poor job at getting them across to the player, the story's nuances are truly brilliant. Read the wiki or steam forums because the story itself is rather lovely and much of it gets lost in gameplay.

I don't get why everyone is complaining about the fact that you have to pay to play most of the game, that's a normal thing these days.
If you bother to pay (and you won't pay more than a normal game to get 3 months plus a good range of gear - and then it's really cheap to renew your licence whenever you miss the game), it's an AMAZING BEAUTIFUL hunting game. It really is ultra real, and if you are opposed to hunting real animals but can see the fun otherwise, then this is the game for you.
It's the only game where you will WALK, and even crawl most of the time and enjoy it. It's a game that makes good finds rare, so when they come they are really rewarding, and challenging. There's a thrill in hunting an animal across the gorgeous (huge) maps and making sure you don't spook it.
You also get to hunt with friends, which is a great pasttime. Grab a beer, get a good microphone and head out into nature with your buddies and enjoy good, old fashioned, manly hunting!
Try it, it's free to try (THATS THE POINT), and you do get to go on a great map and hunt a deer that's as fun as all the other animals. You can even go on the other maps and find other animals, you just can't shoot them (but you can photograph them and see if you want to invest).
Ignore the spoiled brats that want everything free and give this game a go :)
p.s. I've played for over 100 hours, via the website rather than steam ;)

You're free to move around the scene of mayhem as you wish, while all kinds of bandits are shooting at you. Other than that, it's rather linear, but the story is accompanied with your character relating about what's happening in past tense, telling some folk about his deeds.

This game is truly brilliant. At it's core, it's an action-RPG with the ability to stop time and plan out your next sequence of moves, then execute that sequence at hyper-speed. As you play, you will earn or find new abilities (functions), and each one can be equipped either as an active function (press a button and do a thing), an upgrade to another function, or as a passive bonus. The number of possible combinations is near-infinite, and the game really requires and rewards experimentation. The plot, setting and characters are wonderful. Despite the game's relatively short length (around 10-12 hours, probably), I would recommend taking it easy and letting the game breathe. The intracacies of the plot and gameplay can be subtle and vague, and if you try to burn through the game quickly, you will probably miss quite a bit. Take the time to explore, experiment and take in the world and story, and I guarantee you will love Transistor.
Beautiful graphics, haunting music, an engaging combat system, and an ending that made me weep (mostly in a good way). I would definately recommend it.

Another banger by Supergiant Games.
Let me start by saying that Transistor's music is absoultely fantastic. It's composed by Darren Korb (also did the soundtrack for Bastion) it has a futuristic feel to it with a little bit of Noir in there. It's also neatly integrated into the game and its story. The protagonist is a singer for crying out loud.
Her name's Red, she's a singer, and her friend is now a talking sword. That's all you get at the begining of the game. Transistor's story is open ended, surprisingly heartfelt and imaginative. There are no clear-cut solutions or ideologies, the characters have their (sometimes questionable) motives, and it's hard to say what's what at times. The game is also very subtle about its themes. Very much like Bastion, you can speculate and fill in the gaps with your friends. Fun stuff.
Much like the story, the gameplay is brilliantly crafted and also very much open ended. Every bit of it is customisable, and the game makes you feel like you're in control of its systems. To simplify it- it's a real time action RPG. By pressing the right trigger you change it to a turn based structure, but it's more of a special power. The "turn" lasts only a short while but you can trample over the enemies without consequences as they are frozen in time, and you have a bunch of tools that can do the trampling.
Red has a large selection of abilities to chose from, each ability has three functions- active, powerup and passive. You can attach unused abilities as powerups for the ones that are active, or you can use them as passive powerups for your statistics. Some abilities deal damage, some persuade, some create distance between you and the enemy, which you will need, as the enemies are tricky to handle (when they're not frozen in time that is). You will have to mix and match, see what works best, and then change it again. The game encourages experimentation- change your character's presets as many times as you want, it's easy and free of charge. The game's too forgiving? Obliterating enemies left and right? You can make the enemies harder and gain more experience. It's all customisable. Supergiant Games definitely built upon the already well made systems seen in Bastion and greatly improved them.
Heck, the whole thing's really well made. And, well, gosh darnit. Ain't this the prettiest darn game I have ever laid my blue eyes upon. This game's graphics are something special, tell you hwat. Inspired by Art Deco, its futuristic vistas are just... Just beautiful. A little bit confuisng to get through at times perhaps, but with these looks, hey, who's complaining.
The only criticism I have is that its story is too short. Now don't get me wrong, the story is really well made and doesn't drag, but you can finish it in 5-6 hours. Now, that's great, I like a well made story, if it has to be around 6 hours to present itself the right way, the way the author intended, great. but you WILL want to play more of it after you've seen the ending, and it is a shame that you will have to start up New Game+ to do so.
The good news is that the New Game+ mode is really well made and has some additional stuff in it. Everything transfers and the difficulty ramps up. Heck, they even change up the enemy spawns, so it's definitely worth a second playthrough. Plus- there's no way you're going to reach the level cap during your first run through Thransistor, so there's a bunch of new stuff you'll get to play with.
Well, that's a minor gripe, this is A+ material for sure. It's obvious that these guys know what they're doing, and every part of this game has been meticulously crafted with much passion and hard work. Whatcha gonna do next Kasavin? Cause whatever it is, I'm listening.

Ladies and gentlemen, I present you the most understated review in the history of gaming:
Papers please: Not great graphics, interesting gamelay.
Imagine the finest of AAA games run on machines mere mortals can't afford yet and showing you the ultimate humanity can provide in pixelated exellence. Now look at the screenshots for the game and appreciate that I described the graphics (which you could probably run on a 1970's era digital watch) as not great.
Now note I still called the gameplay 'interesting'.
If you appreciate the understatement, buy the game
If you don't, buy the game anyway, note how rubbish it looks compared to how cool it is and learn to appreciate understatement.

A textbook case of trying too hard. I hoped I'd have learned by now that when the vast majority of user reviews cites a game's story as a strong point without any concrete supporting reasons, it typically means that the story is, in actuality, flawed and whatever quality makes it that way is masked by other elements of the game such as music, atmosphere, visuals and other story-enhancing elements that aren't actually part of the story.
It's not hard to see why a lot of people would like this game. The skill system is incredibly clever in its simplicity, variety and potency. It's the only game I've ever played where I haven't found a single skill to be useless or ineffective. This system alone merits praise and hopefully future emulation. The visuals are enchanting and the score haunting and every other superficial and mechanical element is in place to make someone enjoy this game...but beyond that is where things fall apart.
The mystery of the story stretched all the way into my apathy as by the time the world revealed itself sufficiently, I had long stopped caring. It's not impossible to successfully push the exposition of a mystery all the way to the end, but there needs to be adequate engagement in the interim and SuperGiant did not provide. All they gave was an empty world with only the skeletons of characters, minimally fleshed out and ultimately not meriting sympathy or interest.
Worst of all, the conflict made ZERO sense. *PSEUDO-SPOILER* High ranking public servants from the "government" plot to imprison influential, celebrity figures with the goal of abolishing a capricious democracy that renders their work meaningless. *END SPOILER* Are you kidding me? Government drones have an existential crisis and accidentally destroy a city? They should've known when they took their posts that government is ineffective and should be dissolved. In all seriousness though, no suspension of disbelief can make me take this plot seriously. It's like if a waiter reflected on the pointlessness of his job and decided to imprison all restaurant owners to end the drudgery of waiting forever. It just doesn't make sense! And the heroes are a singer and her talking-sword-lover, niether of whom had sufficient backstory to make me care about their relationship?!?...fighting against an army of robots who are just doing their job at the behest of a NON-VILLAIN who accidentally let them run wild?!?!?!?! All of this adds up to a conflict that simply doesn't exist, let alone make sense and all the beautiful music and scenery couldn't pull me back into this heap.
The last - and a minor grievance - is that the gameplay, even the walking speed, could've been a little faster. It felt almost like a turn-based strategy game that ran too fast or an action game that moved too slow.
The most effective stories have a simple premise but are delivered effectively with relatable, interesting, sympathetic characters as the agents of delivery. Transistor had an overwrought premise and failed to deliver it on all fronts and that's what I call trying too hard. Might be worth a purchase at $5 just to see some of the clever ideas implemented and, for aspiring story writers: how NOT to deliver a story. For me, it was too disappointing and even the sale price of $10 now feels like a cold slap in the groin.

, which celebrated its 1-year anniversary last week, is described as “a dystopian document thriller” – quite an intriguing mouthful for a game description, but nonetheless a very fitting description for a truly unique game. Heavily influenced by the border systems present during World War II,
introduces the player to the communist state of Arstotzka, which recently ended a 6-year war with its neighbors and otherwise reclaimed its rightful half of the border town, Grestin.
Winning the lottery would be a nice thing – everywhere but in Arstotzka and in Shirley Jackson’s novel. Unlike Jackson’s novel however, the player gets to live after winning the lottery, but they are forced to take the job as an immigration inspector. And without further ado or formal introduction, day one starts and the player has to face foreigners wanting to immigrate and citizens wishing to return – all with both poor and good attempts to cross the border and (re-)enter Arstotzka.
The gameplay appears extremely simple, but as the game progresses and more regulations are added to the border-security and immigration processes, the harder and more complex the game becomes. The player has to ensure details ranging from name, day-of-birth, sex and passport number to appearance, height and work pass’ are in correct order. Should the player fail to do so, more than three times per shift, a penalty is applied which ultimately hits the player hard as they are under a massive pressure to support a wife, mother-in-law, son and uncle with food, heat, medicine and shelter.
This ultimately introduces a great range of moral choices – should the player bend the rules after hearing some visitor’s heartbreaking stories and let them enter; knowing the consequences? A few achievements are in fact challenging the player’s moral stance – for instance, should an aging woman be allowed to visit her son despite having discrepancy in her papers? Similar, as the entry requirements tightens – following the significant increase in terrorist attacks inside Arstotzka against the oppressive government – more people may be detained. The choice, however, ultimately lays with the player – but as the nearby guard continues to declare his willingness to share his payment, which happens to be based on the amount of detains, the more tempted the player becomes. It becomes a simple matter of survival and thus prioritization.
An interesting aspect to Papers, Please is the sound effects, audio and graphics. There are no identifiable voices (in any language), but rather extremely robotic and inhumane voices – something which follows the unidentifiable, gender less and anonymous queue outside the inspector booth. Both elements together with the Kafkaesque, colourless and overall dystopian environment greatly amplifies the alienation between the state and the people.
The lack of human compassion is stunning, but perhaps very fitting for a totalitarian bureaucracy which values the state above everything and everyone. This, once again, introduces the player’s role – no action is inconsequential, and with every coin having two sides nothing is just black and white. Yet the player is ultimately the only one who can question the procedures and do the unexpected and unwanted; show compassion and empathy. The choices will ultimately impact the player’s family directly as illnesses, hunger and cold all follows rapidly though.
is in truth a unique game which pokes to the player’s moral and human compassion. It introduces the player to a very special and dystopian environment which, if allowed, greatly influences the player. It is not a game for everyone, but those who wishes to find a raw pearl within the ocean of indie-games and for those who treasures great narrative and design, this is the game.

One of the best zombie games out there. Online co-op game based on killing zombies and completing missions.
Achievements are good, most of them being "Get 250 kills with ____" and "Complete ____(map)". Maps are well constructed.
There are two main gamemodes, NMO and NMS. NMO is a story-based gamemode where your task is to complete missions around the map while trying to not get caught by zombie hordes. NMS is a survival-based gamemode where you camp at the map for usually 12 waves of zombies defending three areas, A, B and C. Each area has 100% hp, but whenever a zombie steps on the area the percentage drains. Each wave gets harder and harder with more advanced zombies. These are perfect gamemodes for players to team up to survive and complete achievements.
You search around the map for weapons to use against the zombies. The game has its bugs but overall it's enjoyable.
This is one of my favorite co-op games and I definitely recommend it. 9/10

When I started playing A Machine for Pigs, I expected for it to maintain the mechanics from The Dark Descent. However, upon grabbing the lantern, I knew that this was going to be a horse of a different color. Unlike The Dark Descent, this game focuses more on its admittedly complecated story and does not have as many tense enemy moments. There is no item conservation, no oil, no health pickups, no sanity meter, and no direct connection to the first game. Unless you do some research, you will never find the connection between both Amnesia games. It's almost like the creators made a new game, but slapped Amnesia on the title just to lure fans of the original. The levels are more linear than the first game, so you may be disappointed that there is not a lot to explore. There is also the missing option to directly access custom stories from the main menu. In fact, this whole game is like a custom story that you would download for the first Amnesia.
If the game has these problems, why am I still recommending it? For one thing, it does have some pretty creepy moments. I found the factory setting to be gritty and atmospheric, almost like you could see the filth and decay that it is going through. If you were to think of how blood would crust up and stain the metal cogs and pipes of the machine, you would be in the right mindframe. Sound design is also great, as you will sometimes hear things from seemlingly nowhere. I played with headphones to immerse myself in the game, and that turned out to be a good choice. It wasn't a bad play, but it just doesn't measure up to the tense, dark, and forboding nature of the original Amnesia. For curiousity's sake, it's worth a play. Even if it is just for the familiar Amnesia atmosphere. However, I suggest that you buy this when it is on sale. I got it half-off around the holidays. In retrospect, that was a better choice because had I paid full price, I probably wouldn't be as forgiving to the game.
In conclusion, this game does not meet the same knee-jerk horror of the first one. It is average, but throws in some really good moments. If you are a die-hard Amnesia fan, you can skip this one. It does not have the same impact as the first game. If you are a fan of atmospheric, creepy-looking games, you would probably get some enjoyment out of it. Just wait for the game to go on sale. It is not worth $19.99.

To sum up this page of text, if stories could sell, this game would be worth it despite its ok-ish gameplay. And in many ways stories do sell, just look at the Telltale Games' "Walking Dead" game. However people were expecting a game that "one ups" the previous game, Amnesia: The Dark Descent. It doesn't as far as scare factor goes, however it makes up in story. With that being said, be sure to buy this on a steam sale. It's worth atleast $10, maybe $15.
Gameplay is lacking, it’s definantly a step back from the previous game in that department. And the previous one wasn't particularly scary either. At least they tried however! There are some moments in this game where the level was seemingly designed for patrolling monster areas. It’s confusing!  Also the puzzles, which were also not hard in the first one, were laughable in the second. Really they were not puzzles, just impediments for your "walking sim" (see tags). With a grain of salt however it isn't particularly bad, the setting gives a lot of flavor and variety. Making the walking trip a little bit more enjoyable.
The "H. P. Lovecraftian" story and setting are top-notch; it's very disturbing, tragic, and contemplative. If only stories could sell alone. Clearly you don't need a good one in the case of "Outlast," great gameplay with genuine moments that can make you jump. However the story is... well... let’s just hope that the prequel DLC will have a good one. Although in retrospect the comparison between the two games is like comparing a campy movie and a book in the horror genre section. Getting back to Amnesia. Some of exposition in the pages in game probably should have been addressed in dialogue. There are needlessly vague plot points which are very relevant on how this came about and link directly to the previous Amnesia title. There are a group of people out there who ignore this exposition (A few sentences are just too much for them unfortunately). The dialogue does needlessly beats around the bush at times as well.
Graphics; are not all that impressive. Lot of little details, but some of the textures are not great, clothe seems to be a particular problem. But then again this category was never a selling point, it is enough that it creates a level of immersion that doesn't take you out of the moment. The running movements however for some of the models were a bit clunky. Primarily because of how they were shaped (it just doesn't look like they were meant to run).
The music is also good and very memorable in the parts they were used.  Although there was this moment when the music was too good and didn't fit with the clunky movements on screen (The "Mors Praematura" and London scene, this scene really shows the graphical limitations of running models). The voice acting was very good also, even though were some lines late in the game which were a bit rusty in execution. But I am just being nit-picky in that regard. It is enough that you can sympathize with Mandus in his tragic quest.
Overall Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs leaves much to be desired in gameplay, but the gameplay isn't particular bad. The story was good enough for me to recommend this title. It’s that good. Not to overhype it or anything, but when this game hits a steam sale… buy it, the journey into the depths of despair and desperation is worth it.

FAIR WARNING: THERE WILL NOT BE A TL,DR TO THIS REVIEW.
I am not a beginner at the game, nor have I been playing it for years. I am writing this from a "I have been playing this for a month or two" perspective.
I am going to try to write a serious, honest review about this game.
This game is not Free-to-Play. Do not think that it is. It is free to download, however. Although, to have a positive experience in this program, you will NEED to invest in the game. At the bottom of this review will be what I reccomend you invest in, in order, to have a legitimate, enjoyable experience with the game.
Now, I'm gonna explain the game.
At the very start of the game, you are allowed to kill three species of animals: Mule Deer, Pheasants, and Cottontail Rabbits. You also get one firearm: a .243 caliber bolt-ation rifle. This rifle, however, can only LEGALLY kill one of the animals I have listed, meaning you can only get a real score from Mule Deer. The .243 rifle is simply too powerful to qualify for pheasants and rabbits. At the very start, you can only successfully hunt one species.
Now, you can either go the F2P-grind route, or the "I'll pitch in a few bucks" route. If you choose to be Purely F2P, you will be forced to do missions and receive gm$ to advance in the game. With gm$ you can buy consumables, and one firearm on the market: a crappy single-shot-shotgun, along with individual licenses. Now, to DO these mission, you will need licenses to kill animals in the mission, which probably cost 700gm$ EACH. FOR SEVEN DAYS. AND THERE ARE PROBABLY MULTIPLE ANIMALS TO KILL IN EACH MISSION. NOT TO MENTION 700GM$ IS ALREADY WORTH MORE THAN COMPLETING JUST ONE MISSION. Trying to play the F2P will just be like bending over backwards. You're stuck with bad guns, it's a grind, and guess what? There is no mission looping. If you plan to thrive off of just missions and buying♥♥♥♥♥♥with just gm$, eventually you will have to pay EIGHT DOLLARS to reset all missions just so you can continue being "F2P".
Now, if you have a few dollars to spare, and I mean this, the game becomes enjoyable. The game is fun. Especially when you have friends to hunt with. It becomes a game of coordination, technique, and risk. And you know what? Once you buy firearms, they are there forever, but only as a member will you have infinite ammo. So after you pitch in as much money as you feel satisfied with, you only need to buy new memberships as long as you feel like you enjoy the game.
All in all, "Is it a good game?" Yes. I enjoy it a lot. Why? I don't know. Something about it is pleasurable. It isnt the most visually appealing, but when you spot a crazy looking deer and you nail it in the heart, there is a sense of satifsaftion that you will get that you don't recieve on an everyday basis. I reccomend this game because of the things like that that happen in-game. Also, there is a certain level of variety in the antler system of all animals that piques my interest. I don't know, the antler system is interesting. Random generation is fun, right?
Get it, put a couple bucks in, enjoy this game. It is definitely fun.
Now here's the shopping list:
1. Wayfarer bundle (NOT OFF STEAM) Includes a nice shotgun (can legally kill anything in the game), includes a three month membership, a .357 which is basically a lighter-weight .243, a hat(non-significant), and a turkey caller. 15$
2. A "Parker-Python" bow. Silent, one of the most fun mechanics in the game is bowhunting. Doesn't spook animals, can also kill every animals in the game, and effectively. $7.
3. A set of clothes that protects against all deer species. This should be bought in a bundle. Trapper, Army clothing, Doc Mosignor, or B&C Bundle. $6.84
4. Some callers, to lure in animals. depending on which you choose to buy: $1.30-$2 each. One of the most valuable buys in the game.
---
At this point these buys are just to put more money in the funnel, but these are the more valuable things you should purchase if you have money to burn.
7mm Magnum Bullpup Rifle--$6
Rangefinder scope for bow mention earlier (SO USEFUL)--$3.50
.22 Plinkington Rifle--$5.50
x3-x9 scope for both rifles mentioned--$3.50
OK. Shopping list over.

Quests have to be found manually, especially side quests but this encourages exploration. The game offers a lot more than just quests though, a lot of other options to explore hidden treasures or puzzles and hunting world bosses with friends is most enjoyable.
All in all its a typical MMORPG which even hardcore players would love it, grind is a typical aspect of any online games, if you don't like grinding than you typically don't like MMORPGs so I don't recommend it. Beginners should prepare to research and test class simulation which is available online if you google it and plan ahead, lots of guides and leveling strategies can help.

Call of Juarez is a western-themed arcade FPS game that succeeds at being one thing above all else: fun. This game is incredibly far from a realistic depiction of cowboys, but the sheer fun of it all makes up for it tenfold.
Silas Greaves is also a fantastic protagonist and narrator, bringing with his whiskey-soaked narration a sense of personal bond that grows steadily until the final act of the game. I'd recommend this game at full price, but if it goes on a good sale, I'd 100% recommend it with zero doubts.
