From the makers of bastion comes transistor, a short but unique experience of action and turn based rpg combined into one package. I love bastion and I have looked forward to this game for awhile. My first impression is the game feels like bastion right away because of the voice accompanying you throughout the game and also the artstyle certainly resembles bastion's as well. The strongest aspect of the game is definitely the atmosphere and the story for me. They are unlike any other games I have seen in a long while.
I do not want to spoil the story much, but basically you play as Red, a singer and her boyfriend, a talking sword. You are on a journey to uncover strange happenings around town. The story focuses on a slightly dark scifi theme and a love theme on the side with a dash of light humor. There is somewhat a typical save the world scenario but it is not cliched that much, and I still enjoy the unpredictability up until the very end.
The music sounds contemporary which you might find intriguing. However for me, they do no evoke much emotions, only slight admiration from me. But they suit the game's atmosphere very well! You can unlock the music player by completing tests, similar to dreams in bastion.
Controls feel abit awkward at first because the game does not really explain them well at first. But once you get used  to it, it is not bad at all. You will do fine with mouse and keyboard without a gamepad or joystick. The controls are quite similar to your standard MMO. 4 active skillslots assigned to 1 to 4, and use your mouse to move. There are alternative ways to do it, but i think that is the way to go.
The gameplay feels a little weak compared to bastion simply because it feels like it is caught between action and turn based. Aside from being a standard action rpg like bastion, here you have the option to freeze the game and take all day to decide your next moves while your enemy stands waiting. However, using this option will disable most of your skills for a certain period of time after you finish, leaving you vulnerable (can be bypassed with skill setup). This feature is optional to use throughout the game and you can finish the game without it, with the exception of the final battle.  The beauty here is that you can tailor your skill build to suit your playing style, similar to bastion. Want to play it like a turn based rpg or action rpg? Tune your skills to suit your playing style. Personally I chose to play it like a normal action rpg instead of turn based intuitively, and sorry to say bastion is better here. I think this game is better played turn based style, where you can experiment with alot of different combos. Or you can certainly do both!
You can increase the difficulty of the game according to your taste just like bastion. Except they call it limiters here and you gain bonus xp as the difficulty increases.
The replayability is low because the game is very short and does not have any sidequests other than the tests, similar to the dreams in bastion. You can play the game from the beginning again carrying over your level and skills. The enemy levels up as you do this time. THe maximum level is 30 and easily achieved on the 2nd playthrough if you keep the difficulty high. What is also missing is the scoring system, which also lowers replayability.
Overall this game is short because it is meant to be a low budget game, with minimal to no animation during the story cutscenes and minimal content. However the game is worth your money because even though it is a short game, it is a good one and thus worth experiencing.

Easily one of the best games I've ever played.
Here's my SPOILER-FREE review.
Visually, Transistor is like a dream. Everything looks so smooth and real. The game is very efficient at telling us what kind of a city Cloudbank is.
Story is kept quite vague until the very end. But the telling of the story is unbelievably good. The story is told through a bunch of different characters, so to discover both these people's stories AND the game's main story, you'll have to try a vast number of ability combinations. Boom, linear/boring gameplay dead. Right there.
Red is not a very relatable character. She's an artist, whom even couldn't be understood by the people of Cloudbank. But this just adds to her character, because Transistor is also about discovering Red's identity and personality.
Transistor's fighting system, while seeming repetitive, actually one of the best and most fun fighting systems out there right now. It's quite easy to keep it from being repetitive and cross-combining functions create some very, VERY fun action. It's the fighting system I always wanted to have, but didn't know I wanted it until I've played it.
...and the sounds. Let's just say here that SuperGiant Games knows what they're doing when it comes to creating music & voice over for their games. I feel I have to compare the sounds & music to Bastion, of which OST I still listen to frequently. Transistor's music didn't hit me as hard as Bastion's did. But the overall ambience of the game and the type of story-telling SG chose for this game didn't require it to. The songs are not very specific as they were in Bastion (e.g Zulf's Theme) but rather make a very good background. They fit the scenes very well, and I can't compliment Ashley Barrett & Darren Korb on that enough.
I'm going to talk about Logan Cunningham now. Logan does an AMAZING job. He's more than a narrator this time, he's a "companion character"(Logan's own words) and he makes us feel everything that happens in Cloudbank and around Red.
Overall, Transistor successfully weaves the city and its story around you. Awesome visuals and art, a great and vague story, a very fun combat system and a soundtrack as great as always.
As a SuperGiant Games fan, I expected a lot from this game, especially after a masterpiece like Bastion, and they still managed to overwhelm me with Red's story.

I preordered this game hoping that it would be just as fun and immersive as the first one. Wow, was I wrong. I beat the game in under 2 hours the first time and then proceeded to play it two more times all the way through before uninstalling it. (I have 4 hours on record at this time). This game was simply too easy. They limited the things you could interact with to items that were significant to the puzzles or the back story. NOTHING ELSE! You couldn't even pick up a chair. To make things worse, out of the 5 or so encounters with the monsters, every single one of them was very easy to pass, seeing as they would only chase you in a certain (VERY small) area and couldn't even do things such as break down doors. Dying was also easily avoidable because it took the monsters up to 5 hits to kill you. If you still aren't convinced, they took away the oil lantern and replaced it with a lantern that NEVER runs out. Not only that, but you no longer have an insanity level, so run around in the dark and stare at the monsters to your hearts content. I wont go in depth with the story, but I will say that the ending was not worth the little amount of game time it takes to reach it. It leaves you with too many questions and includes a small twist that most people will see coming. As for getting this game yourself? NO! Never! Amnesia:  A Machine for Pigs is far more of a story-driven adventure than the first installment.  The developers have stripped away the inventory system, as well as the need to find candles and oil for your lantern, and focused entirely on telling the story of Mandus.  While I appreciate the thought that went into the story -- which is hard to comment on without ruining the game -- I found this installment a disappointment overall.  The puzzles (if you can call them that) were extremely simple.  There was no feeling of dread or genuine fright like in the first Amnesia game.  The unlimited oil in the lantern takes away from the experience, and having no need of inventory or most importantly -- the sanity -- leaves this game shallow in the end.  It was so easy that I only died once because of a geometry/clipping issue where I went through a wall and fell out of the game, into a sea of texture maps.  Rarely do you encounter any monsters in this game, and when you do, I few quick turns is all that is needed to lose them.  I applaud the voice acting, the score was decent, but the actual gameplay is no longer here.

Overall, this game is really good, for me. The game is mostly straight to the point and is a really good stress free game. This game is a great time waster, and fits my exact taste. It's not the best decorating game, but it is a very good one. The point of the game is to go around town decorating the insides of buildings for people. Each person wanting their house done are all unique in their own ways and each person wanting their house down, has likes and dislikes. For example one person may love the color blue, while another may hate the color blue. The more likes and dislikes you find out about a place, the better. You see, finding out what a person likes will help guide you to getting a better rating on a house, which means you'll get more gems. Finding out the dislikes in a house will help keep you from using it, as using disliked items will decrease your overall rating (or sometimes an item will be both liked and disliked, if this happens it can go either way. If the item is more disliked it will decrease the score, but if the item is more liked it will increase the score)
Depending on what you like vs dislike, you may not find any interest in this game. I can't speak for you, but I know that I love this game. Of course, to every good game theres flaws and things I don't like, but we'll get to those later. First, here are the things I like about the game!
Now onto suggestions on things that I think would make the game funner
The Crafting Studio ~ Depending on how much gems you have, you can go into the crafting studio and make furniture yourself. You'll be able to alter the looks to fit your taste, and you'll be able to design a pattern or used a previously designed pattern for it. I think this will make the game both more challenging and also more fun!
Your own house ~ I like decorating things to my own taste sometimes. Us players should have a house to do exactly that. Maybe a mansion or something so we can design room after room. That would be fun :) I've always loved decorating in general, but every once in a while I like to decorate something that I too can appreciate
City Events ~ In this game, there should be certain events that happen at random. For example a surprise birthday party for a citizen in the game, and you'll be in charge for decorating the party. Or anything that fit's that line. Maybe a wedding, you're called as the wedding planner and get to decorate the cake, the wedding dress for the bride, etc. I think that would be a fun opportunity for the player to earn some quick cash.
Being able to change the grid size so we can place more items around a place ~ I think it would be super fun to be able to change the grid size of the location you are in, then you will be able to have more room to place items instead of being stuck to placing one item per one square. I think you should be free to choose where exactly you would like to place an item, instead of being stuck to sticking with placing items specific parts of the house only.

Nice decorating game and the price is right. From what I read this game is similar to Animal Crossing: Happy Home Designer though I haven't played it myself to make comparisons.
The game offers up a room with a description of what the owner is looking for and a checklist of clearly explained wants. Completing these gives you currency to buy booster packs which gives 10 random items. You can go further and test different items to find hidden likes/dislikes of the owner - things like color, types of furniture (chair, wall decoration), the theme set the item belongs in, etc. - and try to get the like meter above other thresholds for more boosters after the basic tasks for each room. I feel like the descriptions and wants from the owner get more interesting as you unlock more areas.
More houses and buying repeats of items unlocked from boosters costs gems - currency you earn over time depending on the like meter for each house. It's most likely a design carried over from the mobile game but micro transactions didn't come with. The price of repeat items can get expensive and forces a bit of variety from you.
The artstyle is what it is - you can tell if you'll enjoy it or not from screens. There's only one track but options to mute music/sound effects. Menus are simple to navigate and placing furniture is easy. There's a bit of replay value here - I've been going back through earlier decorated homes when my choice of furniture was extremely limited and fulfilling the requests with furniture that went together better.
My biggest complaint would be finding the hidden likes/dislikes when going for the extra rewards. Sometimes the description gives you hints but besides that I have to keep dropping in different items hoping I hit something. Being able to talk to the owner and ask some generic questions for hints would really help here.
Would I recommend the game? If you're interested at all in the premise of the game then yes.

It's not a bad game, one I'd rank as a 5 or 6/10, and it is fairly cheap.
It plays a little like a puzzle game - you have to decorate houses and there are hidden likes and dislikes which differ for each house.  As you place furniture you expose what those likes and dislikes are.  The more points you make from likes, the more gems the house produces, and dislikes lower your score causing the gems produced to go down.  You then spend those gems to unlock new houses to decorate, and to purchase furniture that you have already unlocked in the catalogue.
In order to unlock new furniture types for use you have to open packs of cards which will give you random pieces of furniture.  You get exactly one piece of furniture for each card you recieve, so recieving duplicate cards just gives you more of that same piece to use in your houses.  Once you have recieved a card of a piece of furniture you can go ahead and use gems to buy more of that piece so that you can place it in different houses, or several in the same house.  The price for buying more furniture raises every time you buy a piece, so it is a good idea to be frugal and wait until you find more cards of that piece than to just keep buying repeats over and over again.
You can not, however, buy booster packs of furniture cards with the gems you earn.  You can only buy the booster packs with pearls.  The houses that you decorate will have a list of objectives to complete and there are 3 rewards to earn for each house by completing those objectives.  You are then rewarded either pearls or booster packs for those objectives.
You have a very limited stock of furniture to use from the start, so you have to use that furniture wisely to make enough gems to unlock more houses.  Many times you can't finish a house's objectives until you have opened up a new location and earned more booster packs.  So in the beginning of the game decorating each house uses a lot more strategy.  As you progress through the game, it becomes easier and easier, but then you can actually start to customize the houses with certain looks as you have a wider selection available to you.
It's not a very indepth game, there are no villagers to interact with, there are no people in the game at all.  When you open a new location there is a general note on what the owners are looking for and then you just experiment with placing furniture from there until you have exposed enough of the likes and dislikes to successfully complete each house.  It's definitely an "Animal Crossing: Happy Home Designer"-Lite game, but at a low price (a decent deal if you find it on sale) it's not a bad time waster for an afternoon.

I highly recommend and can see myself sinking some hours into this :)

Good game, just like Animal Crossing: Happy Home Designer. You spend all of your time developing houses and adding unlocked furniture you either purchase with gems (which you earn from other houses you've developed), or by getting duplicates from booster packs (which you earn for meeting certain goals when developing a house).
Although the game can be fun, I do have a few complaints. After an hour of play, the game feels incredibly repetitive. There is no difficulty increase further in the game, you simply need to meet a new set of main objectives per house, and you'll be rewarded the exact same. You sometimes get stuck with optional goals where you have to go gain more booster packs to unlock needed furniture (on one stage you need a red chair for an optional objective, but none are guarenteed to be unlocked right away). There is also literally nothing else to do but decorate homes. No interaction with villagers, the home owner, or anything, which is where I see it lacking comparted to Happy Home Designer.
Some things I think need to be ironed out are how some items that are disliked are not removable (on one level, you get penalized for black rocks, but can't remove the black rocks). Also the powerup system is weird, where you can upgrade your gem gain without any cost to you (seems like when it was ported the cost was just removed, but the benfits stayed). You are also presented with an option to "get more pearls", although nothing happens.
Overall, the game is alright, just repetitive, and has a few issues since it was ported from iOS. I see getting a few more hours out of playing the game before I get bored with it.

, which celebrated its 1-year anniversary last week, is described as “a dystopian document thriller” – quite an intriguing mouthful for a game description, but nonetheless a very fitting description for a truly unique game. Heavily influenced by the border systems present during World War II,
introduces the player to the communist state of Arstotzka, which recently ended a 6-year war with its neighbors and otherwise reclaimed its rightful half of the border town, Grestin.
Winning the lottery would be a nice thing – everywhere but in Arstotzka and in Shirley Jackson’s novel. Unlike Jackson’s novel however, the player gets to live after winning the lottery, but they are forced to take the job as an immigration inspector. And without further ado or formal introduction, day one starts and the player has to face foreigners wanting to immigrate and citizens wishing to return – all with both poor and good attempts to cross the border and (re-)enter Arstotzka.
The gameplay appears extremely simple, but as the game progresses and more regulations are added to the border-security and immigration processes, the harder and more complex the game becomes. The player has to ensure details ranging from name, day-of-birth, sex and passport number to appearance, height and work pass’ are in correct order. Should the player fail to do so, more than three times per shift, a penalty is applied which ultimately hits the player hard as they are under a massive pressure to support a wife, mother-in-law, son and uncle with food, heat, medicine and shelter.
This ultimately introduces a great range of moral choices – should the player bend the rules after hearing some visitor’s heartbreaking stories and let them enter; knowing the consequences? A few achievements are in fact challenging the player’s moral stance – for instance, should an aging woman be allowed to visit her son despite having discrepancy in her papers? Similar, as the entry requirements tightens – following the significant increase in terrorist attacks inside Arstotzka against the oppressive government – more people may be detained. The choice, however, ultimately lays with the player – but as the nearby guard continues to declare his willingness to share his payment, which happens to be based on the amount of detains, the more tempted the player becomes. It becomes a simple matter of survival and thus prioritization.
An interesting aspect to Papers, Please is the sound effects, audio and graphics. There are no identifiable voices (in any language), but rather extremely robotic and inhumane voices – something which follows the unidentifiable, gender less and anonymous queue outside the inspector booth. Both elements together with the Kafkaesque, colourless and overall dystopian environment greatly amplifies the alienation between the state and the people.
The lack of human compassion is stunning, but perhaps very fitting for a totalitarian bureaucracy which values the state above everything and everyone. This, once again, introduces the player’s role – no action is inconsequential, and with every coin having two sides nothing is just black and white. Yet the player is ultimately the only one who can question the procedures and do the unexpected and unwanted; show compassion and empathy. The choices will ultimately impact the player’s family directly as illnesses, hunger and cold all follows rapidly though.
is in truth a unique game which pokes to the player’s moral and human compassion. It introduces the player to a very special and dystopian environment which, if allowed, greatly influences the player. It is not a game for everyone, but those who wishes to find a raw pearl within the ocean of indie-games and for those who treasures great narrative and design, this is the game.
Glory to Arstotzka.

As I have reached 100 hours in this game, I thought I should share my thoughts.
Factorio is a great game that allows you to create and design your own factories and you have to keep trying to improve to adapt to the new needs when you expand.  A typical day goes like this:
I dream about how to improve my factory.  Send help.

Assuming for some reason you skipped the game description, Factorio is all about building an incredibly efficient logistics network. You're stranded on an alien world and your only hope is to get a distress satellite into orbit to call for help. The trouble is, you don't have the technology to do so. Your logistics network will expand and evolve as you research new technologies necessary to build the rocket and satellite, and you'll be making "friends" with the locals along the way (handshakes are done in the form of bullets).
It really isn't though. Because you start off with only basic technologies, part of the fun of playing this game comes from unlocking higher-tier technologies and implementing them to boost your production speed and capacity. As you progress, you'll be unlocking high-speed conveyer belts, logically operated machines, automated cargo trains, and even a fully functional drone network that can auto-repair damage done by the locals, as well as getting stuff from A to B where there's no room for conveyer belts.
As your production begins to grow in scale, the local population will have more and more bones to pick with you. At first, you can keep them at bay with the starting pistol, but as your production scales up and you eliminate more waves of them with your automated defenses, they'll learn how to protect themselves and attack your defenses much more effectively. As such, you will have to dedicate some of your resources to improving and expanding your defenses.
As a strategy, you will have to decide whether your mounted turret focus will be bullet-fed turrets or laser turrets. The laser turrets are definitely easier to maintain, being that all they require is a power supply, but they consume a LOT of power. The bullet-fed turrets don't consume any power directly, but making the bullets and getting them to each of the turrets in an automated fashion is a material-expensive process (or if you use robots, energy expensive). You might think using both is easy, but each type of turret has a different set of research jobs to upgrade its functionality. So you can either research a max-out on one type, or be only partially upgraded on both. So for the sake of resources, stick with one turret type.
This game will challenge you for a long time to achieve a successful launch in a single world (my shortest success time was 29 hours). It's challenging and at the same time very fun because of all the different ways you can attempt to solve the same problem. My only complaints are that the UI is somewhat lackluster, and the object sprites are lower resolution than is desired on a 1080p monitor. Also, since it's in Early Access and still evolving, the Campaign missions are a bit broken, but that should be getting fixed soon.

This game has to be discussed from both "pay to play" and "free to play" sides. Although this game mostly gets negative feedbacks i will tell m oppinion about the "pay to play" aspect to give the dedicated players an idea of whether this is a good game or not. But before a few things about the game.
The Hunter:
- Beautiful graphics, nicely optimalised to older pc s
- A wide variety of weapons
- Lots of species
- Anatomy, you have to aim
- Realistic there isnt animals in every corner
"Pay to play" option:
Ok... to experience this aspect you have to pay some money for a membership. With a membership you will be eligible to hunt every animals in the game. If you think through the monthly price is not so high, it s totally acceptable. You could buy the shotgun in the shop listed for ingame money, but other than that you cannot buy any weapons or sights, or you could spend some more money on weapons and sights, callers etc. These are really overpriced products, but if you want to enjoy the game you have to do it. After this part you can enjoy the game fully and be able to play the best hunter game in the world. Sure you can spend more money as new weapons come into the store but you can always use the old ones, just choose wisely. The paying community is mostly friendly.
"Free to play" option:
I wouldnt recommend this game as free to play. What you can download is a demo of the game. You can hunt mule deers and rabbits. That should be enough for you to decide if you want to pay for it or not. If you wont pay for it then it s not really a good game, you will get bored fast.
What i recommend for the game is to remove the free to play label, and label it as a demo. Most of the negative feedbacks comes from people who didnt read the limitations and found out ingame that they cannot hunt anything other than mule deer.

I suspect this is the worst game I'll ever recommend.
I was so excited for this game. I read developer interviews talking about how the game would be dynamic and different every time because of the highly advanced AI alien adversary. lol. The alien AI is the worst of both worlds: the scripted parts (and it is unfortunately heavily scripted/static) are ♥♥♥♥♥♥ jump scares, and the non-scripted parts have stupid rules that lead to apparently idiotic alien behavior.
The scripted and non-scripted systems seem to contradict each other. For example, the alien teleports behind running players and instantly kills them, it will break into rooms and lockers with seeming omniscience, and it will pace back and forth next to your hiding spot using its omniscience - meanwhile during scripted jump scares it will drop down right in front of you and not turn around. More than once the alien would drop from an air vent, jump back into the air vent, and then drop back down immediately caught in some kind of loop. During a segment of the game where the alien was supposed to be scripted with heightened aggression (I believe), I repelled the alien with the flame thrower and it literally returned less than 5 sceonds later through a doorway in front of me. The AI is honestly garbage and I can't believe there are players out there that think it's good. The game felt less like outsmarting an opponent and more like being punished for running or waiting on broken automatic doors to let you into the store.
About as bad as the alien AI was the NPC models and animations that look like they were mocapped from melting, flaming Chuck E Cheese robots. I might not have noticed the huge disparity in quality if it had not been for the fact that...
The art direction, graphics, and level design in this game are ♥♥♥♥ing gorgeous. This one factor is so impressive that it's enough for me to muster through the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game play just to see everything in the environment.
tl;dr This game is not fun to play, but you should really crank the graphics up and have a look at it. It's like being in the movies.

From the makers of bastion comes transistor, a short but unique experience of action and turn based rpg combined into one package. I love bastion and I have looked forward to this game for awhile. My first impression is the game feels like bastion right away because of the voice accompanying you throughout the game and also the artstyle certainly resembles bastion's as well. The strongest aspect of the game is definitely the atmosphere and the story for me. They are unlike any other games I have seen in a long while.
I do not want to spoil the story much, but basically you play as Red, a singer and her boyfriend, a talking sword. You are on a journey to uncover strange happenings around town. The story focuses on a slightly dark scifi theme and a love theme on the side with a dash of light humor. There is somewhat a typical save the world scenario but it is not cliched that much, and I still enjoy the unpredictability up until the very end.
The music sounds contemporary which you might find intriguing. However for me, they do no evoke much emotions, only slight admiration from me. But they suit the game's atmosphere very well! You can unlock the music player by completing tests, similar to dreams in bastion.
Controls feel abit awkward at first because the game does not really explain them well at first. But once you get used  to it, it is not bad at all. You will do fine with mouse and keyboard without a gamepad or joystick. The controls are quite similar to your standard MMO. 4 active skillslots assigned to 1 to 4, and use your mouse to move. There are alternative ways to do it, but i think that is the way to go.
The gameplay feels a little weak compared to bastion simply because it feels like it is caught between action and turn based. Aside from being a standard action rpg like bastion, here you have the option to freeze the game and take all day to decide your next moves while your enemy stands waiting. However, using this option will disable most of your skills for a certain period of time after you finish, leaving you vulnerable (can be bypassed with skill setup). This feature is optional to use throughout the game and you can finish the game without it, with the exception of the final battle.  The beauty here is that you can tailor your skill build to suit your playing style, similar to bastion. Want to play it like a turn based rpg or action rpg? Tune your skills to suit your playing style. Personally I chose to play it like a normal action rpg instead of turn based intuitively, and sorry to say bastion is better here. I think this game is better played turn based style, where you can experiment with alot of different combos. Or you can certainly do both!
You can increase the difficulty of the game according to your taste just like bastion. Except they call it limiters here and you gain bonus xp as the difficulty increases.
The replayability is low because the game is very short and does not have any sidequests other than the tests, similar to the dreams in bastion. You can play the game from the beginning again carrying over your level and skills. The enemy levels up as you do this time. THe maximum level is 30 and easily achieved on the 2nd playthrough if you keep the difficulty high. What is also missing is the scoring system, which also lowers replayability.
Overall this game is short because it is meant to be a low budget game, with minimal to no animation during the story cutscenes and minimal content. However the game is worth your money because even though it is a short game, it is a good one and thus worth experiencing.

Easily one of the best games I've ever played.
Here's my SPOILER-FREE review.
Visually, Transistor is like a dream. Everything looks so smooth and real. The game is very efficient at telling us what kind of a city Cloudbank is.
Story is kept quite vague until the very end. But the telling of the story is unbelievably good. The story is told through a bunch of different characters, so to discover both these people's stories AND the game's main story, you'll have to try a vast number of ability combinations. Boom, linear/boring gameplay dead. Right there.
Red is not a very relatable character. She's an artist, whom even couldn't be understood by the people of Cloudbank. But this just adds to her character, because Transistor is also about discovering Red's identity and personality.
Transistor's fighting system, while seeming repetitive, actually one of the best and most fun fighting systems out there right now. It's quite easy to keep it from being repetitive and cross-combining functions create some very, VERY fun action. It's the fighting system I always wanted to have, but didn't know I wanted it until I've played it.
...and the sounds. Let's just say here that SuperGiant Games knows what they're doing when it comes to creating music & voice over for their games. I feel I have to compare the sounds & music to Bastion, of which OST I still listen to frequently. Transistor's music didn't hit me as hard as Bastion's did. But the overall ambience of the game and the type of story-telling SG chose for this game didn't require it to. The songs are not very specific as they were in Bastion (e.g Zulf's Theme) but rather make a very good background. They fit the scenes very well, and I can't compliment Ashley Barrett & Darren Korb on that enough.
I'm going to talk about Logan Cunningham now. Logan does an AMAZING job. He's more than a narrator this time, he's a "companion character"(Logan's own words) and he makes us feel everything that happens in Cloudbank and around Red.
Overall, Transistor successfully weaves the city and its story around you. Awesome visuals and art, a great and vague story, a very fun combat system and a soundtrack as great as always.
As a SuperGiant Games fan, I expected a lot from this game, especially after a masterpiece like Bastion, and they still managed to overwhelm me with Red's story.

Since I just did a review on a bad zombie game and the great George Romero passed away recently I'd figured I come back to this game and do a good review, this game is great in so many ways so to make this easier let's go down a list
The zombies, they are slow but hit hard and can quickly overwhelm you if you corner yourself or if there are just simply too many of them, that is exactly how I like my zombies, while games like Left 4 Dead did cool mutant zombies this gos back to the roots of zombies and does them perfectly, the zombies also look like zombies too, there wasn't a single zombie model I disliked, I also love how there are little kid zombies, that is something I've always wanted to see in games and it makes this game that much darker, the only zombie lore this game doesn't follow is the headshots only rule which is strange considering this game takes place in Romeros universe however headshots do a ton more damage than body shots, I'll let it slide because it is a video game and makes sense in that respect, if I had one gripe about the zombies it would be there aren't enough models, over time I saw a lot of repeating models however this is something most if not all zombie games suffer from so it won't affect my score, 10/10
The Survivors, I love how this game has multiple survivors and voices to choose from, that is a great way of doing it, I do wish some of the models were better and hopefully if this game gets more popluar you could add more character models? That would be awesome, I'll give them a 9/10 but only because a couple of the models had texture issues.
The game modes and maps, there are 2 game modes, a classic survival mode and a more linear objective mode, both are great, tbh I don't know which I like more, Survival mode is easier but Objective mode feels more like a normal game. most if not all of the maps that come with the game are excellent and most fan made ones are good or at least decent there's even a Night of The Living Dead and Day of the Dead map (with a Bub cameo), there is a mall map too but it isn't the mall from Dawn of the Dead but that's ok, the maps provide great atmosphere with help from the music which is also pretty good and atmospheric, I must say bravo developers bravo indeed, another big prop I have to give this game is that it allows you to play by yourself, the last game I played didn't and that sucked, I don't always want to play with people and in the zompocalypse sometimes..Hell a lot of times you'd probably be on your own. 10/10
The weaponry and other items, The weapons in this game are great and pretty various, everything from a kitchen knife to an Automatic shotgun to 3 seperate types of Grenades are in this game, while there isn't a ton of gun variaty there is enough to keep everyone happy and even have several player preferences, it even has a bow and arrow which is easily one of the best but hardest weapons to use. Other items include Flashlights, Hammers and Boards to board up doorways and windows, and medical supplys such as first aid kits to heal, bandages to stop bleeding damage, pills to stave off infection for a decent time and a sort of Anti-zombie epipen that completly cures you of the virus, all of these items play an essential role in surviving, there aren't so many items that it gets confusing but there's also not a lack of items either, there is just enough, another pro of items is that you can't use them if you don't need them, this saves players from wasting stuff which is great, 10/10
Gameplay and mechanics, there aren't many noticable mechanics tbh, it's mostly your typical FPS, grab a weapon, aim, and fire, use items when needed, and do whatever you have to do to survive, the few mechanics that are fresh and somewhat original are being able to board up doors and windows, this is a great mechanic and nice throw back to Night of The Living Dead, another interesting mechanic is that you can hit a button to check your ammo, literally your character takes the clip out and will say how much ammo is left very nice touch, the final and pretty unique mechanic I like is that you have the option to blow your brains out, if you hit K while holding a gun your character will put it under their chin, everything gos pretty quiet, press the mouse button and BAM! you commit suicide, I gotta say this is fantastic game design for 2 reasons, 1 because in the zompocalypse a lot of people would do this, whether out of fear of trying to survive or being cornered by zombies and not wanting to be eaten alive, or because of infection and not wanting to turn. 2 because most games wouldn't have the balls to put this mechanic in, it's a very dark thing most devs wouldn't want in their games, luckily this is a mod game and doesn't have to follow most video game ettiquete.
Overall this is probably one of if not THE best FPS zombie game I have ever played, I love everything about it, it's basic but not too basic, it isn't perfect things in the game could be expanded on but as it stands now it's a very solid game, I've seen big name game companys put out games MMMUUUUUUUCH worse than this in the past 6 or 7 years alone, I highly encourage zombie fans to play this and I also highly encourage the Devs to keep working on this game, with enough support this could become a big game, I'd rate it 11/10, I think George would be proud of this game, if he were still alive and knew of this game he might even support it, R.I.P George Romero.

So ... review time :D, this is the best survival horror game in existence in my opinion. The best game I have played in years.
This was the first game that made me stay under a table for 45 minutes because the patrolling alien had me too terrified to move. It takes you a while to get used to the alien.
To keep this short (or long):
- SPPAAAAAAAACCCE
- awesome experience
- it makes you feel like you're 'playing' the very first alien movie
- mixes the environment with the story really well (again, reminds me of the first alien movie)
- the AI's for the alien are excellent - yes AI's because there are multiple systems that drive the alien
- the alien can really understand your play style and adapt to it - this is more visible on the hardest difficulty level
- the alien can be very unpredictable at times
- don't believe you are Rambo ... start with the lowest or normal difficulty level, starting a first time playthrough on the hardest difficulty level can become frustrating at times
- really good attention to details - very few bugs are present in the game
- whoever made the sounds (SFX) and music for this game deserves a lot of credit, the experience is amazing
- you literally get scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ just from the sounds
- the atmosphere this game has is ... unbelievably well done (I think I've already said this a few times by now)
- the game is created on the CATHODE engine, developed by The Creative Assembly specifically for Alien Isolation in order to handle the sheer amount of lights throughout the game
- the game looks amazing - I wish more developers have this level of quality in their games, really well polished
- the game is optimized very well to use most hardware available on the market, I've played it maxed out @4k using an R9 290, a GTX 1070 and higher than 4k (5120 by 2160) using a GTX 1080Ti and the game was smooth as butter
- has ultrawide support, and mixed with a maxed out FOV - mmm ... very nice
- the achievements (yes, I'm that type of player that collects achievements) are really well done, in my first playthrough i managed to get 41 out of 50 - without having to look on the list to see 'extra' things that i can do along the way
- high replay value, by the time you see the credits ... there's a big chance you'll want to play it again on a different difficulty setting
Speaking of bugs because there are a few (nothing is perfect right ?), there is the occasional alien getting stuck in the vents, humans that occasionally can't see you unless you get really close to them, clipping issues ... etc, however, none of these are present often enough to ruin the experience.
Overall, I highly recommend this game.

Gameplay and Mechanics: 8/10
-There are two methods to combat: Live and Paused. Live is satisfying with the timings, and the game pressures you into thinking on your feet fairly well. You gotta learn from your mistakes before you make them twice or you're gonna really pay for it. Paused combat is triggered by hitting the space bar or when your life bar almost ran out, and it turns the fast-paced One Vs All arena into a more manageable form that lets you plan an amount of action (which can vary) to unleash by unpausing. The benefits are that every action that you loaded while paused will happen so fast, there's almost no opportunity to miss or for the opponent to react, all but ensuring the maximum damage possible (while also being a reliable defensive measure), depending on where you Paused and what your options are. The penalty for Pausing, however, are a global cooldown timer that will count down until you can perform another function. The fludity of these two modes work together in a very satisfying way, and lets you customize your play. Will you smash through the gates and crash through your enemies? Will you go guerrilla and engage the enemy with hit and run tactics? Or will you meticulously plot your onslaught, ensuring maximum carnage while also pathing your way out?
What kept it from rating higher with me is the kind of limited, linear use for several funcions. For example, Get() entices you to engage from a distance, but that distance is shorter than other safer and more rewarding functions. Some others just have a bit too high of a price to pay for their use. As in, cast times and cooldowns. Functions with long casts could have just had a cooldown instead. Would have saved a life.

The lack of interactive characters actually eccentuated the feeling and depth of the game, and really brought the world building to life in a "soft candle lights, guiding you home and warming you along the way" feel, as opposed to "you awaken abruptly to a blinding flashlight piercing your eyelids. An officer asks you your business and directs you where you, or he, think(s) you need to be".
My only complaint was the lack of content, and the somewhat abrupt ending. I still felt like there was so much more I needed to do, wanted to do, and having played Bastion, I ended up just assuming what I was looking for would find me when the time was right. Finishing this game is like finishing any book or series that has a place in your heart: It leaves you wanting more.

Since I just did a review on a bad zombie game and the great George Romero passed away recently I'd figured I come back to this game and do a good review, this game is great in so many ways so to make this easier let's go down a list
The zombies, they are slow but hit hard and can quickly overwhelm you if you corner yourself or if there are just simply too many of them, that is exactly how I like my zombies, while games like Left 4 Dead did cool mutant zombies this gos back to the roots of zombies and does them perfectly, the zombies also look like zombies too, there wasn't a single zombie model I disliked, I also love how there are little kid zombies, that is something I've always wanted to see in games and it makes this game that much darker, the only zombie lore this game doesn't follow is the headshots only rule which is strange considering this game takes place in Romeros universe however headshots do a ton more damage than body shots, I'll let it slide because it is a video game and makes sense in that respect, if I had one gripe about the zombies it would be there aren't enough models, over time I saw a lot of repeating models however this is something most if not all zombie games suffer from so it won't affect my score, 10/10
The Survivors, I love how this game has multiple survivors and voices to choose from, that is a great way of doing it, I do wish some of the models were better and hopefully if this game gets more popluar you could add more character models? That would be awesome, I'll give them a 9/10 but only because a couple of the models had texture issues.
The game modes and maps, there are 2 game modes, a classic survival mode and a more linear objective mode, both are great, tbh I don't know which I like more, Survival mode is easier but Objective mode feels more like a normal game. most if not all of the maps that come with the game are excellent and most fan made ones are good or at least decent there's even a Night of The Living Dead and Day of the Dead map (with a Bub cameo), there is a mall map too but it isn't the mall from Dawn of the Dead but that's ok, the maps provide great atmosphere with help from the music which is also pretty good and atmospheric, I must say bravo developers bravo indeed, another big prop I have to give this game is that it allows you to play by yourself, the last game I played didn't and that sucked, I don't always want to play with people and in the zompocalypse sometimes..Hell a lot of times you'd probably be on your own. 10/10
The weaponry and other items, The weapons in this game are great and pretty various, everything from a kitchen knife to an Automatic shotgun to 3 seperate types of Grenades are in this game, while there isn't a ton of gun variaty there is enough to keep everyone happy and even have several player preferences, it even has a bow and arrow which is easily one of the best but hardest weapons to use. Other items include Flashlights, Hammers and Boards to board up doorways and windows, and medical supplys such as first aid kits to heal, bandages to stop bleeding damage, pills to stave off infection for a decent time and a sort of Anti-zombie epipen that completly cures you of the virus, all of these items play an essential role in surviving, there aren't so many items that it gets confusing but there's also not a lack of items either, there is just enough, another pro of items is that you can't use them if you don't need them, this saves players from wasting stuff which is great, 10/10
Gameplay and mechanics, there aren't many noticable mechanics tbh, it's mostly your typical FPS, grab a weapon, aim, and fire, use items when needed, and do whatever you have to do to survive, the few mechanics that are fresh and somewhat original are being able to board up doors and windows, this is a great mechanic and nice throw back to Night of The Living Dead, another interesting mechanic is that you can hit a button to check your ammo, literally your character takes the clip out and will say how much ammo is left very nice touch, the final and pretty unique mechanic I like is that you have the option to blow your brains out, if you hit K while holding a gun your character will put it under their chin, everything gos pretty quiet, press the mouse button and BAM! you commit suicide, I gotta say this is fantastic game design for 2 reasons, 1 because in the zompocalypse a lot of people would do this, whether out of fear of trying to survive or being cornered by zombies and not wanting to be eaten alive, or because of infection and not wanting to turn. 2 because most games wouldn't have the balls to put this mechanic in, it's a very dark thing most devs wouldn't want in their games, luckily this is a mod game and doesn't have to follow most video game ettiquete.
Overall this is probably one of if not THE best FPS zombie game I have ever played, I love everything about it, it's basic but not too basic, it isn't perfect things in the game could be expanded on but as it stands now it's a very solid game, I've seen big name game companys put out games MMMUUUUUUUCH worse than this in the past 6 or 7 years alone, I highly encourage zombie fans to play this and I also highly encourage the Devs to keep working on this game, with enough support this could become a big game, I'd rate it 11/10, I think George would be proud of this game, if he were still alive and knew of this game he might even support it, R.I.P George Romero.

If i hadto choose between League of Legends and SMITE, I would choose SMITE because it plays better and has a better flow as a game. 4) Competition is fun, friendly but the downside is people may get annoyed if you take their kill.  Honestly this is one downside to all MOBA's and that bugs me, I kill someone I kill someone it's not my issue if someone else wanted the kill.  This i find annoying but a fact of life with MOBA's, and thus part of why it is not my cup of tea.  The emphasis here is winning and not really having fun, I play for fun not to always win.
So overall a GREAT game but not my cup of tea, reccomend you even try it to see if you like it.  If you like it awesome, but I cannot knock this as a bad game even if I do not like it as a player.  As long as you know what your doing, what gear to get, and how to fight properly in it your golden.  So enjoy and many victories!

After spending around 15 hours with Call of Juarez: Gunslinger, it’s tough for me to say whether I’d recommend this game to anyone else. It definitely has its good points: the story is decent and the core mechanics are solid; however, this is almost offset by the absurd boss-battle scenarios and duels. For good or ill, this fourth entry into the Call of Juarez series has very little to do with Juarez or the previous three games. Instead it is the tale of Silas Greaves, a man driven to become a bounty hunter in order to get his revenge on the villains who murdered his brother and left him for dead.
The vast majority of the story is told in flashback as Greaves reminisces in 1910 in a bar in Abilene, KS, holding court with a small audience with varying levels of credulity. You see, Mr. Greaves claims to have met, killed/grievously wounded, or been partnered with some of the Old West’s most famous lawmen and most notorious criminals. As in Pirates of the Caribbean: The Legend of Jack Sparrow, we’re presented with an unreliable narrator whose version of events may or may not reflect actual historical fact. The game nods at this not only with the dialog among the saloon patrons, but also through the “nuggets of truth” found throughout the game. These collectibles provide an actual historical context to the characters, weapons, and events alluded to in the story.
The basic gameplay consists of Greaves moving through an area and taking on a fixed number of foes that appear in specific locations. In addition to shooting from the hip and aiming down his iron sights, Greaves has a “bullet time” ability referred to in this game as “concentration” and it relies on a meter that fills as he takes out enemies. Greaves can carry up to two weapons at once, a long gun (rifle or shotgun) and a pistol, as well as dynamite. Additionally, Greaves earns experience points with each kill (with bonus points for headshots, long shots, kill streaks, et cetera) and upon “levelling up,” he can unlock a skill from one of three trees, corresponding to each of the three main weapons in the game. These skills mostly revolve around enhancing his carrying capacity for ammunition and boosting his concentration duration.
Each level ends with a “boss battle” of a few different types, most equally irritating in the grand tradition of boss fights; this is where the game balances out its fun with tedium and the drudgery of reloads. Some are straight showdowns or “duels” as the game calls them. These involve manipulating Greaves’s focus and speed simultaneously–focus is controlled by holding a circular cursor over your chosen enemy and speed by repeatedly tapping one of two keys to keep his hand close to his pistol. There is also an “honor” mechanic embedded into these duels, as after your focus gets around 75%, you will hear a heartbeat sound and this indicates the earliest time that Greaves can actually draw his gun. If you draw it then, you are drawing first and the game notes that you won your duel dishonorably. This doesn’t seem to have any appreciable effect on the game (there is a separate “duel” minigame where an achievement is apparently linked to winning all duels honorably but it doesn’t seem to have anything to do with the story mode). Greaves is apparently drunk or high in every single gunfight because his focus tends to veer all over the place and his hand will continuously drift to the right, left, or above his gun belt, and I can think of no other plausible explanation for this (aside from Techland just wanting to make these things as annoying as humanly possible).
Another type of mission-finisher is the comically-absurd fixed fight against an overwhelming number of enemies. These are usually Indians for reasons that are only partially fleshed-out in the game’s narrative, mostly the “magical Negro (Indian)” effect. These start out with Greaves in concentration mode so you can attempt to weed out a small number of antagonists before it shifts back to normal. There are a few other variations on the “end-boss” theme too. There is one arena fight in the game where enemies are shooting and tossing sticks of dynamite at you and a few sequences where you have to climb a slope by running from cover to cover to avoid getting torn apart by Gatling gun bullets before you reach the boss.
The story has a single branching point at the end where you determine what Greaves’s ultimate action will be, but you have to negotiate a 2-on-1 duel AND an overwhelming fight against a bunch of ghosts to get to it, so it’s not really worth replaying to see what happens if you choose differently.
I have no basis of comparison between this and the previous Western-themed games in the series, but because the otherwise-decent gameplay is punctuated with frequent and terrible duels and assorted boss battles, at the end of the day, I’d probably recommend Gun over this game.

Amnesia followed the rule of punishing you for looking at the monsters. Sadly, too many things were taken out that made The Dark Descent what it was such as the sanity meter, tinderboxes, oil, and health potions and instead replaced it with regenerating health and no inventory. On its own, A Machine For Pigs could have been a great game. But as much as we would like to ignore the "Amnesia" title, it must be considered a sequel to the 2010 masterpiece. If you're on the fence about purchasing this one, I would wait for a sale to pop up or for the flat price to be lowered.
If there is one thing I need to praise this game for is the story. As much as I loved The Dark Descent's look into the sanity of a human desperate to save his own life, A Machine For Pigs takes this a few steps further and delivers a story, while a short 3-4 hours long, thankfully doesn't overstay its welcome and throws you into what I can only describe as a H.P Lovecraft story come true. Overall, I do recommend this game if you're looking for something that delves deeper into the darkest corners of humanity.

Anyone that played Amnesia: The Dark Descent will recognize the basic premise of this one. Basically, everything is dark and you have to get from one area to the next, solving puzzles and avoiding any enemies that are around. This game is far more simplistic than the original, with the inventory, visible health, sanity, health items, and difficult puzzles all taken out. Doing this allows you to better focus on the story and atmosphere. Even with all those things taken out, this game is still worth a play, espcially if you felt the first one had too much going on all at the same time.
It is not as good as the first one, however. It feels like there are far less enemies, so there is less of a threat and therefore less pressure as you wander around. The first enemy that can actually attack you doesn't show up for quite some time, which both messes with your head and makes things feel less scary after a while. Death in this game means even less than it did on the first one. I got killed once, spawned two feet away, and the enemy that killed me was gone. Maybe it just had to do with where I died, but it made me feel less stressed about whether I got spotted or not. I died in a room late in the game, and all I had to do was redo the room. Not really any pressure to avoid being spotted.
The symbolism in this game is also shoved down your throat as the game goes on. The first one tried to be subtle, and this one throws that out the window. The word "pig" is used far too often: I'm aware it is in the title but it got out of hand after a while. My only other beef has to do with two documents you pick up. I wasn't offended by them, but they were rather sexual and felt out of place for what the game was going for. They felt like they did not belong. It almost felt like they were put in there to test how far the developers could go without getting in trouble. It doesn't hurt the game, but they caught me off guard is all.

All in all, it's a cash-in on the title of Amnesia. It's the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of an amazing horror license, which fell into the wrong hands.

What is there to say about this game? If you've played the first Dark Souls and come to this one, you might find that this one is "easier." To me, it just feels more fluent than the first game. That being said, this game is still a challenging one to go through without slamming your fist onto the nearest surface. Enemies around 98.5% of all corners, very few respites, and a main healing item that you have to find shards of through the game! Getting further through Drangleic and seeing yourself grow as a fighter or a mage will boost your pride and then you'll be crushed as a creature wearing a suit of turtle armor will literally crush you with a hammer. This game has a lot of things to offer, and no matter how many times you fail, are killed, accidentally walk or roll off a cliff, get squished, stabbed, poisoned, cursed, immolated, flattened, blown up, or eaten, once you get through the trial(s) you will feel great about yourself...before you are beaten by the enemies around the corner. If you aim to play DS2 in jolly co-operation, finding someone to help/be helped with a boss fight can be a bit challenging, but don't worry, the enemies and bosses get harder when you summon phantoms/are summoned. PvP is annoying, that's all there is to say about that. Once your journey in Drangleic comes to an end, you can go about playing the DLC, which is about 5 times harder than the game itself! And once you've done everything in your game, you can go to the bonfire in Majula and enter the new game plus cycle, which adds more enemies and makes them harder! With all of that said, this game does have its flaws, like every game. PvP is the biggest annoyance in this game, in my eyes. If you enjoy Dark Souls for the gameplay itself, the lore, the joy of victory, or you're simply a masochist, I would give this game a try if I were you. Of course, there's always the Scholar of the First Sin edition, which makes everything in this version twisted and evil (even by Dark Souls standards), but let's not talk about that. This one here is a good game, worth the purchase. If you can grab the game (and DLC) on sale, all the better!

To Avalanche's credit, they have a very tough act to follow. Just Cause 2 was an incredibly complete game, and the well-established modding + multiplayer communities gave it extra longevity.
Avalanche have added a lot of content to this game, which lead me to think this would be "Just Cause 2 Enhanced". For starters, there's a new, bigger map to play around on, of course. The fantastic grappling hook mechanic is given even more of a spotlight. You can now tether two things at once, and constrict the tethers to pull things together. And the new wingsuit adds even more ways for you to maneuver and travel.
Unfortunately, it seems that adding these features has given the actual gameplay more of a backseat. Combat is clunky and feels slow. Trying to chain moves together becomes mashing the button for the action you want to happen now, then waiting and watching while it happens, then mashing the button for the next action. In particular, climbing into and under helicopters feels incredibly slow. Combine this with an enemy AI that can just keep throwing soldiers and bullets at you, and trying to be a badass quickly becomes very frustrating. You'll find that most of the cool moves you try to pull off will be ruined midway through by the enemy soldiers spamming bullets at you and turning you into a ragdoll for a good fifteen seconds while you mash helplessly to regain control. Furthermore, aircraft and vehicles somehow handle even worse than they did in the previous game, making them next to useless when attacking or in combat. Hijacking a helicopter and using it to strafe an enemy base while dodging SAMs - an activity that was both challenging and fun in JC2 - is both miserable and futile.
It is almost more insulting to be given all of these brilliant new mechanics, and then utterly neutered when you try to use them, than it would be to not have them in a game at all. If you liked JC2, stick with that and flesh it out with mods. Skip this one.

I was so excited for this game. I read developer interviews talking about how the game would be dynamic and different every time because of the highly advanced AI alien adversary. lol. The alien AI is the worst of both worlds: the scripted parts (and it is unfortunately heavily scripted/static) are ♥♥♥♥♥♥ jump scares, and the non-scripted parts have stupid rules that lead to apparently idiotic alien behavior.
The scripted and non-scripted systems seem to contradict each other. For example, the alien teleports behind running players and instantly kills them, it will break into rooms and lockers with seeming omniscience, and it will pace back and forth next to your hiding spot using its omniscience - meanwhile during scripted jump scares it will drop down right in front of you and not turn around. More than once the alien would drop from an air vent, jump back into the air vent, and then drop back down immediately caught in some kind of loop. During a segment of the game where the alien was supposed to be scripted with heightened aggression (I believe), I repelled the alien with the flame thrower and it literally returned less than 5 sceonds later through a doorway in front of me. The AI is honestly garbage and I can't believe there are players out there that think it's good. The game felt less like outsmarting an opponent and more like being punished for running or waiting on broken automatic doors to let you into the store.
About as bad as the alien AI was the NPC models and animations that look like they were mocapped from melting, flaming Chuck E Cheese robots. I might not have noticed the huge disparity in quality if it had not been for the fact that...
The art direction, graphics, and level design in this game are ♥♥♥♥ing gorgeous. This one factor is so impressive that it's enough for me to muster through the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game play just to see everything in the environment.

So ... review time :D, this is the best survival horror game in existence in my opinion. The best game I have played in years.
This was the first game that made me stay under a table for 45 minutes because the patrolling alien had me too terrified to move. It takes you a while to get used to the alien.
To keep this short (or long):
- SPPAAAAAAAACCCE
- awesome experience
- it makes you feel like you're 'playing' the very first alien movie
- mixes the environment with the story really well (again, reminds me of the first alien movie)
- the AI's for the alien are excellent - yes AI's because there are multiple systems that drive the alien
- the alien can really understand your play style and adapt to it - this is more visible on the hardest difficulty level
- the alien can be very unpredictable at times
- don't believe you are Rambo ... start with the lowest or normal difficulty level, starting a first time playthrough on the hardest difficulty level can become frustrating at times
- really good attention to details - very few bugs are present in the game
- whoever made the sounds (SFX) and music for this game deserves a lot of credit, the experience is amazing
- you literally get scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ just from the sounds
- the atmosphere this game has is ... unbelievably well done (I think I've already said this a few times by now)
- the game is created on the CATHODE engine, developed by The Creative Assembly specifically for Alien Isolation in order to handle the sheer amount of lights throughout the game
- the game looks amazing - I wish more developers have this level of quality in their games, really well polished
- the game is optimized very well to use most hardware available on the market, I've played it maxed out @4k using an R9 290, a GTX 1070 and higher than 4k (5120 by 2160) using a GTX 1080Ti and the game was smooth as butter
- has ultrawide support, and mixed with a maxed out FOV - mmm ... very nice
- the achievements (yes, I'm that type of player that collects achievements) are really well done, in my first playthrough i managed to get 41 out of 50 - without having to look on the list to see 'extra' things that i can do along the way
- high replay value, by the time you see the credits ... there's a big chance you'll want to play it again on a different difficulty setting
Speaking of bugs because there are a few (nothing is perfect right ?), there is the occasional alien getting stuck in the vents, humans that occasionally can't see you unless you get really close to them, clipping issues ... etc, however, none of these are present often enough to ruin the experience.
Overall, I highly recommend this game.

-There are two methods to combat: Live and Paused. Live is satisfying with the timings, and the game pressures you into thinking on your feet fairly well. Paused combat is triggered by hitting the space bar or when your life bar almost ran out, and it turns the fast-paced One Vs All arena into a more manageable form that lets you plan an amount of action (which can vary) to unleash by unpausing. The benefits are that every action that you loaded while paused will happen so fast, there's almost no opportunity to miss or for the opponent to react, all but ensuring the maximum damage possible (while also being a reliable defensive measure), depending on where you Paused and what your options are. The penalty for Pausing, however, are a global cooldown timer that will count down until you can perform another function. The fludity of these two modes work together in a very satisfying way, and lets you customize your play. Will you smash through the gates and crash through your enemies? Will you go guerrilla and engage the enemy with hit and run tactics? Or will you meticulously plot your onslaught, ensuring maximum carnage while also pathing your way out?
What kept it from rating higher with me is the kind of limited, linear use for several funcions. For example, Get() entices you to engage from a distance, but that distance is shorter than other safer and more rewarding functions. Some others just have a bit too high of a price to pay for their use. As in, cast times and cooldowns. Functions with long casts could have just had a cooldown instead. Would have saved a life.
Story: 9/10
Exceptionally well-written and heartfully delievered. The narrative was always welcome in the otherwise quiet world. (The casting of which was also brilliant.) The concept was original through and through. Even the scripted interactions with what few characters there were came off very captivatingly. The lack of interactive characters actually eccentuated the feeling and depth of the game, and really brought the world building to life in a "soft candle lights, guiding you home and warming you along the way" feel, as opposed to "you awaken abruptly to a blinding flashlight piercing your eyelids. An officer asks you your business and directs you where you, or he, think(s) you need to be".
My only complaint was the lack of content, and the somewhat abrupt ending. I still felt like there was so much more I needed to do, wanted to do, and having played Bastion, I ended up just assuming what I was looking for would find me when the time was right. Finishing this game is like finishing any book or series that has a place in your heart: It leaves you wanting more.
Music: 10/10
Really no compromise here. I missed the sound when I left.
Overall: 9/10 for $10. Despite it's reviews and how much I genuinely enjoyed it, I wouldn't have paid $20 for it. That would have felt like the Contrast catastrophe...

I first started playing this game when it launched on steam. And took a break due to it's bugs until recently. Me and my friends picked the game up again, since there where promising news. We joined a large player group and started playing on a server.
First the good. This game has good graphics in general. If you slam up those sliders many areas of the map look great. The combat has a learning curve and the recent update added some nice features, if you kick a blocking person with a shield for example, you can now break his block and hit him afterwards.
The building is in my opinion the greatest part of the game. You can build your own castle and roam through your halls. They have drawbridges, furniture and many building items supporting your creativity to the fullest.
I spend hours and hours placing blocks and items, thinking about how i would raid my base and how to prevent this. Awesome stuff I tell you.
Which leads me to the next part, the raids. Raiding is more difficult and way more expensive then in the early days, making it even more rewarding if you succeed. There is nothing like standing on a freshly raided castle and taking their loot, since the raiding is a core and essential part of the game. On the other hand there is nothing worse then your base being gone the next day you log in. But this is the game this is what you singed up for. Don't complain try again and make it safer next time. They now have these things called totems which can protect your base from being removed completely.
I know this is early access, but since this game is on sale more people should know what they are buying. This game has bugs. You can avoid many of them and many have been fixed in the past. Another thing is the engine. With my gtx 770 I get 60 fps if I don't run the game on "ultra" settings. The game is pretty but not very well optimized. If you walk towards a huge base you get massive frame drops, leaving you with 1-5 fps sometimes. I doubt they will improve this by a lot in the beta.
The servers lag a lot. It's great that this game is growing more popular since it leads to full servers. And I have no problem waiting in a queue and to wait until I can play with my mates. The issue I am having is the lag. A full 40 people server is awful. There is no other word to describe it. The nice combat suddenly feels like a stop motion movie and is not decided by skill anymore.
However all these stated things won't keep me from playing the game. The biggest issue are the hackers. We had 3 on our server just yesterday, raiding our chests without any effort. And this was not the first time this happened. This game has little to none cheat protection. And the game being on sale made it just worse.
I really hope they improve this protection in some sort, until then I'd rather recommend to stay away from this game. So you can join the game once it is in a decent state leading to a great experience for everyone.

RoK Review
Reign of Kings is a medieval-styled survival game (think Chivalry mixed with Rust). The objective is to capture the king's castle and claim the throne, granting you respect, power, and taxation over all other players, at the same time as putting you on kill-lists across the map. Nearly every object in the world is collectable and useful in some way or another. Launch siege weapons to invade another castle or find a sneaky way in. The building possibilities are endless. Adorn the world with dozens of decoration options, such as paintable signs and guild banners. Speaking of guilds, this game is a great co-op experience.
Now, RoK isn't without its flaws. In fact, it has many flaws. HUGE flaws. The biggest of which is the hacking. Unless joining a whitelist server, the hackers can make this game unplayable. Some servers have an ungodly amount of lag, but that's easily avoidable.
Overall, I recommend this game for the long run, not so much for right now. Once the devs improve the anti-cheat systems, this will easily be one of my favorite games.

If i hadto choose between League of Legends and SMITE, I would choose SMITE because it plays better and has a better flow as a game.  However I am not a MOBA player, I will play pvp for fun and casually which is to say not to win but to enjoy the game.  Still I would reccomend this game because of many reasons, and I am going to give a short list here so as to not make it a tl;dr review.
1) Graphics are nice, clean, smooth, and beautifully done.  While I am fine even with bad graphics, when they are this gorgeous it is a huge plus.
2) Gameplay is really smooth and much more fluid than League, the level of strategy needed depends on the skill of your opponents but usually is actually indepth.  Each character ha their own intricacies and play style, you will need to take time to get used to them and learn them.  Beginners one huge piece of advice, start on average or easy gods first.  Play some gods with no real knowledge and your in for  world of hurt, so keep what I said in mind if possible.
3) Rewards are good for this game and they often have weeknds or events where you can earn some great things, and their login rewards system is quite well balanced and even allows you to earn gems for the cash shop in the last 2 days.  League could learn a thing or two from HiRez.
4) Competition is fun, friendly but the downside is people may get annoyed if you take their kill.  Honestly this is one downside to all MOBA's and that bugs me, I kill someone I kill someone it's not my issue if someone else wanted the kill.  This i find annoying but a fact of life with MOBA's, and thus part of why it is not my cup of tea.  The emphasis here is winning and not really having fun, I play for fun not to always win.
So overall a GREAT game but not my cup of tea, reccomend you even try it to see if you like it.  If you like it awesome, but I cannot knock this as a bad game even if I do not like it as a player.  As long as you know what your doing, what gear to get, and how to fight properly in it your golden.  So enjoy and many victories!

TLDR at the bottom. Yeah I really like it. I had given up on MMO's but I started messing around with modded skyrim and I was like "Why don't I try ESO again?" You can pickpocket people finally and actually make a ton of money from selling stolen items, which from the last time I played wasn't in the game. Also, you can kill NPC's which is a lot of fun and you get a bounty if you get caught.

I hate to give negative reviews based on technical issues that prevent me from even playing the game, but I have to make an except here. I've been trying to load the game for hours, including hours I've had to spend reading forums and making settings changes on my computer, updating other programs, etc. The game ran when I load the exe files directly, but, of course, wouldn't let me play, because it's an out of date version.
So the problem is entirely the Launcher and the updater. I finally got the Launcher to load, by grabbing the Launcher from the %temp% folder, and now Steam even consistently properly launches the Launcher, but I can't log in, because it says I don't have an account, and that's where my patience runs out. I'm returning the game, and I'm just going to play the dozen new and unplayed games that install and run from Steam without the headache.
While, again, I freely admit that this is a bit of a nitpick, my complaint really is simply a point of professionalism. If Bethesda and Zenimax are going to sell this game on Steam, then the bare minimum expectation is that their launcher is compatible with Steam and that when I try to log in, it shouldn't matter to them where I bought it.
Sadly, it's clear that Bethesda has just gotten lazy, making pieces of buggy garbage with incredible lore that depend on a robust and UNPAID modding community to rescue from Bethesda's incompetence (Congrats, modders, you're unpaid contractors). From crash to desktop bugs when you used autosave mechanics in their games, to busted dialogue and broken items, Bethesda's unprofessionalism and mediocrity has gone on so long that they can't even write a working "out of the box" Steam launcher? Nope, not worth it.
After hours of messing with it, I simply no longer have the interest to play this game. ESO is just going to be a game I don't play. And I think I'm done with Bethesda in general. I know, I know, Fanboys. Bethesda won't miss my money. It'll be even, I won't miss their games, either. That's how capitalism works. Win win.
