Amnesia: A machine for Pigs is (as the credits will state) a game made by The Chinese Room aka Dear Esther. In other words, what you get is Dear Esther's essence wrapped in Amnesia. Don't expect the game to have puzzles or rooms to explore, this thing goes on tracks (nearly) like a steam locomotive and is only supposed to follow the track. I was able to learn in 15-20 minutes what I can open/collect and what are closed/unusable objects. If there is an item to pick, one have to use it. If there is a door that opens, one must go through it. Locked doors and such carry no value, meaning one is not going to run along the rooms to solve how to enter another room like in Amnesia. The game has an excellent atmosphere making this horror story enjoyable. What ruined my gaming experience was expectations for this to be a little more Amnesia than what it was. I was able to enjoy the game as soon as I let go of old Amnesia concept. In Amnesia, one must use light sources to keep sanity, in Piggy one has lantern that has no limits. To put it simply, in Piggy one does not have inventory, one does not need health, oil, any items. Also the the night vision (eyes get used to darkness in Amnesia) is gone. One more thing about tracks and monsters: because this game is supposed to run on tracks, monsters also disappear and appear randomly. Making it sometimes less.. scary. When I started to play the game without using lantern I mainly saw shadows of the monsters or heard the screams. To sum it up, this game has it's strong points and is enjoyable, just don't expect it to be Amnesia/Penumbra.

Factorio is a 2D top-down/slightly-isometric game about building factories, defending them from the local wildlife, and eventually constructing a rocket to reach space.
It is perhaps the most content-rich and stable Early Access game I have ever played, and to top it off, the developers are keeping regular contact with the players and have plenty of ideas that they're working on.
You begin the game with very basic machinery - a Burner Mining Drill, a Stone Furnace, and 8 Iron Plates to your name. From there, you must develop your base and research advanced technologies. Set up electrical systems so you can power Electric Mining Drills instead of pollution-heavy Burners. Build machines that can automatically craft things when given the proper ingredients. Build transport belts to move your products around to different places. Upgrade your electrical systems with solar power and batteries. Move items in bulk over long distances with trains. Set up oil refineries so you can create advanced products like plastic, sulfur, batteries, and explosives. Take the fight to the aliens with armor-piercing ammo for your SMG, Pistol, and Shotgun, or go full Fahrenheit 451 and burn it all to the ground with the Flamethrower. Collect enough resources to build a Rocket Silo, then a Rocket, then a Satellite, and finally launch it all into space and win.
Then do it all again on different settings. Maybe even with mods. Maybe even with friends.
If you get this game, and you should, make yourself available on their Discord channel. Poke around the devs' IRC. Lurk on /r/Factorio. If you don't have friends who own this game, find friends there to play with.
Oh, and I highly recommend saying goodbye to your friends and family. You're gonna be here for a while.

So I have finally found the time to play through Call of Juarez: Gunslinger. And one thing I can say after playing it through is it is essentially a flawless gem for me. The somewhat cell-shaded graphics still look good, the shooting is great and extremely satisfying and the setting is purely awesome. The game itself is entirely story-driven, but the story behind it is really interesting, it incorporates a lot of actual Wild West history as well as plenty of legends. There is enough humor for it to not become too serious and there is enough suspense to keep you interested in what is going on. Great music and absolutely awesome voice acting complete the experience. The collectible “nuggets of truth” are hidden quite cleverly and are not that easy to find and along with a “game plus” mode provide some replayability. On the other hand, the nuggest provide a very interesting insight into speculations about whether the Wild West legends (including people and events) are actually true or not. Other “additional” features include a series of duels (not that interesting for me) and replaying some of the game parts as “shootout” scenes, which are fairly satisfying. If you have ever had even a passing interest in Wild West, please, do yourself a favor and try the demo of this game. The game is EXACTLY like the demo and, if you like it, you will not be disappointed (a demo that actually represents a game well – how common that is nowadays?). I would strongly suggest that you buy this in a pack with Far Cry: Blood Dragon, which is another awesome shooter that I have reviewed last year. If your tastes are anything similar to mine, you will certainly not be disappointed.

For those who want to know: No, this game is not Open World. But so what? Its scenes are absolutely amazing, the adrenaline of the shootouts and the story with real characters put up into a fictional universe get you totally into this game.

Verdict: Passable
While more technically competent than, say, Skyrim, it's an incredibly jerky, ill-paced game that tries to do too much in its time span.  Too many weapons, too many twists, too many bad guys, too many gameplay types.  It's never really content to allow for falling action of any kind.  As soon as you reach the final objective of a mission, it cuts to a loading screen, with hardly a line from one of your squadmates or anything to provide a moment of relaxation, a feeling that you've made it and, for the moment, you're safe.  Alternating between the Rangers and TF141 on a mission-by-mission basis for the first two acts of the game ruins any sense of continuity between the missions -- with each feeling about half the length of a Call of Duty 4 mission -- further exacerbates the lack of fulfilment provided by the end of each mission, because each mission ends on a particularly poor and jarring cliffhanger and you're thrown into the rising action of another mission in another place with different people before you've had a moment to decompress.  It may be that Infinity Ward was trying to keep the tension high.  But, if that is the case, they confused tension with action.  Yes, an all-out firefight can be tense, but it quickly loses its dramatic appeal the more you do it in a given span of time.  And, since you -start- the game in a firefight and do little else besides move from one firefight to the next, aside from some parts of some of the TF141 missions, you're basically forced to keep an adrenaline high for almost the entirety of the game's runtime.  This also prevents even minimal characterization.  So, when characters are killed, there is no emotional impact because there was no time or cause for you to become emotionally invested in them.
While there are some things the game does well, such as the first mission with Roach and Soap and the way the end of "Of Their Own Accord" and the beginning of "Second Sun" tied together (the beginning of "Second Sun" honestly took me by surprise), they are few and far between, lost in the sharp scene changes and deafening non-stop gunfire.
I'd be lying if I said the story lacked drama, but most of what drama it has immediately falls apart when you think about how ludicrous the plot is.  The villain's plan was needlessly complicated, bloody, and destructive, especially given its purpose, which could have been accomplished much easier and cleaner with the clever usage of media and politics.  But what broke my suspension of disbelief was not how out of hand it got, not how far off the deep end the villain had gone to even consider it to be a good idea, but how willing the villain's lackeys were to let him carry on and how freely they seemed to provide their assistance.  It is clear they are trying to top the first Modern Warfare.  However, the first Modern Warfare was already pushing the limits of reason while still trying to set the stakes high.  Modern Warfare 2 front-loads so much ridiculous escalation, much of it climax-worthy material, that you really can't help but think every time "It
get any worse."  And yet it always does, and never in a good way.  If I didn't know any better, I'd say there was a team at Infinity Ward that did nothing but sit around and play "One Up" for the entirety of the script-writing process, just to come up with new ways to turn up the heat, regardless of whether or not they actually made sense in the grand scheme of things.  The scene of using foxholes and trenches to avoid machine gun nests on your approach to a ruined, Russian-occupied White House screams WWII callback.  Aside from that, though, it does little but try to show the player just how bad things are in DC by stirring up patriotic anger.  The same kind of patriotic anger that the game itself practically condemning, both in its plot and in the quotes that are displayed on screen after you die.  And, by this point, the game has gone on far too long with its messages of treason through patriotism for that to be the point.  Not to mention, the game isn't smart enough for it to have ever been the point to begin with.
When they announced the original Modern Warfare, Infinity Ward said they wanted to make the campaign feel a lot more like a film.  And they succeeded.  With a well-paced plot that followed a clear dramatic arc, parallel subplots that contributed to the overall scenario in a positive manner without weighing it down, missions that had their own miniature dramatic arcs, and the sense of danger and urgency needed to justify the faster-paced gameplay, Modern Warfare was a good action movie.  While most of the actors went without characterization beyond "Spec-Ops hardass", "Military grunt", or "Total evil psychopath", such archetypes are pretty much standard for military action movies, and they were neither over-done nor hammed up, and were almost always present, leading to a solid core cast you came to care at least a -little- about by the end.  Combine that with carefully-placed and well-handled twists -- the end of Jackson's subplot in particular was wrung out for as much drama as they could justify -- it was a game that, despite ending up as the spearhead of the subgenre that has taken over the FPS, stands out as an example of trying something new with a franchise without completely butchering the job.  Modern Warfare 2, on the other hand, is the result of trying to capitalize on the success of a new idea without understanding what made the new idea
.
If you're
curious to find out what happened to Soap and Captain Price following the events of Call of Duty 4, or you just want to understand what all the fuss is about, Modern Warfare 2 is worth a play, with some emphasis on "a play", as in the singular.  If not, perhaps you can help unmake the rest of the franchise by silencing
truth, leaving only the deaths of 30,000 Marines, and the sacrifice of the 22nd SAS to avenge them, that the horrors of that week would not return to haunt the future.

Transistor is the second 2D isometric ARPG from Supergiant, the studio that made Bastion. It has a lot in common with that game: very linear story, unlockable character upgrades, heavy emphasis on sound design and art style, and a novel and oblique narrative presentation that relies heavily on excellent voiceover work.
I just finished my first playthrough and thought I would share my impressions.
CORE GAMEPLAY:
ver
Transistor experiments a lot more with the gameplay mechanics than Bastion did, and I enjoyed this aspect a great deal. As in the previous game, you control a single character through what is basically a series of arena battles, and you can customize their loadout of unlockable combat abilities.
Transistor introduces a time-stopping mode where you can strategically plan out several actions in a row. There is a much wider variety of abilities than in Bastion, and experimenting with their synergies is crucial to success; I also found it very enjoyable and addictive. I'm a big fan of turn-based RPGs, and for me the core gameplay loop was much more rewarding than the more-or-less generic isometric shooter mechanics of Bastion.
One thing I found in my first playthrough of Transistor is that the difficulty curve was very inconsistent. It's not a challenging game, but I did die a couple times in the midgame while experimenting with different ability combinations. However, once you discover certain overpowered conbinations, it becomes a complete cakewalk. As in Bastion, there are unlockable debuffs that you can apply to your character in exchange for XP rewards and acheivements, but even stacking all of these debuffs that I could find in the first tplaythough (6 or 7 out of 10), I didn't take a single hit in the final stage, and the last boss went down very, very easily. This really gave me a sense of anticlimax in what was supposed to be a tense and epic finish.
The 2nd playthrough allows you to keep your character progress and ramps up the difficulty. Maybe this will offer a better challenge.
WORLD AND LEVEL DESIGN:
This to me was the weakest part of the game. Not in a visual sense - the game environments are incredible-looking. But under the window dressing, the environment is very same-y: one set of blocks after another. We are supposed to feel anxious that the "evil forces" of the game world are transforming a set of pretty textured blocks, into equally pretty monochrome blocks, both equally (un)interactive.
The enemy design is tolerably diverse, but the levels are all pretty much the same: tiny- to small-sized square areas that you have to clear of enemies before progressing. It's not terrible but it's nothing special either.
The game is also quite short; my first playthrough took 8 hours; this included reading all the terminals, unlocking all the flavor text (by equiping each ability in each slot), completing all the challenges, and even a certain amount of time on the pause screen while I did something else. I spent maybe 2/3 of the in-game time in combat, and the rest exploring the flavor-text, cutscenes, and other stuff. If it had been a lot longer I probably would have become kind of bored; even as it stands, I ended up kind of sprinting through the endgame, partly because of the extreme drop in difficulty once my character hit level 8 or so.
SOUND AND VISUALS:
Transistor is one of the most aesthetically advanced games I've ever seen. The sound and voice work is masterfully done. (I didn't really care for the music, which is also prominently featured, but that's just my own taste.) There are three main voice-acted characters, and all their performances are subtle, emotive, and just a joy to experience.
The visuals are also incredibly well designed. In every inch of the game world there is some kind of eye-popping and novel effect going on: atmospheric animations, interesting use of parallax, foreground, background, and perspective, lovely textures on every surface. It is a deeply beautiful visual world.
In a way, I felt that the visual sophistication was almost too much; during the actual gameplay it can be sort of confusing, and there were places where I literally couldn't figure out how to proceed because the functional components of the environment are buried amid the gorgous props.
The visuals also make the game quite technically demanding for a 2D isometric game; I ran it on my quad-core i5 laptop with integrated graphics; it worked but was a little choppy. Given that it's a short game with pretty simple mechanics, I could actually have lived without a lot of the bling, especially at the $20 price tag. I would rather the developer had put more time into balancing, enemy AI, and world design, instead of the evidently large investment in visual asset design.
Still, it is very very pretty.
STORY:
Whether or not you find the actual story interesting (I thought it was okay, it a little thin,) the way it unfolds through voice and text is simply wonderful. Kudos to the designers for breaking the mold, and I hope that others take notice. There is nary a cutscene to be found; the text is presented in a cool and believable way, and both the playable main character and her narrator-companion are compelling and convincing; this despite one being voiceless and the other, bodiless. It's rare to see a game take risks like this, and even rarer that they pull it off so well.
VERDICT:
I really enjoyed Tranistor and I'd recommend it. However, it's very short, not particularly challenging, and can get repetitive - although I found it far less so than Bastion. Altogether, these things made me glad I got it on a hefty discount.
But if you're interested in strategic ARPGs, novel gameplay design, groundbreaking visuals, sound and narrative, you owe it to yourself to pick this one up in the very next sale.

tl;dr: plays like a puzzler with cool mechanics, amazing art+music, but a really detracting attempt at a plot
I bought Transistor upon the recommendation of a friend and the overwhelming number of glowing reviews it had. I was expecting a really amazing game, but after having finished the game, my opinion is that it is just a textbook example of style over substance.  Don't get me wrong – the artwork is amazing and immersive, the music is exceptionally well done (sans the lyrics), the combat system is interesting and very enjoyable (if not occasionally glitchy). But otherwise... there's nothing here. The entirety of the attempt at a plot is literally just incohesive narration about how some people tried to change everything and it all went wrong. Nothing is actually ever explained, no real motives are revealed (unless you count "We just wanted to change the city for the better!" as a strong motive), and character development never happens. Places are talked about and then visited (but then it's just a level that looks like any other level), enemies are mentioned and then killed, people are vaguely discussed and then, well, suffice it to say that you literally learn nothing after you meet them.
It's really a pity because by silencing the player and forcing them to accept information only through narration and environment interaction, Supergiant Games has full control over the player, being able to make the player believe and feel whatever they want the player to (think Portal-style, for instance). Instead, they completely wasted the opportunity, delivering nothing of substance through any of the channels of storytelling available to them. You never feel anything or root for any characters in this game. I saw another review that likened this game to just a puzzler, and I fully agree.
The failed attempt at a plot was by far the biggest flaw of the game, but I'd like to point out some other things that could have been improved:
The voiceover is interesting at first, but quickly becomes really annoying (this is mostly a side effect of there being no plot to narrate). It basically alternates between rambling about how cool the protagonist is/was, and contempt and confusion about what the antagonists are doing. It narrates and comments on your actions, too, which is amusing until you hate the narrator. The two things it doesn't do are 1. say anything useful or 2. effect emotion in the player, which are things I think narrators in games should do.
The artwork is unique, laying out a steampunk-ish twist in a digital setting and executing it really well. Unfortunately, the designers forgot the other aspect of game art, which is differentiation. With the exception of a plot-spoiling feature, *all the levels look the same*. It's ridiculous. There is so little differentation between the player's regular neighbourhood and the supposedly luxurious and lavish residences of the rich bad guys that I didn't realize how close I was to said bad guys until I was in the same room with them. There were only two levels whose artwork stood out to me as really well designed: the opera house, and the dark walkway near the end.
That's all. I'm including a lot of superfluous details because although reviews are meant for people who haven't played the game, they're primarily judged for merit by those who have, so oddly enough those are the people I have to convince of my opinion. Cool medium-length puzzler. No plot. Possibly not worth your money, and definitely not worth universal acclaim.

The first Dark Souls was a good game with fairly big flaws, which I was thankfully willing to look past to enjoy the overall game. Unfortunately, I cannot say the same for Dark Souls 2. This has got to be one of the most disappointing sequels, one of the most lazily designed, frustratingly awful games I have ever played.
This game has been talked about to death and everyone who played it has their own opinions on it and I can't say much to add to that, if you're interested in a very good in-depth critique, you can check out Matthewmatosis' video on it, he did an excellent job explaining all the flaws in the game.
Dark Souls 2 has improved upon some minor things here and there but is overall a much inferior product compared to its previous installment. Instead of reviewing the game I'm just going to criticize one of the biggest issues I've had throughout this mess.
Dark Souls' combat system is designed to be 1v1, it's painfully obvious, it works fantastically that way and whenever you face more than one enemy, the combat system falls apart and the game becomes a frustrating mess. So in an attempt to make the game "harder", compared to the previous game, Dark Souls 2 includes numerous areas which feature couples, groups and at times full blown hordes of enemies to attack you. The level design in this game is atrocious with some of the worst enemy placement I have ever seen. The game doesn't want to give you a fair challenge, it wants you to die a lot, and it will attempt to do so in any means necessary, even if that means breaking its own rules. Whenever the game let me face one enemy at a time, I blazed through this game; much like the previous Dark Souls, whenever it was fair, it wasn't hard, it was mildly challenging at best. In fact, there were around six or seven bosses in DS2 that I have beaten on my first try, which is an absolute far cry from the previous game where you had to learn the bosses' patterns which meant dying over and over again until you figured it out. But then there are bosses in DS2 which are more than one enemy, and those bosses are frustrating as all hell. I died so many times to the Royal Rat Authority, not because he's hard, he's super easy in fact, but because there were six small rats right before the boss that you have to kill quickly before the Royal Rat Authority drops down to join them. I was a melee character, I had to run in there and kill the rats one by one and more often than not I didn't do it in time and died. This is just the sort of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that's in DS2, it's almost never fair, every time the game introduced me to multiple enemies and I have died, it never felt like it was my fault, it's just From Software hitting ctrl+c, ctrl+v with the enemy placement and giggling away. I mean ♥♥♥♥ing look at this!
This isn't how the game is supposed to work; this is just atrocious game design at its best. This was almost never the case with the first game aside from around two or three bosses and those bosses are easily the worst part of the game, outside of bosses, whenever the game had multiple enemies they had low health and weren't a problem to take care of, but Dark Souls 2 just takes all of this to a whole new level and tells you to go ♥♥♥♥ yourself. The Souls games aren’t about difficulty, because they aren’t hard if you know what you’re doing (and whenever the game is fair), the Souls games are about atmosphere, deep fascinating lore, a bleak and depressing world  that reminds you that we’re all going to inevitably die one day and so on and so forth, they’re not supposed to be hard.
Not to mention the horrible AI at times, the inconsistency in combat (sometimes the enemies have poise, sometimes they don't! Sometimes you hit them, other times you miss point blank! Etc, etc) and the frequent horrific hit detection. But on the basis of what I talked about above, I cannot for the ♥♥♥♥ing life of me recommend this game to anyone. It is one of the most frustrating messes of a game I have ever seen. If you haven't already, go play the first Dark Souls instead of this garbage. Shit♥♥♥♥ almighty what a horrible video game.

Assuming for some reason you skipped the game description, Factorio is all about building an incredibly efficient logistics network. You're stranded on an alien world and your only hope is to get a distress satellite into orbit to call for help. The trouble is, you don't have the technology to do so. Your logistics network will expand and evolve as you research new technologies necessary to build the rocket and satellite, and you'll be making "friends" with the locals along the way (handshakes are done in the form of bullets).
It really isn't though. Because you start off with only basic technologies, part of the fun of playing this game comes from unlocking higher-tier technologies and implementing them to boost your production speed and capacity. As you progress, you'll be unlocking high-speed conveyer belts, logically operated machines, automated cargo trains, and even a fully functional drone network that can auto-repair damage done by the locals, as well as getting stuff from A to B where there's no room for conveyer belts.
As your production begins to grow in scale, the local population will have more and more bones to pick with you. At first, you can keep them at bay with the starting pistol, but as your production scales up and you eliminate more waves of them with your automated defenses, they'll learn how to protect themselves and attack your defenses much more effectively. As such, you will have to dedicate some of your resources to improving and expanding your defenses.
As a strategy, you will have to decide whether your mounted turret focus will be bullet-fed turrets or laser turrets. The laser turrets are definitely easier to maintain, being that all they require is a power supply, but they consume a LOT of power. The bullet-fed turrets don't consume any power directly, but making the bullets and getting them to each of the turrets in an automated fashion is a material-expensive process (or if you use robots, energy expensive). You might think using both is easy, but each type of turret has a different set of research jobs to upgrade its functionality. So you can either research a max-out on one type, or be only partially upgraded on both. So for the sake of resources, stick with one turret type.
This game will challenge you for a long time to achieve a successful launch in a single world (my shortest success time was 29 hours). It's challenging and at the same time very fun because of all the different ways you can attempt to solve the same problem. My only complaints are that the UI is somewhat lackluster, and the object sprites are lower resolution than is desired on a 1080p monitor. Also, since it's in Early Access and still evolving, the Campaign missions are a bit broken, but that should be getting fixed soon.

So I have finally found the time to play through Call of Juarez: Gunslinger. And one thing I can say after playing it through is it is essentially a flawless gem for me. The somewhat cell-shaded graphics still look good, the shooting is great and extremely satisfying and the setting is purely awesome. The game itself is entirely story-driven, but the story behind it is really interesting, it incorporates a lot of actual Wild West history as well as plenty of legends. There is enough humor for it to not become too serious and there is enough suspense to keep you interested in what is going on. Great music and absolutely awesome voice acting complete the experience. The collectible “nuggets of truth” are hidden quite cleverly and are not that easy to find and along with a “game plus” mode provide some replayability. On the other hand, the nuggest provide a very interesting insight into speculations about whether the Wild West legends (including people and events) are actually true or not. Other “additional” features include a series of duels (not that interesting for me) and replaying some of the game parts as “shootout” scenes, which are fairly satisfying. If you have ever had even a passing interest in Wild West, please, do yourself a favor and try the demo of this game. The game is EXACTLY like the demo and, if you like it, you will not be disappointed (a demo that actually represents a game well – how common that is nowadays?). I would strongly suggest that you buy this in a pack with Far Cry: Blood Dragon, which is another awesome shooter that I have reviewed last year. If your tastes are anything similar to mine, you will certainly not be disappointed.

For those who want to know: No, this game is not Open World. But so what? Its scenes are absolutely amazing, the adrenaline of the shootouts and the story with real characters put up into a fictional universe get you totally into this game.
I totally support the buying of this game (I got it in a pack with Far Cry: Blood Dragon, because I wanted Far Cry, but I liked Call of Juarez better).

I got the game for my wife, and now we both play it off and on when it's nice to narrow your focus down to clicking on your pixel farm and watching your horde of frequently unruly Meeseeks-looking helpers ignore the ever-expanding mountain of
right in the middle of everything while babysitting unripe plots at the far corners of the farm.

Transistor is worth buying just for the soundtrack. Seriously, its that good. And the visuals are amazing, the gameplay is fun, and the story is engaging. What more can you ask for? Though it is not perfect. The UI can be pretty clunky, especially when trying to make Function combos which is a really fun mechanic, besides for the UI issues. But if you were expecting Bastion like gameplay, like I was, you won't get that. This is NOT a hack and slash.  Its kind of like the V.A.T.S system from Fallout where you can play in real time, but you can also stop time and plan out moves. Each has pros and cons, real time allows you to spam attacks without cooldown, but if you use the stop time mechanic Turn(), you can plan out moves for maximum damage, but afterwards you are not able to use your Functions till Turn() recharges. Its a very fun system, and one that has a lot of replayability for a few more playthroughs. One of my favorite parts of the game is that nothing is spoon fed to you. You figure out the story and what happened to the city of Cloudbank through expositon from terminals you find through out the game. Even your Functions contribute to the story, with each Function being the soul of dead citizen that the titular sword absorbed. Anyhow, I got carried away. This game is a work of art, nothing less of a masterpeice. Go and buy it. It is a bit on the short side, though I wouldn't really know since I didn't beat it yet. But from what I can tell, it has a lot of replayability. Please, do your brains right side a favor, and please, buy this game. Thank me later.

What can I say to make this review helpful...? Hmm, let's see.
~ Chapter 1. Pros!
This game has action, humour and gore. Imo, that's a big plus. Not to mention, plenty of ways to kill someone or something. Waaay too many ways.
Go past that and what do we have?! Lots of weapons, from different types to different category of element attached to it. Bonus points for stats and rarity on guns!
Reaching the characters- what's to miss?! You got plenty to choose from and more to that, is the fact that you can customize them!
Talking about customizable things? Well, check the rides you get! You can paint those as well! And choose from different types of weapons they can use! That's right! You can use the cars to fight!
Video & audio quality have nothing to miss out as well. They're decent and smooth.
The NPCs are weird and hilarious. Some get even serious.
Plot is decent, worth spending the hours on it; though the side quests and the DLCs are fun to do as well- keep that in mind if you want to level up -it helps a lot!
Co-Op feature! Gather up with your friends and get to experience x4 the fun!
You can replay the game for a harder difficulty and better loot!
~ Chapter 2. Cons!
You can't open doors like in the previous games. (Yeah, I know- a REAL bummer!)
The NPCs have very few lines, apart from the quests ones. Could've been more interaction between the relationship of NPC-Player.
AI respawns mobs, in your face, if it has to. Found myself sometimes wondering: "Where did those guys with big guns came from?! I just went through that area!"
~ Chapter 3. Conclusion!
In my opinion, this game is worth the money. The DLCs are not required, but I'd advice on getting them. Doesn't hurt having something extra in which you get to have fun. And like I said earlier, it's a game filled with action, humour and gore. What's not to like?!

It has been decades, centuries since you, the Chosen Undead, Linked the Fire. The memories have long been forgotten and have faded with the passing of time, the once sturdy armour you wear has already fallen into disrepair and blackened by immolation from the flames, as for your trusty weapons, they have been marred by age, remaining both unused and unremembered by your side, yet despite all this, you feel as though they have never failed you, and that, in all their years, never have they betrayed you when times were tough and the stakes were dire, that they will fight with you until the very end. That is the only thing you are sure of, for everything else seems distant and dreamlike, something from a past long ago, a past that belonged to someone else, perhaps a brave hero remembered for their valiant deeds and actions, perhaps an unknown stranger who took it upon themself to do what no others would or could do, you don't remember. These thoughts drift through your ever-crumbling mind, and all the while disquiet and mental unrest looms ever closer, will these thoughts, will these possessions that once occupied another person's thoughts, in another age, in another time, even be of significance to you? The end approaches now, you see the figure coming through the fog-filled archway facing the place you have waited and pondered all this time, they are here for something, they are here to meet you, for no one has visited this place for several lifetimes. They draw their weapon, it is of an unusual design, as is their garments, but no matter, they are here to fight, for whatever reason, you no longer remember nor do you care, the answers have long lost their importance. As they walk toward you with their guard up in a readied stance, their face filled with equal amounts of awe and defiance, you try to stand, it takes several long minutes, your armour clatters together as you shake off the thick layer of ash that has covered you for as longer than you can fathom. You draw your weapon, it creaks and groans like an old beast nearing the end of its life, you try to flourish it, the movements embedded into your body, but your grip fails you, it has been too long since you last wielded it, the weapon falls to the ground weakly, for a long time you stare at it, trying to remember from whence it came from, out of the corner of your vision you see the figure relax and walks calmly, confidently towards you. Still looking at the ground, you await the your inevitable fate. They pick up the dropped weapon, testing its weight, you look up in surprise, grasping your hand, they place the weapon in your palm, you try to find the words to express your thanks, however having not spoken for so long you only manage a raspy groan, already the figure is taking their position a distance away, once again getting ready to fight you. Now armed, you call up the last vestiges of strength in your body, the final traces of concentration and sanity to aid you in this battle, now blazing with old energies, you charge stone-faced towards your opponent, and they to you. ... You find yourself face down in the ash covered ground, there is a pain emanating from somewhere on your body but it is fading quickly, you try to look up and see the victorious opponent walking towards the dying embers of the flame you have held watch over all this time, a fragment of memory strikes you suddenly, with the last remaining strength you have left, you crawl towards the base of a pillar that pierces up thought the ground, wiping away the charred face and ash, you uncover the writing scrawled onto the surface, you remember now, this was your name, You had a name, that was what as missing all along, a feeling of profound emancipation flows over your mind, and you realize, that with a name you can finally, rest. Rest in the warmth, coming from the newly linked bonfire. A well-earned rest, Chosen Undead. Yep, I think this is definitely the theme that plays for the Chosen Undead's fight when its time for the arrival of the next successor to the Flame.

One of the best indie games I'll never want to play again.  I don't say this in a bad way - it was too effective at what it set out to do.  "Emily is Away" is an AIM simulator where you shape an ongoing story starting as a high school graduate, and continuing on through college.  The story follows conversing with a friend/love interest, and things will unfold differently (somewhat) depending on the conversations you have.
For anyone who was big into AIM during their college years (of which I was), "Emily is Away" hits a little too close to home, and actually was a bit like strolling down memory lane (some good, some bad).  But the game itself is a unique and imaginative concept, and I'd highly suggest giving it at least one playthrough - especially since it's free! Kudos to the developers on the game.

A very neat concept and a cute way of execution, but ultimately, the game falls flat as it fails to really provide any real choice, consequences, or endings other than the same scenario that you'll eventually arrive to. Perhaps that's an artistic liberty to push this unique ending unto the player, making them feel helpless as they attempt to alter the events that lead to the ending, but as far as a visual novel goes, if one could attempt to call this a visual novel, it really could've done much better with multiple paths and endings.
Still though, this game won't take you longer than 30 minutes, if even that. It's worth trying and playing through.

Pros:
1) Absolutely AMAZING music and art style. Of course, both can be subjective but in my opinion, this game is worth 5/10 based on just music and art alone. Some may hate the techno-esque music though.
2) If you liked Ragnarok Online, nostalgia will hit you HARD. ToS is the true successor to the good old Ragnarok Online.
Yeah, that's about it.
Cons:
1) There are so many interesting classes in this game, but they are all horribly IMBALANCED. A few class combinations are just that much stronger and have better synergy than the rest. You need to research and even then, you might not like the playstyle.
2) The high level cap in this game means it takes much more leveling before you get to access the more useful skills in your respective classes. Want to try out different class combinations? Too bad, you have to spend 10-20 hours leveling before you can start to have any meaningful changes in your builds. This means autoattacking for 10 hours for almost every wizard build you want to try, by the way.
3) The above points make the variety of classes meaningless. It just takes up too much time, compared to other MMOs, when you want to try out new classes. The poor class balance makes me feel restricted when deciding what class combinations i want to play.
Even within the same class, its imbalanced. Eg: A scorcerer can summon different types of bosses to aid him, COOL - oh wait, only the templeshooter is considered useful? Out of the MANY bosses in the game? So everyone will be using templeshooters or your DPS will be gimped? Boring.
-------
These are just my main gripes with ToS. There are lots of cons as listed by other reviewers.
I am, however, a casual player and so the slow leveling may not affect hardcore players out there. However, the leveling process is simply BORING to me. Once the nostalgia wore off, playing the game felt like a chore, even when playing dungeons with friends. There's alot of nostalgia, but not so much fun for me.
TL DR:
It's a decent MMO, for a korean grinding game (comes along with the usual gaming restrictions). Play it for the nostalgia, if nothing else.

As the story is told at a bar while the main character recollects his life, levels will change and rewind as he corrects mistakes.  Levels are capped off with good old fashioned duels that will test your reaction speed and focus.  Secrets that give tidbits of info about the Old West spread throughout the levels provide replayability (as does the NG+ mode).
Some minor criticisms of the game--it is definitely on the short side.  I finished my first campaign run in about 4 hours, and took another 3 to replay through on the hardest/no hud difficulty.  Some levels and layouts are reused through the campaign.  Neither of these bothered me that much considering I picked it up on sale for $4.  If you're looking for a short fps experience inbetween bigger or meatier games, Gunslinger is a great choice.
Final sidenote about one of my favorite touches:  your character has an ability called Sense of Death that will proc when a bullet is about to kill you (with a cooldown of course).  Time will slow down, zoom in to show you where the shooter is, then give you a split second to dodge and watch the bullet whiz by you.  Later in the game you can even upgrade this ability to automatically mark your would-be killer for an instant headshot along with some extra bullet time to take out anyone else around.  Very stylish and never felt old!  Also meant you could run around the levels more without hiding behind cover all the time.

I liked this more than Outlast, I also liked the decision to strip away the inventory since it could lead to a more interesting gameplay experience. However, what I don't agree with, is how you're never actually in any real threat aside from two rooms. The story is well written and leaves a lot of room to be desired. All the assets in this game will be available for the Dark Descent and I am very disappointed by the lack of mod support for this game. Perhaps there'll be a way to disable the inventory entirely for Dark Descent? Who knows.
I can tell you what this game "could have" been, it could have been an experience where survival hinged on escaping the monsters and avoiding detection in a stealthy manner. All while doing this, you must search and carry all the items without the use of an inventory. So imagine backtracking into a room you really didn't want to go into, in fears that the monster might or might not still be there. Of course it's scary, but the fact is, the game never requires much backtracking into threatening experiences.
The game isn't dark enough, nobody likes the blue fog really. There are so many people out to disable the blue fog, it's a shame that they didn't just strip it all away. Apparently it's related to the story and serves a purpose, well I say it ruins the experience.
So, with that in mind, the game is what I'd say a disappointment. It's still more scary than Outlast though.

PROS:
= Game looks amazing, with cell-shaded styling going hand-in-hand with more realistic graphics. It truly looks stunning.
= The story is very good, with clever writing, clever use of an unreliable narrator and pitch-perfect voice acting from every voice actor.
= Gameplay is addicting, fast-paced, arcade-ish and action-packed. Rack up a huge combo for more points, then upgrade yourself with those points to score even MORE points!
= Adding on from that, the ability to cheat death helps to curb any frustrations.
= Just the right length for its price and its story.
= Difficulty hovers around the right level; not too easy, not too frustrating. There are no cheap deaths here. Well, sort of.
= Collectables give you a more truthful interpretation of the Wild West and finding them isn't all that frustrating.
= Also, the Joker card details the protagonist from the first CoJ. Genius.
CONS:
= Dueling is pretty crap. You have to be pixel-perfect in every aspect, or you die. Instantly. The final duel in paritcular is pretty frustrating.
= A smaller selection of weapons than I would have liked. Not helped by one of the weapons (the Sawed-Off Rifle) being completely useless and could have easily been replaced by something else, like a pump shotgun. Since most of the guns in this game are anachronistic anyway, it wouldn't have hurt that much to put one in, even as an Easter Egg.
CONCLUSION:
This game is amazing, a fantastic Western FPS. Just so nice to see one of this type after so many "modern" millitary racist corridor simulators. I can only find two real flaws with it, as above, but beyond that it's almost perfect. Great story, amazing graphics, impeccable gameplay with lots of action and joy to be had, not to mention it is light years above The Cartel. Urgh. This game is the spaghetti western counterpart to House of the Dead: Overkill; it's drenched in atmosphere and cheese, parodying itself at every given oppertunity and loving second of it.

The first playthrough for me took about 7.3 hours, despite the fact that I skipped the last challenge room. The whole atmosphere constructed by the art and soundtrack is very immersive. The whole story came together beautifully.
Gameplay:
It's an interesting take on giving players a choice between etiher real-time womanliness combat (which I'm not woman enough to do) or "halting time" so you can plan out a series of executions (use a skill, move, use a skill, use a skill, move, etc.), and even a mix of both.
Have to admit though, the controls on the keyboard aren't too great, and while it isn't a huge issue, I am more inclinded to use the plan-it-out option in fights just to make sure I hit the right things.
Art:
What can I say? It's beautiful. It's breathtaking. It looks like it was a hell-of-lot of work to do, so kudos to the art team. It's really amazing.
Soundtrack:
For me, the fantastic song "We All Become" featured in the reveal trailer stands out the most. Yet, it and every soundtrack/song mixed into the Transistor experience are all really, really well done.
Storyline/Immersion:
I have yet to complete the storyline, but the whole game comes together well. The world is given life and the characters given silent voices. While the story isn't told in a straightforward manner, having the player piece it together on her/his own is a nice variation.
Transistor is a phenomal work of art that everyone should experience. 10/10.

I was not hugely impressed with Transistor; those expecting something remotely as good as Bastion will be dissapointed. While the game is not bad by any stretch of the imagination, it wasn't quite the gem Bastion was.
The soundtrack was really good, but for some reason the developers thought it would be a good idea to hide a lot of it and make it unlockable via challenges. That makes no sense to me. The music that Darren Korb makes is amazing, I do not know why they would not take advantage of it at every turn to create the memorable experiences so many of us had with Bastion. The music being unlockable would not be that annoying to me had the game been more fun.
The game was not very fun for me, the controls felt clunky and while they encouraged experimenting with their system of augmenting abilities with other abilities to make different variations, it had the opposite effect of what they intended. The way the mechanics work, it encourages the player to combine greasy abilities together and just spam them. Their entire "pause and plan the fight" system ended up making boss fights a matter of setting up three of the four abilities to cost more memory than your main one so that when you lost all your health you would just lose the abilities you did not care about. There was no strategy or skill involved, just simple math.
What the game did an amazing job at was the art. The game looks beautiful and stylish, blending great voice acting, beautiful environments and interesting enemy/character designs. The story is also a strong point. It does not show everything to people, and rewards those who take an interest and try to find as much information as possible. All of this coupled with a [SEMI-SPOILER] tragic yet beautiful ending left me liking the entire experience.
TLDR: Great story, beautiful art, good music, mediocre gameplay, not nearly as good as Bastion.

Probably holds the crown for my favourite game of all time, sporting one of the highest amounts of time played on my steam account, and holding a special place in my heart. DS2 is one of those games that is truly the epitome of Marmite, you either love this game and feel a special and somewhat creepy need to smash your head against the wall until you finish it or you find it boring and repetitive. As someone who streamed DS2 for an extremely long time, it held up as one of those games that I always came back to for a cheeky play through.
Story: 7/10
Honestly it could have done with a little tightening up in the story department, you are a chosen undead within the lands of Drangleic, a land filled with a curse that causes people to go hollow and mad and stuff. You set out on a quest to sort of stumble around the lands following some vague advice from some old biddies and an emo redhead. It's one of those games where the story sort of fades into the distance somewhat as you play, the story just is a small nudge in the right direction for a bloodthirsty pit bull with a polearm.
Gameplay: 9/10
I am a huge fan of abusing yourself mentally and physically as you smash yourself endlessly into a boss that seemingly just wont die, and then suddenly killing it and feeling an ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic sense of achievement. This feeling is quickly followed by a sense of overbearing shame when you realised it took you over 30 tries and a few hours of swearing, drinking and button mashing before you killed ancient dragon (or dragonrider ( ͡~ ͜ʖ ͡°) ). The gameplay is very enjoyable, it feels responsive and intuitive, rolling is definitely something you learn to love and moving on to other games without rolling feels strange. There's a weirdly addictive quality to dying endlessly to kill a particular boss, it becomes something you actively look for in games, that is a challenge.
Art & Sound: 7/10
Really DS2 doesn't stand up on its music or it's graphic prowess, although they both are above average when it comes to ambience and building atmosphere. The music is not something I went out of my way to listen to more of and I certainly don't stand at the GORGEOUS VIEW signs for more than a few seconds without thinking "this view is alright and all, but the guy chewing on my♥♥♥♥♥♥probably deserves my attention more".

Absolutely love this game. It'll have you going "just a few more minutes" or "just till the research is done." And then the research is done, and you think another won't hurt. And then it's 2 AM and you're still not tired.
Jokes aside, factorio is a lovely game. While in early access it feels like a finished game. Gameplay is simple. You start off with nothing (I think, it may be a furnace and drill. Doesn't make much of a difference) and slowly begin to automate. First, you automate mining, then refining, then science, crafting, oil refining and so on in the order you please. Science is most likely going to be your first major automation after ore processing and mining, as science is what gets research done, which allows you to "level up" per say, and unlock higher levels items, and weapons, which are needed to defend yourself from the hostile tree-hugging native insects who don't take kindly to your pollution of their homeworld.
And not only can you automate processing, but you can make computers! Fully functional with displays, as long as you are dedicated enough.
All in all, great game for the money, with near infinite replayability.

I wanted to love this game but...
I'll start with some developmental flaws: the performance is unreliable/buggy even on an overpowered PC - it is not optimized. Lots of 'rubber banding', frame rate drops and mysterious lag as well. The controls are shoddy, especially when trying to execute a directional move. This game has been in development for over a year now, there is little reason it should not at least be optimized. That being said, most of the flaws I will further point out are not developmental ones, but design flaws.
The economy. There are instrinsic mechanics set in place to devalue items, thus eventually rendering them useless. Trading between players requires a token. Tokens are purchased with real cash. This can be circumvented by buying one off the market, but the economy makes this difficult since prices keep climbing as silver-farming zones become more congested. You are restricted to selling one item at a time, unless you have a token. I would describe the real money transaction system is 'pay to make it bearable'.
Swarming with bots: This contributes to the poor economic conditions of the game, and high prices on the market attract a lot of RMT activity. This cyclical problem is represented well here. These bots will also be competing with you for farming items and money as they are seemingly an integral and permanent obstacle of the game.
There is a VERY restrictive cap on the amount of dungeons you can run for loot and experience. 3 mission dungeons + 3 loot dungeons (if you purchase a token, otherwise this total is 4) per day leaves you with little to do aside from grinding. There is not much raiding going on here.
The community. The game does not incentivize teamwork. Most things can be done solo, aside from running a few instances a day with strangers. The field bosses are on static timers, and thus are 'poop-socked' by the grand-fathered few. The lack of a socially dependent community results in lots of name calling, greifing, and general unhelpfulness. Asking questions will typically incite a response with the maturity level of a 'Your Mom' type insult or a snarky antisocial retort. New players are looked down upon -  This is just the norm here. Perhaps all the flaws in the game leave the community feeling bereft, and they take their toxicity out on one another.
I put over 200 hours into this game, as well as founding donation cash, believing that it would improve, but it seems that the aforementioned issues continue to spiral downward and compound one another. I really wanted this game to succeed. In my experiences as an MMO player, poor communities and economies stem from bad game mechanics, pay-walls, unchecked exploitation and a pure lack of moderation. This game is a hot, steaming pile of everything that can possibly go wrong in an MMO and a sad dissapointment. Aspiring game developers should use this as a template of what not to do.

However, do not fall into this phsychological pattern and squander your finite time on this planet over this game. It is just not worth it. My advice: find a stable, subscription based MMO with a helpful community and active GMs.

Well another "I think i've spent enough time in the game to make a comment about it"-review.
Tree of Savior has the core to being a good game. You have plenty of classes to choose from, you have a huge world and it has the basics to keep you interested for a long, long time.
Sadly it is plagued by huge performance issues, bots and the incompetence of IMC to use this core they got to make the game a great game.
Once you reach Level 280 (the max level right now) you have pretty much finished the game. You can go into the Earth Tower, which is the only 280 content right now, but only twice a day. That's like saying a guild in WoW that they only have 2 attempts on a new raid boss and then they have to wait 24 hrs before they can try again.
No other dungeon on that level or equipment you could grind that would be fit for that level. High level maps are also pretty bad cause there's no sense in doing them since they don't yield any profitable reward and the monsters hp/dmg grows very steep after 200 making it almost not worth grinding there at all. Which results in those maps being completely empty except for 1-2 maps where grind parties form.
White Knights will then point out that you could farm silver for your attributes, which is not really rewarding and at the current state is not really worth it anyway cause it seems like it's designed for higher levels because the amount of silver you need is just beyond what a normal person could farm anyway.
Also farming "Monster Gems", which will give you +1 to a certain skill, is not really worth it. You can't trade those the normal way so you have to basically find it yourself with a 0,01% droprate (approximately) from monsters that only got like 8-10 on the map sometimes.
The frames drop as soon as there's 10-15 people on the map using their skills and often over time the lag gets worse until the weekly maintenance again (which is on Tuesdays) so sunday and monday are often a real pain in the rear cause the servers are just running poorly (even with steadily declining player numbers)
Then there's the problem of this game being really infested with bots. On certain maps you have 5x the amount of bots than you have human players. And IMC is very slow to react to this problem, too. Some got reported weeks ago and are still botting ruining the economy by farming certain, valuable items.
PvP is rarely existent but due to the performance issues also not something you want to do anyway. Unless you like a clusterfu** of effects while your high end pc is showing you 1-5 fps.
Then again the balance is horrible. The swordsman class is pretty much reduced to being a tank because compared to other classes they nerfed the damage so much that even clerics do more damage...and from all the possible class combinations you COULD choose only a small handful is actually needed and wanted. If you play anything else you will have trouble finding a party for dungeons or grind.
The cash shop in its current form is not pay2win but also doesn't really offer much that would makes you spend money on the game. You could buy tokens but you can also purchase them with ingame currency so there's not really a need to spend real money on the game unless you really want to.
Also the community is toxic as hell with lots of attention seeking trolls and dare you to say one word that isn't english, boy you'll get it...
I really wanted to give this game a fair chance but at this point I think IMC really blew it. There's not even the slightest of info what the next big content update is going to be so you can't even look forward to anything new...and the current patches are pretty much only small fixes and new loading screens.
TL;DR: If you're really interested in the game give it a few months to see how it evolves and if it even survives...if it does okay, if not then you did yourself a favor and saved yourself some pain and disappointment.
///a few months later and to be honest nothing really has changed to the positive. The game has lost pretty much 90% of its population and it's heading straight down the road of being a "pay2win-cashgrab"...really sad.
I thought a few months would help but it didn't help at all....

I was not hugely impressed with Transistor; those expecting something remotely as good as Bastion will be dissapointed. While the game is not bad by any stretch of the imagination, it wasn't quite the gem Bastion was.
The soundtrack was really good, but for some reason the developers thought it would be a good idea to hide a lot of it and make it unlockable via challenges. That makes no sense to me. The music that Darren Korb makes is amazing, I do not know why they would not take advantage of it at every turn to create the memorable experiences so many of us had with Bastion. The music being unlockable would not be that annoying to me had the game been more fun.
The game was not very fun for me, the controls felt clunky and while they encouraged experimenting with their system of augmenting abilities with other abilities to make different variations, it had the opposite effect of what they intended. The way the mechanics work, it encourages the player to combine greasy abilities together and just spam them. Their entire "pause and plan the fight" system ended up making boss fights a matter of setting up three of the four abilities to cost more memory than your main one so that when you lost all your health you would just lose the abilities you did not care about. There was no strategy or skill involved, just simple math.
What the game did an amazing job at was the art. The game looks beautiful and stylish, blending great voice acting, beautiful environments and interesting enemy/character designs. The story is also a strong point. It does not show everything to people, and rewards those who take an interest and try to find as much information as possible. All of this coupled with a [SEMI-SPOILER] tragic yet beautiful ending left me liking the entire experience.
TLDR: Great story, beautiful art, good music, mediocre gameplay, not nearly as good as Bastion.

From start to finish, this game will have you on the edge of your seat. I'd recommend watching it ahead of time just to appreciate how much attention to detail was put into this.
The gameplay is pretty standard survival horror; you sneak around, avoid enemies, fight when absolutely necessary and solve a few puzzles/ do fetch quests. In the gameplay department, there isn't a whole lot of anything new being done. But what it does do, it does well. And the Alien adds a dimension that usually isn't seen within the genre.
The AI of the Alien is unpredicatable and does not repeat its own actions outside of one or two scripted appearances. You can be killed during a section by the Alien, then redo it and not even have the thing show up. It is constantly stalking the player and will learn where you like to hide throughout the game. The sound of it moving around in the vents around you is unnerving and will constantly have you trying to avoid making any noise or dealing with any other enemies.
The storyline is good, if a bit nonsensical with the amount your character is expected to accomplish, and the voice acting is pretty superb. Performance-wise, I had no problems on a GTX 970 with an i5 processor at the highest settings.
I would recommend the game, but would probably say to get it at or under $20. It's good, but it is repetitive, at times stressful, and perhaps a bit too long. After one playthrough, I can't see going through it again any time soon, but will revisit it eventually.

text:
Plantera is an Agriculture Management game with some Clicker elements attached to it.
The game consists of the player building (or planting) their "garden", with different types of trees, bushes and root vegetables. The Clicker elements show up at the very start of the game, you need to click on the fruit/vegetables that fall from your plants to pick them up and gain money to spend on area upgrades or even more plants. Sometimes creatures like moles, foxes and even wolves show up, you can scare them off just by clicking on them.
Plantera has some amazing soundtrack playing while you do your gardening business.
Now for the achievements, Plantera has 29 of them, ranging from leveling up to planting more trees/bushes/roots and clicking on the different creatures as they appear randomly in your garden.
Overall I'd give this game a 9/10, I had a really good time playing it.

You will get carpal tunnel if you play this game. You think I'm joking? Go ahead, buy this game. Plant a tree. Then do whatever you want. Go ahead, I don't care, stop playing if you want. Unfortunately for you however, it is already too late. You have just begun a life-long addiction to clicking on trees. Yup. Every moment playing this game, you'll be thinking "Shouldn't I stop? What is the point of this? Just a bit more gold and I can buy another plant though...Let me just do that and then I'll stop." But you won't stop. Say goodbye to your wrist, and hello to 80 acres of beautiful, digital, fantasy plants.

Nothing particularly interesting happens when you get to the "end" of the game, and the amount of coins you can gain through exiting and coming back a while later caps off at 99 million (which is also the price that items cap off at). I feel that this game would benefit from a "New Game Plus" aspect; right now, you can reset the game and play from the beginning, but there are not any benefits you get from the time you put into the game before the reset.

I bought JC3 with the air, land, and sea expansion pass while on sale for 75% off.  Money well spent.  I love love love games with big open worlds and fast, fluid movement to explore them.  In a number of ways, JC3 brings to mind Prototype, one of my favorites from back in the day.  But, before you buy this game (especially at full price) there are a few things to consider.
1.  I've seen a bunch of reviews where people complained about performance, particularly with respect to memory.  The minimum requirement is 6GB RAM.  I have 8GB RAM and a GTX 750Ti GPU, and I have had virtually no performance issues to speak of.  The game runs smoothly for me, so if you have a PC with decent gaming specs you should be fine (my PC is seriously outdated, note my GPU, and it works fine for me.)
2.  If you are easily frustrated, the learning curve on the wingsuit might bother you.  You move at high speeds, and crashes can kill you.  It takes a while to unlock the ability to land smoothly in the wingsuit.  It is easy to overcompensate and lose control.  At first, I hated the wingsuit.  Then I got the hang of it, and now it is freaking awesome.  It reminds me of gliding in Prototype, but with more capability.  If you practice using the wingsuit, parachute, and grappling hook in tandem, flying around the islands of Medici is extremely satisfying for those who enjoy unique world travel.  If you get the Sky Fortress DLC, you get an alternate glider with enhanced capabilities.
3.  The storyline (what I have played so far) is... meh.  That seems to be the general concensus.  It's not bad, just predictable and simple.  That said, I don't much care.  I love a game with a great story, but I also love a game with a huge vibrant world where I can fly down the side of a mountain; blow up a tank with C4; tether a guy to a propane tank and send him rocketing into the sky; grapple onto an enemy helicopter, throw out the pilot, steer it into a fuel tank and bail out before it explodes... I enjoy the gameplay enough that the basic story doesn't bother me much.
4.  Liberating Medici is repetitive.  Each town, military outpost, etc, is liberated by destroying certain "chaos objects" which are identifiable by their red and white coloring.  However, the number of ways you can accomplish this can keep it fresh.  Blow up a gas tank with a rocket launcher.  Toss a grenade toward some circuit breakers.  Tether a propaganda billboard to a moving truck and let someone else tear it down for you.  Plant C4 on a barrel of fuel and blow it up as soon as a bad guy walks by, perhaps with the proximity sensor upgrade.  Hijack a tank or a military chopper and turn the enemies' weapons against them.  Take a town by stealth or charge in guns blazing, it's up to you.  Repetitive, yes.  But I can blow things up all day and not get bored.  Also, there are random world events (help a guy who ran out of gas, steal a military vehicle with rebel prisoners and get them to safety, etc.) and challenges (wingsuit gliding courses, shooting ranges, street races, etc.) that allow you to upgrade your equipment, if you don't want to spend all your time blowing things up.
Hopefully this will help you decide whether you think you would enjoy the game before you dump any money into it.  I would recommend grabbing it while it's on sale if you get the chance, but I enjoy this game enough that I would, in retrospect, have paid full price for it.  If you like chaotic gameplay, blowing things up, and flying across a huge (400 sq mile) and beautiful game world, this could be a great game for you.  If you prioritize plot over gameplay, have lower PC specs, or get frustrated learning a touchy (at first) new way to travel, maybe give it a pass.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is something you don’t see very often. An old school, single player only shooter. There are a limited number of weapons, three pistols (one shoots hard and slow, another shoots weak but fast and the third one is the average between them), two rifles, and two shotguns. Enemies are little more than well animated, targets in a Wild West themed shoot house, popping up on cue, running short distances until they reach a pre-determined point and spawning in from seemingly nowhere. There are no branching paths save for the opportunity to flank some foes in a select few missions.
You may think I am slagging off the game, but I’m not. All of these aspects are executed brilliantly. Shootouts are fast and satisfying tests of aiming skill and reaction time. Levels are very well designed if linear. The high score mechanics and progression system reward skillful play and encourage you to rack up as high a combo as possible.
QTE’s are peppered liberally through the game, but in the two contexts they are used they are pretty inoffensive. The first and most annoying are little segments where if you hit the right direction you kill an enemy instantly with a bonus to points scored, failure just means you have to aim and shoot at them normally. The second which crops up more often is a “Sense of Death” which grants you the opportunity to dodge a fatal shot in slowmo.  While the penalty for failure in this case is death the game is balanced for this and failing it only sets you back to the last checkpoint. In both cases the time to perform the qte is pretty forgiving and the
Less well realized are the showdowns. Which serve as roughly half of the games boss fights. They try really hard to create the western quick draw duel, tasking you with focusing in on your opponent and letting the tension hit fever pitch before a burst of fatal violence. Unfortunately the focus system feels really floaty and unresponsive. More fatally however the tension and wind up are effective… once. After failing the first time subsequent attempts are not all that satisfying and feel like really bad QTE’s.
In terms of story and art design, the game is simple but executed very well. All the action is framed as the tall tales told by a bounty hunter to some people in a bar. Most of the levels play with this framing device, such as playing out the same event through the perspectives of one eyewitness, how it’s told in the legend, and by the cowboy himself. Another instance see’s apaches swapped out for bandits as he confuses two stories. There is an ambiguity between what is supposed to be real and what is invented to make the story more impressive. The narrative itself is a fairly shallow revenge tale that gets a bit more nuanced as the game goes on, anything more would be veering into spoiler territory.
While the story mode won’t keep you for more than 8 or less hours, there is a new game+ and score attack modes for those who enjoy the core shooting mechanics enough to stay with it past the ending. Overall though, one play through was good enough for me to recommend Call of Juarez Gunslinger.

After the debacle involving a related game that SEGA couldn't even give away, I was excited to see that there had been both a return to sanity and the series' roots.
I would love to see the films take this game as an example of how to tell a story. I am passionate enough to completely discount "Prometheus" and "Covenant" after giving both a fair watch; but the mystery of these Aliens is much more entertaining to me than having unsatisfying answers spoon-fed in between gory Gieger-esque scenes (that are somehow tamer than his work). Why can't these Aliens just be another life-form in this harsh universe? Anyway, apologies to fans of those films for the rant, but they really weren't for me personally. This is just to illustrate my POV before I go further.
"Isolation" lives up to its title admirably and I have rarely been this terrified by a game in a long time. Amanda Ripley is maybe not as tough as her mother, but dealt with a lot more on her first meeting with these creatures. A single enemy pursuing me with this level of intelligence made me wish that "RE3: Nemesis" used the same AI - the threat was real, constant, and at times (admittedly) infuriating. The enemies are clever, even on Novice and I can't count how many times I have seen the Alien vanish from the tracker in the distance, only for it to be right behind the door I'm about to sneak through. Also, do NOT play this while drunk.
The story is subtle and pieced together from what you can find on computers and a damaged flight recorder - one of my favourite moments early in the game is Amanda's discovery of the flight recorder: her reaction and tone of voice could have fooled me that we were playing as her mother. The apple doesn't fall far from the tree here.
The music direction also deserves praise, it raises the tension and keeps the correct mood flowing. The voice acting does not sound over-dramatised as you see lately in other games and characters are fleshed-out and established in a way that is also not overdone. This game has a balance that I really appreaciate.
I do however take exception to the save sysem - it should increase your tension in making it from one save station to another safely, but they are few and far between, and when you get caught by the Alien (and you will), you can sometimes lose a lot of time - this feels more like punishement of the player.
People who love tension will be happy at the amount of threats there are on Savastopol - a xenomorph, lifeless manaquin-esque machines, other humans, the station AI, and more... There are jumpscares dotted here and there to keep you on your toes and a lot of them I could never have seen coming but raised my dread and immersion significantly.
If you're inclined to rage-quit a game normally - don't go into this one head-first: it's hard, and the Alien is VERY intelligent. Any mistake will likely cost you your life, a single bullet can kill you and it's also possible to have an accident on a station this big...
I loved this game on PS3 and more so with a Steam Controller now - thank you for the Linux port. Here's hoping for a sequel!

Dark Souls 2 strays away from what made the first game good, but is still fun to waste a couple hours on. The base product is well done, it would be better if they didn't cut out what eventually became the three overpriced DLCs, but the base game is still entertaining. The lore is not as deep, nor as relatable as the first game, but it's still there. If that's what you're into.
It's intersting, the first game started linnear and then let you loose as they rushed to meet the release date deadline right after Anor Londo. In this game, it does the exact opposite. Completely letting you off the leash straight from the start. This does well in the beginning, seeing how it's near impossible you won't find a path way to go.
Though this system is not without fault, since there are multiple directions, when you finally exhausted mostly every path, it's easy to get lost, forcing me to look on the internet how to get to the next part of the game. An act of which I heavily try to avoid in any RPG related game.
Another issue, the game is easy as hell. The only boss I had problems with was "The Ancient dragon,"  the only reason he was hard was because he killed you in one hit. I saw this to give a false, cheap sense of difficulty when the only reason a boss is hard is not because of their multiple attack patterns, but the amount of damage they dish out. The game also seems to treat you like a child at times when bosses eventually become average mobs. I'm talking about the Rat boss, and the Pursuer.
The last issue I have with this game is that the world isn't held together like it was in the first game. In Dark Souls 1, the world constantly had backgounds of where you once were, and new pathways which allowed you to make your way back to that area. In the end, the whole world was connected, which added heavily to the realism of the game, and it's ability to suck me into it's dark and dangrous world. This game is held together by loading screens, and next to no reminder as to where you were. If I looked at an overhead map of the game, I would have no idea where anything was because none of it fits together in a way I could recognize.
The Graphics were quite acceptional, the frame rate barely slowed, though there were times where it did. Light reflects off the armor you wear, and sometimes even your weapons, and the cloth areas of your outfit flow in the wind in a very believable fashion.
Now comes the treatment of the consumer. B team treated fans of the Dark Souls series like♥♥♥♥♥♥with the release of it's long awaited sequel. Making PC consumers wait one month for its release, (which seems to also be being done with the third game.) lying about the "there will be no DLCs" part, and openly admiting that the day one release version of the game was the "beta version." Makes me quite sick to the stomach that I even bought this game.
The only good things about the game is the combat, which felt very good and well paced with the enemies, it's ability to entertain, and sometimes even surprise. As this games ability to hold its own against the first game, it doesn't even come close.
Also, the story is nonexistant. People will argue there's lots of it. That's a lie though, no one truly knows the story except the creator himself.
