When I think of good games, I think of Mincraft, Terraria, Spore, or Factorio.
PS: This game makes 4 hours feel like 8 minutes.

Absolutely love this game. It'll have you going "just a few more minutes" or "just till the research is done." And then the research is done, and you think another won't hurt. And then it's 2 AM and you're still not tired.
Jokes aside, factorio is a lovely game. While in early access it feels like a finished game. And while you can get to the end goal of putting a satellite in space (I haven't done that yet as of 87 hours!) there isnt a specific way that it's done, every time your factory is different, and highly unorganized until you really get the hang of the game, unlike me. I am part of the church of the flying spaghetti factory.
Gameplay is simple. You start off with nothing (I think, it may be a furnace and drill. Doesn't make much of a difference) and slowly begin to automate. First, you automate mining, then refining, then science, crafting, oil refining and so on in the order you please. Science is most likely going to be your first major automation after ore processing and mining, as science is what gets research done, which allows you to "level up" per say, and unlock higher levels items, and weapons, which are needed to defend yourself from the hostile tree-hugging native insects who don't take kindly to your pollution of their homeworld.
And not only can you automate processing, but you can make computers! Fully functional with displays, as long as you are dedicated enough.
All in all, great game for the money, with near infinite replayability.

Hands down the best F1 game of all time. Seriously, as good as F1 2016 was, unless you're big into previous aero spec regulations, there's not much reason to get the older game instead of this one - even when counting for sales. If you want the best singleplayer F1 experience ever made, there's nothing that should stop you from doing that. And multiplayer? Yeah... well... later on that...
Let's talk about the game in general first - I'm personally a big fan of 2017 aero regulations, which made F1 not only faster than in 2016, but most importantly - fastest of all time. Seriously, look at most track records, most of them were set in 2017. And it shows in the game as well - damn I don't remember having this much fun with an F1 game in a long time, and trust me, I've played most of them. It's an absolute joy to drive in these cars, even the slowest Sauber is aboslutely chewing through corners... not to mention that frontrunner cars are even faster and in certain areas allow you to just go flat out. It feels like you're cheating with grip if you're used to cars from previous 3 seasons.
And even then, just in case you get tired of these aero beasts, the game has classic cars for you to explore, including cars from 1988 to 2010 lifespan. I tried most of them by this point, and while I definitely prefer the modern cars, it's definitely fun to get used to different driving styles - and most importantly, this opens up a ton of options for modders, who can now make different season mods. Just a bit of shame developers didn't also include some extra tracks (3 short variations aren't that much tbh) - but I guess they need to keep some aces up their sleeve to make sure people buy future games as well lol.
Before we get to singleplayer mode, I'd like to say one more thing - this game is all about options. This trend started with 2016 and 2017 just builds on it, you can tweak almost everything. No more preset AI difficulty, you can precisely adjust their skill level just to make them fit your style - this is a big deal, because it eliminates balancing issues that previous games had for some players (like me), who found certain level of difficulty too easy, but the next step was on the other hand too damn hard. Besides AI, you can also adjust HUD positioning, camera (was in 2016 as well) and so much more. More so even for the racing itself, while it's just a cosmetic change, racing in daylight Singapore (or night Monaco) gives the otherwise well known track a fresh vibe.
AI itself is good, once you get the difficulty just right for yourself, you're in for the best time you've ever had in singleplayer racing. They are aggressive, but not murdering crazy, they go for overtakes if they see the chance, you don't scare them away as easily as you could before (it's still possible tho - if you break some clean driving rules), and they hold the line next to you even through corners when you wouldn't expect them in older titles (mostly 2015 and earlier). They even make mistakes at times, which gives them more realistic feel. My only complaint is that they are still way too careful in first lap, nobody really takes alternative lines in first few corners, they just line up behind each other no matter what difficulty you set, allowing for easy 5+ position gaining divebomb.
Now to the singleplayer mode then: The game allows good old quick race, career, championships, time trial and events. Event is a periodically changing challenge showed to all players, in which they can race for best overall score in leaderboard. Quick race and time trial are obvious - but championships, well, that's something new. It reminds me of F1 2013's and 2012 challenges, it's a set of many mini-championships set across different tracks with different rules (spec series, two races per weekend series, street race series, etc.)... it's not really something ground breaking, but it provides some sort of structured progression for people, who for some reason don't want to play career mode.
And about career mode - it builds on very strong foundation from 2016 game, mostly improving on micro-management systems. The game now has straight up RPG-level of car progression with a tree divided into four branches, and additional perks system that improves stuff like pit stop times reliability and such, although this side-system appears to be just statically improving over time, rather than being interactive. My only problem with car progression is, that it mostly relies on grinding out points in practice sessions- you get marginal amount of points for races and qualis themselves, even when you have decent results. I understand the sentiment behind practice being the most effective for it, and while I definitely like that practice has some actual gameplay use now, experienced F1 fans don't really need to go through track acclimatisation and other practices on every track... and so they skip... and as a penalty they get only a small margin of development points.
The second big improvement of the career mode is introduction of actual parts reliability and lifetime system, no more completely random "you get less power because engine appears to be a bit worn" stuff, you can now manage your engine parts and gearboxes through the entire season, with realistic penalties waiting for you in case you fail to fit into rules-mandated part allocation. This is actually way bigger deal than I expected, and micro-managing the car through the season really adds to the fun factor of the game. Mind you, I play in 50% race lengths, not sure how this works with shorter distance races.
And about that multiplayer... well... yeah... I think the general experience is actually worse than in 2016 to be honest. I appreciate in-game ranking profile system and all, but there are too many other issues: Out of like 10 races I only have 4 counted to my in-game profile, because the game randomly disconnected, or people get really laggy and randomly appear in front of you, hitting you... stuff like this really detracts from the multiplayer racing. And this is like 3 months since the games launched. You'd expect them to have this ironed out by now.
Add people who just race online to troll through weaving, kamikaze bombing and stupid crashing (seriously, the game should ban you from online racing for multiple offenses... at least for a day or so), and unless you have a bunch of friends who want serious racing, or get really lucky,... you just won't have as much fun. It's a bit better in longer racing sessions, most trolling happens in short 5 lap races, but it's still fairly problematic. Such a shame, this game would have been a clean 10/10 without these issues.
As for graphics - the game is pretty much on 2016 and 2015 level of graphical detail, although it significantly improved on lighting this time around. Just compare two gameplays on YouTube and you'll immediately notice the difference.
So... if you're in for the singleplayer, just buy it, it's a 9,5/10. The missing 0,5 would be filled by extra tracks DLC (Istanbul park, Bathurst... come on Codies, you already have these tracks scanned for Grid series, just do it!). For multiplayer? You better be off with some more serious racing sim, at least in public lobbies the trolling is beyond acceptable.
Still though - this is the best F1 game yet.

After the debacle involving a related game that SEGA couldn't even give away, I was excited to see that there had been both a return to sanity and the series' roots.
I would love to see the films take this game as an example of how to tell a story. I am passionate enough to completely discount "Prometheus" and "Covenant" after giving both a fair watch; but the mystery of these Aliens is much more entertaining to me than having unsatisfying answers spoon-fed in between gory Gieger-esque scenes (that are somehow tamer than his work). Why can't these Aliens just be another life-form in this harsh universe? Anyway, apologies to fans of those films for the rant, but they really weren't for me personally. This is just to illustrate my POV before I go further.
"Isolation" lives up to its title admirably and I have rarely been this terrified by a game in a long time. Amanda Ripley is maybe not as tough as her mother, but dealt with a lot more on her first meeting with these creatures. A single enemy pursuing me with this level of intelligence made me wish that "RE3: Nemesis" used the same AI - the threat was real, constant, and at times (admittedly) infuriating. The enemies are clever, even on Novice and I can't count how many times I have seen the Alien vanish from the tracker in the distance, only for it to be right behind the door I'm about to sneak through. Also, do NOT play this while drunk.
The story is subtle and pieced together from what you can find on computers and a damaged flight recorder - one of my favourite moments early in the game is Amanda's discovery of the flight recorder: her reaction and tone of voice could have fooled me that we were playing as her mother. The apple doesn't fall far from the tree here.
The music direction also deserves praise, it raises the tension and keeps the correct mood flowing. The voice acting does not sound over-dramatised as you see lately in other games and characters are fleshed-out and established in a way that is also not overdone. This game has a balance that I really appreaciate.
I do however take exception to the save sysem - it should increase your tension in making it from one save station to another safely, but they are few and far between, and when you get caught by the Alien (and you will), you can sometimes lose a lot of time - this feels more like punishement of the player.
People who love tension will be happy at the amount of threats there are on Savastopol - a xenomorph, lifeless manaquin-esque machines, other humans, the station AI, and more... There are jumpscares dotted here and there to keep you on your toes and a lot of them I could never have seen coming but raised my dread and immersion significantly.
If you're inclined to rage-quit a game normally - don't go into this one head-first: it's hard, and the Alien is VERY intelligent. Any mistake will likely cost you your life, a single bullet can kill you and it's also possible to have an accident on a station this big...
I loved this game on PS3 and more so with a Steam Controller now - thank you for the Linux port. Here's hoping for a sequel!

I played this during beta and thought it was easy, boring, and not well thought-out. You can either just quest till your heart is content to enjoy a Skyrim like feel to the game, or you can get involved in dungeons, trials, and pledges in order to make the game feel more like an MMO. The crafting system has been vastly improved from the beta too. There are a lot of armor "sets" that grant extra bonuses for how many items you have of the set equiped (similar to Diablo). Having actual traders makes the game fun too, as there is no server trader or marketboard that everyone can access. Everything is done on a guild basis where the guild have to compete for a trading location. This really makes the player responsible for what they are selling, and keeps prices in game higher on items so that you can actually go gather mats for hours and make loads of money! It's seriously a great game. Pick it up! It's cheap and totally worth it 100%!

Short Review: The game was a disappointment. I was expecting the whole hog and all I got was scrawny pork chops. While I can't recommend-recommend the game, I wouldn't say don't play it. Just expect to feel a little empty inside afterwards, especially if you liked the first game.
Long Review: I am a fan of the first Amnesia game. It had a fantastic setting, dark and gritty and wonderfully oppressive. And it had an interesting lead and while Daniel was a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you could feel for the guy. You got to get inside of his head, got to feel his fear, experience his unknowing at what was going on. You and Daniel got to experience the game together (him with fresh eyes at the horrors he did, you; the player, progressing through the story). And it was a good game. A great game even: Simple enough of a story that it wasn't overly complex and yet engaging.
Then came Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs. When I first started to follow the game's production, I was thrilled that they were making a sequel. I didn't know where they would take the game, since the endings to the first one left little wiggle room for a second, but I was eager all the same. Then I learned Fractional Games wasn't making it. I started to feel a little uneasy about the game then. But it would be alright, right? They wouldn't just hand off one of their titles off to someone that didn't know what they were doing, right?
Then I heard the Chinese Room was making it. Now, when I learned this, I had just finished playing one of their other games "Dear Ester" (Just...biggest waste of money -ever-). Now I started to feel some real dread. I worried about what the game would hold, but I decided to try and keep an open mind.
So when it came out, and I played it, I liked it well enough as I was going through it: The environment was lovely and the little glimpses of the main's children were a nice creepy touch. But then the ending to the game came and I started to feel unsatisfied. And afterwards: Unhappy. The story was complex in the worst possible way. The character's internal narrative bogged down the story, making it difficult to follow in some places and in the end, I felt no sympathy towards him. I was glad he died, he deserved it, no matter how much the game wanted to put some sort of Jekyll and Hyde twist on him.
I also missed the insanity meter, which meant I could stare at something disturbing until the cows came home and Oswald wouldn't get disturbed by it even a little. (Of course, an in game reason is that Oswald is -maybe- more mentally sound then Daniel-I'll-just♥♥♥♥♥♥my-pants-now, but even that doesn't make much sense since just being in the presence of the Orb broke him, While Daniel managed to at least retain his relative sanity until he was pushed to the point he feared for his life and was willing to do ANYTHING to save it)
Anyway: The game was not good. It wasn't bad, but it wasn't good either and not a good follow up to Amnesia: The Dark Decent. It might have done a little better if it didn't carry the tag "Amnesia", perhaps my hopes wouldn't have been so high, but overall, I can't recommend the game on the merit of a bogged down story, unsympathetic and uninteresting characters, and unsatisfactory game play (It's "Dear Ester + Mild Horror elements" really). I will recommend the game though on its visuals and interesting setting though.

Amazing game for the price. Has it all, PvP, Building, RP and Survival. I've been holding off reviewing this game until I've had atleast 500 hours on it.
It's time to review.
Pros

-Some of the funniest gaming experiences I've had have been on this game.
-Building is fun and you can really creative with it, even better than the building system in minecraft.
-PvP - Fast paced and very skill based.
-Roleplaying - Even though I'm orientated towards PvP, Roleplay servers are an entirely differant experience in the game. Putting on a funny medieval voice and catching criminals as the medieval police was a very fun experience.
-Character creation - I still chuckle at the bizzare and ugly character people come up with.
-War time - The King and the guild system really add to the game, go to war with the king or with differant guilds.
Cons
- Don't play this game alone - Whether you get irl friends, steam friends or make friends in game, it just makes the game so much more enjoyable than getting teamed on by yourself by 3 guys.
- Official Server KOS and offline raiding - Although a lot of people like killing on sight and offline raiding, (i'm one of them) a lot of people get fustrated and leave after they die and lose their gear or somebody raids their home. If you're one of these people do not threat, you can still enjoy this game. There are COMMUNITY server with rules and admins who will ban anybody who breaks the rules. Find the right server for you.
- Sieging - Sieging went from being completely overpowered to being completely underpowered. Codehatch are currently working on balancing so in time the siegeing system is a bit unbalanced and it may take a while to break into a base with a trebuchet.
Overall I rate this game a solid 8/10 game. Some balancing issues are needed but overall I am very, very happy with my purchase. Thanks codehatch.

Smite is a fun game to play alone and even more fun to play with friends when you can combo with gods abilities to beat your enemy. The thing that makes Smite fun is the thing that characters are actual gods from mythologies and by playing Smite you will learn a ton about different mythologies and the gods lore. The road to becoming good at Smite takes time to learn what items to buy to your gods to get the most out of them and how the abilities of different gods work in different occasions to beat your enemy.
There are dozen of different game modes and gods to choose from to fit different peoples ways of liking.
Cons of Smite are the occasional bad updates that makes other gods way more dominant than other what leads to repetitive use of few specific gods. There would probably be no cons at all if Hi-Rez Studios would listen what community has to say about the needs of things that updates bring to the game.

Full review on my blog:

Overall, it wasn't that scary, and the experience is closer to Dear Esether in that it's a narrated experience of traversing environments. The puzzles amount to 'pull the lever on the wall right in front of you to open the door' level of difficulty, and unlike Dear Esther, you can be killed by the rare enemies present, but it's still barely a game.
Still, I got it for cheap and enjoyed it for the couple of hours it took to walk through it, but if you're expecting a horror game, it's not going to fill that need.

Do you like puzzles? Do you like being scared? Do you like the "realness" that a fully interactive environment where you can interact with every object brings? If so then avoid the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game. It's on-rails the whole way through and the puzzles boil down to "turn this crank" and "put this box here." I regret every cent of the twenty dollars I spent on A Machine for Pigs.

I gave this game a thumbs up, but this is a mixed review. I enjoyed the game immensely. However, I just don't enjoy it enough to pump funds into it. If it was a one time buy, then you're good to go, then I'd pay real money for it. But having to pay a subscription, I just don't get into it that much.
Now, as far as the game goes, it's very well done. You track animals and kill them. Pretty simple. It's a little "sci-fi", in a way, with your tracker. You see foot prints, your tracker will give you a cone of which direction the animal is heading. Not too bad. But then you find droppings, and the tracker gives you a max range of how far they could have gone. Now you have direction, and how far they could be. Then, you hear a grunt, howl, cluck, etc, and the tracker pings your map exactly where the noise came from.
Now, if that's what you're into, that's fine. Don't get me wrong, that last paragraph was not meant as a complaint, just information. I enjoy the tracker.
The only thing I don't like about this game, is the recurring payments. You can hunt 3 types of animals for free indefinitely, mule deer, a type of rabbit, and something else I can't remember off the top of my head. you have to buy licenses to hunt anything else, or pay a subscription to unlock everything.
It's free to try and hunt and see how the gameplay is, so there's no risk. You might as well try it to see if you're willing to pay money into it. Worst case scenario is you waste some time and realize you don't want to pay.

Still a buggy, unoptimised and crash-filled mess even years after launch. A real shame since the core gameplay is still good, provided you can put up with the braindead AI.

Graphics:
The Graphics are excellent and the map rendering is amazing. This game goes leaps and bounds ahead of Napoleon, Medieval 2, and Rome 1. The absolute detail and effort they put into rendering the landscape, bodies, flora and fauna, and the architecture, as well as the absolute attention to accuracy for time and culture is out of this world.
But alas, this may be the only real vantage it has.
Gameplay:
As much as I enjoy the game in its moments, the times I've played has frustrated the ever living crud out of me. I played Britannica, Rome-Julia (2x), and the Masillia... All I can say is that my play style is aggressive. Britannica, you can't aggressively attack anyone and expand your tribal influence (everyone around you is too powerful or outnumbers you, and your tech and troop choices are low tier number oriented, price oriented), and diplomacy is just as terrible, with no real influence, and no real tangible power to throw weight behind your bids for alliances and pacts between other local and cross-channel tribes...
So I decided do what I have always done: Play as Rome. I thought to myself: "A nation of order, of excellent, professional military prowess (even at its early stages of Republic), and a people readily motivated and highly sophisticated"... Twice... I was absolutely, positively dead f'in' wrong. The people are continuously unhappy, the army is the only real pride, but even then, a nation is not built by warriors alone. Its economic capabilities are hampered as you attempt to lower taxes to ease the "suffering" of the disgruntled, ungrateful peasants who want peace without effort in part of the military, and then the constant f'ing slave revolts. I had two revolts within a matter of 5 turns... 5!!!! And the second revolt took Roma AND the city north of it... In ONE TURN!!!! Which makes no sense as any average army of that time would not have the energy to conduct such a prolonged campaign without serious fatigue and losses...
More importantly, after defeating the first army, the second slave army was twice as powerful, and even MORE EXPERIENCED than the previous army I fought against... This is, of course, after retaking another city from the Etruscans, who, also, are unbalanced in both power and military experience.
And this is all on easy so I can try to understand game mechanics and changes to the game play style... I do FAR better on the previous games, expanding faster and more efficiently than this game, where it seems to take ages to capture just one city or settlement...
So, to see what else was there, I play as Masillia... No different. One single territory, surrounded by hostile or questionable neighbors... So I begin to build up, roughly, a sizable army. I assault into the left hand territory, sending my large army to capture the territory (as per the orders at the beginning of every game, capture 2 territories to show expansion, because reasons)... I face off against another sizable army (a little larger than mine, not too much, something I can handle, I got two Hoplite Heavy Spear units that can do the job if worse comes to worst)... NO! THAT'S NOT WHAT HAPPENSE AT ALL! Instead, enemy has ALL heavy infantry, my Commander's cavalry die like idiots when I try to charge them into a f'ing RANGED unit (light), or die like ABSOLUTE IDIOTS WHEN CHARGING BROKEN ENEMY UNITS! FROM BEHIND!!!! WTF!?
And my Hoplites are just dying. My units outnumber whats left of the enemy force by four whole units (three of them fresh slingers who could help at least boost the numbers), and they just start dying in droves... It was at this point, when unit after unit started fleeing to a near depleted command unit and heavy sword unit, both exhausted, that I decided to quit to windows and uninstall...
It is absolutely ridiculous that, even in the initial stages (all were accomplished within TEN TURNS)... I never made it past 10-15 turns... Ever... In this game... In Napoleon Total War, playing as Great Britain, I've clocked over 120 turns... And I've played ONLY as Britain so far... That says a lot...
The AI is also quite potato... But also extremely blunt and direct... And it seems that with the tying in of inter-clan/tribal politics with ad hoc alliances... It makes you NOT want to expand, because everyone is friends with someone... and ultimately leads you to war with more than just ONE nation/tribe. So it essentially encourages politics... Not war... Contrary to the title of the game... And politics are crap at best. (Example: Britannica, where influence is meaningless, and your power is nothing. YOU CAN'T DO ANYTHING BECAUSE YOU ARE LITERALLY AN INSIGNIFICANT TRIBE)...
I've never been so disappointed in a game, never been so dissatisfied and so completely and utterly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about a game's overall campaign development and battlefield development... EVER. Its almost as if the Game Dev's don't want you to enjoy the game... They want you to be a literal dictator, with all the problems that come with leading a nation... If I wanted to do that, I would've become a politician... Because at least with that, I get benefits... Instead of losing money and pulling hair out of my head because of the stupid crap that happens in this damned game...
Total War forever!!!!!!!

The Barbarians pretty much are all the same with not a whole lot of difference in the skins. Same with the Steppe Barbarians whome also share a combat  style with the Persians and Eastern Empires. The big differance from the last Rome is the naval aspect. While you had no "naval battle map" to fight on, the ships still served a purpose. With Rome 2 they have an even greater use. With Costal cities you can do a combined arms action and beach the ships effectively turning your Marines into ground troops. The flexibilty in troop movements is good but the tactics will always be the same, flank and encircle. Cavalry is fun but limited because the spears are much more effective then the previous Rome. The Roman faction is still by far the best to use and the qaulity of the troops can't be matched. The scope of the map is also great and long lived. While your securing territory in the realm of your influence, at the far end of the map a NPC is doing the same thin on they're end. Eventualy you will clash with an Empire equal in size or greater. Overall the game is worth buying and if you have plenty of hours to sink in this game, you will find this has a huge replay value!

Let me start of by saying that what I write below is from the eyes of a person who has recently finished Transistor.
At the beginning I knew this game was going to be good. The narrative pulled me along - and the world never lost it's curious nature. I found myself wanting to know what was next every moment I played. Something unique about transistor personally, for me. I haven't seen many games that pulled me a long the way it had.
From an Artists perspective - may I just say this game is gorgeous. It's truly beautiful. I tried to savor every single location because of it. The immense use of color and vibrancy in some areas is literally awe inspiring. The designers and Artists who put their time into this game must have really enjoyed the whole process - because I can't fathom anything of this quality being made without considerable love and devotion to it.
Gameplaywise? This game was challenging and fun. The way combat worked was unique to itself - and I enjoyed how much customization your abilities had. It's honestly impressive and fun to sit there figuring out how to build a character. I found myself drawn to a combination of summoning my pet luna and using her in conjunction with other control abilities. But there were so many different ways to go about this.
The soundtrack, well.. how else can I put it? I'd have bought this if it were just /music/ it is so wonderful. But the narrative it flows along with can't be put to the side, either. The narrative the game follows gives quite a few on the songs an amazing meaning to the lyrics and themes - I enjoyed listening to each song and seeing how it told things the story hadn't quite covered.
The story - my god the story. I'm not the toughest guy in the world, but I sure as hell don't cry over nothing. Without revealing too much, let me tell you the person who made this game's story was a genius. It's so beautiful on so many levels. I pride myself on the ability to take something away from a game's meaning and message - and this is a game that has a beautiful message at it's heart.
If I had to say one thing about the ending, I would say it was exactly what I wanted - but not what I had expected whatsoever. You are always on your toes during the whole experience - you never quite see where it's going - and that's the most amazing thing I've ever experienced in a game of 2014. I reccomend this to all of my friends - and pretty much the whole gaming community.
This is something you don't want to miss. It's truly something that won't be forgotten. 10/10

Everything already said here is true: "A Machine for Pigs" is disturbing and occasionally terrifying. The art design is often staggeringly beautiful, despite pushing the game engine to (or sometimes beyond) its limits. The story is awfully familiar and it suffers a bit from an excess of climaxes, but all in all the final scenes are satisfying.
It's also not much of a "game," more of a trolly ride through interesting set-pieces. There's a lot of puzzle-solving to be done, but it's the simplest kind. Some people consider the puzzles to be throw-aways, but I found them welcome breaks between "long exposition" and "creeping around in fear of monsters," both of which are exhausting. In the end I'd say the balance of lever-pulling, storytelling, and scary-stuff-in-the-dark was well-done.
Worth the money? For me it was. Polished? Surprisingly so. Gripping? More-or-less. Just don't expect any brilliant puzzles or any REAL narrative surprises. If you can enjoy the eye-candy and the pretty good yarn, you're set.

Before I start I must explain that the reason I do not recommend this game is not because it is bad in any way, it is because its multiplayer is full of hackers/mods/spam and broken equipment (it also has no developer support).
The game is however very good, the single player has a gripping storyline that is full of action and great cinematic cut scenes. It includes a variety of wepons and settings so that each level is interesting, one level could take place in a desert and the next in a forest. There are intense moments and plot twists that really do get your emotions going, it's possibly one of my favourite story modes of all time. However it's slightly short and on veteran difficulty certain levels can be near impossible without touches of luck.
Single player also comes with 'spec ops' (which can be played co-operatively), spec ops adds another layer of difficulty to the story mode and alters story mode levels to suit a different challenge. It's divided up into a variety of categories including races so the diversity is enough to keep you playing when one type of mission is frustrating you. The frustration is worth it however as when difficult spec ops are completed you feel extremely satisfied.
Overall I would say it is a great game however its lack of developer support and its toxic hacking environment (online) mean it cannot be worth its price tag.

I could write an entire essay/article on this game, I'm not going to for the sheer fact that I'm lazy and hope that whoever reads this will take my word and buy the game.
NOTICE: *Although my steam record says that I have 4.6 hours played, I actually spent a total of about 9-10 hours playing the whole game itself. The reason for why is because I went offline for those good 6 or so other hours. I've played and beaten this game once already.*
Transistor...Oh what to say about this wonderful game that has kept my weekend more than entertaining for me. This game is something that I've been looking for a long time. With it's interesting combat system, the artful use of combining skills and attacks, Transistor and it's creator, Supergiant Games, shows off a more than polished interactive experience that'll be sure to glue your eyes to the screen for countless hours.
The combat system, to me at least, is something that you can compare to VATS from the fallout games, only in a sense that you're able to choose your attacks and inflict them to whoever you wish provided that you have the resources to do it. This system is a big plus for me in that it gives me the choice on a situation and how I'd like to tackle it. It left it to my decision and in doing so, kept me in my chair (may I add that it is an uncomfortable one) for hours at a time.
The storyline was confusing at first, but once I progressed through the story I found that it was a pretty good one. Nothing that blew my mind, but still was a little more than satisfactory.
In short, buy this game. You're not going to regret it, especially if you got it on sale.

The walking animation may be a bit derpy looking, but the rest of the game is absolutely breathtaking. Gorgeous art, perfect storytelling, kick♥♥♥♥♥soundtrack, and a huge amount of variety in combat. The way you learn about the world through customizing your toolkit is brilliant and adds a lot of replayability, which is crucial for such a short game. If the challenge and replay aspects aren't your cup of tea, then a full $20 might be a bit steep for what is a most a six-and-a-half hour game, but experiencing the story unfold through its genius narrative is an experience all of its own.

Plantera is a clicker game where you plant a variety of trees, bushes, and crops to collect gold and plant more. Throughout the game, various animals come to steal the crops, which means setting aside some gold for upgrades like scarecrows or dogs.
It's pretty standard of a clicker game. In fact, it might be a little less substantial than other clicker games, but the adorable style and involvement the game offers is unrivaled. From other clicker games that I've played, it almost wants you to be away from your computer. Which is totally understandable, but Plantera gives you reasons to stick around.
You could click on the various animals that come to steal your things, tap fruit on the trees so that it falls down quicker, and even click the magificent Loot Knight that runs across your screen from time-to-time! If you are active, you'll probably find yourself constantly upgrading your garden with better trees and increasing their plot size.
The only problem that you'll find is that the game goes by incredibly quick. Hence the reason why I said it is much less substantial than other clicker games. Somehow, the world feels rather... lonely. Once you get the upgrades, there is very little use to stick around, save for watching your wallet grow bigger. Without any thing to by, however, it becomes quickly underwhelming.
It would be awesome if they added more crops, but maybe some cosmetic items for your little helpers as a gold-sink. Maybe allow you to plant in different biomes with varying degrees of upgrades and infrastructure. It would also be nice to have a statistics page so I can see how much of my pathetic existence I spent clicking virtual plums!
Overall, I'd consider this game worth the three dollars it is marked at currently. It's a cute clicker game that's a bit rough around the edges. If the developers keep on expanding, this game could be one of the best around!

Anyways, this game is a clicker game. What do you expect? You buy something with your in-game currency and wait for it to produce even more gold. You'll find yourself investing your "gold" in some plants. Instead of telling you to spam the ♥♥♥♥ out of your left mouse button like those generic♥♥♥♥♥clicker games, this game only tells you to wait. Wait as your plants getting ready to be harvested.
But, there's a twist! There's these evil garden invaders trying to steal your crops. You think this is a screen-saver?! NO. Here's where that Clicker game mechanism comes to play. You'll need to protect your garden from these pesky but cute little thieves. TL;DR: 7/10. It has promise, but the game's current content is its community.Your mileage will vary.
Like most survival games, this game is made by the community you play with. If you are someone who wants to log onto a public server, then you will run into hackers, griefers, and a rabid fight for the throne. Some people like that kind of community, I do not. Luckily, I play with friends on a private server where we have a loose set of rules (eg. don't attack without reason, respect the area around everyone's bases, etc) and I'm digging it so far.
The customization of appearence leaves something to be desired (hopefully to be fixed by female models and maybe future armor/dyes), but I'm impressed by how the voxel-based construction works. As long as you place down an "initial" block and build off of that, you can deal with clipping terrain- something that a lot of other survival structure-building games struggle with. It is also easy to remove blocks within your crest as you build (something, again, that a lot of buildings struggle with) so if you make a mistake or decide to move a wall out a few blocks, it's easy to do. Sometimes too easy, I've more than once accidentally made a window! A toggle option would be useful, as a quality of life tweak, but it's nothing major.
I have not experienced a lot of combat, only really facing AI enemies. Larger prey animals are, I feel, sufficiently hard to kill while ducks you can pretty much walk up to and bop on the head. Enemies such as wolves and bears sometimes have strange pathing, losing agro on you to run off somewhere else. The AI in general is a bit odd in places, running off cliffs or into the water to attack you from the riverbed (they have not grasped the concept of swimming yet).
The resource ceiling is fairly low at the moment. Once you get iron tools, weapons, and armor (steel is a very small step up), there isn't much else for you to do aside from build. There are some rare drops from mobs such as livers, diamonds, and 'tears of the gods' but not too much comes from them. I'd be interested to see more a use of these tears (rather than a, as of now, defunct item) or for the plague village to have more of an impact, through items or some other reward.
Glitches happen, as it *is* an alpha. Items will sometimes disappear from workbench output slots (Client-side, so you can get a buddy to grab it. Though, for some reason, you can then only pick them up one at a time... Maybe an ID issue.), phsyics will sometimes eat you and spit you back up toward the sky, balista sometimes will not recognize your commands, etc. Some items seem to have been removed due to bugs, which while better than leaving them in the game leaves a bit to be desired. Some more in-house testing could definitely help but, overall, for its stage in development its issues are fairly smoothed out.
Hunger/thirst seem like unneeded mechanics, hunger moreso than thirst. Pretty much within your first in-game week you have established yourself well enough to, as long as you don't neglect it entirely, manage those stats well enough. Energy is again strange, you can sprint for incredibly long distances but jumping will devour it. As long as you're not bunny hopping everywhere, you'll be fine. Fishing seems pretty much useless, I've spent about an hour trying to catch something to no avail. It could be user error, though. The health system is interesting but confusing at first, and a few tweaks to its UI could be considerable help.
Best way I can describe it is the survival of Rust combined with the building of Minecraft. If you have friends who are interested and you can game privately, then I'd definitely recommend it. If you're looking to play on a public server, or alone, I'd wait a bit longer or do a bit more research. It's not for everybody, and I can see how people can get burnt out by lack of content. Right now the content is the community, and your mileage will vary.

Some people will love Alien: Isolation and some people will hate it. This game really succeeds at ramping up the tension in a way that few other games can match. It's a genuine horror experience. But if you're looking for something that's "fun" in the conventional sense, stay far away from this one. I will recommend it as long as you know what you're getting into. For the right kind of horror fan, this game should be a 10/10. But be warned - this game is not for everyone.
I have to praise the atmosphere. The environments are very reminiscent of the film series, and they are fun to explore. The game is a few years old as of 2017, so the graphics are no longer top-of-the-line, but they are good enough to make the experience feel immersive. The sound design is even better, and might be the best part of the game. I highly recommend wearing your best headphones while playing. You will have to constantly listen for sound cues to see if you're in danger. You're on a space station that is noisy and creaky, and it will mess with your head. Good stuff.
The Alien itself is great. It looks just like it does in the movies. It is powerful, it is fast, and it wants you dead. The AI isn't perfect, but it definitely achieves its main goal: it forces you to stay on your toes at all times. This creature is as terrifying as a video game character can be.
Unfortunately, the tension in this game comes at a cost. Part of the reason you will be so scared to die in this game is that the save points are far apart, so every time you die it's a significant setback. If you get stuck on one part of the game, you might have to play the same 15 minutes over and over. This does help to make the game feel scary, but if that feeling wears off then it just becomes annoying and tedious. I'm playing it on the "normal" difficulty level, and honestly I wish I had picked a lower one because I just want to see more of the game instead of having a burdensome death knocking on my door at all times.
As you progress, the game starts to get repetitive, and the pace of it gets really slow. No matter where you go, the Alien is always nearby. To avoid him you have to find hiding places. So, you sit in a closet and wait around for a few minutes until he backs off. Then you sneak past him so you can find the next closet to hide in. And unfortunately, that is most of the gameplay. So if you ever get tired of hiding in closets and under tables, you will start to hate this game. Alien: Isolation may look like an FPS, but it rarely plays like an FPS. Do not try to fight the Alien, unless you want to see him kill you. Don't fire your gun anywhere near him, because he can hear gunshots and he will come looking for you.
Let's see...what else is there? The story is alright. I like how it fits into the lore of the series, but it never really gets me to care about the characters. The main character is a tough lady engineer - appropriate for the part but nothing special. There are humans and synthetic androids hanging around occasionally, most of which are hostile so you usually just avoid them. The controls are good. I played mostly with a keyboard and mouse, but I also tried an Xbox controller. They are both basically fine. A mouse lets you turn around faster, and a controller lets you peek around corners more carefully. There is a crafting system. I am sick of every game having a crafting system, so I didn't get much out of that, but it is at least functional. I haven't played any of the DLC yet, so I won't comment on that.
So if that a really tense game sounds good to you, then give it a try. If you're not sure and just want to try it, then wait until it's on sale and play on a low difficulty level.

Where to begin...
So do you like playing on a server to have you experience ruined by hackers within in the first few minutes? Do you love playing with a bunch of immature losers on all of the official servers? Do you enjoy spending multiple hours building a decent base to have it torn down via trebuchet within 5 minutes? Do you have fun getting killed in full steel by a person bombarding you with a wood club? Let me start with the positives, then the negatives, then I will give you a summary of my opinion on the game.
PROS:
. The game can be very fun at times when playing on a good server even though it is very rare
. The combat is very enjoyable when its not laggy and glitchy
. Building a base is really fun as well as trying to defend it
. There is a huge variety of weapons that you can craft all of which having advantages and disadvantages.
. A lot of the community servers are really fun to play on sometimes
. Some guilds that you run into have really cool people who want to group up with other guilds to take down the jerks and trolls on the server
. Every once in a while the hackers that take over servers do some hilarious things. One time I was placed on a freeforall deathmatch on the beach with all of the other players
. Trebuchets are really fun to use even though they can be a pain sometimes since their accuracy is inconsistent
. New things are constantly being added into the game
CONS:
. The game has been out for over 6 months and it is STILL ridden with hackers. All of the anti-hack software that the devs make you install to play the game is TOTALLY USELESS!!!!!!
. Every update seems to introduce more bugs then bugs that are fixed
. You will usually spend 5+ hours to build a decent base to have it torn down in 5 minutes. Sieging bases needs WAY more balancing
. There are a lot of annoying trolls in this game. There is virtually no point in making your own stuff since everyone else always tries to KOS and take your stuff that you worked hours upon hours to get
. Any block can be one-shotted with a trebuchet with 5 stones in it. Makes sieging ridiculously OP
. Sometimes the bugs such as respawning with no club are really frustrating and STILL HAVE NOT BEEN FIXED
. Hackers will ruin virtually every server that you will ever join within at least 2 or 3 days of playing
. Blocks are way to expensive and the cost of certain blocks needs to be reduced
. You usually have to wait for a server wipe to get any type of enjoyable experience because servers are usually dominated by just one guild
. The throne room can be blocked up and crested which makes no sense as far as defending your throne
. You have to spend hours of grinding to get situated
. This is a cut-throat kind of game
. There are still a lot of lag issues in the game despite patch
So, is this game worth $20.00? Certainly not. Is the game worth $10.00? Maybe. I would wait till it goes on sale for $5.00 or something to get it like Chivalry is right now. Between all of the hackers, KOSers, annoying trolls, and bugs, this game is virutally unplayable most of the time. Save yourself the heartache. I would wait until this game is officially out of alpha and beta to give it a try. I might give it another review then. If the devs don't make an effort to really fix the game by the time it is released, I wouldn't bother wasting your money on this game. You can still have fun in rare cases, but all of the problems are so much of a turn-off that It will turn you off to playing it a lot of the time. Overall, I would give it a
5/10. If the problems are fixed and the devs add lots more new features and mechanics, I might be tempted to give a much higher rating.

Honestly, this game is a very middle-ground game. It has glitches, lags, and the devs are in the 'bad zone' after their first game.
But, with some friends, and some patience (and the ability to start over again and again without raging), you may find this game good. You can join a roleplay server, and no people will kill you for no reason. If you have friends, then you can make a base quick, and rule your own land.
And, if you're lucky, people may support you enough for you to be king. Kill peasants! Use a gillotine! Get loot from taxes! Anything. And the game's fighting system, though glitchy and strange, is not entirely bad. It's almost like Chivalry.
You have 3 main attacks, a 'kick' ability, and a blocking ability. If you block right, you can counter and score a hit. If they run, throw javelins and rocks. Feint an attack, so they put up their shield, then strike when they lower it.
But really. If you're not into glitches, or hate games without real 'seriousness' then get Rust instead. Otherwise, enjoy a roleplay server, go fishing, and best of all...
Butt-rocks. Use them to escape bonds or to kill yourself. Fun!
TL:DR= The game is fun sometimes, but mostly only on sale or if you've got lots of money to spare should you buy it. Otherwise, get Rust. This game is only really good on roleplay servers, but it's got some good things to it.

After playing for a bit and then not touching the game for almost half a year, I binged the rest of the game in one day. Here are my pros/cons:
Pros:
- Absolutely stunning graphics that haven't aged at all in the past 3 years, with almost photo-realistic environments packed with incredible amounts of detail
- Immersive, high quality sounds
- Runs like greased butter coated in teflon
- Seriously terrifying - you never ever feel truly safe
- Engaging story and characters
- Incredibly intelligent alien AI
- Without a doubt the best Alien game ever made
Cons:
- If you have no other choice, combat against humans, and especially combat against androids, is clunky or just straight up awful
- On higher difficulties it can be more a matter of trial and error to avoid the xenomorph than anything else, to a frustrating extent (You might have heard of the infamous section in the
. I started the game on hard but had to lower the difficulty for this segment)
- Sometimes if you're hiding in a closet or cabinet leaning backwards and holding your breath, letting go of the prompted keys before the xenomorph has been gone for more than 5 or so seconds will cause you to instantly die, with the alien suddenly having teleported back and the game over screen playing with its inner jaw going through the center of your head.
Cons(?):
- If you don't have much patience, stealth in some situations can be frustrating
- Some people might have trouble figuring out where to go
Verdict:
One of the best horror games ever made, that nails the tone and atmosphere of the original Alien better than any other game in the franchise ever has, and likely ever will. Pick this up during a sale and make sure to bring an extra pair of pants.

So about three hours into the game and I noticed something.
The game's titular enemy, the alien, is the worst aspect of the game, at least so far.
It takes 2 hours to show up and when it does it's atmosphere is destroyed.
Until then, I had been fighting enemies with guns, well avoiding them that is.
That was fun, as I knew where they were and it was mostly my fault for being spotted or losing.
The alien is the opposite.
I don't think I've had one death where I genuinely was at fault.
The first time the alien saw me in a closet, I didn't know the button prompts, and couldn't react in the time it gives you, since the game expects you to know about it beforehand.
Then there were the many deaths where the Alien corners me somewhere I can't hide, like in an office where he just sprints up to the door and acts like a natural patrol route.
The AI for the alien is also ridiculous.
It knows what section of the area I'm in, and makes it abundantly clear as it decides it has to hang around 10-15 feet from me at all times. I also can't move because if I can see it, it can see me and I'm already dead.
It has such hightened senses yet prances around me like it definitely does not know that I am under the desk, but it won't give up because its ESP has told it that I'm in the area.
It's as though it's on a trigger to occasionally run right next to where I am to make sure I regularly hide.
The motion detector is annoying too, since it basically turns the game from hiding out of sight of a clever alien murderer, and more like hiding from a pacman ghost, making sure I'm not around when the dot on the screen is.
It's genuinely not fun to play, and the way the alien will fly accross the sections through vents is ridiculous.
I'd believe it weren't just floating from one vent entrance to another if it weren't for the fact that it always travels in a straight line.
Interestingly enough, the game would work so much better without the alien, and therefore it is no surprise that shortly after the game came out, I stopped hearing about it. As though so many people wanted to believe that a truely good Alien game was finally here, when in reality it was just a dissapointment.

Some people will love Alien: Isolation and some people will hate it. This game really succeeds at ramping up the tension in a way that few other games can match. It's a genuine horror experience. But if you're looking for something that's "fun" in the conventional sense, stay far away from this one. I will recommend it as long as you know what you're getting into. For the right kind of horror fan, this game should be a 10/10. But be warned - this game is not for everyone.
I have to praise the atmosphere. The environments are very reminiscent of the film series, and they are fun to explore. The game is a few years old as of 2017, so the graphics are no longer top-of-the-line, but they are good enough to make the experience feel immersive. The sound design is even better, and might be the best part of the game. I highly recommend wearing your best headphones while playing. You will have to constantly listen for sound cues to see if you're in danger. You're on a space station that is noisy and creaky, and it will mess with your head. Good stuff.
The Alien itself is great. It looks just like it does in the movies. It is powerful, it is fast, and it wants you dead. The AI isn't perfect, but it definitely achieves its main goal: it forces you to stay on your toes at all times. This creature is as terrifying as a video game character can be.
Unfortunately, the tension in this game comes at a cost. Part of the reason you will be so scared to die in this game is that the save points are far apart, so every time you die it's a significant setback. If you get stuck on one part of the game, you might have to play the same 15 minutes over and over. This does help to make the game feel scary, but if that feeling wears off then it just becomes annoying and tedious. I'm playing it on the "normal" difficulty level, and honestly I wish I had picked a lower one because I just want to see more of the game instead of having a burdensome death knocking on my door at all times.
As you progress, the game starts to get repetitive, and the pace of it gets really slow. No matter where you go, the Alien is always nearby. To avoid him you have to find hiding places. So, you sit in a closet and wait around for a few minutes until he backs off. Then you sneak past him so you can find the next closet to hide in. And unfortunately, that is most of the gameplay. So if you ever get tired of hiding in closets and under tables, you will start to hate this game. Alien: Isolation may look like an FPS, but it rarely plays like an FPS. Do not try to fight the Alien, unless you want to see him kill you. Don't fire your gun anywhere near him, because he can hear gunshots and he will come looking for you.
Let's see...what else is there? The story is alright. I like how it fits into the lore of the series, but it never really gets me to care about the characters. The main character is a tough lady engineer - appropriate for the part but nothing special. There are humans and synthetic androids hanging around occasionally, most of which are hostile so you usually just avoid them. The controls are good. I played mostly with a keyboard and mouse, but I also tried an Xbox controller. They are both basically fine. A mouse lets you turn around faster, and a controller lets you peek around corners more carefully. There is a crafting system. I am sick of every game having a crafting system, so I didn't get much out of that, but it is at least functional. I haven't played any of the DLC yet, so I won't comment on that.
So if that a really tense game sounds good to you, then give it a try. If you're not sure and just want to try it, then wait until it's on sale and play on a low difficulty level.

Only tossers write lengthy steam reviews so here's a quick list of the reasons you should buy this game.
Playstyle is fluid: You get a bunch of abilities, four of which you can slot. The rest of your remaining abilities can be used to augment the slotted abilities, giving bonus effects or changing the ability altogether. You can swap them around, mix and match and change them as much as you want, to find a playstyle that suits you or just to experiment with new ways to play after every fight, keeping things fresh.
Art style is beautiful: The city looks amazing and intricate. The cutscenes are minimalistic but still amazingly illustrated. It's a very pretty game to look at.
Setting is cool: Futuristic, yet original. It's a city where everything is done by the numbers, to the point where even the sky is painted and the weather is voted on by the residents.  It feels three dimensional.
Story is interesting: It's a game that tells you nothing, but leaves tidbits here and there for you to read so you can put together the bigger picture yourself. It's a little frustrating at times but it keeps you wanting more.
The music is incredible: When people hark on about a game soundtrack, I usually dismiss it. How memorable can some background music be? Transistor's answer: Phenominal. It fits the game and setting, and like the art style, experiencing it is an absolute pleasure. I've never heard a soundtrack like this before.
Short answer: Buy this game. It's bloody good.

This game has a lot going for it: interesting story, beautiful environments, a phenomenal score, and some good scares. It stays with you after you've played it, and I personally plan to play it again.
That said, if there was one thing I would change about this game it would be this: add in some actual gameplay. The game removes many, if not all, of the gameplay elements from the original Amnesia. You're rarely in genuine danger (although the game will definitely make you think that you are), and the few times you are in danger, it can easily be solved by simply running to the next area. There's no need to desperately hide somewhere and wait for the danger to pass, hoping you won't be found. That hurts the game a lot, and I'm a little baffled by its removal. Those terrifying moments were what made the original Amnesia so successful.
I've heard complaints that the game's message is a bit heavy-handed, and while I agree I don't think it hurts the game all that much; I'd rather have the message pushed a little too hard than spend hours trying to decipher it.
That said, I'd recommend this game to fans of the original game and horror fans in general. Despite its flaws, it still has a lot to offer and it's probably one of my favorite games.

Later it's revealed that the antagonist - a group called Camerata - was attempting to kill Red with Transistor during her performance, when this mysterious man jumped in, took the hit in Red's place. Writing this before I start with NG+ ..As someone who loved Bastion; a game which I still need to 100% but haven't for good reason, I'm not surprised by how beautiful this game is.
After completing the first playthrough, there's only one downside I can see. Even with fully exploring levels and listening to all the great and rather touching narrative, the story is pretty short and can be played through within 5 hours. But if anything, I think this game can get away with it because there's a good amount of replay value due to the 'function' mechanics. Not to mention, it does introduce a few new things in new game plus. NG+ / Recursion is a necessity for those seeking to 100% this game as well as playing around with all the different abilities, which I think is great because you may discovering awesome new combos and builds this way. For that matter, the content is built well enough to keep one occupied.
For those who are not obsessed with achievements, the game offers more than enough in terms of story, visuals and sound. The artwork is drop dead gorgeous, it's like Bastion's except sci-fi to put it bluntly. If you break it down, the story isn't really unique or in any way complex, but it's the narration of it that makes it truly shine. ..also much like in Bastion. For me, I found the narrative in Transistor to be more stirring though I think it really depends on how susceptible you are to certain kinds of reading. Words can't describe on how beautiful and enthralling the music is, a more than fitting background that makes way for a remarkable and gorgeous experience for one and all.
It goes without saying that every game's aspects are subject to personal opinion. But if you loved Bastion, you will love Transistor. In any other case, the game is a marvel on it's own and in my opinion, well worth it's price if not for the music alone.

Dustforce truly is a work of art. I don't mean that lightly. The way it's animated plus its music gives it that title in my book. I can find myself playing one level for an hour, maybe even hours at a time. The frustration of losing levels is filled with relaxation and calmness because of the ambient music. The way the levels are crafted is truly mindblowing. They had a system in which you had to perfect a level to earn a key, and you would use that key to earn more levels. In layman's terms, to earn more levels, you had to perfect current levels. They ditched that and added an XP system in which you gain more XP to earn a key the more levels you play and perfect. I'm very glad they added this system and was skeptical about buying it. But now that I did buy it, I do not regret it even for a second. One thing I really love about this game is how you don't have to unlock base levels. In a sense, this game is open world. That sense is that many levels are available to you, and you can choose whether you want to advance into more challenging levels, or stay where you're at. To get an S in completion, you have to sweep up EVERY leaf, and to get an S in Finesse, you have to maintain your combo throughout an entire level.
Another thing I absolutely enjoy about Dustforce is its expasive community. There are lots of Community Workshop maps for you to sharpen your skills on, and lots of people who can set a good example. I'm sure most of the people who get best times on all the levels have a Youtube channel, so you can probably catch them there. The community may or not be active, but it sure is good and friendly.
Overall, in terms of gameplay, music, artstyle, animation, and difficulty (it's not an easy game, but it's not that hard of a game either. It just depends on how much you want to play it), I rate this game:
10/10

It starts off well, but having finished it I feel obliged to point out the lack of danger that was present in the previous Amnesia game. It barely has any character involvement at all. The environment and music are beautiful as they are in Dear Esther, and that makese sense. It's the same developers and the same composer, respectively. The story is also very well written but you won't be able to appreciate it unless you can find the majority of the notes. And that's the only real thing to actually DO in it, besides the occasional simple, boring puzzle and avoiding the occasional pigman who will only spawn at scripted moments and will usually follow a set path, moving around stacks of crates or through hallways. It's only a matter of timing to avoid them. There is no survival elements either, further negating the actual danger in the game and making for poor payoff for the well-designed atmopshere. If this game had all the good elements in it's own right, the story, music, atmosphere and level design as well certain aspects of the first game such as the unpredictable enemies, survival mechanics and intillectually stimulating puzzles I would have appreciated it much more. I'd heard a lot about how dissapointing this game was.
So when I decided to play it, I chose to judge it as its own game. Not an amnesia title.
My conclusion? Even as its own game, I personally hated it.
Why:
Because it failed to involve me whatsoever with its story. It seemed to want to completely distance itself from the player. That's what books and movies are for, and they do it better because they can frame and pace it in an interesting way. In a game, you NEED interaction to make it interesting. Machine for pigs is a series of (more often than not) scripted events, and long periods of nothing happening.
Sure, the environment is impressive. And without threats, or any need for resource gathering, it feels empty. I felt little or no desire to explore it, and there was rarely any form of reward for doing so. One might argue that this makes for a lonely, isolated experience that enhances the fear factor. One might also seek art in something that took little or no skill to craft, because it makes them look or feel more intelligent for doing so. While the environment LOOKS nice, I personally feel that it failed to generate a genuine sense of place. Places have character. Secrets, AI, readables, married together with visual storytelling and sound design, are ingredients for imaginary worlds we call "games". Places CONTAIN things. Events. They are  living things! While AMFP has some of these elements, its missing the most vital ones, and finds pretentious little ways of ruining the stuff that does work. Forced subtitles for posters, for example...because I can't just read it on my own...did Bioshock ever do that?
A machine for pigs never felt living...it was a hollow experience. The story alone is not enough to save it from that. It could have been a novel, and would have been better for it. There is little to nothing that justifies it being a game. While I don't like the whole debate on what the definition of a game is (as it's quite subjective), I feel that a bad game is one that doesn't make effective use of the advantages this medium offers. Interactivity! The Stanley Parable featured nothing but walking, but it still made the player feel like they were somehow interacting with it. Making choices, finding things, etc. AMFP really failed to FEEL like a game for me, so I can only call it a bad one.
For the sake of the things the game did right, I wanted to like it. But I couldn't. There was no reason this amazing environment couldn't have at least had more interactivity than walking and pressing buttons, with occasional glimmers of actual gameplay when a rare enemy was present.
The jumpscares often amounted to nothing, and it wasn't long before I was shrugging them off. It wasn't much longer before I was feeling bored. Eventually, after an evening of giving this game a chance, I simply got too bored to finish. The story didn't intrigue me so much that I needed to finish. Had it felt like I was experiencing the story, as oppoed to feeling dissasociated with it, that could have been different. I'm often more leniant with gameplay issues for games I feel have a good story, such as deadly premonition (though I see no reason a game can't have both up to scratch!). This was simply a case where there was nothing to make the story worth it. It didn't grab my attention as much as it kept me mildly curious. It wasn't enough to make me want to endure any more boredom.
For these reasons, I can only call this a bad game that I want to like, but frankly can't. Forgetting that it's connected to amnesia in any way, I just feel this is bad. It's a poor use of the medium that is unjustifiable, and really ought to have been a novel instead.
If you enjoyed the game and found something of value to you in it, that's great and I'm glad you enjoyed it. This is just my honest feelings, and I'm aware that one man's junk is another mans treasure. If you enjoyed Dear Esther, chances are you'll enjoy this. I hated that game also for the same reasons, so that should give you a good idea of what to expect.

First of all, part of the reason my hours played count is relatively low is because I try to play offline a lot, and I've also poured far more time into the PS4 version of Scholar of the First Sin (SotFS).
But anyhoo, I don't get these haters.
Even if you just get the vanilla version of Dark Souls II, it's still a very lengthy and challenging experience, and better than 99% of games on the market today.
Now, do I necessarily recommend that course of action?  Depends.
If you don't own Dark Souls II at all, and your PC can handle the higher system requirements for SotFS, get that instead.
However, it should be noted that there's a lot of subtle but very real gameplay differences between this vanilla version and SotFS.  Enemy and item placement is quite different, and SotFS has a LOT more enemies than this version does.  And that's not even counting the new areas that version introduces.  Some fans I've talked to also think this version is a bit more balanced than SotFS.
And then there's more obvious stuff SotFS adds like the new areas, bosses, enemies, items, etc.  There's even a new final boss and ending.
And yet, this version still tells a complete story in itself.  As such, there ARE reasons to own this version.  Going through both versions and seeing the differences adds tremendous replay value to the game IMO.  Or heck, you might prefer the difficulty balance and/or enemy and item placement of this version.  Now, I admit, I'm biased.  This is, by far, my favorite game in the Souls series, and as such, I don't mind playing the same game with subtle differences in this case.  It's just that fun.
So to sum up, if you just want one version that gives you the most bang for your buck in the long run, and your PC can handle it, get SotFS.  Whereas get this version if you have an older/less powerful PC, prefer this version's design, or want to compare differences and don't mind owning two versions.
In the end however, I do recommend the game overall... simply based on the fact that it is incredibly fun even by itself.  Yes, there's a bigger, better version of this game available. And if you only get one version, definitely get that one.  But that doesn't mean this version isn't still a heck of a lot of fun, and as such it gets the thumbs up from me.

Liked Bastion? You're in the right place. Super Giant comes back into the limelight with a new title with a familiar yet different feel then Bastion, with plenty of new mechanics, story elements, and music to keep you along for a great, albeit short, ride.
I won't lie to you, the story isn't going to be spoon-fed to you, you might end the game with only a jist of what was going on during your first playthrough. Hell, a few of the small elements of story changed in Recursion Mode (NG+) confused me even more. Super Giant wants you to piece together everything, make what you can out of all the little hints they put in there. If this doesn't sound like your thing, I would probably avoid this game, the story doesn't have a real "huge exposition and revelation" moment and might leave you as a player unsatisfied.
Combat is very much like Bastion with an isometric view of the battle while you perform actions in real time, however the big thing that puts it apart is the turn() system introduced here. Kinda like V.A.T.S. from Fallout, you can pause combat and plan out your next few actions, stringing together movement and attacks and then executing them faster than you could input them normally. This makes for interesting combos and techniques, planning the perfect to take out enemies and get yourself out of harms way. My complaint with combat was when turn() is down you can't attack with any skills (except the one skill that actually allows you to attack with turn() down) and must wait for it's cooldown to be back up to fight in real time. This makes combat frequently using turn(), then run around avoiding things, then use turn() again, rinse and repeat till the room is dead. I feel like combat might of been a bit more exciting if it wasn't necessarily punishing normal play for using turn(), and allowing you to balance the real time and turn based styles of combat. Still, combat remains interesting tactically and exciting with action oriented fights all in one package.
When it came to music and art direction, this game is masterful. The soundtrack really is dynamic and changes on the fly from the Humming of the lead, Red, in turn() mode to the various tracks that play between combat and boss fights will make you want the soundtrack all the more. In addition, Bastion fan's rejoice, the narrator whose voice is so smooth it sounds like he is seducing your ears returns! The game being narrated by this man should be enough to pick up this game if you have ever heard him speak. Art and style is also a huge plus from the white, cell-like Process, to the characters you will "meet" along the way.
I could really go on about this game for hours, but in the end it comes down to this, do yourself a favor, buy this game, you won't regret it.

Absolutely one of the best games I have ever played. All the things that were good about Bastion, with most of Bastion's problems fixed and a bunch of awesome new features thrown in too. Great characters and story (moral ambiguity FTW!), innovative storytelling that interacts with gameplay in a really unique and cool way, and a truly amazing soundtrack (but that goes without saying...) I can't speak highly enough of this game.

Transistor is probably the most beautiful game I've ever played.
As you would expect, it's a lot similar to Bastion in some respects, but it's also more complex and engaging.
Visually, the only other game I ever played that maybe looked better is Journey. Maybe. The writing is superb, subtle where it needs to be, but also quite funny, and, best of all, it actually ties really, really well into the gameplay mechanics. I won't get into details to avoid spoilers, but I'll say that Cloudbank is a fascinating setting, and unlike anything I've seen in other cyberpunk tales.
In my opinion, Bastion's main fault was the simplicity of its combat system. It wasn't bad by any means, but it also didn't allow for a lot of depth. Transistor fixed that and created one of the most engaging combat systems in recent memory in the process. It's a mix of real time and turn-based combat that works surprisingly well, where you can mix and match a number of skills, each of them tied to a character in the game, and the more you use them in different ways, the more you learn about the respective character. It's a great way to keep your playstyle constantly changing, and it ties really well into the story.
Darren Korb is back and his music is as good as ever, possibly even better. Ashley Lynn Barrett voices the protagonist, Red, and the songs she sings are not only beautiful, they're all directly tied to the game's story.
And finally, Logan Cunningham is back, which should be reason enough for you to buy this game.

I have played Medieval II, Shogun II, and Rome II for over 100 hours each at least. Each game is spectacular. Rome II is spectacular. The team has once again done a wonderful job recreating the era to give a real immersive feel to it. Each game has slightly different mechanics, and those are personal preference. Rome II for example has you recruit soldiers through generals instead of settlments. But after 2-3 hours of learning any Total War game you feel right at home. My favourite part of Rome II is how they added so many factions to the map. This creates a unique play-through every time you start a new game. The downside to me though is that not enough of these factions are playable. Considering how many factions are around at the start of the game it does feel a bit like you are getting ripped off when you see the small amount of factions you can choose to play. However this is only my real critcism of the game. Along with that the only other thing I would change is bringing back the family tree aspect, from Medieval II.
I give this game a 4.4/5
The reason for that score is because it's nearly a perfect game, but the lack of factions loses it a half point, and the tiny wish that the family tree was reintroduced loses it 0.1. Of the 3 Total War games I have played, I put this one behind Medieval II, and ahead of Shogun II.

The top-down shooting aspect is something I easily adjusted to, and the crafting mechanics are simple, but not too simple. They are also faster (the crafting mechanics) by shortcutting materials, so instead of needing each component and THEN craft the final product, the game inherently shortcuts all crafting recipes down to how much raw material you have in total to craft the materials to make your final product.
In other words, crafting is simplified, but complex.
Definitely more to this game than meets the eye, and certainly a challenge when you realize that you are surrounded by Aliens at your spawn. Hunker down, fortify, and craft your way to victory, my friends. Or just hunker down and slowly kys, your choice.
