In short, A Machine for Pigs is much different from it's predecessor. I honestly feel bad that Frictional games allowed this title to be released under the Amnesia banner because this just does not live up to the original Amnesia. The sense of horror and complete helplessness that the original had is close to nonexistent in A Machine for Pigs. It is also significantly shorter.
There is basically zero gameplay elements because the inventory has been removed and the enemies in the game which you are supposed to be weary of are few and far between. The Dark Descent also had two central "hub" areas which you could explore around, as to not make the game linear. A Machine for Pigs is COMPLETELY linear and there are basically zero puzzles. The "puzzles" are literally just flip a few switches and move on. That's it. Super dissappointing. Also, as another reviewer mentioned, the game warns you ahead of time when anything out of the ordinary is going to happen by making the lights flicker and your lamp flickers. What is the point of making a horror game when you cue the player into knowing EXACTLY when and where the scary moments are? The design just doesn't make sense.
As far as the story goes, it is overly symbolic and never really draws you in. I feel like the story relies on making you care about the events which are occurring, yet it never does anything to make you care about the events. The best analogy I can make is the story feels like a nightly news broadcast about some random story that you don't care about.
Verdict: Skip this waste of time and play the original Amnesia.
A Machine for Pigs takes about 5 hours to complete.

I've got about 140hrs in this game before it came to steam, which gives a total of ~200.
I have also spent over 100$ for in-game items and licences. I'm guessing the only reason why I played it for so much was the fact, that there aren't any other decent hunting games.
Unfortunatelly I really can't recommend this game to any new players.
First of all, it gets more and more outdated because engine is getting old and has plenty of limitations.
Secondly, the game is not Free to Play at all. Free accounts have access to 2 terrible guns, one bad scope and can only hunt a few animal species. You might be able to spot a boar but you won't be able to shoot it. Frustrating.
You have to buy licences to hunt all the animal species, and you can buy a licence for 3, 6 or 12 months. Yeah, it's a subscription fee, to play this game. And that's not everything.
Then you learn about ethical weapons and the fact, that you need different weapons to hunt different species. Quickly you realise that you need to buy extra wepons and you can only do that with rl money.
So you spend extra 50$ on a proper rifle with good scope, a revolver, pistol holster, a bow, a backpack to carry all that stuff, maybe some camo clothing or a fancy binocs with rangefinder.
Now you can start to hunt and it's quite fun. For a while...
Then you get to the same point I did. You have killed every single animal species, long range, short range, revolver kills, bow kills. What can I do next?
Misssions. Missions reward you with in-game currency that can be used to buy mostly consumable items. Honestly, there is nothing usefull that you can buy for that. Forget about buying guns  or even callers.
It gets worse. Many, many of the missions require you to use a specific weapon to complete them. You either spend rl money on some crappy gun (but I need it for a mission) or just ignore missions completly, since they are a waste of time.
Then you move to competitions.
Some competitions require specific guns but there should be plenty available where you can compete with any gun. To win a comp, usually you need to harvest a highest scoring animal. Most comps last 48hrs, some of them have limited attempts.
Winning a comp gives you a trophy and some em$. That's the currency that is usually only purchaseable with rl money!
You might think that this is solution to all your problems. Win enough comps and be able to afford guns and items.
Sorry to disappoint you.
Unless you are willing to spend countless hours, you won't win a thing.
You might get lucky and bag a winning animal on your first attempt, but chances for that are extremly low. From my experience: winning a comp that wasn't even very popular (not many players competing) required around 12 hours of playing (6hrs a day).
You will find out that most of the players, still playing this game, are massive no-lifers. MASSIVE.
There are competitions that require you to bag as many animals as possible in 48hrs period of time. Regularly you will have players that are willing to spend up to 40hrs online in that period (forget about sleeping etc) just to win a reward that is worth 1-2$.
Soon you will realise that you're better off paying 5$ for a new gun that spending 100hrs doing competitions.
Eventually, there is no reason to keep playing this game. You got every animal, had some fun. Missions are pointless and a cashgrab attempt, competitions are for people with no jobs, who can pay 10+ hrs a day.
Very fun and addictive. However, to do just about anything in the game you have to buy  a subscription.

Q: What is theHunter?

If you want to play more than what you start with, then get a bundle package.  (more details below)
Q: Does it cost anything to play?
A: No!
H: However, the developers have made the game available to you for free.  This is NOT a free trial.  It is the complete game.  You can hunt 2 species right from the start as long as you want forever.  Their business model is genius,  if you like what you see and want more you can pay them for it.
Q: What does it cost if i want more?
A: Well it depends.  The bundle deals are probably a steal on our part,  Their pricing is ultra low.  Avgs 3-4 Dollars per month for unlimited access to the game(KILL ANYTHING). Memberships are based on 3-6-12 month packages.   Their bundles are the same however the perks to a bundle are priceless when compared to manually purchasing them in the shop.
O:  Okay now, the important things to discuss.  If you read any negative reviews (several)  your more than likely to find "its a ripoff" "its not free" "Devs suck".  Well truth be told,  Your all a bunch of idiots.  This isnt just a game, it is a simulation.    "Simulation" as close to reality as you can get being virtual.  The game aspects are what create more playable attractions.  EX: Competitions, Tracking, Spotting Levels.  Leaderboards, Animal Scoring System.  Personal achievments. etc.
If you want to know what the game is like then i will give you the best review i possibly can honestly and in detail.  Honestly speaking im very dissapointed in the reviews that dont justify their responses.  It royally pisses me off.
MY REVIEW
Hunting in its natural form requires patience, and  understanding the behavioral patterns of your prey and overall, the ability to learn from your mistakes.
From the start (Guest non-Member)
As a Guest or non-member you can create single player games and Hunt Loggers Point reserve.  Here you will find Mule Deer, Whitetail, Rabbit, Ferral Hog, Pheasant.  Guests are authorized to hunt Rabbit and Mule Deer by default.  You can continuously hunt them to your hearts content.  (One blunder the Devs did was make default rifle non compliant with Rabbit Hunting,  whether this was intended or not should be fixed,  its a turn off and negative review maker)
When you create your game prior to starting you can choose where you want to start on the map,  After doing so the game loads etc.
1. Right from the start its very important to realize that the game feels slow and characters are slow.  NO♥♥♥♥♥♥  This is a hunting game, not call of freakin Duty.  Slow and Quiet is the game,  and probly the most widely contributed negative review aspect.  "There is no animals to shoot, i run around for hours and cant find anything what a waste"  If you have seen a review like this then read the following.
2.  The AI in the game are astonishing,  they simulate an emense amount of realism in the animals.   "Slow and Quiet"  When you stand up and walk around your a beacon to the world of animals.  So crouch and move slow.  The animals get spooked by 3 Factores.  Movement, Sound, and Smell.  By default your character is Ugly, Smells, and loud as .....
3.  The game takes time to understand,  you need to put in the time to learn terrain the animals, and their patterns.  When you start a new game and you go back to the spot you killed that monster buck,  chances are they wont be there anymore.  The AI is smart, the animals in the game actually avoid overly hunted areas.  Pathfinding actually changes for the animals.  If the Devs did this on purpose, then kudos,  If not your some lucky mofo's.
4.  I had to put in some long hours to actually figure how to find the animals.  It sucked, and i hated it I was one of those Rage Quitters.  Then a friend of mine took me on an actual hunt.  As a guest you can join multiplayer games and hunt every map/reservere.  Just be mindful of the liscenses you carry.  Anyway,  what i learned in that single hour of hunting With my friend, forever changed my opinion of this game.
5.  When you play for the first time, expect to get frustrated if you dont actually have real life hunting habits.  You will be inclined to run everywhere DONT!  You will spook animals and never see them.  Try to find a game with a host that has a high hunter score.  Ask them to show you, or take you on a hunt.  Once you learn the tricks,  the game becomes exciting and fun.
6.  This is very important.   You have been hunting mule deer for hours, now your bored.  You want to kill something else.  But you dont want to pay for a subscription....You can earn em$ (cash currency)  by doing surveys and tasks etc from theHunter website. Transistor is the second game from Supergiant Games, the developers of the critically acclaimed Bastion. Those who have doubts about whether this game lives up to Bastion's expectation can be at ease: Transistor delivers and more.
You play as Red, a famous singer in the city of Cloudbank. One night after a performance, a group of people, the Camerata, attempted to kill Red with a strange, green sword, but she was saved by someone.
Waking up, she found herself next to the corpse of a man, stabbed by that same sword: the Transistor. The sword starts speaking, and not only that, but seems to know her. Urging her to pull it out of the corpse, the two start tracking the Camerata down, seeking answers, while fighting what seems to be robotic creatures sent to hunt them down.
But things may not be as they seem.
The story of Transistor seem simple and straight-forward on the surface, but most of it isn't handed down to the player, instead inferred and concluded from various hints noticed in the environment, character interaction and character profiles. It encourages the player to seek answers along the main character, and leaves a lot up for interpretation. That's something I like in a game.
One downside to the story however, is how short it is. It's far too short, the game is far too short. You'll be left wanting more, even with "recursion", playing a second play through with your stats intact.
The gameplay is a mix of Action RPG and traditional turn-based RPG, using the Turn() system that I will touch upon soon. Red is able to equip up to 4 slots of "Functions", essentially abilities, upgrade those functions with up to two functions a slot, and assign functions as passive abilities, for up to 4 passives.
In battle, Red wields the Transistor. In Diablo style, she can use the numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4 on the keyboard to select an ability, then the right-mouse button to use that ability. Abilities can be offensive, such as shooting a long-range beam or a destructive shockwave, or supportive, such as turning invisible for a period of time or turning enemies friendly.
The Turn() system adds a new depth to the action RPG. It allows Red to stop time momentarily in order to plan and input a certain number of commands: attacking, setting up traps, maneuvering around the map to escape enemy clusters or get behind obstacles, you can do all that. But once all commands are preformed and the Turn() bar is depleted, Red is left (almost) unable to attack until it recharges again; use Turn() at your own discretion, balancing attack and defense.
The game offers the choice of "limiters", handicaps that increase the difficulty of the game in return for better EXP awards. There are achievements you can only get by using limiters, the hardest achieved with all 10 limiters. In addition, there is a "sandbox" unlocked in-game that allows you to tackle specific-themed challenges, like a speed challenge, or a Turn-planning challenge.
Transistor uses an isometric point of view, being able to go in all 2D directions. The sprites are smooth and look good, but the highpoint of the graphics is the artwork. The character portraits, whether in-game or in profiles, are drawn beautifully. The artist, Jen Zee, did a brilliant, detailed job, and it shows even on the OST cover.
Here is where Transistor really shines. The game's OST is amazing. From Ashley Lynn Barrett's beautiful voice in The Spine, In Circles, and other songs, to Darren Korb setting up poignant, melancholic instrumentals that fit the mood perfectly. Tracks play hand-in-hand with gameplay, showing up at specific times for maximum impact, further heightening the experience.
I highly recommend getting the OST along with the game, if you can. Well worth the extra bucks.
Transistor is a beautiful, enjoyable game. It has a bittersweet, albeit short, story that forces the player to think. Brilliant soundtrack, and beautiful artwork. The gameplay won't last you long, but there is decent replayability in it. Try picking it up immediately whenever it's on sale.

Papers, Please is grueling, grim, tedious, and a bad choice if you are looking for lighthearted entertainment. You play a customs agent, trying desperately to make ends meet while filing border corssing papers for a corrupt dictatorship. This game is easily the _opposite_ of what people would normally consider fun.
And yet despite all that, or perhaps because of it, this game is amazing!!!
This is an incredibly well-made game! The attention to detail is amazing! There are countless little human touches everywhere whch constantly break up the inhuman levels of paperwork. And even though all you can do is stamp documents, your choices have a real effect on the world around you. People's lives are changed by your stamp, even yours! There are literally dozens of endings that you can get depending on your stamping decisions. The social commentary is also fatnastic, and the moral dilemmas that the game puts you in -with just your stamp- are gut-wrenching! You will never agonize over a piece of paper like you will in Paper's Please, and you will never look at a DHS or customs agent the same way again!
And that is the game's most amazing accomplishment. Without any traiditonal fun game mechanics Papers, Please manages to be engaging, agonizing, cathrtic, insighful, and a blast to play! You'll just have to pick up your stamp to find out what you've been missing!

I cannot imagine any better emulation of the day-to-day life of an immigration inspector on a recently war torn and still somewhat disputed border of a communist-styled country. There are an ever increasing number of forms, each with their own individual nuances, a few wild characters, and the constant threat of poverty or prison. But then, of course, most of the time is filled with repetitive mundane work. Still, I was surprised how fun this grind could be and I think that is in large part due to its oddly intimate nature. People passes by quickly, but in that short amount of time you learn so much about them. Their height, weight, where they've come from, what they plan on doing for the next few months or so, and possibly even how they react when things turn sour on them. That's an awful lot to learn about a person so suddenly. A character begins to form and you start to feel as if you know them quite well. The same could be said about the setting itself. Without much information or discussion about it, this area, vaguely resembling a former Soviet state, seems not only fully realized but legitimate as well. Though, lots of official looking documents do tend to have that effect.

A fantastic return to beloved series after a truly dreadful third installment, Gunslinger delivers for diehard Call of Juarez fans.
The narrative is quirky in all the right ways, and occasionally breaks the fourth wall but carefully and in appropriate portions. Follow Silas Greaves on a gritty tale of revenge, with a solid ending twist. He'll take on several notable members of gunslinger fame and team up with other in a solid 4-hour romp.
The game oozes AAA quality, with fast-paced shooting, tight and precise controls and even a solid RPG system that doesn't run the show but also stays out of the way and doesn't feel tacked on. There's a minimal difficulty curve throughout and the game heavily touts the narrative to fill in what may have been a lackluster third act.
The visuals take a departure for this installment, turning to a pseudo-cell-shaded masterpiece. This thematic shift fits as if the wild-west were made for thick borderlines and comic book stylings. This again nods to the narrative, which places a high emphasis on dime/graphic novels.
All in all, for a fairly regular sale price of $3.74 USD, you'd be hard-pressed to do worse than Call of Juarez: Gunslinger.

Developers make wierd decisions such as not letting you invert flying controls, binding the boost and throttle to the same key, having the inablility to press buttons at the same time (flying to the left to avoid a helicopter than jumping out at the same time for instance), having to unlock zoom and just overall being a mess.

Shooting silos of gas however feel very powerfull.
The most fustrating thing is that this game continually fights against you imparing your ability to have fun. Oh you want to blow up some building in a helicopter? Sorry the controls suck and you don't have flares to avoid all of the SAM missles. Want to land a plan in the middle of a rural town then hop back in and fly off in style as explosions bellow behind you? Sorry as soon as you hit throttle you go blasting at full speed not giving you enough time to tilt the plane up and avoid obstacles. Want to wind dive near fiery explosions going full speed then at the last second pull up panning the camera behind you as the shockwave propels you forward? Sorry the explosions have a radius of 5 miles and will cause to tuck and inevitably crash to the ground if you try.
Basically this game has a lot of potential but is impaired by its stupid controls and dumb design choices.
TLDR; If you want to experience this game to the fullest buy it on a steep sale, never drive, turn down the voices and play music or a podcast in the background and burn a couple hours. When played in this way the fustration isn't as bad because you're just playing to have fun and waste time.

Plantera is a casual clicker game in which you grow your own garden with various types of plants and trees, and a few farm animals. You click on fruits and vegetables to harvest them and collect money, along with eggs and milk that your animals produce. In addition to clicking to harvest, you also have little blue creatures that help you by passively picking things up for you, which you get when you level up, or when you purchase an expansion to your playable area.
To start, the game gets you to click/collect butterflies to earn your coin. Butterflies appear randomly throughout your play, and will glow when they are ready to be "harvested". Once you get the first few coins, you're ready to plant your first source of income, carrots. From there you collect the carrots to get more money, and plant more carrots, to grow your garden and economy, and thus is the routine for most clickers.
As you collect money from carrots, butterflies and the like, you gain experience that will level you up. Leveling up gives you access to new plants and plant types, and eventually animals. There are three "depths" to your plants; the ground where you plant carrots, turnips, etc, bushes for things like blueberries and raspberries, and trees for various fruits. With five different food producing plants in each category, mixed with 4 animals (chickens, pigs, etc) you can buy, it can become a very crowded yet colourful screen.
All the while you're growing plants, clicking fruits and picking up eggs, there are a few pests that will try to come steal things away, or scare your little blue workers. Magpies will fly down and attempt to steal fruit, and bunnies will try to run from the sides and nab some vegetables, or foxes and wolves will waltz in and try to scare off your workers. All of these can be chased away with a click, or in the case of the foxes/wolves, a few clicks. To help the player from going crazy with hundreds of clicks and chasing away pests there a few bonuses you can buy to help. Of the four bonuses, one is a scarecrow you can place to scare away the magpies, where the other is a guard dog that roams around at random and will bark and scare off any bunnies, foxes, or wolves they bump into.
There are a few other neat little bonuses in the game. The two others that are available to buy are Time, and a Multiplyer. Most clickers will continue when the game is closed, in some facet or another, but in this game your workers will only work by default for an hour after you close the game. It's a neat way to get you to check back into the game often to "wake them up", or you can just buy time which makes them work longer and longer when the game is closed. The other purchasable bonus is pretty straight forward, it's a multiplyer. Each time you buy it, it increase all income by 1X. Other little bonuses in the game come in random appearances. There are moles that will pop up here and there and give you a small sum of money, and ladybugs will spawn each time you level up and are worth a decent chunk of change. However the best is the Loot Hero; a little knight apparently from another game developed by the same company as Plantera that will run from the left side of the screen to the right, scaring away any pest it comes into contact with, and has the added bonus of giving you cash everytime you click him while he's on screen.
The artstyle is easy on the eyes, despite all the clutter than can happen. It's very bright and colourful, and everything is pixelated with some really nice sprites. As such the game never has any performance issues as it's pretty basic and simple.
My only gripes with the game are with the pacing of the "end game", and the lack of content past the first hour or so. The game starts off really fun, you click and gather coins to buy more plants and level up your garden, but you quickly get all 5 in each category, and then there's nothing more, and nothing new. Sure, you still get
benefit to leveling up, extra workers and a star on your plants (which increases the value of the food they produce) but it soon becomes boring and stale. The only purpose to sitting down with the game past the first two hours or so is to get the easy, but time consuming achievements. Most achievements are buying
amount of bushes/trees/animals, or clicking
amount of foxes, moles, etc, which you will get fairly quickly, leaving the two longer ones getting the Loot Hero to appear 50 times, and getting to level 100.
All in all Plantera is visually very pleasing, and starts off being a very fun game to play, but quickly runs out of content to offer and keep you entertained. It's cheap, and perhaps a good way to get into clicker type games, but there are other games that offer more for less, even free. I however got Plantera in a bundle with some other games for 3 bucks (which is the fullsale price of the game) and don't feel I wasted my money, but I would reccomend only buying this game when it's on sale. I wish I could give a "Meh" rather than a thumbs up or down.

Don't let the name fool you. This is NOT Amnesia. It's Dear Esther 2: A Machine for Pigs.
Now, don't get me wrong. I loved Dear Esther. It was a wonderful experiment in video game storytelling, and I enjoyed every minute of it. AMFP, though, was different. I bought the game expecting a long, immersive, and scary journey through one of the scariest game worlds ever created. What I got was less than satisfactory. Too much of what made the first game great was cut, such as the inventory and sanity system, and the game just... wasn't scary. The monsters all looked the same with no fear factor at all, and there were no heart-pounding moments that were so welcome in The Dark Descent to be found. The only real positives I have are praise for the level of detail put into the world, the soundtrack, and the decent story.
If you're looking for a short, narrative-driven adventure that betrays the very name it carries, give it a shot. For everyone else, stay away.

'Papers, Please' is not easy to describe. It isn't what most people would consider a traditional game. There are no points, and winning or losing isn't as black-and-white as you may be used to. You could categorize it as a bureaucracy simulator or an everyday survival game, and that wouldn't necessarily be wrong, but it would definitely miss the point. 'Papers, Please' is — at its heart — an adventure game.
Though everything takes place from within a tiny border checkpoint, the game's drama and tension all comes from the decisions you're forced to make. You'll never feel more anxious stamping a piece of virtual paper than you will when playing this game. You will legitimately hate your supervisor, and you might even care about the people who pass through your little booth.
TL;DR: Get this game if you're looking for insightful, clever political commentary.

Spoiler Free Review:
About 4 hours too long. The game was scary at first. The ambiance is great, the storyline is amazing, it's one of the very VERY few horror games to actually get a reaction out of me. The stealth system was intuitive, and the graphics were incredible. Then it just... drags on. It's like they wanted to finish the game, but instead dragged it out. Forever. And on and on and on and on. It stops being scary, and then just gets tedious as hell. It was good, then just fun, then annoying, then boring, then funny, then just plain tedious. Well worth the play, but once you play through the first few hours, you've got the rest of the game down. Oh my god, and the endless minigames!
Graphics: 10/10. Some of the best I've ever seen. Every cell, every animation, every sweat drop is a work of art.
Sound: 8/10: Some of the ambient ship noises are annoying, and there is an over abundance of scary violins. The rest is great. You spend most of the game relying on it, or terrified of it.
Storyline: 7/10. It stays true to the Alien canon (of which I'm a huge fan). It just drags on near the end. For about 4 hours.
Gameplay: 3/10. Great stealth mechanics. The crafting system is forced in. The weapons feel useless. The rest is just minigames on top of minigames on top of incredibly pointless minigames.

As a result, for those trying to figure out what's going on, part of the experience is lost. However, the combat really makes up for it and the music just sounds fantastic. So, I can safely recommend this game based solely on these two things because that's what I enjoyed the most about it.

Then encounters become almost laughably easy once you understand it and what some of the nastier combos are. - though a brilliant bit of game design makes you try different combinations anyway to unlock more backstory on what's going on. The story is very good and gives you enough information that you generally get what's going on without holding your hand or taking out out of the game for an exposition dump. A few questions remain unanswered, which actually is something I liked - the character spends most of the game on the run from a powerful enemy, so it made sense that I never felt 100% in control of everything. Top notch sound and artistic direction. Between this and Bastion, there may not be anyone that beats Supergiant Games in those departments.
Not everyone will love it, but it definitely has something new to offer and is worth a try.

So as someone who didn't like the first Amnesia enough to finish it but who does like thechineseroom's other stuff, I thought Hamnesia was somewhat better than The Dark Descent (I did at least see it through to the end) but substantially worse than Dear Esther or Korsakovia (which you should totally play if you can actually get it working in any existing version of the Source Engine if you want something they've made which does a much better job of creating an unsettling atmosphere...at least when it doesn't degenerate into a mess of jumping puzzles (which you should feel free to skip over with noclip)).
Uh, anyway, Hamnesia. The writing's alright and the best part of it. I liked some of the ideas in it even if this isn't really my favorite sub-genre, but I think I would've liked them more if it weren't being presented in a game that's trying to be part of the Amnesia franchise, because that doesn't quite feel like the right framework for it, and it also leads to why many people who liked the first game seem to not like this one. Why would that be? They removed or heavily streamlined most of the things I didn't like from TDD, which are most of the things people who were fans of the game DID like, like lugging a bunch of stuff around to solve trivial puzzles, limited resources, and a much higher number of enemy encounters which took more effort to deal with/had bigger consequences. I understand why people like those things, and I even like them myself in some other games, but the way they were done in that game mostly rubbed me the wrong way for some reason, and I didn't miss them at all here. On the other hand, I also understand why people complained that it's too streamlined and there's not enough game left, but it's not nearly at Dear Esther levels.
Getting back to the writing/story for a minute, while it did have some interesting ideas in it, it also didn't really go anywhere unexpected or that wasn't heavily telegraphed way in advance. I'm not really sure why so many people have complained that it's so confusing, because I kind of suspected most of what was going on a third to a half of the way into the game and was thoroughly unsurprised by anything after that. I mean, it's not the MOST accessible game ever, but the plot seems pretty straight-forward to me, especially if you've ever read anything similar before. It does feel like it drags on longer than it needs to though, which is kind of funny because I remember hearing people complain that it was too short. Go figure.

Rome 2 is turn-based epic action strategy. You can compare it to Civilization 5 but graphics are a little better than Shogun 2.
You have Grand Campaign in which you conquer whole world, Multiplayer where you play PvP.
In GC you can build cities, research technologies, train armies, ships, spies, champions, dignitaries.
You have Politics which influences Cultural victory, Economy (talents) income from fields, animals, mines, markets, entertainment and so on which influences Economic victory and standard Military which influences Military Victory.
Game is for patient people as it takes many turns (too much loading time) to get some results. The best part of it are battles which can take from 5 to 60 minutes, but I never spent more than 20 minutes in one. The problem is you have to wait all the time, during late-game when you have conquered almost whole world it takes loads of time to manage your cities, armies and even play battles.
I calculate it takes around 100-200 hours for one Grand Campaign. If you do not have nerves, there is still PvP Multiplayer (also Campaign Multiplayer) for those who like direct action.
This is so far the best Total War game I have played. Multiplayer is a pain to get to work but is fantastic once it gets started.

As a more serious sim racer, mainly spending time on iRacing, I have always enjoyed Codemasters' products (the ones that are actually good like Dirt Rally).  Their F1 releases have always been improving, with F1 2017 being the best of them all IMO.  I've purchased '13, '16, and '17, and can say that they have done a great job keeping pretty realistic as possible, while making it actually playable.  Realistic in regards to feeling like I'm racing in an actual Grand Prix, and with all the assists off and AI difficulty turned up, it can be a real challenge.  Theyve also added in more responsibility while in the pit lane (pit limiter buttion, clutch hold and release), just a few steps closer to manually driving in the pit lane.  The warm up lap is also cool, and now streamlined without a screen change.
My favorite part about their F1 series has been the career.  You can tailor it to your liking, mine being full weekend.  The 3 free practices are excellent, and Qualy can be intense.  As you develop your car over the season (and if your fighting for WDC/WCC) it can get real emotional near the end, happy/anger mgmt.  This gameplay is very unique in the racing game world, so I hope they continue this.
The graphics are always a treat, very well done even if you have a moderate build like me.  Performance wise it is good, though at least every time I run the game, it will lag (offline play) while in the car, could be just me but not real issue.  Does it once and doesn't happen until next time I start the game.  I also only play offline since the AI have been greatly improved, even after release.  In '13, and even '16 I could realy manipulate the AI, as in running them all over the track, causing them to brake very early, etc. A very big no no in a community like iRacing, but for 2017 the AI seem to not take♥♥♥♥♥♥from the player, even running YOU to edge, and being able to go side by side for a sector or two...as James Hunt would say "big balls".  Thats why I've only done career or offline, because I know that Codemasters have developed a very competitive AI.
I could go all day about the Pros, but there are a few cons that need addressing even after a few weeks of release.  Literally just before I wrote this I finished the Mexican GP in my career, 3rd to last race of the season, tied for the WDC.  P1 is 20 sec ahead of me, 6 laps to go, its raining so hard I cant see the course.  The safety car came out because it was so wet, something I didnt know they implemented in this game.  But since P1 had just passed the safety car before it came out, I had to pass it too.  Now this has been a problem before that apparently got "fixed" in a patch, but if you are not within 10 car lengths of the back of the safety car line after some time, you get a drive through.  SInce the track was 15 feet under water it was difficult to catch the back of the line.  They give you about 30 seconds to catch up, which you get a drive through penalty if you dont, and after 3 chances of that,  I was handed 3 drive throughs AND then promptly DSQ from the race.  When I was DSQ, i was literally in line of the safety car.  A little frustrating.  Theres also a problem of cars trying to pass you under safety car (in line) and if you pass them back you are told to hand back the position, or penalty.  Codemasters is lucky that the stewards are not of physical matter or I would start throwing fists.
Overall though, I really recomend this game.  Whether you are a casual player, or a serious sim racer with a wheel, this game will be rewarding.  Theyve nailed the 2017 car handling and lap times too, big plus.  Ive found myself more in tune with the real F1 world when I play these titles too.  And if youre new to F1, watching (or going to) the races themselves really helps when I can do the same exact thing....somewhat.
Oh almost forgot, couldn't be F1 without GRID PENALTIES YAYYYYYYY
EDIT.
As of 10/30/17, Codemasters has released another patch that specifically targets the the two big problems I listed in my review: falling to far back under safety car, and being passed by other cars under safety car without penalty.
Great to see this upkeep from them!

The gameplay has improved once again after 2016. The cars feel a lot smoother and handle much better, especially in wet conditions, which was a terrible thing to do with a controller in the previous game. Now I can enjoy that aswell. The AI is much more challenging than 2016 and before, which makes a race a lot more fun!
Although the gameplay is simply awesome, there are still some flaws. The AI, even though improved, still really likes to stay on the race line, while you're there already and they just bash into you from time to time. The Safety Car has a lot of issues, especially with the "falling too far back" rule, getting penalties like it's Christmas already.
Online is still a 50/50 thing in this game. It's great fun to race against your friends and other real human beings, but the servers still have its issues with connection and stuff. There's not really much to say about.
The mode we all bought the game for is so much better and more enjoyable than 2016's career mode. The highly updated R&D section makes the practice sessions much more fun to get the R&D points, and the fact that upgrades can actually fail makes it much more realistic.
The wear (and swapping) of engine parts and the gearbox adds a lot of realism to the game aswell, which can't be anything but great! In my opinion they completely nailed it this year with the career mode.
It's great fun driving old cars and adds so much more playabilty to the game. Nothing more to say about it. :)

Given their past achievements, it was held to a high standard, but Transistor delivers! Again, we have some wonderful artwork and music to complement great gameplay.
Don’t expect any similarity to Bastion here, besides the top-down isometric view. This is a completely different beast. One major aspect of gameplay is the turn-based approach, which lets you plan out your attacks in sequence. This makes things a lot more tactical rather than guns-blazing, although with some tweaking of skills you could likely pull that off too (I haven’t tried personally, but it seems possible based on the types of skills/abilities present).
The gameplay is engaging and has a good story attached to it. Levels have a good amount of combat and quiet exploring mixed in. Earlier in the game it is possible to get overwhelmed by enemies, especially if you don’t manage skill usage and action points carefully, but once you get a formula working for you it evens out.
This would be another instance (like Bastion) where the length does seem a bit short by most standards, but there are options to prolong your experience such as a hub area with access to various challenges and more varied skill paths to explore. There is also a new game plus mode that lets you keep your skills from a previous play through. Length aside, it is still a fun and quality experience.
Having tried both mouse and keyboard and a gamepad, I was surprised to find I preferred this title with a mouse and keyboard. (I say surprised because Bastion was better for me with a gamepad). But both input methods are equally good a question of personal choice.
In summary, it is a great game and definitely worth at least one playthrough.

As I'm starting my third play-through, I can tell you that this game is absolutely excellent. I'm really biased and I look away from it's flaws to see only how excellent this game just is.  I would honestly call it my game of the year for 2014. It's just that good of a game. With excellent voice-acting, an interesting way of story-telling, an amazing soundtrack, and beautiful visuals, Transistor does not fail to entertain.  To quote my review of Bastion: "Words cannot even explain how much I adore this game" is very accurate to how I feel about Transistor.

If you liked Bastion, it is a safe bet.
If you aren't sure, do it.
Beautiful and creative, it will make you think and do amazing, satisfying combos.

Following in the footsteps of the incredible Bastion, Transistor excels even beyond the world of it's predecessor. Set in a wonderful futuristic world under attack from a robotic army, you play as Red who is trying to piece together the puzzle of why she was the victim of an assassination attempt. The story feels a bit thin at times though where this game really shines is the combat system. The gameplay mechanics of weapon loadout really allow you to play the way you like and it feels completely fluid. Fights take place in realtime but Red has the ability to pause reality and plan her next moves. I would really love a more fully fleshed out version of a game in this world but I was very happy with Transistor as is. 8/10

Transitor starts you off with a mystery that immediately piques your curiosity. You play as Red, a singer who has somehow lost her voice at the same time she came into position of the Transistor, a dimensional sword that serves as the weapon to combat the Process, who are the baddies of the game. The plot unfolds throughout the game via flashbacks and dynamic narration, on par with its predecessor, Bastion. As you progress, the mysteries surrounding Red, the Camerata, the Process and even the Transistor are explained to you and what you end up with is a very rich, detailed background to a fictional world that unfolds into a deep and involving plot.
But Transistor's main gravitas isn't its intricate plot or mysterious characters. It's main selling point comes from its fantastic gameplay. Combat in the game can be played in real-time but it's main focus comes from the tactical planning. You can simply pause the action and plan out your moves. Doing so however, will require a specific portion of a limited meter and different skills will eat up different amounts. I won't go into details regarding the abilities but know that each one can work in a symbiosis with another and various combos can result from it, allowing for a stylishly devastating blow to your enemies.
The use of this battle system is extremely well done and, if I dare say, even surpasses that of AAA titles. Even outside of combat though, the player can simply interact with the environment, digging up background info on the world and characters or simply just enjoying a stroll in the environment.
The art style is very stylish and the music glues everything together. If people thought Bastion was beautiful, they would be very impressed by this too. I don't usually re-play games but I made an exception for this because it wasn't just a game, it was an experience. To enjoy beautiful art and great music alongside tight combat and a colourful plot, Transistor is definitely one game you should never pass up on.

This idea of "Let's make a game where you play as a literal god, in a massive open world sandbox where you can destroy anything, kill anyone, and still be the good guy" is absolutely genius. Just Cause 2 was my favorite game of all time, even topping GTA 5. This game just came along and blew it out of the water, pun intended. So don't listen to the negative reviews about this game being "incomplete" or "repetitive". If youre at all like me, and have a bit of a destructive side to you, BUY THIS GAME. Now as a Rule here: when I started I bought a one month Plus subscription to get the best bang for my buck, so to speak, I also then when I recieved my starter crown coins bought the Imperial Edition Digital Items, so Imperial Race (Because I always play as an Imperial raced character), I also have the Morrowind DLC.
My first few hours with the game we generally fun, starting off in Vvardenfell, due to the Morrowind DLC, Questing and doing all other kinds of things, Now sadly I didnt get to experience the game as intended as I was forced to play Solo due to friends not having the game or not wanting to play it, Which is fair enough, I suppose.
So Far my favourite class is definitely the Nightblade, which I'd made a complete stamina build, Combined with the Blade of Woe from the Dark Brotherhood makes for good kills, but regardless, I've played a few of the other classes, but not any other races, I'm just dead set in 100% Imperial.
The questing was rather fun, I will admit, there is ALOT of unique quests and I rarely found one that was pretty much a carbon copy of another quest just slightly modified. I am glad that they changed the rewards from like 1 gold per enemy to random amounts. There is a fair few things to do in ESO. From Dolmens to Dungeons to simple side quests or even the main story. Each Faction has a set story which takes place at the relative end of all the faction area Side Quests, which just involves a temperary truce to fight Molag Bal, the True Danger to Tamriel.
While most MMOs follow a simular formula of combat, I would generally say this is quite simular but doesnt force you to play a certain way, so E.G You could theoretically be a mage and use a Bow and thats all fine. It is the same with the Skills and Antributes, which frankly makes Elder Scrolls games, what they are with freedom of choice.
Now the game comes off a little expensive for those who don't wish to pay as much or can't for an MMO, as it is a pay upfront for the game as a non-plus member, which you also have to pay for too.
Honestly, I have really enjoyed playing the game so far, but it has it's flaws, but then every game does, I'd have to say I'd rate this MMO atleast a 7-8/10

This game is not made to be ruled by campaigns and pre laid out story lines, this is a game made so the only limitation to your creations is your imagination.  But as with all games it has a few drawbacks that make the game frustrating to play (I am mostly talking about multiplayer). So I will lay out all the pros and cons and you can decide if it's worth buying, while I think it is worth buying personally.
Pros:
1.) Creativity: This game allows you to build your factory without limiting size or what you can do, it is up to you how far you go in your quest to simply produce more materials to advance further and eventually build the rocket to escape the planet if you want to.
2.) Simple graphics: Few other indie games use simple graphics as well as this game does, although a lot of modern gamers would say that simple graphics is a drawback I believe that if you can make it immersive enough with that simplicity it makes the game better.
3.) Multiplayer GAMEPLAY: I say gameplay in all caps because I do not like the way the multiplayer is set up, I will elaborate on that further in the cons but I want to clarify that although playing this game with friends makes it much better as I believe that multiplayer is an important part of a freebuilding creation game such as this. And if you can manage to get multiplayer working it is extremely fun.
Cons:
1.) Confusing for new players: This game has a tutorial in the campaign but although that explains the mechanics for the beginning the game basically expects you to finish the campaign if you want the rest of the mechanis to be explained to you, and as a new player I was confused and my first few factories were not nearly as efficient as they could have been because I wasn't sure how everything works. Some people may like being thrown into a game but I feel many people may not enjoy this part of the game.
2.) Multiplayer setup: I put multiplayer gameplay as a pro above but how terrible it is to actually get a game in your friends is a huge con. The multiplayer system built into the game didn't work at all for me in fact. Me and my friend had to go download a free program called Evolve online which I highly suggest for people looking to play multiplayer easily in this game as well as many other games.
I understand this is a newer game and I hope to see these cons fixed over time, overall the gameplay is amazing and the freebuild-sandbox feeling is great.

Pros:
- Classic cars.
- TrackIR support.
- Much improved graphics and R&D compared to F1 2016, engine/gearbox management.
- The AI are galaxies better compared to previous games... they're still a bit too slow at the start of the race and in the wet, and occasinally they do some stupid stuff (Palmer got a puncture, stopped on the racing line on the exit of the hairpin after the backstraight in Shanghai and got DSQed), but they're much more aggressive when they're attacking and they actually try to defend their position now and don't leave the door wide open. Have had some great battles with them where we were wheel banging for consecutive corners.
- The racing is generally much more enjoyable. The dirty air affect is fantastic, and the difference between old/new tires and different compounds is also much more obvious in battles. During my Russia career race, the SC came out near the end just after my teammate Magnussen had pitted for Ultrasofts. After the SC, he passed 4 cars in 2 laps and then he absolutely left me to suck his balls on my old Supers.
- Best of all though is that the stupid OP slipstream from last years game is gone and the DRS effect is spot on. The difference in engine power between different manufacturers is also very noticable. With my Ferrari engine I can keep Renaults behind me relatively easily on the straights, Honda is obviously snail pace if they're moving at all, and Mercs are definitely beating me.
- The 2017 cars fit my driving style like a glove, even at one of worst and most hated tracks (Shanghai) I was actually competitive!!! More of a personal thing, but meh.
Cons:
- No SLI support.
- While the engine and gearbox management part is great, their wear is too harsh when they don't have any durability upgrades. My gearbox was at 50% wear after 2 weekends, and after 4 I've already pretty much used up 1 of every engine component. I've already taken a 5th unit of everything and a new gearbox (since I messed up one of my qualifyings anyway) and I'm already sure I'm gonna have to take more later on.
- Perez is ridiculously quick...
Got bored very quickly - but what can I expect, its F1.... Force feedback on my G29 also seemed terrible. Refunded

This is a very fun M.O.B.A. genre game with a cast of recognizable gods from respective religious pantheons. Smite has a simillar layout to the game Leauge of legends in that it's main gamemode is a three lane layout leading to the other teams base. All the lanes play a role in team composition and are chosen when you select the roles as follows
1. Jungler, (this is primarily and assassin god) Junglers main focus are the buff camps that spawn in the space between lanes and infiltrating (Ganking) the back line to eliminate the squishier gods (squishy=low hp, defense) *keep note that as of season four any god is playable in any role*
2. Middle lane/ Mid. (this is primarilly a mage god. As a Mid. laner your objective is to take down the towers, pheonix and titan all accessable by the middle lane. After you build the proper items for your playstyle you will most often become your teams backiline using high damage abilities to take out the opposing teams frontline (try and avoid the enemy jungler as they will most likey build to counter you) *keep note that as of season four any god is playable in any role*
3. Attack. Damage. Carry./ ADC (this is most often the hunter class of gods. As the carry you will be placed in the longer of the two lanes ( the side switches depending on if you are on the order team or chaos team ) you will most often be assisted by the teams support. Your high damage basic attacks keep you in the frontline as the teams main damage source but it makes you an easy target in teamfights so always be aware of your posistion while engaging a fight.
4. Solo lane/ solo ( most often the warrior class of god) as the solo lane you will head to the smaller lane on the left or right ( the side switches depending on if you are on the order team or chaos team ) this is the lane that the jungler will assist most often when clearing buff camps. Most of the time spent here will be a one VS. one with the enemy solo laner. Late game ( after the average god level is around 15+ you should rotate to other lanes and assist as a secondary support becoming a frontliner for your team.
5. Support ( this is most often the guardian class of god ) you are your teams imovable sheild keep them alive at the cost of your own and let your team get the kills. (a good support can bring almost any team to victory ) you will move around to lanes that need help or you will follow the enemy support.
*Keep in note these tips are for the Conquest gamemode for smite not the other avalible options*
In general I prefer this game to league in my mind it provides more of a challange considering everything in the game is a skillshot ( with a few exceptions ) and has a much less toxic community my ingame name is Professorslick and ill offer advice on builds for gods if needed ( more often than not the recomended build is viable ) I hope you find this review and tip helpful.

I had a great time with this game. It's intense, spooky, and extremely well-optimized.
Granted, it's not perfect. Most objectives run along the lines of "Go find this generator to power this one door so you can do a thing", which got old by the end of the game. Sometimes the AI enemies were just plain stupid (the androids and humans at least, the alien itself had no problem finding me). The game can be scary at times, but for me, the alien came around so much that it wasn't as scary as it could have been. Then again, this isn't my first horror game, so maybe I'm becoming too hardened for this stuff. The good far outweighs the bad, and I think it's worth the cash, especially if it's on sale. That is, it's worth the cash if you're not too scared and actually play through the game.
It took me about 15 hours to finish and I took the game very slowly (I rarely ever sprinted for fear of the alien hearing). The sound is amazing - hearing the dull thumping of the alien's footsteps come nearer and become faster as he sprints at you is a rush. Visually the game is pretty good and the optimization is top-notch. I played on ultra settings with a perfect framerate on my crappy GTX 650 Ti. Super low-end PCs could likely run it on lower settings. The story is what you may expect from an entry to the Alien franchise; there's a space station, some moron lets the alien in, everyone dies. The gameplay is a lot of hiding and stealth with some FPS gun/melee action mixed in when encountering androids and looters. The game balances stealth and action pretty well.
It's a good action horror and worth the cash, especially if you're a fan of the Alien franchise.

As a big fan of the Alien movies, specially the first one, I played as many Alien games as possible, and most of them followed a basic plot, be a marine and kill Xenomorphs. I am not really into the idea of killing as many aliens as you possibly can with a rifle, that's why I recommend this game. At first I was scared, then I just became dismissive of the Wretches.
And then I got bored.
In the first hour and a half, AMFP was true to the scaring complex seen within TDD. I'd be trying to muffle a scream, pausing the game, being very, very cautious leaning around every corner and putting my head in my heads to try and catch my breath back... and then while I descended, the game descended in atmospheric quality. In the end, I just found myself trudging through the dark with my never-ending light source, not scared in the slightest.
The puzzles... were not puzzles. Those "sabotages" acted more a mere obstacle with which just to step over; no challenge. Everything was spoon-fed. If anything, this made the game act as an interactive novel, in which I didn't feel any sympathy for the characters, nor the true innocents of the game.
While some of the more immersive and explorative features of the original Amnesia were absent, I feel it didn't detract from the game. However, the overall linear feel of the game, and enemy indication feature was a complete buzz kill; there is no adrenaline injected into the atmosphere. Despite that, the scares at the beginning didn't feel cheap at all. In addition, I loved how my enviroment constantly changed around me, and that kept up a certain level of interest for me to complete the game within my 3rd session.
I wanted to get lost in the dark. I wanted to be cowering in a corner behind some boxes with a Wretche's back to me, trying to sniff me out. I wanted ample cause to hide for ages, even when they are long gone. Music, as used in the previous game, could have ramped up that scare factor. The swine are lacklustre and did not carry a sense of intimidation.
Also, the ending felt rushed. The anticipation and my expectations were wasted. Dissapointed.
But nonetheless, this is from a different developer, who may have made the game within their best interests to put a different spin on it whereas their main concern should have been their audience and diehard fans of the previous game.

You can also buy some helpers - scarecrows, dogs, etc., and as you expand the size of your garden you automatically get some helps that wander around picking up produce for you to save some clicking.
As your garden develops you increase in level which gives you access to more valuable crops/livestock, although everything's cost grows exponentially in clicker game style, and as you level up earlier crops get bonus "stars" which increase their value, so it isn't always best to switch to the highest level option you have.
Overall it is a fairly relaxing and well put together game that can keep you occupied for a couple of evenings, there isn't a lot of depth here but it is fine for the type of game it is.

The best Formula 1 game to date.
F1 2017 takes the already amazing formula of an F1 game from F1 2016 and improves it significantly, adding many many new things. The 2017 cars are amazing, feel like a joy to drive, and the handling feels spot on. The career mode has been reworked to add a lot of depth with the new R&D tree and part degredation and management. Classic cars have been added and are an absolute joy to drive along with events for them, new game modes and more.
Handling and Cars
The handling is simply amazing, the cars are ridiculously fun to drive and are ridiculously refreshing to drive after 2016's game. You can drive pretty agressively now, and whilst the handling is a little more forgiving than last year, it certainly doesn't take away from how powerful the cars feel. Driving with a controller also feels significantly more responsive than last years installment.
The classic cars also look and feel great, adding even more fun to the game.
Circuits
Circuits are all around solid and are pretty much exact to the real life stuff. Short additions have also been made to a variety of circuits adding a unique twists to some classic tracks. These are also perfect for the classic cars.
Graphics, sound and optimisation
Graphics are stunning, maybe a little grainy at times, especially with lower settings, but running on the highest settings the game simply looks stunning, an overall great looking game as to be expected.
Engines sound very realistic, along with the weather effects. The classic cars sound absolutely incredible, and it's so refreshing hearing the perfect roar of a V10, and being in control of that power is an experience.
The game seems very well optimised and ran great on my 750ti, and also my 1060. 1060 able to max it out, 750 ti able to run it at reasonable settings very smoothly.

This year's F1 title is a solid addition to the series. If you're into F1, it's a no-question purchase. If you're into racing in general, I'd still highly recommend it but this might not be the game for players that are looking for a massive selection of cars and all the bells and whistles you get in a Forza or Gran Turismo. This is a dedicated motor-sport game.
It doesn't look great on my aging computer but you can tell from other media that it's nice to look at, blah, blah, it's a Codemasters racing game you know what you're getting visually. Sound is excellent, I miss the banshee-wail of the V12 but the classic modes help with that a bit. Game runs smooth, doesn't hog up a lot of memory, loading is pretty quick, the UI is functional, overall it's got solid production value and it feels like Codemasters are still having fun making these games.
But that's not the meat of a racing game. A good racing game need to establish a baseline for the driver, then provide feedback for how to improve your times, and ultimately reward you for that improvement. F1 2017 thankfully checks those boxes. There are a variety of assists that you can fiddle with, and you can also streamline or just automate a lot of the set-up and race strategy and just focus on getting track time. The cars have a bit more weight to them, and correspondingly more grip - making them drive more like an open-wheel car as opposed to a lot of F1 titles where you spend way more time sliding around than you should. There are visual, audio, and rumble cues that will let you know a lot about how you're driving, and the game does a good job of letting you see your sector times and giving you a steady stream of ghost cars from the leader-boards so you can keep improving.
My main complaint is that the AI is... not so great. When you're actually racing for position they don't do a great job of defending, even on the Ultimate difficulty. However when you're lapping a slow car, they'll hold stubbornly to a line when they should let you pass, or slow down/move over suddenly which can (and has been for me) disastrous to some races. They also don't make many mistakes, which is a little disappointing. It'd be nice if the AI would respond to you pressuring them from behind by occasionally dropping a wheel off the track, locking up a tire, or missing their braking point but this doesn't happen often - I think it's a missed opportunity to reward the player for being aggressive.
Multiplayer, at this point, isn't really worth your time. There's stuttering, teleporting cars, d/c issues, and like every other racing game you'll probably get rammed by someone in the first corner because most people are just flat-out bad at racing games. I don't even bother anymore.
It's no Grand Prix Legends or the still-awesome F1'99-'02 Challenge with mods (I don't think anyone would complain if we got more classic F1 cars for this), but as of writing I'm about 20 hours in and I'm only in the initial stages of the different modes and championships - if you sit down with F1 2017 with the intention to see all there is to see (even without 700+ cars to mess with) you're in for a lot of enjoyable racing.

The atmosphere, as you might expect from the trailers, is incredible. What you won't understand from the footage is just how finely woven the storytelling is for a game whose main character has had her voice removed in the story. It starts in medias res (in the middle of the action), and unfolds plot points through beautifully illustrated flashbacks, the transistor's dialogue, and even the game mechanics themselves. Your skills are traces of people, and as you use these skills in more varied ways you unlock more information about the person the trace is from, the world they lived in and the cabal of characters they came in contact with. Combat is clever and surprisingly fast paced for the sort that lets you jump into a paused planning mode. Take advantage of the Sandbox planning areas, Red's humming mechanic and unlocking all the information in traces and limiters. Though your character can't speak, her personality is revealed through the transistor, her input into computer terminals, her actions or lack of during cutscenes, and the soundtrack that you will absolutely not regret buying. The story is deep enough to make sense and propel you forward while still leaving you wide open to theory crafting at the end. My only complaint is that I don't want to leave the game and the <10 hours of gameplay, while bittersweetly satisfying, will not be enough to appease you once you've fallen head over heels in love with this world.

I have almost 3000 hours on this game, why am I writing a negative review? Here I go on why you should run away from this game before you can't get out. Before coming to SMITE, I played WARRAME and RPG's, so from a melee combat prospective this game is fantastic. The problem is evidential towards how Hi-REZ economically has played out, and their game development through the last 2-3 years. I love the character designs, I love the idea of this MMO MOBA, and most importantly I love playing this game. I have invested too many years into this game though, and now I'm stuck with an account worth hundreds of dollars, which is more than half of what it's supposed to be worth.

I love the style of gameplay that is more mechanically oriented, like a fighting game or a strategy game. I would highly recommend this game to any players who have already played MOBA's or games like SMASH in the past. The item system is atleast better than the system that LOL or DOTA offers. SMITE doesn't really offer alot in terms of guidence for new players, in fact SMITE is in the category of games where you can't really get to a higher skill level unless you've played hundreds of hours and watched TWITCH streams consistently. Games that are similar to this are STARCRAFT II and the DARK SOULS franchise in terms of the difficulty in learning the basis and mechanics of the game.
People who use the term "pay to win" usually say it in an hyperbolic sense, but even to play ranked in SMITE you either have to spend endless hours gaining small qantities of in-game currency, or spend 15-30 dollars USD (varies on occasion) on the ultimate god pack. Hi-REZ also has idea of fantasy points, which predominantly eggs on the player to buy skins in order to get in a similar fantasy point level as the people who play in their ELO. Lastly- in terms of fanancial standards- the value that an account can be worth in US dollars can very, and are based on 3 particularly sketchy variants:
1. How many Gems bought from Hi-REZ, which are dramatically overpriced comparitively to what in-game currency is worth in other games, and most importantly, other countries.
2. How many Gems prized to someone from a giveaway, and this usually ends up in glitches and uncertainties in the actual final value the player receives.
3. How many Gems bought by giving money to a third party (a guy who lives in another country), and having them buy gems for you for a much cheaper price. This method can result in a ban, but rarely people get caught.
GARBAGE DEVELOPERS, PERIOD.
On a serious note, the developers are not great. The OG dev's were fantastic, and were people willing to change the game playstyles and options oftenly enough for people to be impressed and happy. Our current devs however, have not changed the games overall mechanics in almost a year and a half. The new dev's focus is to make unique characters, but have a very counterintuitive idea of how to do that, while also not giving the game any new veriety in play. A lot of the abilites of the new characters created have just a pile of abilities and passives from characters made by the previous dev's. Let me also note that the lead developer, AJAX, hasn't actually played enough of his own game to be in the position he's in. Alot of the development went down hill once PALADINS got out of BETA, praise Hi-REZ.
So after reading this, unless if you didn't. I'd like to end on a satirical note.

This game is LOADS of fun. You will be able to sink several hundred hours into this game and still be able to find something to do in it. With 400sq miles to explore, it's easy to say that you will find it hard to not explore somewhere new.
For the players new to the Just Cause series, this game IS playable without having played the previous games as it takes place in a new location where a lot of new characters are introduced. There are a few characters form the other games but their roles become clear very early in the game.
The story (in a nutshell) is simple: There is an evil dictator and Rico, along with the local rebels, are fighting their way to become free again. There is a lot more to the story once you get started but that is the basics of it.
- The gameplay is very fun and exciting.
- Looks amazing.
- Action. There is so much action you could substitute this for a Michael Bay film.
- New gadgets (wing suit, retractable hook and a lot more..)
- Details: The world in this game actually feels like it has been ruled by a dictator and the people want change. There are many times when you will overhear some NPCs talking about how things have changed under this new ruler. While some NPCs just talk about being free, others do something about it.
- The Revolution: The people of this country are tired of the way things are and Rico is hear to help, but not just Rico, there are actual rebels that are there to help. Unlike the other Just Cause games, it's not so much of a one-man show anymore. You can open gates at enemy bases to allow ground troop rebels to join in on the fight and help take down enemys, or take out anti-air guns to allow for rebel choppers to fly in and fire on the base. There are so many ways to destroy bases and take out the enemy, and when rebels join in on the fihgt, it seems like what you're doing is actually helping people who want a change.
- BUGS: With a world this size and this dense, it is no surprise that there are bugs and glitches. However, in the first hour of playing, there was one crash to desktop. This is a huge bummer in major titles like these and it very frustrating. No more crashes as of yet, but it has me slightly on edge.
- Story line / Cutscenes: There are many cutscenes that were not needed to develop story, but I assume it was a way to load the world or change the scene. (For example: In the middle of a mission, there is a cutscene after jumping on shore of an island to see if the person your're looking for is there. The cutscene starts as you jump off of your boat and only has Rico taking a few steps, seeing dead bodies, and saying that the people are dead. Then short loading screen and you just jump back on the boat and go to the next spot where you would do the same thing about three times. There was no point to make that a cutscene (except to throw in some loading screens) and could have been left out.
- Optimization: Not very well optimized and can drop FPS every now and then depending on what's going on.
- DLC: I am not a fan of DLC to begin with, but with this game, you miss out on a LOAD of content if you don't have the DLC. You can still play the main story without it, but in my opinion, I would buy the XL version of the gime while it is on sale.

Dated graphics, tiny playerbase (meaning nobody to co-op with or invade), no storyline at all. One of the hardest things you'll fight in this game is the camera. I've put 53 hours into this game from Sunday night to Saturday morning. I became so determined to take the exact area that real life Rome held that I just couldn't quit playing lol. I fought some of the most brutal battles I've ever faught in a video game, at one point being outnumbered 5300-2300 and killing over 3300 of their men before my last unit fell.
If you like Civilization, I'd say give this game (or one of the other TW's I haven't tried them, but based on the vids I've watched they all play largely the same). You can basically play the entire game like a more complex Civ, on a smaller map, locked into Roman times (due to this, the map feels quite massive). But, you have the added bonus of being able to actually fight the battle and control the troops RTS style. Allowing you to pull off wins in battles that the quick battle claimed you were going to get slaughtered in lol. Though sometimes, the result is the same (or thereabouts).
I played much of the second half of my war for the Roman empire, taking what was the eastern empire. And I did the vast majority of that as I would have in Civ, but the few times I took direct command, I pulled either wins, or significantly more damage on the enemy than what quick match was going to do.
I overlooked this series, and I wish I hadn't, as this is the most fun I've had with a game in quite some time. And I am going to continue to play it, and will be buying other TW games later down the road.
Do yourself a favor, if you like RTS or any of the Civ games, whether it be Civ V, or even Gal Civ, watch some vids on this or one of the other TW games, and see what you think, and give the game a chance. I have 97 hours into Gal Civ, and 65 in Civ V, and as much as I like both of those games, I have no doubt that I will pass them both up with the amount of time I put into this game.

This game isn't what you would expect, but it doesn't mean it's a bad game.
Pretty hard not to remember The Dark Descent when you see the title. But A Machine for Pigs is not a survival horror like the previous game, it's more of a dark tale.
Sharing the game engine and some gameplay from the first Amnesia, this game drops the inventory, but keeps a detailed world, with the help of music fitting perfectly.
The story is quite predictable, but also pretty detailed and well counted.
If you look for a deep survival horror, you might want to look somewhere else. But if you like tormented stories, this is one you must live.
If you need help putting the notes in chronological order, this might be useful.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is the sequel to Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
The game takes place at the end of 1899 in London. You play as Oswald Mandus, a rich industrialist who awakens at the beginning of the game in his mansion with no memory of his recent past. It seems the he has lost his two sons and his wife is may be dead. There is something very strange going down with regard to pigs in and around his home and adjacent factory. You move through the ominous mansion in first person, piecing together your troubled past courtesy of notes, the odd entry in your journal, sound recordings that play on Victrola-like devices and even telephone conversations with a mysterious man who may have your children held captive in the bowels of the factory.
You guide Mandus through the game, you will often face problems that need solving in order to progress. Most of the time you will just have to pull a level or two, sometimes having to retrace your steps in order to find the item that goes into the item-shaped hole. This all sounds very basic, and it is.
In the previous game, Amnesia: The Dark Descent, players had to carefully manage the oil in their lamps, while also attempting to maintain their sanity. A Machine for Pigs abandons this gameplay mechanic entirely. You have a lamp, with unlimited power and any notion of turning insane, simply is not present.
With unlimited supplies, players are free to explore without hindrance; a feature which will make some players happy and others not so much. Those who enjoyed the sense of fear and pressure evoked when running low on supplies in The Dark Descent, will find A Machine for Pigs a little disappointing in this respect.
There are tons of creepy sounds throughout the game and a lot of great music too, some of it is beautiful and haunting, while some is very creepy and vile.
A Machine for Pigs has increased graphics compared to The Dark Decent, but it has less gameplay features that made the game easier and also the survival horror aspect is reduced compared to the first “Amnesia”.
All in all, I can still say that Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is a game that all horror fans should play. The soundtrack alone will make most people feel fear, with the visuals and gameplay certainly not taking much away from the experience.

This game's kind of depressing, so it's hard to play a lot of it. But it's pretty impressive. It did a good job of giving me the feeling of being in the person's shoes and got me to think about how I might act in those situations. It also taught me that it sucks to live in cold-war era Slavic countries. It presents you with interesting moral choices. So if you're looking for a game that's not necessarily "fun," but one that's insightful, go here.

Althoug the game's main premise seems extremelly boring at first glance, it happens to be an amazing experience through the daily issues of a just-hired immigration inspector of the hypothetical communist country of Arstotzka.
Letting people enter is not that simple. Mistakes are not tolerated, which makes you need to pay attention to all presented documents as they'll reveal if the person in question is acting according to Arstotzka rules of immigration or not. And your superiors won't even think about making your job easier: along the game, there are going to be each time more rules and details you'll need to pay attention to in order to not suffer a warning (which lowers your salary). Moreover, Arstotzka has just finished a 6-years lasting war against a neighbour country, so you can expect things to get "hot" during the play.
Quick-thinking, war issues, conspiracy, secret factions, criminals, not being arrested, taking care of your family. These are only a few of the challenges you'll face playing
. Play it at once. This game definitely deserves the green stamp.

Transistor is a beautiful and engaging game.  It has a fragmentary, but effective and at times emotional storytelling style.  A mute protagonist with a stolen voice, and a weapon with nothing but, who spends the entire game talking to Red, the heroine, yet not at all getting dull or old, feeling quite alive as he slowly adjusts and reasons out what's happening.  The soundtrack is amazing and beautiful, and the art style is pure eye-candy, yet accents the story perfectly.  Additionally, the combat goes beyond simple surface depth, as each of the many skills can be used individually, combined with each of the others used as an upgrade, or used as a passive-- and sometimes with surprisingly fun (and explosive) results.
I would fully recommend this beautiful game.  I don't even mind that I paid full price for it!

I love this game.  The narrator and events combine to make a wonderful story, and the unique combat system is quite fun, allowing you to either fight in real time or pause to plan out several quick actions.  One extremely attracive feature to me is the immense variety of options for skill combinations.  And if you enjoy game music, the soundtrack is definitely worth getting.

While the narrative falls disappointingly flat, the game succeeds from a purely mechanical standpoint. The skill customization system is deep, satisfying, and easy to pick up. It's clear that Supergiant spent a tremendous amount of time iterating on this mechanic. It would be Transistor's greatest attribute if it weren't for the music. The ambient soundtrack gives life to this science fiction distopia, but I loved the vocal tracks most of all. They connected to me the otherwise silent protagonist. Making the player character a lounge singer who loses her voice was a brilliant decision too. Supergiant essentially gets everything right that isn't the plot. Plots aren't usually very interesting anyway, so play Transistor for the fun mechanics, fantastic music, and gorgeous art.
