This game is so good, and yet it's so bad. The atmosphere is great. They got every detail of the Alien universe right. It shows through that a lot of care and attention went into making this game. But this is not a fun game. Now, I love stealth games. And I like the alien franchise a lot. But stealth games should be about giving the player tools for outsmarting the enemy. It should give you ample tools to not engage. But the stealth in this game is awful. Enemies are completely unpredictable when they will see you. The lighting makes no sense at all, sometimes large lamps don't even illuminate their immediate surrounding. This makes is hard to tell if it's actually affecting whether enemies notice you. The mechanics are not explained at all, for example I still don't know if shutting down the air purification actually helps you stay unnoticed, how much it affects it if it does, and how long it stays that way (because guess what, it comes back online by itself after a few short minutes). The gadgets are mostly useless, especially against the Alien, and you get far too few crafting components to actually use these items. And the Alien is annoying as hell. It is so fast and unpredictable that it's not fun at all to "outsmart" it. It's mostly just luck. And it also teleports as far as I can tell. And it makes no damn sense anyway. It can't tell that I'm a few feet away, ducking behind some boxes, but shomehow when I get away from it it knows exactly where I went and teleports in front of me (through the vents, I guess). No matter how careful you are, how slow you're moving it will follow you. I was really looking forward to playing this game, but it's a huge letdown in my opinion. I'm just sad that this is canon, so you have to suffer through it to get the story.

I had extremely high hopes for this game. I loved Amnesia and liked Dear Esther, but sadly this game hamfistedly (har?) shoves the sentimental prose of the latter into the engine of the former without utilizing any of the features that made Amnesia so tense and horrifying. The result is a dark muddy slog through an overly literal interpretation of the game's evocative title that's neither frightening nor satisfying.
It's an interesting swing and a miss, but definitely a miss for me.

I am a fan of Frictional games going back to the pre-Penumbra tech demos.  "A Machine for Pigs" is a masterpiece.  It has the best ending of any game I have ever played, and the whole story and atmosphere are amazing.

First of all, this game was not developed by Frictional. It was developed by The Chinese Room: the studio behind Dear Escher. When I discovered that during its development, I became skeptical as to the quality of this game. I did, however, respect that it was a spiritual successor of Amnesia: The Dark Decent, and figured that it still had the opportunity to be an intriguing horror experience. I was incorrect.
My first complaint comes from simplified mechanics, of which there are barely any at all. The inventory system has been removed entirely, and with both health and sanity. Managing health becomes trivial, as there are no situations in which you must do so, while sanity has been removed altogether. Hiding in the darkness no longer has its trade offs, while looking at the monsters does nothing. Monsters now only make your electric lamp flicker from quite distance away, removing the fear of their presence. This is part of another changed mechanic: oil conservation has been done away with as well in favor of the infinite energy electric lamp. At this point, only the levels themselves are left to make the game live up to its predecessor, which they don't.
The game has been designed to be insultingly linear. Each level is a single, straight, path with no choices on how to proceed. The vast majority of monster encounters are scripted, along with a dozen or so out of place shock scares (I could reveal all of them and not spoil the plot). The levels themselves are badly designed and a pain to navigate, with large inaccessible areas and crappy lighting only made worse by the infinite lamp. The puzzles are all remarkably simple now that the inventory is gone. The only thing that makes this worse is the writing of the story.
In the first act, The Chinese Room makes sure you know they made it by coming in so heavy with metaphors that you can't decipher any real context until you are a good amount into the game. As you try to ground yourself in the game's story, TCR continuously throws "deeper meaning" straight at your face until the story becomes completely drowned in its own pretentious metaphors and symbolism by the third act in a way that is relatable to the Matrix trilogy. The only parts of the story that feel as though they actually belong in the Amnesia universe are the references to the original game (albeit with one glaring inconsistency).
TL;DR:
Overall, I disapprove of this game. The mechanics are simplified, the levels are horribly designed, and the story feels like it was written by an undergraduate art student. If you have never played Amnesia: The Dark Decent, buy that instead. If you have played it, then still don't buy this. Wait for SOMA.

Set on what I can only assume is a planet that is excellent for agriculture, Plantera is... another clicker. While I may not have much experience with the clicker genre, I can safely say Plantera is the most fun and interesting clicker I've played to date. It's cute, addictive and would brighten anyone's day, even if only slightly.
One of the best mechanics of Plantera was the clicking itself, which I think is extremely important for a title in the clicker genre. Instead of being forced to click on the same spot over and over, like a traditional clicker, Plantera allows you to freely click anywhere on the screen. This adds some variety and makes the game a little more interesting for the player. Plantera also allows you to build your very own farm, which act as the upgrading system and the way to increase your money growth.
You have little freedom in where you place your various trees and plants, but this didn't ruin the experience for me. The plants will start to grow fruit once planted, very quickly! Once the fruit is grown you can pick it and harvest it, or wait for it to fall off the tree and have a helper pick it up for you and give you the earnings.
Another nice feature was the cameo of Loot Hero, from VaragtP's previous game 'Loot Hero DX'. Every once and a while he'll come rushing past the screen with his giant drill and take out any critters that happened to be in your garden looking for fruit. You are also given the opportunity is click him and gain an abundance of coins that are so helpful for building your garden. I always found myself clicking rapidly as he ran across the screen, trying to get as many coins as I possibly could.
The game is a short journey, only about 7-8 hours, but it's worth playing. I'd recommend picking this up when you can, as the price tag is quite desirable and you'll get some enjoyable playtime out of it. However, at the moment there isn't a lot of replayability for someone that isn't crazy about this game, so think carefully about your purchase.

However, those are the positives of this clicker. It is more like a relaxation tool than a 'keep clicking until your mouse and/or finger breaks' clicker. There isn't a lot to do: just plant some plants and add some animals, make a couple of clicks to get things started and then... Just watch, click whenever or collect the achievements in order.
So, if you are looking for something cute and easy to relax with, Plantera might be your thing. If you're looking something complicated and time-consuming, this won't please you.

I have just over 100 hours on the game so I think it is about time I write a review for this game.  So this is Codemasters' 8th game and they are still unable to make a relatively bug free multiplayer experience; as one of the beta testers I am very dissapointed because the beta had a very good multiplayer system with only a few bugs here and there. Apart from the multiplayer the game has been very enjoyable to say the least. A good handling model that is very hard to master so when you get a good lap together in time trial you feel extremely satisfied with yourself, the new cars are very fun to chuck around and I also would like to add how much playability the career mode has. I am driving for McLaren Honda in mine and have been using 107 to 110 AI difficulty depending on the circuit and it is a refreshing challenge not being able to outqualify and outrace my teammate easily, although recently I have been pulling a few tenths over Alonso! I also think the AI are vastly imrpoved this year but they still can be as stupid as chickens sometimes. For example they are unable to still, after 7 years, let faster cars under blue flags passed without weaving across the track. However, some good things are that you can go side by side on parts of the tracks they would've never dared to on the previous games.
In conclusion, F1 2017 in my opinion is the best game so far and if they can sand off the rough edges it will be a near perfect game. For this I will give it an 8.5 out of 10!

Transistor must be one of my favorite games. Upon launching the game, it strikes with its elegance and polish. As an example, the games goes the unconvetional path of omitting the use of a menu, a great idea, as it lets you get right into the action. Especially the level of animation underlines this elegance. But the real shine of the game is the combat system which presents a great amount of customizability. Notably the pace of a fight is refreshing since the game devides action into a relaxing planning phase and a hectic realtime phase. Another important aspect is the replayability the game offers through a mode called recursion (which I think is what the game is mostly about) and the difficulty customization the user has through so-called limiters, which, in my opinion, is the best way to solve the problem of creating difficulty levels in a game. As was the case with Bastion, the sound tracks in this game always hit, quite literally, the right note.

The most fascinating part of Papers, Please is how so much can spring from what looks like a boring desk job.
To be honest, you are doing approximately the same stuff every day, but there are so many subplots and rule changes going on that you always have something extra on your mind other than the paperwork you're checking. The game is also excellent for keeping you on edge and questioning your morals. You'd be surprised as to how many different endings the game has.

Despite its appearance,
will test you in terms of morality. Are you loyal to
or will you aid the mysterious order? Is it worth ruining people's lives so your family can live? Or maybe your soft side will let illegals through. But what makes
so immersive are the multiple stories going on with the backdrop of a Soviet-esque era in the background, and how you, a simple border guard, can affect them all.
Who knew stamping papers could be so...engaging...

I could whine about the downtime, cry about the grind fest, scream at all the wasted potential in the game mechanics, insult the User Interface and/or rant on and on and on about the lore loopholes tossed at me left and right as a faithful fan of the Elder Scrolls Series. Then I could slap a big thumbs down on this. But I won't. Why?
Well, this game is actually damn good. Those are just flaws. Every game has those. This game is fun. The quests often make sense and I feel motivated to see them through. The storylines are often amazing. The dialogue is awesome most of the time. The game mechanics aren't perfect or even learnable at first, but they're a constant supply of fun. The sound design and visuals are absolutely jaw-dropping. Every character class is flexible and you can poke around and have fun trying whatever you want.
Then, the roleplay elements. Want to be a thief? You got it. Want to be a mage? Go for it. Feel like joining the Dark Brotherhood? That's a thing. Hell, you can be a badass fighter and/or undaunted too. Or a werewolf and a vampire... Not quite the way you could in Morrowind but it just feels like you're actually playing the role. And doing it all feels so perfectly compelling and exciting for many hours. And the developers aren't even done expanding onto the options and the game map yet.
Sure, they take a little money if you want to play a certain race outside of the default faction. Yeah, they want you to buy those fancy mounts and costumes. You might even fall for dropping $50 on an ingame house. But you can do it all without spending any money at all if you're determined to work really hard for it. Yeah, buying the ESO Plus subscription is a huge incentive because you get an infinite crafting bag. But you can create your own guild just to store a lot of items, actually. Sure, paying to play is an option. But just on option. And unlike so so many other modern MMORPG's there's really not a pay-to-win dymanic here at all.
You'll struggle a little with server issues, UI issues, bugs, game items and mechanics that waste potential... But you'll have a hell of a good time.

I'm closing in on 900 hours play-time and I'm just gonna give a small review of how the game-state currently is.
Firstly; This is Elder Scrolls meaning the lore is dark, brooding and extensive so as far as questing and stories go, it's absolutely amazing.
Graphically the game looks solid. Animations are well done in both 1st and 3rd person and the overall aesthetic is incredible from the absolutely gorgeous greendlands of Greenshade to the literal horror that is Coldharbour. The game is gorgeous.
The main thing that keeps pulling me back in is the sheer amount of content that goes hand-in-hand with incredible quality. It's not the generic "Collect the anuses of 10 bears" as quests but more like quests that can affect an actual area. I adore them.
The character building is incredible. Whereas many MMO's are ruled by the meta, this game is not. I've seen countless builds that're incredible. As long as your HP and resource hits a certain threshold then you can quite literally get through all the the content.
- - - Morrowind - - -
My best friend gifted me the expansion with him knowing how much I love this game. In short, I'd say the expansion is worth it. It doesn't add drastic amounts of content but the content it does add is incredible. Giving you an entire new story to play through as well as another incredible area.
Most noteworthy though is the new class; Currently I have 2 Wardens at max level and I'm working on a 3rd. The reason I'm pointing this out is because the class is diverse enough that I can make multiple characters of the same class and they all fulfil their role in a completely new and unique way with my Magicka-based Warden having incredible sustain and my Stamina Warden having absolutely insane burst-damage. And my new Warden? He's a melee-based Stamina character who's currently a master of DoT's.
All in all, ESO is fantastic. It doesn't require a subscription to play [although the content and value it adds is insane] and you never have to spend extra money with the majority of microtransactions just being cosmetics.
I love this game and I'd highly recommend it to anyone who likes in-depth character building, vast amounts of quality content and who just likes Elder Scrolls in general as you can quite literally choose to play this as a completely solo-experience if needed.

All we wanted was to love her. We tried everything. We built up her confidence. We picked her up when she fell down. We lifted her spirits. We were, at least I thought we were, soulmates....
....
I have never been more wrong.
Emily, is without a doubt, the most pathetic and cruel human on the planet. No matter what we did, and no matter what we said, somehow, in Emily's mind, we took advantage of her, even though she is quoted as saying she doesn't regret ANYTHING, nor would take ANYTHING back, we still become the bad guy,..
HOW IS THAT FAIR?!?!?!?!
We tried to rescue her, from an emotionally and possibly physically abusive relationship, with epic toolbag BRAD. Then when she finally comes to her senses and leaves him, she visits us. And that is where it all goes wrong.... NO MATTER WHAT WE DO!
Then, in her delusional mind, she is rescued by EPIC TOOLBAG....BRAD. She treats like a villain, and proclaims BRAD to be the HERO....pshhh. What a load of crap!!!!
We are given NO free will, to truly speak our mind, to let her know how we truly feel about her (aka: WE LOVE HER), and absolutely NO option to win her back. Why give us options to say something, only to take them away, right before our eyes! That is cruelty. We worked up the courage to say it, before a robot from the Matrix came and erased our answers and replaced them with awkward small-talk, made by strangers. This is not even an accurate represenation of real life. You have heartache, but you never give up. You get turned down, but you keep trying, and fighting, and no robot EVER really comes to erase, and then replace your answers.
All in all, it was fun and interesting, and did bring back memories, and left me nostalgic for times past... BUT it left me wanting more. Much, much more. More freedom is needed to make this game more realistic, so that we are at least left with the impression that we can win Emily back. Or at least that we are given the option ourselves to turn down Emily, because quite frankly, she is the worst by the end of the game!
Bye.
